# Fractures and Dislocations — A Practical Course for Health Professionals

This course sets out a systematic approach to the assessment, stabilization, initial management and definitive-treatment principles of fractures and dislocations anywhere in the body, written to be listened to rather than read. It is made for health professionals, students and trained responders: for the paramedic on the way to a call, the nurse taking a handover, the student revising before an examination, and the physician who wants the first ten minutes of an orthopedic problem clear in the mind. It does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which the listener works.

Every injury in the course is taught through the same sequence, and the sequence is worth carrying away on its own: assess the patient, stabilize what threatens life, examine the neurovascular status, immobilize the injury in the position found, obtain the imaging that is indicated, reassess after everything you have done, and then either refer the patient onward or treat the injury definitively within your own scope of practice. Two of those steps are repeated until they become instinct. The neurovascular examination is done before any intervention and again after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The reassessment happens after every intervention, because the complication this course fears most is the one caused by the treatment.

The course runs from the foundations of musculoskeletal trauma, through the primary and secondary survey and the neurovascular examination, and on to immobilization, splinting and patient handling. It then works region by region: the shoulder girdle and shoulder, the humerus, the elbow and forearm, the wrist and hand, the pelvis and hip, the femur, the knee, the leg, the ankle and the foot. It goes on to the spine, the child, the older adult, and the open fracture, then to dislocations and the principles of reduction, to complications, to imaging, and to definitive treatment and rehabilitation. It closes with a set of emergency scenarios, a practical skills laboratory, a decision framework that can be run in the head at the roadside, and four appendices: an algorithm section, a skills checklist, a quick-reference card, and the core principle of the whole course.

Three warnings belong at the front rather than at the back. The first is that reduction, traction and casting are techniques learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. This course describes what they are for, what they must achieve and what can go wrong, and it says plainly that the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training and never to a book. The second is that this course gives no drug, no dose, no route and no frequency. Where analgesia, antibiotics, tetanus protection or sedation must be discussed, it describes who decides, what finding makes the decision urgent, and what the scope of practice forbids; the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and the prescriber. The third is that any number in this course is an illustration. Times, pressures, distances and thresholds differ between services, countries and editions, and every one of them must be confirmed against the current guideline and the protocol of the service you work in.

The injuries in this course do not sort themselves by severity. A fracture that looks trivial can hide a threatened limb, and a limb that looks ruined can often be saved when the responder protects it, controls what is bleeding, records what the nerves and vessels were doing, immobilizes it in the position found, and gets the patient to the right place quickly. That is the whole skill of this subject, and it is more about restraint than about force. What kills and what costs limbs in the first hours is rarely a lack of sophistication; it is a missed compartment, a splint applied over a numb hand, a deformed limb straightened for tidiness, an open wound explored out of curiosity, or a transfer delayed because a finding was never written down.

This is educational material. It does not replace supervised practice, a training program, a certification, or the judgment of a clinician who can examine the patient, and constructed examples used for teaching are illustrations rather than real cases. Used as a companion to proper teaching and to the protocol of your own service, it is a way to keep a difficult subject calm, ordered and close at hand.

# Chapter 1 — Foundations of Musculoskeletal Trauma

Musculoskeletal trauma is the injury that most patients survive and then live with, so it deserves the same care as the injuries that kill within minutes. A broken wrist, a dislocated shoulder and a bruised thigh rarely kill in the first hour, yet each of them can end a career or the independence of a person who was healthy the day before. What decides the outcome is not the fracture alone but every tissue the energy passed through, because the soft tissues around the bone are the hardest to see and to repair. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Bone is a living organ with a blood supply, a covering and a capacity to repair itself, and it is described in two kinds according to how tightly its material is packed. Cortical bone, also called compact bone, forms the hard outer shell and is thickest in the shaft of a long bone. Cancellous bone, also called spongy or trabecular bone, forms a lattice of thin plates inside the ends of the bone, where it spreads the load of the joint across a wider area. The junction between the shaft and the end is the metaphysis, and in a child it is the region where the bone lengthens, so an injury there needs different attention than the same injury in an adult. These names are used in every later chapter, so they are worth learning slowly.

The periosteum is the tough fibrous sleeve that wraps the bone except where a joint surface is exposed, and it is far more than packaging. It carries blood vessels into the cortex, it holds the layer of cells that can make new bone, and it is the reason a fracture in a child may bend rather than break cleanly. In a child the sleeve is thick and lifts from the bone without tearing, so a partly broken bone may stay stable because one side remains intact. In an adult the same sleeve is thinner and tears more readily, which takes away part of the blood supply and part of the healing capacity of the fracture. A fracture that strips the periosteum over a long distance is therefore more serious than its appearance on a radiograph suggests.

Every fracture bleeds, and the blood that collects between the broken ends forms a hematoma that is the first stage of healing rather than a complication to be drained. The size of that collection depends on the bone, and a break of the thigh bone can release enough blood to threaten the circulation, with a figure offered in teaching as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A closed fracture can therefore cause shock without a drop of blood on the skin, which is one reason a patient with a swollen limb and a rising pulse is treated as an emergency. The vessels inside the bone are damaged as well, and a segment of bone may lose its supply altogether, which is one route to a fracture that never heals. Nothing done in the field restores that supply.

A joint is the place where two bones meet, and in a synovial joint the surfaces are covered by articular cartilage, which is smooth, white, springy and has no blood supply of its own. It is nourished by the fluid that fills the joint, and because it cannot be repaired by the ordinary healing process that mends bone, damage to it is the injury most likely to cause years of pain and stiffness. A capsule lined with a membrane holds that fluid in place, and the capsule is strengthened by the ligaments that cross it. Blood inside a joint after an injury, which is called a hemarthrosis, makes the joint swollen, painful and hard to move, and that finding tells the clinician that something within the joint has torn. A joint that fills quickly with blood is not to be manipulated by anyone not qualified to examine it, because the examination itself can add damage.

Ligaments are bands of strong fibrous tissue that connect one bone to another and guide the joint through its range of motion. They resist a pull along their length, and they are injured when a joint is forced beyond the range they allow. The injury is described in words rather than numbers, from a stretch in which the fibers stay intact, through a partial tear in which the joint remains stable, to a complete tear in which the joint no longer holds. The responder notices the swelling and protects the joint, while the judgment about how severe the tear is belongs to a clinician, because a joint that feels loose to one examiner may feel firm to another. Testing the stability of a joint by pulling on it is a clinical skill learned under supervision, and it is not a field test.

Tendons connect muscle to bone and carry the pull of a muscle across a joint into a small area of bone. Because that area is small, the force arriving there during a sudden contraction can be enormous, and a tendon can pull a piece of bone away with it in an injury called an avulsion. Muscle is injured by direct blows, by stretching and by being torn, and the bleeding within a muscle can be considerable, so a thigh that is swollen and tense after a blow needs early assessment rather than exercise. Fascia is the strong sheet of fibrous tissue that wraps muscles, groups of muscles and whole compartments of a limb, and it is the structure that makes some injuries dangerous in a way that is not visible. Evaluating these injuries is the work of a clinician, while the responder recognizes the swelling, protects the limb and reports what has changed.

A compartment is a closed space bounded by bone and fascia, and it holds muscle, nerves and blood vessels with very little room to spare. When bleeding or swelling raises the pressure inside a compartment, that pressure is transmitted to everything within it, and the first structures to suffer are usually the muscle and then the nerve. Fascia does not stretch quickly, so the pressure keeps rising instead of dispersing, and the flow through the smallest vessels fails even while a large pulse at the wrist or the ankle can still be felt. This is why an intact pulse does not exclude a compartment syndrome, and why a limb that is tense, swollen and painful out of proportion to the injury is an emergency. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects it does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late.

Nerves and blood vessels travel along the bone rather than through the middle of a limb, and they often lie directly against its surface where muscle and fascia protect them. That arrangement is efficient in health and dangerous in injury, because a bone that breaks and displaces moves exactly where the vessel and the nerve are lying. A break above the elbow can injure the vessel that supplies the forearm, and a break behind the knee can injure the vessel that supplies the leg, and the nerves of the arm and the leg are exposed in the same way. The findings that suggest damage to a nerve are numbness, tingling, weakness and the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier. The findings that suggest damage to a vessel are pallor, coolness, a diminished pulse and pain out of proportion to the injury, so the field acts are to record them and to send the patient urgently for assessment.

The skin is the envelope of this system, and its state decides how the injury will be managed. When the skin is intact the fracture is called closed, and when the bone or the deep tissues have communicated with the outside the fracture is called open, whether the wound is large or small. An open fracture is contaminated even when it looks clean, because the skin carries organisms that reach the bone and the deep tissues in the moment of the injury. The part played by the responder is limited and precise: cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control the bleeding that can be controlled, record the neurovascular status, immobilize the limb in the position found, keep the patient warm, and arrange urgent transfer. The lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment, and the trained responder works within the procedures the service authorizes. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. Exploring an open wound blindly also adds harm, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room.

Every word that describes position in this course assumes one starting point, called the anatomical position, and every clinician uses the same one. It is a person standing upright, facing forward, with the arms at the sides, the palms turned forward and the feet together and pointing ahead. An injury is described as though the patient were standing in that position even when the patient is lying on a stretcher, so that a description written in one country means the same thing in another. A forearm with the palm turned forward is described as supinated, and the same forearm with the palm turned backward is described as pronated. Without a shared starting point, words such as near, far, up, down, inside and outside would change meaning with every patient, and a record would be useless to the person who reads it next.

Directional terms describe where one structure lies in relation to another, and they are always used in relation to the patient rather than to the observer. Proximal means closer to the trunk and distal means farther from it, so the elbow is proximal to the wrist and the ankle is distal to the knee, however the limb happens to be lying. Medial means toward the midline of the body and lateral means away from it, so the little finger is medial to the thumb when the palm faces forward. Anterior means toward the front of the body and posterior means toward the back, while superior means toward the head and inferior means toward the feet. Superficial means nearer the surface and deep means farther from it, and that difference matters when a wound lies close to fascia. Palmar refers to the palm, plantar to the sole and dorsal to the back of the hand or the top of the foot, and the same side of the body is described as ipsilateral while the opposite side is described as contralateral.

The body is also divided by three imaginary planes, and every description of displacement is placed within them. The sagittal plane runs from front to back and divides the body into a left part and a right part, and the midline sagittal plane divides it into two equal halves. The coronal plane, sometimes called the frontal plane, runs from side to side and divides the body into a front part and a back part. The transverse plane, also called the axial plane, runs horizontally and divides the body into an upper part and a lower part. A fracture may be described as angulated in the sagittal plane, in the coronal plane, or in both, and that tells the clinician which way the far end of the bone has tilted. Rotation is described about the long axis of the bone, which is the axis that the transverse plane cuts across.

The words used to describe how a broken bone has moved are few, and each one answers a different question. Angulation describes a bend at the fracture and is named for the direction in which the far end of the bone points, so a fracture may be angulated toward the front or toward the back. Translation, also called displacement, describes the broken ends sitting side by side rather than end to end, and it is expressed in relation to the width of the bone rather than in units of length. Shortening describes a limb that has become shorter because the ends have slid over one another, and distraction describes the opposite, in which the ends have been pulled apart. Rotation describes a twist about the long axis, and it is the displacement most often missed unless the examiner compares the two sides. Comminution describes a bone broken into more than two pieces, and it warns the listener that the soft tissues are more likely to have suffered.

A joint can also be injured without a bone breaking, and the words for that injury describe how far the joint surfaces have moved apart. A dislocation means the surfaces are no longer in contact at all, and a subluxation means they are only partly out of contact, and both are injuries of the joint as a whole. A joint that has dislocated has almost always torn its capsule and at least one ligament, and it may have injured the cartilage or the bone at the edge of the joint. The joint may slip back into place by itself, which is called a spontaneous reduction, and the examiner then sees only swelling and tenderness and must still consider the injury that has just happened. A dislocation left unreduced may damage the bone or the vessels that supply the head of the bone, and the decision about how and when to reduce it belongs to a clinician working within the local protocol.

The sequence this course follows in every chapter begins with assessment, and the order of the steps is deliberate because each one protects the next. Assessment begins with the scene, continues with the mechanism of injury, and then moves to the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, and the limb is assessed by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing it. Stabilization comes next, and it means keeping the patient warm, controlling the bleeding that can be controlled, and supporting the limb in the position in which it was found. The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Immobilization, imaging, reassessment and definitive care follow in that order, because the complication this course fears most is the one caused by the treatment.

Assessment is more than a search for a broken bone, because the guiding question is what the energy did rather than what the skin shows. The mechanism of injury, the age of the patient, the time of the injury and the illnesses and medicines that affect bone are all part of the history. A patient whose bone is weakened by disease or by long use of a medicine that thins it may break a bone in a fall that would leave a healthy person unhurt. When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, the principle that decides the order is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. A falling level of consciousness, a changed pattern of breathing, a weak or rapid pulse and skin that has become cold and pale all send the responder back to the beginning.

Stabilization of a limb injury in the field is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. A deformed limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Pulling a limb straight may also convert a closed fracture into an open one and release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm and waits for help. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and both levels protect the limb from further movement and from cold. Cold is a complication of trauma, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering.

The neurovascular examination is never skipped and never assumed, and it is performed before the limb is splinted and again afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers and the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and numbness, tingling or the loss of a movement is recorded in the words of the patient as far as possible. The result is written before the splint is applied and after it is applied, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a folded magazine, a padded board, a sling or the body of the patient can each serve, and an improvised device must be checked more often because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace or a surgical fixation. Casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and neither of them is taught from a book in this course.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint is checked for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage or splint to be released by someone authorized to do it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. Either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done, and the decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the care of the patient. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined and reassessed after the picture has been taken.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, or a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, and every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A surgeon may hold the fragments with metal devices, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open or the diagnosis unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

Some patients break bones more easily and heal them less predictably. The bone of a child is more elastic than the bone of an adult, and it has a growth region near each end that can be injured without the bone breaking, so an injury that looks minor and leaves a child unwilling to use a limb deserves the same caution as an obvious break. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break a hip or a wrist in a fall from standing height, and the fracture may be far less painful than its severity suggests. A sign that is treated as reliable may be absent in these patients, and an examiner who relies on one sign alone will miss the injury. The response is not a different sequence but a lower threshold for immobilization and for referral, while the decisions about imaging and about treatment belong to the clinician.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and any change in the condition of the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so such a patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. Where this chapter names a time, a volume or a distance, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services and editions.

To summarize, a fracture is an injury of the whole limb rather than of the bone alone, and the tissues it travels through decide what the patient loses. Bone bleeds when it breaks, so a closed fracture can cause shock without a wound on the skin, and a nerve or a vessel may be torn while the skin stays intact, so the neurovascular status is recorded before any intervention and repeated after every one. The course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, or when the vessels and the nerves are failing and need a specialist. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and the patient is reassessed after every intervention and watched until the handover. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 2 — Types of Musculoskeletal Injury

Every injury of the musculoskeletal system belongs to a small family of named types, and the name is a decision about what happens next. A fracture, a dislocation, a subluxation, a sprain, a strain, a crush injury and the broader group of soft-tissue injuries are told apart by which tissue failed and how completely. That name sets the urgency, the destination, who is called and what will be done on arrival, so the order of the steps matters as much as the words. This chapter follows the order used throughout the course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Energy delivered to a limb does not choose one tissue, and the damage is decided by where the force entered, how fast it arrived and how the tissues were loaded. A pull along a ligament tears fibers, a twist through a joint tears the capsule, a direct blow crushes muscle against bone, and a bending force breaks what resists bending least. The same fall from a bicycle can fracture a wrist in one patient, dislocate a shoulder in another and tear a ligament in a third, and none of them looks dramatic at the roadside. What the responder sees is the sum of all of that, so the examination is aimed at the tissues rather than at the bone alone.

A fracture is a break in the continuity of a bone, whether the bone is cracked, bent, crushed or divided into pieces. A closed fracture leaves the skin intact over the break, while an open fracture has communicated with the outside through a wound that may be tiny enough to mistake for a scratch. The break is complete when the bone is divided across its whole width and incomplete when part of the outer shell stays in one piece, which is common in children, and a bone broken into many pieces is called a comminuted fracture. A fragment pulled away by a tendon or a ligament is called an avulsion, and the findings that suggest a fracture are deformity, swelling, tenderness at one point, a wound over the bone and a limb the patient will not use.

The teaching that a broken bone can be felt to grate is a poor guide, because the sign is often absent and the movement can injure what survived. Being able to bear weight, moving the fingers and feeling only mild pain do not exclude a fracture, and the patients in whom those signs are least reliable are the ones with the most to lose. A child with a crack, an older adult with fragile bone and a patient whose awareness is clouded by alcohol or by an injury of the head may report far less than the injury deserves. Where this chapter names a distance, a time or a threshold, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions.

The words used to describe how a broken bone has moved are few, and each answers a different question about the far end of the bone. Angulation describes a bend at the fracture and is named for the direction in which that end points, while translation, also called displacement, describes the broken ends lying beside one another rather than end to end. Shortening, distraction and rotation describe a limb that has lost or gained length and a bone that has twisted about its long axis, and comminution describes a bone broken into more than 2 pieces. These words matter less to the responder than to the surgeon, but the position in which the limb was found is worth recording, because the limb is splinted as it lies.

A dislocation is the complete loss of contact between the surfaces of a joint, so the bone ends that should meet no longer touch at all. The joint looks wrong, it is held in a position the patient cannot change, and the movement that should be free is blocked by the displaced bone. A dislocation tears the capsule that encloses the joint and damages at least one of the ligaments that steady it, and the nerves and vessels passing close to the joint are at risk. The bone end that has lost its blood supply may die if the joint is not put back within a time that teaching offers as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and nothing in the field is done to put it back.

A subluxation is a partial loss of contact between the surfaces of a joint, so the bones are still touching but are no longer in their proper relationship. It is often less obvious than a dislocation, because the shape of the limb may be almost normal and the patient may be able to move the joint a little. The capsule and the ligaments are torn in a subluxation too, so the joint is unstable even when it looks well and the injury is a different point on the same scale. A joint that has slipped partly out may return by itself, which is called a spontaneous reduction, and the responder then sees only swelling and tenderness while the injury has already happened.

Why does the distinction change what the responder does next? Because the type of injury sets the urgency, the destination and the limits placed on movement. A dislocated or partly dislocated joint can threaten a nerve, a vessel or the blood supply to the bone end, and a delay of hours can turn a recoverable injury into one that is not. A torn ligament with the joint surfaces still in contact is managed with protection, support and a plan made after imaging, while a torn muscle or tendon bleeds into its own compartment and can be more disabling than its appearance suggests. Two patients with the same swelling and the same pain may therefore need to go to different places, and the difference is the tissue that failed.

A sprain is an injury of a ligament, the band of fibrous tissue that joins one bone to another and guides a joint through its range of motion. The ligament is stretched or torn when the joint is forced beyond the range it allows, and the injury is described in words rather than in grades of number. In the mildest form the fibers are stretched and the joint remains stable, in the middle form some fibers are torn and the joint is still held, and in the most severe form the ligament is torn right through. The responder sees swelling, bruising and tenderness over the ligament rather than over the bone, and testing how loose the joint has become is a clinical skill learned under supervision and never a field test.

A strain is an injury of the muscle and tendon unit, in which the fibers of muscle, of tendon or of the junction between them are stretched or torn. It happens when a muscle contracts hard against a load it cannot move, which is why strains cluster in muscles that cross 2 joints and in tendons that carry sudden loads. The patient feels a sharp pain at a specific place, often describes a tearing sensation, and afterward cannot use that muscle with the same power, while bleeding into the muscle produces swelling and bruising that may appear a day later. When a tendon pulls a piece of bone away the injury is called an avulsion and is treated as a fracture, and when a muscle is struck directly and bleeds within its fascia the result is a contusion with a different risk.

The distinction between a sprain and a strain is simple in words and useful in practice, because a sprain is an injury of a joint and a strain is an injury of the muscle and tendon unit that moves it. A sprain of the ankle, the knee or the wrist sits over a joint whose bone ends may also have broken, so an inability to bear weight or tenderness over the bone raises the suspicion of a fracture and sends the patient for imaging. A strain sits over a muscle or a tendon away from the joint line, and the urgent question there is whether the muscle or tendon has torn completely or pulled a fragment of bone with it. Both are soft-tissue injuries, both are painful, and neither is a diagnosis that a responder can confirm by hand in the street.

Soft-tissue injury is the name for damage to everything in the limb that is not bone, which includes skin, fat, fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, joint capsule, blood vessels and nerves. It is sometimes spoken of as the mild part of trauma, and that habit is dangerous, because the soft tissues decide how a fracture heals, whether a limb keeps its blood supply and whether the patient returns to work. A fracture always includes a soft-tissue injury, since bone lies within a sleeve of muscle, fascia and skin that is torn or compressed by the same force. Damage to the soft tissues is often invisible at first, because the blood that has escaped lies deep inside the limb, and the responder who records a wound, a bruise or a change in the color of the skin is documenting what the radiograph cannot show.

A crush injury is the result of a body part being compressed between 2 surfaces, and the damage extends far beyond the point of contact. The force is usually high and applied slowly, so the tissues are squeezed and deprived of blood for as long as the compression lasts, and the visible wound may be small compared with what has happened beneath it. When a large mass of muscle has been crushed and then released, the breakdown products of that muscle enter the circulation and can damage the kidneys and disturb the rhythm of the heart, a condition called crush syndrome. The patient may look surprisingly well in the first minutes after release and then deteriorate quickly, so a limb that has been trapped for a long time is a problem for a physician and for a team rather than for a lone responder.

An open injury deserves a word of its own, because the skin's being broken changes the whole plan. Any wound over a bone may communicate with a fracture, and a small puncture wound from a fall onto a spike or from a bite can reach the bone while looking trivial. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, which is then covered with a sterile dressing if one is available. The bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the neurovascular status is recorded, and the limb is splinted as it lies, because exploring the wound blindly adds harm and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room.

Assessment begins before the patient is touched and follows the same order in every case. The first concern is the safety of the scene and the responder, because a rescuer who is struck becomes a second patient, and protection against infection is part of that same thought. The mechanism of injury and the time it happened come next, together with the age of the patient and any illness or medicine that might have made the bone easier to break. Then comes the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb. The limb is assessed by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing it, and when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot.

Looking is done before touching, and it is done with both sides in view so that the injured limb is compared with the other one. The responder notes the position in which the limb is held and whether it lies at an angle the patient cannot correct, because a limb that is deformed is splinted as it lies rather than straightened. Swelling, bruising, a wound, blood soaking through clothing and skin that has changed color are recorded, with the time each was first seen. A limb that is pale, mottled or cold, or one whose skin has become tense and shiny, is described exactly as it appears, and any ring or tight sleeve is removed if it can be removed without force, since a finger that swells inside a ring can lose its circulation within hours.

Feeling begins away from the site of greatest pain so that the patient does not guard the whole limb, and it moves toward the injury with a light hand. The responder feels for the temperature of the skin, for swelling, for tenderness and for the pulse beyond the injury, and compares one side with the other. Feeling for the grating of broken bone is not a useful test, because the sign is often absent and the movement can injure a nerve or a vessel that survived the accident. Pressing hard on a suspected fracture changes nothing about the treatment and adds to the pain, so the examination is as gentle as it can be and stops as soon as the question is answered.

Stabilization in the field is a small set of acts, and restraint is the most important of them. The limb is supported as it lies, with the hands or with whatever is at hand, and it is not straightened, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Bleeding that can be controlled without exploring the wound is controlled, the wound is covered, and the patient is kept warm, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and the lay first aider does it all with what is available. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint and a dressing within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes, and nothing in stabilization requires a diagnosis, which is why it can begin before the type of injury is known.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterward. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, and presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return. Sensation is tested on both sides rather than at a single spot, and the patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes against resistance that is only the weight of the examiner's hand. Numbness, tingling, weakness, an inability to move a part and a sensation that is reduced or absent are recorded in the words the patient uses, and the lay first aider observes and reports color, warmth and movement while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joint above and the joint below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on a bony point, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a folded magazine, a padded board, a sling or the body of the patient can each serve, and an improvised device must be checked more often because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, and casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least 2 directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography, usually called CT, shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging, usually called MRI, is used mainly for ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. The lay first aider never orders and never interprets imaging, and a radiograph taken soon after an injury does not always exclude a fracture, so a clinician may arrange a further study after a period that teaching offers as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the dressing is checked for bleeding that has soaked through, and the splint is checked for tightness and for pressure at its edges. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation, and reassessment also includes the patient as a whole, because a rising pulse or a falling level of consciousness outranks any question about the limb.

A compartment is a closed space bounded by bone and fascia, and it holds muscle, nerves and blood vessels with very little room to spare, so bleeding or swelling inside it raises the pressure on everything within. The first structures to suffer are usually the muscle and then the nerve, and the flow through the smallest vessels fails while a pulse at the wrist or the ankle can still be felt. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects it does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late. The acts that follow are limited and are defined by the local protocol, because a constricting bandage, splint or cast may be released by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation or a subluxation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, a crushed limb or a fracture in bone weakened by disease is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The receiving facility is told what the responder found rather than what the responder concluded, so that the next team can form its own view. The lay first aider does not decide where a patient goes, the trained responder follows the triage rules of the service, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides on definitive care.

Three words describe the acts that restore and hold the position of an injured part, and all three belong to supervised clinical training rather than to a book. Reduction means restoring the position of the bone ends or of the joint surfaces, and it is done because a bone that lies in a poor position may not heal, may not work and may press on the structures beside it. Traction means a gentle continuous pull that holds the ends in line while the soft tissues settle, and casting means holding a limb in a molded shell while the bone heals. Each can go wrong, because a reduction can injure a vessel or a nerve, can convert a closed injury into an open one and can push a fragment where it should not be, while a cast that is too tight can cause a compartment syndrome. A reduction must not be attempted when the source lists a contraindication, which includes a suspected complex fracture together with a dislocation, fragments caught in the joint, significant compromise of the vessels or nerves that needs a specialist, an open injury, an unclear diagnosis, training or equipment that is not available, and an earlier attempt that has failed. In each of those situations an attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and the qualified decision belongs to the physician or the orthopedic surgeon working within the local protocol, because force is not a technique.

Pain is part of the injury and it deserves to be treated, but no chapter of this course gives a substance, an amount, a route or a frequency, and this one will not either. The decision to give a medicine for pain belongs to a prescriber working within the local protocol, and the responder's part is to report the pain in the patient's own words and to keep the limb supported. A finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is out of proportion to the injury, pain that increases despite support, or pain accompanied by a limb that is becoming tense, pale or numb. Antibiotics and protection against tetanus after an open injury are decided by a clinician and given according to the local protocol, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from this chapter.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the appearance of the skin and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so such a patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision.

Every act described in this chapter belongs to somebody in particular, and the boundaries are part of the teaching rather than a footnote to it. The lay first aider supports the limb, controls bleeding that can be controlled, keeps the patient warm, observes color and warmth and movement, and calls for help, and does nothing that requires training, equipment or authorization. The trained responder and the paramedic examine the limb within their procedures, perform the neurovascular examination, apply splints and dressings with the equipment the service provides, and hand over what they found. The nurse, the physician and the orthopedic surgeon carry the acts that require training, judgment and a license, including the interpretation of imaging, the reduction of a dislocation and the decision about an operation, each according to the local protocol.

To summarize, the injuries in this chapter are told apart by which tissue failed and how completely, because a fracture breaks bone, an open fracture lets the break communicate with the outside, a dislocation separates the joint surfaces completely, a subluxation separates them partly, a sprain tears a ligament while the joint surfaces stay in contact, a strain tears muscle or tendon, a crush injury compresses part of the body and reaches beyond it, and soft-tissue injury is damage to everything in the limb that is not bone. Look for the position in which the limb is held, for swelling, bruising, a wound, an inability to bear weight, tenderness over one point of a bone, a joint that looks wrong, and any change in color, warmth, pulse, sensation or movement. Do the same things in the same order every time, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and record the neurovascular findings before every intervention and after every one. Never straighten a deformed limb, never remove an embedded object, never push exposed bone back into a wound, never explore an open wound blindly, and never test the stability of a joint or the power of a tendon by force. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the source lists a contraindication, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, or when the training and the equipment are not at hand. Cold is treated as a complication and the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it. Call the trained responder, the paramedic or the clinician according to the local protocol, and call early when the skin is broken, when a joint is out of place, when a limb is tense and painful out of proportion, or when the patient is deteriorating. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 3 — Fracture Classification

A description of a fracture is worth only what it predicts, so the words in this chapter are taught as forecasts rather than as labels to be memorized. The same broken bone can be called several things at once, and each name answers a different question about what the injury will do next. A transverse break in a strong shaft behaves unlike a spiral break of the same bone, and the difference matters long before the patient reaches a hospital. Every injury in this course follows one sequence, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Assessment comes first, and it begins with the mechanism of injury rather than with the bone, because the way the energy entered the limb usually predicts the shape of the break. A fall onto an outstretched hand drives force along the arm, while a twisting injury to a planted foot produces a different pattern. The age of the patient, the quality of the bone, the time since the injury and any illness or medicine that weakens bone are part of the same history. The responder records what was seen, what was heard and the position in which the limb was found, and does not name the pattern beyond what the mechanism plainly suggests. Naming the fracture definitively is the work of a clinician who can study the image, so the field description is expected to be revised.

The first and most consequential division is between a closed fracture and an open one, and it is decided by the skin alone. A closed fracture has no communication between the broken bone and the outside world, so the deep tissues stay sealed and the risk of infection is low. An open fracture has a wound that reaches the bone or the deep tissues, whether that wound is a long laceration or a small puncture, and it is contaminated at the moment of injury. The size of the wound does not settle the question, because a tiny wound over a broken bone can open a path into the deep tissues. The lay first aider covers the wound with the cleanest dressing available and keeps hands off it, while the trained responder and the paramedic do the same within the procedures their service authorizes.

The field acts for an open fracture are few. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the neurovascular status is examined and written down, the limb is supported in the position found, and the patient is kept warm while transfer is arranged urgently. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be pressing on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound. The wound is never explored blindly, because a finger or an instrument that enters it can carry contamination deeper and can disturb what was holding the bleeding back. Definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating theater, and the surgeon decides when the wound is taken there, following the local protocol rather than a rule from a book.

A description of the bone is only half of a description of the injury, because the same break can leave a limb quiet or can threaten it. The skin, the muscle, the fascia, the vessels and the nerves have all taken the same energy, and the tissues that were crushed rather than cut heal least predictably. A clean wound and a heavily soiled wound are different injuries even when the bone beneath them looks identical on an image. Swelling that keeps rising after the limb has been splinted is a finding about the soft tissues rather than about the bone. The responder records what can be seen, felt and reported, and leaves the grading of soft tissue injury to the clinician who will treat it.

Stability is a second division, and it is a statement about behavior rather than about appearance. A fracture is described as stable when the broken ends stay in acceptable position under ordinary load, and as unstable when they displace again as soon as the limb is moved. A break with a single clean line across the bone is often more stable than a long oblique or spiral break, because flat surfaces can interlock where slanted ones slide. An examiner may test stability by gentle handling within the limits of the local protocol, and such testing is a clinical skill learned under supervision rather than a maneuver for the field. A responder who hears the word unstable should treat it as a warning that the limb will not hold its position without proper support and early specialist care.

The transverse fracture runs across the bone at close to a right angle to its long axis, and it usually follows a direct blow or a bending force. Because the broken surfaces are broad and flat, they resist sliding, so a transverse break is often described as relatively stable once it is supported. It takes a substantial force to produce such a break, so the soft tissues at that level have absorbed a substantial force as well, and a wound over the bone should be suspected even when none is seen. The periosteum is torn on the side that was stretched and may stay intact on the side that was compressed, and an intact sleeve is one reason these breaks can be held by a well fitted support. The word therefore predicts that the bone will hold position better than a spiral break, but it does not predict that the skin and the muscle beneath it are unharmed.

An oblique fracture crosses the bone at a slant rather than straight across, and its shape carries the answer to how the limb will behave. The slanted surfaces can slide on one another, so an oblique break tends to shorten and to angulate under the pull of the muscles. A force that bends and twists the bone at the same time produces this pattern, and it often injures the tissues lying against the bone. A short oblique break behaves more like a transverse one, while a long oblique break behaves more like a spiral, so these words describe positions on a range. The responder does not straighten the angulation, because movement at the fracture is what the splint prevents, and the final position belongs to the treating clinician.

A spiral fracture winds around the shaft, and it is the signature of a twisting force applied along the length of a limb. A skier whose foot is held while the body turns, or a child whose arm is pulled and twisted, is the kind of constructed illustration that teaching uses, and any example in this course is an illustration rather than a report of a real patient. The line of the break is long, the surfaces are smooth and the ends rotate about the long axis, so the limb may point in a direction the patient did not choose. This is one of the patterns most likely to be unstable, and the twist that caused it may have torn the vessels and the nerves that travel along the shaft. A limb that looks rotated is splinted as it lies, and the examiner compares its resting posture with the other side, because that difference is often more informative than any measurement.

A longitudinal fracture splits along the length of the bone rather than across it, and it is uncommon enough that the word is worth knowing so that not every line is assumed to run the way one expects. It often appears together with another pattern, as a split that extends from a break near a joint into the shaft. Because the split follows the bone, the pieces can separate sideways when the joint above or below is moved. The finding that suggests it is pain along the line of the bone rather than at a single point, together with a joint that cannot be moved comfortably. Only a clinician who can study the image should decide what the line means, because a split reaching a joint surface changes the plan of treatment.

A comminuted fracture is one in which the bone is broken into more than two pieces, and the word tells the listener how much energy passed through the limb. The fragments may be few and large or many and small, and the more numerous they are, the more likely it is that the soft tissues were crushed as well. Comminution predicts difficulty in holding the bone in position, because there is no single pair of surfaces for the ends to interlock, and it predicts slower healing, because the blood supply to some fragments has been cut off. It also raises the chance that a fragment has entered a joint or is pressing on a vessel or a nerve. The responder who hears the word does not change the field acts, but that word should raise the level of concern and shorten the tolerance for delay, and the definitive decision about how such a break is held belongs to an orthopedic surgeon.

A segmental fracture is a serious form of comminution in which the bone is broken at two levels, leaving a free piece of shaft with no connection to either end. The middle piece keeps only the attachments that were not torn, and its blood supply may be poor, so it is at risk of never uniting with the rest of the bone. Because the free segment can move independently, the limb may change shape with the smallest movement, which can injure what is left of the blood supply. The responder supports the whole limb rather than the fracture alone and asks for transfer to a facility where the bone can be stabilized definitively. Deciding how that stabilization is done, whether with a frame outside the limb or a device inside the bone, is the work of an orthopedic surgeon.

An avulsion fracture is one in which a tendon or a ligament pulls a piece of bone away at the place where it attaches. The mechanism is a sudden contraction or a sudden stretch, so the injury often happens without any blow and the patient may describe a snap rather than an impact. It matters because the piece of bone that has moved is the anchor of a structure that moves a joint, and a joint whose anchor has moved may not work even though the fragment looks small on an image. Whether the fragment needs to be returned to its place, and how, is a decision made by a clinician or a surgeon. The responder identifies the loss of movement, records it and supports the limb, and does not test the strength of the structure repeatedly, because that adds pain and can pull the fragment farther from its bed.

An impacted fracture is one in which the broken ends have been driven into one another, so the bone is shorter and the surfaces are jammed together. A fall onto the end of a limb drives the shaft into the softer bone at the end, and this is a common pattern in the wrist of an older adult. Because the surfaces are compressed into each other, an impacted break is often stable, and it may be far less painful than its consequences suggest. Shortening of the limb, a change in the way the hand or the foot is held, and pain on moving the joint above or below are the findings that point to it, and a reliable sign may be absent here. Only the clinician decides whether the position is acceptable and whether it will hold while the bone heals, and the older adult whose bone has lost density deserves a lower threshold for splinting and referral.

A compression fracture is one in which the bone is crushed rather than split, and it is seen most often in cancellous bone, the lattice inside the ends of the long bones and inside the bodies of the vertebrae. The bone loses height and the joint surfaces are driven together, so the injury is a failure of the material rather than a break across a shaft. In the spine this may happen with a fall from standing height or a movement that seems trivial, and it may produce pain that the patient localizes poorly. The responder treats such a patient gently and keeps the spine still until someone qualified has cleared it, because the force that crushed one vertebra may have injured another. Assessment is carried out by a clinician, and the decisions about imaging and about bearing weight belong to that clinician within the local protocol.

The greenstick fracture takes its name from a young branch that bends and splinters on one side instead of breaking in two, and it happens because the bone of a child is softer and more elastic than the bone of an adult. The cortex breaks on the side that was stretched while the opposite side bends and stays intact, and the thick periosteum of a child usually stays in one piece, which holds the fragments together. Because the bone is bent rather than only cracked, the limb may keep a curve after the injury, and straightening that curve is not a field act. An injury that leaves a child unwilling to use an arm or a leg, even without swelling or deformity, deserves the same caution as an obvious break. Correction of the bend and the decision about how to hold it are carried out by someone trained in the care of children's fractures, under supervision and according to local protocol. The lay first aider supports the limb as it lies, keeps the child warm, and does not pull on the limb to see whether the curve will come out.

A buckle fracture, also called a torus fracture, is caused by compression of the cortex, so the bone bulges at one place rather than breaking through. It occurs almost only in children, whose bone can crumple under a load that would break the bone of an adult. The swelling may be modest, the deformity may be absent and the child may move the limb a little, so tenderness over a small area of bone is the finding a responder can record. Because the break does not pass through the whole bone, it is usually described as stable, but stable is not the same as trivial, and the parent must be told what to watch for. The diagnosis is made by a clinician with imaging, and the treatment, often a simple support, is chosen by that clinician in the light of the child's age and the position of the break.

A pathological fracture is one that happens through bone that was already weakened by disease, and it is therefore a symptom as much as an injury. The disease may be a tumor, an infection, a cyst or a condition that softens or thins the bone, and the patient may or may not have known about it. The mechanism is often trivial, such as a fall from standing height or a turn in bed, and pain may have been present for weeks before the bone gave way. Because the bone is abnormal, it heals differently and it may not heal at all unless the underlying condition is treated, so these patients are referred rather than simply supported and sent home. The responder supports the limb, keeps the patient warm and does not test how much weight the bone will take, while the search for the cause belongs to the physician or the orthopedic surgeon.

A stress fracture is a break that follows repeated load rather than a single event, and it is the pattern in which the history matters more than the examination. The bone fails after many repetitions of a force that it could bear once, and the pain begins as a dull ache with activity and settles with rest before it becomes constant. Runners, soldiers and dancers are the groups in which this pattern is most familiar, and any such example in this course is a constructed illustration rather than a description of a real person. The examination may find only a small area of tenderness, and an image taken early may show nothing at all, because the change in the bone becomes visible only after the injury has been present for a time. That is why a normal image does not exclude the injury, and why the clinician may ask for a further study or for a period of rest and review.

These descriptions are not exclusive and they are not arranged in a hierarchy, so one fracture is usually named in several ways at once. A break may be open, spiral, comminuted and unstable, and each of those words answers a different question about the injury. The shape of the line describes the pattern, the state of the skin describes the risk of infection, and the stability describes how the ends behave. A description that omits one of these dimensions can mislead the person who reads it next. For that reason the record is written in a fixed order, so the receiving team sees at once what was known and what was not.

Stabilization and immobilization come next in the sequence, and the classification of the fracture changes nothing about how a responder performs either of them. A deformed limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm and waits for help, while the trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the procedures their service authorizes. Immobilization includes the joints above and below the break, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end, and the splint is padded where it presses on bone. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground, and casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

The neurovascular examination is performed before the limb is splinted and repeated afterwards, and its result is recorded both times, because a finding that was not written before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and numbness, tingling or the loss of a movement is written in the words the patient used. The pattern of the fracture tells the examiner where to look hardest, because a break above the elbow and a break behind the knee endanger the vessels that supply the forearm and the leg. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and movement, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and it is often used to plan an operation. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle, and it may reveal a stress injury before a radiograph does. Either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done, and that decision belongs to the clinician, while the lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging.

Reassessment follows every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by treatment rather than by the injury. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The nurse and the clinician check the limb for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint is checked for tightness and for pressure over a bony point. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, and the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart while the patient is kept warm and referred urgently.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and the vocabulary of classification guides who is called and how quickly. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, a badly comminuted or segmental break, or a fracture in a child across the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals. Every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a book in this course. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves need a specialist, when the injury is open or the diagnosis unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed, because in each case the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. Force is not a technique, and where a substance is needed for pain or for protection against infection, the choice of the substance, the amount and the way it is given belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol.

Every number in this course is an illustration, and each one must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the description of the pattern, and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so such a patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. A patient classified in the field and reclassified in the hospital has not been misled, because a description is expected to change as more is learned.

To summarize, the words used to describe a fracture are predictions about behavior and not labels to be memorized. The first division is between a closed fracture and an open one, decided by the skin alone, and an open fracture is contaminated from the moment of injury, so the wound is covered with a sterile dressing, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back, and definitive closure belongs to the operating theater. The pattern of the break, whether transverse, oblique, spiral, longitudinal, comminuted or segmental, predicts how the bone will hold position and how the soft tissues suffered, while stable and unstable describe how the ends behave under load. An avulsion is pulled off by a tendon or a ligament, an impacted break is driven together, a compression break is crushed, a greenstick or buckle break belongs to a child, and a pathological or a stress break is the sign of abnormal bone or of repeated load. Every injury is handled in one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the provider level is named for every act. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found, the neurovascular status is recorded before and after each intervention, the patient is kept warm, and a limb that becomes tense and painful out of proportion is treated as an emergency. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and they are never taught from a book. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 4 — The Primary Survey

The primary survey is the part of the assessment that happens before anyone has decided what is broken, and it exists because the injuries that kill in the first minutes are rarely the ones that look worst. It searches for the conditions that will end a life within minutes if they are not found, and it searches in a fixed order, so that a frightened or tired responder still does the right thing first. The whole of this course follows one sequence, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the primary survey is the beginning of that sequence rather than a subject beside it. Each step buys the time in which the next can be performed at all, and that is why the order is not a tradition. This chapter is educational material, written for health professionals, students and trained responders, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The rule to carry away is that the limb never comes before the airway, and the reason is that different tissues tolerate a lack of oxygen for very different lengths of time. A brain starved of oxygen begins to suffer within a few minutes, so a patient whose breathing is obstructed, or whose chest is filling with blood, may be dead before a splint has been padded.
