A patient bleeding from a torn vessel can lose the volume that keeps the heart working in a similar span of time, and skin that is cold, pale and clammy says that this is already happening. The limb is the injury that is most visible and least immediately fatal, which is exactly why it captures attention that belongs somewhere else, and a deformed leg is frightening to look at. The order is fixed for that reason, and not because the limb does not matter.

Every act described here is described together with the provider level that may perform it, because a course that teaches the act and forgets the authority gets someone into trouble. The lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment and no authorization, which are calling for help, keeping the head and the neck still when there is reason to fear a spinal injury, pressing on a wound that is bleeding, keeping the patient warm, and staying with the patient. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician work within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, which usually include positioning the airway, suction, oxygen, ventilation with a bag and a mask, splinting, and the control of external bleeding. The paramedic and the nurse may perform the interventions their legislation, their training and their employer's protocol permit, and those permissions differ between countries and between services, so the listener must learn the list that applies where the listener works. The physician and the orthopedic surgeon decide the questions that medicine and surgery must answer, including whether an airway must be taken over, whether a chest must be released, and how an injury will be treated definitively.

The survey does not begin with the patient, because a responder who becomes a second casualty helps nobody. The scene is checked for traffic, fire, electricity, unstable ground, an animal and violence, and personal protective equipment is put on before the patient is touched, because blood and other body fluids carry infection. The mechanism of injury is noted, since it tells the responder what to expect, and the number of patients is counted, because a single responder facing several casualties must call for more help before beginning care. The time of the injury and the position in which the patient was found belong to the history as well, and they are spoken aloud at the handover rather than carried in the memory, because a time that is remembered is a time that drifts.

The first step is the airway, and the question is whether air is moving in and out of the patient. A patient who answers a question in a normal voice has an airway that is open at that moment, and that observation is the most useful one available, though it must be repeated, because an airway can close after it has been open. The findings that say the airway is threatened are a voice that has become hoarse or gurgling, a snoring sound in an unconscious patient, blood, vomit or a lost tooth in the mouth, swelling of the tongue or the throat, and a burn of the face with soot around the nose. A patient who is not breathing, or who breathes only with a noise that can be heard without a stethoscope, is treated before the survey moves on, because every later step depends on this one. The lay first aider opens the mouth, removes only what can be seen and lifted out with a finger, and calls for help, while the trained responder may position the head, use suction and place an airway adjunct within the procedures the service authorizes. Only a clinician trained and authorized to do so takes over the airway definitively, and forcing a device into a mouth or sweeping a finger blindly down a throat adds injury rather than removing it.

The second step is breathing, and it is examined before the chest is examined for broken bones, because the question is whether the lungs are filling and whether the two sides are doing equal work. The responder looks at the rate, the depth and the effort of breathing, at whether the chest rises on both sides, and at the color of the lips and the skin, and listens for air escaping from a wound of the chest. A rate faster than 30 breaths each minute in an adult, or slower than 8, must be acted on, and those figures are illustrations to be confirmed against the current guideline and the protocol of the service, because thresholds differ between countries and editions. A part of the chest wall that moves inward while the rest moves outward is called a flail segment, and a wound that makes a sucking sound with each breath is a finding to be reported at once, because both point to injuries only a hospital can manage. Where the service authorizes it the trained responder assists the breathing with a bag and a mask and oxygen, the paramedic may perform the procedures for a chest that has filled with air or blood under the standing orders of the service, and releasing trapped air with a needle or a finger is reserved for a clinician or for a paramedic trained, equipped and authorized to do it, which this course does not teach.

The third step is circulation, and its first purpose is to find and stop the blood that is leaving the body where a hand can reach it. The responder looks at the skin for pallor, feels it for warmth and moisture, and presses briefly on a nail bed to watch how quickly the color returns. A weak, rapid pulse at the wrist or in the neck, a patient who has become confused or restless, and skin that is cold and sweaty are the signs that the circulation is failing, and they carry more meaning together than any one of them alone. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by direct pressure with a dressing or a clean cloth, and the pressure is held rather than lifted to look underneath, because looking restarts the bleeding. Where bleeding cannot be controlled by pressure and the service permits it, the trained responder or the paramedic may apply a tourniquet according to the protocol of the service, and the time it was applied is written down where it can be seen. Bleeding inside the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis or the thigh cannot be seen, and it is treated by keeping the patient warm, by moving the patient quickly to a place where surgery is possible, and by the interventions the local protocol reserves to a physician or to a paramedic.

A pelvis that is unstable can bleed into the space it encloses without any wound on the skin, so a patient with pain in the pelvis after a fall from a height or a collision at speed is handled gently and is not rolled or pressed upon to test the joints. A pelvic binder, where the service provides one, is applied by the trained responder or the paramedic according to the protocol of the service, and it buys time rather than treating the injury. A broken thigh bone bleeds into the thigh, so a thigh that is swollen and firm tells the responder that a large volume of blood may have left the circulation even though the skin is unbroken. Keeping the patient warm is part of the treatment of shock rather than a courtesy, because cold worsens bleeding and makes the heart work harder, so wet clothing is replaced with dry covering and the patient is insulated from the ground. The quantity of blood that such an injury can hold is taught as a figure, and any such figure is an illustration to be checked against the guideline and the protocol in use where you work, while fluids and blood are given only by those authorized to give them and according to local protocol.

The fourth step is disability, which in the first minutes means the state of the brain and the spinal cord rather than the state of the limb. The responder speaks to the patient and notes whether the answer is appropriate or the patient is drowsy, confused or unresponsive, and compares the two pupils, because a difference between them is a finding to be passed on immediately. The blood sugar is measured by a responder trained and equipped to measure it, since a low blood sugar can mimic an injury of the head and can be corrected by those authorized to correct it, while the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol. The neck and the back are treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear them has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a patient with a suspected injury of the spine is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. A patient whose level of consciousness has fallen since the last check is getting worse, and that change stops the survey and sends the responder back to the airway, while the lay first aider reports the change and keeps the head and the neck still.

The fifth step is exposure, which has two halves that pull in opposite directions. The patient is undressed enough that the whole body can be looked at, because the injury that matters may be hidden under clothing at the back, in the armpit, in the groin or between the buttocks, and a wound that is not seen is a wound that is not treated. At the same time the patient is protected from cold, because the loss of body heat is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and it worsens bleeding and confuses the assessment. A patient who has been lying on a cold road or a wet floor loses heat quickly, so covering is applied as soon as each part has been examined and the removed clothing is put back or replaced.

Throughout the survey the rule is that a problem found at any step is treated before the next step begins, and the survey is then started again from the beginning, because an intervention can change a finding that was normal a moment earlier. The findings that stop the survey and demand treatment are an airway that is not open, breathing that cannot be supported, bleeding that will not stop with pressure, a pulse that cannot be felt in an unresponsive patient, a fall in the level of consciousness, and a new deformity or a change in the shape of the chest. A responder who is alone and cannot both treat and continue must treat what kills first and call for help early, while a service with more than one responder divides the tasks rather than queueing them one behind the other. The lay first aider stops at the limit of what can be done without equipment and without training and calls for the level that can go further, and the trained responder stops at the limit of the equipment, the procedures and the authorization the service provides. The principle behind all these limits is that the responder should do what is within reach and should not improvise what is beyond it.

Only when the survey has been completed, and any problem it found has been treated, does attention turn to the limb, and the patient with the obviously deformed leg is the patient for whom this rule was written. Such a leg is supported in the position in which it was found and is not straightened, not rotated, not pulled and not tested for stability, because a movement that looks like tidying can convert a closed fracture into an open one and can tear a vessel or a nerve that was still intact. The reason is anatomical, since vessels and nerves run along the surface of the bone rather than through the middle of the limb, so they lie exactly where the displaced end of the bone is pointing. The limb is examined by looking for swelling, bruising, wounds, deformity and shortening and by comparing it with the other side, while feeling for tenderness is done gently and only to the extent the patient tolerates. The lay first aider supports the limb with both hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm, and does not move the limb again until it has been splinted or until help arrives.

Before the limb is splinted, the neurovascular status is examined and written down, and this step is never skipped and never assumed, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin beyond the injury, compares the two limbs, feels for a pulse below the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested by touching the skin lightly on both sides, and any numbness, tingling, weakness or loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier is recorded in the words the patient uses. The findings that suggest damage to a vessel are pallor, coolness, a weaker pulse and pain out of proportion to the injury, while the findings that suggest damage to a nerve are numbness, tingling and weakness. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury, because the pressure inside a compartment can rise until the smallest vessels have stopped carrying blood while a large pulse at the wrist or the ankle is still felt, and an absent pulse is an emergency. The lay first aider observes the color, the warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel and reports what has changed, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or the clinician, and its result is spoken at the handover as well as written.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joint above it and the joint below it, because a bone that is held alone can still be moved by the joints at either end. The limb is splinted in the position in which it was found, the splint is padded where it presses on bone, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a folded magazine, a padded board, a rolled blanket, a sling or the body of the patient can each serve, and an improvised device is checked more often than a manufactured one because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the nurse applies and checks those the ward or the emergency department authorizes. Casting, traction and reduction are described in this course only in terms of what they are for, what they must achieve and what can go wrong, because the techniques are learned under supervision on real limbs and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a book. If the limb becomes more painful, more swollen or more pale after the splint is applied, the responder stops and seeks advice, because the splint that was meant to protect the limb has become the thing that threatens it.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment rather than by the injury. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison that carries the information rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the splint is checked for tightness, and a dressing over a wound is checked for blood that has come through it. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain that is out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense, swollen and hard are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects that the pressure inside a compartment has risen does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle, and the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released only by someone the local protocol authorizes to release it, with the limb kept below the level of the heart while the patient is kept warm and referred urgently.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it and to act on the result. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below the injury are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly where it enters a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. An image is requested when the answer it will give changes what is done next, and the lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging while the trained responder does not decide which study is needed.

Definitive treatment begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies, so the last step of the sequence is to refer or to treat according to what the injury is and who is present to treat it. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, a fracture of the pelvis, or a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, are performed by those qualified to perform them and according to local protocol. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the training or the equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed, because in each of those situations an attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. The physician decides what must be done in the emergency department, the orthopedic surgeon decides what must be done in the operating room, and the nurse keeps the record, the observations and the handover in order.

Some patients are harder to survey than others, and the same sequence is used with a lower threshold for calling for help. A child who is injured may be frightened and silent, and a child who is alert and then becomes quiet is getting worse rather than better, so the change matters more than any single number. An older adult may break a bone in a fall from standing height with little pain, and one who takes a medicine that thins the blood may continue to bleed from a place that looks trivial, so the threshold for imaging and for admission is lower. A patient who is pregnant carries two patients to consider, and the position in which she is placed and moved follows the local protocol for her stage of pregnancy. A patient who cannot answer questions because of an injury of the head, a language barrier, deafness, intoxication or sedation is examined as though an injury is present rather than absent, and a sign treated as always present will be believed and will eventually be wrong.

A short constructed illustration may help to fix the order of the survey in the mind, and it is an illustration rather than the record of any real patient. A responder arrives at a road and finds a person lying beside a fallen motorcycle with an obviously deformed thigh, the foot turned outward and the leg shorter than the other, and the patient is calling out in pain. The responder does not begin at the leg, because the patient answers a question, so the airway is open for the moment, and then the chest is watched while both sides are seen to move and the breathing is counted. The skin is cool and clammy and the pulse at the wrist is rapid and weak, so the circulation is failing, and the leg is only one of the places the blood may be going, along with the pelvis, the abdomen and the chest. Help is called for early, the bleeding that can be reached is pressed upon, the patient is covered to keep the warmth in, and only then is the leg supported exactly as it lies and splinted by the trained responder with the equipment the service provides. The neurovascular status of the foot is written down before the splint and again after it, and nothing was straightened, pulled or explored at any point.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and a chapter about a survey is mostly a chapter about what is noticed and what is passed on. The findings of the neurovascular examination are the ones most often lost, because they are written in a hurry by a responder who is about to move the patient, and they are precisely the findings that decide, hours later, whether a limb was already damaged before a splint was applied. Times are written as times rather than as intervals remembered afterwards, and the condition of the patient is described as it was found rather than as it was assumed to be. Where this course names a time, a distance or a threshold, that number is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions.

To summarize, the primary survey looks for what kills in the first minutes, and it looks in a fixed order, which is the airway, then breathing, then circulation, then disability, then exposure, and the limb never comes before the airway, however deformed the limb may be. A problem found at any step is treated before the next step begins, and the survey is then started again from the beginning, because an intervention can change a finding that was normal a moment before. The neurovascular status of the limb is examined before it is splinted and again afterwards, and it is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. A deformed limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the training or the equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed, and force is never a technique. The provider level is named for every act, no drug, dose, route or frequency is given anywhere in this course, cold is treated as a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it. Every number heard here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and your local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 5 — The Secondary Survey

The secondary survey is the examination that begins once the primary survey has been completed and every problem it found has been treated, and it is the step in which the whole patient is looked at from the top of the head to the soles of the feet in a fixed order. Its purpose is to find the injuries that do not kill within minutes and would otherwise be missed, and it is where most fractures and most dislocations are found. The sequence followed in every chapter of this course is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the secondary survey is the part of that sequence in which an injury of a limb is properly assessed. It is not performed on a patient who is still unstable, because such a patient is treated again from the beginning of the primary survey until the airway, the breathing and the circulation are controlled. This chapter is educational material for health professionals, students and trained responders, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The survey starts with the history of the event rather than with the hands, because what happened decides what the examiner looks for and how urgently the patient must be moved. The history begins with the time of the injury, which is written as a clock time rather than as an interval remembered afterwards, and with the position in which the patient was found, because a patient who has lain in one place may have a pressure injury as well as a fracture. The mechanism follows next, and a fall from a height, a collision at speed, a twisting injury of a planted foot, a direct blow and a fall from standing height suggest different patterns of injury that the examiner must consider. The patient is asked what happened in the patient's own words, and those words are repeated at the handover rather than replaced by the examiner's summary, because a patient who remembers striking the head is telling the listener something that no examination of a limb will reveal.

The medical history is gathered at the same time, and it changes what the findings mean rather than merely adding detail. A patient whose bones are weakened by disease, by a long illness or by a medicine taken over years may break a bone in a fall that would leave a healthy person unhurt. A patient who takes a medicine that thins the blood may continue to bleed from a place that looks trivial, and a patient whose heart rate is held down by a medicine may not show the rapid pulse that would otherwise be expected. The names of such medicines, the amounts and the reasons for taking them belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and this course never teaches a listener which substance to give or how much of it to give. The history is also imperfect in predictable ways, because a patient with an injury of the head may repeat the same answer, a patient who has been drinking may deny pain, and a frightened child may say nothing at all. The clinician weighs the history against the examination and treats an unreliable account as a reason to look more carefully rather than as a reason to relax.

The survey needs a patient who can actually be seen, so clothing is removed or cut away where the service authorizes it, and the part that has been examined is covered again before the next part is uncovered. The lay first aider does not undress a patient but keeps the patient warm, covers what is exposed and stays within the acts that need no equipment, while the trained responder, the nurse and the physician expose the body as the local protocol allows. Every part is looked at, including the back, the armpits, the groin and the skin between the buttocks, because a wound in a hidden place is a wound that is never treated and an injury that is never counted. The pull is in two directions at once, since the patient must be exposed to be examined and must be covered to be kept warm, and cold is a complication of trauma. A patient loses heat quickly on a wet road, a cold floor or a metal tailgate, so wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, the patient is insulated from the ground, and the ambulance or the room is warmed where that can be done.

The back cannot be examined while the patient is lying on it, so the patient is turned in one movement by a team, a maneuver usually called a log roll, with one person at the head holding the neck and the shoulders and directing the others. Such a turn is performed only by a team trained and equipped for it and according to the local protocol, because an injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. The purpose of the turn is to look at and to feel along the back, to note any wound, bruising, swelling or step, and to record what is found before the patient is turned back. The turn is not a test of the spine, and the examiner does not press, twist or bounce the patient to see whether it hurts, because a test that moves an unstable segment can convert a survivable injury into a permanent one. A collar, a board or a vacuum mattress is applied where the service provides it and the local protocol requires it, and the same team coordinates the next move as carefully as the first. Where a service has no trained team, the patient is kept still in the position found and help is called for from one that has, and waiting is the safer choice.

The examination then follows the body from above downward, and the order is spoken as it is performed so that nothing is forgotten. The head and the face are examined for wounds, swelling, blood behind the eardrum, bruising around the eyes or behind the ear, and a nose or jaw that has moved, and the pupils are compared with each other more than once. The neck is examined for tenderness, swelling and a step, and it is examined again when the collar is removed by the clinician who is qualified to clear the spine. The chest is watched while it moves, felt for tenderness and for the crackle of air under the skin, and the abdomen is felt gently for tenderness, firmness and distension. The pelvis is pressed once and gently by a clinician, never repeatedly and never to discover how much it hurts, and the back, the buttocks and the perineum are examined during the turn. Every limb is then examined in turn, and findings are described as findings, so the record says what was seen, felt and heard rather than naming a diagnosis the examiner is not qualified to make.

A fracture announces itself through a small set of findings, and none of them is present in every patient, so the examiner gathers them together rather than trusting any one of them alone. The limb may be deformed, which means that its shape differs from the shape of the other side, and it may be shortened when the broken ends have slid over one another. Swelling and bruising appear over the injury and often spread along the limb, and tenderness is present when the bone is pressed gently at a point away from the wound, though the pressure is never applied so firmly that it tests the bone. Movement that is not possible at a joint, or movement in a direction the joint does not normally permit, is a finding that stops the examination of that part and is not reproduced deliberately. A crackling sensation under the fingers, called crepitus, may be felt when the broken ends move against each other, and it is never sought on purpose, because seeking it moves the fracture and adds pain and damage. Shortening, rotation and an open wound each carry more weight than tenderness, and the finding that most changes what happens next is a wound near the fracture, because an open injury needs a different plan.

Several of these findings are unreliable in particular patients, and the examiner who knows this will miss fewer injuries. A child may have a fracture of a bone that bends without breaking and may move the limb almost normally between bouts of crying, and a child who was alert and then becomes quiet is getting worse rather than better. An older adult may break a hip or a wrist in a fall from standing height with little pain and no visible deformity, and the absence of pain is not evidence that the bone is intact. A patient who has been drinking, a patient with an injury of the head and a patient who has received a medicine for pain may report no pain while a serious injury is present, and a frightened patient may deny pain in order to avoid being moved. For all of these reasons the threshold for immobilizing a limb and for referring a patient is lowered rather than raised when the story and the examination do not agree.

Examining a limb without moving it is a discipline rather than a technique, and it rests on three acts that are done in the same order every time. The examiner looks first at the limb as it lies, comparing it with the other side for shape, length, rotation, swelling, bruising and wounds, and at the skin beyond the injury for color and for breaks. The examiner then feels with the fingertips, keeping one hand under the limb to take its weight and sliding the other hand along the surface rather than pressing on the bone, and the patient is asked to say when the touch becomes painful. The examiner asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes and to say what can be felt on the skin, and the answer is recorded in the words the patient uses rather than in the words of the examiner. At no point is the limb straightened, pulled, rotated, lifted by the far end or tested for stability, because the vessels and the nerves of a limb run along the surface of the bone and lie exactly where the displaced end of the bone is pointing. Testing the stability of a joint by pulling on it is a clinical skill learned under supervision, and it is not a field test. The lay first aider supports the limb where it lies and reports what can be seen, while the formal examination of the joint belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

A wound near a fracture is examined by looking at it rather than by exploring it, and the rules about open injuries are short and absolute. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing or with the cleanest covering available, and the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by pressure held over the dressing rather than by lifting the dressing to look underneath. An embedded object is left exactly where it lies and is stabilized in place, because it may be pressing on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound for the same reason. A wound is never explored blindly with a finger or an instrument, since the exploration pushes contamination deeper, tears what remains intact and starts bleeding that was not there before. The neurovascular status is recorded before the dressing is applied and again afterwards, and then the limb is immobilized and the patient is referred urgently. The lay first aider covers the wound and presses on the bleeding, and the trained responder does the same within the equipment the service provides, while the cleaning, the removal of dead tissue and the definitive closure of an open fracture belong to the operating room and to the surgeon who works there.

The neurovascular status of each limb is examined during the secondary survey and examined again after every intervention, and the result is written before a splint is applied and after it is applied. The examiner compares the two sides for color and warmth, feels for a pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes and to describe what can be felt. A pulse that is present does not exclude a serious injury, because the pressure inside a compartment can rise until the smallest vessels have stopped carrying blood while a large pulse at the wrist or the ankle is still felt. A pulse that is absent is an emergency, and so is a limb that has become pale, cold, painful out of proportion to the injury or unable to move. The formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician, and the lay first aider observes the color, the warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel and reports anything that has changed. The result is spoken at the handover as well as written, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards, and the record protects the patient and the responder alike.

Stabilization during the secondary survey means treating each problem as soon as it is found and keeping the patient in a condition in which the rest of the examination can be done at all. Bleeding that can be reached is pressed upon, a wound is covered, a limb is supported in the position in which it was found, and the patient is kept warm and quiet while the survey continues. If a problem appears that threatens the airway, the breathing or the circulation, the secondary survey stops where it is and the primary survey is repeated from the beginning, because an intervention or a new injury can change a finding that was normal a few minutes earlier. The lay first aider stabilizes by holding, by covering and by reassuring, and calls for the level of help that can do more, while the trained responder acts within the equipment, the procedures and the authorization the service provides. A fluid, a medicine for pain or an antibiotic is given only by someone the local protocol authorizes to give it, and the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber rather than to this course. Nothing in the secondary survey is worth a life, so the survey is interrupted as often as the condition of the patient requires.

Immobilization follows the examination and comes before any move of the patient, and it means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joint above it and the joint below it. A bone that is splinted on its own can still be moved by the joints at either end, so a splint reaches past both joints and holds the fracture still. The splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position in which the limb was found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold the limb without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a folded magazine, a padded board, a rolled blanket or a sling can each serve, and a device made by hand is checked more often than a manufactured one because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, the nurse applies and checks those the ward authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is needed. Casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and neither of them is taught from a book in this course. If the limb becomes more painful, more swollen, more pale or more numb after the splint is applied, the responder stops, seeks advice and prepares to release what the protocol allows.

Imaging comes after the examination and after immobilization, and it confirms what the examination has already suggested rather than replacing it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above the injury and the joint below it are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly where it enters a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. Each study is requested when the answer it will give changes what is done next, and the decision belongs to the clinician who is trained to interpret the images and who is responsible for the care of the patient. The lay first aider never orders or interprets an image, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed, although both may describe what they saw and felt before the image was taken. An image is a picture of one moment and it says nothing about how the limb is now, so the patient is examined and reassessed after every study and after every journey to and from the imaging room.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment rather than by the injury. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison carries more information than any single measurement taken on its own. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the splint is checked for tightness and for the pressure it makes, and a dressing is checked for blood that has come through it. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain that is out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense, swollen and hard are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects that the pressure inside a compartment has risen does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late, because time is muscle, and the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart. The constricting bandage, splint or cast is released only by someone the local protocol authorizes to release it, and the release is followed by a further examination and by a further record. A patient whose condition has changed in any way is examined again from the beginning of the sequence, because a change is a finding in itself.

The last step of the sequence is to refer the patient or to treat the injury definitively, and it begins with the recognition that many injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, a fracture of the pelvis or a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, and each of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the training or the equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed, because in each of those situations an attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. The physician decides what must be done in the emergency department, the orthopedic surgeon decides what must be done in the operating room, and the nurse keeps the record and the handover in order. Force is not a technique, and a responder who meets resistance or who sees the condition of the patient change stops at once and calls for the level of care that can take over.

The record is part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and the secondary survey is where most of it is written. Each finding is written before the next intervention rather than reconstructed afterwards, because the order of events is what tells the reader whether a limb was already damaged before the splint was applied. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the patient and the limb were found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention and any change in the condition of the patient are the facts a receiving team needs, and they are the facts most often lost. The words the patient uses about pain and about numbness are quoted rather than translated, since a patient who says that the foot has gone to sleep is describing a different thing from a patient who says that it hurts. Where a number is written down, such as a pulse of 110 beats each minute, that number is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. The same caution applies to any healing time that a service teaches, since 8 to 12 weeks in one hospital is a different estimate in another and must be checked against the guideline in use where you work. Sometimes the patient must be moved before the survey is finished, and the parts that were not examined are then named in the handover as unexamined rather than left to be understood as normal.

A short constructed illustration may help to fix the order in the mind, and it is an illustration rather than the record of any real patient. A cyclist is brought to a small hospital after striking a wall, and the primary survey has found no immediate threat, so the secondary survey begins with the history of the event and with the account of a witness. The patient says that the right shoulder hurts and that the left hand is numb, and the record notes those words as they were spoken. The right arm is looked at where it lies and supported with a hand under the elbow, and the examiner sees swelling and a change in the shape of the upper arm and feels the pulse at the wrist before and after a splint is applied by the trained responder with the equipment the service provides. The left hand is pale and cooler than the right, and the strength of the grip has changed, so the clinician is called at once and the patient is referred to a facility where the vessels can be examined and repaired. The chest is watched while the patient is undressed and kept warm, the abdomen is felt gently, the pelvis is pressed once by the clinician, and the back is examined during a turn performed by the team. Nothing was straightened, nothing was explored, and every finding was written down before the next step was taken.

To summarize, the secondary survey is the head to toe examination that follows the primary survey, and it is where the fractures and the dislocations that do not kill in the first minutes are found. It begins with the history of the event, it exposes the whole patient while keeping the patient warm, and it turns the patient with a trained team when the back must be examined, because an injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so. The limb is examined where it lies by looking, by feeling gently and by asking the patient to move and to feel, and it is never straightened, pulled, rotated or tested for stability, since the vessels and the nerves run along the surface of the bone where the displaced end is pointing. The neurovascular status is examined before any intervention and repeated after every one, and a limb that becomes pale, cold, tense or painful out of proportion to the injury stops the survey and is escalated at once, because a compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis and time is muscle. A wound near a fracture is covered with a sterile dressing and never explored, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room and to nobody else. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the training or the equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed, and no dose, no route and no drug regimen is given anywhere in this course. The provider level is named for every act, every number heard here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and your local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 6 — Neurovascular Assessment

The neurovascular examination is the examination this whole course turns on, because it decides whether a limb survives the journey to definitive care. Is blood still arriving at the hand or the foot, and is the nerve still carrying its messages back? A patient can lie still with a calm face and a steady pulse while the tissues beyond the fracture are being starved, and the only warning is this examination. It needs no specialist equipment and takes less than a minute on each limb once the order is learned. It is performed before any intervention and repeated after every intervention, its result is written down, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

A nerve does not run down the middle of a limb where nothing can reach it. It travels along the surface of the bone, held there by muscle and fascia, and the arteries do the same at the elbow, behind the knee and around the ankle. A bone that breaks and shifts moves into the space where the vessel and the nerve were lying. The soft tissues offer no guarantee either, because the energy that broke the bone passed through them first. A limb can lose its nerve supply, its blood supply, or both, while the skin above it stays unbroken and the wound everyone is searching for never appears.

The sequence this course follows places the neurovascular examination third, after assessment and stabilization and before immobilization, imaging, reassessment and definitive referral or treatment. Assessment decides whether the patient is stable enough for a limb to be examined at all, and stabilization buys the minutes in which the examination means something. The examination then sets the baseline against which every later intervention is measured, because splinting, imaging and treatment all change the limb. Nobody can say what a splint did unless somebody recorded what was there before the splint. A listener who can recite the sequence will not skip the step that a hurry makes tempting.

Assessment begins away from the limb, with the scene, the mechanism of injury, the age of the patient and the time since the injury. It continues with the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because a patient who cannot breathe has no use for a perfect examination of the wrist. Life comes before limb, so a responder with one pair of hands treats the threatened airway first and returns to the limb a moment later. Only when the patient is stable enough does the limb assessment begin, and the limb is examined by looking, by feeling gently and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing it. A falling level of consciousness, a changed pattern of breathing or cold clammy skin sends the responder back to the beginning of the survey.

Stabilization is a small set of acts, and restraint is the most important of them. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with pressure over a dressing, the limb is supported in the position in which it was found, and the patient is kept warm. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm and reports any change in the color or the warmth of the hand or the foot. The trained responder and the paramedic splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and both record the neurovascular findings before the splint goes on. Cold is a complication of trauma, so wet clothing is replaced and the patient is insulated from the ground.

The examination itself is a short list of observations made in the same order every time: pulse, color, warmth, capillary refill, sensation and movement. Pain belongs in the same list, as the warning sense that usually speaks first. Both limbs are examined, the injured one and the uninjured one, and the injured side is compared with the other rather than with a remembered idea of normal. Findings are described as present, absent, reduced or increased, and never left as the single word normal. The order moves from what the examiner can see and feel to what the patient must report, and it makes a change visible at a glance in the record. The whole examination is repeated after every intervention that follows.

The pulse is felt beyond the injury, on the side of the fracture farther from the heart, because a pulse there is evidence that blood is still arriving. In the arm the examiner feels at the wrist on the thumb side, and in the leg at the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle, comparing the two sides whenever possible. A pulse is described as present, diminished or absent, and an absent pulse beyond a fracture is an emergency rather than a note to be filed. A pulse that is present does not exclude a compartment syndrome, an injury to an artery or a nerve that has stopped working, because pressure inside a limb can destroy muscle while a large vessel still carries blood. The trained responder and the clinician feel for pulses as part of the formal examination, while the lay first aider observes color and warmth and reports what has changed.

Color is the first thing the eye notices and the easiest finding to describe. A limb that is pale, waxy or white has lost its blood supply, while a limb that is dusky or mottled is showing that blood arriving is not draining or is short of oxygen. Bruising and swelling change the color of the skin without any injury to the vessels that matter, so the examiner looks at the whole limb and at the other side before drawing a conclusion. In a patient with deeply pigmented skin, pallor and bluish discoloration are judged best at the nail beds, the palms, the soles and the lips. A change in color that appears after a splint has been applied is a reason to look under the splint and reassess.

Warmth is felt with the back of the fingers on both limbs at the same level. The examiner moves a hand from the shoulder toward the fingers or from the hip toward the toes and notices where the limb becomes cooler, because a line of coldness that falls at the fracture differs from a foot that has been cold since the patient left a warm room. A cool limb beyond an injury suggests a failing blood supply, while cold limbs on both sides with cold skin on the trunk suggest that the patient rather than the limb is in difficulty. The limb is kept warm throughout, and the examiner takes care that the examination does not chill the patient. The comparison with the other limb and with the trunk is recorded beside the pulse and the color, and one finding without the other is a puzzle rather than reassurance.

Capillary refill is tested by pressing on a nail bed or on the pad of a finger or a toe until the skin blanches, then releasing the pressure and watching the color return. A delay of more than a few seconds is the finding that is taught, and the number of seconds is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. The test is unreliable in a cold environment, in a patient whose circulation has already shut down and in a darkly pigmented nail bed. It is therefore read with the color, the warmth and the comparison with the other limb, and the trend across repeated examinations is worth more than any single measurement. A capillary refill that becomes slower while the limb lies splinted is a signal to look at the splint before looking for another explanation.

Sensation is tested by asking the patient what the limb feels like, and then by touching the skin lightly in the same place on both sides and asking whether the two sides feel the same. A light stroke with a fingertip is enough for the field, while a pinprick test or the testing of one nerve territory belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician and only where the local protocol allows it. The patient is asked for the words that matter, which are numbness, tingling, pins and needles, a limb that has gone to sleep and a patch that feels dead. It is not enough to touch one spot, because a nerve supplies a territory, so the examiner tests the part of the limb that the nerve in question supplies and compares it with the matching part on the other side. Sensation is unreliable in a patient who has taken alcohol or another sedating substance, in a patient with a head injury and in a frightened child, so those patients need a lower threshold for referral.

Movement is tested by asking the patient to move the part rather than by moving it for them. In the arm the patient is asked to spread and bend the fingers and to lift the wrist up and down, and in the leg to spread the toes and to pull the foot up and push it down. Each movement is compared with the other side, and what the patient could do a few minutes earlier matters as much as what the patient can do now. A movement that has been lost, or that has become weak, stops the examination and sends the responder to the local protocol for a threatened limb. Forcing a joint through a movement the patient cannot perform is never part of this examination, because force may turn a partial injury into a complete one. The lay first aider asks the patient to wiggle the fingers or the toes and reports whether the patient still can.

Pain is the finding that most often arrives before any of the others, and it deserves a place in the neurovascular examination. Pain that is out of proportion to the injury, pain that increases rather than settles, pain made worse when a muscle is stretched gently, and pain that is not relieved as expected are all warnings. The examiner asks the patient to describe the pain and to say whether it is changing, and records the answer with the time. Pain may also be absent or blunted in a patient who has already received a medicine for pain, so its absence proves nothing on its own. Relief of pain is decided by a clinician or by a prescriber working to the local protocol, and this course gives no drug, no dose, no route and no frequency, because the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber. The responder who is not authorized to give such a medicine concentrates on splinting in the position found, on warmth and on the speed of the transfer.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention, and the reason is attribution. If the hand is numb after a splint is applied, nobody can say whether the splint caused the numbness or the fracture did, unless somebody wrote down that the hand was numb before the splint went on. The examination is therefore done before the splint, before the dressing, before the limb is moved and before the patient is lifted, and again after each of those acts. An examination performed once, at the end, after everything has been done, is not a baseline and cannot be used to judge anything. The sequence is repeated at every transfer, because a new team must know what the limb was doing an hour ago.

The record of the examination belongs on the patient and not only in the notes, because the notes travel with a chart while the patient travels on a stretcher. A small card fixed to the splint or a note placed where the receiving team will see it carries the information to whoever unwraps the limb next, and it survives the loss of a folder and the change of a shift. Where local protocol allows writing on the skin, the examiner writes the time and a few plain words rather than a symbol that only one service understands. The card carries the time of the injury, the position in which the limb was found, the findings of each examination and the time of each intervention, so that the next person reads a story rather than a single sentence. Writing the examination is the work of the trained responder, the nurse, the paramedic or the clinician, and the lay first aider reports in the same plain words. A finding that was not written down was not made.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and it is done in the position in which the limb was found. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. An embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and definitive closure of the wound belongs to the operating room. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace or a surgical fixation. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no chapter of this course teaches their technique from a book. The neurovascular examination is repeated as soon as the splint is in place and compared with the record made a few minutes earlier.

A splint can cause the very catastrophe it was applied to prevent, and reassessment is the only thing that catches this in time. Swelling continues after an injury, so a splint that was comfortable an hour ago can become a tight band while the patient waits, and the limb beyond it turns pale, cool, numb and painful. The fingers or the toes are left visible and uncovered wherever the design of the splint allows it, so that the next person can look at them without undoing anything. A bandage is checked for tightness, a sling for pressure on the neck, and the padding for the place where it has shifted and left bone uncovered. If the limb changes, the responder stops, reassesses and follows the local protocol for what may be loosened and by whom, because force is not a technique and neither is waiting.

Imaging comes after the examination and the immobilization, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage and tendons. The neurovascular status is recorded again before the patient leaves for the imaging department, because a limb can become worse in a corridor. An image is a picture of one moment and does not examine anyone, so a normal radiograph never cancels a limb that is pale, cool or numb. The choice of study belongs to the clinician responsible for the care of the patient, and the lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention and at intervals while the patient waits, because the complication this course fears most is the one caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order, that is pulse, color, warmth, capillary refill, sensation, movement and pain, and each one is compared with the record rather than judged on its own. The comparison is the examination, since a pulse that has always been weak is a different finding from a pulse that has just become weak. A new numbness, a new pallor, a limb that has turned cold, a movement that has been lost, a pulse that cannot be found and pain that is worse than it was are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. The splint or the dressing is then examined, the other limb is examined again for comparison, and the patient is kept warm while help is arranged.

Compartment syndrome is the diagnosis this whole examination is arranged around, and it is a clinical diagnosis that nobody makes from a single measurement. Bleeding or swelling inside a closed space raises the pressure there, the smallest vessels stop carrying blood, and muscle and nerve begin to die while the large pulse at the wrist or the ankle can still be felt. The limb becomes tense, swollen and painful out of proportion to the injury, pain is produced when the examiner gently stretches the muscles of the compartment, and the patient may describe numbness in the territory of a nerve that passes through it. A pulse that is present does not exclude the diagnosis, and waiting for the pulse to disappear is waiting for damage that may already be permanent. A responder who suspects compartment syndrome does not elevate the limb above the level of the heart, but keeps the patient warm and refers urgently, because time is muscle. A constricting bandage, splint or cast is released only by someone the local protocol authorizes to do it, and the release is followed by another examination.

What a change means depends on when it was first noticed, and that is why the times are recorded. A pulse lost while the limb lies in a splint is first treated as a splint problem, and the responder looks at the bandage before concluding that the injury has worsened. A limb that was warm and pink and is now pale and cool has lost its arterial supply until proven otherwise, and an injury to an artery is a surgical emergency that needs a facility with an operating room. Bleeding that spurts or will not stop under pressure, a swelling that grows while it is watched, a pulse that cannot be felt and a nerve that has stopped working are hard signs that make the transfer urgent rather than soon. A pulse can also be present at the first examination and gone at the second, because a vessel bruised inside its wall may close over the following hours, which is why the examination is repeated and not merely performed once. None of these findings improves by waiting or by an attempt to restore a position by force.

This illustration is invented rather than taken from any real patient. A man in his thirties falls from a bicycle and holds out an arm with a bend in the middle of the forearm that was not there before; the trained responder supports the limb in the position found, records that the fingers are warm and pink, the pulse at the wrist is present, sensation is intact and the fingers can be moved, and then applies a padded splint. Less than an hour later, in the back of the vehicle, the fingers are pale and cool, the patient says the hand is tingling, and the pulse that was easy to feel is now difficult to find. The responder does not straighten the arm and does not wait for the hospital to notice; the splint is checked for tightness within the local protocol, the findings and the time are written down, and the receiving team is warned before arrival. The examination turns a change that would otherwise be discovered too late into a message that arrives early.

Some patients cannot give a reliable account of their own limb, and the examination has to be adjusted rather than abandoned. A young child who is frightened and in pain may cry without answering and may withdraw the limb, so the examiner compares the two limbs, watches how the child uses the arm and keeps a low threshold for splinting and for referral. An older adult may have thin skin, less padding over the bone, poor circulation and a nerve that has been losing function for years, and a fracture that would be painful in a younger patient may be almost quiet. A patient whose feet have been numb for years from diabetes has no reliable sensation left to lose, so the pulse, the color, the warmth and the comparison with the other foot carry more weight. In all of these patients the trend across repeated examinations is worth more than any single finding, and referring earlier than the rule suggests is never wrong.

Referral does not begin when everything else has failed, and in this subject it begins at the moment a threat to the limb is suspected. The findings that demand an urgent destination are a limb that has lost its pulse, a limb that has become pale and cold, a new numbness or a lost movement, pain that is out of proportion to the injury or increasing under a splint, an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, and any injury in which the vessels or the nerves are known to be involved. The receiving facility needs imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, and the clinician who accepts the patient is told which of these findings is present rather than only that the patient is coming. The emergency medical service is contacted, the transfer is arranged through the local system, and the time at which the limb was last known to be well is stated plainly. A responder who is unsure whether a finding is serious refers and describes it rather than deciding alone, because a transfer that turns out to be unnecessary costs far less than a limb that might have been saved. Whether the call is made by a nurse or by a physician is decided by the local protocol.

Definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends, traction holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation holds the position while the bone heals, and every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught within the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations an attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, because force applied to a limb whose vessels are already compromised removes the last of its supply. The technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training and never to a book.

The provider level is named for every act in this chapter, and the law of the country in which the listener works decides the rest. The lay first aider supports the limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm, observes the color, the warmth, the movement and the feeling of the hand or the foot, and reports any change. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician or paramedic perform and record the examination within the procedures their service authorizes, and apply splints only within their equipment and their protocol. The nurse repeats the examination and escalates to the physician without delay. The physician examines, orders imaging and decides on analgesia and on the urgency of transfer, while the orthopedic surgeon and, where a vessel is involved, the vascular surgeon provide the definitive care. Authorization, equipment and protocol decide what each of these people may do.

To summarize, the neurovascular examination is done before any intervention and repeated after every intervention, and it looks at pulse, color, warmth, capillary refill, sensation, movement and pain on the injured limb and on the other one, in the same order every time. A pulse that is present does not exclude a compartment syndrome, and a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, so the findings are written on the patient and not only in the notes, with the time beside them. The changes that stop a responder are a lost pulse, a limb that turns pale and cold, a new numbness, a movement that has gone and pain that increases instead of settling. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and a constricting bandage, splint or cast is released only by someone the local protocol authorizes. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, no drug, dose or route is given in this course, and a limb with a suspected compartment syndrome is not elevated above the level of the heart. The provider level is named for every act, the patient is kept warm, and when the limb is threatened the clinician and the receiving facility are told at once, because time is muscle.

# Chapter 7 — Principles of Immobilization

Immobilization is the act of holding an injured part still, and in the sequence this course follows it comes after the neurovascular examination and before imaging. The whole order runs from assessment to stabilization, to the neurovascular examination, to immobilization, to imaging, to reassessment, and then to referral or to definitive treatment, and each step exists to protect the ones that follow. A limb that is held still cannot be moved by the patient, by the stretcher, by the vehicle or by the hands of the next person who touches it, and that single fact prevents a great deal of harm. Immobilization is also the step that most easily becomes a second injury, because a splint is a device applied by hand to a limb that is already damaged. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Immobilization has four purposes, and a responder who knows them can improvise when the correct device is not there. The first is to prevent movement at the fracture itself, because the broken ends are the source of most of the damage that follows. The second is to protect the vessels and the nerves that run close to the bone, because those structures are injured by movement rather than by the original force alone. The third is to reduce pain, which is part of the treatment of the injury and not a comfort to be postponed until the end. The fourth is to limit bleeding, because every fracture bleeds and movement keeps the bleeding alive. Each of the four is a reason, and a rule that arrives with a reason attached is a rule that survives a difficult night.

A fracture is not a clean cut. The broken ends are irregular, and the sharp points of bone that appear on a radiograph are hard enough to cut whatever they are pressed against, which includes muscle, fascia, vessels and nerves. Every time the limb is moved, those ends travel through the tissues around them, and the damage is done a second time by hands that meant only to help. Movement can also push a bone end through the skin and turn a closed fracture into an open one, which changes the operation, the antibiotics and the risk of infection for the patient. A clot that has formed between the ends can be disturbed by movement, and bleeding that had stopped begins again. This is why the responder supports rather than examines, and why the first splint is applied to the position in which the limb was found.

Nerves and blood vessels travel along the surface of the bone rather than through the center of the limb, and they pass through places where there is very little room to spare. A break above the elbow can injure the vessel that supplies the forearm, a break behind the knee can injure the vessel that supplies the leg, and the nerves of the arm and the leg lie against the bone in the same exposed way, so the limb may look acceptable while a vessel is kinked or a nerve is stretched. A splint that holds the limb in the position found keeps those structures where they are, and a splint that pulls the limb into a different shape may be the force that tears them. Protecting the vessels and the nerves is therefore the second purpose of immobilization, and it is the one most easily defeated by trying too hard.

Pain is not only a symptom to be noted and set aside. It produces a reflex tightening of the muscles around the injury, that spasm pulls on the broken ends, and the movement increases the pain, so the limb enters a cycle that feeds itself. A limb held still breaks that cycle, and the relief of pain lowers the pulse and the demand on a heart that may already be struggling. Reducing pain is therefore part of the treatment of the injury. Nothing in this chapter allows a responder to give a drug, and where pain relief is needed, the substance, the amount and the route belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol.

Every fracture bleeds into the tissues around it, and the blood that collects forms the hematoma that is the first stage of healing rather than a complication to be drained. That collection also raises the pressure inside the limb, and the rising pressure is part of what slows the bleeding, so a clot knocked loose does more than make the limb swell again. Bleeding continues while the ends move against each other, and in a break of the thigh bone the amount lost can threaten the circulation, with a figure offered in teaching as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Immobilization limits that loss, which is why a swollen limb is splinted early rather than watched. A closed fracture can therefore cause shock without a drop of blood on the skin.

The rule that governs every splint in this course is that the limb is immobilized in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field. The reason is that vessels and nerves lie against the bone, and a piece of bone sitting near a vessel may be the only thing holding a tear closed. Straightening the limb also turns the soft tissue injury into a fresh one, and it can convert a closed fracture into an open wound on the way to the vehicle. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow, with a rolled blanket or with whatever is at hand, and keeps it in the shape it already has. The trained first responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician and the orthopedic surgeon may later correct the position in a facility with imaging and with an operating room available.

A splint that covers only the fracture does not immobilize the fracture, because a long bone is moved by the joint at each end. The joint above the injury and the joint below it are held as well, because it is easy to forget them when the fracture is the only thing in view. The elbow moves the forearm and the wrist moves the hand, so an injury of the forearm is splinted with the elbow and the wrist included, while a splint for the lower limb reaches from well above the knee to below the ankle where the equipment and the local protocol allow it, because the knee and the hip control the thigh bone. Including both joints also protects the joint surfaces, which can be injured by the leverage of a bone that is still free to swing. There are limits, since in some injuries the two joints lie far apart or the position is so painful that a shorter splint is the safer choice, and the paramedic and the emergency medical technician decide within the procedures their service authorizes.

Padding is the part of immobilization that is most often skipped and most often regretted, because a splint presses on the limb where the bone lies just beneath the skin and the skin of an injured limb tolerates that pressure poorly. The pressure of an unpadded device can injure a nerve where it crosses a bony prominence, and the injury is silent at first because the patient may not be able to feel it. Padding spreads the load over a wider area, softens the edge of the device, takes up the small changes in swelling that follow an injury, and absorbs the sweat and the blood that would otherwise stiffen a bandage into a hard ring. It is placed over the bony prominences, over the joints within the splint and along the line of the device, and soft material is folded to a thickness that the local protocol describes, with any figure offered as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline. The reason for padding is therefore not comfort but the prevention of a second injury caused by the treatment.

The splint is then secured firmly enough to hold and not so firmly that it becomes a band around the limb.
