A bandage can stop the flow through the smallest vessels long before it stops a pulse at the wrist or the ankle, and a device tightened until the limb below it changes color has been tightened beyond its purpose. After the splint is applied the limb is checked again, and the check is repeated at intervals because swelling changes the fit. Every service teaches a rhythm for that check, with a figure such as every 15 minutes offered as an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The observations are the same ones made before the splint was applied, and a limb that becomes cooler, paler, more numb or more painful after a splint has been applied has been made worse by the splint.

The material of a splint matters far less than the principle, and that is the most useful thing a listener can carry into a place where nothing is stocked. A rigid device holds best, so a padded board, a rolled newspaper or a walking stick can serve a limb, while a pillow or a folded blanket serves a limb that must be kept in a bent position. A commercial splint is easier to secure, but it still needs padding and checking, and an unfamiliar device should not be used for the first time on a patient. An improvised splint is checked more often because it shifts and because its edges were not designed for skin, and the limb is never straightened to fit the device. An air splint and a vacuum splint mold themselves to the limb and are applied by trained responders within the procedures their service authorizes. A traction splint applies a gentle continuous pull along the line of the limb and is used mainly for an injury of the thigh bone, and it is applied only by a provider trained and authorized in its use, since a device that pulls the wrong way adds harm.

For an injury of the arm or the hand, the familiar arrangement is a sling that supports the forearm with the elbow bent, together with a swathe that binds the arm to the chest so that the shoulder cannot swing. The reason for both is that a sling alone leaves the shoulder free, and the shoulder is the joint above the injury. The hand is positioned so that the fingers point slightly upward where the injury and the local protocol allow it, because a hand that hangs downward swells more, and swelling is the enemy of a limb in a splint. The lay first aider can apply a sling and a swathe, and the trained responder checks the pulse, the color and the sensation in the fingers after doing so. A bandage applied in a crossing pattern is used for some injuries near the collarbone, and applying it correctly is a skill learned under supervision rather than from a description.

The lower limb presents a different problem because it has to carry weight and because the thigh bone is surrounded by powerful muscles that pull on the broken ends. When no splint is available, the injured leg can be bound to the uninjured leg, with padding between the knees and between the ankles, so that the healthy limb becomes the splint and the two legs move as one unit. That binding must be done carefully, because the uninjured leg must not be pulled into an awkward position, and the trained responder or the paramedic may instead choose a rigid splint or a traction device within the procedures the service authorizes. An injury of the hip or of the thigh bone is not treated by binding the legs together where a traction device and a trained provider are available, and the local protocol decides. Nothing here authorizes any provider to pull on a limb to make it straight.

An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until it has been cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and immobilization of the spine is a team task rather than an individual one. A cervical collar, head blocks and a rigid board are applied by trained responders and paramedics who have practiced the procedure, and the way the patient is turned and lifted is decided by the team leader according to the local protocol. The lay first aider does not move such a patient unless the scene is unsafe, and even then the movement is kept to the minimum that the danger requires. Neither walking after a collision nor the absence of pain clears the spine. The reason for the caution is that the spinal cord lies within a canal that a displaced vertebra can narrow, and a cord that is injured is injured permanently.

Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and immobilization puts a patient on the ground and keeps him or her there for as long as the splinting takes. A patient who is losing blood tolerates cold badly, because cold worsens the clotting problem and drives the circulation away from the skin, and a cold patient is harder to assess at every step. Wet clothing is removed where the situation allows it and replaced with covering, and the patient is insulated from the ground as well as from the air, since the ground takes heat away faster than the air does. The lay first aider keeps the patient warm with whatever is at hand, and the trained responder carries the means to do it properly. Every figure about temperature or about time is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

No intervention in this chapter may be performed before the neurovascular status of the limb has been examined and written down. The examination is a short set of observations that a trained responder repeats in the same order every time, so that two records can be compared: the skin is inspected for color and temperature, the pulse is felt beyond the injury, a nail is pressed briefly and the color watched as it returns, and the patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes and to report what is felt. Sensation is compared from one side to the other, and any numbness, any tingling and any movement lost since the previous check are recorded in the words the patient uses where that is possible. The findings are entered before a splint is applied and again after it is applied, because an observation that was not written down cannot be attributed afterwards. The lay first aider can report color, warmth and whether the patient can move and feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse, the physician or the orthopedic surgeon according to the setting.

Reassessment follows every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the previous record, and it is the comparison that carries the value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint is checked for tightness, for slippage, for wet padding and for pressure at its edges. A patient who says the limb feels worse after a splint has given the most useful answer in the whole examination, and that answer is not to be argued with. The responder who finds a change stops the plan that was being followed and reports it before continuing. A reassessment without a written comparison is a memory, and memory fails at the end of a long shift.

Compartment syndrome is the complication this course fears most, and an immobilized limb is one of the settings in which it develops. A compartment is a closed space bounded by bone and fascia, and it holds muscle, nerves and vessels with very little room, so bleeding or swelling inside it raises the pressure on everything within. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that has become tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder. A pulse that is still present does not exclude the diagnosis, and pulselessness is a late sign that must never be awaited. When the condition is suspected, any constricting bandage or splint is loosened or released within the limits of local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Imaging comes after immobilization, and the order matters because a limb that is still free to move will move while it is being positioned for a picture. A radiograph is usually the first study and is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons, muscle and the spinal cord. Either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done, and the decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the care of the patient, while the lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined again after the picture has been taken.

A splint applied in the field is not taken off until someone qualified to replace it decides that it should be, because the limb has just been carried through a journey and a removal repeats the injury. Where an image of the limb is required, the device is removed by the team that will put it back, or the study is arranged so that it stays in place. A cast, a brace and surgical fixation are the definitive forms of immobilization, and each is chosen by the orthopedic surgeon or by the treating physician according to the injury, the swelling and the plan for the bone. Casting is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique of it belongs to supervised clinical training rather than to a chapter of a book. A cast applied while the limb is still swelling can become a band that stops the circulation, so it is checked by the clinician who applied it, and the listener should not attempt any of these treatments.

Reduction means restoring the position of the bone ends, and traction means holding them in line with a gentle continuous pull while the bone heals or until an operation is possible. Both change the shape of the limb, and both are performed by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon with imaging, with analgesia decided by the treating team and with the option of an operating room. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught within the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when the responder lacks the training and the equipment or an earlier attempt has already failed, because in each of those situations an attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot be repaired. Force is not a technique, and resistance is a signal to stop rather than a problem to overcome. The lay first aider never performs a reduction, and the trained responder supports and transports.

Referral is the last step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a diminished or absent pulse, a loss of sensation or movement, a dislocation, a fracture that enters a joint, heavy contamination of a wound, an unstable injury of the pelvis, or a break in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The urgency is decided by the findings rather than by the name of the diagnosis, and the neurovascular findings are what make a referral immediate. The record travels with the patient and is spoken in a fixed order, from the time of the injury and the mechanism, through the position in which the limb was found, to the findings before and after every intervention. The trained responder and the paramedic pass those findings to the receiving facility while the transport is being arranged, and a nurse or a physician who receives such a patient repeats the examination rather than trusting a report.

Some patients are immobilized with more care than others, and a sign that is reliable in a healthy adult may be absent in them. The bone of a child is more elastic than the bone of an adult, and it has a growth region near each end that can be injured without the bone breaking, so an injury that looks minor and leaves a child unwilling to use a limb deserves the same caution as an obvious break. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break a wrist or a hip in a fall from standing height, and the fracture may hurt far less than its severity suggests, while the skin of that patient tolerates the pressure of a splint poorly. A patient with diabetes or with an established neuropathy may not feel a splint pressing on the foot, so the absence of pain proves nothing, and a patient who is confused, sedated or unable to speak cannot report numbness at all. Such patients are checked by looking rather than by asking, and a swollen limb inside a cast applied before the swelling peaked is watched with particular care by the clinician responsible.

An illustration may help, and it is constructed for teaching rather than drawn from any patient. A middle-aged walker slips on wet ground and lands with the weight of the body on one hand; the wrist is bent, the skin is unbroken, and the fingers can be moved but the patient says the hand feels strange. The first aider supports the forearm with both hands in the position found, keeps the wrist as it lies, does not attempt to straighten it, and covers the limb to keep the patient warm. The trained responder records the color, the warmth, the pulse at the wrist and the sensation in the fingers, applies a padded splint that includes the wrist and the elbow, secures it firmly without making it a band, and then repeats the same observations. The hand is supported so that it does not hang down, and the receiving clinician is told what the findings were before the splint and after it.

Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. The scope of practice differs between countries and between services within one country, and an act that a paramedic performs freely may be reserved to a physician elsewhere, so a listener confirms the local rule rather than borrowing one from another system. Courses that teach immobilization assess the learner on a real device, with feedback on padding, on the joints included and on the observations made before and after. A responder who has not practiced the skill supports the limb in the position found and calls for someone who has. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

To summarize, immobilization holds an injured part still in order to prevent movement at the fracture, to protect the vessels and the nerves, to reduce pain and to limit bleeding, and it is applied in the position in which the limb was found. The sequence never changes, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the neurovascular findings are written down before any device is applied and again after every intervention, because a finding that was not recorded cannot be attributed afterwards. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, a splint includes the joint above and the joint below the injury, and the device is padded where it presses and secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band. Pain that increases, numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor, coolness or a limb that becomes tense and swollen means the splint is the problem, so the constricting part is released within local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not raised above the level of the heart and the patient is referred urgently, since time is muscle. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and they are not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear or when an earlier attempt has failed. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, every act is named with the provider level permitted to perform it, and where this chapter mentions a time or a distance it offers an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

# Chapter 8 — Splinting in Practice

Splinting is not the act of tying a device to a limb but the act of deciding what must be held still and who is qualified to hold it. A splint is the simplest life-saving tool in musculoskeletal care, and it is also the tool most often applied badly, because it looks easy and the responder is in a hurry. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone held alone can still be swung by the joint at either end. Its purposes are few and each is a reason: to reduce pain, to limit further displacement, to protect the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone, to slow bleeding into the tissues, and to keep a closed injury from becoming an open one. Pain is not a side issue, because a patient in severe pain breathes badly, moves badly and is harder to assess. A splint also protects an open wound from further contamination and protects the limb from the ground and from the hands of those who move the patient. What a splint does not do is heal, and it never replaces the examination that must come before it.

Whatever material is chosen, the same principles govern its use, and they were learned long before any commercial device existed. The limb is splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Padding goes where the device presses on bone, which means the ankle bones, the heel, the shin, the knee, the elbow, the wrist and the fingers. The device is secured firmly enough to hold the limb without acting as a band that stops the circulation, and a splint that is loose is as useless as one that is too tight. The joints above and below the injury are included, because a splint that stops at the fracture leaves the fracture free to move.

Assessment comes before any material is opened, and it begins with the scene, the mechanism, the time of injury and the condition of the patient rather than with the limb. The primary survey is performed first and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because life comes before limb when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands. The lay first aider looks for danger, calls for help and does not move a patient whose spine may be injured. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician or paramedic record the mechanism and the position in which the limb was found. The nurse and the physician add the history that changes the picture, including illness and medicine that weakens bone. A patient whose bone is fragile may break it in a fall that would leave another person unhurt, so the threshold for immobilization is lower in that patient.

Stabilization is the step between assessment and immobilization, and in the field it means support, warmth and restraint rather than a device. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with direct pressure, and an open wound is covered with a sterile dressing without being explored, because blind exploration adds harm and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. An embedded object is left in place and padded on either side, because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound. The limb is supported with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand until the splint is ready, and a patient with a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and is moved only by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Cold is a complication of trauma, so wet clothing is replaced and the patient is insulated from the ground, from metal and from the wind. Stabilization is performed by the lay first aider with the hands, by the trained responder with the equipment the service authorizes, and by the clinician with the resources of the facility.

The neurovascular examination is performed before the splint is applied and repeated after it, and this rule is the spine of the whole subject. The examiner looks at the color and warmth of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses a nail to watch the color return, and compares both sides. Sensation is tested and described in the words of the patient as far as possible, and the patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes, whichever lies beyond the injury. Movement that was present a moment ago and is now lost is a finding of the greatest importance, and so are numbness, tingling and pain out of proportion to the injury. The result is written before the splint goes on and again after it is secured, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. The lay first aider watches color, warmth and movement, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the clinician.

Commercially made splints are what most responders reach for first, and they fall into a few families that behave differently. A malleable padded splint is a strip of metal covered in foam that is bent to the shape of a limb and held with straps, and it suits the forearm, the wrist and the hand. A vacuum splint is a soft sleeve filled with beads that becomes rigid when the air is drawn out, and it molds to the limb and spreads pressure better than a hard device. A traction splint applies a gentle continuous pull to the leg, and it is used by the emergency medical technician or paramedic only where the service trains and authorizes it, with the technique learned under supervision and not from a book. A commercial splint is fast and familiar, but every one of them can be applied too tightly and must be checked after it is in place.

What a commercial splint does badly is worth saying as plainly as what it does well. It is sized for an average limb, so it is short on a tall patient and loose on a thin one, and a splint that does not reach beyond the joints above and below the injury allows the fracture to move. The metal strip can kink at a pressure point, and the foam can hide a fold in the skin until a blister or an ulcer has formed. The device is unavailable when the service has run out, when the vehicle is far away, or when a passerby finds the patient with nothing in hand. A traction splint demands training, a second pair of hands and attention to the skin and the nerves, and it is not used when the pelvis or the hip may be injured. A commercial splint has a place, but it is not a substitute for judgment, and the responder who has none must know what to do with folded cardboard and a strip of cloth.

A padded board is a rigid straight splint, and its value comes from that rigidity. A wooden board, a length of stiff cardboard or a folded magazine can each hold a limb against movement. The board is wrapped in cloth or foam so that it does not press directly on bone, and it is long enough to span the joints above and below the injury. It is at its best for the forearm, where a straight support along the limb is exactly what the injury needs, and at its worst where a limb must be held bent, as at the elbow or the knee. A rigid splint concentrates pressure at its ends, so the padding is thickest there and the skin is inspected when the device is removed. A board tied with a hard knot can damage the tissues beneath it, so the knot is tied over padding away from the injured part, and the tightness is checked by whoever applied it.

The sling and the swathe are the oldest tools in this subject and still among the most useful. A triangular bandage or a length of cloth supports the forearm against the chest, and a second band around the chest and the arm holds the arm against the body, and the pair together is a sling and swathe. It is at its best for the shoulder girdle, the collarbone, the upper arm and the elbow, where the chest of the patient is the splint and the cloth only keeps the limb against it. It does badly wherever the bone must be held in exact alignment, because it allows the arm to rotate and to slide, and it does badly in a patient who must be lifted, because the band can slip under the weight. The band around the chest must not press on the neck or the opposite armpit, and the hand stays visible so that its color can be watched. A ring or a watch on the injured hand is removed if it comes off easily, because swelling makes it a constriction later.

A pillow is not a splint in the strict sense, and it is one of the most useful things a responder can place under an injured limb. It supports the limb along its length, it conforms to the shape of the body instead of fighting it, and it is soft enough that it cannot cut into the skin. It is at its best for the lower leg, the ankle, the heel and the bent knee, and for the elbow when the arm is held across the body. It does badly because it is compressible and shifts as the patient is moved, so a pillow alone holds nothing still unless it is bound in place. It becomes flat and wet in the rain, and a saturated pillow no longer supports and now conducts cold. It is not a splint for a fracture of the thigh bone, where the muscle around the bone can move the fragments against any soft support.

A rolled blanket or a folded coat can be a soft bolster under a limb or a rigid body when it is rolled tightly and bound. Rolled tightly, it becomes a firm cylinder that is placed along the side of a limb and tied to it. Used as a bolster, it supports a limb in the position found and keeps it from resting on the ground. It is at its best where a rigid device is not available, where the limb needs support rather than grip, and where the pelvis or a second injured limb must be protected from pressure. It does badly because it is bulky, because it absorbs water and blood, and because it loosens as its fibers settle, so it is rechecked more often than a commercial splint. A blanket roll that has been on the ground is contaminated and is not placed against an open wound.

Binding an injured limb to its neighbor is the oldest improvisation in the field and the one that carries the most conditions. A fractured finger is strapped to the finger beside it over a thin layer of padding. The lower leg can be bound to the other leg with padding between the knees and the ankles, which turns two limbs into one rigid unit, and the padding matters because skin against skin produces chafing, sweat and a wound of its own. The method is never used when the other limb is also injured, when the pelvis or the thigh bone may be broken, or when the limbs are unequal in length. It does badly because the swelling of one limb presses on the other and because the patient cannot be moved without moving both. This method belongs to the trained first responder or to the emergency medical technician or paramedic, while the lay first aider waits for help.

Padding is not a comfort but a part of the treatment, because the tissue that dies under a splint dies quietly. The points at greatest risk are those where bone lies just beneath the skin, such as the ankle bones, the heel, the shin, the kneecap, the elbow, the wrist and the knuckles. Cloth, foam, a folded towel or a spare garment can each be used, and it is laid smooth, with no folds and no knots beneath the limb. The padding is thick enough that a finger can slide between the splint and the skin at every point, and that is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the thickness of padding and the frequency of checks differ between services. A wet or blood-soaked pad is replaced, because it loses its cushioning and holds cold against the skin. Any red mark, blister or break in the skin is recorded and reported.

Securing the splint is where most of the avoidable harm occurs, so the materials and the order in which they are used deserve attention. A bandage, a length of cloth, a strip of tape or the straps that came with the device are all acceptable, and each is applied over the padding and not over bare skin. The bands are placed above and below the injury rather than across the fracture, and they are tied firmly enough to hold without pressing the soft tissues. Knots are tied over padding and away from the injured part, with a soft pad under every knot, because a knot over a bone or a nerve can injure it. Tape is not applied directly to fragile skin, and it is never wrapped in a complete circle that could tighten as the limb swells. Once secured, the limb is not moved in order to test the splint, because the test itself can displace the fracture.

An open fracture changes the task from support to protection, and the splint is built around the wound rather than over it. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, and the neurovascular status is recorded before anything else is done. An embedded object is left where it lies and is stabilized with padding on either side so that the splint does not press it deeper, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound. The splint is then applied as for a closed injury, with the dressing left undisturbed and an opening kept clear if the local protocol requires one. No responder irrigates, explores or closes the wound, and no responder removes a foreign body, because definitive care belongs to the operating room and to the surgeon. The lay first aider covers the wound and supports the limb, the trained responder immobilizes and arranges urgent transfer, and the nurse prepares for the care that follows.

Reassessment after the splint is applied is not a courtesy but the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record made before the splint, and it is the comparison rather than any single measurement that carries the information. The examiner checks the color and warmth of the skin beyond the splint, the pulse, the return of color after a nail is pressed, sensation, the ability to move, and the pain described by the patient. The splint itself is checked for tightness, for slippage and for pressure at its edges, and the straps are loosened or retied within the limits of the responder's role if they have become too tight. Findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation are pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, a limb that becomes tense and swollen, and a pulse that was present and is now absent. The lay first aider reports any change at once, the trained responder repeats the examination and documents it, and the clinician decides what the change means.

A compartment syndrome is the complication this whole subject exists to prevent, and it can be caused by the injury or by the splint that was meant to help. The limb becomes tense and swollen, the pain is severe and out of proportion to the injury, and it increases when the patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes. A pulse that is still palpable at the wrist or the ankle does not exclude the diagnosis, because pressure inside the compartment can stop the flow through the smallest vessels while the large vessel continues to beat. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects it does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late. The constricting bandage, splint or cast is released by whoever is authorized to release it within the local protocol, and the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, because that lowers the pressure that keeps the tissue alive. The patient is kept warm and referred urgently, and the receiving team is told that the compartment is in question.

Imaging comes after immobilization in the sequence, and the order matters because a limb that is not yet supported will move again on the way to the imaging room. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions and including the joint above and the joint below so that a second injury is not missed. A splint commonly stays in place for the first image and is removed or opened by the clinician when the image is not adequate, and it is reapplied only after the neurovascular status has been recorded again. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues such as ligaments, tendons and muscle. Either study is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it, and only when it will change what is done. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides which study is needed.

Splinting in the field is a holding action, and definitive treatment begins where the transport ends. A cast or a brace holds the position of the bone while it heals, and both are applied by a clinician or by a technician trained and authorized to do it, with the technique learned under supervision and according to local protocol. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends and traction holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and neither is taught from a book in this course. A surgeon may hold the fragments with metal devices, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, and that decision belongs to the orthopedic surgeon. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations an attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and the splint has a place in both. The time and mechanism of the injury, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and the material that was used are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. The record names who applied the splint, what padding was used, how tight it was felt to be, and when it was last checked. A change in the condition of the patient is reported at once, and a change in the limb is reported in the words of the patient as far as possible. The lay first aider tells the responding team what was done and what has changed, and the trained responder gives a structured handover that includes the mechanism, the findings and the treatment given. The nurse and the physician repeat the neurovascular examination before and after any change to the splint, because the record is only useful if it is used.

Some patients cannot report what they feel, and in them the splint is checked more often and more carefully. A child may not describe tingling and may cry for reasons that have nothing to do with the limb, and the bone of a child bends before it breaks, so the injury may be less obvious than the pain suggests. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break a wrist or a hip in a fall from standing height, and the fracture may be far less painful than its severity implies. A patient who is unconscious, intoxicated, sedated or living with a condition that numbs the feet cannot be asked whether the fingers are tingling, so the examiner relies on color, warmth, pulse and swelling. A patient whose nerve supply is already damaged may have no feeling to lose and no pulse to compare, which makes the first record more valuable and not less. In all of these patients the threshold for immobilization and for referral is lower, while the decisions about imaging and treatment remain with the clinician.

Splinting does not end when the last strap is tied, because the patient may wait and travel for a long time before a clinician sees the limb. The check of color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain is repeated at intervals, and the interval named in any service is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than a rule fixed in this course. The patient is kept warm throughout, because cold makes the vessels narrow and the tissues less able to survive a period of poor flow, and a splint that has become wet is replaced. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart while a compartment syndrome is suspected, and the patient is not left alone with a tight splint. If travel is long, the responders agree in advance who will check the limb and who will be told if something changes. Any change that suggests the circulation or the nerves are failing is escalated at once.

Because the same injury is met by many providers, the scope of practice deserves stating once more in the terms of this subject. The lay first aider supports the limb, keeps the patient warm, covers an open wound and calls for help, and does not straighten, pull, reduce or explore. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician or paramedic apply the splints, the straps and the padding their service authorizes, record the neurovascular status before and after, and do nothing the protocol does not permit. The nurse checks the limb, documents the findings, prepares the materials and reports any deterioration to the physician. The physician assesses the patient, orders imaging, provides analgesia and the other treatment the local protocol allows, and refers the patient when the injury exceeds what the facility can safely treat. The orthopedic surgeon performs the reduction, the traction when it is indicated, the casting and the surgical fixation, and those acts are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. The substance, the amount, the route and the frequency of any analgesia are decided by the prescriber under the local protocol, and this course names none of them, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from a book. What the responder can do is describe the pain, its site, its severity, what makes it worse and what makes it better, and report a change at once.

To summarize, a splint holds an injured limb still, protects the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone, reduces pain, and keeps a closed injury from becoming an open one, and it is chosen from what is available rather than from what is ideal. The commercial splint, the padded board, the sling and swathe, the pillow, the rolled blanket and the limb bound to its neighbor each have a place and each have a failure, and all are judged by the same rules, which are to pad the points where bone lies near the skin, to include the joints above and below the injury, and to secure the device firmly without stopping the circulation. The neurovascular status is examined and recorded before the splint is applied and again afterwards, and the examination is repeated on every journey and after every change, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no book teaches them. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and any limb that becomes tense, painful out of proportion to the injury, numb or pale is escalated at once, because time is muscle. Whoever applies a splint acts within a named scope of practice, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 9 — Patient Handling and Transport

Moving a patient is a treatment rather than a pause between treatments, and it deserves the same care as any other intervention in this course. A patient dragged by the shoulders, rolled by one pair of hands, or lifted by the arm of the injured side can reach the hospital with an injury that no longer matches the one assessed at the scene. Handling therefore runs through the sequence every chapter of this course follows, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter explains what each device and each maneuver is for, who may perform it and what can go wrong, rather than teaching the technique, because every technique named here is learned on a course, on a model and under supervision. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has cleared it, and that rule governs every lift, roll and transfer described here. Clearing the spine is not a single test but a judgment that combines the mechanism of injury, what the patient feels and can move, what the examination shows and what the imaging shows, and it is made by a clinician working within a defined protocol. A patient may have an unstable spine and still be awake, talking and free of pain, so an examination that finds nothing is not the same as an examination that excludes the injury. Spinal precautions are applied on the basis of the mechanism and of what the patient reports, and they are removed only by the person the local protocol authorizes to remove them. The lay first aider and the trained first responder do not clear a spine, the nurse and the physician clear it only as their protocol allows, and no responder clears it because the patient asks to sit up.

Assessment comes before any pair of hands touches the patient, and it begins with the scene rather than with the body. Traffic, fire, electricity and unstable debris are removed or avoided before the responder commits, and personal protective equipment is worn for every patient, because an injured responder becomes a second patient. The number of patients, the mechanism of injury, the time that has passed and the level of consciousness are noted, and then the primary survey proceeds in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Only when the patient is stable enough to tolerate it does the assessment turn to the limbs, which are examined by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move them, never by forcing them. The lay first aider observes and reports, the trained first responder and the emergency medical technician assess within the procedures their service authorizes, and the clinician interprets what the findings mean.

The first decision in handling is whether the patient needs to be moved at all, because the safest place for an unstable injury is usually the position in which it was found. Movement is justified when there is a hazard that cannot be removed, when the airway cannot be protected where the patient lies, when a qualified team has decided that care requires a transfer, or when the space is needed for a patient who is more seriously injured. When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, the principle that decides is that life comes before limb, because a brain and a heart wait for nobody while a limb can wait for minutes. A patient lying on a floor with hands holding the head and the pelvis still is safer than the same patient halfway through an unnecessary move. The lay first aider moves a patient only to escape immediate danger, the trained responder moves within the procedures the service authorizes, and the decision to move for a medical reason belongs to the clinician directing the care.

Stabilization in the field is a small set of acts, and the first of them is restraint, which means holding the injured part still rather than pulling it into a better position. The trained responder supports the head in the position found, holds the pelvis square, or takes the weight of the injured limb with both hands, and keeps that hold until a device has taken over the work. A deformed limb is splinted as it lies and is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what was still intact. Holding is tiring, so the holders are exchanged one at a time, and the new holder takes the load before the old one releases it. The lay first aider supports with whatever is at hand and keeps the patient warm, while formal spinal restraint is a skill of the trained responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic.

The neurovascular examination is performed before the patient is moved and repeated after every movement, and its result is recorded on both occasions. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks about numbness, tingling and weakness. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and the record uses the words the patient used, because a note that says numb tells the next clinician less than a note that says where the numbness begins. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent turns the move into an emergency. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, the trained responder performs the formal examination, and the interpretation belongs to the clinician.

No single responder performs a manual handling technique alone, and this is a rule about physics and about attribution rather than about etiquette. An unstable spine moves as a unit only if the people holding it move as a unit, so a roll, a lift onto a device and a transfer between surfaces all require a team whose members know their roles before the first count. The team has one leader who gives the commands, one person at the head who owns the alignment of the neck, and further pairs of hands along the body, and nobody adds a pull that was not part of the plan. The number of people needed depends on the size of the patient, the equipment and the local protocol, and any figure offered for that is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the procedure of the service. The lay first aider calls for help rather than attempting a roll, the trained first responder joins a team without commanding it, and the emergency medical technician and the paramedic lead the move within their procedures.

The log roll is a way of turning a patient onto the side as a single unit, so that the back can be examined, a device can be placed beneath the body, or a blocked airway can be cleared. What the maneuver is meant to achieve is a turn in which the head, the shoulders, the pelvis and the legs move together, and what it produces when it is done badly is a twist between two parts of the spine, which is the movement the spine tolerates least. The head holder keeps the neck in line with the body throughout, the leader controls the count, and the patient is turned only as far as the task requires and for no longer. A log roll does not move a patient across a room, and it is not attempted on a patient who is fighting the hands that hold the neck. If the patient resists, if a limb cannot move with the body, or if the holders lose their alignment, the leader stops the maneuver and the team returns the patient to the position found, because resistance and a complication are both signals to stop.

The scoop stretcher is a device that separates into two halves, each of which slides under the patient from one side, and the halves are then locked together so that the patient can be lifted without being rolled. It is chosen when a patient found on the ground must be raised onto a stretcher with as little movement of the trunk as possible, and it suits a suspected injury of the pelvis or the hip, where turning can increase bleeding inside the pelvis. The halves are placed by a team that keeps the spine aligned by hand, the locking points are checked before the lift, and the skin is inspected where the device meets the body, because a device that presses on skin causes an injury of its own. The scoop stretcher is applied by the trained responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the choice between it and a simple lift belongs to whoever is leading the move.

The long board is a rigid flat device whose greatest value lies in freeing a patient from a confined space such as a vehicle, so its purpose belongs to the moment of extrication rather than to the journey that follows. A hard surface that does not give transmits every bump of the road to the body, and the pressure it applies to the skin of the back, the heels and the head can cause an injury within a short time, so practice differs between services and countries about how long a patient is carried on one. Some services remove the board as soon as the patient is on a padded stretcher and the spine has been assessed, while others transport on it, and the answer belongs to the current guideline and the local protocol. The board is applied by the trained responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic as part of a coordinated move with the neck held, and the lay first aider never places one.

The transfer from the ground to the stretcher and from the stretcher into the vehicle is the part of the journey in which the most injuries are caused by handling. It is planned aloud before it begins, so that every pair of hands knows which part of the body it owns and where the patient is going. The injured part is supported by the responder who has held it from the start, and the fractured bone is never used as a handle, because the bone is a lever and the soft tissues attached to it take the strain. Where a slide is possible, the patient is moved along the surface rather than above it, since a slide needs fewer hands and moves the spine less than a lift. The patient who is confused, frightened or intoxicated is the patient most likely to be harmed by the hands that are trying to help, so that patient is told what is about to happen and moved with enough people to hold the body securely. The leader watches the patient rather than the device and stops the move the moment the alignment is lost, the patient reports new pain, or a strap or a lock is found to be undone.

A patient trapped in a vehicle presents the clearest example of a decision made for the patient rather than for the injury. When there is fire, the risk of an explosion, rising water or a patient who is not breathing, the patient is removed as quickly as the trained responders can manage, and the spine is protected as well as the situation allows rather than perfectly. When there is no such hazard, the patient is stabilized where the patient lies, the engine is switched off, the neck is held, and the extrication proceeds as a planned move with the equipment the service carries. Rapid extrication is a technique of the emergency medical technician and the paramedic, performed within the procedures their service authorizes and learned in supervised training, and it is not a technique a listener can safely assemble from a description.

An open injury changes the handling of a patient without changing the sequence of care. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by pressure around the wound rather than over the bone ends, the neurovascular status is recorded, and the limb is immobilized in the position found. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the object may be pressing on a torn vessel and the bone may be the only thing holding the wound closed. An open wound is never explored blindly, since the exploration adds contamination, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. The lay first aider covers the wound with the cleanest material available, the trained responder dresses it with the supplies the service carries, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what is done about it in the hospital.

Immobilization during handling means that the injured part, together with the joints above and below it, is prevented from moving while the patient is transferred, and the device is chosen to fit the injury rather than the other way around. A pelvic binder is a device that encircles the pelvis to reduce its volume and to limit movement of the broken ring, and it is applied by responders trained and authorized to apply it, in the place and in the manner the local protocol specifies. A traction splint applies a gentle continuous pull to the leg, and it is described here only in terms of what it is meant to achieve, which is to hold the thigh in line and to reduce movement of the broken ends against each other, because its application is a supervised skill and is not taught from a book. Splinting with a padded board or a sling is the work of the trained responder and the paramedic within their procedures, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required.

A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, and the rule is repeated here because handling is the moment at which the temptation is greatest. Pulling a limb straight may convert a closed fracture into an open one, may tear a vessel or a nerve that was intact, and may release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. Reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, and traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and neither is taught as a technique in this course. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

Some patients change the handling without changing the sequence, and the responder adjusts the threshold rather than the order of the steps. A child is not a small adult, because the head is large in proportion to the body and a device sized for an adult will not hold a small body in line, so equipment and technique are chosen for the size of the patient. An older adult brings thin skin that tears under shear, bone that is fragile and breaks under a hand that grips a rib cage in order to lift, and a stiff spine that will not produce a straight line when a flexible neck is assumed. A pregnant patient is two patients for the purpose of assessment and one patient for the purpose of handling, so the position in which she is carried is decided by the clinician or by the protocol of the service. In all of these patients the lay first aider keeps the patient warm and still and calls for help, while the decisions about imaging and about treatment belong to the clinician.

Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and a patient lying on the ground, uncovered for an examination or waiting in a vehicle loses heat faster than anyone expects. The patient is insulated from the ground, wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, a hat and blankets are used, and the temperature of the vehicle is set for the patient rather than for the crew. Exposure is necessary for the examination and for the transfer, but it is kept as brief as the task allows and the patient is covered again as soon as the hands have finished. Where a service names a temperature or a time for warming, that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the guideline in force and the protocol of the service, because such numbers differ between services and editions.

The vehicle is a treatment space, and it is prepared before the patient is placed in it. The stretcher is locked into its mount, the patient is secured with the straps the service provides, the equipment that may be needed on the way is within reach, and the attendant sits where the face of the patient and the monitor can be seen without unfastening anything. An unsecured patient is a moving mass in a sudden stop, so the injury can be completed by the journey rather than by the fall. Smooth driving is part of the care, which means that the driver avoids the hard braking and the sharp corner that a healthy passenger would not notice, and the attendant asks for a gentler route when the pain of the patient rises with every bump. The driver works within the law and the procedures of the service, and the decision to pass the nearest hospital for one that can treat the injury belongs to the paramedic or the clinician under the protocol in force.

Reassessment happens after every intervention, which in this chapter means after every movement, every application of a device and every transfer. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison rather than any single measurement that carries the information. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the device is checked for tightness and for pressure on the skin, and the record is written at the time rather than reconstructed at the end of the shift. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage, splint or cast to be released by someone authorized to release it, and the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart while the patient is kept warm and referred urgently.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and in the care of a patient who has been moved it has one further purpose, which is to show whether the spine or the pelvis was injured in the first place. A radiograph is usually the first study and is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues. Imaging is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it, the lay first aider never orders or interprets it, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed. An image does not clear a spine by itself, because that decision also depends on the mechanism, the examination and the patient, and it is made by the person the local protocol authorizes. The journey to the imaging room is itself a handling event, so the patient is transferred with the same plan and the same record of neurovascular findings before and after.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and for the patient who has just been moved it begins with the choice of destination. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, a serious injury of the pelvis or an unstable spine is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. That decision belongs to the clinician and to the receiving service under the local protocol, and the paramedic reports the findings on which the decision rests rather than making the choice alone. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, and each of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A surgeon may hold the fragments with metal devices, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, and the choice among these treatments belongs to the orthopedic surgeon who has examined the patient and seen the images.

The handover is part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and it is where the work of handling is either preserved or lost. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the patient and the limb were found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, the devices that were applied and by whom, and any change in the condition of the patient are spoken in a fixed order. It ends with the two things most often left out, which are the findings that remain uncertain and the acts that were not performed because they lay outside the scope of practice of the responder. A constructed illustration is a patient found on the ground, turned once to clear the airway, lifted onto a scoop stretcher and carried to the vehicle, and the useful handover says what was found before the turn, what changed after it and what has not yet been checked, offered as an illustration rather than as a description of any real patient. What is written is written in the same order as what is spoken, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one.

Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on colleagues, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. The lay first aider supports, covers, keeps the patient warm and calls for help; the trained first responder adds the acts the service trains and authorizes; the emergency medical technician and the paramedic carry out the moves, the devices and the transfers their procedures cover; and the physician and the orthopedic surgeon make the decisions that require a license. Nobody in that list performs a manual handling technique alone, and nobody performs an act outside the scope the law and the employer have given to the role. A responder stops when there is resistance, when the alignment is lost, when the pain of the patient changes, when a device does not fit, or when a complication appears, and calls for a higher level of care rather than forcing the move. The record is kept because a finding that was not written before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards, and the spine remains unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so.

To summarize, moving a patient is a treatment, and the safest place for an unstable injury is usually the position in which it was found. Assess the scene and the patient before touching anyone, stabilize by holding the injured part still, examine and record the neurovascular status before every movement and again after it, immobilize with a device that fits the injury, transfer only with a team and a plan, and reassess after each of those steps. Never straighten a deformed limb in the field, never remove an embedded object, never push exposed bone back into a wound, never explore an open wound blindly, and never perform a manual handling technique alone. The log roll, the scoop stretcher and the long board are tools for particular problems, used by a trained responder or a paramedic within the procedures the service authorizes, while the lay first aider supports, covers, keeps the patient warm and calls for help. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when vessels or nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when the training and the equipment are lacking. A patient who is cold, a patient whose pain is rising and a patient whose spine has not been cleared are all referred urgently, because the complication this course fears most is the one caused by the treatment. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 10 — Pain Assessment and Acute Pain Management

Pain is the complaint that brings most injured patients to care and the symptom a responder can act on, so it belongs inside the assessment of every injury. A fracture hurts because the broken ends move, because the periosteum is torn, because muscle goes into spasm and because crushed tissue bleeds, so pain is a reading of the injury itself. Relieving pain is part of treating the injury rather than a courtesy offered afterwards, because unrelieved pain changes what the body does and a patient whose pain is controlled is safer to examine, to move, to image and to hand over. This chapter follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Unrelieved acute pain is not only an experience but a set of bodily events that work against the patient. Pain raises the heart rate and the blood pressure, increases the work of the heart and raises the demand for oxygen when the circulation may already be failing. It makes breathing shallow and rapid, so the bases of the lungs are not filled and secretions are retained, which is one road to pneumonia after an injury that never touched the chest. It slows the emptying of the stomach, raises the risk of a clot in the leg because the patient will not move, and disturbs sleep when healing is most active. Pain also produces fear, and fear amplifies pain, so the two feed each other in a circle that immobilizes the patient further. Each of those effects is a reason to treat pain early rather than to wait for a diagnosis.

Pain is subjective, which means that only the patient can report it, and that report is the standard against which every other sign is judged. It is not one sensation but several at once, with a sharp part from torn tissue, a dull aching part from muscle spasm, a burning part when a nerve is involved, and an emotional part that depends on what the injury means to that person. Culture, age, an earlier experience of pain, the memory of a pain poorly treated, the fear of addiction and the wish not to be a burden all change what a patient says. A listener who hears the patient's own words learns more than a number can carry, because pain described as a tight band is a different problem from pain described as a knife. The part of the responder is to ask, to listen, to believe and to write it down.

In the sequence this course follows, pain is assessed inside the first step, which is assessment, and it never takes priority over the steps that keep a patient alive. The primary survey is remembered as ABCDE, for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and pain is addressed only as far as it interferes with those, because a patient whose airway is obstructed is not soothed first. Once the primary survey is complete, the assessment turns to the limb, and there the pain is examined as carefully as the deformity. The lay first aider may ask where it hurts and report the answer, while the trained responder, the nurse and the physician read the pain in the light of the mechanism of injury and the state of the patient. The order is fixed on purpose, because each step protects the next one.

The history of the pain is taken in a fixed order so that nothing is forgotten, and the questions are simple enough for the lay first aider to ask and to repeat. The first is when the pain began and how it has changed, because pain that worsens over hours tells a different story from pain that was severe at once. The next is where it hurts and whether it travels, since pain running from the hip into the knee points toward the nerve that supplies that region. Then comes what the pain is like, whether sharp, dull, burning or cramping, and how severe it is in the patient's own words. The responder then asks what makes it worse and what makes it better, whether there is numbness, and whether breathing feels short. The mechanism of injury, the age of the patient and the medicines already taken belong in the same conversation, because a bone can break in a fall that would not have hurt a healthy person.

A responder cannot see pain, but the body says a good deal in its place, and those signs are worth reading while remembering that they mislead in both directions. A patient may guard the injured part, hold the limb still, clench the jaw, grimace, sweat, turn pale or become restless, and a child may go quiet and still, which is often worse than crying. None of those signs is a measurement and none is required, because a patient who is calm, still and pale may have severe pain while a patient who is shouting may have very little. The examiner records what was seen beside what was said, and treats the patient rather than the appearance.

Some injured patients cannot describe their pain at all, and the assessment then has to be built from other sources instead of being abandoned. A young child may lack the words and may agree with whatever is suggested, so the child is asked with a tool designed for that age, such as a row of faces, and the parent is asked what is different today. An older adult with a memory problem may be unable to report pain, so the responder watches for a new refusal to move, a new restlessness, a change in appetite or sleep, or a face that has gone blank, because such a patient may carry a fracture nobody suspected. A patient with a breathing tube, a patient who is sedated, a patient who is deaf and a patient who speaks another language all belong in the same group. The part of the lay first aider is to notice and to report rather than to decide.

Certain signs are unreliable in particular patients, and a chapter that teaches them as always present will be believed and will then mislead. A rapid pulse commonly accompanies pain, yet a patient who takes a medicine that slows the heart, such as a beta blocker, may have a normal pulse while in severe pain, and a trained athlete may be the same. A patient with an injury of the spinal cord may have pain from a fracture above the level of the injury and no sensation below it, so the two are assessed separately. Severe pain is not excluded by a score of 0 out of 10, and any such number is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than a measurement to be relied on.

The single finding that must never be explained away is pain out of proportion to the injury that keeps getting worse. Muscle swelling inside a compartment that cannot expand produces pain that is deep and burning and poorly relieved by rest, and that pain is often increased when the fingers or the toes are stretched, which is a clinical test performed by an examiner trained to do it. The pain may be present while the pulse at the wrist or the ankle is still easy to feel, so an intact pulse never excludes the problem, and the skin may look normal when the muscle is already dying. Analgesia does not hide this diagnosis and must not be withheld on the excuse that it would, because a patient whose pain is controlled is easier to examine and to follow; what matters is that pain which does not settle is treated as a warning. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so the responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation.

Pain is recorded in the same way as the neurovascular findings, before an intervention and again after it, in the words of the patient wherever that is possible. The record carries what the patient said, where it hurt, what made it worse, what was done and what changed afterwards, together with the time of each entry, because a note without a time cannot be compared with anything. The comparison is what has value: a pain reported as 6 out of 10 that is now 3 out of 10 has improved, while the same numbers in a patient who is becoming drowsy and cold mean something else, and those numbers are an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. A finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and the same rule applies to a medicine, because nobody can judge whether pain relief helped or a complication began unless the state before it was written down.

Stabilization is the second step of the sequence, and for pain it means making the patient as comfortable and as still as the situation allows while the limb is supported in the position in which it was found. A deformed limb is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what was left intact, and that restraint holds even when pain is the reason someone wants to pull the limb straight. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm and stays with the patient, because presence itself reduces fear and fear reduces pain. The trained responder and the paramedic may immobilize the limb within the equipment and procedures their service authorizes, and the nurse may do the same within the protocol of the facility. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so wet clothing is removed, the patient is insulated from the ground and the injured part is covered.

The neurovascular examination belongs to the third step, it is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and pain is assessed in the same breath because the two are read together. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes and to report what is felt. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and numbness, tingling or the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier is recorded in the patient's own words. Pain that is increasing and pain that has changed in character belong to that examination as much as the pulse, and a pulse that is present never excludes serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the clinician.

Immobilization comes fourth, and one of its purposes is to relieve pain, because a bone whose ends can move with every breath hurts more than a bone held still. The splint holds the joint above and the joint below the injury as well as the broken bone, it is padded where it presses on bone, and it is secured firmly enough to support without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace or a surgical fixation. Casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and neither is taught from a book in this course. Traction is a gentle continuous pull used to hold the ends of a bone in line in certain injuries, and it too is learned under supervision rather than improvised in the field.

Imaging is the fifth step, and it confirms what the examination has already suggested rather than deciding how the pain is treated. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. The clinician responsible for the patient orders the study and interprets it, the lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed. A patient in pain is made as comfortable as the injury allows before the journey, and any medicine given for that journey is prescribed by the authorized prescriber and given by someone whose scope permits it. Because the patient is moved to another room and often left there briefly, the limb and the pain are checked again on return, since an image is a picture of one moment.

Analgesia is the relief of pain with medicines, and in this course it is part of the treatment of the injury rather than a courtesy offered when nothing more urgent is happening. The first principle is that pain is treated as soon as it is recognized and as soon as the patient has been assessed, because a patient in severe pain cannot cooperate with the rest of the examination. The second is that the cause is treated along with the symptom, so a tight splint is loosened and a fracture is immobilized while the medicine is being arranged. The third is that different pains respond to different medicines and that combining them, which is called multimodal analgesia, usually relieves more pain with fewer effects than pushing one medicine to a high amount. The fourth is that relief is measured afterwards rather than assumed, so the patient is asked again and the answer is written down. None of those principles tells the listener what to give, because the substance, the amount, the route and the interval belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol.
