The scope of practice decides who may give an analgesic, and the answer differs between services and between countries, so the listener must know the rule that applies where they work. The lay first aider gives no medicine at all, and in particular does not offer a painkiller from a household supply and does not give a drink to a patient who may need an operation unless the local protocol allows it. The trained responder and the paramedic may give what their service authorizes in writing and what their training and certification cover. The nurse gives a medicine that has been prescribed, in the amount and by the route the prescription names, and administers it according to the checks and the documentation the facility requires. The physician or another authorized prescriber decides the substance, the amount, the route, the interval and the plan for monitoring, and may delegate the giving but never the judgment. Analgesia given outside those limits is not a kindness but an unauthorized act, and it is the patient who carries the risk.

This course gives no amount, no route and no interval for any medicine, and the reason is accuracy rather than caution. The right amount for one patient can be too much for another, because weight, the work of the kidneys and the liver and the other medicines already being taken all change what a body does with a drug. Allergy, pregnancy, breastfeeding, a stomach ulcer or a bleeding tendency, a heart that beats slowly, a lung disease that makes breathing shallow and a previous bad reaction all change the choice before the choice of amount is reached. A patient who has taken an opioid regularly for a long-standing problem needs a different plan from one who has never had any, and a patient with a head injury needs a plan that will not hide a change in the level of consciousness. Because those answers differ between services, countries and editions, every threshold and time named in this book is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the prescriber, not the listener, holds the number.

Every class of analgesic carries effects that the person giving it must be able to recognize, and recognizing them is part of the scope of practice of whoever gives them. The opioid group relieves severe pain and can also slow the breathing, lower the blood pressure, cause vomiting and produce drowsiness that blurs the examination of the head and of the nerves, so a patient who receives it is watched rather than left alone. The nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory group reduces pain and swelling without dulling consciousness, and it can irritate the stomach, cause bleeding and strain the kidneys, particularly in an older patient or one who is short of fluid, and in some patients with asthma it provokes a severe attack. Whatever is given is recorded with the time and the effect, and a responder who sees a patient become drowsy, slow their breathing or drop their blood pressure stops, supports the airway and calls for help at once.

The route by which a medicine is given is a clinical decision that depends on the state of the patient rather than on convenience. A patient who is vomiting, a patient who may need an operation soon and a patient whose stomach is not emptying because of the injury may not be the right patient for a medicine taken by mouth, and the amount that reaches the blood after swallowing can be unpredictable when the circulation is failing. A medicine breathed in reaches the blood quickly and is used in some services for severe pain, with the patient watched throughout and with the equipment and authorization the protocol requires. A medicine given into a vein acts within minutes and can therefore be dangerous within minutes, so it belongs to a monitored setting, to a person trained and authorized to give it and to a plan for what happens if the patient stops breathing. Giving a medicine is a technique learned with a teacher and not from a page.

Local and regional analgesia work by blocking the transmission of pain along the nerve that supplies the injured part, and they can relieve pain very effectively for a period of time. A local anesthetic may be placed around a nerve by a clinician trained to do it, or injected into the space around a fracture by a clinician trained in that technique, and both acts require the training, the equipment, the authorization and the supervision the local protocol sets out. What they can achieve is a patient who can be examined, moved and imaged comfortably, while what can go wrong is a block that spreads further than intended, a toxic reaction to the medicine, an injury by the needle and bleeding where the anatomy was not as expected. Sedation belongs to a clinician working in a monitored environment with the equipment to support breathing, the staff to watch the patient continuously and a plan for an airway that has to be taken over. None of those techniques is taught from this book, none is used on a wound in the field, and the decision to use one belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient.

Certain acts are forbidden in every version of this course, and each is forbidden because it has harmed patients. No medicine is given to relieve pain from a supply prescribed for another person, from a household container whose label has faded or by a route the giver is not trained and authorized to use. A limb is never straightened in the field to make the pain better, because the movement can turn a closed fracture into an open one, can tear a vessel that was still intact and can trap a nerve that was still working. An open wound is never explored blindly and an embedded object is never removed, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound. A medicine is never given in place of an assessment, and a patient who is deteriorating is never settled with sedation instead of being reassessed. A responder who meets resistance, a limb that becomes tighter under the hand or a patient whose condition changes stops what they are doing and calls for help, because force is not a technique.

Reassessment comes after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment, whether the treatment was a splint or a medicine. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value and not any single measurement. The patient is asked again about the pain in the same words as before and the answer is set beside the earlier one, the limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the breathing and the level of consciousness are checked after any medicine that can affect them. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, new numbness, new weakness, a limb that becomes tense and swollen and a patient who becomes drowsy are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage or splint to be released by someone authorized to do it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Some patients need a lower threshold for both assessment and treatment, because the usual signs are less reliable in them. A child may be unable to say where it hurts and may become quiet rather than loud, so a parent is asked what has changed and a tool suited to the age is used, while the decision about any medicine belongs to the prescriber who knows the child's weight and history. An older adult whose bone has lost density may carry a fracture far less painful than its severity suggests and may be unable to report pain because of a memory problem, so the threshold for imaging and referral is lower rather than higher. A patient with a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so such a patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. A patient who is pregnant, a patient who has taken opioids for years and a patient who is dying each need a plan written by the clinician responsible, and the part of the responder is to observe, to report and to keep the patient safe.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and the plan for pain travels with the patient into it. An injury that needs an operating room, a damaged vessel or nerve, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a fracture that enters a joint and a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone are all referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The handover names what the patient said about the pain, what was given and when, how much relief followed and what effect was seen, because the receiving team continues one story instead of starting a new one. In the operating room and afterwards, the surgeon and the anesthesia team decide what will be used for pain, and that plan is theirs to write within the protocols of their institution. Pain that is new, that returns after it had settled, that spreads or that comes with a change in the limb brings the patient back for review. Everything in this chapter is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without it.

To summarize, pain is part of the injury and not a complaint beside it, so it is assessed in the first step of the sequence, recorded in the patient's own words before an intervention and again after it, and treated as part of the treatment. A deformed limb is splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and no medicine is given from a household supply or from another person's prescription. The lay first aider comforts, supports, keeps the patient warm and reports; the trained responder and the paramedic give only what their service authorizes; the nurse gives what has been prescribed, in the amount and by the route the prescription names; and the prescriber alone decides the substance, the amount, the route and the interval, so this course gives no dose and no regimen. Pain out of proportion to the injury, pain that keeps worsening, new numbness, new weakness and a tense swollen limb stop the responder and bring help, and analgesia is never withheld for fear that it will hide such a finding, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. Reduction, traction and casting belong to supervised training and to local protocol, and nothing in this chapter authorizes a listener to perform them. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 11 — Edema and Swelling Management

Swelling is the injury that continues after the injury has happened, and it is treated rather than only watched, because the fluid itself can cost a limb. A limb that swells inside a closed space bounded by fascia has nowhere to put the extra volume, so the pressure rises against the muscle and the nerve within it, and the damage that follows belongs to the swelling rather than to the bone. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and swelling runs through every one of those steps. Two of them are never skipped, because the neurovascular examination is performed before an intervention and repeated after it and its result is recorded, and the reassessment after every intervention is what catches the complication caused by the treatment. This chapter explains why an injured limb swells, what swelling does inside a closed compartment, what a responder may do about it, who may do it, and when swelling stops being a finding and becomes an emergency. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Swelling after an injury is not a mistake of the body but part of its repair, and it begins within minutes of the moment the tissue is torn. A broken bone bleeds from its own vessels and from the marrow inside it, and the blood that collects between the broken ends forms the hematoma that is the first stage of healing rather than a complication to be drained. Torn muscle, torn fascia, torn capsule and torn skin each add their own bleeding, and the inflammatory response that follows widens the small vessels so that plasma leaks into the spaces between the cells. That fluid carries the cells that clear debris and the signals that call repair forward, so a limb that does not swell at all is not automatically a lucky limb. The responder meets the total of all of this as a limb that is larger, tighter, warmer and more painful than it was. The question is how fast it is growing, what it is pressing against, and whether the tissue on the other side of the fascia has room to give.

The body has two places to put this fluid, and the difference between them decides whether the swelling is a nuisance or a danger. The first is the tissue between the cells, where fluid spreads along the limb and produces the soft swelling that leaves a dent when a finger presses into it. The second is the compartment, a closed room bounded by bone on one side and by fascia on the other, which holds muscle, nerves and vessels with very little room to spare. Fascia is a tough sheet of fibrous tissue that wraps a muscle or a group of muscles, and it stretches slowly and reluctantly rather than opening to let the pressure out. When bleeding or edema pours into a compartment, the volume inside a room that cannot enlarge raises the pressure within it, and that pressure reaches everything inside. The same amount of blood is therefore a minor problem in the loose tissue of the thigh and a threat in the tight compartments of the forearm or the leg. The responder cannot see a compartment or feel the pressure inside it, so the examination is a search for what a rising pressure does to the tissues it holds.

As the pressure inside a compartment rises, the first vessels to lose their flow are the smallest ones, and the order in which the tissues suffer is fairly constant. The capillaries and the small veins are compressed first, so the blood that arrives through the artery cannot leave through the vein, and the compartment holds more fluid than it drains. Muscle suffers earliest and most, and nerve is next, which is why the earliest symptoms come from muscle that is being starved and from nerve that is being squeezed. The artery is a thick muscular tube that withstands a pressure which has already closed the smaller vessels, so a pulse felt at the wrist or the ankle does not mean that the muscle inside the limb is being perfused. A pulse that is present therefore does not exclude a compartment syndrome, and a pulse that is absent is a separate emergency with its own urgency. Pain comes from the muscle that is ischemic and from the nerve that is compressed, and it is usually the first thing the patient reports and the first thing that must be believed. A limb that is swollen, tense and painful beyond what the injury appears to explain is not a limb to be observed at leisure.

Swelling has a natural history, and knowing its shape helps the responder decide whether what is being seen is expected or alarming. In an ordinary injury the swelling grows over the first hours, reaches a peak and then slowly settles as the torn vessels seal and the fluid is carried away by the veins and the lymphatics. The height of that peak and the time it takes to arrive depend on which bone was broken, on how much soft tissue was torn and on what the patient has been doing since, and they differ between services and between editions. A figure that names a number of hours is therefore an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. What matters at the bedside is the direction of the change rather than the exact size, because a limb whose swelling increases while the bandage stays the same is telling the responder something that a measurement can only confirm. Swelling that is settling is a patient who can be watched, and swelling that is tightening is a patient who must be seen now.

Assessment of a swelling begins before anyone touches the limb, and it begins with the story. The mechanism of injury, the time it happened, the position in which the limb was found and the illnesses and medicines that affect bleeding and healing are all part of it, because a patient whose clotting is impaired or whose bone is weakened may swell far more than the injury suggests. The account the patient gives of the pain is the most valuable single piece of information in the assessment, and it is worth asking whether the pain is deep, whether it burns, and whether it is growing. The lay first aider gathers what the patient says and reports it, the trained first responder and the emergency medical technician assess within the procedures their service authorizes, and the interpretation of the findings belongs to the clinician. Only then does the examination move to the limb, which is looked at before it is touched and compared with the other side, because a difference between the two limbs is easier to see than an absolute size, and nothing is moved into a prettier position before that comparison has been recorded.

Looking at a swollen limb is a skill with several parts, and each part answers a different question. The color of the skin is compared with the other side, because pallor may mean that flow has failed and a dusky or mottled appearance may mean that the blood is no longer moving through. The surface is inspected for tightness and shine, since skin stretched smooth over a tense limb is a different finding from skin that still moves freely over soft tissue. Blisters may appear over swollen skin, and their presence tells the examiner that the tissue beneath has been under stress for some time. Rings, watches, bracelets, tight sleeves and boots are looked for before the swelling makes them impossible to remove, and the mark left by any of them is recorded. The lay first aider observes and reports these findings, the trained responder and the emergency medical technician document them, and the clinician decides what they mean.

Feeling the limb is the next part of the assessment, and the examiner feels the same place on both sides in the same order. The temperature of the skin is compared, the swelling is pressed gently to see whether it pits and springs back, and the examiner notices whether the limb is soft or tense under the hand. A measuring tape is used at a marked and repeatable landmark, such as a fixed distance from a named bony point, and the mark is written on the skin so that the next examiner measures the same place. The choice of landmark and the size of the difference that matters are local conventions rather than fixed truths, so a difference of 2 centimeters between the two sides illustrates a threshold that some services treat as significant and that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol in force. The examiner also presses along each compartment for tenderness out of proportion to the injury, because a compartment that is tense and exquisitely tender is the finding that changes the plan. Measuring swelling has value only when the measurement is repeated by the same method and compared with the record, and the lay first aider needs no tape to report that the limb looks larger than it did.

Swelling does not always mean the same thing, and where it sits helps to say what has happened. A joint that fills quickly after an injury holds blood inside its capsule, and the joint becomes swollen, painful and hard to move, which tells the clinician that something within the joint has torn. A swelling of the whole limb suggests a larger injury or a failure of the drainage that carries fluid away, while a swelling in a limb with no remembered injury, or in both limbs, points toward a cause that is not trauma at all and deserves assessment rather than a splint. The lay first aider reports what is visible, the clinician decides which of these possibilities is being faced, and nobody in the field reopens a wound to look for a cause.

Several of the signs that a responder would most like to rely on are unreliable, and knowing which ones they are protects the patient. A pulse that can be felt beyond the injury does not exclude a compartment syndrome, because the pressure that closes the smallest vessels is far lower than the pressure that closes an artery. The classical findings of advanced compromise appear late, and by the time they are all present the muscle may already be lost, so the responder acts on the earliest trustworthy report rather than waiting for the whole picture. Pain is the earliest warning in a patient who can communicate, but it is a poor guide in a patient who is sedated, intoxicated, confused or unconscious, in a patient whose spinal cord has been injured, and in a small child who cannot describe it. A limb may also swell deep inside the calf, where the fascia is thick and the swelling is far less visible. Pain out of proportion to the injury, pain that increases when the examiner gently stretches the muscle, a limb that is tense to the hand, and a new numbness or weakness are the findings that matter most. The lay first aider watches and reports, the trained responder and the emergency medical technician perform the examination their service authorizes, and the diagnosis of a compartment syndrome belongs to the clinician who is called to the bedside.

Stabilization of a swollen limb is a small set of acts, and the first of them is to stop adding to the swelling while the patient is moved toward care. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found, and it is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Elevation above the level of the heart is a traditional measure against swelling, and it does reduce the pressure in the small vessels, but it is used within the limits of the injury and never against them. When a compartment syndrome is suspected the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, because guidance on this point differs between services and the safe course is to keep the limb level and to move the patient toward definitive care. A limb whose position is holding a fracture quiet, a limb with an open wound, and a patient whose spine is being treated as unstable are not repositioned for the sake of a swelling. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands or with whatever is at hand and keeps the patient warm, the trained responder elevates within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes, and elevation never delays the transfer of a limb that is tense.

Removing what constricts is the second act, and it is done early because a ring that fits now may not come off in an hour. Rings, watches, bracelets, tight sleeves, tight boots and any elastic garment around the limb are removed before the swelling makes the removal painful and difficult. The lay first aider may remove jewelry and loose clothing that comes away easily, and the trained responder may use the simple measures the service authorizes, such as lubrication, a cool hand or a gentle rotation. A ring that will not move is not pulled, is not forced over a swollen knuckle and is not cut off in the field by anyone who is not authorized and equipped to do it, because a cut ring is a small loss and a torn finger is not. If a constricting item cannot be removed, its presence and its position are recorded and reported before the swelling grows further. Every technique for removing a tight ring or a tight boot is learned under supervision and practiced on a model, and none of it can be learned from listening to a book.

A bandage, a splint or a cast that was comfortable when it was applied can become a tourniquet as the limb beneath it swells, and this is the most common way that treatment causes the very injury it was meant to prevent. The device is checked at the fingers or the toes for color, warmth, sensation and movement immediately after it is applied and again at every reassessment, and the findings are compared with the record made before it went on. A bandage or a splint whose fastenings have become tight may be loosened within the limits of the local protocol, and which provider is authorized to loosen it is written into the protocol that governs the patient. A cast is a rigid shell with no give at all, so a cast that becomes tight is a problem for the clinician, who may split it or remove it with the proper tool and the proper authorization. Cutting a cast blindly is dangerous because the skin beneath the edge may already be broken or blistered, and a cut that reaches the padding and the skin introduces an infection where there was none. Compression wraps carry the same risk, so they are applied only by a provider authorized to apply them, only when the injury and the protocol permit it, and never over an open wound or a limb whose compartments are already tight.

The neurovascular examination is the step that turns a swelling from an impression into a record, and it is performed before any device is applied and repeated after each intervention. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers and the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier is written down in the words of the patient as far as possible. The result is recorded before the splint and after the splint, because a finding that was not written before the intervention cannot be attributed afterwards, and the change between the two records is what carries the information. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and feel, the trained responder performs and records the examination the service authorizes, and the nurse and the physician repeat it and interpret it. Numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor, coolness and pain out of proportion to the injury are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation.

Immobilization is the step that holds the swelling still, and it is done for the fracture and for the soft tissues at the same time. A splint prevents movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. It is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a folded magazine, a padded board, a sling or the body of the patient can each serve, and an improvised device must be checked more often. Cooling a swollen limb is used in some injuries and is applied according to the local protocol and never directly against bare skin, because cold can injure tissue that is already short of blood, and cold is treated throughout this course as a complication of trauma. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, and the patient is insulated and covered before anyone moves.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. Swelling makes that first picture harder to read, because the soft tissues are thicker and the bone edges sit further from the recording surface, so a fracture that becomes obvious once the swelling has settled can be invisible on the first study. A patient whose limb remains painful and swollen after a normal first radiograph is therefore examined again, and a further study may be requested later. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, the trained responder does not decide which study is needed, and the clinician requests a study when the answer it gives will change what is done.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the swelling is compared with the mark and with the other side, and every splint, bandage and wrap is checked for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain that is worse than the injury appears, pain that a gentle stretch of the muscle makes worse, numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor and a limb that becomes tense and hard are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for a confirmatory test and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage, splint or wrap to be released by someone authorized to release it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. The lay first aider reports the change, the trained responder escalates to the receiving facility, and the clinician decides what happens next.

Swelling becomes an emergency when it begins to threaten the tissues inside the closed compartment, and the transition is measured in the damage done rather than in the size of the limb. The diagnosis is clinical, which means that it rests on the history, on the examination and on the account the patient gives, and a single pressure measurement is only one part of a picture that a clinician assembles. Where such a pressure is measured, the threshold and the technique differ between services and between editions, so any figure quoted for it is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The muscle that is starved of blood begins to die before the skin shows anything unusual, and the breakdown products that follow can reach the circulation and the kidneys, which is why the patient is referred to a facility with an operating room and an intensive care unit. Both are reasons to refer urgently rather than to wait for a scheduled appointment, and to write down what was seen and when it was seen. The lay first aider and the trained responder do not make the diagnosis, and their task is to suspect it early, to remove what constricts, to keep the limb level and the patient warm, and to hand the suspicion over in plain words.

Definitive treatment of a swelling that has become dangerous belongs to the operating room, and the operation that relieves the pressure is called a fasciotomy, in which the surgeon opens the fascia that bounds the compartment. That operation is performed by a surgeon with a team, under anesthesia, in a facility with an intensive care unit, and its timing is a surgical decision rather than a field one. Reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, are the other definitive acts this course names, and every one of them is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. None of them is taught from a book, and a responder who has not been trained and authorized does not attempt them, because a reduction that is forced can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. In each of those situations the right act is to immobilize in the position found, to reassess, and to hand the patient to someone qualified to do more, because force is not a technique.

A swollen limb is also a window on the whole patient, and the responder reads it that way. Swelling that grows while the pulse rises and the skin turns pale may be telling the responder about bleeding that continues somewhere the eye cannot reach, and a closed fracture of a large bone can release enough blood to threaten the circulation. A limb that swells after a long period of stillness or after an operation may hold a clot in a deep vein, which is a different emergency with a different treatment, and it is referred rather than massaged. A limb that is swollen, red, hot and painful with a fever suggests an infection, and a limb that swells without any of those features may have a cause in the heart, the kidneys, the liver or the lymphatics that no splint will help. A small child cannot describe the pain an adult would name, an older adult may blister over a splint that would be harmless on a younger arm, and a patient who is sedated, confused or paralyzed by a spinal cord injury may have a compartment that is tight and silent. The record carries the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the size of the swelling and the landmark used to measure it, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and every change in the condition of the patient, and it is spoken in a fixed order so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one.

To summarize, an injured limb swells because bone, muscle and fascia bleed and because the inflammatory response leaks plasma into the tissues, and the swelling becomes dangerous when it rises inside a compartment that cannot expand. The neurovascular status is recorded before any intervention and repeated after every one, because a finding that was not written down before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The responder supports the limb in the position found, removes rings and constricting clothing early, loosens what the local protocol allows to be loosened, keeps the limb level when a compartment syndrome is suspected, keeps the patient warm, and refers urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and they are never attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when training or equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 12 — Clavicle Fractures

The clavicle holds the shoulder out from the middle of the chest and is the only bony link between the arm and the rest of the skeleton, so a break in it changes the way the whole arm hangs. It lies directly under the skin, so the examiner can see and feel what a deeper bone would hide. A fracture of the clavicle is common, and teaching offers it as a little under one in twenty of all fractures in adults, an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter follows the order used everywhere in this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The bone is not a straight rod, and its shape explains where it usually breaks. It curves forward in its inner half and backward in its outer half, so seen from above it looks like a shallow letter S and is narrowest at the middle. Teaching describes about four breaks in every five as falling in the middle third, an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. The inner end is anchored by the breastbone and by the muscles of the neck, while the outer end carries the weight of the arm through the shoulder. When the bone breaks between those anchors, the inner fragment is pulled upward and the outer fragment follows the arm downward, which is why a shortened, stepped contour appears instead of a smooth line.

What makes this small bone more than a small problem is what lies against it and beneath it. The vessels that supply the arm and the bundle of nerves called the brachial plexus pass behind the clavicle, separated from the bone by a thin layer of muscle. The apex of the lung and the first rib lie just below the outer third of the bone, so a fracture that drives fragments toward those structures can injure them without a wound on the skin. The state of the arm and of the breathing therefore matters as much as the state of the bone. The skin over the bone is thin, so a sharp fragment can stretch it until it opens, and a pale, shiny, tented area over the break changes the urgency of the case.

Assessment begins before the bone is touched, with the scene and the story of how the injury happened. The common mechanisms are a fall onto the point of the shoulder, a fall onto an outstretched hand, and a direct blow from a collision or a heavy object. The energy involved decides how much else must be suspected, so the responder asks about the height of the fall, the speed of the vehicle and whether consciousness was lost. The history also asks about illnesses and medicines that weaken bone and about smoking, which slows healing, because such a patient may break a bone in a fall that would leave another person unhurt. The time of the injury and the position in which the arm was found are written down at once.

The first task is not the shoulder but the patient, and the primary survey is remembered by the letters ABCDE, which stand for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. A patient who has fallen from a height may have a collapsed lung, broken ribs, a head injury or a broken neck as well, and none of those will announce itself while everyone is looking at the shoulder. Breath sounds that are absent on one side, a rising pulse, falling consciousness, or skin that has become cold and damp send the responder back to the beginning and away from the limb. Only when the patient is stable enough does the examination turn to the shoulder, and the limb is then assessed by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing it. The principle that orders these acts is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot.

The classic picture of this fracture can be recognized from across the room, though not every patient has it. The patient often sits with the head tilted toward the injured side, the shoulder on that side lower and further forward than the other, and the arm supported across the body by the other hand. The patient may be unwilling to lift the arm above the level of the shoulder, and may guard it against any movement at all. Swelling, bruising and a visible or palpable step in the line of the bone follow within hours, and the contours of the two sides are compared from in front and from the side. A patient who is not in distress and who can move the arm freely may still have a crack in the bone, because a break that is not displaced shows only tenderness and a reluctance to lie on that side.

Gentle palpation along the bone belongs to a trained responder or to a clinician rather than to a passer-by. The fingers follow the line of the bone from the notch at the top of the breastbone to the point of the shoulder, feeling for a step, a gap and an area of greatest tenderness. Grinding the fragments together to feel or hear a crackle is not part of the examination, because moving the broken ends deliberately adds pain and can convert a closed injury into an open one. The skin is examined along the whole length of the bone, and a shiny, pale, stretched area over a prominent fragment, which is called tenting, is treated as an injury that is threatening to open. If the skin has already broken, the wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, and the wound is never explored blindly, because definitive closure belongs to the operating theatre.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding that was not written down before a sling was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the hand, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and feels the pulse at the wrist. Sensation is tested over the shoulder and along the outer side of the forearm and the hand, and the two sides are compared. The patient is asked whether there is numbness or tingling, and is then asked to move the fingers, the wrist and the elbow, and any new weakness is recorded as a change. An absent pulse is an emergency reported at once, and a pulse that is present does not exclude damage, because a pulse can survive an injury that has already reduced the flow through the smallest vessels.

Disability, the fourth letter of the primary survey, includes the neck, and a high-energy injury that breaks a clavicle can also injure the spine. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a patient who must be moved is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. The broken clavicle can act as a distraction, because it is painful and obvious, while a neck injury is neither. A patient who cannot feel or move a limb, or who describes tingling in both hands or in the feet, is referred urgently. The trained responder and the paramedic work within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what further examination is needed.

Stabilization is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The arm is supported in the position in which it was found, because the weight of the arm pulling on the outer fragment causes pain and displacement, and removing that weight is often the most useful thing that can be done at the scene. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, a pillow or a folded garment, keeps the patient warm and waits for help, while the trained responder or the paramedic may apply a sling or a splint within the procedures the service authorizes. Nothing is pushed back into a wound, no embedded object is removed, and no deformed limb is straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a helpful-looking movement can tear what remained intact. Cold is a complication of trauma, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering.

Pain relief is part of stabilization, and the decision about it belongs to a prescriber. The substance, the amount, the route and the frequency are set by local protocol and by the clinician who prescribes, and this course deliberately names none of them, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from a book. The paramedic may give analgesia under the protocol of the service and the authorization of its medical director, while the lay first aider gives nothing and instead supports the arm and reports the pain. Pain that increases instead of settling, or pain out of proportion to the injury, makes the decision urgent. The nurse and the physician reassess the pain after every intervention together with the limb, because a treatment that relieves the bone and leaves the patient worse is not a treatment.

The arm sling is the oldest and still the most useful device for this injury. A triangular bandage, a purpose-made sling, or a length of cloth tied behind the neck all work the same way, supporting the forearm and the elbow so that the weight of the arm is carried by the neck and the trunk instead of by the broken bone. The elbow is kept at the side and the hand higher than the elbow, so that fluid does not pool in the swollen hand, and the material is padded where it crosses the back of the neck. A lay first aider may apply a simple sling as a support while waiting for help, checking that the fingers stay warm and pink and that the bandage does not press on the neck. A sling does not put the broken ends back together, correct a shortened bone or hold the fragments still, so it relieves pain rather than treating the fracture.

The figure-of-eight bandage is the other device a listener will hear named. It passes around both shoulders and crosses at the back, and the theory is that drawing the shoulders backward brings the fragments closer together and holds them there. Studies have not shown that it reliably reduces the displacement or the shortening, and many services have stopped using it. It carries its own harms, including pressure in the armpit, damage to the skin and the nerves of the arm, swelling of the hand, and discomfort that makes the patient loosen it. Where a service still uses it, it is applied by a trained responder or a clinician within the local protocol, never by a lay first aider, and it is checked repeatedly for skin damage, swelling and the state of the fingers. A sling supports the arm comfortably while the figure-of-eight bandage attempts to hold the bone, and the attempt is not reliably successful.

Whatever device is used, the principles of immobilization are the same, and they are checked rather than assumed. The device is padded where it presses on bone or on skin, it holds the limb in the position in which it was found, and it is firm enough to support without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The fingers are examined after application for color, warmth, movement and sensation, and the same examination is repeated at intervals, because a bandage that was comfortable when applied can become tight as the limb swells. The knot of a sling is placed away from the spine and away from the side of the neck that bears the weight, and the armpit is kept dry and inspected for redness or broken skin. The physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, and casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol rather than from a book.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden. The joints at both ends of the bone are included in the picture, because a break at either end may be part of an injury of the joint there. Computed tomography shows the detail of a break that enters a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including the nerves and the vessels. In a child, a view of the other side may be needed, because the growing end of the bone can look like a fracture when it is normal. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the choice and the reading belong to the clinician responsible for the care of the patient.

What the image adds is the position of the fragments, the length of the bone, and the condition of the joints at each end. The clinician looks for shortening, which is judged by comparing the two sides rather than by trusting a single view, and for comminution, which warns that the soft tissues are more likely to have suffered. The image also shows whether a separate piece of bone has been pulled away by a ligament, and whether the shoulder blade, the ribs or the breastbone have been injured as well, because a second injury is easily missed when the first one is obvious. What the image cannot show is the state of the nerves, the vessels and the skin, so the neurovascular examination is repeated after imaging as after every other intervention.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The fingers are checked for color, warmth, movement and sensation, and the pulse at the wrist is felt again. The skin under and around the device is inspected, and the neck and the armpit are checked for pressure or for the beginning of a sore. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A compartment syndrome is unusual after a fracture of the clavicle, but a responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. Within the limits of the local protocol an authorized responder may release a constricting bandage or sling, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently.

Most fractures of the clavicle, in adults and in children alike, heal without an operation, and the treatment is support, time and review by a clinician. The sling is worn until the pain has settled enough for gentle movement, and the clinician then guides the return of movement and strength over the following weeks, with figures such as 6 to 12 weeks offered only as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The patient is warned to return if the pain increases, if the hand changes color or feeling, if the skin over the break becomes tight or shiny, or if the arm cannot be moved at all. The nurse and the physician share the work of review, and the orthopedic surgeon is consulted when healing does not follow the expected course, because practice in this area differs between countries and between editions of the same guideline.

Certain findings turn a fracture of the clavicle into an injury that needs a specialist, and they are worth learning by name. Skin tenting is the first, because skin stretched over a sharp fragment is at risk of breaking and turning a closed fracture into an open one, and an open fracture is contaminated at the moment of injury and needs an operating theatre. Shortening of the bone, marked displacement, and comminution into several pieces are the next, because they predict slower union and a shoulder that may not work as it did. A change in the neurovascular status of the arm, whether it is numbness, weakness, a cold hand or a diminished pulse, requires urgent assessment by someone able to examine the nerves and the vessels. A fracture that fails to unite, which is called a nonunion and which is more likely in a patient who smokes, is referred to an orthopedic surgeon rather than treated with more time in a sling.

Definitive treatment begins with the decision about whether the bone must be brought into a better position and held there, and that decision belongs to an orthopedic surgeon. Reduction means restoring the position of the bone ends, and it may be closed, with the fragments moved through the skin, or open, with the fracture exposed in the operating theatre. Traction means a gentle continuous pull that holds the fragments in line, and casting and bracing hold a limb still while the bone heals. Surgical fixation holds the fragments with metal devices, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, and it is considered for an open fracture, for skin threatened by a fragment, for marked shortening or displacement, and for an injury that involves the nerves or the vessels. Every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, never from a book.

Even where reduction is being considered, there are situations in which the attempt must not be made, and the reason matters as much as the rule. A suspected complex fracture-dislocation, fragments caught inside the joint, and neurovascular compromise that needs a specialist are situations in which an attempt by the wrong hands can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. An open injury, an unclear diagnosis, inadequate training or equipment, and an earlier attempt that failed are the same kind of warning. The responder stops if there is resistance, if the pain suddenly changes, if the pulse or the sensation changes, or if the limb becomes harder to move, because force is not a technique. The lay first aider, the trained responder, the nurse and the physician all work within the same rule, since the bone is not straightened in the field and the technique of reduction belongs to supervised clinical training.

The child with a fracture of the clavicle deserves attention of its own, because the bone and the patient are different. The bone of a child bends before it breaks, so the injury may be a greenstick fracture, in which one side of the bone is broken and the other is only bent, and it may heal quickly with simple support. A newborn may sustain the fracture during delivery, when the infant does not move the arm, a sign called pseudoparalysis that must be distinguished from an injury of the nerves of the arm. A child is often most comfortable in a sling made from a strip of cloth, applied by a carer under the guidance of the clinician and checked for pressure and for the state of the fingers. A child who is repeatedly injured, or whose story does not match the injury, is referred and protected according to local protocol and the law.

The older adult with a fracture of the clavicle often has a bone that broke more easily than the injury suggests. Bone that has lost density breaks in a fall from standing height, and the same fall in a younger person may leave nothing but a bruise, while the fracture may be less painful than its appearance. A patient who uses a walking aid, or who needs both arms to rise from a chair, loses more independence from this injury than a young athlete does. The threshold for immobilization and for referral is therefore lower and the review is arranged sooner, while the decisions about imaging, about analgesia and about treatment remain with the clinician. The same caution applies to a patient whose bone is weakened by a tumor, by a medicine, or by a disease of the bone marrow, and such a patient is referred for assessment rather than treated with support alone.

The complications of this injury are few but worth naming, because each announces itself in a way the patient can describe. A break that fails to unite, called a nonunion, causes continuing pain and a shoulder that cannot be used, and it is more likely in a patient who smokes. A break that unites in a poor position, called a malunion, leaves a shortened and sometimes painful shoulder, and it may limit the reach of the arm above the head. Injury to the brachial plexus or to the vessels behind the bone is uncommon but serious, and it is why the neurovascular examination is repeated. A fragment that presses on the skin can cause it to break down even after treatment, which is why the skin over the break is inspected at every review. A persistent burning pain with changes in the color and the temperature of the hand may be a complex regional pain syndrome, which needs early assessment.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the arm was found, the findings of the neurovascular examination before and after every intervention, the device that was applied, and any change in the condition of the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order. The receiving team then continues a story instead of starting a new one, and a finding that was not recorded before the sling was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, so the record also protects the responder who applied it. A spine that has not been cleared is stated as not cleared, and where this chapter names a time or a proportion, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Because the scope of practice differs between countries, every intervention in this chapter is attached to the level of provider who may perform it, and the listener must confirm that list against their own law and local protocol. The lay first aider supports the limb in the position found, applies a simple sling if trained to do so, keeps the patient warm, and calls for help. The trained first responder adds the observation of the neurovascular status, the application of a splint or a sling within the equipment the service authorizes, and a written record. The emergency medical technician and the paramedic may give analgesia and choose the position of transport under the protocol of the service and the authorization of its medical director. The nurse and the physician examine, assess and refer, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides about imaging and about definitive treatment. Only the orthopedic surgeon, in an operating theatre with the right team, performs reduction, traction, casting or surgical fixation, and every one of those acts is learned with a teacher.

To summarize, a fracture of the clavicle is recognized by the arm held across the body, the shoulder lower on the injured side, swelling and a step in the line of the bone, and the findings that make it more than simple are skin tenting, a badly displaced bone, an open wound, and any change in the neurovascular status of the arm. The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding not recorded before a sling was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The first device is usually a sling, which supports the weight of the arm without putting the bone ends back together, while the figure-of-eight bandage attempts to hold the bone and does not reliably succeed. The limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating theatre and to nobody else. The patient is reassessed after every intervention, the skin under the device is inspected, the patient is kept warm, and a patient with threatened skin, a suspected injury to the nerves or the vessels, or a suspected injury of the spine is referred urgently. Most fractures of the clavicle heal with support, time and review, and the decision about reduction, traction, casting or fixation belongs to an orthopedic surgeon, because those techniques are learned under supervision and never from a book. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 13 — Scapular Fractures

The scapula is the flat bone that lies over the back of the chest wall and gives the shoulder its sliding base, and a fracture of it is a message about force rather than about a broken bone. It has a ridge across its back called the spine, a hook-shaped projection at the front called the coracoid process, a roof called the acromion, and a shallow cup at its outer corner called the glenoid, which receives the head of the upper arm bone. Because the glenoid is part of the shoulder joint, a break that crosses it is an injury to a joint surface and deserves more caution than the same break in the flat body of the bone. Wrapped in muscle and cushioned by the rib cage, the shoulder blade breaks only when the energy arriving there has already passed through the body around it, so a patient may sit up and talk while a torn lung or a bleeding vessel decides whether that patient lives. This chapter therefore treats the scapular fracture first as a marker of injury elsewhere and only then as an injury of the shoulder itself.

Fractures of the ribs on the same side are common, and a rib broken in two places can leave a segment of the chest wall moving against the rest, which is called a flail chest. Air can escape from a torn lung into the space around it to produce a pneumothorax, and blood can collect there to produce a hemothorax, and either can enlarge until it presses on the lung and the heart. The lung itself may be bruised, the collar bone and the breast bone may be broken, and the neck, the back, and the head may have taken the same blow. Because the shoulder blade is protected in this way, its fracture is called a sentinel injury, and it is a reason to look harder at everything else. The first step is to look for these injuries, and only after that to examine the shoulder.

One pattern deserves its own place in the mind even though it is rare. When enormous force pulls the shoulder blade away from the chest wall, the muscles that bind the two together are torn, the nerves of the arm may be stretched with them, and the vessels that supply the arm may be injured at the same time. The shoulder on that side may appear displaced outward while the arm is pale, cool, and pulseless, and such an injury cannot be managed where the patient lies. Any suspicion of it is an emergency, and the patient is moved to a facility with imaging, an operating room, and a vascular surgeon.

Taking the history is part of the assessment, because the answer describes the energy and the energy predicts the injuries. The responder records the time, the height of the fall, the speed of the vehicle, and any loss of consciousness as they were told. A constructed illustration may help: a person thrown from a bicycle at speed and found with a painful shoulder after landing on one side has taken a force that could have reached the lung, the spleen, the neck, and the head. Nothing in that example is a real patient, and it is offered only to show how a mechanism is used.

Every chapter of this course follows one order, and the order protects the patient because each step decides what the next may safely be. The sequence is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. In a scapular fracture the assessment is dominated by the search for the chest injury that often accompanies it, and the shoulder is examined only when the patient is stable enough. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work, and it names the provider level for every act it describes.

Assessment begins at the scene with protection of the rescuer and the patient, and it continues with the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The rule that governs the whole survey is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. A patient speaking in full sentences has a protected airway for the moment, while a patient who is hoarse or drowsy does not, and the difference is acted upon by the trained responder within the procedures the service authorizes. The lay first aider recognizes the problem and calls for help, while the airway itself is managed only by someone trained and equipped to manage it.

Breathing is assessed by looking, listening, and feeling, and in this injury it is the step that most often changes the plan. The responder looks at the rate and effort of breathing, at whether both sides of the chest rise equally, and at the color of the lips. Listening over the chest with a stethoscope belongs to the trained clinician, but any responder can hear a wheeze or a silence where breath should be. Feeling the chest wall may reveal tenderness over a broken rib, a crackling sensation under the skin where air has escaped, or a segment that moves against the rest. Any of those findings is a reason to stop examining the shoulder and to arrange urgent transfer.

Circulation is judged by the pulse, the skin, and the level of consciousness rather than by any single number. A rapid, weak pulse, skin that is pale and cool, and a patient who is anxious or drowsy together suggest that blood is being lost somewhere, and the chest is one of the few places where a large volume can collect unseen. A volume offered in teaching is an illustration only and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The trained responder reports what has changed since the previous set of observations, because a trend is worth more than an isolated reading.

Disability is assessed by the level of consciousness and by movement and feeling in each limb, and it is recorded before anything is given or splinted. Exposure means removing enough clothing to see the whole injured region while covering everything else, because cold is a complication of trauma. A patient who has fallen or been thrown is treated as having an unstable spine until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no single manual handling technique is safe, so the move is made by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Personal protective equipment is worn before contact with blood or body fluid, and providing it belongs to the responding service. The survey is repeated whenever the patient changes, and a patient who deteriorates goes back to the beginning.

Only when the patient is stable does the assessment turn to the shoulder, and even then the history continues. The responder asks whether the shoulder has been injured before and whether the arm could be used at all at the moment of the injury. Medicines that thin the blood, medicines taken for years that weaken bone, and conditions that make bone fragile are recorded, because they change the threshold for imaging and for referral. Inspection comes before touch, with both shoulders uncovered so that the two sides can be compared, and it looks for swelling, bruising, a wound, and the position in which the arm is held. Bruising over the shoulder blade may not appear at once, so a shoulder that looks normal in the first hour can be marked by a broad stain a day or two later.

Palpation begins away from the area of greatest pain and moves toward it, following the bones that can be felt through the skin. The examiner feels the collar bone along its length, both of its joints, the ridge across the back of the shoulder blade, the bony point of the shoulder called the acromion, and the ribs beneath. Tenderness over the body of the scapula, a step in the bone, or a crackling sensation suggests a fracture, and each finding is described in words rather than given a diagnosis. Pressing hard, pulling on the arm, and forcing a painful joint through its range are not part of this examination, because they can turn a stable injury into an unstable one. Feeling for the pulse in the arm is always part of it.

Movement is tested by asking, never by forcing, and a finding taught as reliable is not always present. The patient is asked to lift the arm forward, out to the side, and to rotate it gently, reporting where pain begins rather than pushing through it. A patient who cannot move the arm at all may have a fracture, a dislocation, or a torn muscle, so the finding tells the examiner that imaging is needed rather than which of those it is. Swelling may be modest because the bone lies deep beneath thick muscle, and the arm may still move a little despite a break across a joint surface. Moving the arm for the patient is a clinical test learned under supervision, because doing it without training can displace a fracture or complete a tear.

The examination of the shoulder that must accompany a scapular fracture is the examination of the whole shoulder girdle, because the same force rarely respects the boundary of one bone. A break that crosses the glenoid cup allows the joint to become uneven, which the patient feels as a catch or a block when the arm is rotated. The joints at both ends of the collar bone and the collar bone itself are examined in the same pass, together with the upper part of the arm bone. A dislocation of the shoulder and a fracture of the scapula can occur together, and a squared-off shoulder with the arm held away from the body is a reason to stop and to immobilize.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded in the words of the patient as far as possible. The reason is not administrative: a finding that was not recorded before a sling was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and an injury present from the beginning may be blamed on the person who applied the support. The test covers the nerve supply, the blood supply, and the skin of the whole arm, and it belongs to the trained responder, the nurse, or the clinician. It notes the time, the side, the pulse, the color, the warmth, the sensation in each area, and the strength of each movement. It is repeated after every intervention and read aloud at every handover, because the comparison between two sets is what shows whether the injury is changing.

The nerves of the arm pass through the region of the shoulder in a tight bundle called the brachial plexus, which the scapula lies directly against. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, in the outer shoulder, the outer forearm, the little finger, and the index finger, each served by a different nerve. Movement is tested by asking the patient to make a fist, to spread the fingers, to bend the wrist, and to lift the arm, and weakness is recorded as a change from what the other side can do. Numbness, tingling, a loss of grip, and a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier are findings of the same importance as a break seen on a radiograph. The test is repeated after the arm is supported, because the sling itself can press on a nerve.

The vessels are examined in the same pass, and the findings that matter are the pulse at the wrist, the color and warmth of the hand, and the time for color to return after a nail is pressed. The artery that supplies the arm passes close to the shoulder joint and can be torn by the same force that breaks the scapula. A pulse that is present does not exclude a serious injury to a vessel, because a pulse can survive a tear that is contained by the tissues around it, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency. An expanding swelling around the shoulder, a bruise that grows while the patient is watched, and a limb that becomes cool and pale are reasons to summon help at once. The lay first aider notices color, warmth, and movement and reports them, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or the clinician.

Stabilization comes next, and for a scapular fracture it means the ordinary acts that keep a patient alive and comfortable while the plan is made. The patient is kept warm, because cold worsens bleeding and shock, wet clothing is replaced with covering, and the patient is insulated from the ground. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with direct pressure through a dressing, and bleeding that cannot be controlled is a reason for urgent transfer. The arm is supported in the position in which it was found, with the hand of the patient, a pillow, a rolled blanket, or the body itself, and the support is adjusted until the patient reports less pain. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact.

A wound over the shoulder or the chest wall changes the priority but not the principle. An open injury is contaminated from the moment it happens, and the part played by the responder is limited and precise: cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control the bleeding that can be controlled, record the neurovascular status, immobilize in the position found, keep the patient warm, and arrange urgent transfer. An embedded object is never removed, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and because pushing bone inward drives contamination deeper. The wound is never explored blindly with a finger or an instrument, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else.

Immobilization of a scapular fracture is achieved by supporting the arm, not by binding the chest. The usual device is a sling, which cradles the forearm and takes the weight of the arm from the injured shoulder, and a shoulder immobilizer adds a strap that holds the arm against the side of the body. The sling is applied over the position found, it is padded where it presses on the neck or on the point of the shoulder, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation. The lay first aider trained in basic first aid may apply a simple sling, the trained responder and the paramedic apply the devices their service issues and authorizes, and the nurse or the clinician adjusts the device when the patient reaches care. The material matters far less than the principle, and a triangular cloth or a pillow held in place can serve.

The temptation to wrap a bandage around the chest in order to hold the arm still must be resisted, and the reason is that the same force that broke the scapula may also have broken ribs or bruised a lung. A bandage that encircles the chest limits the movement of the ribs and the depth of every breath, and in a patient with a chest injury it can turn a stable situation into a failing one within minutes. If the chest has been injured, the arm is supported with a sling alone, the strap across the body is left loose, and the patient may sit up if that is comfortable. The chest takes priority over the shoulder in every decision, because a shoulder can be treated tomorrow and a lung cannot wait. Anyone who applies a sling checks the fingers for color and warmth immediately afterwards and at intervals until the handover.

Pain is treated, and the decision about how belongs to the prescriber rather than to this course. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, rising instead of settling, or out of proportion to the injury seen, because that pattern may signal a compartment syndrome or a vessel injury. The responder reports the pain in the words of the patient, records the time of the report and any change, and offers no substance that has not been authorized for that patient by someone qualified to prescribe it. The name of the medicine, the amount, and the way it is given belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from this book. Nothing in this chapter describes a dose, a route, or a regimen, and none should be inferred from it.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. The first study is usually a radiograph of the shoulder taken in more than one direction, because a break invisible in one view may be obvious in another, and the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. A radiograph of the chest is commonly taken as well, since the injuries that accompany a scapular fracture are found in the chest more often than anywhere else. Computed tomography shows the detail of a break that crosses the glenoid or the neck of the scapula, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including the nerves and the tendons of the rotator cuff. Neither the lay first aider nor the trained responder decides which study is needed, and any interval named in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The arm is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement, and pain, the sling is checked for tightness and for pressure on the neck, and the chest is checked for the rate and the effort of breathing. Some findings arrive late, since air can leak slowly from a torn lung and swelling can increase until the skin is tight, so the patient is watched at intervals. Pain that increases instead of settling, a hand that becomes cool or pale, numbing that was not there before, and a chest that becomes harder to fill are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation.

Compartment syndrome is rare around the shoulder, since the bone lies in a broad bed of muscle, but it can occur in the arm and the forearm, and the rule that governs it is the same everywhere. The pressure inside a closed compartment rises after bleeding or swelling, the flow through the smallest vessels fails, and the first structures to suffer are the muscle and then the nerve. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and the finding that raises the suspicion is pain out of proportion to the injury, worse when the muscles are stretched. The constricting bandage or sling is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently, because time is muscle. A pulse that remains present does not exclude the diagnosis, and waiting for it to disappear is waiting too long.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and for most scapular fractures the definitive treatment is not an operation.
