The bone is enveloped in muscle, the blood supply is generous, and the flat body of the scapula tolerates a break that would be unacceptable in a bone that bears weight, so the fracture is usually held in a sling until the pain settles and then moved gently under supervision. An operation is considered when the break involves the glenoid surface and leaves the joint uneven, when the neck of the scapula is displaced, or when the shoulder has been pulled away from the chest wall. The decision, the timing, and the technique belong to an orthopedic surgeon working in a facility with an operating room, and an operation that holds the fragments with metal devices is called open reduction and internal fixation. What the responder contributes is the safe transfer of the patient to that decision, with the record intact and the arm supported, because the shoulder can wait until the patient is safe.

Reduction, traction, and casting are named in this course only so that the listener understands what they are and who may perform them, and the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends, traction holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and a cast or a surgical fixation holds the position while the bone heals. Each is learned under supervision, practiced on models under a teacher, and performed according to local protocol by a clinician or an orthopedic surgeon qualified to do it. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed, because the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

Two groups of patients deserve a lower threshold for imaging and for referral. The scapula of a child still contains a great deal of cartilage, so a break there may be difficult to see and may disturb growth, and a child who will not use an arm after a fall deserves the same caution as a child with an obvious deformity. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break a scapula with far less force than a younger person would need, and the fracture may hurt less than its appearance suggests, so the mechanism is recorded rather than the pain alone. In both groups a sign treated as reliable may be missing, so the threshold for immobilization, imaging, and referral is lower, while the decisions stay with the clinician.

Complications after a scapular fracture are uncommon, but they are not imaginary. A break that crosses the glenoid can leave the shoulder joint uneven and lead to pain and stiffness months later, and the muscles that move the shoulder can lose their attachment, so a shoulder that has healed may still not lift the arm fully. A nerve of the brachial plexus can be stretched by the same force and recover slowly, or not at all, and a patient who notices numbness or weakness weeks afterwards is referred back for assessment. Stiffness of the shoulder, sometimes called a frozen shoulder, is the commonest late problem after any shoulder injury, which is one reason the clinician begins gentle movement early. Rehabilitation begins when the fracture is stable enough to tolerate it, its pace is set by the clinician, the physical therapist directs the program, and progress is measured by what the patient could not do last week and can do this week.

What each provider may do is decided by training, by authorization, and by local protocol. The lay first aider supports the arm with a sling or a pillow if trained to do so, keeps the patient warm, notices color and warmth in the hand, and calls for help. The trained responder and the paramedic perform the primary survey, apply the supports their service authorizes, record the neurovascular findings, and report what has changed. The nurse observes, reassesses, and reports within the procedures of the department, while the physician examines, orders imaging, and decides what treatment is needed, and the orthopedic surgeon decides whether an operation is required and performs it. Everything described here is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, so a course heard in a car teaches the reasons and the limits but cannot confer a skill.

To summarize, a scapular fracture is a break in a bone protected by muscle and by the rib cage, so it usually means that a great deal of energy passed through the chest, the neck, and the arm, and it is treated first as a marker of injury elsewhere. The assessment begins with the scene and the primary survey, in which airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure are addressed before the shoulder is touched, because a patient can talk while a lung is collapsing or blood is collecting in the chest. The shoulder is then examined in full, including the collar bone and both of its joints, and the neurovascular status of the whole arm is recorded before any intervention and repeated after it. The arm is immobilized in the position found, usually in a sling, and the chest is never wrapped, because a band around the ribs can stop a patient from breathing. Imaging is ordered by a clinician, and computed tomography is used when the glenoid or the neck of the scapula is involved. The patient is reassessed after every intervention, a constricting bandage or sling is released within the local protocol if a compartment syndrome is suspected, and the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart. Any suspicion of a chest injury, a torn vessel, a torn nerve, or a shoulder pulled away from the chest wall is a reason for urgent referral to a facility with imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit. Reduction, traction, and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 14 — Shoulder Dislocation

The shoulder trades stability for movement, and it pays for that freedom with the highest rate of dislocation of any joint in the body. A dislocation means the joint surfaces are no longer in contact at all, and in the shoulder the head of the upper arm bone leaves its socket and usually travels forward and downward, which is why this injury is called an anterior dislocation. The patient is almost always in pain, guards the arm and refuses to let anyone move it, and the shape of the shoulder can be unmistakable once the examiner knows what to look for. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work. Every injury in this course is taught through one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the step that protects the patient most is the neurovascular examination recorded before anything is done.

The commonest mechanism is a fall onto the outstretched hand while the arm is lifted away from the body and turned outward, because that position levers the head of the bone against the front and lower edge of the socket until it tears through the capsule and slips out. A direct blow from behind the shoulder, a tackle that forces the arm backward and a violent wrench of the arm in sports can produce the same displacement in other ways. The head usually comes to rest below a bony prominence at the front of the shoulder called the coracoid process, and the socket behind it is left empty. Whatever the mechanism, the energy does not stop at the joint, so the examiner thinks about the whole limb and about the rest of the patient, and the shape of the shoulder is only one part of the picture. Ask what happened, when it happened and whether the shoulder has come out before, and write the answers down, because each of them changes what should be done next.

What the responder sees is described as a squared-off outline, and the phrase is worth unpacking because it is the key to recognition. The normal shoulder has a rounded curve formed by the deltoid muscle lying over the head of the bone, and when the head leaves the socket that curve is lost, so the outer edge of the shoulder falls into a straighter line and the acromion stands out with a hollow beneath it. The arm is held away from the body rather than against it, in a position of slight abduction with the hand turned outward, and the patient supports the forearm with the other hand to ease the pull on the joint. An attempt to bring the elbow across the chest is resisted, and no one should try to prove the diagnosis by forcing that movement. Swelling and bruising appear with time and may be modest at first, so the shape of the shoulder is more useful early than the amount of swelling.

Assessment begins with the scene and with the mechanism, then moves to the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Life comes before limb, so a patient who fell from a height or who is confused after a blow to the head is stabilized before anyone turns attention to the shoulder. The shoulder may be the loudest injury and not the most dangerous one, and a distracting deformity can hide a head injury, a chest injury, an injury of the spine or bleeding elsewhere. Once the patient is stable enough, the history continues with the time of the injury, the position of the arm at impact, whether the shoulder has dislocated before, and whether the patient takes a medicine or has an illness that weakens bone. A patient whose shoulder has dislocated several times may have put it back without help, but that history does not remove the need for examination and imaging, because a repeated dislocation can still carry a fracture or an injury of a nerve. Ask whether the patient can move the fingers and whether the hand feels normal, and record the answer in the words the patient uses.

Stabilization means keeping the patient warm, controlling the bleeding that can be controlled, and supporting the injured part in the position in which it was found. The arm is not pulled, twisted, lifted or straightened, and reduction is not attempted outside a setting where it belongs, because the head of the bone lies against a network of nerves and against the artery that supplies the arm, and a movement that looks helpful can tear a vessel or a nerve that was only stretched. The lay first aider supports the arm with the hands, with a pillow or with a sling improvised from clothing, keeps the patient warm and waits for help. The trained first responder and the paramedic may apply a support within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, without testing the joint by moving it. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering. Nothing is placed under the arm that levers the elbow away from the body, because the position found is the position protected.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding that was not written down before a support was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Begin by looking at the hand for color, swelling and the way the fingers sit, then feel the temperature of the skin and the pulse at the wrist. The pulse is felt at the wrist and, by a trained examiner, at the elbow, and a finger is pressed to watch the color return. Sensation is tested on both sides, and the area to test with particular care is the skin over the outer and upper part of the shoulder, which is supplied by the axillary nerve. That nerve winds around the surgical neck of the bone and is the nerve most often injured when the shoulder dislocates, so its territory is examined before anything is done and again afterwards. Movement is tested by asking the patient to make a fist, to straighten the fingers, to spread them and to bend the wrist. A responder who finds numbness, tingling, weakness or a lost movement does not repeat the test to be sure, but records it, protects the limb and escalates.

An examination that is painful and incomplete is still worth doing, and the record must say what was possible rather than what was assumed. A patient in severe pain may not cooperate with testing of the deltoid muscle, and swelling over the shoulder can blunt the sensation of a light touch, so apparently normal sensation in the first minutes does not exclude an injury of the nerve. The examiner therefore writes down the words the patient used and the movements the patient could perform, and states plainly when a test could not be done, because the next clinician needs to know the difference between a nerve that was working and a nerve that was never tested. The strength of the shoulder itself is not tested by the responder, because asking the patient to lift the arm against resistance moves the dislocated joint and can add harm. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability to move and to feel, and reports any change at once, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the physician.

The axillary nerve and the axillary artery both pass close to the lower part of the shoulder joint, and that anatomy is why movement is feared in this injury. Injury of the nerve is common after a shoulder dislocation and is usually a stretch rather than a tear, so it often recovers, but the recovery begins with a finding that somebody wrote down at the right moment. Injury of the artery is uncommon and dangerous, and it is more likely in an older patient whose vessels are stiffened by disease and in a shoulder that has been out of place for many hours. The findings that suggest damage to a vessel are a hand that is pale or cool, a pulse that is weak or absent, pain out of proportion to the injury, and a shoulder that swells rapidly or bruises widely, and those findings make the injury an emergency. A large collection of blood in the shoulder is not a reason to press on the shoulder, to wrap it tightly or to delay transfer, because pressure applied from outside does not stop bleeding from a torn artery inside.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and in the shoulder that means supporting the arm so that its weight does not pull on the joint. A sling that holds the forearm in front of the body, with the arm as it was found, is the usual support, and a bandage that encircles the chest and the arm may be added by someone working within a protocol that authorizes it. The sling is padded where it presses, secured firmly enough to hold and not so firmly that it becomes a band, and checked after it is applied and again after the patient has been moved. The material matters less than the principle, since a triangular bandage, a strip of cloth or a pinned shirt can each serve. In an anterior dislocation the arm is not forced across the chest and the elbow is not pulled down toward the opposite hip, because that movement levers the head of the bone and can increase the damage. The lay first aider may improvise a sling, the trained responder and the paramedic apply and check support within their procedures, and the nurse or the physician decides what support is used once the patient arrives. Immobilization is a step on the way to imaging and to definitive care, not a treatment that settles the diagnosis.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is the first study, taken in at least two directions, because a dislocation that is obvious from one view may be invisible from another, and the joints above and below are included so that a second injury is not missed. The clinician looks for the empty socket, for the position of the head of the bone, and for a fracture of the rim of the socket or of the neck of the bone, because any of those changes what can safely be done next. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around the joint and is requested when the plain pictures leave the diagnosis in doubt, especially when a backward dislocation is suspected. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle, and it is rarely the first study in an acute dislocation. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, the trained responder does not choose the study, and the decision belongs to the physician or the orthopedic surgeon responsible for the care of the patient. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined afterwards.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison that carries the value rather than any single measurement. The hand and the forearm are checked again for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the support is checked for tightness and for pressure points. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor, coolness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A compartment syndrome is uncommon in the shoulder itself, but it can follow a severe injury of the arm or a bandage that is too tight, and because the diagnosis is clinical a responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation. The constricting bandage or support is released within the limits of local protocol, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because time is muscle.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and a dislocated shoulder is almost always referred, because the joint must be put back into place and the patient must be examined afterwards by someone qualified to do it. Reduction means restoring the surfaces of the joint to their normal contact, and its purposes are to relieve the pull on the nerves and the vessels and to ease pain. A shoulder that has been out of place for a long time is harder to reduce, and any figure offered for a safe interval before reduction is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services and editions. The reduction is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon who is trained and authorized to do it, and the technique belongs to supervised clinical training, not to a book. Whether the patient is given pain relief or sedation, and which substance in which amount, is decided by the prescriber within the local protocol, and no dose, route or regimen may be taken from this course. A dislocation is not reduced in the field or in an ambulance by an untrained hand, because the nerves and the vessels lie against the bone.

There are situations in which an attempt at reduction is not made at all, or is deferred to a place with an operating room and a specialist, and each one has a reason worth saying aloud. A suspected complex fracture-dislocation is not reduced, because the attempt can drive a fragment further into the joint or into a vessel. Entrapped fracture fragments are not worked free by force, because force converts a joint that could be repaired into one that cannot. A limb whose vessels or nerves are failing is not manipulated, because the specialist who will repair them needs to see the injury before it is disturbed. An open injury is not reduced in the field, because the wound must be covered, the contamination must be managed in an operating room, and an embedded object is never removed. An unclear diagnosis is not treated by an attempt, because a backward dislocation handled as an ordinary forward dislocation can be made much worse. Inadequate training or equipment, and an earlier failed attempt, are also reasons to stop, and a failed attempt is not repeated by the same person, because repetition multiplies the damage without improving the chance of success.

After the joint has been put back, the neurovascular examination is repeated and recorded again, and a finding that has changed is reported at once rather than at the end of the shift. The clinician repeats the imaging to confirm that the joint surfaces are in contact and that no fracture has moved, and the limb is supported in the position the clinician chooses. The length of time a shoulder is supported after a first dislocation depends on the age of the patient, on whether the injury is a first or a repeated one and on the practice of the treating service, so any number of weeks offered in teaching is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A patient who is at risk of a further dislocation is taught the movements to avoid and the exercises that maintain movement, and that instruction is given by the clinician or by a physiotherapist within the treating service. The task of the responder does not end at the door of the emergency department, because reassessment after every intervention continues through every movement of the patient.

Several complications are worth naming, because each of them is looked for rather than waited for. A shoulder that has dislocated once is more likely to dislocate again, and the risk is greater in a younger patient and in an injury that tore the front of the socket, so a young patient with a first dislocation deserves a clear plan rather than reassurance alone. A fracture of the greater tuberosity, of the rim of the socket or of the neck of the bone may accompany the dislocation, and it may appear only on a later radiograph or on a computed tomography study. A tear of the rotator cuff is more common in an older patient, and its sign, weakness of the shoulder, may be hidden by pain at first, so a shoulder that stays weak after the pain settles is not a failure of effort. An injury of a nerve that was not recorded before a reduction cannot be attributed afterwards, which is one reason the first examination is written down and kept. Stiffness and lasting loss of movement are the quiet complications, and they are limited by the treatment and by the exercises the treating clinician prescribes.

Some patients need a lower threshold for concern rather than a different sequence. A child who will not use an arm after a fall may have an injury of the growing region near the end of the bone rather than a dislocation, and the examination of a child is limited by fear and by the difficulty a child has in describing what is felt, so the limb is protected and the child is referred. An older adult whose bone has lost density may dislocate a shoulder and break it at the same time, and the fracture may be the part that is missed because the dislocation is so obvious. A patient who has been injured during a seizure, an electric shock or a period of unconsciousness may have dislocated the shoulder backward, and a backward dislocation is easily missed because the arm lies across the body and the shoulder may look almost normal. In every one of these patients the sequence does not change, and what changes is how quickly the patient is passed to a clinician.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the arm was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, what was applied and when, and any change in the condition of the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. The words the patient used about numbness, tingling or weakness are more valuable than any paraphrase, and so are the words the examiner used about what could not be tested. A handover states plainly that the shoulder is dislocated, that the arm was supported in the position found, that no reduction was attempted, and what the neurovascular findings were at the last assessment. A clear handover also names what the responder is worried about, such as a pulse that has become harder to feel or pain that is climbing, because that is what decides how quickly the patient is seen.

Scope of practice decides who performs each act, and the whole list is worth gathering in one place. The lay first aider supports the arm, keeps the patient warm, observes color, warmth, movement and feeling, and calls for help, and those acts need no equipment and no authorization. The trained first responder and the paramedic may apply and check a support, monitor the limb and record the findings within the procedures their service authorizes, and they do not reduce a dislocation, do not test the joint by moving it and do not give medication outside a protocol that names the substance and the circumstances. The nurse assesses, records, reassesses, positions, supports and escalates, and administers medication only as it has been prescribed and permitted. The physician examines, orders imaging, decides on pain relief within the local protocol, and either reduces the joint or refers the patient. The orthopedic surgeon manages the reduction when it is complex, treats the associated fracture, and decides on rehabilitation and on the return to activity.

Pain in a dislocated shoulder is severe, and the response to it is limited by scope of practice rather than by indifference. The lay first aider does not give medication, and the trained responder or paramedic gives pain relief only where a protocol authorizes it, because a substance given by the wrong route or in the wrong circumstance turns one injury into two emergencies. The findings that make pain relief urgent are pain that prevents the patient from cooperating with the examination, pain that is rising, and pain accompanied by numbness, tingling or a change in the pulse, and that combination is reported at once. The substance, the amount, the route and the frequency are decided by the prescriber within the local protocol, and none of them may be taken from this course. The nurse who administers what has been prescribed reassesses the patient afterwards, watching for drowsiness, for a change in breathing and for any change in the limb, because sedation can mask the very findings that matter. Comfort is a clinical objective, and treating it well protects the limb.

The fall that dislocated the shoulder may also have injured the neck or the back, and an injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so. No lone manual handling technique is safe, so the patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires, and the arm is supported during every part of that move. A patient who is confused, who has lost consciousness or who cannot describe the pain may have injuries that are not yet known, and the shoulder is then only one part of a larger problem. The responder keeps the patient warm, keeps the limb supported, records what changes, and hands the patient on with the story intact.

Talking to the patient is a clinical act rather than a courtesy. Explain that the shoulder is out of its socket, that a clinician will put it back, that the arm will not be moved until then, and that the responder will stay with the patient and watch the hand. Ask the patient to report numbness, tingling, a change in the temperature of the hand or pain that is getting worse, and say why that report matters, because a patient who understands that movement may add damage is far easier to keep still. Consent for the examination and for any intervention is part of the same conversation, and a refusal is respected and recorded.

Force is not a technique, and the shoulder is the joint where that sentence is easiest to forget. Pulling on an arm to see whether the shoulder slips back is an attempt at reduction, and it is forbidden to anyone without the training, the authorization and the setting to do it properly. When a movement meets resistance, when pain suddenly increases, when the hand becomes pale or cold, or when a pulse disappears, the intervention stops and the patient is escalated rather than persuaded. An open injury of the shoulder changes the priority rather than the sequence, so the wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the neurovascular status is recorded, the limb is immobilized in the position found, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is transferred urgently to a facility with an operating room. The wound is never explored blindly, exposed bone is never pushed back into it, and an embedded object is never removed, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. Definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else, and a dislocation with an open wound is not reduced by the responder.

To summarize, a dislocated shoulder is an injury of the whole limb, and the squared-off outline, the arm held away from the body and the pain that resists movement are the findings that identify it. The neurovascular examination, and in particular the sensation over the outer part of the shoulder and the movement of the fingers, is performed and recorded before any intervention and repeated after every one, because a finding that was not written down cannot be attributed afterwards. The limb is supported in the position found, the patient is kept warm, the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified has cleared it, and nothing is pulled, straightened or tested by movement. Reduction and its techniques are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol by a clinician trained and authorized to do it, and a reduction is not attempted in the field, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the injury is open, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when a vessel or a nerve is failing, when the equipment or the training is inadequate, or after an earlier failed attempt. Pain relief and every medicine belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and no dose, route or regimen may be taken from this course. The patient is reassessed after every intervention, the findings are handed over in a fixed order, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 15 — Proximal Humerus Fractures

The upper arm bone is called the humerus, and the part of it nearest the shoulder is the proximal humerus, where a break is one of the commonest injuries of the shoulder. The shoulder is built for movement rather than for stability, since a shallow socket on the shoulder blade holds a rounded head in place with muscles and ligaments rather than with the shape of the bones. A break at the upper end of the arm bone therefore damages a region through which every movement of the arm passes, and it happens most often to an older person whose bone has lost density and who has fallen at home, and less often to a younger person who has met a far greater force. This chapter follows the order used in every part of this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Four parts of this small region decide what happens after the break. The head is the rounded part that sits in the shallow socket of the shoulder blade, and it is covered by smooth cartilage that lets the joint glide. The neck just below the head, which surgeons call the surgical neck, is where the bone most often gives way. Two rounded bumps at the top are called the tuberosities, and the tendons of the muscles that rotate the shoulder are attached to them, so a fragment can be pulled out of position by a muscle. A child has a growth plate across the upper end of this bone, from which the arm lengthens, so an injury there is judged differently in a child. The bone here is a thin shell around a lattice rather than a thick tube, which is why it yields to a force that would leave the middle of the bone unbroken.

The patient this happens to is usually not a young athlete, and the reason lies in the bone rather than in the accident. An older adult who falls from standing height at home, often a woman whose bone has thinned with age, can break this part of the arm with a force that would not harm a younger person. A patient whose bone has been weakened by disease, or by long use of a medicine that thins it, may break the bone while turning in bed. In these patients the pain can be far milder than the break suggests, and the patient may sit and talk while holding the arm perfectly still. The other patient is younger and has met a much larger force, such as a fall from a height, a collision at speed, a seizure, or an electric shock, and must be searched for injuries elsewhere. Both need the same sequence, so what differs between them is how low the threshold for referral is set.

The mechanism is worth asking about in detail, because it predicts what else may be broken. The commonest story is a fall onto the outstretched hand, in which the force travels up the arm and drives the head of the bone against the rim of the socket. A direct blow to the outer side of the shoulder is the second common pattern, and it is the one that most often splits the head into several pieces. A sudden violent contraction of the muscles around the shoulder, as in a seizure or an electric shock, can pull the tuberosities away from the rest of the bone. The responder records what happened, when, how far the patient fell, and onto what surface, because those details are used later to judge whether the injury fits the story told. An injury that does not match the described force is reported according to the law and the local protocol of the country.

The way the patient holds the arm is the first thing the responder sees, and it is often more revealing than the swelling. The arm is usually held close against the side of the body, with the elbow bent and the forearm supported by the other hand, and any attempt to lift the arm or turn it outward is resisted. The patient guards the shoulder and turns the whole body rather than the arm, because it is the movement of the shoulder that hurts. That picture is close to the opposite of the one seen in a dislocation, where the arm is held away from the body and the outline of the shoulder looks squared off. Only a clinician can be certain which injury is present, so the responder records the finding rather than naming the injury, in the words the patient used.

Swelling and bruising are late arrivals in this injury, and a shoulder that looks almost normal in the first hour can be marked within a few days. The blood that escapes from the broken bone runs down the arm under the force of gravity, so a bruise may appear at the elbow, along the forearm, or on the chest wall rather than over the shoulder itself. The swelling can increase for a day or two, and tightness of the skin over the shoulder suggests that bleeding within the tissues is continuing. A constructed illustration may help, and it describes no real patient: an older person falls in a garden, keeps the arm still because it hurts, and two days later has a forearm stained with a broad bruise. Because the bruise arrives late, its absence at the first examination never excludes the break.

Assessment begins at the scene, with protection of the rescuer and of the patient, and it continues with the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The rule that governs the whole survey is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. A patient who fell from a height, or who was thrown from a vehicle, is treated as having an unstable spine until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so any move is made by a trained team. Personal protective equipment is worn before contact with blood or body fluid, and providing it belongs to the responding service. Exposure means uncovering enough of the patient to see the whole injured region while covering everything else, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. The survey is repeated whenever the patient changes.

Taking the history is part of the assessment and not a formality that precedes it. The responder asks what happened rather than what hurts, and records the time of the injury, the height of any fall, the surface landed upon, and whether the arm could be used immediately afterwards. Medicines that thin the blood, or that have weakened the bone over years, are recorded because they change the threshold for imaging and for referral. Whether the patient is right-handed or left-handed matters to the plan, since the injury may affect the hand the patient writes and eats with. Whether the patient lives alone also matters, because a shoulder that must be kept still is a shoulder that cannot dress, wash, or cook. The findings of that history travel with the patient to the next provider.

The examination of the shoulder itself begins only when the patient is stable enough to allow it, and it begins with looking. Both shoulders are uncovered so that the two sides can be compared, and the examiner looks for swelling, bruising, a wound, a change in the outline of the shoulder, and the position in which the arm is held. The skin is inspected for a graze, a puncture, or a tenting of the skin over a fragment pressing outward, because any of these makes the injury an open one until a clinician decides otherwise. A wound near the shoulder is covered with a sterile dressing and is never explored blindly with a finger or an instrument, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound. Pressing the skin to see how quickly the color returns is an act any trained responder can perform, while the decision about what a wound means belongs to the clinician.

Palpation follows inspection, and it begins away from the place of greatest pain and moves toward it. The examiner feels the collar bone, the joint at its outer end, the bony point of the shoulder, the ridge across the back of the shoulder blade, and the shaft of the arm bone below the injury, because one force can break more than one of them. Tenderness over the upper part of the arm bone, a step in the bone, or a crackling feeling under the fingers suggests a break, and each finding is described in words rather than given a name. The pulse in the arm is felt during the same pass, and the examination never includes pressing hard on the injured part, pulling on the arm, or forcing the joint through its range. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and can be torn by a movement that looks helpful.

Movement is tested by asking the patient and never by forcing the limb. The patient is asked to lift the arm forward as far as it will go, to move it out to the side, to bend the elbow, and to turn the palm up and down, and to say where the pain begins rather than to push through it. In this injury the shoulder usually moves very little, and that absence of movement cannot be used to tell a break from a dislocation or from a torn tendon. Testing the stability of a joint by pulling on it is a clinical skill learned under supervision and is not a field test. A sign that is taught as reliable is often absent in a frightened, cold, or confused patient, so every movement the patient can still perform is recorded.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated afterwards, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a sling was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. An injury present from the beginning can be blamed on the person who applied the support, and a change not compared with an earlier note is a change nobody can prove. The examination covers the nerve supply, the blood supply, and the skin of the whole arm from the shoulder to the fingers, and it is done on both sides so that the uninjured arm serves as the standard. It belongs to the trained responder, the paramedic, the nurse, or the clinician, while the lay first aider reports only what can be seen without touching the injured part. The record notes the time, the side, the pulse, the color, the warmth, the sensation in each area, and the strength of each movement, and it is read aloud at every handover.

The nerve most often injured with this fracture runs around the neck of the bone, lying directly against it, and it supplies the skin over the outer part of the shoulder and the muscle that lifts the arm sideways. Sensation is tested over that outer patch of skin on both sides and compared, and the patient is asked whether the touch feels the same on each side. The responder then asks the patient to lift the arm out to the side against a gentle resistance, but a shoulder that cannot move because the bone is broken gives no information about the nerve, so weakness in a limb held still is an unreliable sign here. Numbness, tingling, or an area of skin that feels deadened is recorded in the words of the patient as far as possible. The nerves that travel on to the hand pass close by as well, so the grip and the spread of the fingers are tested in the same pass, and any change is reported at once.

The vessel that supplies the arm passes close beneath the shoulder joint, on the inner side of the upper arm, and it can be torn by the same force that breaks the bone. The examiner feels the pulse at the wrist, looks at the color and the warmth of the hand, and presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, comparing one hand with the other. A pulse that is present does not exclude a serious injury to a vessel, because a pulse can survive a tear contained by the tissues around it, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency. An expanding swelling around the shoulder, a bruise that grows while the patient is watched, and a hand that becomes cool and pale are reasons to summon help at once. The formal examination belongs to the trained responder or the clinician, while the lay first aider notices color, warmth, and movement and reports them without delay.

Stabilization means the small set of ordinary acts that keep the patient alive and comfortable while the plan is made. The patient is kept warm, because cold worsens bleeding and shock, wet clothing is replaced with covering, and the patient is insulated from the ground on which the patient lies or waits. Bleeding from a wound that can be controlled is controlled with direct pressure through a dressing, and bleeding that cannot be controlled is a reason for urgent transfer rather than for prolonged effort at the scene. The arm is supported in the position found, with the other hand of the patient, a pillow, a rolled blanket, or a folded garment, and the support is adjusted until the patient reports less pain. A patient who is drowsy, who is vomiting, or who may need an operation is not given anything by mouth, and the decision about any substance belongs to the prescriber. The lay first aider supports the limb, keeps the patient warm, and calls for help.

Pain is treated, and the decision about how belongs to the prescriber rather than to this course. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, rising instead of settling, or out of proportion to the injury seen, because that pattern may signal a compartment syndrome or an injury to a vessel rather than an ordinary break. The responder reports the pain in the words of the patient, records the time of the report and any change in it, and does not offer a substance that has not been authorized for that patient by someone qualified to prescribe it. The name of the medicine, the amount of it, and the way it is given belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from this book. Cooling the shoulder is decided within the local protocol as well, since cold applied too long to skin that is already numb can cause an injury of its own.

Immobilization is achieved by taking the weight of the arm off the injured shoulder and by preventing the arm from swinging, and the two devices that do this are the sling and the swathe. A sling cradles the forearm and the hand and hangs from the neck, so that the weight of the arm is carried by the trunk rather than by the broken bone. A swathe is a broad band that passes around the chest and holds the arm against the side of the body, and together the two keep the shoulder still during a journey over rough roads. The sling is applied over the position found, it is padded where it presses on the neck and on the bony points, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation. The lay first aider trained in basic first aid may apply a simple sling, the trained responder and the paramedic apply the supports their service authorizes, and the nurse or the clinician adjusts the device when the patient reaches care.

One caution belongs with the swathe, and the reason is the same one that governs the immobilization of any injury near the chest. The force that broke the shoulder may also have broken ribs or bruised a lung, and a band that encircles the chest limits the movement of the ribs and the depth of every breath. In a patient with a chest injury the band is applied loosely or left off altogether, and the arm is supported by the sling alone, because a shoulder can be treated tomorrow and a lung cannot wait. The fingers are checked for color, warmth, and sensation immediately after any support is applied and again at intervals, and a hand that becomes cool, pale, or numb is a reason to loosen the support within the local protocol rather than to tighten it. What the support must never be used for is to pull on the arm, to straighten the limb, or to reduce the fracture. How long the support stays in place is decided by the clinician, and any interval a listener has heard is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. The first study is usually a radiograph of the shoulder taken in more than one direction, because a break invisible in one view may be obvious in another, and the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a break that is split into several pieces or that crosses the joint surface, and it often decides whether an operation is needed. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including the tendons that rotate the shoulder, and it is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done. An image is a picture of one moment and does not replace the examination, so the patient is examined and reassessed after the picture is taken. Neither the lay first aider nor the trained responder decides which study is needed.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The arm is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement, and pain, and the sling and the swathe are checked for tightness and for pressure on the neck and on the ribs. Late findings are expected here, since the bruising spreads over days and the swelling can increase until the skin feels tight, so a shoulder that looked comfortable an hour ago is looked at again. Pain that increases instead of settling, numbness that was not there before, a movement that has been lost, and a hand that becomes cool or pale are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. The reassessment is repeated at each handover, and the findings are spoken aloud in the order in which they were recorded.

Compartment syndrome is unusual around the shoulder, because the bone lies in a broad bed of muscle rather than in a closed space, but it can occur in the arm and the forearm, and the rule is the same everywhere. Pressure inside a closed compartment rises after bleeding or swelling, the flow through the smallest vessels fails, and the first structures to suffer are the muscle and then the nerve. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and the finding that raises the suspicion is pain out of proportion to the injury, worse when the muscles are stretched and not relieved by support. The constricting bandage, sling, or swathe is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently, because time is muscle. A pulse that remains present does not exclude the diagnosis, and waiting for a pulse to disappear is waiting far too long.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and for this fracture the decision belongs to an orthopedic surgeon with the images and the patient in front of them. Many proximal humerus fractures are not displaced, or are displaced so little that the shoulder can be expected to work, and those are treated without an operation, supported in a sling with gentle movement begun early under supervision. An operation is considered when the head is split into separate pieces, when the joint surface is broken and left uneven, when the fragments are displaced enough that the shoulder will not lift, when the bone has lost its blood supply, or when the shoulder has also been dislocated. The surgeon may hold the fragments with metal devices, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, or may replace the head of the bone with an artificial one, particularly in an older patient whose bone is unlikely to heal well. The decision, the timing, and the technique belong to the surgeon in a facility with imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit.

Reduction, traction, and casting are named only so that the listener understands what they are and who may perform them, and the technique belongs to supervised clinical training. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends, traction holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and a cast or a surgical fixation holds the position while the bone heals. Each is learned under supervision, practiced on models and on patients under a teacher, and performed according to local protocol by a clinician or an orthopedic surgeon. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique. The same rule governs a shoulder with both a break and a dislocation, because pulling on such an arm in the field can convert a nerve injury that was recovering into one that will not.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the arm was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and the support that was applied are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. What each provider may do is decided by training, by authorization, and by local protocol: the lay first aider supports the arm if trained to do so and calls for help, the trained responder and the paramedic apply the supports their service authorizes and record what they find, the nurse observes and reassesses, the physician orders imaging and decides what treatment is needed, and the orthopedic surgeon decides on and performs any operation. Where this chapter names an interval, a threshold, or a size, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions. A patient who is injured, immobilized, exposed, or waiting is kept warm and covered, because cold is a complication of trauma, and nothing here describes a dose, a route, or a regimen.

To summarize, a break of the upper end of the arm bone is one of the commonest injuries of the shoulder, and it happens most often to an older person whose bone has lost density and less often to a younger person who has met a great force. The patient usually holds the arm close against the side of the body with the elbow bent and the other hand supporting it, and the swelling and the bruising arrive late and spread down the arm, so a shoulder that looks almost normal at first can never be dismissed. The nerve that runs around the neck of the bone and the vessel that passes beneath the shoulder are examined and recorded before any intervention and again afterwards, because a finding not written down before a sling was applied cannot be attributed later. The arm is immobilized in the position found with a sling and a swathe, the support is checked for tightness and the fingers for color and warmth, and the band around the chest is left loose or omitted when the chest has also been injured. The patient is kept warm, is not given anything by mouth if an operation may be needed, and is reassessed after every intervention, with rising pain, new numbness, a lost movement, or a cool pale hand treated as reasons to escalate. Everyone with a suspected break of this bone is referred to a clinician for imaging, and the decision about an operation, about reduction, about traction, and about casting belongs to an orthopedic surgeon in a facility with an operating room and an intensive care unit. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, a wound is never explored blindly, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and force is never a technique. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 16 — Humeral Shaft and Distal Humerus Fractures

The upper arm bone is called the humerus, and this chapter deals with the two parts of it that lie below the shoulder: the shaft, which is the long middle section, and the distal end, which widens into the elbow. A break of the shaft is a break of a bone surrounded on every side by muscle, and its most famous complication is a nerve that stops working for a time. A break of the distal end enters the elbow itself, and what is at risk there is the blood supply to the forearm and the future movement of the joint. The order used in every part of this course is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The shaft of the humerus is nearly cylindrical in its middle and becomes triangular as it approaches the elbow, and it is wrapped in a thick sleeve of muscle that gives the arm its shape. The biceps lies in front of it and bends the elbow, the triceps lies behind it and straightens the elbow, and the muscles of the shoulder attach near its upper end. Because those muscles surround the bone on every side, a break of the shaft bleeds into a closed space and the arm swells, which is one reason this is not the small injury it can appear to be at first. The bone also carries the weight of the arm below the break, and that weight, with the pull of the muscles, produces the deformity and the shortening that the responder sees and feels. Muscle also explains why the broken ends so often settle into a position in which the arm lies across the chest rather than straight down at the side.

Two important structures travel along the shaft rather than through the middle of the arm, and both lie close against the bone. The radial nerve passes from the back of the upper arm around the bone in a shallow channel called the radial groove, or spiral groove, and there it rests directly on the surface of the shaft, while below the groove it pierces a sheet of fibrous tissue near the outer side of the elbow, which is a second place where it can be caught. On the inner side of the arm the brachial artery and the median nerve run together toward the front of the elbow, and the ulnar nerve passes around the back of the inner bump of the elbow, called the medial epicondyle. This arrangement is efficient in health and dangerous in injury, because a bone that breaks and shifts moves exactly where these structures lie, so a break of the shaft can injure a nerve without any wound on the skin.

The distal humerus widens into two columns of bone that end in the rounded surface of the elbow joint, divided into a part that hinges with the ulna and a part that turns with the head of the radius. Above the joint the bone thins into two narrow columns separated by a hollow, and this is where the bone most often gives way, because it is the weakest link between the strong shaft and the strong joint surface. The ulnar nerve lies in a groove behind the medial epicondyle, and the median nerve and the brachial artery cross the front of the joint, both close to a displaced fragment from the distal end. A break that splits the joint surface therefore has consequences beyond the broken bone, because a joint that is damaged and then held still becomes stiff, and the elbow tolerates stiffness badly, so the distal injury is a different problem with a different urgency.

The two injuries reach the patient by different routes, and the history is worth listening to carefully. A break of the shaft often follows a direct blow to the arm, a fall onto the side, or a twisting force such as a throw or a struggle, and it can follow a fall from a height in which the energy is greater. A break of the distal end usually follows a fall onto the outstretched hand with the elbow bent or partly bent, and in a child the same fall is the most common cause of a break just above the elbow. The mechanism matters because it predicts how much energy passed through the limb, and greater energy means a greater chance that the skin, the muscle, the vessels and the nerves have been injured as well.

A patient with a break of the shaft usually arrives supporting the injured arm with the other hand, because the limb is too painful and too unstable to be left unsupported. The arm may be visibly bent, it may be shorter than the other one, and the elbow may point in a direction that does not match the other side. That shortening means the broken ends have slid past one another, because the muscles pull the lower fragment upward while the weight of the arm pulls it downward. Swelling and bruising appear over the hours that follow rather than at once, so an arm that looks almost normal in the first minutes can never be dismissed. The patient may be unable to lift the arm, to bend the elbow or to turn the palm, and each finding is recorded rather than interpreted, because the responder looks, compares the two sides and does not move the limb to find out more.

The distal injury announces itself at the elbow rather than in the middle of the arm. The joint swells quickly, the arm is held at a fixed angle that the patient will not change, and any attempt to move it produces pain. The point of the elbow may look more prominent than usual, and bruising appears around the joint and along the forearm within a short time. A distal injury can look very much like a dislocation of the elbow, and the two cannot be told apart by looking and feeling, so the difference belongs to the radiograph and to the clinician. In a child the same injury may produce almost no visible deformity, and the only sign may be a child who will not use the arm and who cries when it is moved. The responder records the position of the arm, the swelling, the wound if there is one and the neurovascular findings, and then supports what is there.

An open injury deserves separate attention, because the humerus lies just under the skin for much of its length, and a wound over the fracture site means that the bone or the deep tissues have communicated with the outside. Such a fracture is contaminated even when the wound looks clean. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by pressure around the wound and not inside it, and anything embedded is left exactly where it is. Bone that has come through the skin is never pushed back, because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and because pushing it back carries contamination deeper into the arm. The wound is never explored blindly, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. The patient is kept warm, the arm is supported as it lies, and transfer is arranged urgently.

Assessment begins before the arm, and it begins with the scene and with the patient rather than with the fracture. The primary survey follows the steps remembered as ABCDE, which are airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and no limb injury is treated before those steps are complete. A patient who has fallen from a height may have a broken arm and an injured spine, a torn vessel in the chest or bleeding inside the abdomen, and the arm is then the most visible injury rather than the most dangerous one. When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The history includes the time, the mechanism, the age of the patient and any illness or medicine that has weakened the bone, and a break through diseased bone is passed on rather than decided in the field.

Stabilization in the field is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The arm is supported in the position in which it was found, with the hands, a pillow or whatever the responder has, and it is never straightened in order to make it look better. Pulling the arm straight can tear a nerve or a vessel that was still intact, can turn a closed fracture into an open one, and can release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. The lay first aider gives support and warmth, while the trained responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic work within the equipment and procedures their service authorizes. Bleeding is controlled with a sterile dressing and direct pressure, the wound is covered, and the patient is kept warm because cold is a complication of trauma. Nothing is given by mouth when an operation may be needed, and the decision about that belongs to the clinician who will arrange the operation.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding not written down before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color of the fingers, feels their warmth and compares the two arms. The pulse is felt at the inner side of the elbow and at the wrist, and a finger is pressed on a nail to watch the color return. Sensation is tested in the territory of each of the three nerves of the arm, in the web space between the thumb and the index finger, in the pulp of the index finger and in the little finger. Movement is tested by asking the patient to lift the wrist against gravity, to spread the fingers and to touch the thumb to the little finger, and each is compared with the other hand. The result is written in the words of the patient as far as possible, so that the receiving team can compare it with the next examination.

The radial nerve is the structure this chapter fears most in the shaft injury, and when it stops working the patient cannot lift the wrist or straighten the fingers, a finding called wrist drop, while the back of the hand between the thumb and the index finger feels numb. The deficit may be there from the moment of the injury, or it may appear after the arm has been moved, splinted or examined by someone. A nerve that was working before an intervention and is not working afterwards must be reported at once, because the intervention may have caused it and the plan may need to change. The finding is documented in the same words each time, so that the next examiner can see not only that the wrist does not lift but also when it stopped lifting. Testing the nerve by asking the patient to push hard against painful resistance is not a field test, because pain can imitate weakness. Only a clinician can judge the meaning of the deficit, and it is the surgeon who decides whether the nerve must be inspected.

Some findings are unreliable in particular patients, and a responder who relies on a single sign will miss the injury. An intact pulse does not exclude severe damage to the vessels or to the compartments of the arm, because the flow through the smallest vessels can fail while a pulse at the wrist remains strong. A patient who has been drinking, who has an injury to the brain, who is in severe pain or who is a frightened child may be unable to cooperate with a test of sensation or movement, and in an older adult the pain may be less than its severity suggests. The examiner therefore compares the two sides, repeats the examination after every intervention and records what could not be tested as clearly as what could. It is never correct to write that the neurovascular status is intact when the examination was not performed.

Immobilization means preventing movement at the fracture and at the joints above and below it, because a bone held alone can still be moved by the shoulder and by the elbow. For the shaft injury the arm is carried across the body in a sling that takes the weight of the forearm, with a swathe that binds the arm to the chest as far as the injury allows. The support is applied over the position found, padded where it presses on bone, and fastened firmly enough to hold yet loosely enough to let the fingers stay warm and pink. When the chest has also been injured, the band around the chest is left loose and the arm rests against a pillow instead. A trained responder, a paramedic or a nurse authorized by protocol may apply a padded splint along the sides of the arm, and a splint from the shoulder to the hand belongs to that training and to the local protocol rather than to this book. The purpose is not to make the arm look straight but to keep it from moving, and a support that straightens a bent arm has failed.

The distal injury is immobilized with the elbow at the angle in which it was found, and that angle is never forced open or forced closed. A splint applied along the back of the arm and the forearm, padded and shaped to the position found, is the support a trained responder or a clinician may use within the local protocol, and it holds the elbow still while the patient is moved. The arm is then carried across the body in a sling, with the hand supported and the fingers visible so that the circulation can be watched. Nothing is wrapped around the elbow tightly enough to compress it, because the swelling of this injury is rapid and a band that was comfortable when it was applied may be dangerous an hour later. An improvised support from a padded board, a rolled blanket or a folded magazine can serve while help is coming. The check is the same at every level: color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, before the support is applied and after it is applied.

A deformed arm is not straightened in the field, and no listener may learn from a book how to reduce, to apply traction or to cast this injury. Reduction means restoring the broken ends to their proper position, traction means holding them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting means holding the position while the bone heals, and all three are skills learned on real patients under supervision and performed according to local protocol. The reason for that restraint is anatomy, because the radial nerve, the median nerve and the brachial artery lie against the bone where a movement of the broken ends can tear them. A reduction is not attempted, even by a clinician, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when a fragment or the nerve is caught between the ends, when the vessels or the nerves need a specialist, when the equipment or the training is inadequate, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations an attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is never a technique.

Imaging confirms what the hands have already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it. The first study is usually a radiograph, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it must show the whole bone with the joints above and below, because a second break or a dislocation may sit at either end. The elbow needs particular care, because a break of the distal end and a dislocation can look alike and an angled view is often needed to see the joint surface. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break that enters the joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, tendons, cartilage and muscle. A break of the shaft together with a break of the forearm on the same side, called a floating elbow, is a serious combination that needs a surgeon and an operating room. The trained responder does not decide which study is needed, the lay first aider neither orders nor interprets one, and because an image is a picture of one moment the patient is examined again after every journey to the imaging room.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with what was recorded before, and the comparison has value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the support is checked for tightness and pressure points. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a forearm that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. The most feared of these is a compartment syndrome, in which pressure inside the closed space of the arm or the forearm rises until muscle and then nerve are starved of blood, while a pulse at the wrist can still be felt. A responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle, so within the limits of local protocol a constricting bandage or splint is released by a nurse or a clinician authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm and referred urgently.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. Any patient with an open injury, an absent pulse, a new nerve deficit, a suspected compartment syndrome, a break that enters the elbow joint, a displaced break at the distal end, or a break of the shaft together with a break of the forearm is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. A child with a break just above the elbow is referred urgently, because the bone there is thin, the displacement can be great and the blood supply to the forearm can be threatened. A patient whose arm cannot be supported comfortably, whose pain is not controlled or whose neurovascular findings change in any way is also referred without delay. The referral is a spoken and written handover, and it carries the time, the mechanism, the position in which the arm was found, the support applied and the neurovascular findings before and after each step. When the responder is uncertain whether a patient needs a specialist, the answer is to ask the receiving clinician rather than to wait and see.

Definitive care differs between the two injuries, and in both cases it belongs to the orthopedic surgeon and to that surgeon's team. Many breaks of the shaft heal well in a splint or a brace applied by the treating clinician, and some need an operation in which the fragments are held with a metal plate or with a rod placed inside the canal of the bone. The choice depends on the break, the soft tissues, whether a nerve or a vessel is injured and on the patient, and it is not a decision for the responder or for this book. A nerve that has stopped working is usually watched for a period decided by the surgeon, because most such injuries recover on their own, while a trapped nerve or one that fails to recover may be explored and repaired in the operating room. A displaced break of the distal end in an adult is usually treated with an operation, because the joint surface must be put back together accurately and the elbow must be moved early rather than held still. In every case the technique belongs to supervised clinical training, and no part of this course teaches a listener to perform it.

Some patients deserve a lower threshold for imaging and referral rather than a different sequence, and complications explain why the reassessment is never skipped. The bone of a child is more elastic than the bone of an adult and has a growth region near each end, so a child's break may look minor and still disturb growth, while an older adult with thin bone may break the shaft in a fall from standing height. A patient treated for cancer elsewhere may break the arm through a deposit of tumor, called a pathological fracture, and in such a patient the pain may be far less than the injury suggests. A break of this bone may fail to unite, which is called a nonunion, or unite in a position that leaves the arm shortened or bent, which is called a malunion, and the elbow may stiffen after a distal injury even when the repair was good. The radial nerve may fail to recover, the median and ulnar nerves may be injured, and a compartment syndrome not recognized in time can leave a clawed hand and a useless wrist. Some of these complications are caused by treatment, and that is why this course asks the same questions after every intervention.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the arm was found, the wound if there was one, the support applied and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. Any change in consciousness, breathing, pulse or skin color sends the responder back to the beginning, because the limb is never the priority over the airway, and a patient with this injury may also have an injured spine, which is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so. Comfort belongs to the treatment as well, so the responder records the pain in the same way each time, because a patient in severe pain cannot cooperate with an examination, and medicine for pain is given only by a clinician or a paramedic authorized to give it, while the substance, the amount and the route belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber. Warmth is provided throughout, because cold worsens pain and hides the color of the skin, and everything here is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that defines what may be done unsupervised.

Where this chapter names a time or a distance, it names an illustration rather than a standard, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions, and they must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Every figure in this chapter is therefore a teaching example and not a threshold to apply without checking it. Practice also differs in where the line is drawn between a break treated in a brace and one that needs an operation. What can be learned from a book, and what this course teaches, is what to look for, what to record, what to do with the hands, and who to call.

To summarize, the upper arm bone can break in its shaft or at its distal end, and the two injuries look alike on the outside while carrying very different dangers. A break of the shaft produces a bent and shortened arm, and its particular risk is the radial nerve that runs in the groove against the bone, so a patient who cannot lift the wrist or who feels numb on the back of the hand has a finding to be recorded before anything is applied and again afterwards. A break of the distal end enters the elbow itself, threatens the brachial artery, the median nerve and the ulnar nerve, and can leave the joint permanently stiff, so it is always referred. The sequence is to assess with the primary survey first, to stabilize by supporting the arm as it lies, to examine and record the neurovascular status before and after every intervention, to immobilize with a sling and a swathe or with a padded splint applied within the local protocol, to image through a clinician, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. A deformed arm is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the injury is open, when a fragment or the nerve is caught between the ends, when the vessels or nerves need a specialist, or when the training and the equipment are not there. A suspected compartment syndrome is acted on at once by releasing the constricting bandage within the local protocol, without elevating the limb above the level of the heart, and by referring the patient urgently, because time is muscle. Everyone with a suspected break of this bone is referred to a clinician, the arm is supported and the patient kept warm throughout, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 17 — Elbow Dislocation
