The elbow is a joint a person uses all day, and injuring it changes ordinary life quickly. A dislocation means the joint surfaces have lost contact, and most often the forearm moves backward. It is one of the dislocations in which delay damages the arm, because the artery and the three nerves lie close against the bone. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Three bones meet at the elbow, and their arrangement explains much of what follows. The humerus widens at its lower end into two columns, with an epicondyle on each side. The ulna lies on the side of the little finger and carries the olecranon, the point felt at the back of the elbow. The radius lies on the side of the thumb, and its flat upper end, the radial head, turns when the palm is turned over. A capsule surrounds the joint and is reinforced by ligaments on each side, so the joint is stable in health and unforgiving when it is disrupted.

Four structures lie close to the elbow, and each can be injured with it. The brachial artery runs down the inner side of the arm and passes in front of the joint, where it divides into the vessels of the forearm and the hand. The median nerve travels with that artery, directly in front of the joint surface from which the ulna moves away. The ulnar nerve runs behind the inner epicondyle in a shallow groove, and it tingles when the elbow is struck. The radial nerve winds around the outer humerus, supplies the muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers, and carries feeling from the back of the hand.

The usual mechanism is a fall onto an outstretched hand, with the arm taking the weight of the body and the elbow partly bent. The force travels up the forearm and drives the ulna and the radius backward while the humerus stays, levering the olecranon over the lower humerus. The energy of the injury predicts the damage, so a young person with a violent mechanism is more likely to have broken bone as well. In a constructed illustration of the kind used in teaching, a young adult lands on one hand during a game, and the arm is found bent the wrong way with the point of the elbow standing out behind.

What the responder sees is a limb whose outline has changed. The elbow is held partly bent and cannot be moved further, because the joint surfaces are no longer engaged. The point of the elbow sits too far back and too high, with a hollow where it should be, and the forearm looks shorter than the other one. A dislocation with a wound over it is treated as an open injury, and the responder does not test how far the joint moves or try to put it back.

One injury is easily mistaken for the other, and the difference matters. A break of the humerus just above the joint can push the lower fragment backward and produce much the same shape. That break may also injure the artery and the median nerve, and it can be the more dangerous of the two. No field test separates them reliably, and the responder is not expected to settle the question at the scene. The safe position for both is the position found, supported and immobilized without any attempt to straighten it.

The reason this dislocation is urgent is the narrow space through which the artery and the nerves must pass. When the surfaces separate, the artery in front of the joint is stretched, and it may be torn, kinked or bruised. A joint left out of place adds a second problem, because swelling inside the closed sleeve of the arm raises the pressure in the compartments of the forearm. Time is muscle, and delay also makes the reduction harder, because swelling and early scar make the joint resist every attempt to return it.

Assessment begins before the limb is touched. The primary survey is performed in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and the limb waits until the patient is stable enough. A patient who fell from a height may have a head injury, a spinal injury or blood inside the abdomen, and any of those comes first. The history includes the time, the height of the fall, the medicines taken and whether this joint has dislocated before. The lay first aider observes and reports, while the structured examination belongs to the trained responder, the paramedic, the nurse or the physician under the procedures their service authorizes.

The neurovascular examination decides how urgent the case is, and it is done before and after every intervention. The pulse is felt at the wrist on the thumb side, and in the elbow crease or the upper arm if the wrist pulse cannot be found. Capillary filling is tested by pressing a fingernail until it blanches and watching how quickly the color returns. Sensation is tested in the area of each of the three nerves, and movement is tested by asking the patient to spread the fingers, bring the thumb across the palm and straighten the wrist against gravity. Every finding is spoken aloud and written with the time, and the lay first aider reports only what the patient says and what can be seen.

The record is written before any intervention, because a finding cannot be attributed afterwards if it was never noted before. If the patient could not feel the little finger before the splint was applied and still cannot feel it after, the splint is not the cause. The examination is repeated in the same order after every intervention, and the two records are compared rather than each being judged on its own. A change in any finding is an emergency, and the patient is referred without further delay.

An intact pulse at the wrist is reassuring but not a guarantee, and treating it as one is the commonest error made with this injury. The artery can be torn while the pulse remains palpable, because blood reaches the hand through smaller vessels around the elbow. The vessel may also be bruised rather than divided, so a clot forms slowly and a hand that was pink on arrival is pale an hour later. Pain that grows rather than settles, a hand that becomes cold or loses its color, and a forearm that becomes tight and hard matter more than the pulse. The examiner therefore repeats the whole examination, and a responder who finds any of those changes stops and escalates.

Two findings point directly at a torn artery, and both require immediate action. The first is an expanding swelling at the elbow, especially if it is tense and enlarging while it is watched. The second is a mass that beats in time with the pulse, which is called a pulsatile hematoma, and it is handled by covering it and supporting the limb. A wound that keeps bleeding despite firm direct pressure, or that bleeds in spurts, is treated the same way, with a sterile dressing and urgent transfer to a facility with an operating room.

Each nerve gives its own pattern of loss, and the pattern tells the clinician where to look. Injury to the ulnar nerve weakens the spread of the fingers and the pinch between thumb and index finger, and it removes feeling from the little finger. Injury to the median nerve weakens the bending of the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger, and the movement that brings the thumb across the palm. Injury to the radial nerve weakens the straightening of the wrist and the fingers, so the hand hangs down when the arm is lifted. None of these tests is perfect, and the absence of a clear loss does not exclude damage.

One complication changes the whole plan of care. The median nerve can be caught within the dislocated joint, trapped between the humerus and the ulna. A joint held open by a trapped nerve will not return to its place, and this is one reason a reduction must never be forced. A reduction is also not attempted when a fragment of bone is caught in the joint, when the joint surfaces are shattered, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the team lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. When the clinician meets resistance, the attempt is stopped and the patient goes to an operating room.

Not every dislocated elbow arrives dislocated, because the joint sometimes slips back into place by itself. The shape of the limb may then look almost normal, and the examiner sees only swelling, bruising and tenderness. The patient still cannot use the arm comfortably, and the joint is still unstable. A swollen elbow after a fall that cannot be moved through a full range deserves the same immobilization and referral as an obvious deformity. The absence of a deformity is a finding to interpret with care, not a reason to relax.

Stabilization in the field is a short list of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened, because straightening pulls on the artery and the nerves. The lay first aider supports the arm with a pillow, a folded garment or both hands, keeps the patient still and warm, and waits for help. The trained responder or the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and procedures the service authorizes, holding the elbow comfortably. Nothing is given by mouth, because a patient who may need an operation should arrive with an empty stomach, and covering is added against cold.

An improvised splint is padded where it presses on bone and firm enough to hold without stopping the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a rolled magazine, a padded board or a folded blanket can each serve. The trained responder checks the pulse, color, warmth and sensation in the hand after the splint is applied. If the hand becomes pale, cold or painful, the splint is loosened within the limits of the local protocol and the patient is referred urgently. Nothing is ever pushed into the joint, an embedded object is left where it lies because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and a dislocated joint is not manipulated by anyone.

Pain relief is part of humane care, and a book that teaches a dose is a dangerous book. The responder needs to know who decides, what makes the decision urgent and what the scope of practice forbids. The substance, the amount, the route and the timing belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and they differ between services, countries and editions. Relief becomes urgent when the patient cannot be moved or examined because of pain, and when the pain is out of proportion to the injury. The physician or the advanced practice nurse authorized to prescribe decides what is given, and the paramedic gives only what the service protocol permits.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it exists to catch the complication caused by the treatment. The hand is checked for color, warmth, pulse, capillary filling, sensation and movement, and the splint for tightness. The findings that stop the responder are pain that increases instead of settling, numbness or tingling that is new, a movement the patient has lost, and a forearm that becomes tense, swollen and hard. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome acts without waiting for confirmation, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. The constricting bandage, splint or cast is released by someone the local protocol authorizes, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently.

Imaging is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it, and it answers questions the examination has already raised. A radiograph is taken in at least two directions, and the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not hidden. The clinician looks for a break of the radial head, of the coronoid process of the ulna, of the medial epicondyle and of the lower humerus, because each changes what must be done. Computed tomography is used when a fragment is unexplained, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for ligaments, cartilage and tendons. An image is a picture of one moment, so the limb and the neurovascular status are checked again after imaging.

Reduction means restoring the joint surfaces to their proper contact, and it relieves the stretch on the artery and the nerves. It is performed by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon trained and certified to do it. The technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training and to the local protocol, and no book can teach it safely. Before the attempt the neurovascular status is recorded, and after it is recorded again, because the value lies in the comparison. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment or the median nerve is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the team lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and the correct act is to stop and escalate.

The complications of this injury are the reason it is watched for so long. The joint stiffens easily, because the capsule thickens and the muscle tightens, and a joint held still for a long time may never regain its range. New bone can form in the soft tissues around the joint, a process called heterotopic ossification, and it can block movement permanently. The artery can clot after the joint has been returned to its place, and the swelling that follows any reduction can raise the pressure in the compartments of the forearm. The median nerve may be injured at the moment of injury or during the reduction, and the ulnar nerve may suffer if the elbow is kept bent for a long time. Infection follows an open injury that is not treated properly, and instability follows a joint whose ligaments and bone have not healed in a way that holds.

Definitive treatment depends on what the injury turns out to be, and the decision belongs to the orthopedic surgeon. An unstable joint may need a hinge that allows controlled movement, and a joint with a trapped fragment or a shattered surface may need reconstruction. An open injury needs thorough cleaning in an operating room, and definitive closure of the wound belongs there and nowhere else. A patient whose arm remains pulseless after reduction needs a surgeon trained in the repair of blood vessels. Traction, casting and the surgical holding of fragments are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and this course describes what they achieve rather than how to carry them out.

Referral is a decision made early and reviewed often, not a formality at the end of the sequence. Every patient with a dislocated elbow, a suspected dislocation that has reduced itself, a break around the elbow, a wound near the joint, a lost pulse, a numb hand or a tense forearm is referred to a facility with imaging, an orthopedic surgeon and an operating room. A simple dislocation treated where the right skills and follow-up exist may be managed there, but the decision to keep the patient belongs to the clinician who accepts responsibility for the outcome. The responder states plainly what was found, what was done, what changed and what is still unknown, and gives the times. The receiving team should be able to continue a story rather than to start a new one.

The elbow of a child behaves differently, and one difference matters more than any other. The ends of a child's bones are made of cartilage that does not appear on a radiograph in the same way as bone, so an injury that has moved the growing part can be hard to see. The elbow of a child is also the site of an injury in which the lower humerus breaks just above the joint, which can look like a dislocation while endangering the blood supply of the forearm. A child who will not use an arm, holds it still or cries when it is moved deserves radiographs and a clinician's examination. The scope of practice does not change because the patient is a child, but the threshold for imaging and referral is lower.

Age changes the elbow in ways that alter both the injury and the recovery. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break the radial head or the lower humerus in a fall from standing height. The same patient often has less muscle to protect the joint and more difficulty regaining movement, so rehabilitation matters as much as the operation. A patient who has dislocated an elbow before may do so again with less force, because the capsule and the ligaments have been stretched. In each of these patients an examination that relies on a single sign will mislead, and the response is a lower threshold for imaging and referral.

Some of the signs taught for this injury are less reliable than they sound. The pulse at the wrist may be present with a torn artery, and it may be absent for a moment in a patient who is cold or shocked and then return. The apparent shortening of the forearm is a comparison between two limbs, so it can be missed if only one arm is examined. The point of the elbow cannot always be felt clearly once the joint has swollen, and a wound may be small enough to hide under a sleeve. Sensation testing depends on the ability of the patient to describe what they feel, and age, fear and other injuries all affect that.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order. A delay of 6 hours is a common threshold for concern in teaching, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The record travels with the patient, because the comparison is worthless if the earlier finding cannot be produced. A patient whose condition changes during transport is reassessed, and the change is reported before the handover.

A constructed illustration may hold the sequence in mind. A middle-aged person trips on a step and falls onto one outstretched hand, and the elbow is found bent with the point standing out behind. The arm is supported in that position with a pillow, the hand is examined and the findings are written, and no one straightens the limb. The receiving clinician records the neurovascular status again, orders radiographs and checks for a break of the radial head and the coronoid process before any attempt to put the joint back. If the joint returns smoothly and the hand remains well, the patient is protected briefly and then begins supervised movement, and if it does not, the patient goes to the operating room. The example is an illustration and not a real patient, and every decision in it belongs to the clinician and to the local protocol.

The order is worth walking through once more. The first step is to assess, which means the scene, the mechanism, the primary survey in the order remembered as ABCDE and then the limb. The next is to stabilize, which means keeping the patient warm, controlling the bleeding that can be controlled and supporting the limb in the position found. Only then comes the neurovascular examination, performed before any intervention, recorded and repeated after every one. Immobilization follows, applied by the trained responder within the authorized equipment, and imaging comes after that, ordered by the clinician who will interpret it. Reassessment follows every intervention, and the last step is referral or definitive treatment, which belongs to the physician, the orthopedic surgeon and the vascular surgeon.

Transport adds its own hazards. The splinted limb is secured so that it cannot swing against the stretcher or the door, and the patient is positioned so that the whole patient can still be assessed. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. A patient with this injury and a mechanism that could have hurt the spine is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. The patient is covered against cold throughout the journey, and the hand is checked repeatedly, because a hand that was pink at the scene can become pale in a cold ambulance.

Rehabilitation begins when the joint has been reduced and held safely, and it is supervised rather than self-taught. The aim is a joint that moves again without becoming unstable, and the balance between movement and protection changes with the injury. A program that starts too late leaves a stiff elbow, and one that forces movement through pain can dislodge a fragment or stretch a ligament that is trying to heal. The patient is taught what to watch for at home, including increasing pain, numbness, a cold hand and any change in the shape of the limb. The number of weeks named for any stage of this recovery must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Two situations demand that the responder move faster than usual. The first is the arm that remains pulseless after the joint has been returned to its proper position, because the hand has a limited tolerance for a lack of blood. The second is the forearm that becomes tense, swollen and painful out of proportion to the injury, especially when the pain increases on stretching the fingers. In both situations the constricting device is released within the limits of the local protocol, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm. The patient is transferred urgently to a facility with a vascular surgeon. The responder does not explore the wound, does not remove an embedded object and does not push exposed bone back into the limb, because what to do with the vessel belongs to the surgeon.

An open dislocation, in which the joint has communicated with the outside, is treated as a contaminated wound from the first moment. The responder covers it with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the limb in the position found and arranges urgent transfer. The wound is not irrigated with anything improvised, not packed tightly and not explored, because the wound will be cleaned properly in an operating room. Protection against tetanus and the use of antibiotics are decisions made by the prescriber under the local protocol, and the wound itself makes the decision urgent. What the responder must not do is take a dose, a drug name or a schedule from a course that is listened to rather than read.

To summarize, a dislocated elbow is a joint whose surfaces have lost contact, most often with the forearm driven backward, and it is one of the dislocations in which delay damages the arm, because the brachial artery and the median, ulnar and radial nerves lie against the bone that has moved. The course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly, because definitive closure belongs to the operating room. An intact pulse does not exclude a torn artery and does not exclude a compartment syndrome, so the neurovascular examination is recorded before every intervention and repeated after every one. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment or the median nerve is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the team lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and the patient is reassessed after every intervention and watched until the handover. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 18 — Radial Head and Olecranon Fractures

The elbow holds two fractures that behave like opposites, and the difference between them is the difference between rotation and a pull. A radial head fracture is recognized when the patient cannot turn the palm up and down without pain, while an olecranon fracture is recognized by a gap at the back of the elbow that widens because the triceps pulls the broken piece away. Both injuries arrive at the same joint after a fall, and both are missed by a responder who looks only at the swelling. This chapter follows the order this course keeps everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. It names the provider level for every act, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The elbow is where three bones meet, and each of these two fractures belongs to a different one of them. The humerus ends in two rounded columns with a spool between them, and that spool is the hinge on which the forearm swings. The ulna runs to the wrist on the side of the little finger, and its upper end carries the olecranon, which is the point of the elbow and the lever on which the triceps pulls. The radius runs beside the ulna on the side of the thumb, and its upper end is a disc called the radial head, which turns against the rounded part of the humerus while the forearm rotates. The radial head is therefore a pivot and the olecranon is a lever, so the examination of one fracture tests rotation and the examination of the other tests straightening against resistance.

A radial head fracture usually follows a fall onto an outstretched hand with the elbow slightly bent, so that the force travels up the radius and drives the head against the humerus. The same fracture appears when the elbow is forced sideways, because the head is then crushed against the bone by the angulation of the joint. The energy may continue along the forearm and injure the wrist, which is why the wrist is examined in every patient whose elbow has been hurt. An illustration, offered as a constructed example and not as a description of any real patient, is a cyclist who lands on one hand and feels the pain on the outside of the elbow rather than in the wrist where the force entered. The mechanism is the first clue, and it is obtained before the limb is touched, because a patient in pain will guard the arm once the examination begins.

An olecranon fracture usually follows a direct blow to the point of the elbow, as when a person falls backward onto it, or a sudden violent contraction of the triceps that tears the bone apart where the tendon joins. Because the olecranon lies directly under the skin with almost no muscle over it, a blow there often breaks the skin as well as the bone, and an open injury is more common at this site than at most others in the body. The weight of the falling body, the hardness of the ground and the thinness of the covering are all part of the reason. A wound over the point of the elbow after a fall is therefore treated as an open fracture of the olecranon until a clinician has shown otherwise, and the wound is covered rather than inspected.

Neither fracture is obliged to arrive alone, and the examiner who finds one looks for the others. The elbow may have come apart at the moment of injury and gone back into place by itself, leaving a radial head fracture and a fracture of the coronoid process behind, and that combination is unstable even when the joint appears to be sitting in place. A radial head fracture may also travel with a torn membrane between the two forearm bones and an injury at the wrist, so that the whole forearm rather than the elbow alone has lost its length. When the diagnosis is in doubt, an elbow that has just been dislocated is treated as unstable and is referred. The responder does not test the joint to discover which of these is true.

Recognition of the radial head fracture begins with the patient's account and with a careful look from a step back. The elbow is held slightly bent, often with the forearm resting halfway between supination and pronation because any attempt to turn it further hurts. Swelling appears on the outside of the elbow, over the soft spot below the small bony prominence on the outer side of the humerus, and the point of greatest tenderness is found there with one finger rather than the whole hand. The examiner compares the two sides and may notice that the injured elbow has lost the last part of its straightening. The finding that gives this fracture its personality is a block to rotation, and the way to look for it is to ask rather than to push. When a piece of the head has been caught between the bone ends, rotation stops suddenly against a hard stop that will not clear with waiting, and deciding whether a stop is mechanical or simply produced by pain belongs to a clinician.

Recognition of the olecranon fracture is usually easier and sometimes too easy to trust. The back of the elbow is swollen, bruised and tender, and the examiner may feel a gap between the broken piece and the shaft of the ulna, with the piece riding higher than it should when the arm is bent. A scrape or a small wound over the point of the elbow is looked for in every case, and the patient is asked whether bone was visible at any moment. The ability to straighten the elbow is the sign most often taught for this fracture and the sign most often misleading. A fibrous expansion of the triceps may still transmit the pull across a widely separated break, and a painful elbow whose fracture has not moved at all may also refuse to straighten. The test is performed by asking and never by forcing the arm against the patient's resistance, because a sign that can be present in the wrong patient is a clue and not a test that decides.

Assessment follows the same order in this chapter as in every other, and the order exists because each step protects the next. The responder begins with the scene, checking for danger, noting the number of patients and the time of the injury, and considering the mechanism. The primary survey follows, remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and the limb is not examined in detail until the patient is stable enough to tolerate it. Life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The history then carries as much weight as the examination, so the age of the patient, the delay since the injury, and any illness or medicine that weakens bone or thins the blood are asked and recorded, because each answer raises the chance of a complication.

Examination of the limb is done by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move, and never by forcing movement. The responder looks at both arms from the front and from the side, comparing the position of the two elbows, the amount of swelling and the state of the skin from the shoulder to the fingers. Feeling is done gently, beginning away from the injured area and finishing with one finger over the point of greatest tenderness, so that the patient does not guard before the examination is complete. The joints above and below are checked, which here means the shoulder, the wrist and the small joints of the hand, because the force that broke the elbow may have injured them as well. Clothing is cut away rather than pulled over the broken limb, because a sleeve dragged over a fractured elbow moves the joint and may displace a fragment that was still in place.

Stabilization of an injured elbow in the field is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The arm is supported in the position in which it was found, with a sling, a pillow, a folded garment or the hands of the first aider, and it is never straightened, because the vessels and nerves lie against the bone around the elbow and a movement that looks helpful can tear what stayed intact. Straightening a deformed elbow may also convert a closed fracture into an open one, or release the pressure that a collection of blood was exerting on a torn vessel. The patient is kept warm, because cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and wet clothing around the arm is replaced with dry covering. Nothing is given by mouth to a patient who may need an operation.

Who may do what is stated plainly, because scope of practice is not a formality. The lay first aider supports the arm with the hands or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm and still, and calls for help, and nothing more is required of that level or permitted to it without training. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician or paramedic may apply a sling or a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and they record the neurovascular findings before and after doing so. The nurse and the physician in an emergency department may assess the limb, arrange imaging and give treatment within the protocol of the facility. The orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive treatment the fracture needs, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol rather than from any book.

The neurovascular examination is done before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down in words. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the hand, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and feels the pulse at the wrist on both the thumb side and the little finger side. Sensation is tested on both hands for comparison, and movement is tested by asking the patient to spread the fingers, bend the wrist and touch the thumb to each finger in turn. The pulse is never used alone to decide that the vessels are safe, because the elbow carries a rich network of smaller vessels that can keep the hand supplied even when one of the two main branches below the elbow has been torn. A pulse may therefore be present while a vessel is injured, and a hand that is pale, cool or slow to refill is a warning even when the pulse can be felt.

Three nerves pass around the elbow within a short distance of the bone, and each has a recognizable territory in the hand. The nerve that winds around the back of the humerus supplies the muscles that lift the wrist and straighten the fingers, so an injury to it shows as a wrist that droops and fingers that cannot be held out against gravity. The nerve that passes behind the bony ridge on the inner side of the elbow supplies most of the small muscles of the hand, so an injury to it shows as a hand that cannot spread the fingers or grip firmly, with numbness along the little finger. The nerve that passes through the front of the elbow supplies the muscles that turn the palm down and the deep muscles that bend the fingertips, so an injury to it may show only as an inability to pinch the tips of the thumb and the index finger together. Testing all three is quick, and it is repeated after every intervention.

Recording the findings is part of the treatment rather than a task that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the arm was found, the color, warmth, pulse, sensation and movement before the splint, the same observations after the splint, and any change in the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order. The receiving team then continues a story instead of starting a new one, and a change is recognized because there is something recorded to compare it with. The first question the surgeon will ask is not what the swelling looks like but what the arm could do before the splint was applied.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and at the elbow that means supporting the shoulder as well as the wrist. The arm is placed in a sling that carries the weight of the forearm, usually with the elbow bent at a right angle, and the sling is adjusted so that the hand sits higher than the elbow and the fingers remain visible. A collar and cuff, a broad arm sling or a padded splint may each be used, depending on what the local service authorizes. The exact angle at which the elbow is supported is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services differ, and the position of comfort is often the safest choice in the field. A patient who is more comfortable with the arm hanging is allowed to keep it there while the sling is prepared around that position.

A point of mechanics helps the responder understand why the arm is not forced into a tight bend when the olecranon is broken. The triceps pulls the fragment toward the shoulder, and bending the elbow increases the gap, so an olecranon fracture held tightly flexed may separate further while it waits. A radial head fracture behaves differently, because the joint surfaces are pressed together by the same movement and its fragments are not under the pull of a strong tendon. A splint or sling around a swollen elbow can also become a band, so padding is placed where the device presses on bone and the device is secured firmly enough to hold the arm without compressing the swelling. Every device is checked again after a short interval, and after any movement of the patient or change of position, because an improvised support shifts as the patient is moved.

An open injury at the elbow changes the priority of everything that follows, and the olecranon is one of the places where an open injury is most often seen. A wound over the point of the elbow is covered with a sterile dressing, and bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by pressure around the wound rather than by probing inside it. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and the bone carries contamination deeper when it is moved. The wound is never explored blindly, and definitive cleaning, repair and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. Tetanus protection and antibiotics are decided by a clinician according to the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the timing and the route are not described in this course.

Pain is treated as a finding to be recorded and as a symptom to be relieved within the limits of each provider's scope. The lay first aider offers reassurance, stillness and warmth and gives no medicine at all. The trained responder or paramedic may give analgesia only when the service protocol authorizes it and only after the neurovascular examination has been recorded, because a medicine that dulls the pain may also hide the change that matters most. The nurse and the physician decide what is appropriate, and the substance, the amount and the route belong to the local protocol and the prescriber rather than to this course. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain out of proportion to the injury, or pain that appears when the fingers are gently straightened, because those findings suggest a compartment syndrome rather than ordinary fracture pain.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph of the elbow is taken in at least two directions, and the side view is taken with the elbow truly sideways, because a view that is slightly rotated hides the fracture line and misleads the reader. Views taken with the forearm turned into different positions are often needed to show the radial head, and a fracture there may appear only as a faint line. Blood inside the joint pushes the pad of fat at the front of the elbow away from the bone, and that shadow on the side view means that something inside the joint is injured without saying what it is. Computed tomography shows the shape of the pieces when the fracture is comminuted, magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues including the ligaments and the cartilage, and both are ordered by the clinician responsible for the patient. A radiograph that looks normal in a patient with tenderness exactly over the radial head does not exclude a fracture.

Children deserve a separate word, because the ends of their bones are not yet bone. The upper end of the radius is largely cartilage in a young child, and cartilage does not show on a radiograph, so a fracture through it may be invisible even when the child will not use the arm. The age at which the bony center of the radial head appears is given in teaching as about 4 years, an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the range among healthy children is wide. The examiner therefore relies on tenderness, swelling, the refusal to use the arm and the mechanism, and refers a child whose elbow is tender over the radial head even when the radiograph is reported as normal.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with what was recorded before, because the comparison is what carries the information rather than any single measurement. The examiner checks the color, warmth, pulse, sensation and movement of the hand, asks about the pain, and looks at the fit of the sling or splint for tightness or a crease that presses on the skin. Pain that increases instead of settling, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a forearm that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. The front of the forearm is the compartment most often affected after an elbow injury, and the smallest vessels there fail while a pulse at the wrist can still be felt, so the diagnosis is clinical, time is muscle, and the responder releases whatever constricts the limb within local protocol, keeps the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, and refers urgently.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and for these two fractures the decision turns on what the joint can still do. A crack of the radial head that does not block rotation and has not moved is usually treated without an operation, with a short period of support followed by gentle movement, because the elbow stiffens faster than almost any other joint. A radial head fracture that blocks rotation, or that has lost its shape, or that travels with instability of the whole forearm, is treated by an orthopedic surgeon, and the choice among removing a fragment, holding it with metal or replacing the head belongs to that surgeon. An olecranon fracture that has separated is pulled apart by the triceps, so it is treated by an operation that holds the pieces while the bone heals, and one of these two fractures punishes stiffness while the other punishes delay. All of those acts are learned under supervision, and none of them is taught from a book.

Reduction is the act of restoring the position of the bone ends, traction is a gentle and continuous pull that holds them in line, and casting or surgical fixation holds the position while the bone heals. Each of them is described here so that the listener understands what is being done and why, and none of them is taught here as a technique, because the feel of a joint that is about to yield and the moment to stop are learned with a teacher, under supervision, and certified by an authority. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. Each of those situations can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. For these two fractures the elbow is not manipulated, not straightened, not pulled and not rotated to see whether it moves better afterwards, and force is not a technique.

One pattern deserves special attention, because it is easy to treat as an elbow problem when it is really a problem of the whole forearm. When the force of a fall travels up the radius, it can tear the membrane that connects the two forearm bones and injure the joint at the wrist, so that the radius slides toward the hand and the forearm loses its length. The finding to record is pain at the wrist and tenderness along the space between the two bones, and the decision about how to manage it belongs to the orthopedic surgeon. Older adults deserve the same attention for a different reason, since bone that has lost density breaks with little energy and the fracture may be far less painful than its severity suggests. An older adult who has fallen and now has pain on the outside of the elbow is treated as having a fracture until a clinician decides otherwise.

The choice of where to send the patient should be made early rather than at the moment of departure. A facility that can take radiographs, examine a limb and call upon an orthopedic surgeon is needed when the elbow is deformed, when a wound over the point of the elbow is present, when the pulse or sensation has changed, when the forearm is tense, or when the patient is a child with tenderness over the radial head. When the distance is long, the responder says plainly what has been found and what is feared, so that the receiving team can prepare. The care is shared, and each level reports what it has done and what it cannot do, using the same order every time. Everything in this chapter is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision.

A constructed illustration, offered as a teaching example and not as a description of any real patient, may help to fix the sequence in mind. A woman of middle age trips on a step and falls onto her outstretched hand, and afterward holds her right arm bent with the palm facing neither up nor down. Her wrist is not tender, and the only tender spot she can identify is on the outside of the elbow over the radial head. The first aider supports the arm as it lies and keeps her warm, while the responder records that her fingers are warm and pink and that turning her palm upward reproduces the pain. A splint is applied in the position found, the hand is left visible for later checks, and the findings are recorded again after the splint. At the hospital a clinician orders radiographs and decides the definitive treatment.

To summarize, the elbow holds two fractures that behave like opposites, and the radial head fracture is recognized by tenderness on the outside of the elbow with pain or a hard block when the palm is turned, while the olecranon fracture is recognized by swelling over the point of the elbow, a gap that widens because the triceps pulls the fragment, and often a wound over the bone. The ability to straighten the elbow is unreliable in both directions, and a normal radiograph in a patient with tenderness exactly over the radial head does not exclude a fracture, so the arm is splinted in the position found and never straightened, because the vessels and nerves lie against the bone. The neurovascular status is examined and recorded before any splint and repeated after every intervention, the fingers are left visible so that the hand can be watched, and the limb is kept warm. Pain out of proportion to the injury, a tense forearm, a changing pulse or new numbness stop the responder and prompt urgent referral, because a compartment syndrome is diagnosed clinically and time is muscle. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, an open wound is covered and never explored, an embedded object is never removed, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound. Reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when training or equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed. Every figure here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, no dose, route or regimen is given, and the course remains educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 19 — Forearm Fractures

The forearm is two bones rather than one, and that fact decides almost everything about how its fractures behave. The radius lies on the thumb side and the ulna on the little finger side, and the two are joined along most of their length by a strong sheet of fibrous tissue called the interosseous membrane. Together the bones, that membrane and the joints at each end form a ring, and a ring cannot fail in only one place. A fracture of one bone is therefore treated as an injury of the whole forearm until someone qualified has shown otherwise, and the examination and the imaging must reach the elbow above and the wrist below. This chapter follows the order used in every chapter of this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively.

The reason the forearm has two bones is rotation. When the radius turns around the ulna the palm turns from facing forward to facing backward, and that movement places the hand where the eye and the work need it. A fracture that heals with the bones in the wrong rotational relationship, even one that looks straight on a picture, costs the patient the ability to turn the palm, and that loss is felt in eating, in dressing and in every task that asks the hand to be turned. The examiner compares the two sides, notes which way the palm and the thumb are pointing, and records that before anything is applied to the limb.

The ulna is easy to feel along its whole length because its border lies just under the skin, and that same lack of covering is why a break of the ulna is more likely than most fractures to open through the skin. The nerves of the forearm travel in the spaces around the bones, with the median nerve on the palm side, the ulnar nerve along the little finger side of the ulna, and the radial nerve winding around the upper radius. The arteries follow a similar path, one on the thumb side and one on the little finger side, and the hand is fed by both of them. A pulse at the wrist may therefore survive the loss of one artery while the other is already compromised, which is one reason the examination looks for more than a pulse.

Forearm fractures arrive by a small number of routes, and the mechanism tells the responder what else to suspect. A fall onto an outstretched hand drives force up the radius from the wrist and is the commonest route to a break of the lower forearm. A direct blow, a fall from a height, a road collision or a crush sends energy across both bones at once and is the setting in which the two are broken together. A raised forearm used to shield the head can produce a break of the ulna near the elbow together with a dislocation at the elbow, and a fall onto a fixed hand can produce the mirror image at the wrist. The responder records the mechanism in the words of the patient or of a witness, because the pattern of injury is often written in that account.

Assessment begins before any hand is laid on the limb. The responder looks at the position of the arm, the shape of the forearm, the direction in which the palm and the thumb are facing, and whether the skin is broken. A forearm that is bent, shortened or twisted is left exactly as it is found, because the broken ends may be lying against a vessel or a nerve, so a well meaning attempt to make the limb look straight can tear what is still intact. The responder asks about pain, about numbness or tingling in the hand and about whether the fingers can be moved, and compares what is said with the other side. Tenderness is sought along both bones and at the elbow and the wrist, because pain in either joint points to a second injury that a break of one bone alone would not explain. The findings are said aloud and written down with the time, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards.

The rule that governs this region is that a break of one bone is presumed to have injured the other bone or the membrane between them until that has been excluded. A single break can displace only if the ring has failed somewhere else, so the examiner looks for tenderness over the other bone, for a step in its surface, and for pain when the forearm is turned. The membrane can tear without a second fracture, and that injury alone can allow the two bones to come together and to block rotation. When any part of this picture is present, the responder stops testing, immobilizes the limb in the position found, and refers the patient to a clinician who can examine and image the whole forearm.

The findings of a both bone injury are usually plain, and they are worth describing in the order in which a listener would notice them. The forearm looks shorter than the other one, it is bent, and the hand hangs or points in a direction the patient cannot correct. The smooth ridge of the ulna, which should run as one continuous line under the skin, is interrupted by a step, and the width of the arm is increased by swelling that is already present at the first examination. The skin over that ridge is examined with particular care, because a sharp end of bone lying just beneath it can break through during handling, and a wound of any size means an open fracture. The palm may lie face down when the patient is sure it was face up before the injury, and that single observation tells the examiner that the bones have rotated.

Two patterns of injury show how closely the elbow, the forearm and the wrist are bound together. In the first, the ulna breaks near the elbow and the head of the radius slips out of its joint at the same time, and the injury at the elbow is easily missed because attention is drawn to the obvious break below it. In the second, the radius breaks near the wrist and the joint between the two lower ends of the bones is disrupted, so the ulna rides out of line at the wrist while the radius alone appears broken on the picture. Both patterns carry the names of the clinicians who first described them, and both show that the ring has failed in two places. The treatment of both belongs to an orthopedic surgeon, and neither is corrected in the field.

Stabilization of a forearm injury is a small set of acts performed in a fixed order, and the first of them is restraint. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found, with the hands, with a pillow, or with whatever padding is at hand, and it is never straightened, because force applied to a deformed forearm can convert a closed injury into an open one and can release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. Bleeding from an open wound is controlled by the pressure that can be applied, without blind exploration of the wound and without removing anything embedded in it, and exposed bone is covered and left where it lies. The patient is kept warm, wet clothing is replaced with covering, and the limb is protected from the cold ground, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. The lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment and calls for help, while the trained responder and the paramedic act within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes.

Transport is part of stabilization and not a separate errand. A patient with a forearm injury is moved in the position of greatest comfort, usually sitting if there is no other reason to lie flat, with the forearm supported across the chest and never allowed to hang by the side, because a dependent hand swells quickly. The limb is supported by the hands of the responder and by the splint together, and the movement is planned aloud before it is made so that no one pulls on the injured arm. Where the mechanism could have loaded the spine, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and such a patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and in the forearm it is the step that decides how urgently the patient must move. The examiner looks at the color of the hand and at whether the fingers are pale, dusky or mottled, and feels the temperature of the hand against the other side. The pulse is felt at the wrist on the thumb side and on the little finger side, and the time taken for color to return after a nail is pressed is noted. Sensation is tested in the web between the thumb and the index finger, along the little finger and over the back of the hand, and the patient is asked to spread the fingers, to make a fist, to bend the wrist and to straighten the thumb, because each of those movements depends on a different nerve. A pulse that is present does not exclude injury to an artery or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency that overrides everything else.

The forearm holds several closed compartments, and the one on the palm side is the one most often threatened by bleeding and swelling after a fracture of both bones. Because the fascia does not stretch, the pressure inside rises rather than dispersing, and the smallest vessels fail first, so muscle and nerve are starved while the pulse at the wrist may still be easily felt. The earliest and most reliable finding is pain that is out of proportion to the injury and that increases rather than settles, particularly when the fingers are straightened by someone else, and it is followed by a limb that feels tense and hard to the touch. Numbness and tingling in the fingers, weakness, and a hand that feels cool or looks pale come later, and a responder who waits for them has waited too long. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so the responder acts on suspicion within the limits of the local protocol and does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late. The arm is not elevated above the level of the heart, because that lowers the pressure that is keeping what flow remains, and the patient is referred urgently.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured bones and of the joints above and below them, and in the forearm that means the support must span the elbow and the wrist. A support that holds only the bones between the two joints allows the broken ends to move every time the elbow or the wrist is used, and that movement is exactly what it was meant to prevent. The splint is padded where it presses on a bony point, it is applied over the position in which the limb was found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. A sling supports the weight of the forearm and is adjusted so that the hand is not left hanging below the elbow, since a dependent hand swells. Casting, traction and definitive immobilization are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a book in this course.

The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the nurse may do so within the standing orders of the ward or the clinic, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization the injury requires. The moment the splint is secured, the neurovascular examination is repeated in the same order and compared with what was recorded before, because a splint that is too tight shows itself first in the fingers and not in the forearm. The responder checks that the fingers are warm, that their color is normal, that they can be moved and that sensation has not changed, and asks whether the pain has changed. If the pain is worse, if the fingers tingle or feel numb, or if the hand has become pale or cool, the splint is loosened at once by whoever is authorized to do it and the patient is escalated. An intervention that is followed by a worsening examination has failed, and the correct response is not to wait and see.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and for a forearm injury it must show the whole length of both bones together with the elbow above and the wrist below, since a picture of the shaft alone hides the dislocation that so often accompanies the break. Computed tomography is used when the pattern near a joint is complex or when the relationship of the fragments is unclear, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including the membrane between the bones and the ligaments around the joints. Each study is requested only when the answer it gives will change what is done, and the choice belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient. The lay first aider never orders or interprets an image, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed.

An image is a picture of one moment, and it does not replace the examination or the reassessment. A fracture can be present when the first picture looks normal, particularly in a child, and a fracture can displace after the picture was taken, so a limb that is more painful or more swollen than the image suggests is treated according to the limb and not according to the picture. The same caution applies at the other end of life, where a bone that has lost density can break with little force and where the injury may hurt less than its severity suggests. Where this chapter names a time, a size or a distance, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions.

The reassessment that follows immobilization is repeated at intervals, and its purpose is to catch the complication caused by the treatment rather than the one caused by the injury. Swelling inside a splint or a cast has nowhere to go, so the limb is checked for the pain, the tightness and the loss of movement that mark a rising pressure, and the fingers are checked for warmth, color, movement and sensation. A bandage that encircles the limb, a cast applied over an arm that later swelled, or a splint secured too tightly can each produce the harm, and each is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do so. The pain of a forearm fracture should settle with support and with the measures the local protocol provides for comfort, and pain that climbs despite them is the finding that stops the process and sends the patient for urgent review.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and in the forearm the decision turns on how many parts of the ring have failed and how well the soft tissues have tolerated it. A fracture of both bones in an adult is treated as an unstable injury and is referred to an orthopedic surgeon, because the two bones cannot hold each other in place and the position a splint achieves is lost as the swelling changes. A break of one bone with tenderness or instability at the other bone, at the elbow or at the wrist is referred for the same reason, since the second injury is the one that will limit the arm if it is missed. An open fracture, a limb with a failing pulse, a hand that is numb or weak, and any suspicion of a compartment syndrome are referred urgently to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. A fracture that enters a joint, a fracture in a child that crosses the growth region, and a fracture in a patient whose bone is weakened by disease or by long use of a medicine are also referred, because each needs a judgment that cannot be made where the patient lies.

Definitive treatment of a forearm fracture aims at three things, which are to restore the length of the bones, to correct the rotation so that the palm can turn again, and to hold both until the bone heals. A clinician may achieve this by reduction, which restores the position of the broken ends, followed by a cast or a brace in the injuries that will hold their position, and by an operation in those that will not. In an operation the surgeon may expose the bones and hold the fragments with metal plates and screws, an act called open reduction and internal fixation, or may pass a rod inside the canal of each bone, a method used particularly in children so that the growth regions are not crossed. Traction may be used as a temporary measure to hold the limb in line with a gentle continuous pull while the patient waits, and it is applied only by those trained and authorized to apply it. Every one of these acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training and never to a book.

Pain is treated, and the listener will not find a substance, an amount, a route or a frequency in this course. The decision about which medicine to give, how much, and by which path belongs to a prescriber working within the local protocol, and the responder's part is to report the pain, to support and immobilize the limb, to keep the patient warm, and to ask for help early rather than late. A finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, rising or out of proportion to the injury, because that finding may mark a compartment syndrome, and pain that is masked is not pain that has been treated. The lay first aider gives nothing by mouth and nothing by any other route, and the trained responder, the nurse and the paramedic give only what the protocol of their service authorizes them to give. Sedation, tetanus protection and antibiotics are likewise decisions for a clinician, and where the injury is open the finding that makes them urgent is the wound itself.

Swelling deserves its own attention because it is the complication that a well applied splint can cause. The forearm has little room to spare, and fluid that collects after a both bone fracture can raise the pressure inside the compartments within hours, so the limb is watched rather than merely supported. A hand that is allowed to hang below the elbow will swell, which is why a sling is adjusted so that the forearm lies level or slightly raised, and why the fingers are left visible at all times. Cooling may be part of the local protocol, but it is never applied so as to numb the limb, never left in place without checking the skin beneath it, and never allowed to delay the referral of a patient whose pain is climbing.

Children break the bones of the forearm more often than adults do, and their injuries differ in ways that change the response. The bone of a child is more elastic, so it can bend without breaking, and it can break on one side only, with the other side intact and the bone bowed rather than separated. None of that is a reason to be casual, because the growth region near each end of the bone can be injured without an obvious fracture, and an injury there can shorten or deform the arm for life. A child who will not use the arm, who cries when the forearm is turned, or whose hand looks pale or feels cool is referred without debate, and the decisions about reduction and about casting belong to a clinician trained in the care of children.

The elbow and the wrist lose their movement quickly when they are held still, and the rotation of the forearm is the hardest of all to regain once it has been lost. This is why the fingers, the thumb and the shoulder are moved as soon as the treating clinician permits, even while the forearm itself is held, because a shoulder that is not moved while the arm is in a sling can become painful and stiff in its own right. Rehabilitation is prescribed and supervised by the treating clinician together with a physical therapist or an occupational therapist, and its pace is set by the surgeon and by the local protocol rather than by the impatience of the patient. The responder's part is to explain why the fingers must keep moving, to keep the arm supported and warm, and to pass on any increase in pain, swelling or numbness instead of dismissing it as part of recovery.

The record is part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time and the mechanism of the injury, the position in which the forearm was found, the state of the skin, the findings of the neurovascular examination before and after every intervention, and every change in the condition of the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. A handover that says only that the arm is broken leaves the next clinician to guess what the arm was like before the splint went on. Every technique named in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, and a constructed example used in teaching is an illustration rather than a real patient.

A deformed forearm is never straightened in the field, because the broken ends may be lying against the vessels and the nerves, and the movement that makes the limb look better can take away the hand. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, since the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and the bone carries contamination inward. An open wound is never explored blindly; it is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the neurovascular status is recorded, the limb is immobilized in the position found, and the patient is referred urgently, with definitive closure left to the operating room. The stability of the two bones is never tested by pulling or twisting them, because that examination is a clinical skill learned under supervision and not a field test, and a test performed in the field can turn a stable injury into an unstable one. Nothing is given by mouth to a patient who may need an operation, no medicine is given outside the local protocol, and no transfer is delayed for the sake of a tidier dressing or a straighter limb.

To summarize, the forearm is a ring formed by the radius, the ulna, the membrane between them and the joints at each end, so a fracture of one bone is presumed to have injured the other or the membrane until that is excluded, and the examination and the images must include the elbow above and the wrist below. What to look for is a forearm that is bent, shortened or twisted, a palm that faces the wrong way, a break in the smooth ridge of the ulna, a wound, tenderness over the other bone, and pain in either joint, and what to record is the color, warmth, pulse, sensation and movement of the hand before any intervention and again after every one. What to do is to support the limb in the position found, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, to cover a wound and an embedded object without removing or exploring anything, to immobilize the forearm and both joints, to keep the patient warm, to reassess after every act, and to refer a both bone injury, an open injury, a failing pulse, a numb or weak hand and any suspected compartment syndrome urgently to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. What never to do is to straighten a deformed limb, to push exposed bone back into a wound, to test the stability of the bones by pulling or twisting them, to give any medicine outside the local protocol, or to delay a transfer for a tidier appearance. The neurovascular examination is never skipped and never assumed, reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the person to call is the clinician responsible for the patient and the receiving facility that can treat the injury definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 20 — Wrist Fractures

The wrist is the part of the arm that people break most often, and the bone that breaks is usually the lower end of the radius, the bone on the thumb side of the forearm that carries most of the weight of the hand. Beside it lies the ulna, thinner and ending a little lower, joined to the radius in a way that lets the palm turn from facing forward to facing backward. An injury here can look dramatic and still heal well, or look modest and still threaten the fingers, so the responder trusts the examination rather than the appearance. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What is written here is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, the protocol of your service, or the law of the country in which you work.

The lower end of the radius is broad and flat where it meets the small bones of the hand, and that broad surface carries most of the load when a person catches a fall. The ulna carries less of that load, but it provides the pivot that lets the forearm rotate, and the joint between the two lower ends is part of the injury whenever the radius is displaced. On the little finger side of the wrist a person can feel a small point of bone called the ulnar styloid, which is where the ligaments that steady the arrangement attach, and it is often broken at the same time. Because the two bones and their joints work as one unit, an injury of one is treated as an injury of both until somebody qualified has shown otherwise.

The median nerve is what makes this fracture more than a broken bone. It passes through a fibrous tunnel at the front of the wrist together with the tendons that bend the fingers, and the tunnel has no room to give. The nerve lies just under the skin across the front of the joint, and the lower end of the radius lies directly behind it, so a bone that tilts backward presses the nerve against the roof of the tunnel. That nerve carries sensation from the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger and the thumb side of the ring finger, and it carries the movement that turns the thumb across the palm. The ulnar nerve runs along the little finger side and supplies the little finger and the adjacent part of the ring finger, while a branch of the radial nerve supplies the back of the hand between the thumb and the index finger.

The commonest mechanism is a fall onto an outstretched hand, in which the weight of the body travels up the arm while the hand is fixed against the ground. The force bends the lower end of the radius backward, and the more it tilts, the more the shape of the wrist changes. A fall from a height, a road collision, a direct blow from a heavy object, and a fall in which the hand is trapped all injure the same region with more energy behind them, so the soft tissues suffer more. A fall onto the back of the hand, or a blow that drives the hand forward instead of backward, produces the opposite tilt, and the names used for the two shapes differ between countries and between editions of the same text. The mechanism tells the responder what else to suspect, because the same fall that broke the wrist may have injured the elbow, the shoulder, the neck or the head.

Most listeners have seen the shape called the dinner-fork deformity, named after the curve of a fork that lies on a table with its handle raised. The lower end of the radius tilts backward, the hand follows it, and the back of the wrist takes on a step that a hand can feel before the eye is certain. The responder does not need the name in order to act, because the shape is only a sign, and a wrist that looks almost straight may still be broken. What matters is that the deformity is seen, described in plain words and left exactly as it was found. Straightening it is not a field act, however tempting the shape looks, and the reason is the nerve and the vessels that lie against the front of the bone.

A wrist is never treated on its own, and the assessment begins with the scene and with the patient rather than with the arm. The primary survey comes first, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. A patient who fell hard enough to break a wrist may also have a head injury, a chest injury or bleeding elsewhere, and a patient who is confused after a fall cannot be considered as a wrist alone. When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, the principle that decides the order is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. Only when the patient is stable enough does the examination turn to the wrist, and the wrist is then examined by looking, by feeling and by asking, never by forcing.

Assessment of the wrist itself begins with questions, and the answers shape everything that follows. The responder asks when the injury happened, how it happened, which hand the patient uses for writing and for work, and what the patient was doing in the moment before the fall. The age of the patient matters, because the bone of a child bends where the bone of an adult snaps, and the bone of an older adult may break with very little force. Illnesses and medicines that weaken bone belong in the history, as does an earlier injury or operation on the same wrist, since an old injury can make a new one harder to read. The responder asks whether the fingers can be moved, whether they feel normal, and whether the pain is spreading up the arm or into the hand. A patient who cannot remember the fall, or who was found on the floor with no account of it, is assessed for a medical cause of the fall as well as for the fracture.

The first look is taken before anything is touched, and it is compared with the other side. The responder notes the position of the hand, the shape of the wrist, the direction in which the palm and the thumb are turned, and whether the skin is broken. Swelling can hide a deformity and can also disguise how far the bone has moved, so a wrist that swells quickly is watched rather than squeezed. Skin that is stretched and shiny over a bone pressing from beneath is a warning that the cover may give way, and such a finding is reported at once even while the skin is still whole.
