A wound near the wrist makes the injury open until a clinician has shown otherwise, and even a small puncture is treated as a communication with the deep tissues.

Feeling and asking come next, and both are done gently. The examiner feels along the bones for tenderness and for a step in the surface, and compares the two wrists without pressing hard on the injured one. The hollow at the base of the thumb on the back of the hand is felt for tenderness, because the small bone inside it, called the scaphoid, is the bone most often missed when a wrist is injured, and it may not be visible on the first radiograph for some days. The examiner asks the patient to move the fingers and the thumb, and never pulls or pushes the wrist to test how stable it is, because that test belongs to a clinician and can convert a closed injury into an open one. Sensation is tested on the pads of the fingers of both hands, and the patient is asked whether the two sides feel the same.

Stabilization of the wrist is a small set of acts whose most important member is restraint. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found, with a pillow, a rolled blanket or the patient's own body, and it is never straightened in the field. An object embedded in the wrist is never removed, and bone that has come through the skin is never pushed back into the wound, because both may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and both carry contamination deeper. A wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, and the wound is never explored blindly. The lay first aider does these acts with whatever is at hand and calls for help, while the trained responder works within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes. Definitive cleaning and closure of an open injury belong to the operating room and to nobody else.

Stabilization also belongs to the whole patient, and it continues while the limb is being handled. The patient is kept warm, because cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and wet clothing is replaced with covering while the ground beneath the patient is insulated. If the fall was from a height, or the patient struck the head or the neck, the spine is treated as unstable until somebody qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. Whether the patient may eat or drink before definitive care is decided by the receiving team, not by the responder and not by this course. The handover carries the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, and the neurovascular findings with the times at which they were taken.

The neurovascular examination is the step that must never be skipped, and it is performed before any intervention and again afterwards. The examiner looks at the color of the hand and fingers and at the warmth of the skin, and compares one side with the other. The pulse is felt at the wrist on the thumb side, and the examiner presses briefly on a fingernail and watches the color return, a test that is quick and that can be repeated without hurting the patient. Sensation is tested in each finger, with the median territory of the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger and the thumb side of the ring finger given particular attention, because that is the nerve this fracture threatens most often. The patient is asked to bend and straighten the fingers and to spread them, and any movement that has become weaker than before is recorded as a change. Pain is treated as a finding rather than as a complaint, and the patient is asked to describe it, because pain out of proportion to the injury is the earliest signal of a compartment that is filling.

The result of that examination is written before the limb is immobilized and written again after, and it is written so that another person can compare the two. A finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and a numbness discovered after splinting will be blamed on the splint when it may have been present from the moment of the fall. The patient's own words are kept where possible, since a patient who says that the fingers feel like wood is describing a change that no measurement in this course can replace. A second examiner repeats the observations in the same order, and the value lies in the comparison rather than in any single finding. The record travels with the patient, and it is part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it.

Some patients cannot give a reliable examination, and the responder must know that before trusting a reassuring answer. A young child may be too frightened to say what can be felt, an older adult who is confused may answer at random, and a patient who has been drinking or who has a head injury may not report numbness at all. In such a patient the examination is repeated at intervals, the limb is compared with the other side, and the threshold for immobilization and for referral is lowered rather than raised. A pulse that can be felt does not exclude serious damage to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that cannot be felt is an emergency. Consider an illustration, and only an illustration: an older patient with a broken wrist who says the hand is fine, whose answers grow vague as the hours pass, and whose fingers are found to be cooler and duller than those of the other side is a patient who must be seen again and moved urgently. A sign that is absent in one patient is not a sign that is absent in the injury.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is held alone can still be moved from either end. The material matters less than the principle, and a padded board, a folded magazine, a pillow or a sling can each serve, so long as it is padded where it presses on bone and secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band. The lay first aider supports the limb and does not apply a formal splint, while the trained responder and the paramedic apply splints and slings within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. The physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace or an operation, and that decision is made with the images in front of them. Whatever is applied, the fingers are left visible and able to be examined, because the hand is the part that will show the complication first.

A splint that is too tight is the complication this course fears most, and it can happen with the best material and the kindest intention. The responder checks that the fingers have not become swollen, pale, cool or numb since the splint was applied, and that the skin at the edges of the material is not being rubbed or pinched. An improvised device shifts more than a manufactured one, so it is checked more often, and a sling that holds the arm too high or too tightly can press in the wrong place. If any of those findings appears, the responder does not adjust the limb or remove the device unless the local protocol authorizes it, and instead reports the change and gets the patient seen. Cold is part of the problem as well, so the hand is covered and not left exposed on a cold surface.

The neurovascular examination is repeated after the splint is applied, and this second examination has the same standing as the first. The examiner checks the color and the warmth of the fingers, the pulse, the return of color after pressure on a nail, the sensation in each finger and the ability to move the fingers. The two records are then compared, and any deterioration is reported as an emergency rather than as a detail. Numbness that appears only after a splint has been applied suggests that the splint is the cause, and the constricting material is released within the limits of the local protocol by somebody authorized to do it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart when a compartment syndrome is suspected, and the patient is not left waiting in a corridor for a radiograph while the hand is changing. The purpose of the examination is to notice the complication while it can still be reversed.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. The images of the wrist are read with particular attention to the joint surface of the radius, to the ulnar styloid, and to the small bones of the hand, including the scaphoid at the base of the thumb. That bone may look normal on the first radiograph and still be broken, which is why tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb is treated as a fracture until it is shown not to be, a practice whose details differ between services. Computed tomography shows the detail of a break that reaches into the joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues and for the bone that the radiograph cannot settle. The lay first aider never orders or interprets an image, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed.

A second radiograph is often taken after a splint has been applied or after a reduction has been performed, because what matters is where the bone lies inside the device and not only how it looked before. The image is a picture of one moment, and the limb must still be examined after the picture has been taken, since a film cannot report pain, sensation or the tightness of a bandage. Some wrists are imaged again during the following days and weeks, because a break can move inside a cast as the swelling settles, and a break of the scaphoid may become visible only on a later study. The responder's part is to keep the limb supported, to keep the patient warm, and to pass on what has changed since the last observation.

Pain in a broken wrist is treated by a prescriber, and the responder must not be able to take a prescription from this course. The name of the substance, the amount, the route and the frequency belong to the local protocol and to the clinician who knows the patient, and no dose appears here on purpose. What the responder contributes is the finding that makes the decision urgent, which is pain out of proportion to the injury, pain that increases while the limb is at rest, or a patient whose pain is not controlled by the plan already in place. A nerve block at the wrist is a procedure for a clinician trained and authorized to perform it, and a reduction performed under sedation belongs to a clinician working with monitoring and help in a setting that can manage the airway. Whether tetanus protection is needed after a wound is a decision for the prescriber, who weighs the wound, the history of the patient and the local protocol, and the responder's part is to report the wound and the time it happened. Anything given by a responder is given only under a protocol that authorizes that responder to give it.

Reassessment after every intervention is the step that catches the complication caused by treatment, and in the wrist there are two complications to watch. The first is compression of the median nerve inside its tunnel, in which the numbness present at the start spreads or deepens, the thumb weakens, and the hand becomes clumsy. The second is a compartment syndrome of the forearm, in which the pressure inside a closed space of muscle rises, the pain becomes severe and out of proportion, the forearm is tense and swollen, and the fingers hurt when they are moved by the examiner. The diagnosis is clinical and belongs to a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects either of them does not wait for confirmation that will arrive too late. The constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol by somebody authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently. A limb that becomes worse after a splint has been applied is a limb whose splint must be examined again, not a limb to be tolerated.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and it begins with the recognition that some wrists cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open injury, a damaged nerve or vessel, a suspected compartment syndrome, a break that reaches into the joint, a break in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone, a suspected break of the scaphoid, or a wrist that has dislocated as well as broken is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The interval that makes an open injury urgent is measured in hours rather than days, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs between services and countries. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, casting, which holds the position while the bone knits, and surgical fixation, in which a surgeon holds the fragments with metal devices in an operation called open reduction and internal fixation. Each of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique does not come from a book, this one included.

A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and the reason is that force applied to the wrong thing tears what is still intact. A responder who meets resistance stops, because resistance is information and force is not a technique. Traction is sometimes used in a fracture clinic as a temporary way of holding a wrist while other decisions are made, and it is applied there by people trained to do it, never in the field and never as a substitute for the transfer of the patient. The listener is not being taught to reduce a wrist, and no chapter in this course teaches reduction, traction or casting as a skill to be learned from a book.

After the wrist has been treated the work is not finished, and the hand must be observed as carefully as before. The cast or splint is checked for tightness and for pressure over the bony points, the neurovascular status is recorded again, and the patient is told in plain words what change should bring them back. Stiffness of the fingers is the outcome that costs the most in the long run, so the fingers are kept moving when the treating clinician allows it, and how soon and how much is decided by that clinician and by the therapist rather than by the responder. In a child the injury may cross the growing part of the bone, and healing there needs follow-up for a longer period than the fracture alone suggests, while in an older adult the same fall may be the first sign that the bone is weak, and that question belongs to the treating team. Every interval named in this chapter, including the weeks that a bone takes to knit, is an illustration that must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such numbers differ between services, countries and editions.

To summarize, the wrist is the part of the arm that people break most often, and the break is usually at the lower end of the radius, with the ulna and its styloid often involved at the same time because the two bones work as one unit. The median nerve crosses the front of the joint inside a narrow tunnel, so a backward tilt of the bone, swelling or a tight splint can take away the feeling in the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger and the thumb side of the ring finger, and the same nerve can be compressed into a clumsy, weak hand. The dinner-fork shape and the tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb are signs to be recognized and recorded, not corrected, and a limb is splinted in the position in which it is found and is never straightened in the field. The neurovascular status is examined before any intervention and after every one, with the color, the warmth, the pulse, the sensation in each finger and the movement of the fingers written down with the time, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. An embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Cold is a complication of trauma, the spine is treated as unstable until somebody qualified has cleared it, and pain, antibiotics and tetanus protection are decisions for the prescriber, with the substance and the amount left to the local protocol. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint is shattered, when a fragment is trapped, when the nerves or vessels are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the training or equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 21 — Carpal Dislocations

The wrist is a place where many small bones meet, and that is the reason an injury there can hide from the person who examines it. A carpal dislocation means that one or more of the small bones of the wrist have moved out of the line they keep with each other and with the forearm, so the hand may lose not only its comfort but its feeling and its grip. It is one of the injuries this course calls subtle, because the wrist may look puffy rather than deformed, because the patient can still move the fingers, and because a radiograph taken from one direction alone may appear almost normal. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter keeps that order exactly. What follows is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The carpus is the group of small bones between the forearm and the bones of the hand, and there are eight of them, arranged in two rows. The row nearer the forearm holds the scaphoid, the lunate, the triquetrum and the pisiform, while the row nearer the fingers holds the trapezium, the trapezoid, the capitate and the hamate. The lunate sits in the middle of the near row and takes its name from its shape, which is that of a half moon. It is the keystone of the wrist, because the forearm bone called the radius rests on it and the capitate, the largest bone of the far row, sits in a hollow on its far surface, so that the two form a ball resting in a cup. The scaphoid bridges the two rows on the thumb side and swings like a link whenever the wrist bends, and short, strong ligaments with a fibrous capsule hold the whole arrangement together, so it is the ligaments rather than the bones that decide what happens when the wrist is injured.

On the palm side of the wrist the carpal bones form an arch, and a broad band of fibrous tissue stretches across the arch to make a passage. Through that passage run the tendons that bend the fingers and, with them, the median nerve, which gives feeling to the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger and half of the ring finger, and which works the short muscles at the base of the thumb. The passage has no room to spare even in health, so anything that narrows it presses on the nerve. This is why the median nerve appears again and again in injuries of the wrist, and why it is the nerve an examiner asks about first. The ulnar nerve, which gives feeling to the little finger, passes outside the passage on the other side of the wrist, and the radial nerve supplies feeling over the back of the hand, so a carpal dislocation can injure any of the three, although the median nerve is the one most often caught.

The usual mechanism is a fall onto an outstretched hand, with the wrist bent back and the weight of the body arriving through the palm. The force travels along the radius into the lunate and then into the capitate, and the lunate is levered against the bones around it until the ligaments that hold it give way. A low energy fall may stretch or partly tear those ligaments, or break the scaphoid, while a fall from a height or from a moving vehicle may tear them completely and carry the far row of carpal bones off the back of the lunate. The injury is best understood as one spectrum rather than several diseases, because at one end the ligaments are stretched, in the middle the link between the scaphoid and the lunate fails, and at the far end the far row of carpal bones moves out of place, which is called a perilunate dislocation, or the lunate itself is driven forward out of its socket, which is called a lunate dislocation. When a break of the scaphoid travels with the dislocation, the injury is called a trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture dislocation, and it is the most unstable of the group. The energy of the injury predicts the damage, so a violent mechanism deserves more suspicion than a simple fall, although thin bone may give way in a fall from standing height.

Carpal dislocations are uncommon compared with fractures of the radius, and that rarity is part of the danger, because an uncommon injury is not the first one a busy clinician considers. A large share of perilunate injuries are reported as missed at the first visit, and the size of that share differs between published series, so any figure offered here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than a fixed truth. The reasons for the delay are easy to understand, because the wrist is swollen, the patient can still move the fingers, and the dramatic deformity that turns the wrist into the shape of a fork when the radius is broken is absent. A dislocation of the carpus may leave the wrist looking only puffy and slightly out of shape, and the tender point that would give it away lies deep beneath the swelling. In teaching, this injury is often described as a sprain that will not settle, and that is exactly the story a listener should distrust, because the mechanism, the swelling and any change in the feeling of the hand are the three findings that should keep the question open. An older adult with thin bone may instead break the radius, or break it and dislocate the carpus at the same time.

Assessment begins long before the wrist is touched, and it begins with the scene and with the patient as a whole. The responder asks how the injury happened, how far the patient fell, whether the patient landed on the hand, how much time has passed, and whether the same wrist has been injured before. The patient is asked about numbness, tingling and weakness of the grip, because those symptoms may be the only clue that the median nerve is involved, and the age of the patient and any illness or medicine that weakens bone are part of the history as well. If the patient is intoxicated, confused or unable to answer, the history is taken from a witness, and the examination is described as incomplete rather than reassuring. The primary survey comes before everything else, with its steps remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because life comes before limb. Only when the patient is stable enough does attention turn to the wrist, and even then the wrist is examined without being forced.

The limb is examined by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, and never by forcing it. The examiner compares the injured wrist with the other one, because the difference between the two sides is more reliable than any single finding taken alone. Swelling may be the only visible change, and it can arrive quickly, which is one reason the first examination is the most informative one ever performed on that patient. Tenderness is often greatest over the hollow at the base of the thumb between the tendons, where the scaphoid lies, and it may also be found at the back of the wrist over the lunate. The contour of the wrist may be lost rather than obviously deformed, and a wrist that looks merely puffy is not thereby cleared of serious injury, so a finding that is absent proves nothing and a wrist that is swollen and painful out of proportion to the story told is treated as a serious injury until someone qualified decides otherwise.

Swelling is the great masker of this injury, and it deserves its own warning. A wrist that fills with fluid swiftly hides the loss of contour, hides the tender point over the lunate and hides the loss of the normal hollow at the back of the wrist. A swollen wrist is also harder to examine, so a clinician who arrives later will find fewer signs than the responder who arrived first, which is one reason the first record matters so much. The amount of swelling does not measure the severity of the injury, because a modest sprain can swell dramatically while a complete dislocation can swell surprisingly little at the beginning. A sign that depends on the examiner's fingertips, such as the exact shape of the wrist, is unreliable in a swollen limb and unreliable in inexperienced hands, so the response to that uncertainty is not to guess but to immobilize, to record what was found, and to refer the patient for proper assessment.

Stabilization is the second step of the sequence, and in an injury of the wrist it is a small set of deliberate acts. The wrist is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bones, and the bones of the wrist are small enough that a pull on the fingers moves them. A deformed wrist is not pulled back into line by anyone in the field, for the same reason that governs every other limb in this course, which is that force applied to a joint whose ligaments are already torn can tear what remained intact. The lay first aider supports the wrist with the hands, a folded cloth or a pillow, keeps the patient warm, and waits for help, while the trained first responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the procedures their service authorizes. Rings, watches and bracelets are removed early, before the swelling arrives, and a ring that is already tight is not pulled over a swollen finger but is cut away by someone with the proper instrument and the authority to use it. The patient is protected from cold, because cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and a wet sleeve is replaced with dry covering. Pain is treated within the local protocol, but the choice of substance and the amount belong to the prescriber, and this course teaches no dose, no route and no regimen.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the hand and compares the two sides, then feels the pulse at the wrist on the thumb side, where the artery lies close to the surface, and compares it with the other hand. A nail is pressed briefly to watch the color return, and the examiner notes how quickly it does so rather than stating a threshold as a rule, because the figures that describe it differ between services and editions. Sensation is tested on both hands, and the examiner asks specifically about the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger and the inner half of the ring finger. The patient is asked to spread the fingers, to bend them, and to bring the thumb away from the palm against gentle resistance, which is the movement produced by the muscles at the base of the thumb. The formal examination of nerve function belongs to the clinician, while the lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel.

Among all the findings, a change in the median nerve is the one that alters the plan. When the lunate is driven forward it presses on that nerve inside the passage, and the patient reports tingling in the thumb and the first two fingers, or cannot feel a light touch there, or finds the thumb weak. In some patients this comes on slowly over hours and in others it is present on arrival, and either pattern carries the same meaning, because a nerve that stays compressed for a short time can recover while a nerve compressed for longer may not. The absence of these symptoms does not exclude a dislocation, and their presence does not prove one, so the finding is weighed with the mechanism and the rest of the examination. A patient who cannot report sensation, because of intoxication, confusion, a head injury or a language barrier, is treated as a patient whose nerve status is unknown and therefore as one who needs urgent assessment. That judgment belongs to the clinician who takes over, and the duty of the responder is to hand over the uncertainty clearly.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it. In the wrist that means supporting the wrist together with the joint at the base of the fingers and, on the other side, the joint at the elbow, because a splint that holds the wrist alone can still be moved by the joints at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, so a padded board, a folded magazine or a commercial splint can each serve, and an improvised device is checked more often because it shifts as swelling changes. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and they check the fingers and the pulse after the splint is in place. A rigid plaster cast is not the answer during the acute phase, because swelling inside a closed ring of plaster can turn the cast into a tourniquet, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, while a circumferential bandage applied by someone without the training to judge it is a hazard whose fingers are checked and rechecked.

There is one act that a listener must never take from this chapter and attempt, and that act is reduction. Reduction means restoring the small bones of the wrist to their normal relationship, and in a carpal dislocation it needs sedation or anesthesia, imaging during the attempt, and the strength to overcome the pull of the forearm muscles, which is far greater than a pair of hands can manage. It is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training rather than to a book. A failed attempt may injure the median nerve further, may push a bone through the skin and convert a closed injury into an open one, or may drive the lunate farther out of place. Traction, which means a steady pull on the hand to draw the bones apart, is not a field technique for the same reason, and neither is casting, because neither can be done safely without knowing what lies beneath the skin. A reduction is not attempted when the diagnosis is unclear, when the injury is open, when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the equipment or the training is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed, because each of those situations can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it. A plain radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions, because a displacement seen from the front may be invisible from the side and the reverse is equally true. For the wrist, the view from the side shows whether the lunate still sits in line with the capitate, and a conclusion drawn from a single image taken from the front is not enough, so the clinician asks for further views when the story and the examination do not fit the first picture. Computed tomography shows more detail of the small bones and of the joints between them, and it is often needed, because the plain images of a carpal injury can look deceptively ordinary. Magnetic resonance imaging shows the ligaments, the cartilage and the bone that has lost its blood supply, and a normal report never clears a patient whose history and examination point to a carpal dislocation, because an image is a picture of one moment in a changing injury and the patient is examined and reassessed after it has been taken.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The hand is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint or bandage is checked for tightness and for points of pressure. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a hand that becomes tense, shiny and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. If a compartment syndrome is suspected, the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of local protocol, the wrist is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. A patient whose fingers were pink and sensitive before the splint and are pale and numb after it is a patient whose splint is the problem until someone proves otherwise. The responder says aloud what has changed, and says it to the person who will make the next decision.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and for a suspected carpal dislocation the answer is referral rather than a splint and a quiet journey home. The reason is that the small bones of the wrist are held in place by ligaments, so a dislocation means those ligaments have failed, and a splint supports the wrist without restoring the alignment of bones that are already out of line. A wrist that feels deceptively comfortable after splinting may still be dislocated, and the swelling that follows will make it harder, not easier, to put right. Delay carries specific penalties, because the median nerve is compressed by the displaced lunate, the cartilage is worn by bones that rub in the wrong place, and the lunate may lose its blood supply and die, a change that cannot be undone afterwards. The patient is therefore referred without delay to a facility where the wrist can be imaged properly, where a reduction can be performed by someone qualified, and where operative treatment is available, and a patient with numbness or weakness in the territory of the median nerve is referred as an emergency, with the receiving team told about it explicitly.

Definitive treatment of a carpal dislocation belongs to the hand surgeon and to the operating room, and the part of the listener is to understand its purpose rather than its steps. The surgeon first restores the relationship of the bones, which may be done as a closed procedure guided by imaging or as an open operation in which the joint is inspected directly. Because the ligaments that held the carpus are torn, the surgeon repairs or reconstructs them and holds the bones with metal pins, screws or a plate while the tissues heal, and the general name for the open operation is open reduction and internal fixation. A cast or a brace may be worn after the operation, and the timing of its removal and the start of movement belong to the surgeon and to the therapist rather than to the patient or the responder. Rehabilitation is slow, because a wrist that stiffens takes the function of the whole hand with it, and it is guided by a therapist working to the instructions of the surgeon. Published accounts of how long the wrist is protected differ between centers and between surgeons, so any period named in this course is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

What can go wrong is worth stating plainly, because it explains the urgency. The lunate has a fragile blood supply, and a lunate that is left out of place may die, a change called avascular necrosis, after which the bone collapses and destroys the joints above and below it. The scaphoid carries the same risk, particularly when it is broken near the end closest to the forearm, and a scaphoid that fails to unite causes pain and arthritis that may appear long after the fall. The cartilage of the wrist can be worn away by a joint that is not aligned, and the result is arthritis that limits grip and rotation years later. The median nerve can lose function permanently if it is compressed for too long, leaving a hand that cannot feel or grip properly, and the wrist itself can become stiff. Every one of these outcomes is more likely when the diagnosis is delayed, which is the argument for examining carefully, imaging properly and referring early rather than waiting to see whether the wrist improves.

A constructed illustration may help to fix the pattern in mind. A young adult falls from a ladder onto one outstretched hand and is brought to an urgent care center with a wrist that is swollen but not obviously deformed. The skin is intact, the fingers move and the pulse at the wrist is present, but the patient says that the thumb and the first two fingers feel asleep and that the thumb feels weak. A radiograph taken from the front appears nearly normal, and the clinician asks for a view from the side, which shows that the small bone in the middle of the wrist is no longer in line with the bone of the forearm. Nothing is straightened, the hand is splinted in the position in which it was found, the neurovascular findings are written down again, and the patient is transferred to a hand surgery service, where the joint is put back into place and the torn ligaments are repaired. That patient is invented for teaching and is not a real person, and the lesson of the illustration is that the numb thumb and the single direction of the first radiograph were the two findings that mattered.

Scope of practice runs through every step of this injury, and it is worth saying plainly who may do what. The lay first aider supports the limb, keeps the patient warm and still, removes a watch or a loose ring when that can be done without force, and calls for help. The trained first responder and the paramedic may splint, may record the neurovascular findings, may give what the local protocol authorizes for pain, and may transport the patient, but they do not reduce a dislocation and they do not interpret an image. The nurse observes, records, reassesses, prepares the patient and reports any change, working within the rules of the institution and the instructions of the treating clinician. The physician examines the patient, orders and interprets the imaging, decides about analgesia and sedation, and performs or arranges a reduction within the local protocol and the training that person holds. The orthopedic surgeon or the hand surgeon provides operative treatment and defines the plan for rehabilitation, and the therapist carries it out. When a responder is unsure whether an act lies within their scope, the safe answer is to do the things that need no permission, such as support, warmth, recording and calling for help, and to leave the rest to the person who is authorized to do it. The record follows the patient, because the position in which the wrist was found and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are what let the receiving team continue a story instead of starting a new one.

To summarize, a carpal dislocation is a tearing of the ligaments that hold the small bones of the wrist in line, and it may look like a sprain, because swelling hides the deformity while the fingers still move. The mechanism of a fall onto an outstretched hand, the swelling that arrives quickly, and any numbness or weakness in the thumb and the first two fingers are the findings that keep the question open. The sequence is followed in order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the neurovascular findings are recorded before every intervention and repeated after it. A wrist is splinted in the position found and is never straightened or pulled in the field, a ring that is already tight is not pulled over a swollen finger, and an open wound is never explored blindly. A radiograph taken from one direction alone may look normal, so a normal report never clears a patient whose history and examination suggest this injury, and computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging may be needed. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no listener should attempt them from a book, because a failed attempt can damage the median nerve or open a closed injury. A suspected carpal dislocation is referred urgently rather than splinted and sent home, and it is referred as an emergency when the median nerve has changed, because time is muscle and a wrist put right early works best.

# Chapter 22 — Metacarpal Fractures

A metacarpal fracture is a break of one of the five long bones that form the frame of the palm, and no other bone of the hand breaks as often. The injury seldom kills, yet the hand is the instrument with which a person works, eats and cares for others, and a hand that heals in the wrong rotation can cost a patient a trade. The energy of the injury travels through muscle, tendon, nerve and vessel as well as through bone, so this chapter is about the whole hand. The order of work is the same as everywhere in this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the provider level is named for every act. This is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Five metacarpals run from the wrist to the knuckles and are numbered from the thumb side outward, and each has a base, a shaft, a neck and a head. The base meets the wrist, the neck is the narrow region before the knuckle, and the head forms the knuckle at the metacarpophalangeal joint. The first metacarpal belongs to the thumb and sits apart, with a saddle-shaped base that lets the thumb swing across the palm. The second and third are almost rigidly locked into the wrist and form a fixed pillar that carries the force of a grip, while the fourth and fifth have mobile bases. That difference in mobility decides how much displacement a broken bone can leave behind.

Around the metacarpal heads lies the apparatus that makes the fingers work, and it may be damaged with the bone or instead of it. Each metacarpophalangeal joint is steadied by a collateral ligament on either side and by a tough plate on its palmar surface, and those ligaments are slack when the joint is straight and tight when it is bent. That is why a hand is never left with the fingers held out flat for days, because a ligament that stays short will not easily lengthen again. Between the metacarpals lie the interosseous muscles, which draw the fingers apart and together, and the tendons that straighten the fingers run over the back of the hand in a layer so thin that a small wound can injure them. The nerve that supplies most of the small muscles of the hand runs close to the fifth metacarpal.

The way the hand was injured tells the responder what to suspect before the hand is examined. A direct blow from a hammer, a door or a machine commonly breaks a shaft or a neck, and a fall onto the outstretched hand drives force along the second and third rays and may break a metacarpal base or the wrist. A twisting injury, such as a hand caught in a strap, tends to produce a spiral break of a shaft, and the spiral pattern is the one most likely to rotate. The commonest of all is a blow delivered with a closed fist against a firm object, which breaks the neck of the fifth metacarpal, the bone of the little finger.

When the neck of the fifth metacarpal breaks, the head tilts toward the palm and the knuckle of the little finger sinks, which is why the injury is also called the dropped knuckle. A small prominence may be felt in the palm where the tilted head presses forward, and the shape can resemble a claw, with the knuckle bent backward and the first joint of the finger bent forward. That appearance alone does not prove which structure is injured, and tenderness over the neck of the bone, swelling and pain on gripping are what a responder can act on. A constructed illustration is a patient who struck a wall and can still bend the little finger, because a broken bone does not stop movement.

Rotation is the deformity that decides the fate of the hand, and it is judged by looking at the fingers rather than at the hand. When a metacarpal twists, the whole finger beyond it turns, and a turn of a few degrees at the bone becomes a large overlap at the fingertip, an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The examiner asks the patient to bend all the fingers toward the palm and looks at where they point, because the fingers of a normal hand converge toward the base of the thumb. When the little finger rides over or under its neighbor, the fracture has rotated. The fingernails give a second view, since their planes should stay roughly parallel, and a third test uses the tendons, because extending the wrist makes the fingers curl, so a finger that takes no part has rotated.

Rotation and angulation are not the same problem, and the difference is why one patient goes home and another goes to a surgeon. Angulation is a bend at the break, and in the fifth ray a bend of some degree may be accepted because the mobile base of that metacarpal lets the hand compensate, with the amount quoted in teaching varying between services and editions. Rotation is a twist, and it does not remodel, because the finger is not turned by a joint that can adapt but fixed by a bone in the wrong plane. Rotation in the index and middle rays is worse still, because those rays have little mobility at the wrist, so any rotation is referred to a clinician.

Assessment begins with the scene and with the patient rather than with the hand. The responder checks for danger, puts on the protection the situation requires, and works through the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The rule that decides the order of work when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The lay first aider then recognizes the injury, supports the hand and calls for help, while the trained responder, the nurse and the physician work within what the law and the local protocol allow.

The history of a hand injury is short to take and it changes what is done. The responder asks which hand is injured, whether it is the dominant hand, and what work the patient does, because those answers set the urgency of the referral as much as the fracture does. The patient is asked how the injury happened, whether the skin was broken, and whether the hand struck anything that could cut it, and the question about the mouth is asked directly rather than left to chance. Protection against tetanus and any illness or medicine that weakens bone are recorded, and the decisions that follow belong to the treating clinician and to the local protocol.

A wound over a knuckle after a blow to the mouth is a human bite, and it is one of the most easily missed emergencies of the hand. The tooth cuts a small opening over the metacarpophalangeal joint or over the tendon that straightens the finger, and it carries organisms from the mouth into the joint, the tendon sheath or the tissue beneath the skin. The wound often looks trivial and may be hidden by the position of the hand at the moment of the blow, because a cut over a knuckle in flexion slides beneath the skin when the finger is straightened. The patient may be reluctant to say what happened, so the examiner looks at the skin over every knuckle of a hand that has been in a fight. A human bite is an open injury and is referred urgently, while the substances used against infection are decided by the prescriber according to the local protocol.

The hand is examined in a fixed order that no responder has to invent, which is to look, to feel and then to ask the patient to move. Inspection begins with the position of the whole hand at rest and compares it with the other side, because an injured hand is often held differently before any swelling appears. Swelling, bruising, a wound, a deformity at a knuckle and a change in the contour of the back of the hand are all recorded as findings rather than as diagnoses. Palpation moves along each metacarpal from base to head, feeling for the one place that hurts most, and the examiner feels the knuckle, the base of the thumb and the wrist in turn. The fracture is never deliberately rocked to produce a grinding sensation, because that test adds pain and can displace what was stable.

Movement is asked for rather than imposed, and the patient is never made to move a hand against pain. The patient is asked to make a fist, to straighten the fingers, to spread them apart and bring them together, and to touch the thumb to the tip of each finger, and the examiner notes which of those acts is lost. A finger that cannot be straightened against resistance suggests a torn tendon over the back of the hand or the knuckle, and a finger that cannot be bent suggests a tendon injury on the palmar side or a bone blocking the movement. Weakness of the small muscles that spread the fingers apart may point to the nerve close to the fifth metacarpal rather than to the bone, and every movement is compared with the other hand.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Sensation in the hand belongs to three territories, and the examiner tests the little finger and the ulnar border of the ring finger for the ulnar nerve, the thumb, the index and the middle fingers for the median nerve, and the web between the thumb and the index finger for the radial nerve. Numbness or tingling in the little finger after a fracture of the fifth metacarpal changes the plan, because the nerve to the small muscles of the hand runs close to that bone. Both hands are compared, and the patient's own words for the feeling, such as pins and needles or a dead finger, are written as far as possible.

The blood supply of the hand comes from two arteries at the wrist, which join in the palm to form arches from which the digital arteries arise. The examiner looks at the color of the fingers, feels their temperature with the back of the hand, presses briefly on a fingernail to watch the color return, and feels for the pulse on both sides of each finger. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury, because the small vessels and the compartments can fail while the large pulse continues, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency. When a digital pulse cannot be felt, a clinician may test the supply from the two arteries at the wrist by pressing on one and then the other while the patient opens and closes the hand. The finding is recorded for each finger, and a finger that becomes pale, cool or painful after a splint is applied is reported at once.

Stabilization in the field is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The hand is supported in the position in which it was found, and a deformed hand is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves of the hand lie close to the bones and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. That decision belongs to a clinician who is trained, equipped, supervised and authorized to make it, and no responder at any level performs it outside a properly equipped clinical area. The lay first aider supports, covers a wound with a sterile dressing, keeps the patient warm and calls for help, while the trained responder and the paramedic act within the procedures their service authorizes.

An open injury of the hand is treated as contaminated from the moment it happens, because the skin carries organisms that reach the bone and the deep tissues as the wound is made. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled with pressure around the wound and not inside it, and never explores the wound with a finger or an instrument. The neurovascular examination is recorded before the dressing is applied where that is possible, and the hand is immobilized in the position found and kept warm. Definitive closure of an open wound of the hand belongs to the operating room and to nobody else.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured bone and of the joints above and below it, and the position chosen is the one that leaves the hand useful. The hand is placed in what teaching calls the position of function, in which the wrist is slightly extended, the knuckles are bent, the middle joints of the fingers are gently bent, and the thumb is carried away from the palm. The knuckles are bent because their collateral ligaments are tight in that position and slack when the joint is straight, so a hand held still is held with the joints that will not stiffen. The amounts quoted in teaching, such as a wrist extended by some degrees, are illustrations to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The practical details of a hand splint decide whether it helps or harms. It is padded wherever it presses on a bony point, applied over the position found, and secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation, and nothing is ever wrapped tightly around a finger, because a finger has little room for swelling. A sling supports the weight of the arm, and rings, watches and tight bracelets come off the injured hand before the swelling arrives, while a ring that cannot be removed is left alone and reported rather than cut or pulled by an untrained hand. The trained responder and the paramedic apply a splint within the procedures their service authorizes, the nurse and the physician choose the definitive immobilization, and the surgeon decides when the position of the bones must be changed. Swelling is expected, so the hand is raised when the patient is sitting or lying, and a cold pack wrapped in cloth may be applied by a responder authorized to do so. The patient is kept warm, because cold is a complication of trauma, and a patient who may need an operation is kept without food and drink by instruction of the clinician.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and the hand is imaged in more than one direction so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with a view from the front, a view from the side and an angled view commonly used together because the bones overlap. The joint above and the joint below the injured bone are included, so that a second break at the base of a metacarpal or in the wrist is not missed. A special angled view of the metacarpal heads may be requested when a break of a knuckle is suspected but not seen, and computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break that enters a joint. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, tendons and cartilage, and ultrasound may be used in some services, though its availability differs between countries. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not choose the study.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The examiner looks at the color and warmth of the fingers, feels the pulses, tests the sensation, asks the patient to move the fingers and asks about the pain, then checks the splint for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, a finger that has turned pale or cool, and a hand that has become tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A patient whose pain is controlled by the measures the local protocol allows, and whose hand stays warm, pink and movable, can be watched, but a patient who is getting worse is not watched further by the responder.

Compartment syndrome of the hand is uncommon and devastating, and it begins with pain that does not match the injury. The hand has several small compartments between the metacarpals, each bounded by bone and by the fascia that wraps the interosseous muscles, and pressure that rises inside one of them shuts down the smallest vessels while the pulse at the wrist continues. The hand becomes tense and swollen, the pain is worse when the fingers are straightened passively, and the patient may describe a deep ache or a burning that is not relieved by the measures the protocol allows. The diagnosis is clinical, so the responder does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late, and within the limits of the local protocol the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released by someone authorized to release it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart unless the local protocol for the hand directs otherwise, and the patient is referred urgently, because time is muscle.

Pain is treated in the hand as it is treated anywhere else, and the limits of this course are fixed. A patient in pain is assessed, the injury is immobilized, the swelling is managed and the clinician is told, while the choice of substance, the amount and the way it is given belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and no dose, no route and no regimen appear anywhere in this course. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that rises despite the measures taken, pain out of proportion to the injury, or pain that comes with numbness or with a hand that is becoming tense. The lay first aider gives no substance, the trained responder gives only what the service authorizes and carries, and the nurse and the physician act within their own license and the law of the country.

Definitive treatment begins with a decision about whether the position of the bones must be changed, and that decision belongs to a clinician. Reduction means restoring the broken ends to a better position, and it is done to relieve pressure on skin, nerve or vessel, to let the bone heal in a useful shape and to make later movement possible, and it is performed with the patient made comfortable, in a clinical setting, by a trained clinician whose technique was learned under supervision rather than from a book such as this one. What can go wrong is worth saying plainly, because a listener who understands the risk will not improvise: the bone ends may injure a nerve or a vessel as they move, a closed injury may be opened by the attempt, and a break that was stable may become unstable. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

Most metacarpal fractures do not need an operation, and the majority are treated by holding the hand in a useful position and then moving it as soon as the clinician allows. The splint or cast, the position it holds and the length of time it stays are prescribed by the clinician, and a figure such as a few weeks is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A break of the neck of the fifth metacarpal that angulates but does not rotate is often tolerated, and a residual bump on the back of the hand is a cosmetic finding in many patients. Certain fractures are referred to a surgeon, among them any rotation, an open fracture, a wound over a knuckle after a blow to the mouth, more than one bone broken, a break that enters a joint, a break of the base of the thumb metacarpal, and a hand with a nerve, vessel or tendon injury. Surgery may hold the fragments with wires through the skin, with screws, with plates or with a device outside the skin, and every operation on the hand is performed by a qualified surgeon.

The thumb is not a finger, and a fracture of its metacarpal is not treated like the rest of the hand. The first metacarpal is shorter and set apart, and its base carries the whole force of a pinch and a grip. A break that runs through that base and into the joint at the wrist is unstable, because the tendon that pulls the thumb away from the palm drags the lower fragment with it, and teaching gives such breaks names, one for a break into two parts and one for a break shattered into more than two. A patient with a painful, swollen thumb base after a fall is referred for imaging and for a decision by the clinician, and a responder never pulls on the thumb to test it.

The age of the patient changes the urgency of a hand injury even when the sequence does not change. A child's metacarpal still has a growth region near its ends, and an injury through that region can disturb the growth of the bone or of the whole ray, so a child who will not use a hand after a fall is referred even when the first radiograph looks modest. An older adult may break a metacarpal in a fall from standing height because the bone has lost density, and the fracture may hurt far less than its severity suggests. A bone that breaks without a strong injury may be weakened by disease, and such a break is referred for assessment of the bone as well as of the fracture.

Some errors are made so often that they deserve to be named. The first is to treat a hand injury casually because it is small, when the hand is the part of the body that most often decides whether a patient returns to work, and the second is to miss a rotation because the examiner looked at the hand rather than at the fingers. The third is to miss a human bite because the wound was small and the patient did not say, and the fourth is to leave a ring on a hand that is about to swell. The fifth is to apply a splint that is too tight and then fail to look at the fingers again, the sixth is to straighten a deformed hand in the field, and the seventh is to accept a pulse as proof that the vessels are safe. Scope of practice frames all of it, since the lay first aider supports and calls, the trained responder and the paramedic work within the procedures their service authorizes, and the surgeon decides when the bones must be repositioned. The record and the handover are part of the treatment, so the time, the mechanism, the position found and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written in a fixed order, and a possible injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified clears it.

To summarize, a metacarpal fracture is an injury of the whole hand, and the bone that broke is only one of the structures the energy passed through. The fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal after a blow with the fist drops the knuckle and tilts the head toward the palm, and angulation there may be tolerated while rotation never is. Rotation is judged by looking at the fingers rather than at the hand, by the way they converge when the patient makes a fist and by the planes of the nails. The sequence is the same as everywhere in this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the neurovascular findings recorded before every intervention and repeated after it. The hand is splinted in the position found and never straightened in the field, the knuckles are kept bent in the position that leaves the hand useful, rings come off early, wounds are covered and never explored, and a wound over a knuckle after a blow to the mouth is treated as a human bite and referred urgently. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, no dose or route or regimen appears in this course, and a responder who suspects a compartment syndrome releases nothing outside the local protocol and refers the patient at once. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 23 — Phalangeal Fractures and Finger Dislocations

A finger that is fractured or dislocated is the injury most often called minor at the moment it is seen, and that habit is what costs hands. The phalanges are the small bones of the fingers, and the joints between them carry a wide range of movement through a very small space, so a finger left slightly out of line can leave a hand that will not close around a cup or a tool. This chapter follows the order used everywhere in this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. It is educational material for health professionals, students and trained responders, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The fingers are built from phalanges, and the thumb has two while each of the other four fingers has three. The bone nearest the hand is the proximal phalanx, the one beyond it is the middle phalanx, and the one at the tip is the distal phalanx, and each has a base facing the hand, a shaft, and a head that carries the joint surface. The joints are named from the bones they join, so the metacarpophalangeal joint lies between the metacarpal bone of the hand and the proximal phalanx, the proximal interphalangeal joint lies between the two phalanges nearest the hand, and the distal interphalangeal joint lies between the two furthest from it. In the thumb the corresponding joint is called simply the interphalangeal joint, and a clinician locates an injury by naming the bone and the joint in that way, so the record uses the same words and the next examiner finds the same place.

Such small bones deserve a chapter of their own because the hand heals by stiffening. Swelling collects in the loose tissue around the joints and tendons, the ligaments and the joint capsule shorten while the hand rests, and the fine gliding that lets a tendon draw a finger through its full arc is lost once that tissue becomes thick and stuck. The window in which this stiffness can still be turned back is measured in days rather than months, and a figure used in teaching, such as 3 weeks of rest for a joint, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and editions differ. Early care therefore aims at protected movement rather than perfect stillness, and the clinician chooses the position that keeps the ligaments and joint surfaces under the least tension while the responder keeps the hand in the position found until that decision is made.

The mechanism of injury is the first clue and often the only clue available before anything can be seen. A direct blow crushes a finger between two hard objects, a fall onto the outstretched hand drives a finger backward at a joint, and a twisting force passed through a ball or a leash bends and rotates it at the same time. The injury patients most often dismiss is the jammed finger, which was bent backward in sport and now hurts and swells, because that same description covers a sprain that will settle and a fracture or dislocation that will not. Age matters as well, since the growing end of a phalanx in a child can be injured without the shaft breaking, so a child who will not use a hand after a fall deserves the same caution as an adult with an obvious deformity.

Assessment begins with the scene and with the patient rather than with the finger, so the responder makes sure the area is safe, notes the time of the injury, and asks what happened, what the patient felt at the moment of impact, whether the hand has been used since, and what has already been done to it. A hand injury can accompany a fall from a height, a road crash or a fight, so the primary survey is completed first, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Only when the patient is stable enough does attention turn to the hand, because life comes before limb and a finger can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The lay first aider observes and supports, the trained responder assesses within the procedures the service authorizes, and the diagnosis belongs to the clinician.

The first part of the local examination is looking, and the responder looks at the whole hand rather than the sore finger alone, with both hands in view at once so that the injured side can be compared with the uninjured one, because swelling crosses the spaces between the fingers quickly and a second injury is easily missed. Swelling, bruising, a wound, a torn nail, blood beneath a nail and any unnatural bend are all recorded. The most important observation in the hand is rotation, which becomes visible when the patient bends the fingers gently toward the palm, because instead of lying side by side one fingertip crosses over or under its neighbor. That observation is unreliable in a patient who cannot move the fingers because of pain, so its absence proves nothing and an examiner who cannot see it does not conclude that rotation is absent. A finger with a wound over a joint, with exposed bone, or with a nail driven into the nail bed is looked at, covered with a sterile dressing and left alone, because it is not examined by probing.

Feeling comes next, and it is done lightly along the bone and around the joints, comparing the two hands as the examination goes. The responder palpates the length of each phalanx on its sides and along its back, feeling for a step, a gap, a sharply localized tender point and the joint lines above and below the injury. A crackling sensation beneath the fingers, which is called crepitus, suggests that the bone ends are moving against one another, and it is a reason for gentleness rather than for repeated testing. Tenderness directly over a joint line suggests that the joint has been injured even when the bone feels whole, and the examiner also feels the temperature of the finger and the tightness of its skin, because a finger that becomes tense and shiny is describing pressure inside a closed space.

Movement is tested gently and by the patient, because the responder does not move an injured finger through a range that causes pain or meets resistance. The patient is asked to bend and to straighten each finger as far as comfort allows, and the difference between the two hands is noted rather than a measurement. A finger that will not straighten at all may have an injured tendon rather than an injured bone, and a finger that will not bend may have a dislocation or a fragment caught in the joint. Testing a finger against resistance, or pulling on it, is a clinical skill learned under supervision and is not a field test, so the responder does not do it. The record states what the patient could and could not do at that moment, in the patient's own words as far as possible, because the ability to move may change after any intervention.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Each finger carries two digital arteries and two digital nerves, one along each side, and they lie close to the bone, so an injury that displaces the bone puts them at risk. The examiner looks at the color of the finger and of the nail bed, feels the warmth of the skin against the other hand, and presses briefly on the nail to watch the color return, which is called capillary refill. Sensation is tested on both sides of each finger, and the patient is asked to report numbness or tingling in ordinary words, since the pulse of a single finger is often too small to feel reliably and its absence alone proves nothing. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability to feel and to move, the trained responder and the clinician perform the formal examination, and every result is recorded before and after each intervention without exception.

Stabilization of an injured hand is a small set of acts, and the first of them is restraint. A deformed finger is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the digital vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Pulling a finger straight can also turn a closed injury into an open one by pushing a sharp bone end through skin that had not yet been torn, so the lay first aider supports the hand with a pillow or a soft roll of cloth, keeps the arm against the body and waits for help. The trained responder and the paramedic may splint the hand within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, examining the neurovascular status before and after they do it. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the hand is insulated, wet clothing is replaced with covering, and a ring that threatens to become tight is dealt with early within the local protocol instead of by force.

Immobilization of a finger has two aims at once, which are to hold the injured part still enough to heal and to keep the joints that are not injured moving enough to avoid stiffness. Buddy strapping binds the injured finger to an uninjured neighbor with tape or with a manufactured strap, so that the healthy finger acts as a splint, and it is used for stable fractures of the middle phalanx and for some injuries of the distal phalanx. It may be applied by a trained first responder, an emergency medical technician, a paramedic or a nurse, and only to an injury assessed as stable, because strapping a rotated or unstable finger in place conceals the problem and lets it set in the wrong position. The strap is placed around the middle of the finger rather than over a joint, it leaves the tip visible so that color, warmth and sensation can be checked, and it is never wrapped so tightly that it stops the circulation. A padded splint or a custom splint may be applied by those authorized to use one, and the position chosen for a hand that must be rested is the position of function, the relaxed posture in which the wrist is slightly extended, the knuckles are bent and the fingers curve as though around a small ball, because there the ligaments along the sides of the joints are at their longest and a hand held in that posture loses less movement than a hand held flat.

Some finger injuries look small and are not small, and the open injury over a joint is the clearest example. A wound that lies over the metacarpophalangeal joint, or over any interphalangeal joint, is treated as an open injury until a clinician decides otherwise, because a joint entered by a wound is contaminated even when the wound is small. The constructed illustration is the hand of someone who has struck another person in the mouth, where a small wound over a knuckle opens the joint beneath. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the hand in the position found and arranges urgent transfer, while the wound is never explored blindly, an embedded object is never removed, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound. Protection against tetanus and the decision about antibiotics belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, so no substance, no amount and no route is given in this course, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to an operating room and to nobody else.

Not every phalangeal fracture behaves the same way, and the purpose of the responder is not to classify them but to recognize which ones have stopped being minor. A fracture of the shaft that runs as a long spiral is unstable because the two ends can rotate around one another, and rotation is the displacement that a splint cannot control and that only the eye will catch. A fracture that enters a joint, which is called an intra-articular fracture, can leave a step in the joint surface that wears the cartilage away and limits movement for years. A fracture at the base of the thumb, a fracture of the distal phalanx that has a wound, and a fracture beneath a nail that has torn the nail bed are injuries that need imaging and a clinical decision rather than a bandage and reassurance. A sign that is taught as reliable may be missing in a patient whose bone is weakened by disease or by long use of a medicine that thins it, so a lower threshold for immobilization and referral takes the place of a confident diagnosis.

A dislocation of a finger is a complete loss of contact between the joint surfaces, and a subluxation is a partial loss of contact, and both tear the capsule and at least one ligament of the joint. The joint most often dislocated in the hand is the proximal interphalangeal joint, the middle joint of a finger, and it usually comes apart toward the back of the hand when the finger is bent backward. The finger looks shortened, it is bent at an angle, and the patient holds it stiffly away from the others, while the skin over the joint may be tight because the bone end is pressing against it from within. The joint at the base of the thumb is dislocated far less often but is more serious, because the ligaments that steady the thumb are large and the bone ends can become trapped between the tendon and the skin.
