Any dislocation of a finger is referred to a clinician, because the decision about how and when to restore the joint belongs to someone trained and equipped to make it.

The rule that a deformed limb is never straightened in the field applies to the finger as firmly as to the thigh, and it is the rule most often broken in the hand because a finger looks easy to pull straight. Force is not a technique, and a finger pulled on by someone without training can be turned from a dislocation that could be reduced gently into one that cannot be reduced at all, because a fragment of bone or a tendon can become caught between the surfaces. A reduction is not attempted when the injury is open, when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught within the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. Each of those situations rests on the same reason, which is that the attempt can add an injury that the receiving clinician then has to repair, and the responder stops at the first sign of resistance or of a new complication. Describing what a reduction is meant to achieve and what can go wrong is the work of this chapter, while the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training and to local protocol.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below the injury included so that a second injury is not missed. The hand is difficult to image because its bones overlap when the fingers lie together, so the clinician may ask for views taken with the fingers separated and for the request to state which finger and which joint are in question. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break that enters a joint and helps the surgeon decide how to treat it, while magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues such as ligaments, tendons and cartilage, and neither study is ordered routinely. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging and the trained responder does not choose which study is needed, because that decision belongs to the clinician, and an image is only a picture of one moment.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, so the finger is checked for color, warmth, capillary refill, sensation, movement and pain and the strap or splint is checked for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, a finger that becomes cold and pale and a finger that becomes tense and shiny are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A bandage, a strap or a splint that has become constricting is released by someone authorized to do so within the limits of the local protocol, because waiting for a formal diagnosis wastes the time in which muscle and nerve can still be saved. The hand is not elevated above the level of the heart when a compartment syndrome is suspected, the patient is kept warm and referred urgently, and a ring that fitted in the morning can become a tourniquet by evening.

A compartment syndrome can occur in the hand, and although it is uncommon it is the complication this course fears most, because it is caused by the treatment as often as by the injury. The hand is divided into compartments bounded by fascia, and the small muscles within them are packed tightly between the bones, so bleeding or swelling raises the pressure against structures that have almost no room to expand. The earliest and most dependable finding is pain that is greater than the injury explains and that increases when the fingers are moved, while the later findings of pallor, coolness, an absent pulse, numbness and paralysis appear only once the damage is advanced. An intact pulse does not exclude the diagnosis, because the pressure that stops the flow through the smallest vessels is well below the pressure that would stop a pulse at the wrist. The constricting bandage, strap or splint is released within the limits of the local protocol, the hand is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm and transferred urgently to a facility where the compartments can be opened if that becomes necessary.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some finger injuries cannot be managed where the patient is sitting. A patient is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and, when the injury is severe, an intensive care unit, and the reasons include an open injury, a joint that has been entered, a finger that is rotated or scissored, a dislocation that is present or suspected, an unstable or comminuted fracture, an injury of the thumb, more than one finger injured in the same hand, an injured tendon or nerve, a neurovascular status that is worsening, and a child with an injury near the growing end of the bone. A crushed fingertip, an amputation at any level and any hand in which the blood supply of a finger is in doubt are transferred as emergencies rather than booked for a later appointment. A patient whose pain is increasing, whose finger is swelling inside a splint or whose sensation is changing is referred without waiting for the next clinic day. When the responder is unsure whether an injury is minor, arranging review is safer than offering reassurance, because a finger watched for a week has often lost movement it will never regain.

Definitive treatment of a phalangeal fracture or a finger dislocation begins with a decision about what the finger will have to do once it has healed. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends or of the joint surfaces, traction holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or splinting holds the position while healing proceeds, and each of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A surgeon may hold the fragments with fine wires, with screws or with small plates, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, and a dislocation that cannot be brought back by gentle means needs an operation to remove whatever is caught between the surfaces. The purpose of all these treatments is to restore alignment, to preserve the joint surface and to allow movement as early as the tissues permit, and the complication that threatens that purpose is stiffness rather than an imperfect line. A hand surgeon or an orthopedic surgeon decides what is needed, and none of the acts named in this paragraph is taught by this course or may be attempted by a listener who has not been trained and authorized to perform it.

The work of recovery after a hand injury belongs mostly to the patient, and the task of the clinical team is to make sure the patient knows what to do and what would mean stopping. Hand therapy, provided by a therapist trained in the rehabilitation of the hand, uses exercises, splints and advice about swelling to regain movement without pulling a healing bone out of place. Adherence is the strongest single influence on the outcome in many hand injuries, because the exercises that restore movement are uncomfortable and are easy to abandon once the pain settles. A patient who reports that the finger is becoming stiffer rather than looser, or who cannot move it as the therapist described, needs review rather than encouragement.

Two groups of patients need a lower threshold for referral than the rest. In a child the ends of the phalanges contain a growth region, and an injury there can disturb the length and shape of a finger for the rest of life even when the shaft is intact, so a child who will not use a hand after an injury is examined and imaged rather than watched at home. In an older adult the skin is thinner, the bone is more brittle and the joints stiffen faster, so a finger that would recover in a younger patient may lose its movement within days, and the fracture may be far less painful than its severity suggests. Patients whose bone is weakened by disease or by a long course of a medicine that thins it may break a finger in a fall from standing height, and where a sign is unreliable the answer is a lower threshold for immobilization, for imaging and for referral, while the decisions themselves belong to the clinician.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the hand was found, the findings of the neurovascular examination before and after every intervention and what has been applied are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. Where this chapter names a time or a distance, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. A hand injury in a patient who is intoxicated, confused or unable to cooperate is treated with the same care as any other, with attention to the airway while the hand is protected, and anyone whose spine may have been injured is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so.

To summarize, a fractured or dislocated finger is a small injury with a large consequence, because the hand heals by stiffening and a finger left out of line or left still loses the grip the patient needs. Look at both hands together for swelling, deformity and rotation, feel along the bone and around the joints, ask the patient to move the fingers and record what they can do, and examine the color, warmth, capillary refill and sensation of every finger before any intervention and again after it. The order of this course is followed in the hand as everywhere else, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the provider level is named for every act. A deformed finger is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, force is not a technique, buddy strapping is used only on an injury that has been assessed as stable, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. An open wound over a joint is covered with a sterile dressing and never explored blindly, an embedded object is left where it is, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound. Pain that increases, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a finger that becomes cold and pale or tense and shiny are the findings that stop the responder, so a constricting bandage or splint is released within the limits of the local protocol, the hand is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm and transferred urgently, because time is muscle. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 24 — Pelvic Fractures

The pelvis is a ring of bone that carries the weight of the upper body into the legs. When it breaks, the injury is a bleeding injury before it is a bone injury, because blood collects behind the abdominal cavity, where nothing is seen from outside and nothing can be pressed by a hand. The patient may be pale, restless and thirsty while the skin over the pelvis shows only a graze. The pelvis therefore belongs to the first minutes of care and not to the later examination of the limb. This chapter keeps the order that every chapter of this course follows, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

To see why the bleeding is so heavy, the pelvis has to be understood as a container as well as a ring. The two hip bones meet in front at the pubic symphysis and behind at the sacroiliac joints, and strong ligaments close the ring. Inside it lie the bladder, the urethra, the rectum, the great vessels of the legs and the roots of the nerves of the lower limbs. The bone itself is rich in blood, and the veins of the pelvis form a wide, thin-walled network that lies against the bone. A ring rarely opens at one point alone, because the force that breaks it usually disrupts a second place as well.

Several sources bleed at once in this injury, which is why it is so hard to control. Torn bone surfaces ooze, torn veins bleed steadily into the loose space behind the peritoneum, and a torn artery may bleed under pressure. Teaching offers a figure of about 3 liters for what some patients lose, an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries and editions. A fracture that opens the ring increases the room available, and a break near the sacroiliac joint lies close to the great vessels. None of this bleeding is visible, and none of it can be stopped by pressing on the skin.

The mechanism tells the responder how much energy passed through the patient. A side impact in a vehicle crash, a motorcycle collision, a pedestrian struck by a vehicle, a fall from a height, a crush between heavy objects and a blast most often break the pelvis. In a young person the bone is strong, so a pelvic fracture means great energy and raises the chance that other organs are injured too. In an older person whose bone has lost density, the same ring may break in a fall from standing height. A sudden pull of a muscle can avulse a small piece of bone in a young athlete. The energy, rather than the appearance, is the first question.

A patient who cannot stand or bear weight is treated as having a broken pelvis until a qualified clinician decides otherwise. Pain may be felt in the groin, the hip, the lower back, the buttock or the perineum, and it may be reported as coming from the hip. A leg may lie turned outward or shortened, and the patient may be unable to lift a straight leg. Bruising may appear over the pubis, the groin, the scrotum, the labia or the flank, and it may take hours to show. A gap where the two pubic bones meet, or a wound near the perineum, is a serious finding. The responder records what is seen, felt and reported, and does not test the ring.

The signs are not always present, and a chapter that teaches them as certain will be believed and will then be wrong. Some pelvic fractures cause surprisingly little pain, and an older adult may walk a few steps with a break of a pubic ramus. There may be no bruising in the first hour, no deformity and no complaint beyond a reluctance to move. Intoxication, a head injury, a spinal injury and the pain of another wound can all hide the pelvis. A patient who is confused or unconscious cannot describe pain, so the responder falls back on the mechanism, the vital signs and the whole picture.

The pelvis belongs to the primary survey because it is one of the places where a patient can bleed to death while the examination of the limb is still being arranged. The survey follows the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and the control of massive bleeding sits inside the step for circulation. A pulse that seems normal may rise as the loss continues, and the change over minutes is more useful than any single measurement. Exposure is what reveals the wound at the perineum, the swelling of the thigh and the blood at the opening of the urethra. When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, life comes before limb.

No responder springs the pelvis, and that prohibition is the most important sentence in this chapter. Springing means pressing inward on the two iliac crests, rocking the ring, pulling on the legs to compare their length, or pressing again and again on the pubic symphysis to see whether it moves. Each of those movements can dislodge the clot that holds a torn vein closed, restart bleeding behind the peritoneum, drive bone into a vessel or a nerve, and cause pain that itself worsens the bleeding. The judgment about the stability of the ring belongs to a clinician who will act on the answer, and it is made once, gently, with the plan already decided. The hands of the responder support and cover, and do not test.

The neurovascular examination is done before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is written down, because a finding not recorded before a binder was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of both feet and feels the pulse at the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle on each side. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and the words the patient uses for numbness or tingling are written as far as possible. The pelvis shares its nerves with the legs, so a weak foot or an area of numbness may be the first sign that the ring has pressed on a nerve root. A pulse that is present does not exclude damage to a vessel, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency.

Some findings in this region are examined only by a clinician, and the task of the responder is to notice them and to report them. Blood at the opening of the urethra, blood in the urine, an inability to pass urine, a swollen scrotum or labia and a laceration of the perineum all change the plan. A urinary catheter is not passed when the urethra may be torn, and that decision belongs to the physician, or to the nurse acting under a protocol that names who may decide. A gloved examination of the rectum or the vagina is a clinical examination and not a field test. The lay first aider reports what is visible, and the trained responder does the same unless the local protocol says otherwise.

Stabilization of a suspected pelvic fracture is a short list of acts, and restraint is the most important of them. Bleeding that can be seen is controlled with direct pressure and a dressing, and an embedded object is left in place and stabilized. The patient is kept flat, moved as little as possible and protected from cold with blankets, insulation from the ground and the removal of wet clothing, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. A deformed limb is splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, since the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone. The lay first aider acts without equipment, the trained responder and the paramedic act within the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician directs the care.

A pelvic binder is a device that wraps the ring at the level of the hips, and it is used to reduce the volume of the pelvis and to limit movement so that the clotting of the patient can work. It is a measure for the control of bleeding during transfer, and not a treatment that makes the fracture safe or removes the need for urgent referral. It is applied by a trained responder, a paramedic or a physician according to the training and the local protocol that govern it, while a folded sheet may serve where the service authorizes that practice. Applied wrongly, it damages skin, sits too high or too low and does nothing, or gives false reassurance while bleeding continues behind it. The reassessment after it is applied matters as much as the act of applying it.

Certain acts are forbidden in this injury, and each prohibition has a reason attached to it. The responder never asks a patient with a suspected pelvic fracture to stand, to walk or to lift a leg in order to test weight-bearing, because the test can complete a bone that was only cracked and start bleeding that was not happening. The responder never straightens a deformed limb, never pulls on a leg to compare lengths, never pushes exposed bone back into a wound, never removes an embedded object and never explores an open wound blindly. The patient is not sat up, and is not rolled from side to side without a team and a plan. Force is not a technique.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the ring, of the spine that rests on it and of the joints above and below the injury until someone qualified has cleared them. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until it has been cleared by a person qualified to clear it, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. A patient with a suspected pelvic fracture is therefore moved by a trained team, with the precautions and the equipment that the local protocol requires. A scoop stretcher, a vacuum mattress or a firm transfer surface may be used by those trained in it, and the legs are left where they lie. A traction splint is not a device for the pelvis, and every device is checked after it is applied.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph of the pelvis is not a screening test for every patient who has fallen, and that decision belongs to the clinician who has examined the patient and weighed the mechanism. Computed tomography shows the ring, the sacrum and the joint surfaces in detail, and it is used when the patient is stable enough to travel to the scanner. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues and can show an injury that a radiograph misses in an older adult. A normal image does not exclude a fracture, and the patient is examined again after the picture has been taken.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single number. The responder checks the level of consciousness, the breathing, the pulse, the color and the warmth of the skin, the pain, the abdomen for swelling, the wound for fresh bleeding, the device for tightness and the legs for movement and sensation. A patient who becomes more restless, more pale or more confused while the pulse rises is still bleeding, even if the pelvis looks unchanged. A deterioration that does not respond stops the process and sends the patient onward at once.

A pelvic fracture is dangerous because its bleeding is hidden, so the responder reads the whole patient rather than the injured part. Blood that collects behind the peritoneum does not swell the abdomen in the way that a bleeding spleen does, and it does not bruise the skin over the pelvis. A rising pulse, a falling blood pressure measured by those authorized to measure it, skin that is pale, cool and damp, thirst, restlessness and a reduced production of urine all suggest that the loss is continuing. In an older adult, a medicine that thins the blood may make the loss faster and the signs appear sooner. No single measurement is decisive, and the trend over minutes is what the receiving team will want to hear.

Definitive treatment of an unstable pelvic fracture belongs to the trauma team, the orthopedic surgeon and the interventional radiologist working in a facility with an operating room and an intensive care unit. Bleeding may be controlled by packing the pelvis in the operating room, by a procedure that blocks the bleeding vessel from inside under imaging, or by a device that holds the ring from the outside. The choice depends on the patient, the injury and the resources of the hospital, and definitive fixation of the ring is a later decision. None of these treatments is described here as a technique to be learned from a book, and none of them belongs to the responder.

Reduction, traction and casting are named in this course because a listener must know what they are, why they are done, what they are meant to achieve and what can go wrong, while the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training and to the local protocol. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends, traction holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation holds the position while the bone heals. In the pelvis these acts are performed in an operating room by a surgeon trained in them, and they are not attempted in the field or by anyone without the training and the equipment. A reduction is not attempted when the ring is unstable and the patient is bleeding, when the injury is open, when a vessel or a nerve is failing, when the diagnosis is unclear, when training or equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed.

An open pelvic fracture is one in which the bone or the deep tissues have communicated with the outside, through a wound in the buttock, the perineum, the vagina or the rectum. The wound may be small and easy to overlook under clothing or blood, and it may communicate with the bowel, which contaminates the deep tissues at the moment of injury. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes, keeps the patient warm and arranges urgent transfer. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. Closure and the decisions about infection and tetanus belong to the operating room and to the prescriber.

The pelvis rarely travels alone, and the responder should expect more than one injury. The bladder and the urethra may be torn, the rectum and the vagina may be opened, the vessels and the nerve roots that leave the pelvis may be damaged, and the spine, the thigh bone, the chest, the abdomen and the head may be injured in the same event. A fracture of the thigh bone on the same side increases the loss of blood and changes the way the limb lies. The responder notices, records and reports each finding in the order in which the patient was examined. Treating the obvious wound while the hidden bleeding continues is the commonest way to lose a patient who arrived talking.

Some groups of patients need a lower threshold for suspicion and for referral. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break the pelvis in a fall from standing height, and that break may be stable enough to be treated without an operation, so an event that looks minor to a young responder may be serious for that patient. A child has a more elastic pelvis, so the ring bends before it breaks, and a pelvic fracture in a child is rare and usually means very great energy and other injuries as well. A pregnant patient carries two lives, and the uterus, the placenta and the position of the patient belong to the clinician and to the local protocol, while the responder protects, warms and transports. The sequence of care does not change, but the degree of concern does.

Pain in a pelvic fracture is a finding, a burden and a risk, because pain drives the pulse, the breathing and the movement that the injury cannot afford. Relieving pain is part of the care of the patient, and the decision about how to relieve it belongs to the clinician or to the paramedic authorized by the local protocol. The responder who may not give a medicine still helps, by supporting the limb, by reducing movement, by keeping the patient warm and by watching for a change. The name of the substance, the amount and the way it is given are set by the local protocol and by the prescriber, and no listener should be able to take a prescription from this course.

Communication is part of the treatment, and it begins before the patient reaches the hospital. The emergency medical technician or the paramedic sends a pre-alert according to the local protocol, naming the mechanism, the time of the injury, the suspected pelvic fracture, the vital signs, the findings before and after each intervention and the treatment given. The receiving team prepares the room, the blood, the imaging and the operating room while the vehicle is still moving, and that preparation depends on a clear message. The nurse who receives the patient repeats the story back and records it, and the physician decides the next steps. Handover is given in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one.

The scope of practice for every act has to be said plainly, because the law and the training differ between countries and services. The lay first aider supports the limb, covers a wound, keeps the patient warm and calls for help, and does nothing that needs equipment or authorization. The trained first responder and the paramedic immobilize, apply the devices their service authorizes, monitor and report, and they act within the procedures written for them. The nurse observes, records, reassesses and gives the care that the nursing protocol allows. The physician examines, orders imaging and decides about transfer, while the orthopedic surgeon and the interventional radiologist perform the definitive procedures.

Every number in this chapter is an illustration and not a rule. The volume of blood that can be lost into the pelvis, the time within which a patient must reach an operating room, the pressure at which a device is applied and the interval between observations differ between services, countries and editions, and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is used. A figure remembered from a book and applied in a different service can lead to a device that is too tight, a transfer that is too late or an observation that is never made. What does not differ is the order of the work, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively.

Stability of the pelvic ring is a judgment about which parts have moved and whether the ring can still carry the weight of the body. A break in one part with the rest of the ring intact behaves differently from a break that opens the ring at two points and lets the halves move independently. The clinician makes that judgment from the examination and the images, and it decides whether the patient needs an operation, how soon, and where. The responder cannot make that judgment and does not need to, because the safe course is the same in every case. The pelvis is treated as unstable, protected from movement, kept warm and moved toward a team that can decide.

A constructed illustration may make the order of the work easier to hold in mind, and the patient in it is imagined rather than drawn from any real case. A person is struck by a vehicle and lies on the road, awake but restless and pale, with pain in the groin and a leg that will not move. The responder checks the scene, protects against blood and moves through the primary survey, and in the step for circulation notices the pelvis. The pelvis is not sprung, the wound at the perineum is covered, the patient is kept flat and warm, and the neurovascular status of both feet is recorded before anything is applied. The ring is supported with the device the service authorizes, the findings before and after are written down, and the patient is transferred to a trauma team with the message that a pelvic fracture is suspected. Nothing required the responder to decide whether the ring was stable, and nothing was done twice.

When a complication is suspected, the response is to stop and to escalate rather than to press on. Force is not a technique, and a maneuver that meets resistance has already answered the question it was asked. A constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol by a person authorized to release it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm and referred urgently, because the diagnosis of a compartment syndrome is clinical and time is muscle. The same principle applies to the pelvis, where a patient bleeding behind the peritoneum cannot be helped by more pressure from outside but only by a team that can stop the source.

Pelvic fractures teach a lesson that runs through the whole of musculoskeletal care, which is that the bone is often the least dangerous part of the injury. A broken ring may hold a clot that a single careless movement destroys, a wound that looks small may communicate with the bowel, and a patient who is talking may be losing blood into a space that no one can see. The value of the responder lies in recognizing the pattern early, in protecting the patient from movement and from cold, in recording what was found before and after every act, and in handing the patient to people who can stop the bleeding. Recognition, protection, record and referral are four words that carry most of the work.

To summarize, a pelvic fracture is a bleeding injury before it is a bone injury, because the pelvis is a ring with great vessels, wide veins and a large hidden space behind the peritoneum, and the loss can continue without a mark on the skin. The pelvis belongs to the primary survey, and a patient with a mechanism of high energy, pain in the groin, the hip or the perineum, or an inability to bear weight is treated as having a broken pelvis until a qualified clinician has decided otherwise. The responder never springs the pelvis, never asks the patient to stand or to lift a leg, never straightens a deformed limb, never pushes bone back into a wound and never removes an embedded object, because each of those acts can restart bleeding or damage a vessel or a nerve. The order of the work is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the neurovascular findings recorded before and after every intervention. Warmth, restraint, documentation and a clear handover to a trauma team are the contribution of the responder, and every act is named for the level of practice that is allowed to perform it. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no medicine and no dose is given in this course, because the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 25 — Pelvic Trauma Management

The pelvis is a ring of bone, and a ring that gives way in one place has almost always given way or torn somewhere else as well, so an injury of the pelvic ring is a bleeding problem before it is a bone problem. The bones enclose a rich network of veins and the arteries that supply the buttock, the thigh and the organs within the pelvis, and those vessels lie in a space that can accept a very large volume of blood without a drop of it appearing on the skin. A patient can therefore be bleeding to death from a pelvic injury while the abdomen looks flat and the skin looks unmarked, and the fracture may still look like nothing at all. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work. Its subject is what is done for the patient with a pelvic injury, and it follows the order this course uses everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively.

The bleeding from a broken pelvis comes chiefly from torn veins, from the raw spongy surfaces of the bone, and from branches of the arteries that run along the back of the ring. The veins that cross the pelvis are large and thin-walled, so they tear rather than seal, and the space behind the lining of the abdomen has room to accept a volume that teaching quotes in liters for an adult. That figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the volumes named in different services and different editions do not agree. The consequence that matters is not the number but the direction of the thinking, since until someone qualified has shown otherwise, a pelvic fracture is treated as a source of major bleeding. A broken ring is also a mechanical problem, since every movement of the patient can open it further.

A pelvic fracture in a young adult is usually the mark of great force, such as a vehicle crash, a motorcycle crash, a pedestrian struck, a fall from a height or a crush. Whatever the mechanism, the patient is approached in one order, and that order is the spine of this chapter. The first step is assessment, the next is stabilization, then the neurovascular examination, then immobilization, then imaging, then reassessment, and only after that the decision to refer or to treat definitively. Two of those steps are non-negotiable in every patient, because the neurovascular examination is performed and recorded before any intervention and repeated after it, and because the reassessment after every intervention is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment.

Assessment begins before the patient is touched, with the scene, because a responder who is injured adds a second patient to a difficult rescue. The hazards are counted, the number of patients is noted, and the mechanism is read from the wreckage as well as from the story, because the direction of the force predicts where the energy has gone. The primary survey follows, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Catastrophic bleeding that can be seen is controlled first by the trained first responder or the paramedic, using the equipment the service provides and within the procedures it authorizes. The lay first aider calls for help, does not move the patient unless there is immediate danger, keeps the patient warm and stays with the patient. Only when the patient is stable enough does the examination turn to the pelvis and the limbs.

The pelvis is examined by looking before it is examined by hand, and the eyes are asked specific questions. A limb that lies rotated outward, a leg that appears shorter than the other, bruising over the perineum, swelling of the scrotum or the labia, blood at the opening of the urethra, blood at the anus and any wound all point toward the ring. The trained responder may then press the ring gently and once, feeling for movement between the two halves of the front of the pelvis, and writes the finding down. What must not happen is the repeated springing, rocking and re-testing of the pelvis that turns the patient into a demonstration for each new pair of hands, because every movement can break the clot that has begun to seal a torn vein. A pelvis that feels firm under gentle pressure may still be broken, so the absence of movement is not reassurance. Three examinations belong to the clinician rather than to the responder, and they are the internal examination of the rectum and of the vagina, the passing of a tube into the bladder, and the probing of a wound near the perineum. Each of those acts can do harm in untrained hands, because a channel that is partly torn can be made completely torn by a tube pushed blindly through it. The responder looks, reports, protects those regions and lets the clinician decide.

Stabilization of the ring is the act that buys the most time, and the device that most services use is a wide band called a pelvic binder. It is placed around the pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters, which are the prominent bony points on the outer side of the upper thigh, and not at the level of the crests of the iliac bones. The reason is mechanical, since the front of the ring is closed by bringing the two halves of the pelvis together at the joint between them, while a band placed higher, over the crests, can press the wings of the pelvis apart instead. A commercial binder is designed for that level, while an improvised one is a folded sheet or a wide strip of cloth, at least 15 centimeters wide, a figure offered as an illustration to be confirmed against the guideline in force and the local protocol. The band is applied over the clothing where possible, it is centered, it is wide enough that the pressure is spread rather than focused, and it is tightened firmly but never so tight that it acts as a tourniquet. The trained first responder and the paramedic apply the device within the procedures and the equipment their service authorizes, and the lay first aider at most presses the knees together gently or holds a folded sheet in place under the direction of a dispatcher until trained help arrives.

A pelvic binder is a bridge and not a treatment, and a listener who understands that will not be surprised when the patient remains unstable after a neat band has been applied. The binder closes the volume of the ring and gives the clot a chance to form, but it does not stop arterial bleeding and it does not replace blood, warmth or an operating room. It is left in place during movement, during imaging and during transfer, and it is not removed by anyone who is not qualified to decide what happens next. The decision about when it comes off, and what is done in its place, belongs to the receiving team and to the physician. The skin beneath the band and the tightness of the band are checked at every move and at every reassessment, because a device left too long or made too tight causes an injury of its own.

The log roll is the maneuver by which the patient is turned as a single unit so that the back can be seen, and in a pelvic injury it is performed once, by a team, with the spine protected. It must not be repeated for the convenience of a new examiner and it must not be repeated to prove a finding, because every roll moves the ring, disturbs a clot and can displace an unstable spine. The lay first aider does not roll a patient alone, since no lone manual handling technique is safe where a pelvic or spinal injury is suspected. The pelvis and the spine are injured together often enough that a pelvic injury is treated as a spinal injury until the spine has been cleared by someone qualified to clear it, the neck is kept in line while the airway is managed, and a collar is applied according to the local protocol. Clearing the spine is a clinical decision made with examination and imaging together, and it is never made by a responder at the roadside.

Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and the patient with a pelvic injury is at risk from the moment of the crash. The patient lies on the road or on a hard floor, clothing is cut away so that the pelvis can be seen, blood is lost from the circulation, wet clothing holds the cold against the skin, and the back of an ambulance loses its warmth every time the doors open. Cooling makes the clotting system fail, so a patient who is allowed to become cold bleeds more and then bleeds still more, and that spiral is difficult to interrupt once it has begun. Prevention starts with insulation from the ground, continues with the removal of wet clothing and its replacement with dry covering, includes covering the head and the hands, and includes warming the vehicle before the patient is loaded. Warmed fluids are a physician's decision within the local protocol, and the temperature is measured wherever the equipment allows, because a falling temperature is a finding to be reported rather than a detail to be tolerated.

The neurovascular examination is performed and recorded before the binder is applied and again after it is applied, and it is repeated at every reassessment because the trend of the findings matters more than any single set. The examiner feels for the pulse at the back of the ankle and on the top of the foot, notes the color and the warmth of the skin, presses a nail briefly to watch the color return, tests sensation on the front and the back of the leg and in the region that would touch a saddle, and asks the patient to move the ankle and the toes. The result is written with the time, before the intervention and after it, because a finding that was not recorded before a binder or a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious bleeding inside the pelvis, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency that forces the fastest possible transfer. The lay first aider notices color, warmth, and whether the patient can move and feel, and reports a change at once, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

Nerves that run through the pelvis can be injured by the broken bone, by the bleeding around it, or by pressure from a device, and the findings are easy to miss in a patient who is distracted by pain. The large nerve bundle that leaves the spine and passes through the pelvis supplies the muscles of the leg and the foot, and its injury may show as a foot that will not lift, a leg that feels numb, or a limb weaker than the other one. Numbness in the region that would touch a saddle, the inability to pass urine, and the loss of the tone of the anal sphincter are findings that suggest pressure on the lowest nerves of the spine, and they are urgent because that injury can become permanent within hours. Such a finding is reported immediately by whoever notices it, and it is acted upon by the clinician, since decompression and definitive care belong to a surgical service. A binder that is too high, too tight or badly centered can press on nerves as well, which is a further reason to check it whenever the patient is moved.

Circulation is judged from the whole patient rather than from the pelvis alone, and the signs are the ones taught in the first weeks of every clinical training. A pulse that rises, a blood pressure that falls, skin that is pale, cool and damp, a nail that stays white after it is pressed, thirst, restlessness and then confusion all point to a circulation that is losing ground. A single set of observations can look reassuring in a young patient who is compensating, and the patient who improves for a few minutes and then worsens again is often the patient who is bleeding once more. The observations are therefore repeated and compared, and the comparison is what is reported. The responder's part is to recognize the pattern early, to keep the patient warm and to move the patient toward blood and an operating room.

The decisions about fluid and blood belong to the physician and to the local protocol of the service, and this course describes the reasoning without ever supplying the prescription. Where the service authorizes it and the training certifies it, the paramedic or the nurse obtains access to a vein so that the physician's decision can be carried out without delay, and nothing is given on personal authority. Which fluid is used, how much is given and how quickly it runs are matters for the physician, who weighs the risk of continued bleeding against the risk of dilution and knows the stock of the hospital. Strategies differ between countries and between editions of the same guideline, and one service may deliberately keep the pressure lower than usual until bleeding is controlled while another follows a different path. The same boundary applies to every medicine that might be considered around a pelvic injury, whether for pain, for infection or to support the clotting of blood, because the substance, the amount and the way it is given belong to the prescriber and to the protocol. What the responder can do is the same in every service, which is to recognize shock, to keep the patient warm, to protect the access the protocol permits, and to say aloud that the patient is deteriorating.

Immobilization of a pelvic injury begins with the binder and continues with everything else attached to the pelvis. The legs are kept together and still, and the trained responder may bind the ankles and the knees to one another with padding between them, provided the local protocol permits it, since a leg that swings freely moves the ring. The patient is lifted and carried on a device that supports the pelvis and the spine together, used by people who have practiced with it. A deformed limb is splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Where a thigh bone is broken as well, a traction splint may be used by a responder trained and authorized to use one, and the technique belongs to supervised practice. Nothing is achieved by pulling on a leg to make a pelvis look straighter, and definitive alignment belongs to the operating room.

Imaging for a pelvic injury begins with a radiograph of the pelvis, which is usually made early in a patient with major trauma because it answers a question that changes what is done. The single picture shows the ring from the front and reveals gross displacement, and computed tomography then shows the ring in three dimensions, the joints of the pelvis, the sacrum and the volume of blood collected behind the lining of the abdomen. The decision to image, and the choice of study, belong to the clinician responsible for the patient, and that decision is never made by the lay first aider or by the responder. The binder is left in place while the pictures are made unless a clinician directs otherwise, and the team that makes the images is told that it is there. No image replaces the examination, and a first radiograph that looks normal does not exclude a fracture of the ring, because some breaks are seen only on another view or on a later study.

Reassessment happens after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment rather than the complication of the injury. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, so that the direction of travel is visible to whoever reads it next. Several findings should stop the responder and force an escalation, and they include pain that increases rather than settles, new numbness or tingling, a foot that becomes pale or cool, a pulse that disappears, an abdomen that becomes distended, a patient who becomes confused, and a binder that has slipped, loosened or become too tight. Pain and swelling in a thigh that is tightly bandaged may mean a compartment syndrome, which is a clinical diagnosis and an emergency, and the response within the local protocol is to release whatever is constricting the limb, to keep the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, to keep the patient warm, and to refer urgently, because time is muscle. A responder who suspects that condition does not wait for confirmation and does not watch quietly.

An open pelvic fracture is one in which the bone or the deep tissues have communicated with the outside, and the wound may lie in the perineum, in the buttock, in the groin, or within the rectum or the vagina where it is not seen at a glance. The part played by the responder is limited and precise, which is to cover the wound with a sterile dressing, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, to record the neurovascular status, to immobilize the pelvis, to keep the patient warm and to arrange urgent transfer. A wound is never explored blindly, an embedded object is never removed, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and because the deep tissues are contaminated from the moment of the injury. Cleansing, removal of dead tissue and definitive closure belong to the operating room, and they are done early by the surgical team rather than improvised at the roadside. The responder says clearly what was seen, what was covered and what was left alone.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and for a patient with a pelvic injury the question is rarely whether to refer but where, how and how soon. The destination that can treat this injury has imaging, an operating room, an intensive care unit and, where such a service exists, the ability to block a bleeding vessel from inside the artery without opening the abdomen or the pelvis. Not every hospital has all of those, so the nearest hospital is not always the right one, and the physician and the receiving center decide together and early. The responding team's part is to ask for that decision as soon as the injury is suspected, to prepare the patient while the decision is made, and to follow the destination the system names rather than the destination that seems convenient. Figures quoted for transfer times are illustrations to be checked against the guideline in force and the local protocol, since the geography of one region is not the geography of another.

The preparation for transfer is a short list of acts performed in a fixed order, and the order is part of the treatment. The first is to control what can be controlled where the patient lies, which means bleeding, airway, breathing, warmth, the binder and any splint. The next is to make the record complete, with the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which each limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention and the trend of the pulse, the pressure and the level of consciousness. Only then is the patient moved onto the carrying device, with the spine protected and the pelvis supported, and only then is the journey begun with the monitor, the covering and the access that the protocol provides. During the journey the observations are repeated, the binder and the splints are checked whenever the patient is handled, and any change is reported before arrival rather than at the door. A patient who becomes unstable on the way is a patient for whom the receiving team must be warned in advance.

The handover carries the story rather than a set of numbers, and it is spoken in an order that the receiving team can follow without having to ask. It states how old the patient is, what happened and when, what was found on the primary survey, what the pelvis looked like and whether the ring moved, what the neurovascular status was before the binder and after it, what was done and by whom, what has changed since, and where the patient was going before arriving here. Everything given to the patient is named with the person who authorized it, which is why a spoken chapter gives no amount and no schedule. A handover that ends with the question of what the receiving team would like next respects the fact that the definitive decisions belong to them.

Children, older adults and pregnant patients change the weight of the findings without changing the sequence. A child's pelvis is more elastic than an adult's, so it takes greater force to break, and a break in a child is therefore a marker of severe energy and a reason to look harder for injuries elsewhere. An older adult may break the pelvis in a fall from standing height, may bleed slowly and for a long time, and may be taking a medicine that prevents clotting, so the history of those medicines is part of the assessment and is reported to the physician. A pregnant patient carries two patients, and the care of the mother and of the child must be planned together, with the position of the mother on the carrying device chosen according to the local protocol and the stage of the pregnancy. In each of those patients the threshold for immobilization, for warmth and for urgent transfer is lower rather than higher.

A constructed illustration may help to hold the sequence together, and it is invented for teaching rather than drawn from any real patient. A motorcyclist is thrown from the machine, is awake and pale, and has a fast pulse and a leg that lies turned outward, while the responder keeps the head in line and the team applies a binder at the level of the greater trochanters over the clothing. The patient is rolled once onto a vacuum mattress after the back has been examined, wet clothing is cut away and replaced with dry covering, and the ambulance is warmed before the doors close. The neurovascular findings of both feet are written down before the binder and after it, warmth is maintained through the journey, the receiving hospital is warned, and the handover ends with the trend of the observations rather than with the fracture. Nothing in that illustration is a technique, and every act in it was performed by someone trained and authorized to perform it.

What a listener must never do is easier to state than what to do, and it is worth saying plainly before the summary. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, the pelvis is never sprung repeatedly to confirm a finding, a pelvic binder is never removed by someone who is not qualified to decide what happens next, a wound is never explored blindly, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and no medicine is given on personal authority. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no part of this course teaches them as techniques to be acquired by listening. Nothing said here replaces training, certification, supervision, the protocol of the service or the law of the country in which the listener works.

To summarize, a pelvic injury is a hemorrhage problem before it is a bone problem, because the ring surrounds large veins and an artery-rich space that can hold a great volume of blood while the skin stays unmarked. The order is always the same, and it is to assess, to stabilize, to examine and to record the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the provider level named for every act. The pelvic binder is placed at the level of the greater trochanters and not on the crests of the pelvis, it is a bridge to definitive care and not a treatment, and it is not removed by anyone who is not qualified to decide what comes next. The log roll is performed once, by a team, with the spine protected, and the pelvis is never sprung or rocked repeatedly. Cold is treated as a complication and not as a detail, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and the decisions about fluid, blood and medicine belong to the physician and to the local protocol. The patient is reassessed after every intervention, and the destination is a center that can image the injury, operate on it and care for it in an intensive care unit.

# Chapter 26 — Hip Fractures and Hip Dislocation

A fracture of the hip is one of the injuries most likely to end the independence of an older adult, and it is one of the few fractures whose outcome is decided as much by how the patient is handled in the first hours as by the operation that follows. The hip is a deep ball and socket joint, and the bone that breaks most often in this region is the femur, the long bone of the thigh, at the point where its head meets its shaft. A hip dislocation, in which the head of the femur leaves the socket altogether, is far less common and far more urgent, because the blood supply of the head runs along the bone and can be torn by the displacement itself. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows that order for both injuries. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The hip joint is formed by the rounded head of the femur sitting in a cup-shaped hollow of the pelvis called the acetabulum, and the fit is deep and stable because the socket surrounds more than half of the ball. Strong ligaments spiral around the joint and the capsule that encloses it is thick, which is why the hip dislocates only under great force while the shoulder, with its shallow socket, dislocates easily. The neck of the femur angles from the head to the shaft, and the blood that keeps the head alive travels along that neck in small vessels that run beneath the capsule. Those vessels are already stretched and compressed in a displaced fracture of the neck, and they are stretched again when the head leaves the socket. The head of the bone has almost no blood supply of its own, so when the vessels along the neck are torn the bone dies, a process called avascular necrosis, and that is why both injuries in this chapter are treated as urgent.

Hip fractures are grouped by where the break lies in relation to the capsule, and the grouping matters because the blood supply of the head is at risk in one group and not in the other. A break of the neck of the femur, just below the head, is called intracapsular because it lies inside the capsule, and it interrupts the vessels that run along the neck, so the head may lose its supply. A break between the neck and the shaft, through the prominences called the trochanters, is called intertrochanteric, and it lies outside the capsule, where the bone is rich in blood and heals more readily. A break just below the trochanters is called subtrochanteric, and it usually follows greater force and is more likely to bleed. The examiner in the field does not make this distinction, because it belongs to imaging and to the orthopedic surgeon, but the distinction explains why one phrase, a broken hip, describes two injuries with different futures.

The patient who most often breaks a hip is an older adult whose bone has lost density, and the injury usually follows a fall from standing height or less. The bone of an older person is thinner and more brittle, and the muscles that would once have absorbed the fall are weaker, so a force that would leave a younger person bruised snaps the femoral neck or the trochanteric region. In a younger patient the same fracture follows a road crash, a fall from height or a bicycle injury, and it may be accompanied by other injuries that are more immediately dangerous, so a break of the hip in a young patient raises the suspicion of greater force and of injury elsewhere. A constructed illustration may help: an older woman who cannot rise after a fall in her kitchen and a young cyclist thrown over the handlebars may both arrive with a broken hip, and both are handled in the same order.

The findings that suggest a hip fracture are pain in the groin, the thigh or the knee, an inability to bear weight, and a limb that lies shortened and rotated outward, with the knee and the foot turned away from the other side. Pain on any movement of the hip is common, and the patient often holds the leg still and resists any attempt to move it. The knee may hurt more than the hip, because the nerve that supplies the hip also supplies the knee, so a patient who complains only of knee pain after a fall still needs the hip examined by a clinician. These signs are helpful, and none of them is reliable enough to build a decision on by itself. A fracture that is impacted, with one broken surface driven into the other, may allow the patient to walk, and a patient with dementia may not report pain at all. The consequence for the listener is a low threshold, so that any older adult who falls and cannot walk as before is treated as having a hip injury until someone qualified has excluded it.

Assessment begins before the limb, with the scene, the mechanism of injury and the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. An older patient lying on a hard floor after a fall may be cold, frightened, dehydrated and in pain, and the fall may have been caused by an illness rather than by an accident, so the responder asks what happened before the patient reached the ground. Life comes before limb, and when one pair of hands must choose, the airway, the breathing and the circulation are dealt with first while the hip is supported in the position found. The lay first aider recognizes the injury, calls for help, keeps the patient warm and does not move the patient unless the scene is unsafe. The trained responder and the paramedic examine within the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what is done next. A patient who is drowsy, whose pulse is weak and rapid or whose skin is cold and pale sends the responder back to the beginning of the survey.

The history that matters for a hip fracture is short and practical. The responder tries to learn the time of the fall, the height of the fall, what the patient was doing, whether the patient could stand afterwards and how long the patient has been lying there, because each of those answers changes the urgency. The medicines the patient takes, the illnesses the patient lives with, whether the patient walks with a frame or a stick, and where the patient lives and with whom all belong to the story, because they decide where the patient should be taken and how much support will be needed afterwards. Pain is assessed by asking, by looking at the face and the posture and by noticing which movement the patient avoids, and it is recorded rather than estimated silently. Constructed examples in this course are illustrations only, and no real patient is described.

Stabilization of a suspected hip fracture in the field is a small set of acts, and restraint is the most important of them. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and because pulling the limb may turn a closed fracture into an open one. The leg is not pulled, not rotated, not measured against the other leg again and again, and not lifted by the ankle, and nobody tests how far the hip will move. The lay first aider supports the leg with the hands, with a pillow or with a rolled blanket, keeps the patient warm and waits for help. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint or a binding within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician decides what immobilization is needed for the journey. Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced, since an older patient loses heat quickly and cools further while lying still.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding that was not written before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the foot, feels the pulses at the ankle and the foot, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the ankle and the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and numbness, tingling or a movement that has been lost is recorded in the words of the patient as far as possible. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, and reports any change, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or the clinician. One limit must be said plainly: this examination describes the limb below the injury, and no bedside test shows whether the blood supply of the femoral head has survived, which is why a displaced break of the neck and every hip dislocation are threats to the head until imaging and the surgeon say otherwise.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, so far as that can be done without force. In a suspected hip fracture the limb is supported from the hip to the foot, a pad is placed between the knees, and the leg is held in the position found until a stretcher is ready. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, is applied over the position found, and is secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation, and an improvised device must be checked more often because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints and bindings within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. Traction, which is a gentle continuous pull applied along the limb to hold the broken ends in line and to reduce spasm, is sometimes used while a patient waits for surgery, and it is applied only by a clinician acting under local protocol, because the pull, the counter-pull, the padding and the skin all need supervision. Traction is not a technique to be learned from a book, and this course does not teach it, nor does it teach casting, nor does it teach reduction.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and for a suspected hip fracture it is taken in at least two directions so that a break in one plane is not hidden, with the joint above and below included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography gives more detail of a fracture around the socket or of a break that is hard to see, and it is also used to plan an operation. Magnetic resonance imaging shows bone and soft tissues together and can reveal a fracture of the neck that a radiograph did not show, which matters in a patient who cannot bear weight and whose first picture looked normal. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed, because that decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient. A normal radiograph does not exclude a hip fracture, so a patient who cannot walk as before is kept still and referred even when the picture is reported as normal.

Reassessment happens after every intervention and is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison matters more than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the splint is checked for tightness, and the skin over the heel and the sacrum is checked for damage, since an older patient who lies still can be injured by the surface itself. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. Compartment syndrome is uncommon in the thigh but it happens, and a responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation: within the limits of local protocol a constricting bandage or splint is released by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm and referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. A change in the level of consciousness, in the breathing or in the pulse is also a reason to stop and escalate, since a hip fracture in an older patient may be only one part of a larger illness.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and for a hip fracture it almost always begins with a call to a hospital that has an orthopedic surgeon. A patient with a displaced break of the femoral neck, a fracture broken into several pieces, a suspected dislocation, an open wound, or signs of damage to a nerve or a vessel is referred urgently, and the reason is that the period in which surgery gives the best result is short, with the first 24 to 48 hours offered in teaching as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since practice differs between countries and editions. Definitive treatment is decided by the orthopedic surgeon and may be a surgical fixation, in which metal devices hold the bone while it heals, or a replacement of the joint, in which the damaged head and sometimes the socket are exchanged for an artificial one. Some patients are treated without an operation because surgery is too dangerous for them, and that decision belongs to the clinical team. Reduction, traction, casting and every operation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them can be learned from a book.

A hip dislocation is a different injury, and it is rare because the socket is deep. The head of the femur is driven out of the acetabulum by great force, most often in a road crash when the knee strikes the dashboard or in a fall from a height, and the head usually comes to rest behind the socket, which is called a posterior dislocation. Less often it comes to rest in front of the socket, which is called an anterior dislocation. In the common posterior dislocation the limb is shortened, the knee is bent and the leg is turned inward toward the other leg, while in the anterior dislocation the limb is held out to the side and turned outward. The findings are taught as typical and not as certain, because a fracture of the socket or of the head can change them, and an examiner who expects one attitude may not see the other. The sciatic nerve, which passes behind the hip, is the nerve most often injured, and its damage shows as numbness or weakness below the knee, so the neurovascular examination before and after any intervention is the record that matters. A dislocation of the hip is often accompanied by a fracture of the acetabulum or of the femoral head, by a knee injury or by a head injury that takes priority.

A dislocated hip is an emergency for the blood supply of the femoral head, and the reason is anatomical. The vessels that feed the head run along the neck, and when the head leaves the socket those vessels are stretched and compressed, so the bone is starved of blood from the moment of the injury until the joint is put back. If the head is starved long enough it dies, and the dead bone collapses months or years later, which is the outcome called avascular necrosis, and the risk rises with every hour of delay. The responder's part is precise and limited: recognize the injury, keep the limb supported in the position found, record the neurovascular status, keep the patient warm and arrange the fastest safe transfer to a facility with an orthopedic surgeon. The responder does not attempt to put the joint back, does not pull on the limb, does not straighten it and does not test the joint. Reduction of a dislocated hip is performed by a clinician, usually under sedation or anesthesia in a controlled setting, and the substance, the amount and the route belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, so no listener can take a regimen from this course.

There are situations in which a reduction must not be attempted at all, and the reasons are worth carrying because force applied in the wrong place can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. An attempt is not made when a complex fracture and dislocation are suspected together, when a fragment of bone is caught between the joint surfaces, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the person present lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. In each of those situations the correct act is to stop, to immobilize the limb in the position found, to record what was found before and after, and to move the patient to someone qualified to decide. Resistance is a signal to stop and not a problem to be overcome, because force is not a technique, and the rule protects the patient from an act that only felt helpful.

Some patients need a lower threshold than others. A child with hip pain who refuses to walk needs urgent assessment by a clinician, because several conditions in a child's hip present in the same way, and the examination and the imaging belong to the clinician. A patient whose hip has already been replaced can dislocate it with an ordinary movement such as bending to pick something from the floor, and the findings may be milder, so a replaced hip that becomes painful and loses its range of movement is treated as a dislocation until someone qualified has excluded it. A patient with dementia may be unable to report pain, and the responder then relies on what is seen, on the position of the limb and on the account of whoever found the patient. A patient who has fallen and cannot get up may have lain there for hours, and cold, dehydration and pressure damage may be more urgent than the fracture itself. A patient with a hip injury can also have an injury of the spine or of the pelvis, and the pelvis and the spine are each treated as unstable until they are cleared by someone qualified to clear them.

Handling and transport decide whether the work done before is preserved. The patient with a suspected hip fracture is moved by a trained team using the equipment and the precautions the local protocol requires, with the limb supported and the body kept in line, and no lone manual handling technique is safe however strong the responder is. A scoop stretcher, a vacuum mattress or a long board may be used, and which one is chosen belongs to the service, since a suspected injury of the spine or of the pelvis changes the plan. The lay first aider does not lift the patient unless the scene is unsafe, and waits with the patient for the team. The limb is supported through every transfer so that the broken ends do not move, and the leg is never used as a handle. The patient is covered and insulated from the ground, because cold is a complication of trauma and pain increases with it. The handover then names the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention and any change in the condition of the patient, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one.

The complications of a hip fracture begin before the operation and continue long after it, which is why the injury is treated as an emergency rather than as a nuisance. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head can follow a displaced break of the neck or a dislocation and may not show itself for months, and nonunion, in which the broken ends fail to join, is more likely when the blood supply was damaged. Blood collects around the fracture and inside the thigh, and a hip fracture can lose more blood than a listener expects, with teaching figures offered as illustrations to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because estimates differ between services and editions. An older patient who lies still after the injury is at risk of pressure sores, of a clot in the deep veins of the leg and of its passage to the lungs, of chest infection and of confusion, and those complications are prevented by early assessment, careful handling, warmth, pain relief decided by a clinician and above all by early surgery and early movement. The risk of death in the year after a hip fracture is high enough that it must be said aloud, and it is one more reason why the injury is never dismissed as a simple break in an old person.
