Pain relief in a suspected hip fracture is decided by a clinician, and the responder's contribution is to handle the limb gently, to immobilize it and to describe the pain clearly enough for someone else to act. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, that rises instead of settling or that comes with numbness, tingling, weakness or a limb that becomes tense, because those suggest a complication rather than ordinary injury pain. Analgesia, antibiotics, tetanus protection and sedation are prescribed by those whom the law and the local protocol authorize to prescribe them, and the substance, the amount, the route and the frequency are theirs to choose; this course gives no dose, no route and no regimen, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from it. The lay first aider gives nothing unless the local protocol and a competent authority have trained and authorized that act. What the responder can always give is warmth, reassurance, a supported limb and a calm voice, and those are not small things to a patient who is frightened, in pain and unable to move.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position of the limb when it was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, the level of consciousness and any change in the condition are written or spoken in a fixed order. Nothing that was not recorded before a splint was applied can be attributed afterwards, and nothing that was not reported can be acted on by the team that receives the patient. Where this chapter names a time, a volume, a pressure or a distance, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. Every skill described here is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

To summarize, a hip fracture is a break of the femur at or near the joint, and in an older patient it may follow a fall from standing height while in a younger patient it follows great force. What to look for is pain in the groin, the thigh or the knee, an inability to bear weight and a limb that lies shortened and rotated outward, remembering that an impacted fracture may still allow walking and that a patient with dementia may report nothing at all. What to do follows the order this course uses everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the findings written before and after every intervention. The limb is supported in the position found, the patient is kept warm, the neurovascular status is recorded and the patient is moved promptly to a facility with imaging and an orthopedic surgeon. What never to do is to straighten the limb, to pull on it, to lift the patient by the leg, to test how far the hip will move, or to remove an embedded object. A hip dislocation is rare and is an emergency for the blood supply of the femoral head, and the responder recognizes it, supports the limb, records the neurovascular findings and transfers the patient urgently, but never attempts to put the joint back, because reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique belongs to that training and to no book. Who to call is the emergency service and the receiving hospital, and the handover names the time, the mechanism, the position found and every change since. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 27 — Femoral Shaft Fractures

A fracture of the thigh bone is one of the few fractures that can kill a patient before anyone decides whether the leg needs an operation. The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, and the force that breaks it usually injures the trunk as well. The thigh then fills with blood that nobody can see, and the limb shortens as the muscles around it pull. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The femur has three parts, and the difference between them decides how each injury is managed. The proximal femur ends in the head that sits in the socket of the pelvis, and the distal femur widens to form the surface of the knee joint. Between them lies the shaft, a long tube of thick bone with a narrow cavity in the middle that holds marrow. The shaft is surrounded on all sides by the muscles of the thigh, which are wrapped in fascia and confined by the deep fascia of the limb. Those muscles form a closed space in which a large volume of blood can collect unseen, and they are strong enough to move the broken ends a long way.

The mechanism tells the responder how much energy passed through the patient, and in the thigh it is usually a great deal. A head on collision, a fall from a height, a struck pedestrian and a motorcycle crash are the usual ways a healthy adult breaks a femoral shaft. In a child the same bone can break in a fall from a bicycle, and in an older adult it can break in a fall from standing height when the bone is already weak. A thigh that breaks under a force that seems trivial is a finding worth reporting rather than a reason to relax. The mechanism is the first piece of the assessment, because it predicts what else may be injured and how quickly the patient may deteriorate.

The reason this fracture is treated as a life-threatening injury is hemorrhage, and the hemorrhage is invisible. A closed fracture of the femoral shaft can release 1 to 2 liters of blood into the muscles and tissues of the thigh. Any such number is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because estimates differ between services, countries and editions. In a person of small body size that loss can cause shock before the skin shows more than swelling. Injured muscle also loses the ability to hold fluid inside its vessels, so the loss continues after the injury has happened.

Shortening is the sign that follows from the anatomy, and it is the one most often seen. The muscles pull the lower fragment upward while the upper fragment is held near the hip, so the broken ends override one another. The same pull rotates the lower limb outward, so the foot of the injured side may lie turned away from the other foot. Angulation adds a bend at the fracture, and the thigh takes on a shape the eye can recognize from the foot of the bed. The responder compares the two limbs without lifting them and records the difference instead of trying to correct it.

What the responder sees is a thigh that is swollen, tense and changed in shape, with the knee and the foot lying in an unusual direction. What the responder feels is warmth, firmness and often exquisite tenderness over the fracture. What the patient reports is severe pain in the whole thigh, pain made worse by movement, and an inability to bear weight on that leg. A patient whose level of consciousness is reduced by a head injury, by alcohol or by another substance may report nothing at all. In that patient the swelling and the posture of the limb are the only evidence available.

Because the force is great, the thigh must never be allowed to take all of the attention. The same impact can tear the aorta, collapse a lung, lacerate the spleen or the liver, and break the pelvis, the ribs, the spine or the skull. The principle that orders the response is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. Bleeding inside the chest, the belly or the pelvis may be larger than the bleeding in the thigh, and it may be the reason the patient is deteriorating. The responder therefore completes the primary survey before turning to the limb, and treats the patient rather than the radiograph.

Assessment begins before the patient is touched. The scene is made safe, personal protective equipment is put on, and the mechanism is established from the patient and from witnesses. The primary survey then proceeds in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Circulation here means the search for hemorrhage, both the visible kind and the kind hidden inside the thigh, the chest, the belly and the pelvis. Exposure means undressing the patient enough to see the whole body, and it is followed at once by covering the patient again, because cold is a complication of trauma.

The history is gathered while the examination proceeds, and it has a fixed content. The time of the injury matters because the condition of the patient changes with time and because the receiving team will ask for it. The list of medicines matters because a patient whose blood clots slowly loses more blood and reaches shock sooner. The illnesses matter because a bone weakened by a tumor or by a long illness may have broken before the fall rather than after it. Whether the patient is pregnant, and whether the patient carries a pacemaker or an artificial joint, are part of the handover as well.

Stabilization of the patient with a thigh fracture is a small set of acts performed in a deliberate order, and the first of them is restraint. A deformed limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field. The vessels and the nerves of the thigh lie close against the bone, so a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Pulling the limb straight may also convert a closed fracture into an open one, and it may release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with a rolled blanket, keeps the patient warm and waits for help.

Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled at once, which usually means a dressing over a wound if one exists. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be pressing on a torn vessel and its removal may release the bleeding. Exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because that carries contamination deeper without restoring the bone to a useful position. The patient is kept flat or in the position that best protects the airway, and the injured limb is supported on a padded surface. Wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, because a patient who is losing blood cannot afford to lose heat as well.

Traction is the act of applying a gentle and continuous pull along the long axis of the limb. In the thigh it is used to overcome the pull of the muscles that have shortened the limb, and to hold the fragments in better alignment. Its purpose is not to set the fracture, but to limit further movement and further bleeding, to ease pain and to make the limb safer to transport. Traction is applied through a device fixed to the leg and to the body, and it transmits a steady pull while the patient lies on a stretcher. A well applied device can leave a patient calm on the way to hospital, while a badly applied one can injure skin, press on the perineum or damage vessels and nerves.

Traction of the femur is applied only by those who are trained and authorized to apply it, and the authority comes from the service and the protocol rather than from the possession of a device. In most services the people who apply it are the emergency medical technician and the paramedic who have completed the training and whose service permits it. In the hospital it is applied by the orthopedic team, and the lay first aider never applies traction at all. The technique itself, with its straps, its counter-pressure and its check of the pulses before and after, belongs to supervised practical training with a qualified instructor. What this chapter can do is describe what traction is meant to achieve and what can go wrong.

A device that causes increasing pain, that changes the shape of the limb, that reduces the pulse, or that produces numbness or tingling is adjusted or removed at once by someone authorized to do so. Force is not a technique, and stopping is a decision that a trained responder is expected to make. Over-traction can pull the fragments apart and can injure the vessels and the nerves. Pressure from straps can damage skin over the ankle, the knee or the pelvis, so the device is checked for tightness and for pressure over bony points after it is applied. Where the trained responder cannot apply traction safely, immobilization alone is the better answer.

Several situations make traction the wrong choice, and the reason is always a specific risk. A suspected fracture of the pelvis is the clearest of them, because the device presses against the pelvis and can open a pelvic injury and increase the bleeding hidden there. An injury to the knee or to the bones below the knee is another, because the device pulls through those injured structures, and a partial amputation is a third. An open fracture with a wound along the line of the device, a fragment caught in the joint, and a limb with a failing pulse or a numb foot are also reasons to leave the device off. In each of those situations the responder immobilizes instead and explains the reason to the receiving team.

Where no traction device is available, the trained responder may immobilize the injured limb by binding it to the uninjured limb, with padding between the knees and between the ankles. This is an improvised measure, and it is checked more often than a manufactured device because it shifts with movement and can tighten during transfer. The binding must be firm enough to prevent movement and loose enough to permit the circulation, so the toes and the foot are examined after it is applied. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, but the decision to bind one limb to the other belongs to the trained responder working within the local protocol.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is recorded. A finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, which is why the record is part of the examination. The examiner looks at the color of the foot, feels its temperature, and compares the injured side with the uninjured side. The pulses sought are the pulse in the groin, behind the knee, behind the inner ankle and on the top of the foot. Sensation is tested on the top and the outer side of the foot, and the patient is asked to move the ankle and to spread the toes.

A pulse that is present does not exclude a serious injury to the vessels, because a large vessel can be torn while the smaller ones below it still produce a pulse. A pulse that is absent is an emergency, and a limb that is pale, cool or painful out of proportion to the injury is an emergency for the same reason. Numbness, tingling, weakness and the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier suggest damage to a nerve. These signs are not equally reliable in every patient, because a patient with a head injury, a patient who is confused or intoxicated, and a frightened child may not cooperate. Where a finding is uncertain, the responder says so rather than recording a normal result that was never obtained.

Compartment syndrome of the thigh is uncommon when the femur alone is broken, but it becomes a real risk after a crush or a long period in shock. The findings are a thigh that is tense and swollen far beyond what the fracture explains, and pain that increases rather than settling. Pain that is made worse by stretching the muscles of the thigh is another warning finding. The diagnosis is clinical, and the examiner must not wait for a measurement that will arrive too late, because time is muscle and muscle that has died cannot be replaced. The responder who suspects it releases any constricting bandage or splint within the limits of the local protocol, keeps the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, keeps the patient warm and refers the patient urgently.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, so a fracture of the femoral shaft is immobilized in a way that also controls the hip and the knee. The device is padded where it presses over bone, which in the thigh means the prominences of the pelvis, the knee and the ankle. It is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a traction device, a padded board, a pillow bound in place or the uninjured leg itself can each serve. Casting, skeletal traction and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a book.

Because the energy that breaks a femur often passes through the spine, the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. The neck is stabilized with the device the service uses, and the patient is rolled as a unit by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. A patient whose level of consciousness is reduced, whose neck or back hurts, or who has been in a high energy crash is presumed to have a spinal injury until a qualified examiner decides otherwise. Immobilizing the thigh must never become a reason to drag the patient or to roll the patient alone. Where the two needs compete, the airway and the spine take precedence over the appearance of the leg.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do so. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden. The hip and the knee are included because a break of the neck of the femur is a recognized companion of a break of the shaft. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break and is also used to examine the chest, the abdomen and the pelvis. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, and the lay first aider neither orders nor interprets any study.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, the pulses, sensation, movement and pain, and the device is checked for tightness and for pressure over bony points. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling and a foot that has become pale or cool are the findings that stop the responder. A patient whose pulse rises, whose skin becomes cold and clammy or whose level of consciousness falls is bleeding somewhere, and the thigh may not be the place.

One complication deserves separate mention, because it appears after the patient reaches the hospital and is often mistaken for something else. Fat embolism happens when fat from the marrow of the broken bone enters the blood and travels to the lungs and the small vessels of the body. It typically appears a day or so after the injury, though the timing varies and any number given for it is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The picture is a patient who becomes short of breath, restless, confused or drowsy, with a rapid pulse and a rash of tiny red spots across the chest and neck. The diagnosis belongs to the hospital team, while the responder supports the airway, keeps the patient warm and calls for urgent help.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and for a fracture of the femoral shaft it almost always means transfer to a facility with an operating room, imaging, a supply of blood for transfusion and an intensive care unit. The decision about where the patient goes belongs to the service and the local protocol, and a hospital without orthopedic surgery is a stop on the way rather than a destination. The orthopedic surgeon and the trauma team decide what operation is performed and when, and the guiding rule is that the patient must be stable enough to survive it. In a patient who is still bleeding, an operation on the thigh may be delayed while a temporary measure holds the bone. The timing differs between services, and any figure offered for it is an illustration to be confirmed against the local protocol.

Several operations are used, and a listener should be able to recognize their names without being able to perform them. The most common permanent treatment is a metal rod passed down the canal inside the bone, which is called intramedullary fixation, and it holds the fragments in line while the bone heals without a cast. An external frame with pins that pass through the skin is used when the soft tissues are badly damaged or when the patient is too unstable for a long operation, and it is often temporary. Skeletal traction, in which a pin is placed through the bone near the knee and a weight pulls the limb, remains a definitive method where surgery is not available. Open reduction and internal fixation, in which the surgeon exposes the fracture and holds the pieces with plates and screws, is used for fractures that extend into the knee or the hip.

An open fracture of the femoral shaft is an emergency at a different level from a closed one. The bone or the deep tissues have communicated with the outside, and the wound is contaminated at the moment of injury whether it looks clean or not. The part played by the responder is limited and precise, which is to cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control the bleeding that can be controlled, examine the neurovascular status, immobilize the limb in the position found, keep the patient warm and arrange urgent transfer. Tetanus protection and antibiotics are decisions for the prescriber and the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route and the frequency belong to them and not to this course. Definitive closure belongs to the operating room, and a responder who explores the wound or pushes exposed bone back into it adds harm.

The same injury behaves differently at the two ends of life. A child's bone bends before it breaks, so a child who refuses to walk after a fall may have a fracture that no one can see. The growth region near each end of the femur can be injured without the shaft breaking, and that can affect the length of the leg for life. A fracture of the femoral shaft in a young child is often treated without an operation, by holding the limb in line in a device or in an enclosure that includes the trunk and both thighs, and a clinician trained to do it applies it. An older adult whose bone has lost density or contains a tumor can break the thigh in a fall from standing height, or even while turning in bed, and the pain may be far less than the injury suggests. In both patients the response is the same sequence with a lower threshold for immobilization and for referral.

Pain is a finding and not merely a complaint, and it is part of what the responder records. The lay first aider eases pain by supporting the limb in the position found, by reducing movement, by keeping the patient warm and by explaining what is happening. The trained responder may be authorized to give a medicine for pain under a written protocol, and which medicine is used and in what amount are matters for the service and the prescriber. No dose, no route and no regimen appears in this course, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from it. The finding that makes the decision urgent is severe pain that is not eased by immobilization, because that may mean a compartment syndrome or an injury that has been missed.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the device used, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and any change in the condition of the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order. It is worth saying aloud that the limb was not straightened and that no object was removed, because the absence of an act is as important to record as its performance. Speaking to the patient is part of the treatment as well, so the responder explains what has been found and what will happen next, in plain words. A receiving team that knows which findings are firm can repeat the examination and trust the record second.

Transport is decided by the service, and the destination is chosen for the care the patient needs rather than for the distance. Reassessment continues during transport, and any change in the pulse, the breathing, the skin or the level of consciousness is reported before arrival. The levels of practice named in this chapter are easy to keep in order. The lay first aider supports the limb, keeps the patient warm and calls for help, while the trained first responder and the emergency medical technician immobilize with the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. The paramedic works within a broader protocol, and the nurse, the physician and the orthopedic surgeon receive the patient, repeat the examination, order the images and plan the definitive operation.

Several acts are forbidden in every chapter of this course, and they are forbidden here together with their reasons. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and because the pressure holding a torn vessel closed may be the only thing preventing more bleeding. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound. An open wound is never explored blindly, because the exploration adds injury and does not change what must happen next. Traction is never applied by someone who has not been trained and authorized to apply it, and reduction, skeletal traction and casting are never learned from a book.

Numbers in this course are illustrations and never rules. A volume of blood lost, a pressure inside a compartment and a time to the operating room are figures that differ between services, countries and editions. Each of them is confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is used to make a decision about a patient. The fracture of the femoral shaft is treated as a life-threatening injury because it bleeds into a space nobody can see, because the force that broke it often injured the trunk as well, and because the patient may change from stable to critical while the limb is being splinted. And it happens to people who were healthy that morning.

To summarize, a fracture of the femoral shaft is a limb injury that is also a threat to life, because the thigh can hide a large hemorrhage and because the force that broke it often injured the trunk as well. The course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the neurovascular findings are recorded before any intervention and repeated after every one. A swollen and shortened thigh is supported and splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, traction is applied only by those trained and authorized to apply it, and reduction, skeletal traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. An embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. No dose, no route and no regimen is given in this course, because the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and the local protocol. The patient is kept warm, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and the patient is reassessed after every intervention and handed over in a fixed order. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 28 — Distal Femur Fractures and Traction

The distal femur is the widened lower end of the thigh bone, where it divides into two rounded condyles and meets the shin bone to form the knee. When it breaks, the joint is often involved, and a break between the condyles can separate them from each other and from the shaft above. The injury deserves respect, because the knee is the joint a person needs in order to walk and because the vessels and the nerves of the leg pass immediately behind the bone. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The shape of the lower thigh bone explains much of what happens when it breaks. Above the knee the bone narrows into the shaft, and the place where the shaft flares into the condyles is the supracondylar region, where the bone is thinner and lies closer to the skin. The condyles roll and slide on the top of the shin bone, and between them lies a deep notch that holds the crossing ligaments of the knee. The capsule of the knee is attached above the condyles rather than at the joint line, so the condyles lie inside the joint cavity, and that is why a break here fills the knee with blood. In a child the growth region lies just above the condyles and is the busiest in the body, so an injury there can change the length and the shape of the leg for life.

The force that breaks the lower thigh bone divides these patients into two groups. In a young adult the cause is usually a high energy event, such as a vehicle collision in which the knee is driven into the dashboard, a fall from a height or a motorcycle crash. In an older adult the same break may follow a fall from standing height, because the bone has lost density, or an even smaller force when a knee replacement has already been placed. A fracture that crosses the bone around an implanted joint is a familiar companion of this injury, so the responder asks whether the patient carries such an implant. Sport, a fall from a bicycle and a direct blow each account for a share of these fractures, and in a child a simple fall is enough.

Muscle decides the direction in which the broken ends travel. The large calf muscle takes its origin from the back of the bone just above the condyles, so the lower fragment is drawn backward while the shaft is pulled forward by the muscles at the front of the thigh. The result is a limb that looks bent at the knee and a lower fragment that tilts toward the back of the leg, which is exactly where the vessels and the nerves lie. The limb may also be shortened and rotated, so that the two legs no longer match. What the responder sees is a swollen thigh and a knee that is filled and tense, and what the responder must not do is to correct that shape by pulling on the limb, because good intentions can convert a pressed vessel into a torn one.

Assessment begins before the patient is touched, because the scene and the mechanism are part of the examination. The lay first aider makes the scene safe, puts on personal protective equipment where available, counts the helpers, and notes how the injury happened and how long ago. The trained first responder then works through the primary survey in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Circulation here means the search for hemorrhage, both the visible kind and the kind hidden inside the thigh, the chest, the belly and the pelvis, and the principle that orders the response is that life comes before limb. Exposure means undressing the patient enough to see the whole body, and it is followed at once by covering the patient again, because cold is a complication of trauma. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, which is examined by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing it.

What the responder finds at the limb is a set of observations rather than a diagnosis. The thigh may be swollen, the knee may look fuller than the other side, and the whole limb may lie in a shape the eye recognizes as wrong. A fracture that has not displaced may leave the limb looking almost normal, so the absence of deformity must never exclude this injury, and the inability to lift the leg against gravity may be the only evidence when consciousness is reduced. Pain is a finding and not merely a complaint, so the lay first aider eases it by supporting the limb, by reducing movement, by keeping the patient warm and by explaining what is happening. The trained responder may give a medicine for pain under a written protocol, while the substance, the route and the amount belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, and no dose, no route and no regimen appears here. Pain that increases despite immobilization is the finding that makes the decision urgent, because it may mean a compartment syndrome or an injury that has been missed.

Stabilization is a short list of acts performed in a deliberate order, and the first of them is restraint. A deformed limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and because the pressure holding a torn vessel closed may be the only thing preventing further bleeding. Pulling the limb straight may also drive the sharp end of the bone through skin that was intact. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with a rolled blanket, keeps the patient warm and still, and waits for help. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with a dressing, an embedded object is never removed, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, while wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, because a patient who is losing blood cannot afford to lose heat as well.

A knee that fills with blood deserves a word of its own. The capsule of the knee holds very little room, so even a modest amount of blood raises the pressure inside the joint and produces a knee that is tense, hot and extremely painful. Whether the joint should be aspirated is a decision for the clinician and the local protocol, because an aspiration performed in the wrong circumstances introduces infection into a joint that cannot afford it. What the responder records is the size of the swelling and whether it is increasing, because a knee that grows tighter over minutes is a different report from one that has looked the same since arrival. Nothing is bound tightly over the knee to reduce the swelling, and the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart when there is any question about the circulation.

The vessels behind the knee are the reason this fracture frightens orthopedic surgeons. The artery that supplies the leg below the knee passes through a tunnel behind the joint, tethered above by a fibrous opening in the muscles of the thigh and below by the muscle that forms the calf, so it has very little slack to give. A fragment that tilts backward, a knee that has also dislocated, and the swelling that follows either one can compress or tear that artery. The findings that suggest the artery is failing are a foot that is pale and cool, a pulse that cannot be felt and pain out of proportion to the injury, while numbness and tingling suggest that a nerve has been injured. A pulse that can still be felt does not exclude serious injury, so any of those findings means that the limb is immobilized in the position found and the patient is sent urgently to a facility where a surgeon can examine the vessels.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is recorded, because a finding not written down before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color of the foot and compares it with the other side, feels its temperature, and presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return. The pulses to be sought are the pulse on the top of the foot and the pulse behind the inner ankle, and each is compared with the uninjured limb. Sensation is tested in the space between the first and the second toe and on the outer side of the shin, and the patient is asked to pull the foot up, to push it down and to spread the toes. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician perform this examination in the field, and the nurse and the physician repeat it in the hospital. No sign in it is perfectly reliable, because a patient who is unconscious, confused or in severe pain cannot cooperate, so the responder records what was found and says plainly what is doubtful.

Traction is a principle before it is a device. Traction means a gentle and continuous pull along the long axis of the limb, held steady for as long as it is needed, in order to overcome the pull of the muscles that have shortened the limb. Its purpose is not to set the fracture, and it is not a way of putting a dislocated joint back into place, because a pull applied to force bone ends into position can tear vessels, nerves and skin. What traction is meant to achieve is a limb held in better alignment, less movement at the fracture, less bleeding from the broken ends, less pain and a safer journey to hospital. It may be a temporary measure, a definitive treatment or a bridge to an operation, and which of those it is belongs to the clinician who plans the care.

Skin traction is the gentler of the two forms, and it works by attaching a device to the skin of the leg and letting a weight pull through it. The device may be straps fixed to the sides of the leg with adhesive, or a boot or a bandage or a manufactured splint that grips the limb, so the pull is transmitted through the skin rather than directly to bone. It is used for modest amounts of pull, for a limited period, and often while a patient waits for an operation. It is applied by a nurse, a physician or another clinician trained and authorized to apply it, according to the written protocol of the service, and never by the lay first aider. The risks are blisters, abrasions and pressure over the bony bumps on either side of the ankle, and a strap can also press on the nerve that winds around the small bone below the knee. Skin traction also slips, and a device that has slipped delivers less pull than the clinician intended while looking as though it is still working.

Skeletal traction is the more powerful form, and it places a metal pin through the bone so that the pull reaches the skeleton directly. The pin is usually placed through the lower end of the thigh bone itself or through the upper end of the shin bone below the knee, and the choice belongs to the orthopedic surgeon. It is used when a stronger and more sustained pull is needed, when skin traction has failed or would damage the skin, or when the limb must be held in line for weeks because no operation is available. Skeletal traction is applied only by a clinician trained and authorized to do it, in a clean environment and with sterile technique, and the anesthesia that makes it tolerable is a decision of the physician and the local protocol. The placement of the pin, the choice of the weight and the check of the pulses before and after belong to supervised practical training with a qualified instructor and never to a book. This course describes what the device is for and what can go wrong, and it stops there.

Because a pin passes through skin and bone, skeletal traction has complications of its own. The pin site can become infected, which is why it is cleaned, dressed and inspected according to the local protocol and why redness, discharge and new pain at the site are reported at once. The pin can loosen or migrate, the weight can be disturbed by a well meaning visitor or by a patient who slides down the bed, and the counter pull can be lost when the bed is moved. A pull that is too strong can hold the fragments apart rather than in line, can stretch a nerve, and can press on skin until it breaks down. The examination that accompanies traction is the same neurovascular examination performed at every other step, carried out before the device is applied, immediately after it is applied, and again after every adjustment of the weight. Increasing pain, a limb that changes shape, a weaker pulse, numbness, tingling, a pale or cool foot, and skin that breaks down under a strap stop the process at once, and the weight is never increased to overcome resistance, because force is not a technique.

Traction is the wrong choice in a set of situations, and in each of them the reason is a specific risk rather than a rule to be memorized. A suspected fracture of the pelvis is the clearest of them, because the device presses against the pelvis and can open an injury that was closed, and an injury to the knee or to the bones below the knee is another, because the pull and the pin pass through damaged structures. An open fracture with a wound along the line of the device, a partial amputation, and a fragment caught inside the joint are also reasons to leave the device off. A limb with a failing pulse or a numb foot is not treated with traction by a responder, because that patient needs the surgeon and the operating room. Traction is not applied when the diagnosis is unclear or when the responder has not been trained and authorized to apply it. Traction is never used to pull a deformed limb straight in the field, and it is never a substitute for immobilization or for the images the clinician needs, so in those situations the limb is immobilized in the position found and the reason is explained to the receiving team.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and this fracture lies close enough to the knee that the knee itself must be included. The device supports the limb from the upper thigh to the ankle, it is padded where it presses over bone, which at this level means the bony bumps at the knee, the small bone below the knee and the ankle, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation. The knee is splinted in the position in which it was found and is never forced straight, because the vessels and the nerves that lie behind the joint are at risk from any movement. The material matters less than the principle, so a padded board, a pillow bound in place, a manufactured splint or the uninjured leg bound alongside with padding between the knees can each serve. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician apply splints within the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician and the orthopedic surgeon decide what definitive immobilization is required, and casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do so. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the hip and the knee included so that a second injury at another level is not missed. Computed tomography is used for this fracture more often than for most, because the break between the condyles and the surface of the joint is frequently more comminuted than the first radiograph suggests. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, and at the knee it can show injury to the ligaments and to the cartilage that the radiograph does not reveal. In a child the growth region at the lower end of the thigh bone is difficult to assess, and the clinician may ask for images of the other leg for comparison, because an image is a picture of one moment.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because it is the comparison that carries the information and not any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, both pulses, sensation, movement and pain, the splint or the traction device is checked for tightness, and the skin is inspected wherever a strap or a pin rests against it. Pain that increases instead of settling, numbness, tingling, weakness, a foot that becomes pale or cool, and a limb that grows tense and swollen are the findings that make the responder stop and escalate. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed, acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage or splint to be released by someone authorized to do it, keeps the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, keeps the patient warm and refers the patient urgently.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and for this fracture it usually means transfer to a facility with an operating room, imaging, a supply of blood and an intensive care unit. The orthopedic surgeon with the trauma team decides what is done and when, and the patient must be stable enough to survive an operation. An open fracture at this level is an emergency of its own kind, because the wound is contaminated from the moment of injury whether it looks clean or not. The lay first aider covers such a wound with a sterile dressing and the trained responder controls the bleeding that can be controlled and immobilizes the limb in the position found, while definitive closure belongs to the operating room, because neither explores the wound blindly or pushes exposed bone back into it. A plate and screws applied to the side of the bone hold the condyles together and reattach them to the shaft, and a metal nail passed upward through the knee into the canal of the bone can hold the same fracture from within. A frame outside the limb, with pins through the skin, is used when the soft tissues are badly damaged, and in an older patient the surgeon may replace the knee joint and use the stem of the replacement to hold the fracture.

Not every fracture of the lower thigh bone is treated with an operation, and where surgery is not available or not safe, traction may be the definitive treatment rather than a bridge to something else. A fracture that has not displaced, a patient who could not survive an operation and a service without an orthopedic operating room are all situations in which a clinician may hold the limb in line with a continuous pull for weeks. That choice belongs to the orthopedic surgeon, and the pull is maintained and adjusted only by those trained and authorized to do it. The goal is a limb of the right length, in line, with a knee surface able to bear weight and a knee that does not become stiff while the bone heals. Stiffness of the knee is in fact the disability that follows this fracture most often, even when the bone has been repaired well, because the joint was filled with blood, the muscles of the thigh were injured and the patient was asked to keep the limb still. A knee that becomes hot and painful weeks later may be infected, while a swollen and painful calf may hold a clot in a deep vein, so both findings are reported to the clinician, while the rehabilitation program that restores movement is designed by the treating team with a physical therapist.

The injury behaves differently at the two ends of life. In a child the growth region at the lower end of the thigh bone is the most active in the body, and an injury that crosses it can slow the growth of the leg, stop it altogether, or produce an angulation that worsens with every year the child grows. A fracture at this level in a child is the business of an orthopedic surgeon from the first hour, even when the radiograph looks modest. A child who refuses to walk after a fall, whose knee is swollen or whose leg hurts when it is moved should be assumed to have a significant injury until a clinician decides otherwise. The older adult brings a different set of problems to the same fracture, because the bone is thinner, so a smaller force is enough and the mechanism may sound trivial. Such a patient may carry a knee replacement, may take a medicine that thins the bone or prevents clotting, and may live alone. The fracture may hurt far less than its appearance suggests, so the threshold for immobilization and for referral is lower in this group, and the decisions about how quickly an operation is performed belong to the treating team and to the local protocol.

The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the device used, the name of the person who applied it, the pull that was set and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order. It is worth saying aloud that the limb was not straightened and that no object was removed, because the absence of an act is as important to record as its performance. Because the energy that breaks a lower thigh bone often passes through the trunk, the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. Transport is decided by the service, and the destination is chosen for the care the patient needs rather than for the distance, because a hospital without orthopedic surgery is a stop on the way rather than a destination, and during transport the same neurovascular observations are repeated so that any change is reported before arrival.

The levels of practice named in this chapter are easy to keep in order, because every act described here has an owner. The lay first aider supports the limb in the position found, controls the bleeding that can be controlled with a dressing, keeps the patient warm and still, calls for help, and observes color, warmth, movement and feeling, but never applies traction and never straightens the limb. The trained first responder applies splints, performs the neurovascular examination and records it, and works within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes. The emergency medical technician and the paramedic work within a broader protocol, may apply a traction device where the service trains and permits it, and may give a medicine for pain only under a written protocol. The nurse performs the neurovascular examination, checks the skin beneath straps and pins, maintains the traction the clinician has ordered and reports any change at once. The physician examines the patient, orders and interprets the images, decides about pain relief and about the referral, and performs a reduction only where training, equipment and protocol allow it, while the orthopedic surgeon decides about skeletal traction and about the operation.

To summarize, a fracture of the lower thigh bone is an injury of the knee as much as of the thigh, because the condyles lie inside the joint and because the vessels and the nerves of the leg pass immediately behind the bone. What to look for is a swollen thigh, a knee that is filling with blood, a limb that is shortened or bent, and any change in the pulses, the color, the warmth, the sensation or the movement of the foot. What to do is to follow the order every chapter of this course follows, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What never to do is to straighten a deformed limb in the field, to remove an embedded object, to push exposed bone back into a wound, to explore an open wound blindly, or to attempt traction, reduction or casting without training and authorization. Traction is a gentle continuous pull that holds the limb in line and reduces bleeding, pain and movement, it is not a way to set a fracture, and it is avoided in a suspected pelvic fracture, in an injured knee and in a limb whose pulse is failing. A knee that tightens, a foot that pales and pain that increases instead of settling are reported at once, and who to call is decided by the service and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 29 — Patellar Fractures and Knee Dislocation

The knee is the largest joint in the body and one of the most often injured, and two of its injuries belong together in one chapter because they could hardly be more different. The patella is the small bone that sits in front of the joint inside the tendon of the quadriceps muscle, where it acts as a pulley and gives that muscle a longer lever in the last part of straightening, and it can be broken or dislocated; that injury is immobilized and referred. The knee itself can dislocate, with the thigh bone and the shin bone losing contact, and that injury is an emergency not only for the joint but for the whole limb, because the artery that supplies everything below the knee runs directly behind it. Both are handled through the same sequence that every chapter of this course follows, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

A direct blow, such as the knee striking a hard surface in a fall or an occupant's knee hitting the dashboard of a vehicle, crushes the patella against the thigh bone behind it. The result is often a fracture with several fragments, sometimes described in teaching as a starburst pattern, and the cartilage on the back of the bone is usually damaged at the same time. Because the quadriceps tendon and the fibrous expansions on each side of the knee, called the retinacula, may stay intact, the fragments can remain together and the patient may still be able to straighten the knee. An indirect mechanism works differently, because when the knee is partly bent and the quadriceps contracts violently, or when the patient catches a fall on a partly bent knee, the muscle pulls the patella apart against the attachment below. The break is then usually a transverse one with a gap between the ends, and the tearing reaches the fibrous expansions on each side, so the extensor mechanism fails.

The patient with a broken patella usually arrives holding the knee still, with the joint swollen and the skin over the front of the knee tight and shiny. Blood inside the joint from the fracture, called a hemarthrosis, fills the pouch above the patella and makes the whole knee look round rather than knobbly. The examiner may feel a gap or a step in the bone, and pressing the patella against the thigh bone causes sharp pain, though that is not a test to repeat. The most useful single observation is whether the patient can straighten the knee against gravity and hold it straight, because that movement is the work of the extensor mechanism and it fails when the mechanism is torn. A patient who cannot lift the straightened leg, or who can hold it straight only with effort, is treated as having a disrupted extensor mechanism until a clinician decides otherwise. The sign is not perfectly reliable, because severe pain may prevent the attempt, a partly torn expansion may still allow weak straightening, and a child may simply refuse to try, so the responder records what was seen and leaves the judgment to the clinician.

Dislocation of the patella is a different injury in a different patient, and it is common in young people who play sport. The kneecap almost always leaves the joint outward, driven off its groove by a twist of the body while the foot is planted and the knee is nearly straight. Some patients are more likely to dislocate because their joints are generally loose, because the groove in the thigh bone is shallow, or because the patella sits higher than usual, and a previous episode is a strong clue in the history. The patient holds the knee slightly bent, refuses to straighten it, and describes the kneecap as having moved sideways, and the patella may still be visibly displaced to the outer side of the knee. It often slips back into place by itself as the knee bends, however, so the examiner may see only a swollen and painful knee with tenderness along the inner edge and no obvious deformity at all. That is why the story matters: something moved, the knee became painful and swollen, and it has not felt right since, and a fragment of cartilage or bone may have been knocked loose inside the joint.

A dislocated patella is not a sprain and it is not put back by the responder. The reduction of a patellar dislocation is performed by a clinician, usually with the knee gently straightened and the kneecap guided back into its groove while the muscles are relaxed, and the technique is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, never from a book. A first attempt can drive a loose cartilage fragment deeper into the joint, and an attempt made against tense muscle can damage the joint surface, which is why the clinician also wants to know whether the reduction was difficult. After the joint has been put back it is held in whatever position and with whatever device the local protocol directs, and the patient is referred, because a knee that has been dislocated must be examined again once the swelling and the pain have settled. The lay first aider and the trained responder do the same thing while they wait: they support the knee in the position found, they keep the patient warm, and they do not test the joint.

Dislocation of the knee itself is a much rarer and much more dangerous injury, and it is the reason this chapter is written. The thigh bone and the shin bone are forced out of contact, and with them go the ligaments that hold the knee, in most cases several at once. It follows high-energy trauma such as a road traffic collision, a fall from a height or a heavy blow to the front of a bent knee, but it also follows injuries of much lower energy, particularly in a patient who is very heavy or whose joints are unusually lax. The energy of the mechanism therefore does not tell the listener how bad the knee is, and a knee dislocation must be suspected whenever the story and the examination do not fit a simpler injury. The joint frequently returns to its own position before the patient is seen, and that is the trap, because the limb may look nearly normal while the artery behind it has already been torn. The responder who hears that the knee was deformed at the scene and is straight on arrival is hearing a dislocation, whether or not anyone used the word.

Behind the knee the popliteal artery passes from the thigh into the calf, and it is tethered above where it leaves the canal of the thigh muscles and below where it passes beneath the fibrous arch of the calf muscle. Because it is fixed at both ends and lies against the back of the joint, it cannot move out of the way when the bones shift, and it is stretched or torn by the displacement. The nerve that lifts the foot, the peroneal nerve, wraps around the neck of the smaller bone of the lower leg just below and outside the knee, and it is injured in a similar way. Its loss is seen as a foot that drops when the leg is lifted and as numbness or tingling over the front and outer side of the lower leg and the top of the foot, and although that injury does not threaten the limb, it changes the patient's life and is recorded in the same way as the pulse.

The neurovascular examination is the step that decides the fate of a leg, and it is performed before the limb is splinted, again after the splint is in place, and again after every other intervention. The examiner compares the two limbs, feels for the pulse at the front of the ankle and behind the inner ankle, and notes the warmth and the color of the skin and how quickly the color returns when a nail is pressed and released. Sensation is tested on both sides, on the top of the foot and between the first two toes, and the patient is asked to pull the foot up and to push it down and to report any numbness or tingling in their own words. A pulse that is present does not exclude injury to the artery, and this is the finding most often trusted wrongly, because the inner lining of the vessel can be torn while a channel remains open. Many services compare the blood pressure measured at the ankle with the pressure measured in the arm, because a value much lower at the ankle points to an injury that needs urgent study, but the threshold used is an illustration for the local protocol rather than a fixed law. The absence of a pulse is an emergency that stops everything else.

Assessment begins away from the limb, because a patient whose knee has been dislocated has often been injured elsewhere as well. The first step is the safety of the scene and of the responder, and the next is the mechanism of injury, which tells the team what to expect and where to look. The primary survey follows, in the order remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and it is performed before the knee is examined in detail, because life comes before limb and a limb can wait for minutes that a brain cannot. Bleeding inside the chest, the abdomen or the pelvis, a head injury or a spinal injury takes precedence, and the knee is supported in the position found while those problems are addressed. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the knee itself, and then it is done by looking, by feeling gently and by asking the patient to move the joint, never by forcing it. A limb that was deformed and is now straight, a knee that is grossly swollen, a calf that feels tense and a pulse that has changed are findings that are recorded at once and reported to whoever will receive the patient.

Stabilization of these injuries is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The knee is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the artery and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that appears helpful can complete a tear that was only partial. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient still and warm and waits for help, while the trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. Any device that presses on the back of the knee is padded so that it does not add pressure to the artery. Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering. A knee that is open, with bone or deep tissue visible, is covered with a sterile dressing once the bleeding that can be controlled has been controlled, and nothing is pushed back into the wound.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and around the knee that means supporting the hip and the ankle as well as the knee itself. The trained responder and the paramedic apply a splint that holds the limb in the position found, and a device that extends from the upper thigh to beyond the ankle is often used for transport because it controls the knee and the ankle together. Padding is placed where the device presses on bone, particularly over the bony points of the ankle and the hip, and the limb is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The splint is checked immediately after it is applied and then at intervals, because swelling inside a limb can turn a splint that was comfortable into one that is dangerously tight. Casting, bracing and surgical fixation are different matters altogether, they are performed by clinicians, and the technique of each is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do so. A radiograph of the knee is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. For a broken patella the radiograph shows how many fragments there are and how far apart they lie, and the clinician may ask for an additional view taken from a particular angle to see the joint surface. Computed tomography gives finer detail of a fracture with many fragments, particularly where it enters the joint, and magnetic resonance imaging shows the ligaments, the menisci, the cartilage and any loose fragment once the limb is safe; the second study never takes priority over the question of the artery. When injury to the artery behind the knee is suspected, the clinician may arrange a study of the vessels, and the decision about which study, and how quickly, belongs to the team responsible for the patient.

Reassessment happens after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record written before, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The toes are checked for color, warmth, movement and sensation, the pulse is felt again at both places on the ankle, the splint is checked for tightness, and the patient is asked whether the pain is the same, better or worse. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a calf that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. The knee is one of the places where compartment syndrome follows dislocation even when the artery was never torn, because bleeding inside the closed compartments of the calf raises the pressure until the muscle and the nerve begin to die. A responder who suspects that condition does not wait for confirmation and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage or splint to be released by someone authorized to do it, and the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart. The patient is kept warm and referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Definitive treatment of a patellar fracture turns on three questions that belong to the orthopedic surgeon. Does the extensor mechanism still work, so that the patient can straighten the knee against gravity and hold it straight? Is the joint surface still smooth, and is there a step between fragments large enough to wear out the cartilage behind the bone? And is the skin intact, or has the fracture communicated with the outside? When the answers are that the mechanism works and the surface is smooth, many such fractures are treated without an operation, held in the position the surgeon chooses and allowed to heal while the patient follows a program of supervised exercise. When the extensor mechanism is torn, when a fragment has separated, when the joint surface is uneven, when a piece of bone or cartilage is loose inside the joint, or when the injury is open, an operation is usually needed to bring the fragments together and hold them while they heal. The surgeon may use wires, screws or strong sutures, and an operation that opens the joint to see and fix the fragments directly is called open reduction and internal fixation; every one of those decisions and techniques belongs to the surgeon, is learned under supervision, and is performed according to local protocol.

The treatment of a patella that has dislocated depends on what the first episode left behind. A first dislocation in a young patient is often treated without an operation, with a period of protection chosen by the clinician and then a program of rehabilitation supervised by a physical therapist, whose work is to strengthen the muscle that holds the patella in its groove and to teach the patient to use the leg safely again. An operation may be needed when a fragment has been knocked loose, when the joint surface is damaged, or when the patella will not stay in place without help. The responder's part in this is small and does not change: support the knee, immobilize it in the position found, examine and record the neurovascular status, arrange the transfer, and never attempt to reduce the joint.

A knee that has been dislocated is treated as an emergency for the limb from the moment it is recognized. The joint is put back by a clinician in a controlled environment where the airway, the blood pressure and the rest of the patient can be watched, and where the examination of the vessels can be repeated before and after the reduction; this is not an act for the field, for the ambulance, or for anyone working alone in a corridor. If the artery behind the knee is injured, the repair is a matter of hours rather than days, and the interval quoted in teaching is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the time a limb can survive without blood is not the same in a warm patient and a cold one. The joint may be held after reduction with a frame that lies outside the limb, called an external fixator, or with a brace or a cast chosen by the surgeon, while the vessels and the soft tissues are watched. The ligaments that were torn are often repaired or reconstructed later, once the limb is safe, because saving the leg comes before rebuilding the knee. A patient whose knee has been put back and whose pulse is present is still watched with repeated neurovascular checks, because the inner lining of a stretched artery can tear and clot over the hours that follow, and the period of that observation is an illustration for the local protocol.

An open injury at the knee adds urgency to everything already described. When the bone or the deep tissues have communicated with the outside, the wound is contaminated at the moment of the injury even when it looks clean, and the risk to the limb rises sharply, whether the injury is a broken patella or a dislocated knee. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm and arranges urgent transfer; nothing is removed from the wound and nothing is pushed back into it. Protection against tetanus and the use of antibiotics are decisions for the clinician and the prescriber, and the substance, the amount, the route and the timing belong to the local protocol, so that a listener cannot take a prescription from this course. Cleaning the wound and repairing the deep structures are done in the operating room, and definitive closure belongs there and nowhere else. A patient with an open injury at the knee is referred to a facility with an operating room, imaging and an intensive care unit, and is not kept for observation in a place that cannot treat what may be found.

Children and older adults bring their own cautions to these same injuries. The patella of a child is largely cartilage, so a violent contraction of the quadriceps can pull a sleeve of cartilage and bone off its lower or upper edge, and because cartilage does not show on a radiograph the picture may look almost normal while the extensor mechanism is torn; a child who cannot straighten the knee, or who will not bear weight, is referred even when the radiograph is reported as showing nothing. Some children also have an extra center of bone formation at the upper outer corner of the patella, called a bipartite patella, which is a normal variant and not a fracture, and deciding which it is belongs to the clinician. In an older adult, bone that has lost density breaks more easily and holds fragments less well, so a patella can be fractured by a fall that would leave a younger person unhurt, and a knee dislocation may follow an injury of surprisingly low energy. Arteries that are already narrowed tolerate a period without blood flow badly, so the threshold for urgent assessment in an older patient is lower rather than higher. The examiner is not reassured by a calm patient, by a knee that looks straight, or by a radiograph that shows no break.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and around the knee they carry the findings that decide whether a limb survives. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the knee was found, whether it was ever deformed, and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. A single line saying that the knee was deformed at the scene and straight on arrival is worth more to the vascular surgeon than a page of description, because it converts a swollen knee into a suspected dislocation with an artery at risk. Any change in the pulse, the color, the warmth, the sensation or the pain is reported immediately to the clinician responsible, and where this chapter names a time or a threshold it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Some rules are absolute, and every act in this chapter has a name attached to the level of provider who may perform it. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field; a dislocated knee or patella is never reduced by anyone but a clinician; and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, never from a book. An embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly. If an attempt at any maneuver meets resistance, or if a new numbness, a new weakness or a lost pulse appears, the responder stops, records what has changed, supports the limb and escalates. The lay first aider supports the limb, keeps the patient still and warm and calls for help, using no splint and no treatment; the trained first responder and the paramedic splint and dress within the procedures their service authorizes; the nurse observes, records and reassesses; the physician examines, orders the images and performs the reductions the local protocol permits; and the orthopedic surgeon, with the vascular surgeon when an artery has been injured, decides about and performs the operations. For the patella, look for a swollen knee, a kneecap that moved and perhaps moved back, and the inability to straighten the knee against gravity; for the knee itself, suspect a dislocation whenever it was deformed at any point in the story or the pulse, the color, the warmth or the sensation below it has changed. Everything in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision.

To summarize, the patella can be broken or dislocated, and the knee itself can dislocate, and the two injuries share a joint while sharing almost nothing else. A broken patella is examined for the ability to straighten the knee against gravity, immobilized in the position found and referred, and the surgeon decides whether the fragments, the joint surface or the extensor mechanism require an operation. A dislocated knee is an emergency for the limb, because the artery behind the joint is fixed at both ends and is torn or stretched when the bones move, and because the joint often reduces itself and leaves a limb that looks deceptively ordinary. Suspect it whenever the knee was deformed at any point, and treat a pulse that is present as no guarantee, because the inner lining of the artery can be injured while blood still flows. Follow the sequence in every case, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. Never straighten a deformed limb in the field, never reduce a knee or a patella outside a controlled clinical setting, never remove an embedded object, never push exposed bone back into a wound and never explore an open wound blindly. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, an injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified clears it, cold is treated as a complication, and the patient is reassessed after every intervention and watched until the handover. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 30 — Tibial Plateau Fractures

The tibial plateau is the upper surface of the shin bone where it faces the thigh bone inside the knee, and a break through it is an injury of a joint surface that must carry the weight of the body. A patient with this fracture usually arrives with a knee that has swollen within hours, that will not take weight and that hurts when it is bent. The upper end of the shin bone is soft inside and thin at its rim, so a force along the leg drives the surface down rather than breaking it cleanly across. The soft tissues around the knee then decide both how dangerous the injury is and what may be done about it, which is why skin, swelling and pulses matter as much as the bone. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The tibial plateau is formed by two rounded surfaces on top of the shin bone, the medial plateau on the inner side of the knee and the lateral plateau on the outer side. Between them rises a small bony peak called the intercondylar eminence, where the ligaments that cross the center of the knee take hold. The lateral plateau is smaller and slightly domed, the medial plateau is larger and slightly hollowed, and together they receive the weight of the body through the rounded ends of the thigh bone.
