Beneath a thin shell of joint surface the upper shin bone is built of spongy bone rather than dense bone, which is why a force down the leg dents the surface instead of cracking it across. The front of the same region carries a bony bump where the tendon of the quadriceps muscle attaches, and a fracture may run into it. In a child the region also contains the growth plate just below the joint, so an injury there can disturb the growth of the leg.

A plateau fracture is rarely a break of bone alone, because the force that drives the joint surface down also stretches or tears the structures that hold the knee together. The menisci are two rings of tough fibrous cartilage between the thigh bone and the shin bone, and they are commonly torn when a plateau is split or driven down. The ligaments that cross the center of the knee and those along each side may be stretched, partly torn or completely torn at the same time, and a piece of the bony peak between the plateaus may be pulled away with one of them. Because the joint surface is damaged, blood collects inside the knee, and that collection makes the joint swell, feel tense and refuse to move. No responder can tell from the outside which of these structures is injured, and that judgment belongs to a clinician who can examine the knee once pain and swelling allow. The responder records what can be seen, which is a swollen knee, a limb that will not take weight and a patient who holds it still.

The force that produces this fracture travels along the line of the leg and is usually a combination of a direct blow and a bending movement at the knee. A common history is that of a pedestrian struck by the bumper of a vehicle on the outer side of the knee, which drives the shin bone outward and breaks the lateral plateau, and that mechanism is why the injury was once taught as the bumper fracture. A fall from a height onto a straight leg and a landing in sport load the joint in the same way. The direction in which the knee bends decides which plateau breaks, because a force that drives the knee outward damages the outer surface while a force inward damages the inner one. A fracture of the medial plateau generally follows a more violent mechanism and is more often accompanied by injury to the ligaments and to the structures at the back of the knee. The energy of the mechanism therefore matters more than the size of the break on an image, and a small crack may belong to a limb with a torn artery behind it.

The soft tissues do not simply cover this fracture, because they decide what can be done and when it can be done. Swelling around the knee can become so great that the skin over it is stretched and shiny, and blisters may appear over the front and sides of the knee within a day or two. Skin stretched by swelling is skin at risk of dying, and the surgeon planning an operation will look at it and decide whether the knee is ready. Where the bone has communicated with the outside through a wound, the fracture is open, it is contaminated at the moment of injury, and it needs urgent surgical care rather than treatment in the field. The leg below the knee is divided into closed compartments of muscle bounded by bone and fascia, and bleeding or swelling inside one of them can raise the pressure enough to suffocate the muscle and the nerve within it. That complication, called a compartment syndrome, is why a swollen leg after a plateau fracture is watched closely rather than merely covered.

The patient with a fractured tibial plateau most often holds the knee slightly bent and refuses to straighten it, because straightening stretches the joint and hurts. The knee looks swollen and round rather than bony, and bearing weight causes sharp pain along the joint line on the side that was struck. A visible deformity is often absent, which is one of the traps of this injury, because a break of the joint surface can hide beneath a knee that only looks bruised and puffy. Some patients describe a knee that gives way, and the injury is mistaken for a sprain until the swelling fails to settle and walking remains impossible. Not every patient tells this story, and one sign taught as always present will mislead. An older adult whose bones have lost density may be treated for a sprain after a fall from standing height, a replaced knee may break around the implant, and a child may hurt so little that the injury is noticed only because the child refuses to run. The responder therefore records what was seen and felt, and leaves the diagnosis to the clinician who can image the limb.

Assessment begins before the knee is touched, with the safety of the scene, the number of patients and the mechanism of injury. The primary survey comes first, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because a patient who has fallen from a height may have injuries that kill faster than a broken knee. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, and the principle that decides the order is that life comes before limb. The history includes the time since the injury, the height of any fall, whether the knee was struck on the inner or the outer side, and whether the patient has been able to stand since. The patient's age, the illnesses that affect bone and the medicines that thin it belong to the same history, because they change how easily the bone broke and how well it may heal. The person who performs this assessment is whoever arrives first, whether a lay first aider, a trained first responder, an emergency medical technician, a paramedic, a nurse or a physician, and each works within the procedures their service authorizes.

Examination of the knee follows the primary survey and is done by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move the limb, never by forcing it. The examiner looks at both knees together, comparing their shape, the position of the limb and the color of the skin, and looks for a wound, a blister or an area of stretched and shiny skin. Feeling is done gently and from the unaffected side inward, noting where the pain begins, whether the joint feels tense and whether the skin is warm. The patient is asked to lift the leg and to bend and straighten the knee a little if they can, and an attempt that causes severe pain is stopped rather than repeated. Testing the stability of the knee by pulling it from side to side is a clinical skill learned under supervision and is not performed by a responder in the field. The limb is left in the position in which it was found, and that position is written down together with the time.

Stabilization means keeping the patient alive, keeping the limb from moving and keeping the patient warm, in that order. The painful knee is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves of the leg lie close to the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient still and waits for help. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. Bleeding from a wound is controlled by direct pressure with a dressing, an embedded object is never removed, and exposed bone is never pushed back inside. A patient with an injured limb loses heat quickly, so wet clothing is replaced with covering and cold is treated as a complication of trauma.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention, repeated after every intervention and recorded both times, because a finding that was not written down before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner compares the two legs and looks at the color and the temperature of the skin of the foot and the toes. The pulse is felt where the artery crosses the front of the ankle and again behind the inner ankle, and it is described as strong, weak or absent. A nail is pressed briefly and released, and the time the color takes to return is noted. Sensation is tested on the top of the foot, between the first two toes and on the sole, and the patient is asked to report numbness or tingling in their own words. Movement is tested by asking the patient to pull the foot up, to push it down and to turn it inward and outward, and the injured side is compared with the other.

The artery that supplies everything below the knee passes at the back of the joint and lies against the bone, and because it is held at both ends it cannot move out of the way when the bones shift. The nerve that lifts the foot winds around the small bone of the lower leg just below and outside the knee, and its injury shows as a foot that drops when the leg is lifted and as numbness over the front and outer side of the lower leg. An intact pulse does not exclude damage to a vessel or to a compartment, because a pulse can still be felt while the flow through the smallest vessels has failed, and an absent pulse is an emergency that stops everything else. A compartment syndrome is the complication this chapter most wants the listener to suspect early, and its earliest sign is pain far worse than the injury appears to explain while the leg becomes tense and swollen and stretching the muscles by moving the foot causes severe pain. A responder who suspects this complication does not wait for confirmation, releases any constricting bandage or splint within the local protocol and by someone authorized to do it, keeps the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, keeps the patient warm and refers urgently.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is held alone can still be moved from the knee or the ankle. For a suspected plateau fracture the knee and the ankle are both supported, and the limb is held in the position found without any attempt to bring it into a better line. A splint is padded where it presses on bone and secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a padded board, a folded blanket, a vacuum splint or the body of a second person can each serve, and an improvised device must be checked more often because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while a nurse or a physician may apply a temporary device in a treatment area. Casting, traction and the devices that hold a limb for weeks are applied under the direction of the orthopedic surgeon and are learned under supervision, never from a book.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below so that a second injury is not missed. On a plain radiograph the clinician looks for a step in the joint surface, for a fragment driven down into the bone beneath it and for a split that runs from the joint into the shaft. Computed tomography is used when the joint surface must be seen in detail, and it shows how far the surface has been driven down, how many pieces there are and which way the split runs, all of which change the surgical plan. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including the menisci, the ligaments and the cartilage, and for a suspected fracture that plain films do not show. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined and reassessed after it has been taken.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison carries the value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint is checked for tightness, for slipping and for points where it presses on the skin. The knee is watched for increasing swelling, for a wound that was not there before, for blisters and for skin that has become shiny and tense. Pain that increases instead of settling, numbness, tingling, weakness and a leg that becomes hard and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A patient whose pain is eased but whose leg is tense is not reassured by the absence of pain, and a patient whose knee was comfortable an hour ago and is now rigid is not watched for another hour. Each reassessment is recorded and handed over in the same words, so that the next team continues a story rather than starting a new one.

Referral decides where the patient will be treated, and for this injury the answer is usually a facility with an orthopedic surgeon, an operating room and imaging. A patient with an open fracture, a foot without a pulse, a leg that is tense and painful out of proportion, or a knee that cannot be moved at all is referred as an emergency. So is a patient whose joint surface is displaced, whose knee is unstable, whose skin is stretched over a swelling, or whose fracture is so comminuted that the surface lies in many pieces. A child with a suspected injury across the growth region below the knee belongs with a surgeon who treats children, and an older adult whose bone is thin belongs with a surgeon who can weigh fixation against replacement. A patient with a knee replacement already in place and a patient with several injuries need the same urgent referral, whatever the first radiograph appears to show. Referral does not end the responder's task, because the limb is splinted, the neurovascular status is recorded, the patient is kept warm and the handover is completed before the patient leaves.

Definitive treatment begins with the decision about whether the joint surface can be left to heal without an operation, and that decision belongs to the orthopedic surgeon. A fracture that is not displaced, that leaves the surface of the joint smooth and level and that leaves the knee stable may be treated without surgery, and the patient is then supported in a device that holds the knee while the bone heals. What that device is, how long it stays and how much weight the patient may put on the leg are decisions made by the surgeon and the local protocol, and the periods used for such matters are illustrations to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Casting and bracing are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and this chapter does not teach the technique of either. A patient treated without surgery is watched closely, because a fracture that looked stable can move as the swelling settles, so the limb is examined and imaged again as the surgeon directs. Exercise of the joints that are not held still, and of the muscles of the thigh, is begun when the surgeon allows it, and a physical therapist carries out the program.

When the joint surface is broken in a way that will not heal smoothly, an operation is needed, and it is performed by an orthopedic surgeon in an operating room. The surgeon opens the knee, restores the position of the fragments, fills the space beneath a driven down surface with bone graft or a substitute material, and holds the pieces with plates and screws in a procedure whose name is open reduction and internal fixation. Sometimes the soft tissues are too damaged for a plate to be placed safely, and the bone is then held from outside the skin with pins and bars in a frame, which may span the knee while the swelling settles and the skin recovers. The technique of every one of these operations is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of it is taught from a book. The operation may be delayed until the soft tissues are ready, and how long that delay may be is a matter for the surgeon and the local protocol rather than a rule in a chapter. The aim of all of it is a joint surface that will carry weight without pain and a limb that can move.

The complications of a tibial plateau fracture are worth naming, because the patient is watched for them rather than merely treated and sent away. The joint surface may settle out of position as the bone heals, and a surface that is not smooth wears the cartilage of the knee and leads to arthritis years later. Infection is a risk of any operation and a greater risk after an open injury, and it may appear days or weeks after the patient has gone home. A blood clot may form in the deep veins of the leg and a piece of it may travel to the lungs, which is why a patient with a swollen painful calf and breathlessness is assessed urgently. Injury to the artery or to the nerves of the leg may be present from the moment of the fracture and may not recover, and a compartment syndrome can leave a foot that does not work. The patient and the family are told what to watch for, and a responder who meets such a patient later records the findings and refers.

Pain after this injury is severe, and relieving it is part of care rather than a courtesy. The decision about which medicine is given, how it is given and how often belongs to a physician, a nurse practitioner or another prescriber working within the local protocol, and the substance and the amount are never taken from a course listened to in a car. A responder who is not authorized to give a medicine does not give one, and a responder who is authorized gives only what the protocol names and only in the way the protocol names. What makes the decision urgent is a patient in severe pain, a patient whose pain is rising despite support and splinting, and a patient whose pain is out of proportion to the injury, because that last finding may be the first sign of a compartment syndrome rather than a call for more medicine. An open fracture also raises the questions of protection against tetanus and of antibiotics, and both decisions belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol. Positioning the limb, splinting it, keeping the patient warm and explaining what is happening are acts of comfort that every level of responder can perform.

Reduction, traction and casting appear in the treatment of knee injuries, and a listener must understand what they are without ever learning to perform them from these words. Reduction means restoring the position of bones that are out of place, and for a fracture of the tibial plateau it means lifting a joint surface that has been driven down and holding it while the bone heals. Traction means holding a limb with a gentle continuous pull, and it is used mainly for injuries of the shaft of the thigh bone rather than for a plateau fracture, though the principle of supervision applies wherever it is used. Casting means holding a limb in a rigid shell while the bone heals, and it is applied by a clinician or a trained technician under the direction of the orthopedic surgeon. All three are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique belongs to that training and never to a book or a recording. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the knee was found, the condition of the skin and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story rather than starting a new one. Where the patient is transferred, the receiving facility is told in advance which injuries are suspected and what has been done, because an open fracture or a tense leg changes what must be ready on arrival. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and a patient who fell from a height with a broken knee is exactly the patient in whom that rule applies, so movement is performed by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Everything described here is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. Where this chapter names a time, a distance or a period, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services and editions.

To summarize, the tibial plateau is the weight bearing surface of the shin bone at the knee, and it is broken by a blow along the line of the leg that drives the joint surface down while the skin, the ligaments and the compartments of the leg are injured with it. What to look for is a knee that swells quickly, that will not take weight and that cannot be straightened, with tenderness along the joint line, stretched and shiny skin, a foot that cannot be felt or moved as well as the other, and pain far worse than the injury appears to explain. What to do is to assess the whole patient first, to support the limb in the position found, to examine and record the neurovascular status before and after every intervention, to immobilize the knee and the ankle, to keep the patient warm and to transfer the patient to a facility with imaging and an orthopedic surgeon. What never to do is to straighten the limb in the field, to remove an embedded object, to push exposed bone back into a wound, to explore a wound blindly, to test the stability of the knee, or to attempt a reduction, because force is not a technique. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome acts at once, releases any constricting device within the local protocol, keeps the limb at the level of the heart and refers urgently, because time is muscle. No dose, no route and no regimen appears in this chapter, since the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and the prescriber, and every figure named here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

# Chapter 31 — Tibial Fractures

The tibia, the shin bone that runs between the knee and the ankle, carries the weight of the body, and its sharp front ridge can be felt through the skin of every healthy leg. Along most of its length it lies directly beneath the skin, with almost no muscle over its front and inner surfaces, so a blow that would only bruise a thigh can break it and tear the skin from within. The fibula beside it carries little of the load, but the two bones are joined at both ends, so an injury to one is often an injury to the other. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Blood reaches the shaft of the tibia mainly through a vessel that enters the bone near its middle and runs inside the canal, so the inner part of the shaft depends on that supply more than on the muscle around it. The periosteum, the tough sleeve that wraps the bone, adds a smaller supply along the surface, and it is stripped away by the same force that breaks the bone. When a fracture tears that sleeve over a distance, a fragment may lose much of its supply, and the lower third of the tibia is where this matters most. That is one reason a fracture of the shin bone heals more slowly than a fracture of the thigh bone, and why a break that looks modest can take months to unite.

The mechanism tells the responder what to expect. A bumper of a car, a falling object, a kick or a heavy door produces a direct blow, and the bone breaks at the point of impact with skin and muscle bruised above it. A twisting force, as in a fall while skiing, produces a long spiral break that may run up to the knee or down to the ankle, while a fall from a height drives the bone along its length. High energy damages soft tissue far beyond the bone, so the energy involved is a better guide to danger than the size of the wound, because skin may be nearly intact over muscle that has been crushed.

Because the front and inner surfaces of the tibia lie directly under the skin, this is the long bone most often broken open, and the wound may follow a modest blow rather than a violent one. A spike of bone tears through the skin from within, so the wound may be no larger than a buttonhole. A small hole in a trouser leg or a stain on a sock may be the only sign, and the wound can be hidden by the position of the limb or by the swelling. Clothing is cut away rather than pulled over the leg so that the whole limb can be seen, and the patient is covered again at once to protect against cold. The search for a wound belongs to the assessment and is performed by the trained responder or the clinician, while the lay first aider covers what is already visible.

Any fracture with a wound that communicates with the broken bone is an open fracture, however small the wound and whatever it looks like. The wound is contaminated at the moment of injury, because the skin carries organisms that reach the bone. An open fracture needs surgical cleaning, and the decisions about infection and tetanus belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol. Surgeons describe such a wound by its size, by the damage to skin and muscle, and by whether a vessel supplying the foot has been torn, and those words belong to the treating team. What the responder contributes is the time, the appearance of the wound, whether bleeding was controlled, the neurovascular findings before and after immobilization, and the treatment given. A wound near a fracture is covered and reported, and the responder does not judge whether it is deep enough to matter.

Assessment begins before the limb is touched. The responder makes the scene safe, notes the mechanism, and works through the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. A patient with a broken shin may also have a broken pelvis, a broken thigh or an injury to the head, and those injuries can kill within minutes while the leg can wait. The rule that decides the order is that life comes before limb, so a falling level of consciousness, a changed pattern of breathing, a weak pulse or skin that has become cold and pale sends the responder back to the beginning. The primary survey and the decisions it forces belong to the trained responder, the paramedic, the nurse or the physician, each within the scope that the local service authorizes.

The history adds what the examination cannot show. The responder asks when the injury happened, how much energy was involved, and whether the leg gave way before the fall rather than because of it. Medicines and illnesses that weaken bone, smoking, diabetes, poor circulation in the legs and previous surgery on the same limb all change what the fracture means for this patient. An older adult may break the shin in a fall from standing height, and a person whose bone is fragile may break it with no fall at all. In a child the story matters as much as the injury, because a story that does not fit the findings is a warning to be passed on and recorded.

Looking at the limb comes next, with the patient covered except for the leg. The leg may lie at an angle, it may be shortened, or the foot may point inward or outward when the knee is straight, and any of those findings means the bone ends are no longer in line. The injured leg is compared with the other one, which is the only useful standard available in the field. Swelling may be modest at first and grow while the responder watches, and blisters may form over skin stretched by fluid beneath it. A wound, a stain of blood, a patch of pale or dusky skin and a foot that is not the same color as its partner are all recorded. Nothing is straightened, nothing is pulled, and nothing is measured by force so that the shape can be written down.

Feeling the limb is done with the flat of the hand and with care, because the examination itself can do harm. The responder feels the temperature of the skin, the swelling and the tension in the calf, and compares each finding with the other leg. The sharp front ridge of the tibia is tender wherever it is broken, but the bone is not moved in order to prove that it moves. Tenderness at the knee and at the ankle is looked for, because a twisting force that breaks the shaft may also injure a joint. The compartments of the calf are felt for a hardness out of proportion to the injury, and a calf that is tense is an emergency. Formal palpation belongs to the clinician, while the responder supports the leg, covers the wound and feels without moving anything.

The neurovascular examination of the foot is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and it is recorded in words. The examiner feels for the pulse behind the inner ankle and for the pulse on the top of the foot, and compares both with the other side. The color and the warmth of the foot are noted, and a nail is pressed briefly to see how quickly the color returns. Sensation is tested in the web between the first and second toes, which belongs to the nerve that lifts the foot, and on the sole. The patient is asked to pull the foot up, to push it down and to spread the toes, and any movement that has become weak or lost is recorded as a change. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or the clinician.

A pulse can still be felt in a leg that is developing a compartment syndrome, so a present pulse does not replace the search for pain and tension. The pulse on the top of the foot cannot be felt in a small number of healthy people, so it is compared with the other foot and read with color, warmth and sensation. Pain, swelling and distress can make movement and sensation hard to test, and the responder says so in the record instead of writing that sensation was normal. An absent pulse, a foot that is pale and cold, or a loss of movement that was present a moment earlier is an emergency that is reported immediately. The examination is repeated after the splint, after the dressing and after any transfer, because a finding not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards.

Stabilization of the limb is a small set of acts, and the most important is restraint. The responder keeps the leg in the position in which it was found, supports it with the hands or with padding, and does not test it. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by firm pressure around the wound and by a sterile dressing laid over it, and the dressing is not lifted to look underneath. An embedded object is left in place and stabilized, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the bone may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. The wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room and to nobody else. The lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment, the trained responder and the paramedic work within the equipment their service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what comes next.

Keeping the patient warm is part of stabilization rather than a comfort that follows it. The injured leg is insulated from the ground, wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, and the patient is shielded from wind and rain while waiting for help. Cold worsens bleeding and shock and makes the patient more difficult to assess, and a patient who is already losing blood tolerates cold badly. The covering is checked again each time the patient is moved, and the responder who has only a coat or a blanket uses it. Everything else that might be done for the limb waits until the patient is warm and the life threats are treated.

A deformed leg is not straightened in the field, and this rule has a reason the listener can picture. The vessels and the nerves of the lower leg lie against the bone, and the vessel behind the knee and the nerve at the neck of the fibula are close to the surfaces a broken tibia may injure. Pulling a limb straight may tear what remained intact, and it may also convert a closed fracture into an open one by driving the bone through the skin. It may release the pressure that a collection of blood was placing on a torn vessel, and bleeding that had stopped then begins again. The limb is therefore splinted in the position found, however unnatural it looks, and the correction of the deformity is left to those who can see the vessels and the nerves. Force is not a technique, and resistance is a signal to stop.

Pain is treated as a finding and not as a request. The responder asks about it in the patient's own words, notes where it is and whether it is growing, and reports pain out of proportion to the injury, because that is the earliest warning of a compartment syndrome. Relief of pain is decided by a clinician, or by a paramedic acting under a written protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route and the timing belong to the prescriber and to local protocol. A listener must not be able to take a prescription from these words, and no dose and no regimen is given here. What the responder may do is reduce the pain of movement by immobilizing and supporting the limb and keeping the patient warm. The decision to give nothing, or to wait for a senior clinician, is itself a clinical decision and belongs to the person accountable for it.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone splinted alone can still be moved by the knee and by the ankle. A rigid splint is padded where it presses on bone, which for this injury means the heel, the ankle, the knee and the head of the fibula, and it holds the leg from the thigh to below the foot. The splint is applied over the position found and secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and the toes are checked after it is secured. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and a device that applies traction is used only where the service trains and authorizes it. The physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace or a surgical fixation, and each is learned under supervision.

A splint applied too tightly becomes a complication of the treatment, and the leg is where this happens most easily. As the limb swells, a bandage that was comfortable at the roadside can begin to act as a tourniquet, and pressure rises inside a compartment that cannot expand. The responder therefore examines the toes, the color of the foot and the tightness of the straps at the interval the local protocol sets, and compares them with the record made after the splint was applied. A constricting bandage or splint is released only by someone the local protocol authorizes to do it, because releasing it in the wrong way can also cause harm. The patient is not left alone with a fresh splint, and a leg that becomes more painful, more tense or more numb inside its splint is an emergency.

Compartment syndrome of the leg is the complication this chapter fears most, and the responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation. The lower leg is divided into four compartments by bone and by sheets of fascia, and the front one is affected most often. The earliest finding is pain and tension, and the pain is out of proportion to the injury and grows worse rather than better, while a limb that hurts when the toes are stretched is the classic warning. Numbness between the first and second toes, a weak lift of the foot and a calf that feels hard like wood come later, and the pulses may still be present. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects it acts within the local protocol and arranges urgent transfer. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm while the transfer is arranged.

The record is part of the treatment and not a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the leg was found, the wound, the treatment given and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order. Pain that is increasing, a change in color or warmth, a loss of movement or sensation and a rise in the pulse are recorded in the same way. The condition of the other leg is the standard against which every later observation is compared. A finding that was not written before the splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and the note travels with the patient.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the whole bone and both joints included. The knee and the ankle are examined even when the pain is in the middle of the leg, because the force that broke the shaft may also have broken one of them. Computed tomography shows the detail of a break that reaches a joint or is broken into several pieces, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues and for a suspected stress injury. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, the trained responder does not choose the study, and the surgeon decides when the images are complete. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined afterwards.

An overuse injury, common in runners, dancers and soldiers who train in new boots, begins as a small crack that hurts with activity and eases with rest, and it may not appear on an early radiograph. If training continues, the crack can grow across the bone and the leg can break completely, and any figure quoted for the time away from training is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and local protocol. The responder advises the patient to stop the activity and arranges assessment, and does not ask the patient to run on it. The decision about imaging and about the return to training belongs to a clinician, and a stress injury that is ignored is a fracture that could have been prevented.

Reassessment happens after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison has value and no single measurement does. Color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement, pain and the tightness of the splint are checked, and the wound is checked for bleeding that has soaked through. Reassessment follows the dressing, the splint, every move of the patient and every period of waiting, and the result is recorded each time. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, a tense swollen calf and a foot that has become pale or cold are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and for the tibia it is rarely a step the responder completes alone. Almost every fracture of the tibial shaft is assessed by an orthopedic surgeon, and a fracture that is open, deformed, pulseless or numb is referred at once. The same is true of a fracture that enters the knee or the ankle, a fracture in a child, a fracture in a leg with poor circulation or with nerve damage from diabetes, and a fracture that cannot bear weight. The receiving facility needs imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, and the handover names the time, the wound and the neurovascular findings. The lay first aider calls for help and stays with the patient, the trained responder arranges transport within the local protocol, and the nurse and the physician prepare to receive the patient. Nothing here authorizes anyone to keep such a patient at home.

Definitive treatment is described here so that the listener understands what is being done, and not so that the listener can do it. Fractures of the shaft that are not displaced are held in a cast or in a functional brace while the bone heals, and those devices are applied and monitored by clinicians trained in that work. Many displaced fractures are held with a metal rod passed down the canal of the bone or with a plate and screws, and a severe open injury may be held with a frame outside the limb. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends, traction is the gentle continuous pull that holds them in line, and casting or surgical fixation holds the position while the bone unites, and each is learned under supervision. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations a well meant attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot.

Healing of the tibia is slower than healing of most other long bones, and the patient should hear that early. The lower third of the bone has the poorest supply and the least muscle cover, and a fracture there may take months to unite, while every figure quoted for the time to union and for weight bearing is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Weight bearing is allowed only when the surgeon responsible says so, because a leg loaded too early can lose the position won in the operating room. The patient is taught to move the toes and the ankle as far as the splint allows and to report new pain, numbness or a change in the color of the foot. Smoking, poor nutrition and poorly controlled diabetes slow healing, and those are matters for the treating team. The listener's part is to keep the appointments and to bring the patient back when something changes.

A fracture that does not unite, a fracture that unites at an angle so that the leg is not straight, an infection that settles into the bone after an open injury, and stiffness of the knee and the ankle are the outcomes that follow the most severe injuries. Pressure from a splint or a cast can damage skin over the shin, the heel or the ankle, and a patient with nerve damage may not feel it happening. A leg that becomes hot, swollen and more painful days after the injury, a wound that begins to discharge and a fever send the patient back to the clinician rather than to the pharmacy. The responder does not clean, probe or repack a wound in the field and does not adjust a cast.

A child's bone bends before it breaks, and the same fall may produce a crack that is hard to see or an injury to the growing region near the knee, so a child who will not use the leg is treated with the caution owed to an obvious break. An older adult with fragile bone may break the shin in a fall from standing height, and the injury may hurt less than its severity suggests. A patient with diabetes and damaged nerves may not feel the pain of a splint that is too tight, and a patient with poor circulation may lose the foot as well as the fracture. A patient who cannot describe pain because of a head injury, sedation or a language barrier is examined more often and not less. None of these patients receives a different sequence, and all of them receive a lower threshold for immobilization and referral.

The handover is the moment when the story must survive a change of hands. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the leg was found, the wound, the neurovascular findings before and after each intervention and the treatment given are passed on in a fixed order. Gloves and eye protection are used whenever blood or body fluid may be present, and the level of protection is set by the local protocol, because an open tibial fracture exposes the responder as well as endangering the patient. The receiving nurse repeats the neurovascular examination on arrival and at the interval the local protocol requires, and reports any change at once. A leg that has been splinted is never left unobserved while the patient waits for an operating room. Everyone who touches the patient works within the scope of practice the local service and the law define.

To summarize, the tibia lies just under the skin, so even a modest blow can break it and open the skin, and a fracture with any wound near it is treated as an open fracture and referred urgently. The order never changes: assess the patient and the limb, stabilize by covering the wound, controlling bleeding and keeping the patient warm, examine the neurovascular status of the foot and record it, immobilize the leg in the position found, image when a clinician orders it, reassess after every intervention, and then refer or treat definitively. Look for the wound that may be small, the deformity that is never straightened in the field, the swelling that grows, the pain out of proportion, the tense calf and the foot that is pale or cold. Reduction, traction and casting belong to supervised clinical training and to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the diagnosis is unclear, the injury is open, the vessels or nerves are failing, a fragment is caught in the joint, or the responder lacks training and equipment. Keep the patient warm, record every finding before and after every intervention, and call for a team that can reach an operating room. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 32 — Fibular and Combined Tibial and Fibular Fractures

The fibula is the slender bone that runs down the outer side of the lower leg, and it carries so little of the weight of the body that it could be taken away without destroying the ability to walk. It is a strut rather than a column, and yet it holds two things that matter far more than weight bearing: the outer side of the ankle joint, which it forms at its lower end, and the nerve that winds around its upper end on its way to the muscles that lift the foot. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it keeps to the fibula and to the injury in which both bones of the lower leg are broken. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The fibula begins just below the knee at a small rounded head, narrows into a neck, and runs down as a shaft that is thin in its middle and widens again into the lateral malleolus, the bump on the outside of the ankle. It is joined to the tibia along almost its whole length by the interosseous membrane, a strong sheet of fibrous tissue, and again at both ends by ligaments that allow very little movement. The tibia, the fibula, the membrane between them and the two joints at their ends together form a ring, and a ring broken in one place is usually broken or bent in another. That idea explains these injuries better than any list of types, because a break anywhere in the ring directs the examiner to look at the rest of it. A tender ankle in a patient with a fracture higher up the fibula is not a coincidence but the second part of the same injury.

The common peroneal nerve, also called the common fibular nerve, gives the fibula its reputation, because it leaves the back of the knee, wraps around the neck of the fibula just beneath the skin, and then divides to supply the muscles that lift the toes and turn the foot outward. Around the neck of the fibula it lies against bone with very little muscle to shield it, so a direct blow, a tight bandage, a splint that presses there, or the displaced end of a broken bone can injure it. The findings are a foot that cannot be lifted, a slap of the foot on the ground when the patient tries to walk, numbness over the outer side of the lower leg and the top of the foot, and a loss of the ability to turn the foot outward against resistance. A nerve already injured before the splint was applied must not be blamed on the splint, so the examination is done before any intervention and again afterwards, and a change is treated as an emergency.

The mechanism decides how much energy passed through the leg, and the energy decides how much of the soft tissue has been damaged. A direct blow to the outer side of the leg, as from a bumper, a falling object or a boot, breaks the fibula at the point of impact and bruises the muscle beneath the skin. A twisting force on a planted foot, common in ball games and in a fall on stairs, produces a spiral break that may run a long way along the bone. A fall from a height or a road traffic crash drives the force along the leg and may break both bones into several pieces and tear the membrane between them. The same words describe the injury in a young athlete and in an older adult, but the energy required is very different, and so is the meaning of the same crack.

When only the fibula is broken, the leg usually still takes weight, because the tibia continues to carry the body, and the patient may walk in with a sore outer leg and nothing more. That is exactly why the injury is dangerous to dismiss, since the fracture itself is rarely the whole story. The examiner looks for tenderness along the whole fibula, at the head and neck beside the knee, and at the ankle, and compares the two sides before deciding that the injury is confined to the shaft. Tenderness at the front of the ankle, between the two bones, suggests that the fibrous joint binding them has been torn and that the ankle mortise, the socket that holds the ankle bone, has lost its grip. An isolated fracture with a quiet knee, a quiet ankle and a normal neurovascular examination may be a modest injury, but the decision about how to treat it belongs to a clinician and not to the responder who first touches it.

A fracture of the fibula above the ankle may be the least painful part of an injury whose true damage lies at the ankle, because the force that tears the membrane between the bones has to escape somewhere. The ankle swells, the patient cannot bear weight, and the tenderness sits over the ligaments of the outer ankle rather than over the broken bone. In the same way, a painful ankle after a twisting injury may conceal a fracture of the fibula higher up, so the whole length of the bone is examined in both directions. This is why the joint above and the joint below are assessed whatever the patient points to first, and a responder who examines only where the patient complains will miss the injury that decides the outcome.

When both bones are broken, the leg loses both of its struts, and the injury becomes a different problem in kind rather than in degree. The membrane between the bones may be torn over a long distance, so the two fragments are no longer tied to one another, and the broken ends can slide, overlap, tilt and twist. The leg can shorten, the foot can turn outward, and the whole limb can move as a unit above and below the break, which is what the examiner means by an unstable leg. An unstable leg is immobilized in the position found before it is moved anywhere, because every movement of the limb moves the bone ends with it, and a bone end that moves can tear a vessel, stretch a nerve, cut the skin from within and turn a closed fracture into an open one. The responder does not test how unstable the leg is, because the test itself does the harm.

Assessment begins with the scene and with the story, and the story is taken while the limb is being supported rather than examined. The responder asks about the mechanism, the time of the injury, whether the patient could stand afterwards, whether the skin was broken and by what, and whether the foot felt normal at the moment the leg gave way. The medical history matters as much as the accident, because a bone thinned by age, by disease or by long use of a medicine that weakens it may break in a fall that would leave a healthy person unhurt. A patient whose sensation is already reduced by diabetes may feel very little, and medicines that make the blood slower to clot make bleeding into the leg more likely. Tetanus protection is a decision for the clinician who knows the local schedule and the patient's history, and the part of the responder is to ask and to report, never to decide.

Looking is the first act of the examination and it is done with the limb still supported, comparing one side with the other. The responder notes the shape of the leg, the direction in which the foot points, whether the limb looks shorter, and where the swelling and the bruising have appeared. A foot that has turned outward while the patient lies still is a warning that the leg is rotating at the fracture, and it is never corrected by hand in the field. The skin is inspected from the knee to the toes, including the back of the calf and the heel, because a small wound at the level of the break may be the only sign that the fracture is open. Any wound is covered with a sterile dressing, an embedded object is left exactly where it is, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the limb.

Feeling the leg follows looking, and it is done gently, from the head of the fibula beside the knee down to the lateral malleolus at the ankle, and then around the ankle and along the front ridge of the tibia. The examiner is looking for the place that is tender, for a step in the bone, and for the joint that is swollen, while remembering that a patient in shock or distracted by pain may report very little. Crepitus, the crackling of broken ends rubbing together, is not deliberately sought, because seeking it moves the fracture and adds pain without information. Movement is asked for rather than imposed, so the patient is invited to move the toes and to lift the foot if it is comfortable, and a movement that is refused is information too. The limb is never straightened and never used as a lever to see what happens, and testing the stability of the knee, of the ankle or of the bones themselves is a clinical skill learned under supervision and is not a field test. Palpation and the request to move belong to a trained responder, a nurse or a clinician, within the limits of the local protocol.

The neurovascular examination is never skipped and never assumed, and it is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the foot, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and feels the pulse on the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle. Sensation is tested on both legs and compared, including the outer side of the lower leg, the top of the foot and the sole, and the patient is asked to lift the foot and to turn it outward. The result is written before the splint is applied and after it is applied, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. A formal neurovascular examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the physician, while the lay first aider reports what the patient says about feeling and movement. Any change after an intervention stops the responder and prompts escalation.

Some of these signs are less reliable than they look, and a listener who trusts one of them alone will be misled. A pulse that remains palpable does not exclude a compartment syndrome, because the pressure inside a compartment can stop the flow through the smallest vessels long before it stops the flow through the main artery. A patient whose nerves are already damaged by diabetes or by alcohol may have little pain and may not notice numbness that is new, so the injury is found late. Swelling may be modest in a leg that is bleeding into a deep compartment behind the bone, and a foot drop may be present from the moment of the injury rather than appearing afterwards. The response to that uncertainty is not a different examination but a lower threshold for immobilization, for repeated reassessment and for urgent referral.

Stabilization means keeping the patient still, keeping the limb in the position in which it was found, controlling the bleeding that can be controlled, and keeping the patient warm. A deformed leg is supported with the hands, with a pillow, with a rolled blanket or with the uninjured leg, and it is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and the pressure a displaced fragment is applying to a torn vessel may be the only thing holding the bleeding back. An open wound is covered with a sterile dressing and is never explored blindly, an embedded object is left in place, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room and to nobody else. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering. The lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment, and the trained first responder and the paramedic work within the procedures their service authorizes.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, which for the lower leg are the knee and the ankle. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and its purpose is to stop the bone ends from moving rather than to put them back where they belong. The material matters less than the principle, since a padded board, a folded blanket or the uninjured leg can each serve, and an improvised device is checked more often because it shifts. For the unstable leg in which both bones are broken, the limb is immobilized before it is moved at all, and it is then moved only as part of the whole patient, with one person supporting the leg while others move the body. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, the nurse works within the same limits, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required. Casting, surgical fixation and every device that holds a reduced fracture are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a book in this course.

Moving a patient with an unstable leg is a team task rather than a solo skill, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. If the patient must be turned, the whole body is turned as a unit while the leg is supported through the fracture and across both joints, and a spine injury is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so. The limb is lifted along its whole length and never by the foot or by the knee alone, because the weight of the lower leg hanging from a broken shaft bends the fracture and pulls on the tissues around it. A patient who must wait is kept warm, kept still and watched, and the waiting time is used to repeat the neurovascular examination and to record what it shows. The number of responders and the method of movement are set by the procedures of the service and by the equipment available.

Traction is a gentle continuous pull that holds the bone ends in line, and devices that apply it exist for the thigh and, in some services, for the lower leg, but whether such a device is used, and by whom, belongs to the local protocol and to the equipment the service carries. A device of that kind is applied only by a responder trained and authorized to use it, it is never improvised around a fractured lower leg, and it is checked before and after application because a splint that pulls too hard can injure skin, vessels and nerves. Reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, and casting, which holds the position while the bone heals, are acts learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and this course describes what they are meant to achieve and what can go wrong rather than how they are done. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. When the fibula is broken, the whole length of the bone is examined, because a fracture at one end is often accompanied by an injury at the other. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break and of the ankle mortise when an operation is being planned, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including the membrane between the bones, the ligaments and a suspected stress injury that an early radiograph does not show. Either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done, and the decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the care of the patient. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the splint is checked for tightness, and a dressing over a wound is checked for bleeding that has soaked through. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, pain when the toes are stretched gently upward, a calf that becomes tense and swollen, numbness between the first and second toes and a foot that cannot be lifted are the findings that stop the responder. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed, releases a constricting bandage or splint only within the limits of the local protocol, keeps the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, keeps the patient warm and refers urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

The fibula itself usually heals well, because it is wrapped in muscle over much of its length and has a generous blood supply, so an isolated fracture of the shaft often unites without difficulty. The tibia is a different matter, since its lower third lies just under the skin and depends on a supply that a high energy break can damage, and a fracture there may take months to unite or may fail to unite at all, with a period of 8 to 12 weeks offered in teaching as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Infection follows an open injury, which is why the wound is covered, the limb is immobilized and the patient reaches an operating room as soon as the service can arrange it. A nerve that was stretched may recover slowly over weeks to months, while one that was cut does not, and rehabilitation belongs to a physiotherapist working within a plan the treating clinician sets.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with a fracture of both bones, an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a fracture near the knee that has caused a foot drop, a fracture with a torn membrane at the ankle, a fracture that enters a joint, a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone, or a fracture in a limb with poor circulation is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. An isolated fracture of the fibular shaft with an intact tibia, a quiet knee, a quiet ankle and a normal neurovascular examination may be treated without an operation, but that judgment belongs to a clinician who has examined the patient and seen the images. The decision about how urgently a patient must travel is made by the clinician or by the service protocol, and the responder who is unsure treats the injury as urgent and says so in the handover. Nothing in the field is helped by waiting to see whether the leg gets better on its own.

Definitive treatment of these injuries takes several forms, and which of them is used depends on the bone that is broken, the state of the soft tissues and the needs of the patient. A fracture of the fibula alone may be treated with support, with a walking boot or with a cast, while a break of both bones is usually held with a metal plate and screws, with a rod passed down the canal of the tibia, or with a frame of pins and bars outside the limb when the soft tissues will not tolerate an operation. An operation that puts the fragments back into place and holds them with metal devices is called open reduction and internal fixation, and it is performed by an orthopedic surgeon in an operating room. Sometimes the surgeon repairs the fibula first to restore the length of the leg and then fixes the tibia, and sometimes the fibula is left alone because the tibia carries the weight. Each of those decisions is made with images, with an examination under anesthesia and with the judgment of a surgeon, and none of it is a field decision.

This chapter describes no dose, no route and no drug regimen, because the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol. Pain is treated by the clinician who can assess it, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, increasing, out of proportion to the injury, or accompanied by a limb that is tense, cold or numb. A responder at any level may make the patient more comfortable by supporting the limb, by keeping the patient warm and by explaining what is happening, and a trained responder may give an analgesic only under the standing orders and the authorization of the service. Antibiotics for an open injury and protection against tetanus are decisions for the clinician, and the part of the responder is to report the wound, the time of the injury and what is known of the patient's immunization. Sedation for any procedure belongs to a clinician working in a monitored setting, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from this book.

Two groups of patients deserve a lower threshold for immobilization and for referral. A child's fibula has a growth region at each end, and an injury near the ankle that looks like a sprain may damage the growing part of the bone, so a child who will not use the leg, or who limps for days after a fall, is examined rather than watched. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break the fibula and the tibia in a fall from standing height, and the pain may be far less than the severity of the injury. An athlete may have a stress fracture of the fibula that hurts only with running and that an early radiograph does not show, so a persistent pain in the outer leg after training deserves assessment rather than another session. The record and the handover are part of the treatment, and the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are handed over in a fixed order. A leg that was unstable when it was splinted is described as unstable, so that nobody blames an intervention for a finding that came before it.

To summarize, the fibula carries little weight and much importance, because it forms the outer side of the ankle and because the nerve that lifts the foot winds around its neck just beneath the skin. A fracture of the fibula alone may be a modest injury, but the knee and the ankle are examined with it, since a break at one end of the bone often means an injury at the other. When both bones are broken the leg is unstable, and it is immobilized in the position found before it is moved anywhere. The order is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status before and after every intervention and to record it, to immobilize the joints above and below, to image when a clinician orders it, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and cold is treated as a complication. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the diagnosis is unclear, the injury is open, the vessels or the nerves are failing, the joint is shattered, a fragment is trapped, or the responder lacks training and equipment. Keep the patient warm, record every finding, and call for a team that can reach an operating room. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 33 — Acute Compartment Syndrome

Acute compartment syndrome is the emergency this course returns to more than any other, because it is common enough to meet on an ordinary shift and quiet enough to be missed while the limb still has a pulse. It happens when bleeding or swelling raises the pressure inside a closed space bounded by bone and fascia until the smallest vessels can no longer carry blood to the muscle and the nerve within it. The muscle suffers first and the nerve a close second, so the patient loses feeling and power before the limb looks dramatic, and by then the harm is usually done. Everything in this chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work. The course teaches every injury through one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows that order from beginning to end.

A compartment is a box whose walls are bone and fascia, and it holds muscle, nerves and blood vessels with very little room to spare. Fascia is a tough sheet of fibrous tissue that wraps muscles and divides a limb into these boxes, and its important property here is that it does not stretch quickly. The lower leg is usually described as holding four compartments and the forearm three, with several more in the hand, the foot and the thigh, and each holds a group of muscles that share a nerve and a supply of blood. When the pressure rises inside one box the tissue cannot move aside, so the pressure is passed to every structure within it instead of dispersing. This anatomy is not a detail reserved for the surgeon, because it tells the responder which limb is at risk and which finding must be reported without delay.

The pressure inside a compartment rises for a small number of reasons, and a responder who knows them will suspect the problem earlier. The most common is bleeding from a broken bone, especially a break of the shaft of the shin bone or of the two bones of the forearm, because the bone lies within or beside a compartment. A crush injury does the same on a larger scale, and so does the return of blood to a limb whose artery was blocked or repaired, because tissue starved of blood swells when the flow comes back. A burn that encircles a limb creates a tough layer of dead skin that acts like a band, and so can a tight bandage, a splint strap or a plaster cast. Bleeding into a compartment is more likely in a patient who takes a medicine that thins the blood, so the list of medicines belongs in the history. As a constructed illustration, a person pulled free after being trapped under a fallen weight, with a leg that is tense and painful out of proportion to the wound, must be suspected of this at the roadside.

The process is a matter of pressures, and understanding it explains why the limb can look deceptively well. Blood reaches muscle through the smallest vessels, and those vessels stay open only while the pressure inside them is higher than the pressure around them. As the tissue pressure climbs it first narrows and then closes those vessels, so the muscle is starved even though the large artery is open and a pulse can still be felt at the wrist or the ankle. Anything that lowers the patient's blood pressure makes this worse, because the pressure driving blood into the tissue falls while the pressure inside the compartment stays the same. The nerve suffers early, which is why numbness and tingling may come before the loss of a pulse, and the muscle suffers in hours rather than days, though that window differs between patients and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The diagnosis is clinical, and a responder who waits for the limb to look dead before acting has waited too long.

The findings that matter are few, and the first of them is pain that is out of proportion to the injury. The patient describes pain that is severe, deep and unrelenting, and that grows instead of settling after the limb has been splinted. Gently stretching the muscles of the compartment produces pain, and this pain on passive stretch is the finding that most often raises the alarm, though it is not present in every patient and is lost once the nerve has failed. The compartment itself feels tense and firm, and that tension is compared with the same place on the other limb. Sensation is diminished or changed in the area the nerve of that compartment supplies, and the patient may report pins and needles, numbness or a limb that feels asleep. Weakness, or the loss of a movement the patient could perform minutes earlier, follows, and the responder records each of these findings in the words of the patient where that is possible.

The signs taught as the classic picture of this emergency are the signs of a limb that has already been lost, and that is the trap this chapter most wants to close. Absent pulses, a pale or mottled color, cold skin and paralysis appear late, after the muscle and the nerve have suffered damage that may not be reversible. A palpable pulse does not exclude the diagnosis, because the large vessels remain open while the small ones have closed, and this single misunderstanding sends more patients to harm than any other. The responder therefore treats pain and tension, rather than pulse and color, as the findings that demand action, and reports all of them together. Waiting for the classic picture is the same as waiting for the damage to be done.

Some patients cannot report the pain on which the diagnosis depends, and in them the threshold for suspicion must be lower rather than higher. A young child may cry, refuse to use the hand or become quiet and withdrawn, and may not localize the pain at all, so a limb a child will not move is taken seriously. A patient who is unconscious, confused, deeply sedated or intoxicated cannot describe pain, and the examination must then rest on tension, color and the comparison with the other limb. A patient who has received a nerve block or an epidural anesthetic may feel no pain at all while the muscle is dying, which is why that decision belongs to a clinician who has weighed the risk. Where a sign is unreliable in the patient in front of you, say so in the record, and let the record carry the uncertainty forward.

The injuries that most often produce this emergency are worth knowing, because they set the level of suspicion before the examination begins. A break of the shaft of the shin bone is the classic, and a break of the upper part of the shin bone is close behind it, because both lie within a compartment that cannot expand. A break of both bones of the forearm is the other classic, and it is the injury that most often leaves the lasting contracture of the hand when it is missed. A break just above the elbow in a child, a dislocation of the elbow, a break of the bone at the lower end of the forearm and a break of the heel bone are all followed with particular care. The thigh, the upper arm, the hand and the foot can each be affected, and the thigh is dangerous because a large volume of blood can be lost within it. A compartment syndrome can also occur with no broken bone at all, so a normal image never removes the diagnosis.

The sequence begins with assessment, and assessment begins before the limb is touched. The responder makes the scene safe, notes the number of patients and the mechanism of injury, and records the time the injury happened, because that interval matters to the team that receives the patient. The primary survey comes next, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and it is completed before the limb is examined in detail. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, and it is done by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move, never by forcing a movement. Life comes before limb when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, and a falling level of consciousness or a rising pulse sends the responder back to the beginning.

Stabilization of a limb that may be losing its muscle is a short list of acts, and restraint is the most important of them. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Rings, watches, tight sleeves and any band that encircles the limb are removed by the trained responder or the clinician, because a ring that fits now may not fit later. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with direct pressure, an open wound is covered with a sterile dressing, and an embedded object is left in place because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel.
