The limb is kept at the level of the heart and is never raised above it, for reasons this chapter explains. The patient is kept warm and insulated from the ground, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated immediately after it, and its result is written down at both times. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin and at the swelling of the limb, feels the pulse beyond the injury and compares it with the other side, and presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return. Sensation is tested in the area the nerve supplies and compared with the other limb, and the patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes and to say whether the movement is normal. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, and reports any change at once. The trained responder and the paramedic perform the formal examination within their training and their service procedures, and the nurse and the physician examine, document and compare. A finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and that is the whole reason for the rule.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, so that a splinted bone cannot still be levered by the joint at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, is applied over the position found, and is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. Nothing that encircles the limb is tied so tightly that a finger cannot be slipped beneath it, and nothing adds pressure over a wound. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required. Casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and neither of them is taught from a book in this course.

A cast, a splint, a bandage or a dressing that has become tight is the one cause of this emergency that a caregiver can remove, and removing it is treatment rather than an afterthought. The bandage is unwound, the straps of the splint are released, and a plaster cast is opened together with the padding beneath it, because a cut shell still lined with a tight band continues to constrict. That act belongs to the clinician, or to the provider the local protocol authorizes, with the equipment and the training the protocol requires, and it is not a task a lay first aider improvises. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, because raising it lowers the pressure that drives blood into the compartment and can deepen the starvation. Cold packs are not applied and the limb is not massaged, because both narrow the vessels the muscle is fighting to keep open, and the patient is not asked to exercise the fingers or toes as a test. After the constriction is released the limb is supported, the patient is kept warm, and the release is judged by repeating the examination.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison rather than any single measurement that has value. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the splint is checked for tightness, and the patient is asked whether the pain is better, the same or worse. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain that appears when the muscles are stretched, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes more tense and more swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A patient whose urine has turned dark after a crush injury is reported as well, because that finding belongs to the breakdown of muscle and to the team that will treat it. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for confirmation and acts within the local protocol, or escalates by another route without delay.

Imaging comes after stabilization, and it answers a different question from the one that matters most here. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joints above and below included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues such as muscle, ligament and cartilage, while neither of them measures the pressure inside a compartment. The clinician responsible for the patient orders and interprets the study, and requests it only when its answer will change what is done. Imaging never delays the referral of a patient in whom this emergency is suspected, and a report that shows a fracture and nothing more does not remove the diagnosis. An image is a picture of one moment, so the patient is still examined and reassessed after the picture has been taken.

Measuring the pressure inside a compartment is a clinical test rather than a field one, and it is performed by a clinician who has the equipment and the training the local protocol requires. The figures taught as thresholds differ between services and between editions of the guidelines, so a reading within 30 millimeters of mercury of the diastolic pressure is named only as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. What matters more than any single value is the trend over time, the difference from the patient's own blood pressure, and the clinical picture, because one reassuring reading does not exclude the diagnosis. Only a clinician measures and interprets this pressure, and the responder's part is to report the findings that made the measurement necessary. Where the equipment or the trained person is not available, the patient is referred rather than watched until the test can be arranged.

Several other conditions produce a swollen, painful and tense limb, and a responder does not have to separate them at the roadside, but should know that they exist. A clot in a deep vein produces swelling and pain, usually with a limb that is less firm and a patient in less distress, and its confirmation and treatment belong to a clinician. An infection of the skin and the tissue beneath it reddens and warms the limb and may be accompanied by fever, and that distinction is made by the physician rather than by the responder. An injury to a major artery can produce pallor, coldness and a loss of pulse, and it is a surgical emergency in its own right, so it is reported in the same breath as the suspicion of a compartment syndrome. The responder's task is to describe what is seen and felt, to record it, and to hand both to the team that can decide.

Definitive treatment for an established compartment syndrome is an operation called a fasciotomy, and it is performed in an operating room by an orthopedic or vascular surgeon working with an anesthesia team. The surgeon opens the skin and the fascia over the compartment so that the pressure can escape and the muscle and the nerve can be supplied with blood again, and the wound is usually left open at first and covered with a sterile dressing. The operation is urgent, because muscle that has been without blood for hours does not recover, and the surgeon may return to look at the tissue again before deciding how the wound will be closed. Damage already present when the patient arrived cannot be undone by the operation, which is why it is not a substitute for early recognition. The technique of the operation is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and it is not taught from a book.

A fasciotomy is a large operation, and like every operation it has complications of its own, which the surgeon explains to the patient and the family. Bleeding, infection, injury to a nerve or a vessel, and a wound that takes weeks to close are all possible, and a patient who becomes unwell after the operation is reported to the surgical team at once. When the diagnosis is made late, muscle that has died is replaced by scar tissue that shortens as it heals, and in the forearm this produces a hand with fingers that curl and cannot be straightened, a condition remembered as a contracture of the forearm. Sensation and strength may never return, and in the worst case the limb itself is lost, which is why this course treats the tense limb as a race against the clock. The chapter asks the listener to suspect the problem early and to say so plainly, because a picture of the pressure will not arrive in time to make the decision.

Every act in this chapter belongs to a named level of practice, and the levels are worth saying together because the listener may be any one of them. The lay first aider recognizes a limb that is swollen, tense and painful beyond the injury, supports it in the position found, keeps the patient warm, does not raise it, does not apply cold, and calls for help without waiting to be certain. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician perform the same acts and add the splint, the formal neurovascular examination and the reporting of every change, within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. The paramedic may release a bandage or a strap within those same procedures, and transports the patient urgently while alerting the receiving facility in advance. The nurse examines the limb, records the findings before and after each intervention, keeps it at the level of the heart, and escalates to the physician without delay. The physician makes the clinical diagnosis, orders imaging, may measure the pressure and may open a cast, and the orthopedic or vascular surgeon performs the fasciotomy and any definitive treatment of the fracture.

Medicines appear in this emergency in a few narrow places, and none of them is a regimen this course will give. Severe pain is treated, because a patient in agony is not made safer by withholding relief, but the substance, the amount and the manner of giving it belong to a prescriber working from the local protocol, and this course names none of them. A nerve block or an epidural can remove all feeling from the limb and hide the pain that is the earliest warning, so that decision belongs to a clinician who has weighed the benefit against the risk and who will keep examining the limb. A patient with an open wound over a fracture, or with a crush injury, needs decisions about protection against infection and against tetanus, and those decisions also belong to the prescriber and to the protocol. A listener must not be able to take a prescription from this book, and everything said here about a medicine describes who decides rather than what to give.

A short list of things that are never done in the field protects more limbs than any technique, and each has a reason attached. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened, because the vessels and nerves lie against the bone and because a closed injury can be turned into an open one by a movement that looks helpful. An embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and exploration adds injury and infection. A reduction is not attempted in the field, nor anywhere when the joint surfaces are shattered, a fragment is caught in the joint, the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, the injury is open, the diagnosis is unclear, the responder lacks training or equipment, or an earlier attempt has failed. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and force is not a technique, so a responder who meets resistance stops and escalates. A patient with a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and in this emergency they carry the whole story of a limb. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, its appearance, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and every change in the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order. The receiving team is told plainly that a compartment syndrome is suspected, because that sentence changes how quickly the patient is seen and who sees the patient first. Everything described here is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. Where this chapter names an interval, a pressure or a distance, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. A course cannot certify a hand, so the listener is asked to use this chapter to recognize, to report and to refer rather than to act beyond the scope the law allows.

This emergency is quiet, and that is the quality that makes it dangerous, because the limb that is being lost often looks better than the injury would suggest. The patient may be calm, the wound may be small, the pulse may be present and the skin may be pink, while the muscle inside is starved and the nerve is beginning to fail. The responder who has heard this chapter is asked to trust pain, tension and the passage of time over the reassurance of a pulse, and to say the word compartment out loud to the team that receives the patient. Prevention here is not a device or a medicine but a habit of examination, repeated at every stage and recorded at every stage. A limb that is watched by someone who knows what to look for has a chance, and a limb left unexamined because it looks well is the limb this chapter was written to save.

To summarize, acute compartment syndrome is a raised pressure inside a closed space of bone and fascia that starves the muscle and the nerve, and the diagnosis is clinical, so it is made from the history and the examination rather than from a picture. What to look for is pain out of proportion to the injury, pain that grows instead of settling, pain when the muscles are gently stretched, a compartment that feels tense and firm compared with the other limb, and numbness, tingling or weakness in the area the nerve supplies. What to do is to assess the patient first, to support the limb in the position found, to keep the patient warm, to record the neurovascular status before and after every intervention, to immobilize, to image when a clinician orders it, and then to reassess. The constriction is released within the local protocol by the provider authorized to do it, the limb is kept at the level of the heart and never raised above it, cold and massage are not applied, and the patient is referred urgently, because time is muscle. What never to do is to straighten a deformed limb in the field, to remove an embedded object, to push exposed bone back into a wound, to explore an open wound blindly, to raise the limb above the heart, to apply cold, or to delay referral while waiting for a test. Call the emergency service and the receiving facility early, speak the words compartment syndrome when you suspect it, and work only within the scope of practice the local protocol and the law allow, because this course is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 34 — Malleolar Fractures

The ankle carries the whole weight of the body through a surface no wider than the palm of a child, thousands of times a day and without complaint. Two bony prominences frame that surface, the medial malleolus on the inner side, which is the lower end of the shin bone, and the lateral malleolus on the outer side, which is the lower end of the slender calf bone. With the back edge of the lower shin bone they form a socket that grips the ankle bone, and that grip is what makes the joint steady enough to walk on. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The medial malleolus is the inner corner of the lower tibia, pointing downward just beneath the skin with almost nothing between it and the air. The lateral malleolus belongs to the fibula, sits a little lower and farther back, and can be felt by anyone as the bump on the outside of the ankle. Behind the lower tibia lies a third prominence, the posterior malleolus, which cannot be seen from outside and is found by an examiner who feels the back of the joint or by the radiograph. The upper surface of the lower tibia, the plafond, is a slightly curved ceiling of smooth articular cartilage, and the ankle bone rolls beneath it inside the socket. That socket is a ring in which the tibia, the fibula and the strong ligaments binding them all take a share, so a break of one malleolus sends the examiner to look at the other one.

The inner side of the joint is held by a fan of ligament called the deltoid ligament, which runs from the medial malleolus to the bones of the foot and is strong enough that a violent force often breaks the bone instead of tearing it. The outer side is held by three ligaments, one from the front of the lateral malleolus to the ankle bone, one below it to the heel bone and one behind, and they are injured far more often because the foot rolls inward so much more easily than outward. A torn ligament lets the ankle bone tilt within the socket, so a patient whose bones are intact may still have an unstable joint full of blood. Between the two bones of the lower leg lies a firm fibrous joint that allows the fibula to move only a very little and holds the socket at a constant width, and when that binding tears the socket widens. The examiner therefore thinks of that binding whenever an ankle is swollen and the patient cannot bear weight.

The position of the foot at the moment of injury is the most useful piece of history a responder can obtain, because the direction of the force tells the examiner where to look. When the foot rolls outward while the leg twists inward on a planted foot, the ankle bone turns within the socket and presses the lateral malleolus outward, so the bone may break at the level of the joint or well above it. The same force stretches the inner side, so the medial malleolus may be pulled off as a fragment or the deltoid ligament may tear instead. When the foot rolls inward, the ankle bone tilts, the outer ligaments are stretched and torn, and a piece may be pulled from the tip of the lateral malleolus or a break may run across the bone just above the joint. A fall from a height drives the ankle bone upward into the ceiling of the socket and may break the front or the back edge of the lower tibia as well. These patterns are named and sorted in the textbooks and the names differ between them, so what matters at the bedside is the story of the force and the two prominences that hurt when touched.

Swelling is the finding that hides the injury, and that is why an ankle fracture is missed in the first hour more often than almost any other fracture in the body. The joint fills with blood from the torn bone ends and ligaments, and the soft tissues around the malleoli are loose enough to accept a great deal of it, so within minutes the ankle can double in size and the prominences can no longer be felt. A displaced ankle then looks like a broad, tense and shining swelling rather than an obvious step in the bone, and the deformity may show only as the direction in which the foot points. Comparing the injured ankle with the other one is therefore part of the examination, because the healthy side shows what this patient is normally like. A patient who cannot bear weight and whose tenderness lies over the bony prominences rather than the ligaments has a fracture until a clinician with images decides otherwise.

Looking at the injured ankle is the first act of the examination, and it is done with the limb supported and the other ankle in view for comparison. The responder notes the shape of the joint, the direction in which the foot points and the position of the heel, because that direction is the visible record of the force that broke the bone. The skin is inspected from below the knee to the tips of the toes, including the back of the heel, since a small wound can be the only sign that the injury communicates with the air. A wound over a malleolus makes the fracture an open one even when it is only a puncture, and the management of the whole patient changes at that moment. The skin over the medial malleolus is thin and lies directly upon the bone, so it is the skin most likely to be torn from within by a fragment or to break down under the pressure of swelling, and a pale or dusky patch there must be reported at once.

Assessment begins with the scene and with the story, and the story is taken while the limb is supported rather than examined. The responder asks how the injury happened, in which direction the foot was forced and at what time, and whether the ankle took weight afterward. The medical history matters as much as the accident, because a bone thinned by age, by disease or by medicine may break under a force that would leave a healthy ankle unhurt. Before the ankle is examined at all, the responder decides whether the patient is stable, because the ankle can wait for minutes that the airway, the breathing and the circulation cannot. The steps of that first survey are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and a broken ankle found during that survey does not change the order of it. A patient who fell from a height or was thrown from a vehicle may have injuries of the spine, the chest, the pelvis and the abdomen as well, so a falling level of consciousness or skin that has turned cold and pale sends the responder back to the beginning. The scene is checked for anything that can still injure the patient or the responder, personal protective equipment is used according to the procedures of the service, and only when the patient is stable enough does the examination turn to the limb, which is examined in the position in which it was found.

Feeling the ankle follows looking, and it is done gently, with the limb supported and the two sides compared. The examiner feels the medial malleolus, the lateral malleolus and the back edge of the lower tibia, presses along the whole length of the fibula up to the head beside the knee, and feels the base of the bone on the outer edge of the foot, because a twisting injury can break more than one bone. Tenderness greatest over a bony prominence suggests a fracture, while tenderness greatest over the soft tissue below and in front of the malleolus suggests a ligament injury. Crepitus, the crackling made when broken ends rub together, is never deliberately sought, because seeking it moves the fracture, and the tests that pull the ankle sideways belong to supervised clinical training rather than to the field. Movement is asked for rather than imposed, so the patient is invited to move the toes and to turn the foot gently if that is comfortable, and a refused movement is information too. A patient who cannot bear weight is treated as having a fracture until images say otherwise, the limb is never straightened and never used as a lever, and a patient who cannot cooperate has a limited examination recorded rather than a normal one. The trained responder, the nurse and the physician each examine within the limits that their training, their equipment and the local protocol allow.

The neurovascular examination of the foot is never skipped and never assumed, and it is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the foot, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and feels the pulse on the top of the foot and the pulse behind the medial malleolus. Sensation is tested on both feet and compared over the top of the foot, over the sole and along the outer border of the foot, because different nerves supply each of those areas. The patient is asked to move the toes, to spread them and to lift the foot upward against a gentle hand, and any movement that was possible a moment earlier and is now lost is written down at once. The findings are recorded in the words of the patient before a splint is applied and again after it is applied, because a finding not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. A formal examination of this kind belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the physician, while the lay first aider reports what the patient says about feeling and movement and keeps the foot warm. Some of these signs are less reliable than they look, because a patient whose nerves are already damaged by diabetes or by alcohol may not notice numbness that is new, and swelling may be modest in an ankle that is quietly bleeding. The answer to that uncertainty is a lower threshold for immobilization, for repeated reassessment and for urgent referral.

A pulse that can still be felt does not exclude serious injury, and that lesson belongs to the ankle as much as to any other part of the body. Pressure inside a closed space can stop the flow through the smallest vessels long before it stops the flow through the main artery, so a foot with a strong pulse may still be losing its muscle and its nerve. The lower leg is divided into four compartments and the ankle sits below them, so bleeding from a fractured malleolus can raise the pressure in the leg as well as fill the joint. Pain out of proportion to the injury, pain produced by stretching the toes gently upward, a foot that is tense and swollen, numbness and a foot that cannot be lifted are the findings that stop the responder. The diagnosis is clinical, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late.

Stabilization means keeping the patient still, keeping the ankle in the position in which it was found, controlling the bleeding that can be controlled, and keeping the patient warm. A deformed ankle is supported with the hands, with a pillow, with a rolled blanket or with padding on either side of the joint, and it is never straightened in the field, however alarming its shape appears. The reason is not tidiness but anatomy, because the vessels and nerves of the foot pass close to the bone, and a displaced fragment may be pressing on a torn vessel in the position that looks wrong to the eye. Pulling the joint straight can tear what remained intact, can release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed and can cut the skin from within, turning a closed fracture into an open one. An open wound over the ankle is covered with a sterile dressing and never explored blindly, exposed bone is never pushed back into it, and an embedded object is left exactly where it is, since definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering.

A splint for the ankle is built around one principle, which is that it must prevent movement of the joint without pressing on the two bony prominences that are already injured. The support is placed along the position in which the joint was found, it is padded where it touches the malleoli and the heel, and it is secured firmly enough to hold the foot steady without becoming a band that stops the circulation. It is long enough to control the foot and the lower leg together, so that the ankle cannot be twisted by the weight of the foot hanging from it, and the toes are left uncovered so that color, warmth, movement and sensation can be checked and rechecked. The material matters far less than the principle, since a padded board, a folded blanket or a pillow bound in place each serve, and an improvised device is checked more often because it shifts as the patient is moved. The ankle is not forced into the square resting position of a healthy joint, because forcing it is another way of straightening a deformed limb. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, the nurse works within the same limits inside a facility, and the lay first aider supports the limb by hand and waits for help.

Reduction, traction and casting are the treatments that restore and hold the position of the bones, and this course describes what they are meant to achieve, what can go wrong and who is qualified to perform them, never how they are done. A reduction brings the displaced malleoli and the ankle bone back into their proper relation, a process sometimes held with traction applied as a gentle continuous pull, and a cast or a surgical fixation holds the position while the bone heals. Each of those acts is learned with a teacher and performed according to local protocol, and none of them can be learned from a book. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught within the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. Force is not a technique, resistance and a new finding are signals to stop rather than to push harder, and the whole of the field role is to support the limb, keep the patient warm, record the neurovascular findings and speak plainly to the patient.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. The ankle is also pictured through a view that looks straight into the socket, since a fracture of one malleolus can let the ankle bone tilt in a way that a single straight picture does not show. The whole length of the fibula is examined when a lateral malleolus is broken, because the force that breaks the bone at the ankle can break it again beside the knee. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, of the back edge of the lower tibia and of the socket when an operation is being planned, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the ligaments, the cartilage and the growing part of the bone in a child. Either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done, and the lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging while the trained responder does not decide which study is needed. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined and reassessed after it has been taken.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with what was written before, and it is the comparison that carries the value rather than any single measurement. The foot is checked for color, warmth, the two pulses, sensation, movement and pain, the splint is checked for tightness and for pressure over the malleoli, and any dressing over a wound is checked for bleeding that has soaked through. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, pain when the toes are stretched gently upward, numbness between the first two toes, a foot that cannot be lifted and a joint that becomes tense and shiny are the findings that stop the responder. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed, releases a constricting bandage or splint only within the limits of the local protocol, keeps the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, keeps the patient warm and refers urgently. The position in which the limb is kept while the patient waits differs between services and editions and is confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some ankles cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with a break of both malleoli, a break of the back edge of the lower tibia, a fracture that has displaced the ankle bone within its socket, an open injury, a suspected compartment syndrome, a foot whose pulses or sensation have changed, or a limb with poor circulation is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The decision about how urgently a patient must travel is made by the clinician or by the service protocol, and a responder who is unsure treats the injury as urgent and says so in the handover. Waiting to see whether the ankle settles on its own helps nobody, and the swelling that hides the deformity also hides the moment at which the skin becomes unsalvageable. Two groups deserve a lower threshold for immobilization and referral, and the first is children, whose lower tibia and fibula carry the growth regions that lengthen the leg, so a twisting injury that looks like a sprain may run through that region rather than through the joint. A child who will not use the ankle or who limps for days after a fall is therefore examined rather than watched, and an injury across the growing part of the bone can disturb the growth of the leg for years. The second group is older adults, whose bone has lost density and whose skin has grown thin, so a fall from standing height can displace an ankle, the pain may be far less than the severity of the injury, and the skin over the malleolus may break down within hours. A patient who lives alone or who cannot keep weight off the limb needs a plan for care rather than an appointment, and the receiving team is told the time of the injury, the mechanism and every neurovascular finding with the time at which it was recorded.

Definitive treatment takes several forms, and which is used depends on the bones that are broken, the state of the socket and the needs of the patient. A stable fracture that holds its position may be treated with support while the bone heals, with weight bearing allowed at a stage the treating clinician sets. A displaced fracture is usually held with plates and screws placed on the bone, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, performed by an orthopedic surgeon in an operating room. When the socket has been torn open between the two bones of the lower leg, a screw or a tight binding may be placed across them for a period that teaching gives as several weeks, an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. When the skin and the soft tissues are too damaged to tolerate an operation through them, the surgeon may place a frame of pins and bars outside the limb and wait for the swelling to settle. After any of those treatments the ankle is stiff and swollen for weeks, and rehabilitation belongs to a physiotherapist working within a plan the treating clinician sets, since the goal is a joint that carries weight and not merely a bone that has joined.

This chapter describes no dose, no route and no drug regimen, because the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol. Pain is treated by the clinician who can assess it, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, increasing, out of proportion to the injury, or accompanied by a foot that is tense, cold or numb. A responder at any level may make the patient more comfortable by supporting the ankle, keeping the patient warm and explaining what is happening, and a trained responder may give an analgesic only under the standing orders and the authorization of the service. Antibiotics for an open injury and protection against tetanus are decisions for the clinician, and the part of the responder is to report the wound, the time of the injury and the state of the patient's immunization. Sedation for any procedure belongs to a clinician working in a monitored setting with the equipment and the staff the protocol requires, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from this book.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the ankle was found, the state of the skin and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a patient who fell from a height is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Where this chapter names a time, a distance or a period of healing, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. Everything described here is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, and a responder who is unsure about any part of this chapter treats the ankle as urgent, keeps the patient warm, records what is seen, and calls for help rather than for reassurance.

To summarize, the ankle is a small joint that carries a great load, and its two malleoli are the lower ends of the tibia and the fibula, held into a socket by ligaments that decide whether it stays steady. The direction in which the foot was forced at the moment of injury tells the examiner which side to expect to be broken, and the swelling that follows within minutes hides the deformity and most often leads a broken ankle to be dismissed as a sprain. Assess the patient first, remember that life comes before limb, and record the neurovascular status of the foot, including color, warmth, the two pulses, sensation and movement, before any intervention and again after every one. Stabilize by supporting the ankle in the position found, never straightening it in the field, covering any wound with a sterile dressing, leaving an embedded object in place and keeping the patient warm. Immobilize the joint and the joints above and below it, pad the bony prominences, leave the toes uncovered for the checks that follow, and let only a trained responder or paramedic apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes. Image only when a clinician orders it, reassess after everything you do, suspect a compartment syndrome and act on it, and refer a displaced, open or unstable ankle, a foot whose nerves or vessels have changed, a child with an injury across the growing part of the bone, or an older adult with thin skin over a displaced joint. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and reduction is not attempted when the joint is shattered, a fragment is trapped, the vessels or the nerves are failing, the injury is open, the diagnosis is unclear, the responder lacks training and equipment, or an earlier attempt has failed. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 35 — Syndesmotic Injury and Ankle Fracture-Dislocation

Two injuries of the ankle are taught together in this chapter because one of them is quiet and the other is loud, and both are missed for the same reason. The first is an injury of the strong bands between the two bones of the lower leg, a structure called the syndesmosis, which is easy to overlook because the ankle may look almost normal and the patient may still walk. The second is the ankle fracture-dislocation, in which the joint is out of place and the skin stretched over the bones is at risk of tearing from the inside, and it is one of the few injuries in this course in which a delay of hours changes what the patient keeps. Both are taught through the order this course follows everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The lower leg is built from two bones, a thick one on the inner side called the tibia and a slender one on the outer side called the fibula, and at the ankle they form a bracket rather than a simple hinge. The bracket holds the lower ends of both bones together above a bone of the foot called the talus, so the talus sits in a socket and the foot can bend up and down within it. The two bones are not fused, because the socket must widen a little when the foot bends up, and that movement is possible only because the bones are bound to each other by strong fibrous bands. Those bands together are the syndesmosis, and the most important of them lie at the front of the ankle, at the back of the ankle, and along the two bones as a sheet called the interosseous membrane. The sheet runs far up the leg, and its work is to keep the two bones moving as one unit while holding the talus centered. When the bands are torn or a bone is broken, the socket can open wider than it should and the talus then shifts or turns inside it, which is the beginning of both of the injuries in this chapter.

The usual mechanism is a twisting force applied to a planted foot while the leg turns the other way, which is why the injury appears in sport, in a fall on a step and whenever one part of the body stops and the rest keeps moving. The energy that tears the ligaments on the outer side of the ankle may instead travel between the two bones, and it may also break the fibula at the ankle or, less often, break it far above the ankle near the knee. A foot driven upward into the socket with great force can injure the syndesmosis and the front of the lower end of the tibia at the same time, and a fall from a height delivers exactly that energy. A patient who describes a crack heard at the moment of the injury and who cannot bear weight deserves the same urgency as a patient whose ankle is visibly out of place. The mechanism is therefore recorded in the words of the patient or of a witness, because it tells the receiving team what to look for.

A syndesmotic injury is missed because its tenderness lies above the joint line, in the space between the two bones, rather than over the prominent bone on the outer side of the ankle where a sprain is expected. The ankle may be only slightly swollen, the skin may show no bruise at the beginning, and the patient may take several steps before the pain becomes sharp, which is how the injury comes to be called a sprain and sent home. Several examinations are taught for it, among them pressing the two bones of the lower leg together above the ankle and turning the foot outward against resistance. Those tests are not perfectly reliable, and their meaning differs in a patient with an old injury, with a nerve condition, or who cannot cooperate because of pain, so a negative test never takes the injury off the list. What the responder can do is simpler and safer, which is to look for the swelling, ask where it hurts most, record that the pain is above the joint line, protect the limb, and pass that description to the clinician who will examine it.

A ligament on the outer side of the ankle heals in a few weeks in most patients, while an injured syndesmosis heals more slowly and less predictably, and the reason lies in how the two bones are loaded. Every time weight passes through the leg the talus presses outward on the socket and tries to widen it, so the torn bands are pulled apart with each step instead of being brought together, and healing tissue that is stretched again and again may lengthen rather than rejoin at its original length. The blood supply of the region also arrives from the ends of the bones rather than through the middle of the bands, so a tear lying between the two bones has less to work with. A period of healing offered in teaching for this injury is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the true time differs with how much was torn and with the treatment chosen. The practical point that follows is simple, because an injury allowed to bear weight before it is assessed can become worse while the patient believes it is improving.

An ankle fracture-dislocation is defined by the position of the bones rather than by the number of them that are broken. The talus is no longer sitting in the socket, and the bones that form the socket have broken, torn away from their ligaments, or both. The injury therefore includes the displacement of the joint, a break of the bone on the inner side or the outer side or both, and often a tear of the syndesmosis, and it may also include a break of the back of the lower end of the tibia. The foot may lie turned outward or inward, or it may be pushed backward or forward, and the whole limb looks wrong in a way that even an untrained bystander recognizes. Because the joint surfaces are no longer in contact, the injury is unstable by definition, and no splint makes it stable.

The emergency in this injury is not the broken bone but the skin, because bones that have moved can press the skin from the inside until it tears. The skin over the inner side of the ankle is thin, and it lies directly over the lower end of the tibia, so a foot displaced outward can drive that bone against it with the force of the whole injury. What the responder looks for is skin that has become pale, white, shiny or tight, a crease or a dimple that was not there before, blisters filled with blood, or a small wound that may look like an abrasion but that leads down to the bone beneath it. A wound of that kind turns a closed injury into an open one, and from that moment the deep tissues are contaminated. Skin can survive under such pressure only for a limited time, and a figure taught for that window is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, which is why the patient is moved to a place where a clinician can act instead of waiting for a routine appointment.

Assessment begins before the limb is touched, because a patient with a deformed ankle may have a more dangerous injury elsewhere. The responder considers the scene, the mechanism, the time of the injury and the age of the patient, and then performs the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The limb is examined only when the patient is stable enough, because a life comes before a limb. Both legs are uncovered and compared, and a shoe or a boot is cut away rather than pulled off, since pulling can move the bones and can hide the deformity from the next examiner. The responder does not ask the patient to stand on the injured limb to prove the injury, because weight bearing loads the syndesmosis and can widen a socket that is already unstable. The lay first aider looks, keeps the limb still and calls for help, while the history, the examination and the decision about what a finding means belong to the trained responder and to the clinician.

Stabilization means keeping the patient alive, warm and still while the limb is supported in the position in which it was found. A deformed ankle is never straightened in the field, and the reason is anatomy rather than caution, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bones of the ankle and a limb that is pulled straight can tear what remained intact and can turn a closed injury into an open one. Bleeding from a wound is controlled by pressure around the wound and never by pressing on exposed bone, and an embedded object is left where it lies because it may be holding a torn vessel closed. Exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, and a wound is never explored with a finger or an instrument, because blind exploration adds injury and contamination while adding nothing to the plan. The limb is supported on a pillow or on whatever is at hand, the toes are left visible, and the patient is insulated from the ground, since cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. Wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, and the patient is not left on a cold surface while the responder waits for transport.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any splint is applied and repeated after every intervention, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner feels for the pulse behind the inner ankle, which is the posterior tibial artery, and for the pulse on the top of the foot, which is the dorsalis pedis artery, and compares each with the other side, since either may be faint or absent in a healthy person. Color, warmth and the time it takes for color to return after a nail is pressed are noted, and the toes are checked for sensation on the sole and in the web space between the first and second toes. The patient is asked to move the toes and the ankle, and any movement weaker than on the other side is recorded. A pulse that can be felt does not exclude serious injury to the vessels, to the nerves or to a compartment, while a pulse that cannot be found is an emergency to be reported at once. The trained responder or the paramedic may perform this examination and record it, while the interpretation of an abnormal finding belongs to a clinician.

Compartment syndrome is the complication this course fears most in the lower leg, and it can follow an injury that looked modest at the beginning. The compartments of the lower leg and of the foot are closed spaces bounded by bone and by a tough sheet of fibrous tissue, and bleeding or swelling inside one of them raises the pressure until the flow through the smallest vessels fails. The earliest and most reliable finding is pain that is greater than the injury appears to explain and that grows instead of settling, together with pain when the muscles of the compartment are gently stretched, an act performed by a clinician. A limb that is tense and swollen, a foot that is numb over the sole or the toes, and toes that cannot be moved are late findings, and a pulse that can still be felt does not exclude the diagnosis. When a responder suspects it, the constricting bandage or splint is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, so an ankle injury is held together with the foot and with the leg and not with the ankle alone. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position in which the limb was found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, and a commercial splint, a folded blanket, a padded board or a pillow bound in place can each serve, although an improvised device must be checked more often because it shifts. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands and with whatever is at hand, while the trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. The splint is checked after it is applied, the toes are left visible so that their color can be watched, and any ring or tight band below the injury is removed before swelling makes that impossible. A cast is not a splint, a cast is applied by a clinician, and no field responder decides that one is needed.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. For the ankle that means the whole length of the fibula is part of the picture, including the part just below the knee, because a tear of the syndesmosis can accompany a break far above the joint. A radiograph may appear nearly normal when the syndesmosis is torn, since the widening of the socket may show itself only when the foot is loaded, so a normal film does not clear the patient. The clinician may then need a view taken while the foot is stressed, a computed tomography study or a magnetic resonance imaging study, because computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break while magnetic resonance imaging shows the bands themselves. Either study is requested when the answer will change what is done, and neither the lay first aider nor the trained responder decides which study is needed.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison carries the value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the skin is checked for new tightness, blistering or a wound, and the splint is checked for tightness, for slipping and for pressure over bone. Pain that grows instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, and a responder who finds that a pulse has disappeared or that the toes have gone pale reports it at once rather than adjusting the splint alone. The nurse who receives the patient repeats the same examination, records it, and keeps the limb visible so that a change is noticed early.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step, and for both of the injuries in this chapter it begins with the recognition that the decision belongs to someone else. A patient with an unstable syndesmosis, a fracture-dislocation, a wound over the joint, a damaged nerve or vessel, or a tense swollen leg is referred to a facility that has radiography, an operating room and an intensive care unit, and the referral is urgent rather than routine. The orthopedic surgeon decides whether the two bones of the lower leg must be held together while the bands heal, a judgment that depends on how far the socket widens under load. When the joint is judged unstable, the hold may be provided by a screw or by a flexible device placed across the two bones, and the surgeon may also use plates and screws to hold a broken bone, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation. Some ankles are treated without an operation, in a cast or in a walking support with restricted weight bearing, and which route is taken differs between countries and between surgeons. Recovery is then measured in weeks and months, and the plan is adjusted by the treating team, while the responders have no part in that choice and only have to deliver the patient in the best possible condition for it.

Reduction is the word for restoring the position of the joint and of the bone ends, and in an ankle fracture-dislocation it is done to take the pressure of the bone off the skin before the skin dies. That pressure is the reason the injury is treated as an emergency, and the act itself is a clinical procedure performed with sedation, with monitoring and with imaging available, by an emergency physician or an orthopedic surgeon according to the local protocol. The responder never performs it, never pulls on the foot to improve the look of the limb, and never allows a bystander to try, because force applied by an untrained hand can tear the skin further, break a bone that was intact, or injure the vessels behind the inner ankle. The technique, the amount of force and the way the limb is held afterwards are learned under supervision on real patients and are not taught from a book, and no chapter of this course can take the place of that training. What the field responder gives instead is time saved, which is the one thing that reliably protects the skin.

There are situations in which even a qualified clinician does not attempt a reduction, and the reason is always that the attempt can make the injury worse rather than better. It is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment of bone is caught between them, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when the person present lacks the training or the equipment. An earlier failed attempt is also a reason to stop, because repetition adds injury without adding position, and resistance felt during any attempt is a signal to stop rather than to push harder. The listener should hear the pattern rather than the list, which is that whenever the harm of trying is greater than the harm of waiting for the right hands, the patient is moved instead. Traction, which holds the bone ends in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting, which holds a position while the bone heals, are learned in the same supervised way, and both can cause skin damage, loss of position, stiffness or a compartment syndrome when they are done without training or follow-up.

Some acts are set aside in every chapter of this course because they turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the neurovascular status is recorded, the limb is immobilized, and the patient is referred urgently, while definitive closure belongs to the operating room and to nobody else. Antibiotics and protection against tetanus are decisions for the prescriber and the local protocol, and no dose, no route and no regimen are given in this course, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from these words. Pain relief follows the same rule, and the responder who covers the wound well, splints the limb in the position found and reports the findings has done the part that belongs to the responder.

The same injury behaves differently in different patients, and a course that teaches one picture will be believed. An older adult whose bone has lost density can break an ankle in a fall from standing height, and the skin over that bone may be thin and slow to heal, so a pressure sore from a splint is a real complication of the treatment. A patient with diabetes may have lost the sensation of the feet long before the injury and may report little pain while the joint is badly displaced, so the absence of pain is not evidence that the injury is minor. A child has a growth region near the ends of the tibia and the fibula, and a twist that tears a ligament in an adult can injure that region or pull a small piece of bone away with the band in a child, which changes both the treatment and the follow-up. A patient whose bone is weakened by disease also breaks more easily, and the mechanism may look trivial in the history. In all of these patients the order of the steps does not change, but the threshold for immobilization and for referral is lower, and the decisions about imaging and about treatment belong to the clinician.

Everything the responder has noticed is written down or spoken in a fixed order, because the receiving team continues a story rather than starting a new one. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the state of the skin, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, the splint that was applied and by whom, and any change in the condition of the patient are recorded and handed over in that order. An ankle injury caused by a fall from a height or by a heavy blow is treated as part of a whole patient, and an injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, with no single manual handling technique regarded as safe. The patient who must wait is kept warm, covered and observed, and the limb is left visible so that a change in color or in swelling is noticed by whoever is nearest. Where this chapter names a time, a size or a period of healing, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions.

The two injuries of this chapter can be brought together in a constructed illustration. A middle-aged person hurries down a step, plants the foot and turns the body, and feels a sharp pain above the outer ankle rather than over the prominent bone, while the ankle is only slightly swollen and the person walks to the car. By that evening the leg is tense, the sole of the foot is numb and the pain is severe, and the clinician finds a widening of the socket that the first radiograph did not show. In another constructed illustration an older person slips on ice, the foot turns outward, and the ankle is visibly out of place with pale, tight skin over the inner side of the joint. The responder supports that limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm, records the pulses and the sensation, sends the patient to a facility with an operating room, and does not touch the joint. Neither example is a real patient and neither carries any institutional detail, and they are written only to show that the loudness of an ankle injury is no measure of its severity.

To summarize, the syndesmosis is the set of strong bands between the two bones of the lower leg, and an injury of it is missed because the tenderness lies above the joint line. An ankle fracture-dislocation is an unstable injury in which the joint is out of place and the skin over the bones may tear from the inside, which makes it urgent rather than routine. The order is always the same, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the neurovascular findings recorded before and after every intervention. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly, while definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are performed by qualified clinicians, learned under supervision and carried out according to the local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open, or when training and equipment are lacking. The skin of the ankle sets the clock, so the patient with a fracture-dislocation goes to a facility with an operating room without delay, and every patient is kept warm, reassessed after each intervention and handed over with a clear record. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 36 — Calcaneal Fractures

The heel bone, the calcaneus, is what a person lands on when the feet arrive first, and it is what gives way when a body falls from a height onto a hard surface. It is the largest bone of the foot, it forms the whole of the heel and the back of the arch, and it carries the weight of the body at every step. A break of the calcaneus is therefore rarely a small injury, because the force that broke it traveled through the whole skeleton first, and the same force may have broken the spine, the pelvis or the other heel without the patient noticing. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The calcaneus lies beneath the ankle bone, the talus, and the two form the joint that lets the foot turn on uneven ground. Its upper surface carries smooth facets that meet the matching surfaces of the talus, and behind them the bone narrows into the heel that strikes the ground. At the back the tendon of the calf, the Achilles tendon, attaches to the bone, and along the sole a tough band called the plantar fascia runs from the heel to the toes, so the bone is loaded from above and pulled from below. On the inner side a shelf of bone, the sustentaculum tali, projects beneath the talus and supports it, and the tendons that turn the foot inward glide over that shelf. On the outer side the bone is thin, and the tendons that turn the foot outward pass close against it.

The force that breaks a heel bone is usually an axial load, which means a load directed straight up the line of the leg while the foot is planted. A fall from a height onto the feet does this, and so does a jump from a wall, a fall from a ladder, a fall down stairs, and a heavy object falling onto a seated patient. The talus is driven downward into the calcaneus like a wedge and, being harder than the bone beneath it, splits the heel along the lines of least resistance. Where that split runs decides much of what follows, because a break that stays outside the joint surface behaves differently from one that crosses it and steps the cartilage out of line. Whether the joint surface is involved is the question every classification asks, and the names of the categories differ between systems, so the listener should hold the question and let the surgeon hold the labels. The mechanism is the most useful history a responder can obtain.

Because the energy arrives from below, the examiner must look above the heel, and the spine is the structure most often missed. A patient who lands on both feet transmits the force through the legs, the pelvis and the spinal column, and a compression injury of the thoracic or lumbar spine can exist beside a broken heel in a patient who reports only the foot. The pelvis, the hips, the knees, the other heel and the head are examined in the same pass, and the patient is turned only once, by a team using the precautions the local protocol requires, because a spine that has not been cleared is treated as unstable until someone qualified clears it. The history begins with the height of the fall, the surface landed on and whether the patient could stand at once, and it ends with a search for every place the same fall could have injured. A responder who records only the foot has recorded half of the injury.

Both heels are broken in a substantial proportion of these patients, and the second heel is often the quieter one, so both are examined and compared rather than merely inspected. A patient may say that one foot hurts more, may refuse to put either down, or may be unable to say which foot struck first, and a swollen heel on the less painful side is easily dismissed when the other side is deformed. Comparing the two sides reveals the widening, the flattening of the arch and the loss of the normal inward tilt of the heel. This is a clinical comparison and not a diagnosis, and the definitive answer comes from imaging ordered by a clinician. In a patient who is intoxicated, confused or in shock from other injuries, even the comparison may be unreliable, so the threshold to image both heels is low.

Assessment begins before the foot is touched, with the scene and with the patient. A fall from a height can injure several body regions at once, so the primary survey is completed first, in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. A patient with a broken heel may also be bleeding inside from a torn organ, may have a head injury, or may have an injured spine, and the limb is examined only when the patient is stable enough to allow it. The lay first aider keeps the patient still and warm and calls for help, and the trained responder or the paramedic continues the survey within the procedures the service authorizes. Where the fall happened and how long the patient has been lying there are part of the assessment, and when two correct actions compete for the same hands, life comes before limb.

The heel itself is examined by looking first. It is swollen and broadened, the skin over it is tight and shiny, and the normal curve of the outer edge of the foot is lost, so the foot sits flatter and lower than the other one. Bruising appears on the sole early, and bruising that reaches the sole after a fall points to the bone rather than to a sprain of the ankle, though it may take hours to appear and its absence proves nothing. The skin is inspected with particular care along the inner side of the heel, where the bone lies just beneath the surface and a sharp fragment can split the skin from within, turning a closed injury into an open one without any outside wound. Blisters filled with blood may form over the heel within a day, and they signal badly contused soft tissues rather than an intact bone.

Palpation is done gently and with a purpose, which is to find where the tenderness lies and whether the bone behaves as one piece. The examiner presses the two sides of the heel together between the fingers and the thumb, and a sharp increase in pain is the classic bedside sign of a broken heel, though it is absent in some patients and unreliable in one who is intoxicated, sedated or distracted by another injury. Pressing upward against the sole also causes pain, and neither maneuver establishes the diagnosis by itself. What the responder looks for is not one sign but the pattern of a swollen and widened heel, tenderness over the bone, pain on squeezing, and an inability to bear weight. Bone tenderness in a patient who cannot walk is enough to immobilize the foot and to ask for an image, and the choice of image belongs to the clinician.

Every step from this point onward is preceded and followed by the neurovascular examination, recorded in a fixed order so that the receiving team can compare it with its own findings. The examiner feels the pulse behind the inner ankle and the pulse on the top of the foot, notes the color and temperature of the skin, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and compares each finding with the uninjured side. Sensation is tested on the sole and on the outer border of the foot, where nerves run close to the bone and near the heel. The patient is asked to curl and spread the toes and to turn the foot against resistance, and any movement that was possible a moment earlier and is now weak is recorded as a change. Numbness or lost sensation on the sole, an absent or diminished pulse, and pale, cool skin make the injury urgent. The lay first aider reports what the patient says rather than testing it, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or the clinician.

Swelling in the foot can become a compartment syndrome, and the foot holds more than one closed space in which pressure can rise. The deep space of the foot and the space around the heel bone are the ones most often involved after this fracture, and the pressure rises because the broken bone bleeds inside a space that cannot expand. The findings are pain that increases instead of settling, pain when the toes are stretched upward, a foot that is tense and tight to the touch, and numbness or tingling in the sole, and the pulse may remain present while the tissue is starved, so a normal pulse never excludes the diagnosis. The diagnosis is clinical and belongs to a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation. Where local protocol permits, an authorized responder releases the constricting bandage or splint, the foot is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and transfer is arranged as an emergency. Only the operating room can open those spaces, and that decision belongs to the surgeon.

Stabilization of a broken heel is a small set of acts, and the first of them is restraint. The foot is left in the position in which it was found and is never straightened, pulled into line or manipulated in the field, because the fracture lies inside a tight envelope where nerves and vessels lie against the bone, and because moving the fragments may push a sharp edge through intact skin. The patient is kept still, and the heel is supported from below with the hands, a pillow or a folded blanket so that its weight is not hanging on the injured tissues. Bleeding from an open wound is controlled by pressure around the wound and not inside it, an embedded object is left where it is, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and for the foot that means holding the ankle as well as the heel. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a padded splint that runs behind the calf and under the sole, with the foot supported at the angle in which it was found and the heel free of hard pressure, using the equipment and procedures their service authorizes. A pillow tied around the foot and leg, a rigid board padded with clothing, or a commercial splint can each serve, and an improvised device is checked more often. Nothing is bound tightly around the heel itself, because the swelling can double the size of the foot within hours and a band that was comfortable at the roadside can behave like a tourniquet on arrival. A cast is not applied during the acute phase of a swollen heel, and casting is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol rather than from a book.

Elevation is the next act, and it is done with one exception that must not be forgotten. Raising the injured foot above the level of the heart lets the swelling drain toward the body, and for a swollen heel without any sign of a compartment syndrome that is what the patient needs. The foot is raised on a pillow or a folded blanket while the knee is supported, so that the limb is not left hanging, and the position is held during transport and in the waiting area. The exception is the foot in which the pressure inside a compartment is already too high, because elevation then lowers the pressure driving blood into the tissues and can make the starvation worse. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome therefore keeps the foot level, refers the patient urgently, and asks rather than guesses. How high and for how long belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician. A plain radiograph of the foot is usually the first study and is taken in more than one direction, and the heel often needs a view taken along the line of the bone through the sole, because the ordinary side view alone can hide a break that runs across the joint surface. The whole foot and the other heel are often included, and a patient who fell from a height also needs images of the spine and the pelvis, requested on the basis of the mechanism rather than the reported pain. Computed tomography shows the detail around the joint surface when the surgeon needs to know how many pieces there are and where they have moved, while magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for soft tissues and is rarely needed here. Only the clinician decides which study is required, and the responder neither orders nor reads images, while the patient is examined again after every study and every intervention.

One measurement appears repeatedly in the descriptions of this fracture, an angle drawn on the lateral radiograph between two lines, one along the upper surface of the heel bone and one along its under surface. The normal value lies within a range that differs slightly between texts, and a heel flattened by the fracture reduces that angle toward zero and sometimes reverses it, which describes in numbers the flattening an examiner can feel with a hand. The number is not for the responder to estimate, and any figure attached to it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Around that angle the fracture is sorted into those that spare the joint surface and those that cross it, those with two large pieces and those ground into many, and those that split the bone lengthwise. The names differ between countries and editions, and the practical questions are whether the joint surface is broken, whether the skin is open, how badly the soft tissues are injured, and what else the fall has broken.

Definitive treatment is chosen by the orthopedic surgeon together with the patient, and it depends on the pattern of the break, the state of the soft tissues, the other injuries and the needs of the person who must walk on that foot again. A fracture that does not enter the joint surface, that is not displaced, and that is found in a patient who cannot safely undergo an operation may be treated without surgery, which means a period of immobilization, no weight through the foot, elevation and a gradual return to walking under supervision. That program is prescribed by the treating clinician, and the responder's part is to keep the foot still and elevated and to ensure the patient takes no weight until someone qualified says so. Weight bearing before the bone has held is one way a good result becomes a painful flat heel, and no listener should decide this for themselves. The plan, its duration and its exceptions belong to the treating team and the local protocol.
