An operation is often offered when the joint surface is broken and the pieces are out of line, because a heel that heals flat and wide wears out the joint above it and turns the foot outward. The operation is called open reduction and internal fixation, which means the surgeon opens the area, restores the position of the pieces and holds them with metal devices. A heel is difficult to operate because the skin and the fat beneath it are thin and easily damaged, and the swelling can be severe, so the surgeon may wait several days for the soft tissues to settle before operating. The timing, the approach and the choice of implant are surgical decisions, and the responder has no part in them. Reduction, closed or open, is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, it is never taught from a book, and the same applies to traction and casting. Force is not a technique, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered beyond reconstruction, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when an earlier attempt has failed.

The complications of a broken heel arrive slowly, and most are caused by the shape the bone settles into rather than by the break itself. A heel that heals wide and flat changes the way the foot meets the ground, the outer edge of the ankle presses against the bone beneath it, and the tendons that turn the foot outward begin to rub and snap, so the patient reports pain on the outside of the ankle months later. The joint beneath the ankle bone develops arthritis when its smooth surfaces were stepped out of line, and that pain is felt deep in the foot and is worse on uneven ground. The pad of fat under the heel can be damaged or displaced, leaving pain on the sole with every step, and a small nerve can be caught in the scar, producing burning or numbness along the outer border of the foot. Wound problems, infection, stiffness and a foot that swells for months are also common, and a patient who smokes or has diabetes is at greater risk.

An open injury of the heel is treated as a surgical emergency, and the responder's part in it is narrow and exact. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by pressure around the wound and not by probing inside it, the neurovascular status is recorded, the foot is immobilized in the position found, and the patient is kept warm and transferred to a facility with an operating room. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back, because the object may be plugging a torn vessel and because bone that has been outside the body is contaminated. Protection against tetanus and the use of antibiotics are medical decisions, and a listener must not be able to take a prescription from this book, so the substance, the amount, the route and the timing belong to the prescriber and the local protocol. Any break in the skin over the heel makes that decision urgent, and the clinician who examines the wound decides. Definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else.

Not every broken heel comes from a fall from a height, and the examiner who waits for a dramatic story will miss the quiet ones. A person whose bone has lost density may break the heel in a fall from standing height or in a misstep, and a patient who takes a medicine that thins the bone, or a steroid over a long period, breaks it more easily still. In such a patient the swelling may be modest, tenderness may be the only finding, and the ability to take a few steps does not exclude the fracture, so the threshold for immobilization and imaging is lower rather than higher. Age also changes treatment, since the risks of an operation rise with the illnesses that come with age, and those judgments belong to the treating team rather than the responder.

Reassessment is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment, and it is performed after every intervention and at every handover. The examiner repeats the same observations in the same order, compares them with what was recorded before, and treats any change as meaningful. The foot is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint for tightness, pressure over the bony points, and the position of the foot within it. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness or tingling in the sole, weakness of the toes, a foot that becomes tense and shiny, a wound that begins to smell, and a patient whose pulse and breathing are changing are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome acts within the local protocol, where an authorized person may release the constricting bandage or splint, and does not elevate the limb above the level of the heart. The record of the change, the time it was noticed and the action taken travels with the patient and is part of the treatment.

Referral is the final step of the sequence, and for the bones of the heel it is the usual one, because the definitive decisions need an orthopedic surgeon and an operating room. A patient with a fracture that enters the joint, a badly comminuted break, an open wound, a suspected compartment syndrome, damaged nerves or vessels, a break of both heels, or any injury of the spine or pelvis is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The transfer is arranged early rather than after the swelling has worsened, and the receiving team is told the mechanism, the time of the injury, the state of the skin, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and what has already been done. During the transfer the foot stays splinted and elevated unless a compartment syndrome is suspected, the patient is kept warm, and the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified clears it. The lay first aider does not decide the destination, and the nurse or physician who arranges the transfer works within the local protocol for the region.

An illustration, constructed rather than drawn from any real patient, shows how these pieces fit together. A man in middle age falls a single story from a ladder onto a concrete floor, lands on both feet, and tells the responders that his left foot hurts. His left heel is swollen, broad and tender when squeezed, his right heel is tender as well although far less swollen, and he has a tender area over the lower back that he attributes to lying on the ground. The responders record that both feet have a pulse and normal sensation, splint both feet in the position found with the heels supported and free of hard pressure, keep him warm, and take him to a facility with imaging rather than to the nearest clinic. The images show a break of the left heel that crosses the joint surface, a smaller break of the right heel that does not, and a compression injury of the spine, and the orthopedic surgeon plans the treatment of all three. The point is that the second heel and the spine were found because the mechanism guided the examination rather than the pain.

Everything in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on one another, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, and the provider level is named for every act because a course that ignores scope of practice can harm the patient who follows it. The lay first aider supports the foot, keeps the patient warm and still, and calls for help. The trained first responder and the paramedic splint the foot in the position found, record the neurovascular findings, and work within the equipment and procedures their service authorizes. The nurse and the physician examine, record, request imaging, reassess and refer within the local protocol, and the orthopedic surgeon decides about reduction, external support, operation and weight bearing. No listener should attempt a reduction, apply traction or apply a cast on the strength of a spoken lesson, and no listener should straighten a deformed foot in the field for any reason. Where this chapter names a time, a distance or a threshold, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions.

To summarize, the calcaneus is the heel bone, it breaks when a load is driven up through a planted foot, and the same fall may have broken the spine, the pelvis or the other heel, so the examination always looks above the foot as well as at it. The findings to look for are a swollen, widened and painful heel, tenderness over the bone, pain when the heel is squeezed, bruising that reaches the sole, blood blisters, a wound on the inner side, and an inability to bear weight. Both feet are compared, because the second break is often quieter. The order remains to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The foot is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Elevation is used for swelling but not when a compartment syndrome is suspected, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 37 — Talar and Midfoot Injuries

The talus and the midfoot are small structures that carry a large share of the weight of the body, and injuries to them are among the most easily missed in the whole skeleton. The talus passes the load of the body from the leg into the foot, and it is almost entirely covered with joint cartilage and has no muscle attached to it. The midfoot is the group of small bones and joints that holds the arch and passes force from the heel to the toes. When the talus breaks, the danger is that it loses the blood supply that keeps it alive, and when the midfoot is disrupted, the danger is that joints which must line up exactly heal out of line. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace supervised training, certification, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The talus sits like a keystone between the two bones of the lower leg above it and the calcaneus below. The body is the block that forms the ankle joint with the tibia and the fibula, the neck is the narrow bridge that turns forward and inward, and the head is the rounded end that meets the navicular bone. Almost the whole surface of the talus is covered with cartilage and no tendon or muscle attaches to it, so its nourishment arrives only through the soft tissue around it. Blood reaches it at a few small points, mostly through the neck and through a canal between the talus and the calcaneus, and from there it flows backward to fill the body of the bone. In most bones a break does not threaten the life of the bone, because the supply is rich, but in the talus it enters through the very part that most often breaks, so a fracture of the neck can leave the body with no blood at all.

Talar injuries are produced by force driven up through the foot rather than by a blow that arrives from the side. The ordinary causes are a fall from a height, a fall down stairs, a motor vehicle crash in which the foot is pressed against a pedal, and any landing in which the full weight of the body arrives on a planted foot. The position of the foot at the instant of impact decides which part of the bone fails. When the foot is forced upward toward the shin while the leg is fixed, the neck of the talus breaks, and that is the injury which carries the greatest risk to the blood supply. When the force arrives with the ankle held in a neutral position, the body of the talus may be driven between the two bones of the lower leg and split, while a small fracture of the lateral process on the outer side follows a combination of upward and inward twisting.

The difficulty of these injuries is that the foot often looks far better than it feels. Swelling fills the hollows around the ankle and the heel within a short time, and a swollen foot hides the bony landmarks an examiner would otherwise use. A fracture of the talar neck may produce no visible deformity until the broken ends move apart, and the patient may describe only a deep ache in the middle of the foot. A fracture of the lateral process is easily mistaken for a sprain of the ankle, because the tenderness lies on the outer side of the joint and the ligaments that are usually injured lie immediately beside it, so the examiner who finds tenderness there also presses on the talus itself. A fracture of the posterior process causes pain at the back of the ankle, and bruising that appears on the sole should raise the question of a deeper injury, because blood has traveled from a structure the examiner cannot see.

The midfoot is the region between the hindfoot, which is the talus and the calcaneus, and the forefoot, which is the metatarsals and the toes. It contains the navicular, the cuboid and three cuneiform bones, together with the joints among them and with the bones behind and in front, two of which let the foot twist as the heel strikes and lock the arch as the foot pushes off. The most important row of joints in the midfoot is the one where the midfoot meets the metatarsals, and its keystone is the base of the second metatarsal, which is set back into a notch between the cuneiform bones and held there by a strong ligament running from the medial cuneiform. That ligament is the last structure to give way when force drives the front of the foot away from the back, and when it tears the arch loses its shape. A displacement of a few millimeters that would be unimportant in the shaft of a long bone is a serious injury here.

Midfoot injuries are produced by the same axial load that breaks the talus, usually with a twist added, and the classic description is a foot that stays planted while the body rotates above it. That is what happens when a person steps into a hole, slips on a step, or lands awkwardly from a height. The energy may be very low, and that is why the injury is underestimated, because a person can tear the midfoot ligament by stepping off a curb and the injury may be treated as a sprain for weeks before the foot fails to recover. A direct blow, a heavy object dropped on the foot, and a crush in a doorway produce a different pattern, often with several bones broken and the soft tissues badly bruised. In a vehicle crash the foot is driven against the floor or the pedals, and the same energy may also fracture the ankle or the bones of the lower leg, so the whole limb is examined rather than the part the patient mentions.

The findings of a midfoot injury are few, and each of them can be dismissed by an examiner in a hurry. The patient is tender over a precise line across the middle of the foot, where the midfoot meets the metatarsals. Swelling appears quickly and may obscure the tender line, so the examination is repeated once the swelling has settled, and bruising may appear on the sole rather than on the top of the foot. The ability to walk a few steps does not exclude a serious injury to the midfoot. Widening of the foot compared with the other side, or a step felt with the finger along the line of the joints, suggests that the arch has separated, and pain at that same line when the front of the foot is twisted gently against the back is the most useful sign the examiner can produce. A foot that has been walked on for several days may present with nothing more than persistent swelling and a patient who says the foot does not feel right.

Assessment begins away from the foot and works toward it, because a foot injury is rarely the injury that kills. The scene is made safe, the mechanism is established, and the primary survey is completed in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, and a foot that is bleeding heavily is controlled while the survey continues, because life comes before limb. The history includes the height of the fall, the surface struck, the position of the foot at impact, and the time, together with what makes this patient different, such as diabetes, loss of sensation in the feet, and medicines that thin the bone. A patient with a distracting injury or a reduced level of consciousness may never mention the foot, so the foot is examined in every patient who has fallen from a height. The lay first aider reports what was seen and when, the trained responder adds what was found, and the diagnosis belongs to the clinician.

The examination of the injured foot follows the same rule as the examination of every other part, which is to look, to feel, to ask the patient to move, and never to force. The examiner looks at the position of the foot, the shape of the arch, the swellings, the wounds and the color of the skin, then palpates in a fixed order from the heel to the toes, comparing each spot with the other foot. The patient is asked to curl the toes, to bend the ankle up and down, and to turn the foot inward and outward, and the examiner stops at the first movement that is lost or that sharply increases the pain. The examiner does not test the stability of the midfoot by twisting it and does not pull on the foot, because both are clinical skills learned under supervision and both can convert an injury that was stable into one that is not. A foot that cannot be examined properly because of pain is splinted and reassessed rather than examined through the pain.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any splint is applied and repeated after every intervention, and its result is recorded in words, because a finding that was not written before a splint went on cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner feels for the pulse on the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle, and notes whether each is strong, weak or absent, remembering that in some healthy people one of those pulses cannot be felt at all, so an absent pulse alone is not proof of injury. The skin is checked for color, warmth and the time a pressed nail takes to refill, and sensation is tested over the web of skin between the first and second toes and along the borders of the foot. Movement is tested by asking the patient to curl the toes and to bend the ankle, and a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier and cannot perform now is recorded at once. Numbness, tingling, a cold and pale foot, and pain far worse than the injury explains are all findings that stop the examination and send the patient for urgent assessment.

Compartment syndrome of the foot is the complication this chapter fears most, and it is caused by the injury and sometimes worsened by the treatment. The foot is divided into several closed compartments by sheets of fibrous tissue, and bleeding or swelling inside one of them raises the pressure on the muscles, the nerves and the small vessels within it. The earliest and most reliable finding is pain out of proportion to the injury that becomes worse rather than better, particularly when the toes are gently stretched. A tense, shiny and swollen foot whose sensation is changing, and a foot whose pain does not respond to the measures the local protocol allows, are reasons to act, and a pulse that is still present does not exclude the condition. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so the responder does not wait for a confirmation. The constricting bandage, splint or cast is released by someone authorized to do so within the local protocol, the foot is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently.

Stabilization of the injured foot in the field is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The foot is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, however deformed it looks, because vessels and nerves lie against the bones of the foot and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact, turn a closed injury into an open one, or release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. The lay first aider supports the foot with the hands, rests it on a pillow or a folded blanket, keeps the patient warm and waits for help. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment their service authorizes, and both of those levels protect the foot from further movement and from cold. Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, so the foot is insulated from the ground and the patient is covered. Nothing is given by mouth except on the decision of the receiving team, and any substance, route or amount belongs to the prescriber and to the local protocol.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved from either end. For an injury of the talus or the midfoot this normally means a padded splint that supports the lower leg, the ankle and the whole foot in the position found, with the foot held at a right angle when that can be reached without force. The splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a walking boot, a rigid shoe or an operation. Casting is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no chapter of this course teaches a listener to cast a limb, to reduce a fracture or to apply traction from a book, while a cast applied too tightly can cause the very compartment syndrome the splint was meant to prevent.

An open injury of the foot is a special emergency because the soft tissue covering the talus and the midfoot is thin, so bone that lies barely under the skin can be exposed by a modest wound. An open fracture is contaminated even when it looks clean, because the skin carries organisms that reach the bone and the deep tissues in the moment of injury. The part played by the responder is limited and precise, which is to cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control the bleeding that can be controlled, record the neurovascular status, immobilize the foot in the position found, keep the patient warm, and arrange urgent transfer, while the lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment and the trained responder works within the procedures the service authorizes. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and because bone that has come out carries contamination back in. Exploring an open wound blindly adds harm, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. Antibiotics and tetanus protection are decided by the clinician and follow the local protocol, and the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and for a suspected injury of the talus or the midfoot the clinician usually needs pictures of the ankle and of the whole foot as well. Views taken while the patient stands and puts weight through the foot may reveal a separation that a picture taken lying down cannot show, but they are taken only when the clinician judges them safe. Computed tomography shows the detail of the talar body, of the talar processes and of the small joints of the midfoot, and it is the study that finds the injury when the first radiograph looks nearly normal while the foot is clearly injured. Magnetic resonance imaging is used for stress injuries of bone, for ligament damage, for cartilage and for the early detection of avascular necrosis. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed, while the clinician remembers that an image is a picture of one moment and that the patient must still be reassessed after it.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what carries value. The foot is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint is checked for tightness and for pressure over the bony points. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a foot that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. Reassessment is also the moment to notice that the patient has become drowsy, pale, short of breath or cold, because a foot injury may be only one part of a larger set of injuries. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, so the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart while the patient is kept warm and referred urgently.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and injuries of the talus and the midfoot cannot be managed where the patient lies. A fracture of the talar neck or body, a displaced fracture of a talar process, and any injury that has separated the joints of the midfoot are referred to an orthopedic surgeon, almost always at a facility with computed tomography, an operating room and an intensive care unit, because the talus lives on a slender blood supply and the midfoot lives on precise alignment, and both are decided in the hours after the injury. A patient whose foot is clearly injured but whose first radiographs are reported as normal is referred for reassessment rather than sent home, and the lay first aider does not decide where a patient goes. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, open reduction and internal fixation, which holds them with metal devices, external fixation, which holds the bone from outside the skin, and fusion of a joint, which removes a painful joint surface that cannot be saved. Every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a page of this course.

A reduction of a talar or midfoot injury must not be attempted when the source lists a contraindication, and there is a reason behind every item on that list. It is not attempted when the injury is a suspected complex fracture with a dislocation, because the fragments and the joint surfaces are arranged in a way that only an operating room can rebuild, or when a fragment of bone is caught in the joint. It is not attempted when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, because a second attempt can finish what the first injury began. It is not attempted when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. In every one of those situations the attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is never a technique. The same discipline applies to traction, which is a gentle continuous pull that holds bone ends in line and is used only where a qualified clinician directs it.

Several complications are common enough to be expected rather than surprising, and the patient is warned about them before leaving care. Avascular necrosis of the talus is the slow death of the bone that follows an injury to its blood supply, and it may declare itself only after weeks or months, a period that is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Post-traumatic arthritis is the wearing away of a joint surface that healed out of line or was damaged at the moment of injury, and it is why a midfoot injury that seems minor is treated seriously. Malunion, which is healing in an unacceptable position, and nonunion, which is failure to heal at all, both change the shape of the foot and the way it takes weight, while infection may follow any open injury and appear after the patient has left the hospital. Stiffness and persistent swelling are expected to some degree and are managed by rehabilitation, and the findings that bring a patient back urgently are fever, a wound that becomes red or discharges, pain that increases after it had begun to settle, and a foot that becomes numb or cold.

Two groups of patients deserve a lower threshold for imaging, immobilization and referral. A child's foot contains growth regions near the ends of the bones and several centers of bone that have not yet joined, and an injury there may be invisible on a radiograph while it can still disturb growth, so a child who refuses to walk after an injury is treated with the same caution as a child with an obvious break. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break the talus or the midfoot in a fall from standing height, and the injury may be far less painful than its severity suggests. A patient with diabetes and loss of sensation in the feet may not feel the injury at all, and a foot that is warm, swollen and painless in such a patient is an emergency that needs a clinician rather than a new pair of shoes. The unconscious patient, the patient with a spinal injury and the patient with several injuries cannot report pain in the foot, so the foot is examined early and the finding is recorded before anything is applied to it.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the foot was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and the splint that was applied are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a patient with a foot injury and a possible spinal injury is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that defines what may be done without supervision, and where this chapter names a period or a threshold it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, the talus carries the weight of the body into the foot on a blood supply that enters through its narrow neck, so a fracture there can kill the bone slowly, while the midfoot is a row of small joints that must line up exactly, so a displacement of a few millimeters is a serious injury. The findings to keep are tenderness over a precise line across the middle of the foot, bruising on the sole, a widening of the foot compared with the other side, and tenderness over the outer side of the talus that is worse than the ligaments beside it. These injuries are missed because the foot looks better than it feels, so the clinician is asked early for the imaging that shows the detail of the bone and the joints. The sequence is always the same, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status and record it before and after every intervention, to immobilize in the position found, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the scope of practice is named for every act. A deformed foot is splinted as it lies and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and definitive closure of an open wound belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, never from a book, and who to call is the orthopedic surgeon at a facility with imaging and an operating room. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 38 — Metatarsal and Toe Injuries

The metatarsals and the toes are the part of the skeleton that meets the ground first, and they are also the part most often dismissed as too small to matter. Five long bones carry the weight of the whole body into the floor at every step, and the toes finish that movement and push the body on. When one of these bones breaks, the shoe no longer fits and the step becomes painful, so the patient loses more than a fracture. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace supervised training, certification, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The five metatarsals are numbered from the inner side of the foot outward, and each has a base at the midfoot, a shaft, and a head that meets the first bone of a toe. The first is the thickest and the shortest, and with two small sesamoid bones beneath its head it carries most of the body weight through the great toe. The second is the longest and is set back into a notch between the bones of the midfoot, while the third and fourth are more free to move. The fifth ends in a broad base where a tendon from the leg attaches. The junction of the shaft of the fifth metatarsal with its base is supplied by a small branch that enters there and nowhere else. A break there can therefore leave part of the fracture without blood, which is why this bone has a reputation for failing to heal.

The toes contain the phalanges, and their number differs between the great toe and the rest, with two in the great toe and three in each of the others. The great toe carries the load at the end of the step, so its joint must stay straight and in line, while the lesser toes balance the sole and spread its pressure. The nails protect the tips of the toes and the tissue beneath them, and the nail bed must heal flat and smooth if the nail is to grow without a ridge or a split. Nothing in a toe is large, and that is precisely why an injury there is underestimated by the patient and by the examiner alike.

Injuries of the metatarsals and the toes come from two kinds of force, and telling them apart is part of the assessment. A direct blow breaks the bone under the point that was struck, as when an object is dropped on the foot, a foot is crushed under a wheel, or a bare foot strikes a hard edge. These injuries often involve more than one bone, and the swelling may become the more serious part of the injury. An indirect force arrives through the foot rather than against it, as a twist, an awkward landing or a repetitive load, and it usually breaks a single bone at a place the examiner can predict. A twist of the ankle that pulls on a tendon can tear a small piece from the base of the fifth metatarsal, while the same twist often sprains the ligaments beside it, so the examiner who finds tenderness there also feels the bone below it.

Repetitive load without a single moment of injury produces the stress fracture, the injury this chapter knows as the fracture of the marched foot. A person who marches, runs, dances or stands for long hours in boots that are new or worn thin loads the same small segment of bone thousands of times, and bone that is tired faster than it can repair itself develops a fine crack. The second and third metatarsals are the usual sites, because they are the longest and the least mobile of the five. The pain begins as a dull ache in the ball of the foot that appears with activity and fades with rest, and at this stage the foot looks almost normal. If the load continues, the crack can extend across the bone and the injury becomes a complete fracture, so an ache that returns with every march deserves an examination rather than a new pair of socks.

Assessment of the foot begins with the patient's own account, and that account is worth more than any single sign. The primary survey is completed first, in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and only then does the assessment turn to the limb. The time of the injury, the force behind it, the position of the foot at impact, and whether the patient has been able to walk on it since are the first questions. The examiner also asks about the days before the injury, because a stress fracture has no single moment to report, and about diabetes, loss of sensation in the feet, poor circulation, and medicines that thin the bone. The lay first aider reports what was seen and heard and when, the trained responder adds what was found on examination, and the diagnosis belongs to the clinician.

The local examination looks at the foot before it touches it, and it looks at both feet side by side. The examiner notes the position of the toes, any unnatural bend, a toe that sits above or below its neighbor, a great toe that no longer points straight, and any wound or break in the skin. Swelling appears quickly over the top of the foot and around the base of the fifth metatarsal, and it can hide the shape of the bones within a short time of the injury. Bruising may appear late, and blood that has traveled along the sole or around the heel suggests that the injury reaches deeper than the skin shows. The examiner asks whether the shoe of the injured foot has become tight, because a foot swelling inside a shoe is a foot whose circulation must be checked.

Palpation follows a fixed order so that nothing is skipped, and it begins away from the place the patient points to. The examiner feels along each metatarsal from its base to its head, then presses gently across the row of metatarsals at once, because a crack in a shaft often hurts when the whole row is squeezed. The base of the fifth metatarsal is felt on its own, because a fracture there follows a twisted ankle closely and is mistaken for a sprain of the ligaments beside it. The examiner does not test the stability of a toe by pulling on it and does not move a toe that is clearly deformed, because both are clinical acts that can add damage. A patient who can walk does not thereby exclude a fracture, since many people walk on a broken toe for days before they seek help. When the patient presents days after the injury, the swelling has softened and the foot may look ordinary, and feeling along the bone belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

Stabilization of an injured foot in the field is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The foot is supported in the position in which it was found, and a deformed toe or a displaced metatarsal is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie close against the bone. Pulling a toe straight can turn a closed injury into an open one and can release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. The lay first aider supports the foot with the hands, keeps the patient warm, and waits for help, while a shoe that has become tight as the foot swells is cut away by someone authorized to do it. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and because cold is a complication of trauma, the foot is insulated from the ground.

The neurovascular examination of the foot is performed before any splint or strap is applied, repeated after every intervention, and recorded in words. The examiner feels for the pulse on the top of the foot and for the pulse behind the inner ankle, and remembers that in some healthy people one of those pulses cannot be felt at all. The color and the warmth of the skin are noted, and the examiner presses briefly on a nail and watches how quickly the color returns. Sensation is tested in the web of skin between the toes and along both borders of the foot, and the patient is asked to describe numbness or tingling in ordinary words. Movement is tested by asking the patient to spread the toes, to curl them and to bend the great toe upward, and any movement lost since a moment earlier is recorded at once. Numbness, tingling, a foot that has become cold and pale, and pain far greater than the injury explains are the findings that stop the examination and send the patient for urgent assessment.

A lesser toe that must be held still is often strapped to the toe beside it, and the neighbor then acts as a splint, which means that two toes depend on one piece of tape. The examiner records the color, the warmth, the capillary refill and the sensation of the injured toe and of its neighbor before the strap is placed, and again afterwards. A finding that was not written before the tape went on cannot be attributed to the tape afterwards. The strap is placed around the middle of the toe rather than across a joint, so that the joint can still bend, and a small pad is placed between the two toes where skin would otherwise press on skin. The tape is never wrapped so tightly that it leaves a groove in the skin or stops the flow through the small vessels, and the tip of every strapped toe is left visible. Strapping is used only on a toe that has been assessed as stable, because a toe that is rotated or badly displaced is held in the wrong position by a strap and then heals there. A trained first responder, an emergency medical technician, a paramedic or a nurse applies the strap only within what the local protocol allows, and the toe is examined by a clinician when there is any doubt about it.

The circulation of a strapped toe is examined by looking, by feeling and by asking, in that order. The examiner looks first at the color of the tip and of the nail, comparing the strapped toe with the same toe on the other foot and with its neighbor. The neighbor is now part of the same dressing and can be harmed by it. The nail is pressed briefly, and the time the color takes to return is compared between the two toes, while the skin is felt for warmth with the back of the examiner's hand. The patient is asked whether either toe feels numb, tingling, painful or different from before the strap was applied. If either toe is pale, blue or cold, or cannot be felt, the strap is released by someone authorized to do it within the limits of the local protocol and the patient is referred urgently. A toe lost to a piece of tape is a complication caused by treatment, and the great toe is generally not strapped to its neighbor, because it is wide and carries the weight at the end of the step.

Immobilization of the forefoot has one purpose, which is to stop the metatarsals and the toes from bending while the bone heals, because bending keeps a crack open and keeps it painful. The device most often used is a shoe with a stiff sole that does not bend at the ball of the foot, so that the metatarsals are protected from the force of the step. A walking boot, a rigid sandal or a plaster shoe may be chosen instead, and practice differs between countries and clinics. The physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides which device suits a particular fracture, while the nurse or the trained responder may fit the device and teach its use within the local protocol. Casting, which means molding a rigid shell around the foot and the ankle, is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and it is never taught from a book, because a cast applied too tightly can cause the very complication it was meant to prevent. Whatever is chosen is checked for fit and for pressure over the bony points, and the skin beneath it is inspected regularly.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions and including the joint above and the joint below the injury. Views taken while the patient stands and puts weight through the foot may show a widening that a picture taken lying down cannot show, and they are taken only when the clinician judges them safe. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex fracture, particularly one that enters a joint, while magnetic resonance imaging can find a stress fracture before it is visible on a radiograph. The first radiograph of a stress fracture is often reported as normal, and a repeat study after a period of protected weight bearing may show the new bone, so that period is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, the trained responder does not decide which study is needed, and an image is only a picture of one moment.

Many injuries of the metatarsals and the toes are treated without an operation, and the two devices that do most of that work are the stiff-soled shoe and the strap. A single crack through the shaft of the second, third or fourth metatarsal that has not moved is usually held in a stiff-soled shoe while the bone heals. A fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal that was pulled off by a tendon, and in which the fragment has not separated widely, is often treated in the same way. A simple fracture of a lesser toe, and a toe that a clinician has put back into place and that is sitting straight, may be held with strapping to the next toe and a stiff sole. Protected weight bearing, rest from the activity that caused the injury, and a follow-up appointment are part of the treatment rather than advice added at the end. The decision about which injury belongs in a shoe and which belongs in an operating room belongs to the clinician, and the responder's part is to immobilize in the position found and to arrange the assessment.

Some fractures of the metatarsals must be referred, and each reason explains a rule that would otherwise sound arbitrary. A fracture of the first metatarsal is referred because this bone carries the weight of the step together with the great toe and forms part of the arch, so a break that heals out of line changes the way the whole foot accepts load. A fracture of the fifth metatarsal at the junction of the shaft and the base is referred because the blood supply enters there and only there, so the bone may fail to heal. Several metatarsals broken at once, a fracture that has moved, a fracture that enters a joint, a fracture with a wound near it, and a foot crushed so badly that the swelling is tense and spreading are all injuries for the orthopedic surgeon. A fracture in a patient whose bone is weakened by disease or by a medicine is referred with a lower threshold, because the usual signs of trouble may never appear. Children are referred as well, because the ends of these bones contain growth regions that can be injured without a visible break and can later disturb the shape of the foot.

The toes bring their own list of injuries that have stopped being minor. A fracture of the great toe that enters its joint or that has moved, a dislocation of any toe, and a fracture that has a wound over it are referred rather than strapped. A nail torn from its bed, a nail bed that has been cut, and blood collected beneath a nail that lies over a fracture are injuries that need a clinician, because a nail bed that does not heal flat leaves a nail that grows in two pieces. The examiner does not pull off a partly detached nail and does not probe beneath it. A crush injury of the toes, an injury in which the skin is broken over a joint, and an injury in which the patient cannot feel or move a toe are also referred urgently. Any toe injury in a patient with diabetes or loss of sensation is treated as serious from the first moment, and when the diagnosis is unclear the patient is referred rather than reassured.

A dislocated toe is a joint whose surfaces are no longer in contact, and the toe may look shortened, bent to one side or crossed over its neighbor. The responder supports the toe in the position in which it was found, straps it only if a clinician has judged it stable, and never pulls it back into place. Reduction, which restores the joint surfaces to their normal position, is performed by a clinician according to the local protocol, and the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training. It is not attempted when a complex fracture with a dislocation is suspected, when a fragment of bone is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and a specialist is needed, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. In each of those situations an attempt can turn an injury that would have recovered into one that cannot, and force is never a technique. After a toe has been reduced, the clinician decides whether strapping and a stiff sole will hold it or whether a surgical device is needed.

An open injury of the foot deserves particular care, because the skin here is thin and the bones lie close beneath it, so a modest wound can expose bone. An open fracture is contaminated even when it looks clean, because the organisms on the skin reach the bone and the deep tissues at the moment of injury. The part played by the responder is limited and precise, which is to cover the wound with a sterile dressing, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, to record the neurovascular status, to immobilize the foot in the position found, and to arrange urgent transfer. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. A wound is never explored blindly, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. Antibiotics, tetanus protection and pain relief are decisions of the clinician that follow the local protocol, and the substance, the route and the amount belong to the prescriber.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the strap, the shoe and the splint are each checked for tightness while the foot is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a foot that becomes tense and shiny are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. The foot is divided into several closed compartments by sheets of fibrous tissue, and bleeding or swelling inside one of them raises the pressure against the muscles, the nerves and the small vessels, so the earliest dependable sign is pain that grows worse when the toes are gently moved by someone else, and an intact pulse does not exclude it. The constricting strap, bandage, shoe or cast is released by someone authorized to do so within the limits of the local protocol, the foot is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm and referred urgently, because time is muscle.

Some patients deserve a lower threshold for imaging, immobilization and referral, and the reason lies in what their feet cannot tell them. A child's bones contain growth regions near the ends, and an injury there may be invisible on a radiograph while it can still disturb growth, so a child who refuses to walk is treated with great caution. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break a metatarsal in a fall from standing height, and the fracture may hurt far less than its severity suggests. A patient with diabetes, with poor circulation or with loss of sensation in the feet may not feel the injury at all, and a foot that is warm, swollen and painless in such a patient is an emergency that needs a clinician. The same caution applies to a patient who cannot return for follow-up, because the safety of treatment in a stiff-soled shoe depends on someone looking at the foot again. The response is not a different sequence but a lower threshold for immobilization, for imaging and for referral, while the decisions themselves belong to the clinician.

Advice at the end of the visit is part of the treatment, and the patient is told how long the stiff sole is to be worn, a period to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The patient is told to keep the shoe dry, to check the skin under it, and to return if it becomes loose or if the skin becomes red or painful. The person who marches is warned that a return to full training too early can reopen a stress fracture, and that the return is guided by the clinician. Some complications are common enough to be expected rather than surprising, and a fracture of the fifth metatarsal may fail to heal, so that the pain over the outer border of the foot never settles. A toe or a metatarsal that heals in the wrong position leaves a toe crossing over its neighbor or a shoe that rubs in a new place. Post-traumatic arthritis produces pain and stiffness that appear gradually, infection may follow any open injury, and in a foot that has lost its sensation a poorly fitting shoe can produce a pressure sore that becomes an ulcer.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it. The time of the injury, the force behind it, the position in which the foot was found, the state of the skin, and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order. The record also names the device that was applied, whether it was a strap around two toes, a stiff-soled shoe, a splint or a dressing, and who applied it. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a patient whose foot was injured in a fall is moved by a trained team. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, and any period or threshold named here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, the metatarsals carry the weight of the step and the toes finish that step, so a small break there changes the way a person walks and can cost months of pain and altered gait. The findings to keep are swelling over the top of the foot, bruising that appears late, tenderness on one spot along a metatarsal, tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal after a twisted ankle, and the dull ache in the ball of the foot that comes with marching. The sequence is always the same, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status and record it before and after every intervention, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. A deformed toe or foot is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, force is not a technique, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and reduction is not attempted when the joint is shattered, when a fragment is caught in it, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open, or when the diagnosis is unclear. A strapped toe is examined together with the neighbor it is strapped to, and the constricting strap or shoe is released within the limits of the local protocol when a toe becomes pale, cold or numb, when pain increases, or when the foot becomes tense and shiny. The foot is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm and referred urgently, and the first metatarsal, the fifth metatarsal at the junction of the shaft and the base, and every open or crushed injury go to the orthopedic surgeon. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 39 — Cervical Spine Injuries

The neck is the narrowest and the most mobile part of the spine, and it carries the heaviest load per unit of bone in the body, which is the head. It lets the head turn, nod and look up, and for that freedom it gives up the protection the ribs and the trunk muscles give the rest of the spine. Inside it lies the spinal cord, with almost no room to spare around it. An injury here can kill within minutes by stopping the breathing, or leave a patient paralyzed from the neck down while the skin stays unbroken. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows that order for the bones of the neck. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The cervical spine is built from seven bones stacked in a curve that bows gently forward. The first is a ring rather than a block, and it carries the skull the way a hand carries a bowl. The second has a peg that points upward into that ring, and that peg is the pivot on which the head turns, which is why a break of the second bone is so often an injury of turning. The remaining bones have a body in front, a disk between one body and the next, and small joints at the back that guide each segment on the one below. Strong ligaments run along the front of the bodies and along the back of the canal, and one runs inside the canal behind the cord, where it limits how far the neck can bend forward. Because the neck moves more than any other part of the spine, it depends on those ligaments more than any other part does, and a torn ligament can be as dangerous as a broken bone.

Within the canal lies the spinal cord, and at every level a nerve root leaves the cord and passes out between two bones toward the arm. The cord carries the fibers that move and feel the arms and the hands, the fibers that serve the trunk and the legs, and the fibers that drive the diaphragm, the muscle of breathing. Those fibers for the diaphragm leave the cord high in the neck, so an injury at the top of the neck can stop the breathing while the heart is still beating, and an injury lower down can leave the breathing weak and the cough useless. Through channels in the bones pass the arteries that carry blood to the back of the brain, so a break that tears one of those arteries can cause a stroke hours or days after an injury that looked minor at the time. The cord is therefore not the only structure at risk in the neck, and a responder who thinks only of the bones will miss the vessels.

The mechanism of injury is the first thing that should raise the suspicion of an injury to the neck, and the useful question is what happened to the head rather than what happened to the neck. Any sudden change in the speed of the body while the head keeps moving bends the neck past the range its ligaments allow, and the cord is squeezed between the bones in front of it and the ligament behind it. A collision between vehicles, a fall from a height, a dive into shallow water, a direct blow to the head, being struck by a vehicle as a pedestrian, a heavy object falling onto the head, a tackle in a contact sport and a hanging are the mechanisms taught as significant. A fall from a height greater than 1 meter belongs on that list in many services, though that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and countries differ. The violent mechanisms come to mind first, and they are not the only ones.

A fall from standing height can break the neck of an older patient whose bone has lost density, and a fall from a bed or a chair can do the same in a patient whose spine has been weakened by disease or by a medicine that thins the bone. The neck of a patient whose canal is already narrow may be injured by a movement that would leave a healthy young person unhurt, and such a patient may feel a dull ache rather than a sharp pain. Any patient who has been found unconscious, and any patient who cannot give a clear account of the injury because of intoxication, a head injury, a young age or a language the responder does not share, is treated as having an injured neck until someone qualified to do so has cleared it. The rule that follows is short, and it is that the absence of neck pain is not the absence of an injury to the neck.

What the responder looks for in the neck is tenderness in the midline at the back, felt with the patient lying still while the examiner presses gently on each bony point. Pain on any movement, muscle spasm that holds the head to one side, and a step or a gap felt between two spines all suggest a broken or a displaced segment. The patient may hold the head with both hands to keep it still, a striking sign when it is seen. Bruising, a scrape or a wound of the face and the scalp points to a blow that reached the head, and blood behind the eardrum may be the only mark of a break at the base of the skull. None of these findings is reliable on its own, and several may be absent in a patient with a serious injury. Tenderness and the story of the mechanism together decide whether the neck is treated as injured, and that decision belongs to a clinician rather than to a single sign.

Some patients describe a brief numbness, a tingling or a burning in the hands or the feet immediately after the injury which has gone by the time the responder arrives. Such a symptom warns that the canal was narrow or that the cord was touched, even if it lasted only a moment, and it changes the way the patient must be handled. The same is true of a weakness that lasted for a few minutes and then passed, and of an odd feeling in the hands that the patient dismisses as the effect of landing on an arm. The responder records those words as exactly as possible, because the patient may not repeat them to the next clinician, and a symptom that was never written down cannot be used later. A patient who reports such an episode is treated as injured and referred for assessment, and the meaning of the episode belongs to the clinician who examines the cord.

Assessment begins with the danger to the rescuer and then with the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The airway is the first place where an injury of the neck changes what a responder does, because the usual way of opening an airway tips the head back and moves the neck. The trained first responder and the paramedic open the airway with the jaw thrust, which moves the jaw instead of the neck, while a second person holds the head in the position found, and the lay first aider supports the head and follows the dispatcher. Breathing may be shallow and the cough weak when the cord has been injured, so the chest is watched rather than assumed. Circulation may show the strange pattern of a slow pulse with warm, dry skin after a cord injury, which is not the same as the shock of blood loss and is not treated as though it were.

Stabilization of the neck means that the head, the neck and the trunk are kept in one line and moved as a single block, and the position preserved is the position in which the patient was found. The trained responder holds the head with both hands, without pulling, without turning and without straightening, and keeps holding until the patient is secured or the spine has been cleared. That hold is called manual in-line stabilization, and it is a team skill learned under supervision and practiced, because one responder who tries to hold a head while moving a patient will fail. Traction is never applied by hand in the field, since a pull on the neck may distract a broken segment and stretch the cord. The lay first aider is taught to tell the patient not to move, to support the head gently and to wait. A child is not held in the same way as an adult, because a child's head is large in proportion to the trunk and the padding that keeps the neck in line differs accordingly.

A rigid collar is a device that surrounds the neck and limits some of its movement, and it is applied by a trained responder, a paramedic, a nurse or a physician working within the local protocol. The collar does not remove movement, it does not replace the hands of a trained responder while a patient is being moved, and it does not clear the spine. A collar of the wrong size is worse than none, because one that is too small fails to support the head and one that is too large pulls the neck into extension, and both errors can move a broken segment. A collar that is too tight presses on the veins of the neck, which raises the pressure inside the head, and it presses on the skin, which can cause a sore within hours in a patient who cannot feel it. The collar is checked after it is applied, the skin beneath it is inspected whenever the patient is turned, and it is adjusted or removed only by someone the local protocol authorizes. The responder who applies a collar records the neurovascular examination before and after, because a change that was not recorded before cannot be attributed afterwards.

The long board is a tool for moving a patient a short distance out of a vehicle or away from a hazard, and it is not a bed. A patient left on a hard board for a long journey suffers pain, pressure sores and difficulty breathing, and many services remove the board as soon as the patient is on a mattress, according to their own rules. Turning a patient with a suspected injury of the neck requires a team working on a count, with one person holding the head and enough hands to keep the trunk in line, and that maneuver is learned under supervision. A helmet is left in place unless it blocks the airway or prevents care, and removing one takes 2 trained people, a figure to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Every one of these acts is a team act, and no single manual handling technique is safe when it is used alone.

The neurovascular examination of a patient with a suspected injury of the neck examines the cord, the nerve roots and the arteries, and it is performed before any intervention and repeated after it. The examiner asks the patient to shrug the shoulders, to lift the arms, to bend the elbows, to extend the wrists, to grip the fingers and to spread them, and compares the two sides, because a difference is more informative than any single grade. The legs are tested in the same way, and the level of feeling is mapped by asking where a light touch is felt, beginning at the shoulders and moving down the arms, the chest, the abdomen and the legs. The lowest level at which feeling is normal is recorded in a sentence, with the time, and the same sentence is repeated after every intervention. Reflexes and the internal examination of the bowel belong to a clinician and are not field tests, and a responder says plainly that an examination was not performed rather than guessing at it.

Immobilization here means preventing movement of the injured part and of the segments above and below it, and in the neck that means the head, the neck, the trunk and the pelvis move together or do not move at all. The head is supported in the position in which it was found, with the collar, with blocks or rolled towels on each side, and with the trunk secured to whatever surface the patient is lying on, as the protocol directs. Padding is placed behind the head of a child and, in some adults, under the shoulders, because the shape of the body decides where the gap lies. A deformed neck is supported as it lies and is never straightened in the field, because the cord and the vessels lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Splints, collars and boards are applied by trained responders, paramedics, nurses and physicians within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician or the spine surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required.

Imaging is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it, and it confirms what the examination has already suggested rather than replacing the examination. A radiograph of the neck is usually taken in 3 views, one of them through the open mouth so that the second bone can be seen, and the junction between the neck and the chest often needs a special position, so the views are local practice to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Computed tomography shows the bones in fine detail, and in many services it has replaced the plain radiograph as the first study for an adult with a significant mechanism, because it finds breaks that a radiograph hides. Magnetic resonance imaging shows the cord, the disks, the ligaments and the blood within the canal, and it answers the question when a patient has a deficit and the bones look normal. A responder never orders imaging, never interprets it and never tells a patient that a scan was normal, because the spine is cleared only by someone qualified to clear it.

The second bone of the neck deserves special attention, because the peg that points upward from it is the pivot of all turning of the head and it has a fragile blood supply. The peg may break near its tip, at its base where it joins the body of the bone, or through the body itself, and the break at the base is the one that most often fails to heal because the supply to that part is poor. In an older patient the mechanism is usually an extension of the neck in a fall, and the injury may cause little more than a dull ache at the top of the neck and a headache at the back of the head. The examination is unreliable here, because tenderness may be vague and the nerve findings may be normal, so the diagnosis is made by good imaging rather than by the hands. The care of that break may be a rigid collar, a special device that holds the head with a ring and pins, or an operation, and the choice depends on the pattern, the age of the patient and the state of the bone. All of those treatments are decided and performed by a spine surgeon in a hospital, and the techniques belong to supervised clinical training and never to a book.

The neck of an older patient is often already narrowed before any injury happens, because the disks lose height, the joints at the back grow spurs and the ligaments inside the canal thicken with age. That patient's cord has less room than the cord of a young person, and a movement that would be harmless in youth can bruise it. The cord is pinched between the spur in front of it and the folded ligament behind it, and the deficit that results is often strange, in that the arms are weaker than the legs, the hands burn, the fingers are clumsy and the bladder may fail. The radiograph may show no fracture at all, and a responder who relies on it will conclude that the neck is fine while the cord is injured. The deficit can worsen over the first hours and days, so such a patient is referred urgently to a hospital with imaging of the cord and a team able to watch the breathing and the blood pressure. The care of the airway, of the blood pressure and of the cord belongs to the physician and to the team in the intensive care unit, and the responder's part is to recognize the pattern, protect the neck and move the patient quickly.

A cord can also be injured when no bone is broken and no joint is displaced, and this possibility is why a normal radiograph is never allowed to end the assessment. In young children the spine is elastic and the cord is not, so the bones may bend and spring back while the cord is stretched, crushed or torn, and the injury may be present with normal images. In adults a disk may burst into the canal, a small vessel inside the canal may bleed and press on the cord, or an artery that supplies the cord may be injured. The findings to look for are weakness, numbness, tingling, a loss of the ability to move the arms or the legs, difficulty breathing, and a loss of control of the bladder or the bowel. A child who will not move the neck, who cries when picked up or who is unusually quiet after a fall deserves the same caution as an adult with an obvious fracture. The responder does not decide whether the cord is injured but instead recognizes that it might be, protects the neck and sends the patient to a place where the cord can be examined.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and in the neck that means after the collar is applied, after the patient is moved, after any attempt to open the airway and after every turn. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison and not the single measurement carries the meaning. The findings that stop a responder are a falling level of consciousness, breathing that becomes weaker or noisier, new weakness or numbness in the arms or the legs, a patient who can no longer lift an arm that moved a moment before, and pain that increases instead of settling. A collar that has become too tight, a strap that presses on the chest and a board that has become unbearable all cause harm of their own, so the device is checked at each stage. A patient who vomits while lying flat is at risk of drawing the vomit into the lungs, and turning that patient is a team act performed within the local protocol with the head, the neck and the trunk kept in line. A patient who is losing cord function is referred urgently, and the responder does not wait for a second examination to confirm what the first one found.

Referral begins with the recognition that an injury of the neck cannot be managed where the patient lies, and the destination is chosen at the same time. A patient with a nerve deficit, a displaced break, a break of the second bone, an unstable neck or a neck that cannot be cleared is taken to a hospital where a spine surgeon, an intensive care unit and imaging of the cord are available. The receiving team is told before arrival what happened, what was found, what was done and what is still uncertain, in that order, so that the next team continues a story instead of starting a new one. The spine is not cleared over the telephone and is not cleared by the responder, however confident the examination appears. A patient with a normal examination but a dangerous mechanism is transferred for assessment rather than sent home, and that decision belongs to a clinician who has the imaging and a validated rule. A collar or a supporting hold is a precaution and not a diagnosis, and the symptoms that should bring the patient back are explained in words the family can repeat.

Definitive treatment begins with the question of whether the spine is stable, and everything that follows depends on the answer. A stable injury may be treated with a rigid collar or a molded brace, worn for a period that the treating clinician sets and that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the skin beneath it is inspected regularly, because a patient with altered sensation may not feel a sore forming. Some injuries are treated with traction, which is a gentle and continuous pull on the head meant to restore the alignment of the bones or to hold it while healing proceeds, and it is applied only in a hospital by a qualified team with imaging and monitoring at the bedside. Some injuries need an operation to take pressure off the cord and to join one bone to the next with grafted bone and metal devices, so that the neck becomes stable without external support. Those techniques, and the reduction of a displaced segment, are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no chapter of this course teaches the technique itself. Pain relief and every medicine are chosen by the prescriber under the local protocol, and neither the substance nor the amount can be taken from this book.

Throughout the prehospital phase the aim is not to make the injury better but to keep it from becoming worse. The patient is kept still, kept warm, kept informed and kept covered, because cold worsens clotting, raises the work of breathing and makes an agitated patient fight the people who are helping. A patient who pulls at the collar and tries to sit up needs calm words and a plan rather than force, and the plan is made within the local protocol by the team leader, because a struggle moves the neck more than a controlled turn. The responder does not examine the neck by asking the patient to move it, does not test the strength of the neck, and does not remove the collar unless the protocol allows it and the spine has been assessed. Where a patient must be moved urgently because of fire, traffic or another hazard, the move is made as a team with the head controlled. Every number named in this chapter is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services differ in their equipment and in their rules.

To summarize, the neck protects the cord in a canal with almost no reserve, and an injury there can stop the breathing or paralyze a patient while the skin stays intact. Suspect it after any violent mechanism, after a fall in an older or a weakened patient, after a blow to the head, and in any patient who cannot give a clear account of what happened, because the absence of neck pain proves nothing. Follow the sequence in order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and name the provider level for every act. The trained team holds the head in the position found without traction, applies the collar and the board, and keeps the patient warm, while the lay first aider supports the head and never straightens a deformed neck. Record the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, reassess after each one, and escalate at once when the breathing weakens, when new weakness or numbness appears or when the level of consciousness falls, and the emergency service of the area is called for any patient who cannot be moved safely by those present.
