A normal radiograph does not exclude an injury of the cord, especially in a child, in an older patient whose canal is narrow, and in a patient with a broken peg of the second bone. Reduction, traction and the fitting of specialist devices are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique is never taken from a book. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 40 — Thoracic and Lumbar Spine Injuries

The thoracic and the lumbar spine are the part of the skeleton that carries the weight of the body above the pelvis, and an injury there can change a life more completely than any broken limb. The thoracic spine is the segment to which the ribs are attached, and the lumbar spine is the heavier segment below it. A fracture in this region may be painful and obvious, or it may produce no more than a tenderness that a tired examiner misses at the end of a long shift. Because the spinal cord and the nerves that leave it travel inside this column, the same force that breaks a bone can also interrupt the messages that move a leg or empty a bladder. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

A vertebra is built around a block of bone in front, called the body, and an arch behind it, and that arch encloses a canal through which the spinal cord and its nerves pass down the body. Behind the canal the arch closes into a spinous process, which is the bony point a hand feels in the middle of the back, and on each side of it lie the facet joints, where one vertebra meets the one above and the one below. The bodies of the thoracic vertebrae are smaller and are held by the ribs, which give the chest its stiffness, while the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae are larger because they carry more weight. The discs between the bodies are cushions that let the column bend and absorb load, and the ligaments along the front and the back of the bodies hold the whole stack together. This arrangement explains why a healthy spine bends and twists without harm and why the same spine fails when the force arrives faster than the tissues can yield.

The spinal cord does not run to the bottom of the column, because it ends in the upper part of the lumbar spine, and below that level the canal holds a bundle of nerves that continues downward like a horse's tail. That bundle is the reason an injury at the top of the lumbar spine can injure the cord itself, while an injury lower down injures the nerves of the bundle one by one, and the two produce different pictures. The cord usually ends somewhere between the lowest thoracic vertebra and the second lumbar vertebra, though the exact level differs from person to person, and any figure offered in teaching must be confirmed against the current anatomy text and the local protocol. The nerves of the bundle supply the muscles that move the feet and the ankles, the sensation of the saddle area, and the control of the bladder and the bowel. This is why a patient who cannot feel the inner thighs or who cannot pass urine after a fall from a height is treated as a surgical emergency rather than as a patient with back pain.

Two mechanisms produce most of the injuries in this region, and the history often names one of them before the examination begins. The first is a fall from a height, in which the patient lands on the feet or on the buttocks and the force travels straight up the column, so the vertebra that fails is usually one of the junctional vertebrae where a stiff segment meets a mobile one. The second is a flexion injury, in which the column is bent forward beyond what the ligaments allow, as happens in a collision when a seated body is thrown forward against a belt or when a heavy load falls across the back. A third mechanism combines both, bending the spine and then loading it, and those injuries tend to be the most unstable because more than one column of the spine has failed. The mechanism is not a diagnosis, but a force arriving from above and along the line of the column raises the suspicion of an injury to a vertebral body even when the patient complains only of a sore back.

What the responder looks for in this region is simple, and it must be looked for on purpose. The patient is asked where the pain is, and the answer is often a single point that the patient can cover with one finger, which is more useful than a vague ache across the whole back. The examiner looks at the line of the spinous processes from the side and from above, and looks for a step, which is a place where one bony point sits out of line with the ones above and below it, and for a gap, which is a space where a bony point should be. Swelling, bruising and a tightening of the muscles beside the column are common, and the muscles may stiffen so much that the usual curve of the back is lost. Tenderness is found by pressing gently along the line of the spines and beside it, and by pressing on the pelvis and on the chest to see whether the pain is reproduced from a distance.

None of those findings is reliable on its own, and a listener who trusts one of them will miss an injury. A step in the line of the spines may be absent in a fracture that has collapsed evenly, and it may be present in a patient whose spine was curved before the injury. Tenderness may be masked by another painful injury, by alcohol, by a medicine that dulls pain, or by a patient who is confused and cannot say what hurts. A constructed illustration may help, in which a patient in their thirties who fell a short distance from a ladder, who walked to the ambulance and who has no numbness or weakness still has a fracture of a vertebral body that only imaging will show. The lesson is not that such a patient can be sent home, but that the absence of a dramatic sign is not evidence of an uninjured spine.

The assessment of a patient who may have injured this region begins with the same steps as any other trauma, which are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The reason is not a formality but a fact about energy, because the same fall that breaks a vertebra often breaks ribs, bruises a lung, tears the spleen or the liver, or fractures the pelvis, and any of those can kill before the spine is considered. A patient who is short of breath, whose chest does not move evenly on both sides or whose abdomen is tender and tight is treated for that problem first while the spine is protected at the same time. Life comes before limb and limb comes before the fine detail of a bony injury, so the examination of the back waits until the patient is stable enough to be turned. The lay first aider keeps the patient still and calls for help, while the trained responder and the paramedic assess within the procedures their service authorizes.

When the patient can speak, the history is taken in a fixed order and written down, because the answers decide how much caution the rest of the care requires. The questions are how far the patient fell, onto what surface, in what position the body landed, whether the patient could move the arms and the legs afterwards, and whether the patient stood up and walked. It matters whether there has been back pain or back surgery before, whether the bones are weakened by age or by disease, and whether a medicine that thins the bone has been taken for a long time. A constructed illustration is a patient in their seventies who slipped on a wet floor at home, who felt a sudden pain in the middle of the back and who has no weakness at all, because a bone that has lost density can break under a force that would leave a younger spine unhurt. Every figure in that history, including the height of the fall, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The burst fracture is the pattern for which this region is best known, and its name describes what has happened rather than how severe it is. In a burst fracture the vertebral body is broken into several parts by a force that arrives along the line of the column, and the fragments are pushed outward in all directions, including backward into the canal where the nerves lie. It follows a fall from a height or a heavy load more often than a simple fall on the level, and it may be present in a patient who has no neurologic deficit at all, which is why the examination alone cannot rule it out. When a fragment presses on the cord or on the nerves of the bundle, the patient may have numbness, weakness or a change in the control of the bladder, and those findings make the injury a surgical emergency. Computed tomography is the study that shows the fragments and the canal, and it is requested by a clinician trained to interpret it, while the responder protects the spine and does not try to judge stability from the story alone.

Another pattern follows a flexion force, in which the upper part of the body is thrown forward while the lower part is held, and the injury runs through the back of the spine rather than the front. A seat belt across the abdomen, the handlebars of a bicycle or a heavy weight falling across the back can each produce it, and the injury may open the back of the spine like a book, tearing the ligaments that hold the vertebrae together. Because the tear is in soft tissue, a radiograph taken soon after the injury may look almost normal, and a patient who is walking with pain may be sent away before the imaging that shows the injury is arranged. A fracture of this kind is treated as unstable even when the bones look nearly lined up, because the ligaments that would resist movement have failed. The names given to these patterns belong in the specialist's report, and the task of the responder is to recognize a mechanism that could have produced one and to protect the spine while help is arranged.

The neurovascular examination of this region is recorded before any intervention and repeated after it, and here it has two parts, one for the cord and its nerves and one for the limbs. The examiner asks the patient to move the ankles, the toes and the feet against resistance and compares the two sides, because a difference between them is more telling than an absolute weakness. Sensation is tested with a light touch on both sides of the body from the chest downward, and the patient is asked whether the feeling is the same on the left and on the right and whether the saddle area between the legs feels normal. The tone of the muscles and the reflexes are examined by a clinician, because a limb that is floppy and a limb that is stiff point to different levels of trouble. The most intimate parts of that examination, which include the sensation around the anus and the tightening of the anal muscle, are performed by a clinician, with a colleague of the same gender as the patient present when local protocol requires it, and they are never performed by a lay first aider.

The findings that make an injury of this region an emergency are worth naming slowly, because a patient may describe them in ordinary words rather than medical ones. A patient may say that the legs feel heavy or that one foot drags, that the inner sides of the thighs feel numb as though a band were drawn around them, or that the saddle area has lost its feeling altogether. A patient may say that passing urine has become difficult, that the bladder feels full but will not empty, or that control of the bowel has been lost, and any of those statements is treated as a nerve emergency. Back pain that is worse at night, pain that wakes the patient from sleep and a loss of weight without a reason are findings that suggest a cause other than injury and are referred for assessment. No responder waits for the picture to become complete, because the nerves of the bundle are compressed from the moment of the injury and time is nerve rather than muscle.

Stabilization of a patient with a possible injury in this region is mostly a matter of restraint, and the first act is not to move the patient at all unless there is a reason that cannot wait. A fire, a falling wall, a rising flood or a patient who is not breathing are such reasons, and in every other case the patient is kept in the position found until a team with the right equipment arrives. The head is held in a neutral position by two trained hands when a trained responder is present, but this is not a technique that one person can perform alone while also assessing or moving the patient, and no lone method of handling is safe. A patient lying on the back, on the side or in a heap on the ground is left as found, with the body supported so that the head, the trunk and the pelvis stay in one line. Covering the patient, insulating them from the ground and replacing wet clothing with dry covering are part of this step, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort.

Moving a patient with a possible spinal injury is a team task, and the number of hands required is decided by the equipment and the local protocol rather than by the strength of one rescuer. The aim is that the head, the trunk and the pelvis move together without twisting, and that the patient is not dragged, folded or pulled by the arms. A scoop stretcher, a vacuum mattress or a rigid board is chosen according to what the service provides, and a rigid board is a tool for lifting and for the short distance to the stretcher rather than a bed for a long journey, because pressure on the skin and discomfort increase the longer a patient lies on it. Padding is placed under the head and the shoulders so that the neck is not forced into a bend, and the older patient with a curved upper spine needs more padding rather than less. Straps are checked twice, once before the move and once after it, and the patient is told what is about to happen at each stage, because fear makes muscles rigid and rigid muscles move a broken spine.

Immobilization of the thoracic and the lumbar spine is not the same problem as immobilization of the neck, and a device that is right for one region may be useless or harmful for the other. The whole column is kept in one line by supporting the body from the head to the pelvis, so the head is held, the trunk is secured and the legs are kept straight and together, and a collar alone does not immobilize the thoracic or the lumbar spine. A collar, side blocks and straps are applied by the trained responder and the paramedic within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and the decision that a patient no longer needs a device belongs to the clinician who clears the spine. The lay first aider supports the head and the body with the hands and with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm and still, and waits. Any device is checked for tightness and for pressure on the skin, because a strap that is right at the moment it is applied can become too tight as the patient swells.

Some patients make every part of this care harder, and the responder should recognize them before the move rather than during it. A patient who is agitated, confused, intoxicated or frightened may fight the hands that are holding the head, and such a patient is treated as having an unstable spine while the cause of the agitation is also assessed, because head injury and low oxygen are common reasons for it. A child has a larger head in proportion to the body, so a board that fits an adult tilts the young neck forward unless padding is placed beneath the shoulders, and the spine of a child also bends rather than breaks in some injuries. A pregnant patient is positioned according to local protocol and with the advice of the receiving team, because the precaution that protects the spine may also reduce the flow of blood to the womb. An older patient whose spine has stiffened with age breaks it in a way that resembles a long bone rather than a stack of vertebrae, and that injury is missed when the mechanism seems too minor to cause harm.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it rather than by the responder who protects the patient. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken from the front and from the side, and it may be repeated with the patient turned in a way the local protocol allows so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden. Computed tomography shows the fine detail of the bone and of the canal, and it is the study that shows a burst fracture and its fragments most clearly. Magnetic resonance imaging is the study for the cord, the discs and the ligaments, and it is used when the neurologic findings and the plain images do not explain one another. The trained responder does not decide which study is needed and the lay first aider never orders or interprets an image, but both help by reporting the mechanism and the findings they recorded, because those decide what is asked of the imaging.

Reassessment after every intervention is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment, and in this region it has a particular meaning. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what carries the value rather than any single measurement. The patient is asked again about the movement of the legs, about feeling in the saddle area and about the ability to pass urine, because a change in any of those is the finding that stops the responder. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse and pain, and a strap is loosened or a device changed only within the limits of the local protocol and by someone authorized to do it. Pain that rises instead of settling, a new numbness, a new weakness and a patient who becomes restless without a reason are all findings that prompt urgent referral, and the patient is kept warm throughout.

Referral begins with the recognition that some patients cannot be cared for where they lie, and a suspected injury of the thoracic or the lumbar spine is one of them. A patient with a step in the line of the spines, a neurologic finding, a high-energy mechanism with pain in the middle of the back, a known weakness of the bone or a fall from more than standing height is referred to a facility with imaging, a spine service, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The receiving team is told the mechanism, the level of the pain, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention and any change in the condition of the patient, because a story that continues is safer than a story that starts again. Transfer is arranged by the service that owns the decision, and a patient who must wait is kept warm, still and observed rather than left alone. A patient with no pain, no tenderness and no neurologic finding may still need imaging, and the decision about how much imaging is enough belongs to the clinician who examines them.

Definitive treatment of an injury in this region ranges from a brace to an operation, and every decision belongs to a specialist working within the local protocol. A brace holds a stable injury in a position that allows it to heal, and it must be made and fitted by someone trained to do it, because a brace that is too loose does not hold and one that is too tight injures the skin over a bony point. An operation may be needed to take pressure off the cord or the nerves and to hold the bones in line with metal devices while they heal, and its timing depends on the neurologic findings and on the general condition of the patient. Traction may be used for some injuries of the cervical spine to hold the column in line with a gentle and continuous pull, and it is applied only in a unit with the equipment and the staff to watch the patient. None of these acts is learned from a book, so they are described here only as what they are meant to achieve, who performs them and what can go wrong, and the technique itself belongs to supervised clinical training.

Complications in this region arrive in two directions, from the injury and from the care, and a listener should be able to name both. The injury itself can leave a patient with a weak leg, a numb saddle area or a bladder that no longer empties, and those losses may be permanent if the pressure on the nerves is not relieved in time. The care can add harm when a patient is moved with the column twisted, when a device presses on the skin for hours, or when a fracture that no one suspected is loaded by an eager examination. For that reason a patient with a suspected injury here is never asked to sit up, bend forward or lift a leg while lying on the back, the back is never massaged and a hot pack is never applied. The findings that make a responder stop and ask for more help are a new weakness, a new numbness, a loss of bladder control and pain that increases, and anyone who is unsure of the next step stops and calls for the person qualified to decide.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and in this region they carry more weight than in almost any other. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the patient was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention and every change in the condition of the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order. The spine is treated as unstable until it has been cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and clearing it means an examination, a decision about imaging and a record of that decision rather than the disappearance of the pain. The lay first aider, the trained responder, the paramedic, the nurse and the physician all write down what they saw and did, because a finding that was not recorded before a device was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Any number spoken in that handover, including a time or a distance, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, the thoracic and the lumbar spine carry the weight of the body, and an injury there threatens the nerves as much as it threatens the bone. The patient is assessed in the usual order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because a broken spine rarely comes alone and life comes before limb. The responder looks for the tender point, for a step or a gap in the line of the spines and for a mechanism that fits a fall from a height or a flexion force, and remembers that a burst fracture may leave the patient walking and that the absence of a dramatic sign proves nothing. The neurovascular examination is recorded before any device is applied and repeated afterwards, and it includes the movement of the legs, the feeling of the saddle area and the control of the bladder and the bowel. The patient is not moved unless there is a danger that cannot wait, the head, the trunk and the pelvis are kept in one line by a trained team using the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes, and no lone method of handling is safe. Reduction, traction, casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no part of their technique belongs in a book. The spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, every number in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the patient is kept warm, observed and handed over with the whole story written down. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 41 — Spinal Neurological Assessment

A suspected injury of the spine is the one injury in which the broken bone matters less than the question of whether the nervous system inside it still works, because a vertebra will heal and a spinal cord will not. A patient may arrive walking and talking and lose the use of a hand an hour later, and only an examination repeated in the same order will notice that change. This chapter follows the sequence this course uses everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The examination is a clinical skill, so this chapter says what is looked for, why it matters and who may perform each act, and it does not teach a technique that belongs to supervised training. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country in which you work.

The spinal cord lies inside a canal formed by the vertebrae, and the column of bone and the cord within it must be thought of and examined together. In an adult the cord ends near the first or the second lumbar vertebra, and below that point the canal carries a bundle of nerve roots called the cauda equina. Each segment of the cord gives rise to roots that leave between the vertebrae, and each root supplies a strip of skin and a group of muscles, so the bone that is broken and the cord that has suffered are not always at the same level. The cord can also be injured while the bone remains whole, and in a child it may be hurt with nothing abnormal on a radiograph, a pattern called spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality.

The decision to treat a spine as unstable begins with the mechanism of injury and with what the patient cannot tell you. A fall from a height, a dive into shallow water, a vehicle collision, a crushing blow to the trunk and a fall in sport all carry enough energy to break the spine in a patient who feels comfortable. In an older adult a fall from standing height is enough, particularly when the head is thrown back and the neck is forced into extension. The patient who is intoxicated, confused, unconscious or distracted by a painful injury elsewhere cannot report pain or weakness reliably, and is treated as having an unstable spine until someone qualified clears it. The lay first aider does not make this judgment alone but suspects the injury, keeps the head and trunk still, and calls for a team.

Assessment begins before the spine is touched, and it begins with the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Life comes before limb, because a blocked airway and a failing circulation kill in minutes while a damaged cord cannot be repaired by any hurry at the roadside. The disability step is the first neurological observation, and it records the level of consciousness, the movement of the limbs, and the size and the reaction of the pupils. Only then does the examination turn to the spine, and it turns to it with the neck already supported, because an assessment that moves an unstable spine is part of the injury rather than part of the care. The lay first aider performs no formal examination of the spine but keeps the patient still and warm and calls for help.

Stabilization means that the head, the neck and the trunk are kept in the position in which they were found and are moved as one unit. No traction is applied to the neck and no attempt is made to straighten it, because a pull on the head is a force delivered to an injured column, and that technique belongs to supervised clinical practice. The trained first responder and the paramedic hold the head with both hands, or apply the collar, the blocks and the straps their service authorizes, saying aloud what they are doing so that the team moves together. A patient on the ground is turned by a team using the method the local protocol describes, and no single responder performs a lone manual handling technique, because one pair of hands cannot control a spine. The patient is then insulated from the ground and kept warm, since cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding that was not written before a collar was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. In a suspected spinal injury the first examination is whatever the patient can do at the moment of first contact, taken where the patient lies rather than after the patient has been moved. Numbness, tingling, weakness and the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier are the findings that matter, recorded in the words the patient used. Each finding is written with the time at which it was made, since a weakness noticed at one moment and recorded later has lost the interval that would have shown how fast the injury is moving. The physician interprets the record, while the responder at every level contributes to it by repeating the observations and reporting them unchanged.

The examination is carried out with the patient lying still, the examiner working from the side so that nothing is leaned across the face or the chest. Gloves, eye protection and the other items of personal protective equipment are worn whenever there may be blood or body fluid, because a rescuer who becomes a patient helps no one. The patient is told what will be done before it is done, consent is asked for each part, a chaperone is present for the genital or the anal region, and the patient is covered apart from the area being tested. The limbs are then examined in a fixed order, with the arms before the legs in most protocols, and the examiner compares the two sides at every step, because a limb is judged against its partner rather than against a memory of what is normal.

Sensation is tested with a light touch and with a pinprick, and the two are not the same test, because one travels in the pathways that carry position and vibration and the other in those that carry pain and temperature. The skin is mapped into strips called dermatomes, each supplied mainly by the root of one spinal segment, so a strip of altered sensation points toward the segment that is injured. That map is drawn from averages rather than sharp borders, because the strips overlap and the arrangement differs between one person and another. The patient's eyes are closed and the answers are given in words, such as sharp or dull, which even a patient who cannot use the word pain can supply. The sharp end is never pressed hard enough to break the skin, and the examiner records what the patient feels rather than what the map predicts.

A few landmarks let a listener place a level without a chart. The top of the shoulder marks the fourth cervical segment, the outer upper arm the fifth, the thumb and the index finger the sixth, the middle finger the seventh, and the little finger the eighth. The inner side of the arm at the armpit marks the second thoracic segment, the nipple line the fourth thoracic, the umbilicus the tenth thoracic, and the groin the first lumbar. On the leg, the front of the thigh marks the third lumbar segment, the inner leg above the knee the fourth, the top of the foot the fifth, and the outer foot and the little toe the first sacral. The skin around the anus is supplied by the lowest sacral roots, and these landmarks are approximate in every patient and never replace testing the person in front of you.

The sensory level is the lowest segment at which sensation is normal on both sides, and it is an estimate rather than a measurement, written for the right side and for the left side separately because the two may differ. The word level is used in three senses, since the level of the bone injury is what imaging shows, the sensory level is the lowest segment with normal sensation and the motor level is the lowest segment with normal power, and the three do not always agree. A level that has moved upward since the last examination is one of the most urgent observations in this course, because it means the injury is extending toward the segments that supply the diaphragm. A level that has moved downward often signals recovery, but it is not a reason to relax the observation.

Movement is examined segment by segment, and the examiner tests the key movement each segment supplies rather than every muscle in the limb. Strength is described on a scale that runs from 0, which is no movement at all, to 5, which is movement against full resistance, and the useful middle of that scale is described in words. The words are movement that can be seen but cannot lift the part against gravity, movement that can lift against gravity but not against resistance, and movement that acts against resistance but is weaker than the other side. The examiner asks the patient to perform the movement and then resists it gently, and never forces a joint through a range the patient cannot achieve. A painful limb may be moved weakly for that reason alone, and the record should say so, because pain and weakness are different findings with different meanings.

In the arm, bending the elbow is supplied mainly by the fifth and the sixth cervical segments, straightening the wrist by the sixth, straightening the elbow by the seventh, bending the fingers by the eighth, and spreading the fingers by the first thoracic segment. In the leg, bending the hip is supplied mainly by the second lumbar segment, straightening the knee by the third, lifting the foot upward by the fourth, lifting the great toe by the fifth, and pushing the foot downward by the first sacral segment. The movement of the diaphragm belongs to the third, the fourth and the fifth cervical segments, so an injury high in the neck threatens breathing, and such a patient is watched for a weak cough and a quiet voice. The trained responder supports ventilation within the procedures the service authorizes, while the physician decides whether a definitive airway is needed.

The single most useful question in the whole examination is whether the lowest sacral segments still work, because their function separates a complete injury from an incomplete one. Those segments are tested in three ways: by sensation around the anus, by the pressure the patient feels when a finger presses deeply in the anal canal, and by a voluntary contraction of the anal sphincter. Any one of the three that is present means the injury is incomplete, and an incomplete injury may recover useful function far more often than a complete one. When all three are absent the injury is described as complete at that moment, and the word complete describes the examination rather than the future. The finding is written with the time and the name of the examiner, because prognosis and the choice of treatment will turn on it, and a test that is omitted is not a negative test.

The examination that gives this information is a rectal examination, and it belongs to a clinician or a trained examiner acting within the local protocol, not to a first aider and not to a responder at the roadside. It is performed with gloves, with a lubricant permitted by the service, with a chaperone present, and only after the patient has been told what will be done and has agreed. The examiner notes whether sensation is present, whether the patient feels deep pressure and whether the sphincter contracts around the finger, and each observation is recorded separately. A patient may refuse, and a refusal is respected and written down rather than argued with. The absence of the examination is recorded as an omission and never as a normal finding, and the local protocol decides whether it is done at the scene or deferred to the receiving facility.

Immediately after a severe injury the cord may stop working without being destroyed, a state called spinal shock, in which the limbs are floppy and the reflexes are absent below the level of the injury. In that state the examination cannot tell a complete injury from an incomplete one, because the functions that would answer the question are temporarily silent. The end of the state is marked by the return of the reflex that contracts the anal sphincter, and that test belongs to a clinician. Until the reflex returns, repeated examinations are recorded in the same words so that a comparison remains possible, and no conclusion about completeness is drawn from an absent reflex alone. A patient in spinal shock may lose control of the bladder, which a clinician manages according to the local protocol. The responder's part is to notice the flaccid limbs, keep the patient warm, record what is seen, and say plainly that the picture may change.

A cord injury high in the neck or in the upper part of the thoracic spine may remove the nerve supply that keeps the blood vessels narrowed, and the patient then has a low blood pressure with a pulse that is slow rather than fast. That pattern is called neurogenic shock, and it differs from the shock caused by bleeding, in which the pulse is usually rapid and the skin is cold and clammy. The two may exist in the same patient, and the responder must never assume that the cord injury explains a low blood pressure. The physician decides whether fluid or a medicine to support the blood pressure is needed, and that decision belongs to the prescriber and to the local protocol. This course names no substance and gives no amount, no route and no frequency, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from it.

Several patterns of incomplete injury are recognized, and the picture at the bedside differs with each. In central cord syndrome the arms are weaker than the legs and the loss of sensation is patchy, and the pattern is seen most often in an older person whose canal is already narrowed after the neck is forced backward. In anterior cord syndrome the injury spares the back of the cord, so the patient loses movement and the sensation of pain and temperature below the level while still feeling vibration and the position of a limb. In the pattern named after Brown-Sequard one half of the cord is injured, and the patient has weakness and loss of position sense on the same side with loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side. When the roots below the end of the cord are injured instead, the patient has floppy weakness of both legs, numbness in the saddle area and retention of urine, and that is a surgical emergency referred urgently for decompression.

Nothing in the field examination of the neck requires the patient to move it, and the responder never asks for that movement. The patient is not asked to touch the chin to the chest, to turn the head or to lift the head from the stretcher, because each of those movements is a test of an unstable column performed with the cord as the instrument. The absence of neck pain does not clear the neck, and the presence of pain does not prove that the spine is broken. The clearing of the cervical spine is a decision made by a clinician who has the examination, the imaging and the authority the local protocol requires, and the decision is recorded. The lay first aider holds the head still if trained and waits, because waiting is the safest act available at the roadside.

The examination is repeated after every intervention and at intervals set by the local protocol, because a spinal injury can change in either direction while the patient lies still. The change this course fears most is the one caused by the treatment rather than by the injury, which is why the examination is repeated after a collar is applied, after the patient is rolled and after the patient is lifted. The times named for those repetitions differ between services and between editions of the same guideline, so a figure such as every 15 minutes is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the previous record, and the comparison is what has value rather than any single result.

Deterioration announces itself in a small number of ways, and the examiner listens for all of them. The sensory level moves upward, or a limb that could be lifted a moment ago cannot be lifted now. The patient reports new numbness in the hands, new tingling in the feet, or a change in the way the chest feels when breathing. Breathing becomes shallow or the cough becomes weak, the voice changes, or the patient becomes restless and then drowsy, and the bladder may become distended with no urge to pass urine at all. Any one of those findings stops the responder, prompts a repeat of the full examination and leads to an urgent escalation, because an injury rising toward the segments that supply the diaphragm threatens life rather than walking.

The record is part of the treatment, and in a spinal injury it is the only way a later change can be proved. It carries the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the patient was found, the observations of the primary survey, and the neurological findings on each side and in each limb. It carries the time of each examination and the name of the examiner, and the exact words the patient used to describe what was felt. It also carries what was not examined and why, since an omission recorded is a gap that can be filled while an omission unrecorded looks like a normal result. The handover to the receiving team follows the same order, so that the next clinician continues a story instead of starting a new one.

Immobilization and examination are performed together rather than one after the other, because the collar that protects the neck also hides it. A wound, a swelling and a piece of glass in the hair are all found by looking before the collar is placed, and the skin beneath the collar is checked afterward by trained staff according to the local protocol. The collar is applied by the trained responder or the paramedic in the size and manner the service authorizes, and a collar that is too large can pull the neck while one that is too tight can press on the vessels. The examination is repeated after the collar, the blocks or the straps are applied, because the device itself can change what the patient is able to do. Nothing in this chapter authorizes a responder to remove a collar that another clinician has placed, and a collar removed for any reason is replaced and the fact recorded.

Each act in this sequence belongs to a named level of practice, and the sequence fails when those levels are blurred. The lay first aider recognizes the mechanism, keeps the head and trunk still with the hands if trained, keeps the patient warm and calls for help, and performs no examination of the spine. The trained first responder performs the observations of the primary survey, applies the spinal motion restriction the service authorizes, and reports the findings without interpreting them. The emergency medical technician and the paramedic may perform a limited neurological check within their own procedures and repeat the observations during transport. The nurse repeats the observations, records them and reports any change to the physician, who performs the complete examination, orders the imaging and decides on the destination. The orthopedic surgeon or the spinal surgeon decides whether the column must be stabilized or the cord decompressed, and the classification of the injury on the impairment scale belongs to an examiner trained and certified in it.

Imaging is ordered by a clinician, it answers a question the examination has raised, and it never replaces the examination. A radiograph of the spine is often the first study, and computed tomography gives far better detail of the bone, the alignment and the canal. A study of the blood vessels of the neck may be added when the injury is high in the neck, because an artery there can be torn by the same force that broke the vertebra and the tear can cause a stroke. Magnetic resonance imaging shows the cord, the disks, the ligaments and the blood within the canal, and it is used when the examination has found a deficit the bone does not explain. The images are read by a clinician trained to read them, and the responder neither orders nor interprets them, because a normal study at one moment does not clear a spine the examination has not cleared.

Reassessment follows the patient through every move, since each move is an intervention. It is repeated after the roll onto the board, after the lift onto the stretcher, after the collar is adjusted, on arrival at the receiving facility and at every handover, and each set is compared with the one before it. Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and for a spinal injury it means transfer to a facility with imaging, a spinal surgeon, an operating room and an intensive care unit. An operation may relieve the pressure on the cord and stabilize the column with metal, and the technique, the timing and the choice of operation belong to the surgeon and to the local protocol. What the responder contributes is the accurate record of the examination, because the surgeon's decision rests on how the patient has changed since the injury.

The spine of a child bends farther than the spine of an adult while the cord tolerates less stretching, so a child may injure the cord with no break in the bone. The child may be too young to describe numbness, may be frightened into silence and may answer a question to please the examiner, so the examination is performed with a parent present and by a clinician whenever possible. An older adult with a narrow spinal canal or a spine stiffened by arthritis is a different patient with the same sequence, since the neck may be forced backward in a fall from standing height while the radiograph looks ordinary. In both groups the pain may be less than the injury suggests, and the record then says which parts of the examination were completed and which were not. The threshold for immobilization and for referral is lower in both groups, and the decisions about imaging and treatment remain with the clinician.

Nothing in this chapter can be learned from listening alone, and the listener should hear that as a limitation rather than as a formality. The examination of the spine, the testing of sensation, the grading of movement, the clearing of the neck and the classification of a cord injury are learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. The numbers and the intervals named in this chapter differ between services, between countries and between editions, and each one must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A responder who is uncertain about the level of practice that authorizes an act asks before performing it, and asking is a sign of competence rather than of doubt.

To summarize, a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and the examination of movement and sensation in each limb is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, because the change that matters is a comparison and not a single observation. The sequence is the one this course follows everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and each step belongs to a named level of practice. Assessment begins with the primary survey remembered as ABCDE and with the principle that life comes before limb, stabilization keeps the head, the neck and the trunk in the position found, and cold is treated as a complication. The examination records sensation and movement on both sides, the level of any loss and the sacral sparing that separates a complete injury from an incomplete one, and the testing of the lowest sacral segments belongs to a clinician or to a trained examiner within the local protocol. A rising level, new weakness, new numbness or a change in breathing is a reason to stop and to escalate at once, and any person with a suspected spinal injury and any neurological finding is referred urgently to a facility with imaging, a spinal surgeon and an intensive care unit. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, an open wound is never explored, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

# Chapter 42 — The Child's Skeleton

A child is not a small adult, and nowhere is that plainer than in the skeleton, which is still growing and behaves differently from the moment of injury onward. The same energy that breaks an adult's bone may bend a child's bone, buckle it, split it along a plane an image cannot show, or injure the region that makes the bone grow. That difference changes what the responder looks for, what the responder may do, and what the family must be told about the years ahead. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Every long bone of a child lengthens at two regions, one near each end, and each is built in layers that explain what follows. The shaft is the diaphysis, separated from the end of the bone by a flared zone called the metaphysis, which is thin-walled and blood-rich. Between the metaphysis and the end lies the growth plate, also called the physis, a layer of cartilage whose cells divide, mature and become bone in an ordered sequence that lengthens the bone, and beyond it lies the epiphysis, which carries the joint surface. Because cartilage does not absorb x-rays the way bone does, the plate appears on a radiograph as a gap and the centers of bone in the epiphysis appear as separate pieces, so the growing skeleton can look like one that has been broken in several places. Only a clinician should read that appearance.

The growth plate is the weakest link when a force arrives as tension or as shear, which is why an injury that would tear a ligament in an adult can separate the plate in a child. The cartilage cells stand in columns with little to resist a sideways pull, and the zone where those columns are replaced by bone is the most fragile part of the structure. A force along the length of the bone is therefore transmitted to the plate rather than to the joint, so the joint may survive while the region that produces growth is disturbed. A child who cannot move a joint after a twisting injury is therefore not merely a child with a sprain. Tenderness that lies exactly over the plate rather than over the joint line must be recorded, because the responder is often the only person who can describe where it was before a splint covered it.

Clinicians describe injuries of the growth plate in several patterns, and the names differ between editions and countries, so the reason for a pattern matters more than its label. In the mildest pattern the fragment separates through the plate itself, with no break in the bone on either side, and in the next the break runs through part of the plate and out through a corner of the metaphysis, taking a small triangle of bone. A third crosses the plate and exits through the epiphysis, so the joint surface is involved, a fourth combines those, and the last is a crush of the plate in which nothing appears displaced. That last pattern is often recognized only in hindsight, when the bone stops growing, so tenderness over a plate deserves review even when the first image is reassuring.

An injury to the growth plate can leave a bridge of bone across the cartilage, and that bridge acts as a staple, tethering one side of the bone while the rest lengthens. The result is an angular deformity that worsens with time, or a limb shorter than its partner, and the amount depends on which plate was injured, how much growth remained and how much of the plate was damaged. A plate near the knee or the ankle can change the length of a whole limb, and the head of the thigh bone has a blood supply that is easily disturbed in a child, so an injury of the hip is an emergency even when the child seems comfortable. The decisions that follow belong to the orthopedic surgeon, and the part played by everyone else is recognition, protection, accurate recording and prompt referral.

The periosteum is the tough fibrous sleeve that wraps the bone except where a joint surface is exposed, and in a child it is thicker, stronger and far more active than in an adult. It carries vessels that feed the outer bone, it holds the cells that can make new bone, and it can bend without tearing when the bone beneath gives way, which is why a child's bone often breaks on one side only while the other side merely bends. Such an injury is called a greenstick fracture because it resembles what happens to a young green stick of wood, and because the sleeve stays intact it is usually stable and may hold the ends so close that the limb looks almost straight. The same sleeve can bend without any break at all, leaving the bone permanently curved in a pattern called plastic deformation, which is easy to dismiss as a bruise until the curve is compared with the other side.

The activity of that sleeve explains why children heal so quickly and why their healing is not always a comfort. New bone forms along the periosteum within days, so a repeat image taken about 2 weeks later can show a fracture the first image did not, a timing that differs between services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Speed of healing also means that a fracture which is going to heal in a poor position will do so quickly, so a deformity that needs correcting has to be recognized early. The periosteum can slip between the broken ends, a finding called interposition, and it is one reason a reduction may fail no matter how carefully a qualified clinician attempts it. Interposition is not diagnosed or treated in the field, because that examination belongs to the orthopedic surgeon, while the responder records that the bone is not straight and that the plate is tender.

The bone of a child is softer and more porous than the bone of an adult, because it contains more water and more protein and less mineral, and that changes the way it fails. It absorbs energy by bending before it breaks, so the same force may produce an incomplete injury, a bulge in the surface, or a curved bone rather than a snapped one. A fall on an outstretched hand that would snap an adult's wrist may instead compress one side of the child's bone into a small ridge, called a buckle or torus fracture, which is tender but rarely displaced. A child with such an injury may still move the limb, may still use the hand and may have no swelling, so the absence of an obvious deformity proves nothing. The softer bone is also more forgiving of small errors of alignment, but only up to a point, and no responder decides how much to accept or corrects anything.

Because the bone is softer and the plate is weaker, the tissues that give way first in a child often differ from those in an adult, which has a practical consequence for recognition. A ligament that would tear in an adult may stay intact while the bone to which it is attached is pulled away, an injury called an avulsion fracture, and the fragment may be small enough to be missed. A similar pull near a joint may separate a growth plate instead of tearing a ligament, and the two look alike from outside because both produce swelling and pain in the same place. The responder records what the child will and will not do, where it hurts, and what the limb looked like before and after immobilization, and does not test the joint by pulling on it, because that skill is learned under supervision.

Remodeling is the process by which a growing bone corrects the shape it has been left in, and it is why a child's fracture is judged by different standards than an adult's. It works in three ways at once, because new bone is laid down on the side under strain, old bone is removed from the side that is not, and the growth plate itself can realign as it lengthens, so the bone slowly straightens. How much correction is possible depends on the age of the child and the growth that remains, on how close the fracture lies to a plate, and on whether the deformity lies in the plane in which the nearby joint moves. A bend in the plane of the elbow or the knee remodels far better than one that is not, and a limb left rotated or shortened does not remodel at all, because growth cannot untwist a bone or lengthen one that has healed too short.

Remodeling is measured in months and years rather than days, and it is not a promise that every deformity will disappear. A fracture that is to be corrected by growth must lie in a position the plate can correct, the family must understand that reviews will continue long after the pain has gone, and someone must watch for the deformity that does not improve, because a bone that has healed bent may need an operation later. A child's fracture also sometimes overgrows, because healing stimulates the plate near the break. Growth continues for years, so a damaged plate may produce a deformity only after a growth spurt, and a limb left short may change the way a child walks, while some of those outcomes are unavoidable and some are the price of delay.

Recognition of a fracture in a child depends less on what can be seen than on what the child will and will not do. A child who will not use an arm, who will not bear weight on a leg, who holds a limb still and refuses to let it be moved, or who cries when it is handled is describing an injury even when there is no swelling and no bruise. A very young child may show nothing except irritability, a refusal to feed, or a cry that changes when the limb is touched, while a trivial mechanism such as a fall from a low height can produce a real fracture because a child is light and the forces are small. Comparing the two sides is a habit worth keeping, and so is examining the whole child, because a child who has fallen often has more than one injury.

Assessment begins with the scene, the mechanism, the age of the child and the time since the injury, and the history includes illness that affects bone, medicines that thin it, and anything that has made the child's bones fragile. The primary survey comes next, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, with the whole child rather than the injured limb as its subject. A child compensates for blood loss by raising the heart rate and tightening the vessels and may look well until that compensation fails, so a child who becomes quiet, pale or drowsy after an injury is more worrying than the same behavior in an adult. Life comes before limb whenever two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, and exposure is followed at once by covering the child again, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. The limb is assessed only when the child is stable enough, and only by looking, by feeling gently and by asking.

Among the injuries a child may bring to a responder are those that were inflicted, and the features that raise that possibility are worth knowing even though the judgment belongs to others. Concern is raised when the explanation does not fit the injury, when a child who cannot yet walk has a fracture, when injuries of different ages are found together, or when help has been delayed without good reason. The correct acts are to keep the child safe and warm, to avoid interrogation or accusation, to record what was seen and said in the words used, and to pass the concern to the clinician in charge. The duty to report is set by local law and local protocol, and a responder who suspects such an injury does not send the child home to be brought back later.

Stabilization of an injured limb in a child is the same small set of acts as in an adult, and the first of them is restraint. The limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact or turn a closed fracture into an open one. A deformed limb is supported by hand, by a pillow or by whatever is at hand, and the child is kept warm while help is arranged. An open wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, and an embedded object is never removed, because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. The lay first aider performs only the acts that need no equipment, the trained responder and the paramedic work within the equipment and procedures their service authorizes, and nobody in the field explores an open wound blindly, because definitive closure belongs to the operating room.

Cold deserves its own place in the care of an injured child, because a child loses heat faster than an adult and has less reserve to replace it. The surface of a child is large in relation to the weight, the skin is thin, and the layer of fat beneath it is small, so a limb left uncovered on cold ground loses warmth quickly. Wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, the child is insulated from the ground, and a hat or a blanket over the head helps, because much heat is lost there. A young child who is cold may not shiver but may instead become quiet and sleepy, which can be mistaken for calm. Because cold worsens bleeding and complicates every injury, warmth is part of the treatment of the fracture, and any temperature, time or distance named in this chapter is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such figures differ between services and countries.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the child to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and in a child the testing may have to be turned into a game or done while the caregiver distracts the child, because numbness and tingling are reported by the child and not by the examiner. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the child's ability to move and feel, while the formal examination of pulses and sensation belongs to the trained responder or the clinician. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency.

A compartment syndrome is harder to recognize in a child, because a frightened child may cry for other reasons and a quiet child may be assumed to be comfortable. The limb that is tense, swollen and painful out of proportion to the injury is an emergency at any age, and pain that increases instead of settling, pain not relieved by the measures available, and a child who cannot be comforted are the findings that should stop the responder. Numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor and coolness come later, and waiting for them is waiting too long, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. A responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation, does not elevate the limb above the level of the heart, releases a constricting bandage or splint only within the local protocol and only when authorized, keeps the child warm, and refers urgently. The substance and amount of any medicine for the pain belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, and no dose, route or frequency may be taken from this course.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, is applied over the position found, and is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. In a child these principles demand more care, because the limb is small and the child may wriggle against whatever is applied. The material matters less than the principle, since a folded magazine, a padded board, a sling or the body of the caregiver can each serve, and an improvised device must be checked more often because it shifts, while a sling holding the arm against the chest is often the whole of the immobilization a child's upper limb needs before transfer. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, and casting, traction and surgical fixation are learned under supervision rather than taught from a book.

Whatever is applied must be checked, and in a child the checking is repeated more often than in an adult because the limb is small and the margin between firm and too tight is narrow. The fingers or toes beyond the splint are watched for color, warmth, swelling and the ability to move, and a digit that becomes pale, cool or painful is a signal to loosen the device within the local protocol and to seek advice. A child who becomes distressed after a splint is applied is telling the responder something, and the answer is not to wait and see whether the distress passes. Because a child's fracture may swell for hours, a device that fits at one moment may be too tight later, so the family must be told what change should bring them back, and instructions given on transfer are part of the immobilization.

Imaging confirms what the examination has suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do so, never by a responder in the field. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. In a child the reading is more difficult, because the growth plate appears as a gap and the bony centers at the ends of the bones appear as separate pieces that can be mistaken for fragments. A fracture through the plate may not be visible at all on the first image, so a clinic may review the child after about 1 to 2 weeks, when new bone begins to show, though that interval differs between services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Children are more sensitive to radiation than adults, so the clinician weighs the benefit of every study.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement, and the limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain while the splint is checked for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation, and in a child the same findings may appear as distress that cannot be soothed. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome acts within the local protocol rather than waiting for confirmation, and the child is kept warm, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the receiving team is warned, and the transfer is not delayed for a test that will be repeated at the hospital. Medicines for pain are chosen and given only by those the local protocol authorizes, and a responder whose scope of practice forbids giving a medicine says who will.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the child lies. A child with a suspected injury of the growth plate, a displaced fracture, a fracture that enters a joint, an open fracture, a damaged nerve or vessel, a suspected compartment syndrome, a fracture of the thigh bone, a joint that will not move, or an injury that does not match the explanation given is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Transport is arranged with the limb immobilized and the neurovascular findings handed over. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, and every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. When the growth plate is involved, timing matters more than in an adult, because the longer a displaced plate waits the greater the risk to the cartilage that is trying to grow. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open or the diagnosis unclear, when the training or equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed, because an attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. Force is not a technique, and in a child it can damage the plate and change the length of the limb for life.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and in a child they carry information that no later examiner can recover. The age of the child, the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and any change in the condition are written or spoken in a fixed order, so the receiving team continues a story rather than starting a new one. The fact that a child cried when the limb was touched belongs in the record in those words. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a child with a suspected spinal injury is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision.

To summarize, a child's skeleton is not a small adult's skeleton, and the growth plate, the thicker and more active periosteum, the softer bone and the greater remodeling explain why the same force produces a different injury, a different recovery and a different future. A child who will not use a limb, will not bear weight, or cries when the limb is handled has described a fracture even when nothing can be seen, and tenderness over the growth plate or a joint that will not move makes the transfer urgent. The course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and a constricting splint is released only within the local protocol by someone authorized to do it. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open or the diagnosis unclear, when the training and the equipment are missing, or when an earlier attempt has failed. A child is kept warm, a suspected spinal injury is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, an injury that does not fit its explanation is reported through the proper channel, and the child is reassessed after every intervention. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 43 — Common Pediatric Fractures

A child who has fallen and now holds one arm against the chest is a common sight in pediatric emergency care, and the injury is seldom the one an adult would suffer from an equal fall. A child's bone is softer and more elastic, and the sleeve around it is thicker than the sleeve around adult bone, so a bone may bend, buckle or crack on one side instead of breaking in two. This chapter follows the order used in every chapter of this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the level of practice for each act. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The differences begin in the tissue rather than in the size of the bone. The periosteum is the tough sleeve that wraps the bone, and in a child it is thick and firmly attached at the ends, so it often stays intact on one side of a break and holds the broken ends near each other. A crack on one side with a bend on the other is called a greenstick fracture, and a bone that is compressed and bulges without a clear crack has a buckle fracture, which is common in early childhood. Because a child's bone remodels as the child grows, a bend may straighten over months while a twist about the long axis does not, which is one reason a forearm injury in a child is never dismissed as minor.

Near each end of a long bone in a child lies a growth region, a band of cartilage in which new bone is made and from which the bone lengthens. An injury that crosses that band may disturb the length or the shape of the bone for the rest of childhood, and the damage may not show at the first examination, because cartilage does not appear on a radiograph as bone does. A growth region can be mistaken for a fracture line, and a fracture through it can be mistaken for the ordinary appearance of a growing bone, so the image is read by a clinician who knows the appearances of childhood. Tenderness over the end of the bone, swelling, and a child who will not use the limb raise suspicion even when the radiograph is normal, and the responder records them, immobilizes the limb and refers.

Assessment begins with the scene, the mechanism and the child, and only then turns to the limb. The time of the injury, the height of the fall, the surface struck and whether a vehicle was involved all belong to the story, because the same fracture means different things after a stumble and after a road crash. The primary survey comes first, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because a child who is drowsy or bleeding elsewhere is treated before an arm is examined. A child may be unable to say where it hurts, may be too frightened to answer, or may cry whenever the limb is touched, so the parent is the historian and the child's behavior is the finding. The limb is examined by looking, by feeling and by asking the child to move it, never by forcing a movement the child resists, and a movement the child will not make is itself a finding.

Sometimes the story does not fit the injury, and that mismatch is a clinical finding rather than a moral judgment. A child who is not yet mobile cannot break a thigh bone by rolling off a sofa, a bruise in the shape of a hand is not caused by a fall, and injuries of different ages suggest more than one event. When the mechanism does not explain the injury, or when the caregiver delays seeking help for reasons that do not hold, the responder records what was said and what was seen and reports it along the path that the local protocol and the law require. That duty belongs to every health professional and every trained responder, and it is carried out without accusation, while the child is immobilized and referred exactly as any other child would be.

Stabilization of the injured limb in a child is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. A deformed arm or leg is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what was left intact. The limb is supported by the hands of the first aider, by a pillow or by whatever is at hand, and the child is kept warm, because cold is a complication of trauma. A child who may need sedation or an anesthetic is kept from food and drink, a decision that belongs to the treating clinician. The lay first aider supports and warms the child, the trained responder and the paramedic apply the splints and slings their service authorizes, and both keep the parent with the child whenever it is safe.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and in a child it takes patience rather than force. The examiner looks at the color and warmth of the hand or foot, compares the two sides, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and feels the pulse beyond the injury. A pulse may be hard to find in a plump or frightened child, and the examiner's own pulse may be mistaken for the pulse of the child, so the finding is checked on the other side and recorded with its uncertainty. Sensation is tested lightly on both sides, and the child is asked to move the fingers or the toes, because a movement that has disappeared is the clearest sign of a nerve that is no longer working. The record made before the splint is applied is the only thing that can be compared with the record made afterwards.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. In the upper limb this usually means a support that holds the elbow and the wrist, and in the lower limb a splint that holds the knee and the ankle, applied over padding that protects the skin and the bony points. The device is secured firmly enough to hold the limb without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and the fingers or the toes are left visible so that color, warmth and movement can be checked. The trained responder and the paramedic apply these devices within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

A radiograph is usually the first study in a child with a suspected fracture, and it is taken in at least two directions, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed.
