The appearances of growth make a child's image harder to read, so the clinician may ask for a view of the other side or for a repeat image after an interval, and any interval chosen is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Computed tomography is used when the detail of a complex break around the elbow will change what is done, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues and for the growth region. The lay first aider never orders or interprets an image, and a normal radiograph does not exclude a fracture in a child who will not use the limb.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and in a child it rests more on observation than on words. The limb is checked again for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the support is checked for tightness, and the findings are compared with the record made before it was applied. A child who becomes quieter is not necessarily better, because a limb that is losing its blood supply becomes painful and then numb, and the child may simply stop crying about it. Where a compartment syndrome is suspected, the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the child is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that a child's fracture is not always treated where the child lies. A child is referred to a facility with imaging and with a clinician trained in the care of children when the injury is open, when the pulse or the sensation has changed, when a compartment syndrome is suspected, when the fracture crosses a growth region, or when treatment will need sedation or an operating room. The receiving facility is told what was found, what was done and what changed, in a fixed order, so that the next team continues a story instead of starting a new one. The level of practice is named with each act, since the lay first aider supports and warms, the trained responder and the paramedic examine and splint, the nurse monitors and reassesses, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides about imaging, reduction, casting or operation.

The fracture that matters most in this chapter is the break of the bone just above the elbow, called the supracondylar fracture. It is the commonest fracture of the elbow in childhood, and it happens most often when a child falls onto an outstretched hand with the elbow partly straight, so that the force travels up the forearm and out through the thin part of the bone above the joint. The child holds the elbow bent and refuses to use the arm at all, while the elbow swells quickly and a deformity may appear, though in a plump arm the change in shape can be hard to see. This is not a sprain and it is not a pulled elbow, and a child who will not use an arm after a fall is treated as having this injury until a clinician has said otherwise.

The vessel that supplies the forearm and the hand passes in front of the bone at the elbow, and the median, radial and ulnar nerves pass close to the same place, so a displaced break can kink the vessel, tear it or trap a nerve. The forearm is also divided into tight compartments by fascia, and the swelling that follows the injury raises the pressure inside them, which can shut off the blood supply to muscle and nerve even while a pulse can still be felt at the wrist. A pulse that is present therefore does not exclude a hand that is at risk, and the findings that matter are a hand that is pale, cool and slow to refill, a child who will not move the fingers, and pain that grows instead of settling. This is the injury above all others in this chapter that can cost the limb, and the same anatomy explains why straightening a displaced supracondylar fracture is a hospital procedure and never a field procedure.

The response to a suspected supracondylar fracture is made of restraint, warmth, a careful record and speed. The limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found, the neurovascular status is recorded before and after the splint is applied, and the arm is never straightened, pulled or reduced outside a hospital, because the fragments lie against the vessel and the nerves. The child is kept warm and is given nothing by mouth, since sedation or an anesthetic may be needed, and is transferred urgently to a facility where an orthopedic surgeon and a clinician experienced in the anesthesia of children are available. The definitive treatment of a displaced supracondylar fracture is decided by the orthopedic surgeon and may include a reduction under anesthesia and the holding of the fragments with wires, and every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

Fractures of the forearm are among the commonest fractures of childhood, and they often involve both bones, the radius and the ulna. The mechanism is usually a fall onto the outstretched hand, and the result may be a greenstick crack on one side of the bone, a buckle at the end of the bone, or a complete break with displacement. The child guards the forearm, holds it against the body and will not turn the palm up or down, and there is swelling, tenderness along the bone and sometimes a visible bend. The forearm is a tight space in which muscle, vessels and nerves are packed against the bone, so the swelling that follows a fracture of both bones is the finding to watch most closely, and the limb is supported and the child referred for imaging and for the decision about treatment.

Two things decide how a fractured forearm will work months later, and both belong to the clinician rather than to the responder. The first is the alignment of the bones in rotation, because a forearm that has healed with a twist loses the turn of the palm, and that loss disables a child far more than a small bend that growth would have straightened. The second is the condition of the soft tissues, because a forearm that has been swollen and tight can leave a hand that is stiff and weak even when the bone has healed. The part of the responder is to immobilize the limb as a whole, including the elbow and the wrist in the support that is applied, and to check the fingers before and after that support is applied. The trained responder and the paramedic do so within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and if the pain increases or the fingers become pale, the child is reassessed at once and referred urgently.

A fracture of the clavicle is one of the commonest injuries of childhood, and it is usually caused by a fall onto the shoulder or onto the outstretched hand. The child holds the arm still against the body and is unwilling to lift it, the shoulder on the injured side sits lower and further forward than the other one, and the head may be tilted toward that side. There is tenderness over the bone, and sometimes a visible step in its outline that will later become the firm bump of new bone. The vessels and nerves that supply the arm pass behind the clavicle, so the neurovascular status of the hand is recorded before anything is applied and again afterwards. Most fractures of the clavicle in a child heal well with support and time, and the choice of support belongs to the clinician, while the trained responder applies the sling the local protocol authorizes. A fracture of the inner part of the clavicle, where the great vessels lie, a fracture that opens the skin, a pale or numb hand, and a child who is unwell all make the injury urgent and require immediate referral, and no one pulls on the arm or attempts to straighten it.

The clavicle can also break at birth, and that injury is seen in the nursery rather than in the field. A newborn with a fractured clavicle does not move the arm on that side, a finding sometimes called pseudoparalysis, and the arm lies still while the other arm and both legs move normally. The injury may be mistaken for a stretch of the nerves of the arm that happens during a difficult delivery, and the two can occur together, so the infant is examined by a clinician who can distinguish them. A firm bump that appears over the fracture some weeks later is new bone forming as it heals rather than a tumor, and the family is told that it is expected, though the judgment about any swelling belongs to the clinician.

The pulled elbow, also called the nursemaid's elbow, is not a fracture at all, and it is one of the few injuries in this chapter that a clinician can usually settle quickly. The head of the radius, one of the bones of the forearm, is held against the bone of the upper arm by a ring of ligament, and in a young child that ring is slack enough that a sudden pull on the hand lets the head slip part of the way out of it. It happens most often between the first and the fourth year of life, a range that must be checked against the version of the guideline and the protocol that govern your service, because such figures differ between services and countries. The child stops using the arm, holds it slightly bent with the palm turned down and cries when the arm is moved, yet there is no swelling, no deformity and no bruising, which is exactly why the injury is sometimes dismissed as a refusal to use the arm.

The treatment of a pulled elbow is a specific, gentle maneuver that returns the head of the radius into its ring, and the maneuver is learned in supervised clinical training and performed according to local protocol rather than read about in a book. It may be performed by a physician or by a trained provider whom the local protocol authorizes, and it is not an act for a lay first aider, for a bystander, or for anyone who has not been taught it with a teacher. A radiograph is often normal in a pulled elbow, so a normal image does not exclude it, and the maneuver is not attempted when there is swelling, bruising, tenderness over the bone, a deformity, a wound, or any change in the pulse, the sensation or the movement of the hand. It is not repeated, because repeated attempts turn a simple injury into a swollen elbow that can no longer be assessed. The aim of the maneuver is that the child uses the arm again, and where the child does not, the clinician reassesses and images the elbow, while a fever or a hot and swollen joint in a child who is unwell points to an infection that belongs to the clinician at once.

The toddler's fracture is a crack in the bone of the lower leg that is easy to miss and easy to remember once it has been seen. It is usually a fine spiral or oblique crack in the tibia, the larger bone of the lower leg, and it happens in a young child who twists the leg while learning to walk, steps into a small hole or falls while running. The child refuses to put weight on the leg, crawls or asks to be carried, and may be perfectly content while sitting still, while the leg shows no swelling, no deformity and no bruise. The tenderness is found only by pressing carefully along the bone, and a missed toddler's fracture leaves a child in pain and hides the possibility that the history is not the whole story.

Radiographs in a toddler's fracture are often normal at the first visit, and that is what makes the injury dangerous to the careless. A clinician may therefore ask for the leg to be imaged again after an interval, or may use another study, and the choice of study and the length of the interval belong to the clinician who knows the local protocol. The age of the child is usually between the first and the third year, and that range is another illustration, to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because practice differs between services and editions. The part of the responder is to think of the injury in a child who will not walk, to immobilize the leg as the local protocol allows, to keep the child warm, and to refer with the record of what was found.

Of the injuries in this chapter, some threaten the limb within hours and others threaten the child's comfort for days, and knowing which is which is the first skill of the responder. The supracondylar fracture of the elbow is the clearest emergency, because the vessel and the nerves of the forearm lie against the broken bone and the swelling inside the forearm can close the circulation to the hand. An open fracture of any bone is an emergency, and the wound is covered with a sterile dressing while the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled and the child is referred for an operating room. A fracture of both bones of the forearm with a tense, swollen compartment is an emergency too, and so is any limb with a pulse that is fading or a hand that is pale and cold. The fracture of the clavicle, the pulled elbow and the toddler's fracture seldom threaten the limb, but each of them can be missed, and where the responder is uncertain, the child is treated as if the worse injury were present.

Comfort is part of the treatment of a child and it is never an afterthought. Pain makes a child move, and movement makes the injury worse, so a supported limb and a child who is kept warm and near a parent will often settle before anything else is done. Where a medicine for pain is needed, the substance, the amount and the way it is given are decided by a prescriber authorized to decide them and are recorded according to the local protocol. For an open fracture, protection against tetanus and the use of an antibiotic are decisions for the prescriber, and this course names no dose, no route and no regimen, so no prescription can be taken from it.

A child loses heat faster than an adult, because the surface of a small body is large in relation to its weight, so warmth is a treatment rather than a courtesy. Wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, the child is insulated from the ground, and a hat and a blanket are used whenever they are available, while the injured limb is left visible enough to be checked. The record and the handover carry the rest of the care, and the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order. An injury of the spine in a child is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no single manual handling technique is safe on its own, so a child who has fallen from a height is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires.

To summarize, a child's bone bends before it breaks, so a fracture that looks minor may still involve a growth region, a nerve or a vessel, and the child may be unable to say where it hurts. A child who will not use an arm or a leg is assessed, stabilized, examined for the neurovascular status, immobilized in the position found, imaged, reassessed, and then referred or treated definitively, and the neurovascular findings are recorded before and after every intervention, because a finding that was not recorded cannot be attributed afterwards. The supracondylar fracture of the elbow is the injury that most often threatens the limb, an open fracture and a tense swollen forearm are emergencies, and the fractured clavicle, the pulled elbow and the toddler's fracture are the injuries most often missed. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and no one attempts a reduction when the diagnosis is unclear, when the injury is open, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, or when the person lacks the training and the equipment. The maneuver for a pulled elbow, the reduction of a fracture, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and this course teaches only what they are for, what can go wrong and who is qualified to do them. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, no dose and no regimen is given here, and the child who is getting worse is escalated at once. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 44 — Growth Plate Injuries

The growth plate is the layer of cartilage near each end of a child's long bone where the bone lengthens, and an injury to it differs from a broken shaft because the tissue that was damaged is the tissue that was going to make the limb grow. A plate that is bruised, split or crushed may heal, and the bone may still stop lengthening or grow crooked years later. This chapter therefore asks the listener to look past the bone that shows on an image and to think about the plate that does not. The course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The plate is built in layers, and hearing them in order explains why it fails where it does. Nearest the end of the bone lie small rounded cartilage cells that divide slowly and serve as the store from which the plate is renewed. Farther toward the middle of the bone the cells multiply and line up in columns, and then they enlarge, take in water and prepare their matrix for calcification. The last layer is invaded by vessels from the shaft, which bring in the cells that lay down bone on the cartilage scaffold, so that the plate moves away from the middle of the bone and the bone grows longer. The layer of enlarged cells is the weakest part of the structure, because the matrix between the cells is thin, and that is the layer a pulling or a shearing force tears. A ring of fibrous tissue at the edge of the plate holds it in position, and when that ring is torn the plate may bridge to the shaft as it heals.

Because the plate is the weakest link in the growing skeleton, the tissue that gives way first in a child often differs from that in an adult. A joint that would tear a ligament in an adult may instead separate the plate, and a force along the length of the bone is spread across the joint and into the plate, so an injury that seems to spare the joint may still disturb growth. Rotation is the displacement most easily missed, because a limb can look straight while it is twisted, and a twist recognized late heals as it lies and does not remodel. The responder records the position in which the limb was found and compares it with the other side but does not test the joint by pulling on it, because that examination belongs to a clinician and can add damage.

An injury of the plate announces itself less clearly than a broken shaft, so the responder takes the history seriously and the examination gently. The child may hold the limb still, refuse to use it or cry when it is handled, and yet the limb may look straight, may not swell for hours and may still move through most of its range. Tenderness that sits exactly over the plate rather than over the joint line is the finding that matters most, and it is easily lost once a splint has covered the limb, so it is written down at the first examination. Pain with a twist, pain when the bone is squeezed along its length and a reluctance to bear weight all point to the plate and not only to the joint.

Clinicians describe injuries of the plate in a small set of patterns, and the descriptions matter more than the numbers attached to them, because the number is local language while the pattern is anatomy. This group is often called the Salter-Harris classification, and the names and their order differ between editions and countries, so a listener who hears a number should ask what it describes. In the mildest description the fragment separates through the plate itself, leaving the bone on both sides intact, and this is the pattern that may not show on the first image at all. In the next, the break runs across part of the plate and exits through a corner of the shaft, carrying a small triangle of bone with it, and this is the commonest description in childhood. A third crosses the plate and leaves through the end of the bone, so that the joint surface is broken as well, and a fourth combines the third and the second. The last is a crush of the plate in which nothing looks displaced, and it is often recognized only afterwards, when the bone fails to grow.

What the listener should carry away is not the order of the numbers but the four questions those patterns answer. The first is whether the joint surface is involved, because a break that enters the joint can leave the surface uneven and the joint arthritic in later life. The second is whether the plate has moved, because a displaced plate must be brought back into position by someone qualified to do it, and that decision belongs to the orthopedic surgeon. The third is whether the blood supply to the end of the bone is at risk, because the head of the thigh bone and the head of the radius in a child have supplies that tear easily. The fourth is how much growth remains, because a plate that is nearly closed has little future to lose, while the same injury in a toddler may change the length of the whole limb.

Assessment begins with the scene and the mechanism, and in a child it also includes the age, the time since the injury and anything that has made the bones fragile. The primary survey comes next, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. A child compensates for blood loss by raising the heart rate and tightening the vessels and may look well until that compensation fails, so a child who becomes quiet, pale or drowsy is more worrying than the same behavior in an adult. Life comes before limb whenever two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, and exposure is followed at once by covering the child again, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. Only when the child is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, and the limb is assessed by looking, by feeling gently and by asking the child to move it, never by forcing it.

Some children cannot describe their pain at all, and the examination has to be built from what someone else can see. A baby who has not yet learned to speak, a child whose development is delayed, a child with a condition that alters sensation, a child who is sedated in an intensive care unit and a child too frightened to answer may each present with a fracture and no complaint. A baby may stop moving one arm and hold it still, and a child may refuse to feed, sleep badly or cry in a way the caregiver has never heard before. The caregiver is the expert on that child's normal behavior, so asking what is different today is more useful than asking where it hurts. A change in the use of a hand, a limp that was not there yesterday and a cry that changes when the limb is touched all describe an injury even when no swelling is present.

None of those signs can be relied upon to be present, and the reverse matters just as much, because a child who is using a limb may still have an injured plate. The absence of swelling, the ability to move the joint and the absence of visible deformity are all unreliable in a plate injury, and a responder who rests on any one of them will miss the child who is quiet rather than loud. Pain out of proportion to the injury is the finding this course teaches the listener to take most seriously, and in a child it may appear as distress that cannot be soothed rather than as an answer the child can give. A child who cannot report numbness cannot be asked to, so the examiner tests sensation by comparison and by watching the face.

Stabilization of an injured limb in a child is a small set of acts, and the first of them is restraint. The limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact and can disturb the plate. The lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment, which are supporting the limb with the hands or a pillow, keeping the child warm and staying with the child until help arrives. The trained responder and the paramedic work within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and neither straightens a deformed limb, pushes exposed bone back into a wound or removes an embedded object. A child loses heat faster than an adult, so wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, the child is insulated from the ground and the head is covered.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return and asks the child to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and with a small child the testing is often turned into a game or done while the caregiver distracts the child. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the child's ability to move and feel, while the formal examination of pulses and sensation belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency.

A compartment syndrome is harder to recognize in a child than in an adult and is more easily missed, because a frightened child may cry for reasons that have nothing to do with the injury and a quiet child may be assumed to be comfortable. The limb that is tense, swollen and painful out of proportion to the injury is an emergency at any age, and pain that increases instead of settling and a child who cannot be comforted should stop the responder. Numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor and coolness come later, and waiting for them is waiting too long, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. A responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation, does not elevate the limb above the level of the heart and releases a constricting bandage only within the local protocol and only when authorized. The substance, the amount and the route of any medicine for pain belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and no dose may be taken from this course. A child in a cast whose pain is rising must be seen rather than observed.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, is applied over the position found and is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. In a child the margins are narrow, so the device is checked again after it is applied and the part beyond it is watched for color, warmth, swelling and movement. Padding that presses over the tender plate may add pain and hide the very finding the next examiner needs, so the padding goes over the bony points and the tender region is left undisturbed. A folded magazine, a padded board, a sling or the body of the caregiver can each serve, and a device that leaves the part beyond it pale, cool or painful is loosened only within the local protocol and by someone authorized to do it. Casting, traction and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them can be learned from a book.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do so, never by a responder in the field. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. In a child the reading is more difficult, because the plate appears as a gap, the centers of bone at the ends of the long bones appear as separate pieces and small extra centers that are entirely normal can look like fragments that have been pulled away. An image of the other limb may be taken for comparison when the clinician is unsure, and that decision belongs to the clinician. A break through the plate may not be visible at all on the first image, so a clinic may review the child later, and any interval quoted for that review is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Computed tomography shows the detail of a break that runs into a joint and is used when that detail will change what is done, and magnetic resonance imaging shows cartilage and soft tissue and is the study a clinician may choose when a plate injury is suspected but not seen. Magnetic resonance imaging can also show a bridge of bone forming across the plate before the deformity appears. Children are more sensitive to radiation than adults, so every study is weighed against the answer it will give. Ordering an image, choosing between the studies and reading the result are the work of the clinician responsible for the child's care, and the responder's part is to describe the mechanism, the tenderness over the plate and the neurovascular findings. An image is a picture of one moment, and the child must still be examined and reassessed after it has been taken.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement, and the limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain while the splint is checked for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen stop the responder and prompt escalation, and in a child the same findings may appear as distress that cannot be soothed. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome acts within the local protocol rather than waiting for confirmation, and the child is kept warm while the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart. The receiving team is warned before the child arrives, and the findings travel with the child in a fixed order.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the child lies. A child with a suspected injury of the growth plate, a displaced fracture, a fracture that enters a joint, an open fracture, a damaged nerve or vessel, a suspected compartment syndrome or an injury that does not match the explanation given is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. A suspected plate injury deserves that referral even when the image looks reassuring, because the finding that decides the outcome may not be visible yet. When the plate has moved, the timing of definitive care matters more than in an adult, and the decision about when and how belongs to the orthopedic surgeon. Transport is arranged with the limb immobilized, the child warm and the neurovascular findings handed over. Nothing in this chapter permits a responder to reduce a plate injury, to apply traction or to reduce a joint, because those acts are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

Definitive treatment of a plate injury may be an operation, and what the surgeon does is decided by the pattern and by the growth that remains. A displaced fragment may be brought back into position and held, a fragment blocking the joint may be removed and a bridge of bone that has formed across the plate may be taken away in the hope that growth resumes, and every one of those acts belongs to the orthopedic surgeon in an operating room. A bridge that is not removed acts as a staple, tethering one side of the bone while the rest lengthens, so the limb becomes crooked or shorter than its partner. That outcome may appear only after a growth spurt and may be measured in years rather than weeks, which is why a child with a plate injury is followed until growth is finished. Some angulation in a young child is accepted and left to remodel, and that acceptance is a considered plan made by a surgeon who expects to review the child again. The family must understand that the pain will go long before the watching ends, because a family that understands the plan is far more likely to return for the reviews that make it safe.

An open injury in a child deserves its own considerations, because the wound and the plate change each other's meaning. An open fracture in a child is sometimes produced by less energy than the same injury in an adult, but the wounds of farm equipment, of a mower or of a road crash carry heavy contamination, and any such example is a constructed illustration. The wound may be small and may look almost clean while the plate beneath it is crushed or displaced, so an open injury is never judged by the size of the hole in the skin. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the limb in the position found, keeps the child warm and arranges urgent transfer. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. An open wound is never explored blindly, because definitive closure belongs to the operating room and to nobody else.

An open injury near the plate is an emergency for the limb and sometimes for the life, because contamination that reaches a damaged plate can destroy the growth of the bone and infection in an open fracture can become a general illness. Whether the child needs an antibiotic, whether tetanus protection is required and how the wound is cleaned belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and this course names no substance, no amount, no route and no frequency. What the responder must decide is only how quickly the child reaches a facility with an operating room and an intensive care unit, and how to keep the wound covered, the limb still and the child warm. Because a plate injury and an open wound may occur together, a child with a wound over a joint or over the end of a bone is treated as having a plate injury until a clinician says otherwise. The neurovascular examination is recorded before the dressing is applied and after it is applied, so that a change following the dressing can be recognized.

Among the injuries a child may bring to a responder are those that were inflicted, and an injury of the growth plate is one of the patterns that must raise that question when the story and the injury do not match. Concern is raised when the explanation offered does not account for the force the injury required, when the account changes between the people who tell it, when there has been a delay in seeking help without a reason that fits and when a child who cannot yet walk or roll has a fracture. Concern is raised again when injuries of different ages are found together, when the family has made repeated visits for injury and when the injury lies where a fall cannot reach, such as the trunk, the ears, the neck or the buttocks. In a young infant, a break through the corner of the shaft near the plate and fractures of the ribs are descriptions that clinicians treat as inflicted until they are explained, and a responder does not have to make that judgment in order to act on the concern. The question is raised by the mismatch, not by the responder's certainty, and every example here is a constructed illustration.

The correct acts are to keep the child safe and warm, to treat the injury that is present and to pass the concern to the clinician in charge in the words in which it was raised. The responder does not interrogate the child, does not question or confront the family in front of the child and does not say aloud what is suspected, because a confrontation can place the child in greater danger and can spoil an investigation. What was seen, what was said, who was present and the exact words used are written in the record, together with the time the child arrived and the time the injury was said to have happened. The duty to report is set by local law and local protocol, and the reporting is done through the channel the protocol names and by the person the protocol names. A clinician, not the responder, decides whether the injury was inflicted, but a responder who suspects it does not send the child home to be brought back later, and the concern is recorded even when the explanation seems satisfactory to everyone else.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and in a child they carry information that no later examiner can recover. The age of the child, the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the tenderness over the plate and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written in a fixed order. Where an injury was inflicted, the record also carries what was observed about the account itself, because that observation may be the only thing that prevents the next injury. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a child with a suspected spinal injury is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Everything described here is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that defines what may be done without supervision, and any time, age or distance named is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, the growth plate is the cartilage layer where a child's bone lengthens, and it is the weakest link in the growing skeleton, so a force that would tear a ligament in an adult may separate the plate in a child. The descriptions of these injuries matter more than the numbers attached to them, because what decides the outcome is whether the joint surface is broken, whether the plate has moved, whether the blood supply to the end of the bone is at risk and how much growth remains. A child who will not use a limb, will not bear weight, cries when the limb is touched or simply stops feeding has described an injury even when nothing can be seen. The course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and a constricting splint or bandage is released only within the local protocol and by someone authorized to do it. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the training is missing or when an earlier attempt has failed. An open injury in a child is covered, immobilized and transferred urgently, no substance and no amount is named in this course for pain, for infection or for tetanus, and an injury whose story does not match the child is reported through the channel that local law and local protocol name. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 45 — Osteoporosis and the Fragile Skeleton

Osteoporosis is a disease in which the amount of bone and the arrangement of its material have both fallen far enough that ordinary loads break it. The fracture is the event that brings the patient to care, while the disease is the reason the event was possible, and the two must be kept apart. A bone loses strength in two ways at once: it loses mass, so that less material carries the load, and it loses architecture, so that the material it retains is badly placed. This chapter is educational material for health professionals, students and trained responders, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Bone is rebuilt throughout life, and the balance of that rebuilding decides how strong it is when a force arrives. Cells called osteoclasts dissolve small packets of bone, and cells called osteoblasts lay down new bone in the space that has been cleared, so the skeleton is not a fixed structure but a surface that is continually resurfaced. In the first three decades the building usually outpaces the taking down, and a person reaches a peak bone mass that is set partly by inheritance and partly by hormones, nutrition, muscle pull and physical activity. After that peak the balance slowly turns, and loss begins in both men and women, though it accelerates in a woman after menopause because the hormone that restrained resorption has fallen away. Nothing in that process can be felt by the patient, and that silence is the first thing to understand about the disease.

A long bone has a dense outer shell called cortical bone and an inner lattice of thin plates and struts called cancellous or trabecular bone. The shell carries bending and twisting loads and gives the bone its stiffness, while the lattice spreads the load of a joint across a wide area at the ends of the bone. In osteoporosis the shell thins from the inside and the lattice loses whole struts rather than merely becoming thinner, and a lattice that has lost its connections does not recover them by gaining thickness later. Strength is therefore not one property but three: how much material is present, how well it is arranged, and how sound the material itself remains.

The disease is common, and most of the people who have it do not know that they do. It causes no pain, no swelling, no limp and no visible change until a bone fails, so a patient cannot be asked whether the skeleton is fragile and cannot be believed if the answer is no. Inheritance matters, so a family history of a broken hip in a parent is a useful piece of information, and a small body frame, a low body weight and a history of weight loss all raise the probability. A previous fracture after a minor injury is one of the strongest warnings available, because it says that the skeleton has already failed once under an ordinary load. The responder who hears any of this does not make a diagnosis, but neither does the responder treat the patient as though the bones were ordinary.

The illnesses and medicines that weaken bone are numerous, and a chapter can only show the shape of the list. The most common medicine cause is the group of steroid hormones used for asthma, arthritis and inflammatory disease, because they reduce the formation of new bone and increase its removal at the same time. Other conditions work through nutrition or absorption, including disease of the small bowel, celiac disease and previous surgery on the stomach, and others work through hormones, including an overactive thyroid, an overactive parathyroid and low testosterone in a man. Chronic kidney disease disturbs the mineral balance of bone, and some cancers settle in bone and hollow it from within, while multiple myeloma does so in a scattered and destructive pattern. Smoking, heavy drinking, long use of some medicines and years of poor diet belong on the same list.

The first sign of a fragile skeleton is usually a fracture, and it is usually a fracture caused by a mechanism that would not have broken a healthy bone. A fall from standing height is the classic example, but the force may be smaller still, and a cough, a sneeze, a bend to pick something up, a stumble off a curb or a hard embrace have each been enough to break a vertebral body or a rib. This is the idea of the fragility fracture: an injury whose severity is out of proportion to the energy that caused it. In a teaching illustration, an older woman who catches her foot and lowers herself to the ground with one hand returns with a painful wrist, and the wrist is treated while the reason the wrist broke is never mentioned; the second visit is the one that changes her life. The responder cannot prevent the second fracture alone, but the responder can make sure that the first one is described accurately enough for someone else to act on it.

Every bone in the body can be involved, but a few sites carry most of the burden. The bones of the spine, especially in the middle of the back and the lower back, are the most common, and the hip, the wrist and the shoulder are next. The pattern has some logic in it, because the sites that carry the richest cancellous lattice lose their strength earliest. A patient who has had two such fractures deserves a careful review of why, and that review belongs to a clinician.

The energy of the injury and the injury itself must always be compared, and a mismatch is a piece of information. A break of a large bone from a fall down a flight of stairs tells the examiner that the forces were large and the bone may be ordinary. A pathological fracture is one in which a disease process in the bone, most often a cancer that has spread there or a disease of the marrow, has weakened it before the injury happened, and it may occur with no remembered injury at all. Pain in a bone that is present before it breaks, or pain that wakes the patient at night, is a finding that must be reported rather than explained away as strain. The responder's work is to notice the mismatch, to describe it in plain words, and to pass it on; the naming of the underlying disease belongs to the clinician who can investigate it.

The spine deserves its own warning because the fracture there is the one most often missed. A vertebral body can lose height quietly and cause nothing more than a dull ache or a change in posture, and the patient may believe that the pain came from lifting a bag or from sleeping awkwardly. Loss of height over the years, a gradually stooped posture and a new hollow at the back of the neck are all visible findings that suggest old compression fractures, and they are found by looking rather than by asking. Because the bone is fragile, the spine of an older adult who has fallen must be treated as injured until someone qualified to clear it has done so. No lone manual handling technique is safe for such a patient, and the precautions are those the local protocol requires.

The hip is the fracture that frightens patients most, and it can present in ways that do not look like a hip at all. A patient may complain only of pain in the knee, because the nerves of the hip joint also supply the knee, and the hip itself may be moved with little discomfort. The classic picture of a leg that is short and turned outward is helpful when it is present, but it is absent often enough that its absence proves nothing, and some patients with a fractured hip can still bear weight a few steps. A radiograph taken on the day of the injury may look normal when the fracture is a crack that has not displaced, and that is why a patient whose pain and inability to walk do not match the image needs further assessment. The responder keeps such a patient still and does not test the limb by asking the patient to walk on it, because the test can complete a fracture that was only a crack.

A break of the wrist is the fragility fracture of middle life, and it usually follows a fall onto the outstretched hand. The hand and the forearm may be visibly deformed, and the patient guards the limb and will not use it, but the amount of deformity is a poor guide to the amount of damage. The upper end of the arm bone is broken in the same way, often by a fall from standing, and the patient may only report that the shoulder hurts and will not lift. A break of the pelvis in an older adult after a low energy fall is a serious injury with a risk of bleeding, and a break of a rib after a cough carries a risk of lung injury. Every one of these findings is handled in the same order, and none of them is handled by force.

Assessment of the patient begins before the limb is touched, and the first questions are what happened, when it happened and how the patient is now. The mechanism of injury, the age of the patient, the time of the injury, the medicines the patient takes and the fractures the patient has had before are all part of the history, and so is a history of falls. A fall that was not explained by a slip must be treated as a medical event until it is explained, because a faint, a stroke or a disturbed heart rhythm can present as a broken bone. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, and the order is deliberate because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The steps of the primary survey are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and they are performed before any splint is applied.

The limb itself is assessed by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, and never by forcing it. The examiner looks for swelling, bruising, deformity, a wound, a shortened limb or a limb that lies at an unnatural angle, and compares the injured side with the other side. The examiner feels the temperature of the skin, the tenderness of the bone and the tightness of the muscle compartments, and asks whether the feeling in the fingers or the toes has changed. Pain is a finding and must be recorded in the words of the patient, including where it is, when it began and what makes it worse. A fracture in a fragile bone may be far less dramatic than its severity suggests, and a patient who can move the limb may still have a fracture, so movement alone never excludes one. Equally, an older patient with confusion may not report pain at all, and a new reluctance to move a limb or a new confusion after a fall deserves the same seriousness as a complaint.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is written down. The examiner looks at the color of the skin, feels its warmth, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail or a fingertip to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and numbness, tingling or the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier is recorded and reported. A pulse that can be felt does not exclude serious injury to a vessel or the start of a compartment syndrome, and a pulse that cannot be felt is an emergency. In a patient with fragile bone the examination is more important rather than less, because a fracture can complete during handling, a nerve can be compressed by a fragment, and a break of the spine can threaten the spinal cord. The formal examination belongs to the trained responder or the clinician, while the lay first aider observes and reports.

Stabilization is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Straightening a deformed limb can also convert a closed fracture into an open one and can release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. In a fragile skeleton the surrounding bone is weak as well, so a force applied to one part of the limb can break another part, and handling must be gentle and deliberate for that extra reason. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. A wound near the broken bone is covered with a sterile dressing and is never explored blindly, and an object embedded in it is left in place. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground, wet clothing is replaced with covering, and an older patient is kept warm from the moment of the injury.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, and in an older patient the padding must also protect thin skin that tears easily and skin that has already been damaged by pressure. The splint is applied over the position found and is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and the neurovascular status is checked and recorded after it is in place. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace or a surgical fixation. Casting is a technique learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and it is never learned from a book.

Pain in these patients is real, and it is also a signal that must be respected rather than silenced without thought. The decision to give any medicine for pain belongs to a prescriber working within the local protocol, and this course gives no substance, no amount, no route and no frequency, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from a book. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, pain that is rising despite the splint, or pain that is out of proportion to the injury, because that combination suggests that the circulation of the limb is failing. An older patient with confusion or memory loss may be unable to describe pain, and a new restlessness or a new confusion after an injury is treated as a possible sign of it. The responder's part is to describe the pain accurately, to record what has already been given as far as it is known, and to escalate rather than to improvise.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below are included so that a second injury is not missed. In a patient with fragile bone the image is harder to read, because the bone contains less mineral and therefore casts a fainter shadow, and a fracture line may be visible only as a subtle change in the pattern of the bone. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break and is particularly useful around a joint, while magnetic resonance imaging shows soft tissues and can reveal a fracture that a radiograph has not, including a crack in the neck of the thigh bone. Either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done, and that decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the care of the patient.

A normal image does not exclude a fracture when the examination suggests one, and this is especially true in a fragile skeleton. A crack that has not separated may be invisible at the moment of the injury, an overlapping shadow may hide it, and pain may prevent the positioning that would reveal it. In the spine, a compression fracture may show only a slight loss of height in one vertebral body, and the change may be missed unless the examiner looks for it deliberately. A second image taken after some days may show the fracture more clearly as the bone edges resorb, and further imaging may be needed for a patient whose pain persists despite a reassuring first study. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed, because an image that is read by the wrong person can close a question that should stay open.

A measurement of bone mineral density is sometimes used to confirm the disease and to estimate the risk of a future fracture, and it is performed and interpreted by a clinician. The report compares the patient with a reference group of young adults and gives a figure that describes how far the patient lies from that reference, and any such number in this course is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the protocol of the service you work in. The measurement is one part of a judgment that also weighs age, previous fractures, medicines, falls and general health, and no single figure decides anything on its own. The responder's task is to know that such a measurement exists, to mention it in the handover when it is known, and to leave the ordering and the interpretation where they belong.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A splint or a cast can become tight as swelling grows inside it, and a bandage that was comfortable an hour ago can become a tourniquet, so the limb is checked again after every change. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, which may permit a constricting bandage, splint or cast to be released by someone authorized to do it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and in this group of patients referral is the rule rather than the exception. A patient with a fragility fracture of the hip, the spine, the pelvis or a joint surface is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, because these injuries need more than a splint. The timing of an operation for a fractured hip is a matter of local protocol and current guidance, and any interval named in this course is an illustration to be checked against the guideline in force where you work. The receiving team needs to know the mechanism, the time, the position in which the limb was found, what was done, and the neurovascular findings before and after each intervention. The part played by the responder is to recognize, to stabilize, to immobilize, to record and to transfer without delay.

Definitive treatment of the bone may include reduction, which restores the position of the broken ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, casting, which holds the position while the bone heals, and surgical fixation, in which a surgeon holds the fragments with metal devices or replaces the worn joint. Each of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a book in this course, which describes only what they are for, what they must achieve and what can go wrong. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique. A responder who meets resistance stops, supports the limb in the position found and escalates, because the decision to proceed belongs to someone qualified to make it.

The second half of definitive treatment is aimed at the skeleton itself, because the fracture that has just been treated is a warning about the fracture that has not yet happened. Whether a patient should take calcium, vitamin D or a medicine that slows the removal of bone is a decision for a physician, and this course gives no substance, no amount, no route and no frequency, because those belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol. What the responder can contribute is the recognition that a fracture happened after a minor injury, that the patient has lost height, that a parent broke a hip, or that the patient has been taking a steroid medicine for years, and the habit of saying so in the handover. Preventing the next fall is part of the same work, and it includes reviewing the medicines that cause drowsiness, checking vision, making the home safer and encouraging strength and balance exercise where the patient is able. The first fracture is the diagnostic event, and the second fracture is the one that must be prevented.

Handling and transport deserve special care in a patient whose bones are fragile and whose skin is thin. A patient who has fallen and whose spine has not been cleared is moved only by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires, because the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so. Pressure injuries begin within a short time on a hard surface, so the patient is padded and lifted rather than dragged, and every contact point is checked during the wait for transport. Fracture of the ribs and of the pelvis makes breathing and coughing painful, so the patient is encouraged to breathe deeply at intervals and is watched for signs of a chest infection. Nothing in this paragraph replaces the manual handling technique that must be practiced with an instructor on a suitable model.

Some patients with fragile bones do not fit the familiar picture, and the responder must keep room for them. A younger adult may have a secondary cause of bone loss, such as a long course of steroid medicine, an eating disorder, an untreated hormonal condition or a period of immobility, and their fracture is as significant as that of an older patient. A child may have a rare condition that weakens bone, and a fracture in a child from a mechanism that seems too small must be reported rather than dismissed, since the same finding may also raise a question about how the injury happened. A patient who lives in a care home may arrive with a fracture that was noticed only when they stopped standing, and the absence of a clear story is not evidence that nothing happened. In all of these patients the sequence is unchanged, and the threshold for imaging and for referral is lower rather than higher.

To summarize, osteoporosis is a disease of bone amount and bone architecture that causes no symptoms until a bone breaks, so the first sign is usually a fragility fracture caused by a force too small to break a healthy skeleton. The responder assesses the scene, the mechanism, the age, the medicines and the history of previous fractures, performs the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, and then examines the limb by looking, feeling and asking the patient to move it without ever forcing it. The neurovascular status is examined before any intervention and repeated after every one, and it is recorded, because a finding that was not written down before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Such a patient is kept warm, handled gently, and splinted in the position found, and a deformed limb is never straightened and an embedded object is never removed. Imaging is ordered and interpreted by a clinician, and a normal radiograph does not exclude a fracture when the examination suggests one, so a patient whose pain persists is reassessed rather than reassured. Fragility fractures of the hip, the spine, the pelvis and the joints are referred to a facility with an operating room and an intensive care unit, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, never from a book. Every number in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, the patient is reassessed after every intervention, and the first fracture is the moment to ask why it happened.

# Chapter 46 — Fragility Fractures in Older Adults

A fragility fracture is a break in a bone that has lost its strength, and the force behind it is often no more than a fall from standing height. The bone gives way before anything violent has happened to the body, so an injury a young person would walk away from leaves an older patient on the floor. The difference between this patient and the patient of the earlier chapters is not the fracture pattern but the body around it. The bone has thinned, the skin has grown thin and dry and tears where it would once only bruise, the heart and lungs have little reserve, and the reflexes that answer a stumble are slower. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names who may perform each act.

Assessment begins before the patient is touched, with the scene and with the story it tells. The lay first aider notes what the patient fell onto, how the limb lies, and whether the patient is awake and breathing, and nothing is moved until that much is known. The next questions decide the course of care. When was the patient last seen well and walking, where do they live, who is with them, and can they get up. The hours spent on the floor matter more than the minutes in the ambulance, because cold, pressure, thirst and fear accumulate while the patient waits, so a patient found after a long night arrives weaker than the fracture alone explains. The fall itself is often the symptom of something that is not an injury, so the responder notes where the patient was, what they were doing, and whether the fall is remembered. The history is taken from the patient when the patient can give it, and from the family or the caregiver when the patient cannot.

The primary survey comes before the limb, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Life comes before limb, because a brain and a heart cannot wait. In the older patient this survey is quick but never superficial, because a fall may be the first sign of an illness that is not an injury at all. The airway is checked and kept clear, the chest is watched for equal movement, and the ribs are felt for tenderness, because a rib broken in a fall can lead to an infection of the chest in the days that follow. The pulse and the skin are felt for shock, the level of consciousness is recorded, and the body is exposed enough to find the second injury that the first one hides. Only then does the assessment turn to the limb, which is looked at, felt and asked to move, and never forced.

Confusion is the finding that makes this chapter necessary, because in an older patient a change in the mind may be the only sign of a fracture. A patient who was lucid at breakfast may be drowsy, restless, frightened or unnaturally quiet after a fall, and that change is treated as an injury until someone qualified has shown that it is not. The confusion may come from the fracture itself, through pain, blood loss and fear, or from a medicine, an infection, a low blood sugar, a stroke or a blow to the head, and it may also be the reason the patient fell in the first place. A patient who repeats a question, who cannot say where they are, or who has stopped speaking needs to be examined rather than reassured, and the lay first aider never attributes confusion to old age. The responder reports what has changed, when it changed, and what the patient was like before, because that comparison tells the clinician whether the mind or the injury came first.

Pain in the older adult is real, and it is far more often underreported than absent. The patient may say discomfort rather than pain, or may say nothing at all and simply stop moving it. A patient with a memory problem may show the pain as agitation or as a face that tightens when the limb is moved, and that expression is a finding worth recording. Pain is measured with the tool the local service uses, at rest and on moving, and it is measured again after every intervention. Relief of pain belongs to the prescriber, because the substance, the amount, the route and the interval belong to the local protocol and to the clinician who knows the patient's kidneys, stomach and heart. The responder measures and records the pain, supports and immobilizes the limb, and reports pain that is not controlled, while the lay first aider gives nothing by mouth unless a protocol authorizes it, and nobody gives a medicine taken from the patient's own supply.

The medicines an older patient takes change both the chance of the injury and the response to it. A medicine that reduces the clotting of the blood means that a fall which would leave a bruise can instead bleed, and the blood may collect in the thigh, in the pelvis, in the wall of the abdomen, or inside the skull, where it is dangerous and cannot be seen. A medicine that slows the heart can hide the rapid pulse that would otherwise announce blood loss. A medicine that lowers the blood pressure, a sedative, or a medicine taken for sleep can make the patient unsteady, and some medicines weaken the bone and thin the skin over years of use. The responder asks what is taken, writes the names down or brings the boxes, and never stops, changes or advises a medicine, because that decision belongs to the prescriber and to the local protocol.

The skin of the frail patient is part of the injury rather than a covering over it. It is thin, it has lost the padding beneath it, and it tears under shearing forces that a younger person would not notice, so a wound over a fracture may have been made by the fall, by a rescuer's hand, or by the tape that held a dressing. Any break in the skin near a broken bone is treated as an open fracture until a clinician has shown otherwise, because the deep tissues may have communicated with the outside even when the wound is small. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm, and refers the patient urgently. No embedded object is ever removed, no exposed bone is ever pushed back into a wound, and no wound is ever explored blindly. Cleaning and closure belong to the operating room, and the nurse or the physician who dresses such a wound before that acts within the protocol of the local service.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. In the older patient this examination is harder, and it is never skipped for that reason. The examiner looks at the color and the warmth of the skin, compares the two sides, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, feels the pulse beyond the injury, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides, and in a patient who cannot answer, the response to a light touch and the change from the previous record carry the information. Sensation may already have been reduced before the injury by diabetes or by disease of the nerves, so the comparison with the other limb is worth more than any single test. A pulse that is present does not exclude a threatened compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and movement, and the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

The hip is the fracture that most often decides whether an older patient walks again, and it deserves the most careful assessment. The patient usually cannot put weight on the leg, and the leg may lie shorter than the other and turned outward, but a fracture whose ends are still packed together can allow the patient to stand and even to take a step, so the ability to walk does not exclude the injury. Pain is felt in the groin or the thigh and is worse when the hip is moved or when the heel is pressed upward with the leg straight. The general condition matters as much as the limb, because a fracture of the hip can bleed a large volume into the thigh and the pelvis, and the older heart may answer with little more than a rising pulse when the patient sits up. The neurovascular examination of the leg is recorded before anything is applied, and the skin over the sacrum, the heels and the elbows is inspected.

Management of the suspected hip fracture in the field is a study in restraint. The limb is supported and immobilized in the position in which it is found and is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks tidy can tear what remained intact. A pillow between the knees keeps the legs from crossing, and the patient is lifted by a team with a device the local protocol authorizes, never by one pair of arms. Traction applied to the leg is not a field treatment for this fracture, and the reduction of a displaced hip belongs to the orthopedic surgeon in an operating room. The definitive decision, whether the bone is held with metal or the joint is replaced, belongs to the surgeon and to the patient, and the part played by the responder is to deliver a warm, comfortable and documented patient early. Any target for the time to an operation, such as a period counted in hours, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the protocol of the local service.

The vertebra is the fragility fracture most often missed, because it may follow no fall at all. A patient who bends to lift a bag, who sits down heavily, or who stumbles onto the buttocks may break one of the blocks of the spine, and the pain is felt in the middle or the lower part of the back, worse on standing and easier on lying flat. Such a fracture is often called a strain for weeks, and the patient simply becomes less willing to go out. The loss of height and a posture that has become bent forward are signs that appear with time, and they speak of fractures that have already happened. A broken vertebra is also a warning about the future, because bone that has broken once is likely to break again, so the treating team arranges the assessment and the prevention that follow. The responder's part is to suspect the injury from the story and the posture, to keep the spine still, and to describe the mechanism in words rather than in a diagnosis.

The spine is treated as unstable until it has been cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and no lone manual handling technique is safe in a patient with a possible injury of the spine. The examination belongs to a clinician, or to a trained responder working within a protocol, and it includes the sensation of the trunk and the limbs, the strength of the legs, the ability to pass urine, and the feeling around the saddle area, where the nerves that serve the bladder and the bowel lie. Numbness there, weakness of both legs, or the inability to pass urine after a fall are findings that stop the responder and send the patient to a facility with imaging and a surgeon without delay. A rigid collar or a board is applied by those trained and authorized to apply it, and it is removed as soon as the clinician who clears the spine permits, because a hard board under a frail patient becomes a pressure injury within a short time. The patient is kept warm, the head is kept in line with the body, and the transfer is made by a team that has agreed on the plan before the lift begins.

The wrist is the commonest fragility fracture of all, and its danger is the nerve that runs through the canal on the palmar side of the joint. A fall onto the outstretched hand leaves the wrist swollen, tender and sometimes deformed, and the deformity may be obvious or almost absent. The skin over the wrist is thin and a small tear is easily missed under the swelling, so it is looked for deliberately. The examiner asks about numbness or tingling in the thumb and the first fingers, tests the sensation of the fingertips, feels the pulse at the wrist and watches the color of the hand, because that nerve can be compressed by bleeding and swelling rather than cut by bone. The fingers and the thumb are moved and the movement is recorded, because a tendon can be injured even when the bone is only slightly out of place. The trained responder supports the position found with a splint or a sling within the local protocol, the hand is left at the level of the heart rather than raised above the head, and the patient is referred for imaging and for the decision about an operation.

The upper end of the humerus is broken by a fall onto the shoulder or by a direct blow, and it is the fracture in which the examination most easily misleads. The patient has pain and swelling around the shoulder and often cannot lift the arm, yet a patient with a fracture may still raise it a little, and a patient whose tendon is torn may not raise it at all, so the loss of movement alone does not separate the two. The examiner looks for bruising that spreads down the arm, feels the bone gently, and tests the sensation over the outer part of the shoulder and the strength of the muscle that lifts the arm away from the body, because the nerve that supplies it runs close to the bone. The trained responder supports the arm in a sling within the local protocol, and a pillow under the elbow keeps the weight of the arm from pulling on the fracture. The decision about an operation belongs to the orthopedic surgeon, and the responder does not test the shoulder by moving it or by lifting the arm.

The pelvis of an older patient can break with the same small force, and the fracture may be described by the patient as pain in the hip, in the groin or in the lower back. A pelvic fracture from a fall in a frail patient is usually a break of the ring rather than the massive disruption seen after a high-energy crash, and it may be stable, but it can still bleed and it makes every movement painful. The responder does not press on the pelvis to see whether it moves, because that test causes pain and adds nothing the field can use. The patient is kept flat and still, the legs are supported, and the warmth and the pressure areas are attended to while help is arranged.
