A pelvic binder is applied by trained responders to the patient with suspected bleeding after a high-energy injury, and whether it helps in the low-energy fracture of a frail patient is a clinical decision for the treating team. Signs of shock are watched for continuously, because a pelvic fracture can bleed into the space behind the abdomen with no swelling that can be seen.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and in the older patient it is done with padding and with patience. The splint is applied over the position found, padded where it presses on bone, and secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. Devices that are rigid and narrow are the ones most likely to injure thin skin, so the skin is inspected before the device is applied, the straps are kept away from bony prominences, and the device is checked for tightness each time the patient is moved. The patient is turned at the interval the local protocol sets, and the skin under every strap and edge is inspected, because a sore that was not recorded on arrival will be attributed to whoever touched the patient last. Casting, the application of plaster or a synthetic shell to hold a bone while it heals, is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and it is never taught from a book, because a cast that is too tight around a swelling limb can cost the limb. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints and cover the patient against cold within the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, and cold is treated as a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort.

Early mobilization and good control of pain are the two measures that most often decide whether the patient walks again. The complications of lying still gather quickly in a frail body, and they include pressure injuries, infection of the chest, clots in the veins of the legs, loss of muscle, constipation and confusion. Each of them is easier to prevent than to treat, and each of them begins in the hours before admission rather than in the days after it. Pain that is not controlled keeps the patient from breathing deeply, from coughing, from moving and from sleeping, so it feeds the very complications that immobility creates. The plan for getting the patient up, for taking weight through the limb and for returning home belongs to the treating team of physician, surgeon, nurse and physiotherapist, and it is decided together with the patient and the family. The part that belongs to the responder is to relieve what can be relieved within the scope of practice, to immobilize well, to move the patient without leaving them on a hard surface, and to hand over a patient who is warm and comfortable.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below so that a second injury is not missed. The hip is a special case, because a fracture there can be invisible on the first radiograph, and a patient who cannot bear weight with a negative image is kept for further study rather than sent home, a decision that belongs to the physician. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging shows bone and soft tissue together and can tell an old fracture of the spine from a new one. The clinician orders a study when its answer will change what is done, and the first aider never orders or interprets an image. A picture is a record of one moment, so the patient is examined and reassessed after it has been taken, and an ordinary image never cancels an abnormal examination.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention and compared with the record, because the comparison is what carries the value rather than any single measurement. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint, the bandage and the cast are checked for tightness and for pressure. The whole patient is checked as well, because a frail patient changes for reasons that have nothing to do with the limb, and a new confusion, a faster rate of breathing, a falling blood pressure or a temperature that has appeared belong in the handover. The findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation are pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, a pulse that cannot be felt, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen. When a compartment syndrome is suspected, the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. Force is not a technique, and a responder who meets resistance stops and asks for help.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and in this population it often decides the rest of the patient's life. A patient with a suspected fracture of the hip, a fracture that has opened the skin, a suspected injury of vessels or nerves, a suspected compartment syndrome, a fracture that enters a joint, or a fracture of the spine is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit by the clinician or by the responder within the local protocol. The handover names the age of the patient, the time of the fall, the ability to walk before it, the medicines, the neurovascular findings before and after each intervention, and the treatment already given. Definitive treatment of the hip may be an operation to hold the bone with metal or to replace the joint, and that choice belongs to the orthopedic surgeon together with the patient and the family, while the assessment of bone strength and the plan that may prevent the next fracture belong to the clinic that follows afterwards. Reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting, which holds the position while the bone heals, are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique of each belongs to supervised clinical training rather than to a book. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed.

More than one injury is common, and the second one is easily missed when attention has fixed on the obvious fracture. The head, the ribs, the hands, the feet and the other hip are examined, and the patient is asked about every region rather than only the painful one, because a frail patient may not volunteer a second source of pain. A pulse that looks ordinary does not exclude bleeding. The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality, and the time of the fall, the last time the patient was seen well, the position in which the limb was found, the state of the skin on arrival, the medicines, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and any change in the condition are written and spoken in a fixed order. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on one another, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. Where this chapter names a time, a distance or a figure, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the protocol of the service in which you work, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions.

To summarize, a fragility fracture is a break caused by little force in a bone that has lost its strength, and in an older patient it may announce itself as confusion, as a refusal to stand, or as pain in the back that is called a strain. Look for the hip that cannot bear weight even when the patient can still take a step, for the wrist that has swollen after a fall onto the hand, for the shoulder that will not lift, for the pelvis that hurts in the groin, and for the spine that hurts on standing and eases on lying. Assess the whole patient before the limb, keep the patient warm, treat the spine as unstable until someone qualified has cleared it, examine the neurovascular status before and after every intervention and write down what you found, immobilize in the position found with padding over the skin, and reassess after everything you do. Never straighten a deformed limb in the field, never remove an embedded object, never push exposed bone back into a wound, never explore a wound blindly, never move a patient with a possible injury of the spine alone, and never give a medicine outside your authorization. Pain is relieved by the prescriber within the local protocol, and reduction, traction and casting belong to supervised clinical training rather than to a book. Call for help early and refer a suspected fracture of the hip, an open fracture, a failing limb or a suspected compartment syndrome to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, and say who the patient was before the fall, because the ability to walk yesterday is part of the picture today. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 47 — Recognizing the Open Fracture

An open fracture is a break in which the bone, or the deep tissue around it, has communicated with the outside world, so that the inside of the limb has become continuous with the environment. The wound may be a long laceration with bone visible in its depth, or a puncture no larger than the head of a pen, and the size of the wound says very little about the severity of the injury beneath it. What makes it different is what the tear has let in, which is organisms from the skin and the ground, foreign material, and air, carried into a space that was sterile a moment before. Such a fracture is contaminated at the instant of the injury, even when the wound looks clean and even when it is washed at once. The open fracture is the injury in which the recognition made by the first person on the scene changes the patient's future more than any later decision does. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The wound and the bone are connected by a story that the responder has to reconstruct from what the patient says and what the limb shows. A wound made from the outside inward, by a blade, by a fall onto a sharp edge, or by a machine, carries surface organisms and foreign material into the limb along its track. A wound made from the inside outward, by the sharp end of the broken bone pushing through the skin and then withdrawing, is a puncture in a limb that may look almost undisturbed, and it is the pattern most often underestimated. In that pattern the bone end has traveled through the skin and then back into the limb, and it may carry a cuff of skin and cloth into the depth of the wound. The observer cannot tell the two patterns apart from the appearance of the wound alone, so any wound on a limb with a suspected fracture is treated as though it communicated with the bone, and the lay first aider does not need to make that judgment, only to report the wound and keep everything still.

A puncture hides a serious injury for three reasons, and each of them can be defeated by a systematic look. The first is position, because a wound in the fold behind the knee, in the armpit, under the edge of a boot, or beneath matted hair is not seen unless the limb is fully exposed and turned. The second is that the wound stops bleeding early and is then hidden by a dressing, a sock, or dried blood, so that the clinician who arrives later sees only a stain. The third is that the patient may not connect a small hole with the pain of a broken bone and may not mention it unless asked where the skin was broken. Full exposure of the limb is the way such a wound is found, with the patient kept warm and the spine protected according to the local protocol, and clothing is cut away rather than pulled over the injury.

Contamination is not a single substance, and the likely organisms differ with the place where the injury happened. Skin carries organisms of its own, so a wound made by a fall on a paved road in a city is contaminated by those organisms and by grit. A wound made in a field, a stable, or a yard where animals are kept carries soil, manure, and plant material, and the organisms that arrive with them are more numerous and harder to treat. A wound in contact with standing water or with clothing soaked in animal waste is contaminated in a way that changes the urgency of referral but never changes the field acts, which remain the same. The responder records what the patient was doing, where the injury happened, and how long ago, because those three facts are asked for first, and describes the wound in the words of what is visible rather than giving it a name. Naming the severity of the contamination is a judgment made later, in the operating room, by the surgeon who can see the depth of the injury.

Every injury in this course is approached through the same order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and an open fracture is the injury in which that order is most easily broken. The temptation is to look at the wound first and to lose sight of the patient, and the result can be a patient who bleeds, becomes cold, or stops breathing while the wound is being examined. Assessment therefore begins with the scene and the mechanism, passes through the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and only then turns to the limb. When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain cannot. The open fracture is a wound that must be covered early, but covering it takes seconds and does not delay the search for a cause of shock. The rest of this chapter follows the order named above, and each step names who may perform it.

Assessment of the open fracture is a history and a look, and the history is unusually valuable because the wound cannot be re-created afterwards. The responder asks the time of the injury, the mechanism, the environment, whether the patient could move the limb afterwards, and whether anyone has touched, washed, packed, or dressed the wound. Medicines that affect bleeding and the ability of tissue to resist infection, illnesses such as diabetes, and the state of protection against tetanus are recorded as facts, because the decisions that follow from them belong to the receiving clinician. In the examination the whole limb is exposed and compared with the other side, the wound is described without probing it, and the position in which the limb was found is written before anyone moves it. Tenderness, swelling, deformity, crepitus, and the wound itself are recorded as findings rather than as a diagnosis, and a finding not written down when it was obtained will be argued about later. The lay first aider reports what was seen and done, the trained responder records the observations in a fixed order, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what the findings mean.

Stabilization of an open fracture begins with bleeding, because an open wound on a limb can bleed in a way that a closed one cannot. The lay first aider presses firmly on the wound with the cleanest material available and keeps pressing, without lifting the material to look underneath it. The trained responder works with personal protective equipment, which protects both the patient and the responder, and covers the wound with a sterile dressing while maintaining pressure. When bleeding cannot be controlled by pressure, a trained responder or paramedic may apply a manufactured tourniquet within the procedures the service authorizes, and the time is written down, because a tourniquet without a record is a hazard of its own; the technique belongs to supervised training. A dressing that has become soaked is reinforced with another dressing rather than lifted away, and the limb is left in the position in which it was found. The patient is kept warm from below as well as above, wet covering is cut away rather than pulled over the injury, and the patient is shielded from wind and from the ground, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort.

Three acts are forbidden in the field, and each is forbidden for a reason that can be said in a single sentence. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be pressing on a torn vessel and its removal may release bleeding that cannot then be stopped. Exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the act pushes contamination deeper and can turn a dirty wound into a deep and dirty wound. An open wound is never explored blindly with a finger or an instrument, because the exploring finger cannot see the vessels and nerves in the depth of the wound and carries its own organisms into it. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing and stabilized in place, and the patient is moved with the dressing and with the object left undisturbed. Definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else, because a wound closed in the field over dead tissue and contamination is a wound that will open again with infection.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and in the open fracture it has a second purpose, because the wound itself may have divided a nerve or a vessel. The examiner looks at the color and temperature of the skin beyond the wound, feels the pulses on both sides and compares them, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, tests sensation, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to a vessel or to the deep tissues, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency, although a pulse may occasionally be absent for a time in a limb that is still viable. Numbness, tingling, weakness, a cold and pale limb, and pain out of proportion to the injury are recorded and reported rather than explained away. The lay first aider observes warmth, color, and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse, or the clinician.

Immobilization of the open fracture follows the same principles as immobilization of any other fracture, with one addition, which is that the dressing must stay where it was placed. A splint is applied over the position in which the limb was found and it includes the joint above and the joint below, because a bone splinted alone can still be moved by the joints at either end. It is padded where it presses on bone, it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and it keeps the wound covered without pressing on it. A deformed limb is not straightened to make the splint fit, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact, and because straightening may turn a closed injury into an open one. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required. Casting, traction, and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of the three is taught from a book in this course, and the neurovascular status is examined and recorded again once the splint is in place.

Imaging is ordered by a clinician and interpreted by a clinician, and it confirms what the examination has already suggested rather than replacing it. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly one that enters a joint, and it is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, and here it is requested only when the question it answers matters more than the delay it causes, with the safety screening for metal and implants belonging to the clinician who orders it. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed. An image is a picture of one moment, and the limb must still be examined afterwards, and in a patient who is unstable the imaging is deferred until the patient is stable enough to travel.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention and compared with the record made before it, and in the open fracture the observations include the wound and the dressing as well as the limb. The examiner repeats the same observations in the same order, which are color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement, and pain, together with the tightness of the splint and whether blood has struck through the dressing. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage, splint, or cast to be released by someone authorized to do it; the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. Reassessment is repeated while the patient waits, and any change is spoken aloud to the team and written in the record, and a wound that begins to smell or to discharge is reported at once.

An open fracture is a different problem from a closed one because contamination has entered a space that the body cannot easily clean, and because the same energy that broke the bone has often destroyed the tissue that would have defended it. Muscle that has been crushed loses its blood supply, and muscle without a blood supply dies and becomes a culture medium rather than a barrier. Periosteum stripped from bone leaves a segment of bone without a blood supply, and dead bone is both unable to heal and unable to resist organisms. The result is that an open fracture has two problems to solve at once, the mechanical problem of a broken bone and the biological problem of contaminated, dead tissue, and the second decides the outcome of the first. Cleaning the wound, removing dead tissue, and deciding what may safely be left in place are surgical acts performed in an operating room with anesthesia, and the number of operations needed cannot be known in advance. Antibiotics and protection against tetanus are decisions of a prescriber, made under the local protocol and never announced as a substance or an amount in this course.

An open fracture that communicates with a joint is more urgent than the same wound in the middle of a bone, and the reason lies in how a joint is built. The surfaces of a joint are covered by cartilage that has no blood supply of its own and is nourished by the fluid inside the joint, and that fluid is an excellent medium for organisms, so infection inside a joint can destroy those surfaces within a short time. A wound over the knee, the elbow, the ankle, or the wrist therefore deserves a high index of suspicion, because the bone may lie close to the skin there and only a thin layer of tissue may stand between the wound and the joint space. The signs that suggest the joint has been entered are a wound that discharges clear or blood-tinged fluid, droplets of fat in the wound fluid, or a joint that fills and becomes tense, but each is unreliable and none can exclude the injury. Air within a joint seen on imaging is a strong finding, and it is a finding made by a clinician rather than by the responder. The responder treats a wound near a joint exactly as a wound over a bone, which is to cover it, to immobilize the limb, to record the neurovascular status, and to refer without delay, because the question of whether the joint was entered is answered in the operating room.

A fracture that happens on a farm, in a stable, or in any place where animals and soil are present is a different problem for reasons that can be stated but not dismissed. Soil and manure carry a wide range of organisms, some of which resist the treatments available in an ordinary hospital, and plant material carries fragments that are not visible on a plain radiograph. A wound that has been dragged through soil or bedding is contaminated along its whole track rather than at its surface, and washing the surface does not reach the depth. Farm machinery crushes rather than cuts, so the wound at the skin may be small while the muscle, the vessels, and the bone beneath are extensively damaged. The responder records the place, the contact with animals, the machinery involved, and the time, because those details change which specialist the patient needs. The wound is covered, nothing is poured into it, and nothing is probed, because the substances that would clean such a wound are used in an operating room under anesthesia and not in a field, so a wound that looks trivial on a farm is referred with the same urgency as one that looks severe.

Delay changes the problem in several ways, and a patient who arrives days after the injury is not a patient for whom the urgency has passed. Swelling that develops over time makes the limb tense and makes the neurovascular examination less reliable, and the wound may have been covered by a dressing that hides its depth. A delay allows contamination to establish itself in the deep tissues and allows dead muscle to become a focus that the body cannot clear, and the infection that follows may involve the bone itself. A wound treated at home with a leaf, a powder, or an oil is recorded as a fact, with the substance named if the patient can name it, and the responder never applies a substance to the wound in response. The patient may have eaten, which matters to the anesthesia team and to nobody in the field, and the time of the last meal is recorded. The patient who waited may also be dehydrated, frightened, and in pain, and that pain is reported to the clinician who decides what may be given, because analgesia is a medical decision and the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber.

Every act in the care of an open fracture has a provider level attached to it, and a chapter that leaves the level unsaid invites someone to act beyond that training. The lay first aider covers the wound with the cleanest material at hand, presses on bleeding that can be controlled, keeps the patient still and warm, and calls for help, and does nothing else. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician or paramedic expose the limb, cover the wound with a sterile dressing, apply pressure, splint within the procedures the service authorizes, record the neurovascular status before and after each intervention, and report the environment and the time. The nurse observes, records, reassesses, prepares the patient for transfer, and carries out the orders that the local protocol and the prescriber authorize, without deciding the substance or the amount of any medicine. The physician examines the wound, orders imaging, decides what analgesia and what protection against infection are needed, and refers the patient onward, while the orthopedic surgeon cleans the wound, removes dead tissue, stabilizes the bone, and closes the wound in the operating room, where the true extent of the injury is finally seen. Reduction, traction, and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique of each belongs to supervised clinical training rather than to this book, and the record is part of the treatment and not a formality that follows it.

Referral is not a single telephone call but a transfer of responsibility, and the open fracture is referred to a facility that has an operating room, imaging, and an intensive care unit. The receiving team needs the age of the patient, the time and mechanism of the injury, the environment, the wound as it was first seen and how it changed, the neurovascular findings before and after each intervention, the treatment already given by anyone, the medicines that matter, and the state of protection against tetanus. The responder says plainly what was done and what was not done, because a transfer that hides a delay repeats that delay in a new place. The patient is kept warm and still during the journey, the wound stays covered, and the limb stays splinted, with the splint checked at intervals and the neurovascular status examined again if the patient's condition changes. If the patient becomes unstable on the way, the nearest facility able to stabilize the patient takes priority over the facility able to repair the fracture, because life comes before limb. The grading of an open fracture describes how much soft tissue has been destroyed and how heavy the contamination is, and it is assigned by the surgeon in the operating room, and whatever grade is finally recorded, the part played by the responder is to have recognized the injury, to have protected the patient, and to have sent the patient to the right place in time.

Two groups of patients deserve a lower threshold for referral, and the reasons are different in each. In a child the bone is more elastic, the periosteum is thicker, and the region near each end of a long bone contains the growth area, so a wound on a child's limb may accompany an injury that is not obvious on a radiograph and may threaten the future growth of that limb, and such a child is referred where a pediatric orthopedic surgeon can be reached. In an older adult the skin is thin and the blood supply to it is poor, so a wound over a fracture heals badly and an infection spreads easily, and a fracture that stretches the skin over a displaced bone end may kill that skin and behave as an open injury even before the skin breaks. A patient whose bone is weakened by disease or by long use of a medicine that thins it may sustain an open fracture in a fall from standing height, and the small energy of such a fall must not be read as a small injury. The same lower threshold applies to a patient who has had surgery on that limb, to a patient with a prosthesis, and to a patient whose sensation is already reduced, because there the usual signs are less reliable. The sequence does not change for any of these patients; only the threshold for imaging, for immobilization, and for referral becomes lower.

A few rules in this chapter exist to prevent the responder from causing a harm that the injury has not yet caused. Force is not a technique, so if an attempt to move or to position a limb meets resistance, the attempt stops and the limb is supported where it lies, because the tissues that resist are the ones that would tear. Nothing is poured into a wound, nothing is placed inside it, and no attempt is made to line up the bone ends, because reduction and traction are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when fragments are caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, or when the responder lacks the training or the equipment. A tourniquet is used only by a provider trained and authorized to use it, and its time is recorded, because a device that saves a life in one minute can cost a limb in the next. The patient is kept warm at every stage, since cold worsens bleeding, weakens the defense against infection, and makes the patient harder to assess. The wound is not closed in the field, and it is not left open to the air either, because a dressing protects the wound and shows the receiving team how much it has bled. Every number quoted here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such figures differ between services, countries, and editions.

To summarize, an open fracture is any break in which the bone or the deep tissue has communicated with the outside, so the whole limb is exposed and inspected before the injury is judged. What to look for is a wound anywhere on an injured limb, soil or plant material inside the wound, a wound near a joint, a delay before care arrived, and an injury that happened among animals, because each changes the urgency without changing the sequence. What to do is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the neurovascular findings recorded before every intervention and repeated after every one. What never to do is to straighten a deformed limb, to remove an embedded object, to push exposed bone back into a wound, to explore a wound blindly, to pour anything into a wound, or to close a wound in the field. What to do next is to cover the wound with a sterile dressing, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, to splint the limb in the position found, to keep the patient warm, and to refer urgently to a facility with an operating room. Antibiotics, analgesia, and protection against tetanus are decisions of a prescriber under the local protocol, and the substance and the amount never come from this course. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 48 — Initial Management of the Open Fracture

The first minutes after an open fracture are spent on a small set of decisions that are simple, few, and unforgiving, because what is done then decides whether the limb can be saved and whether the patient survives to have it repaired. An open fracture is a break in which the bone or the deep tissue around it has communicated with the outside, so the wound has carried organisms, foreign material, and air into a space that was sterile a moment earlier. Initial management is not a small version of definitive treatment; it is a holding action that buys time without adding harm. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows that order and names the provider level for every act it describes. Three problems compete for attention at once, which are bleeding that will not stop, contamination that cannot be cleaned in the field, and a bone that will not hold still, and of the three the first is the one that kills soonest. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, the rule that decides the order is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. Assessment therefore begins with the scene rather than with the wound, and a responder who is not safe cannot help anyone, so traffic, machinery, electricity, fire, and unstable ground are dealt with first and the patient is moved only when moving is safer than staying. The primary survey follows, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and the wound is covered only when the survey allows a pause of a few seconds. A patient with an open fracture may be bleeding from a torn vessel in the limb, may be bleeding from another injury that has not been looked for, or may be bleeding nowhere that can be seen, and the last of those is the most dangerous because a break of a large bone can hide a liter of blood inside a thigh. Exposure means that the whole patient is examined, and it is done with the patient kept warm, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort.

The history of an open fracture is unusually valuable, because the wound cannot be re-created and the story of how it was made explains what is inside it. The responder asks when the injury happened, what made it, where it happened, and whether the patient was in contact with soil, manure, standing water, or machinery, because those facts tell the receiving surgeon which organisms to expect. It matters whether the wound was made from the outside inward by a blade or a sharp edge, or from the inside outward by the sharp end of the bone, although the two cannot be told apart by looking and any wound on an injured limb is treated as though it reached the bone. The patient is asked whether the limb could be moved afterwards, whether any part of it felt numb or dead, and whether anyone has washed, packed, dressed, or poured anything into the wound, and every answer is written down as a fact rather than as an opinion. Medicines that affect bleeding, illnesses such as diabetes, previous surgery on the limb, and the state of protection against tetanus are recorded, because the decisions that follow from them belong to the receiving clinician. The lay first aider gives the story in plain words, the trained responder takes a structured history in a fixed order, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what the story means.

The examination of the limb begins with looking, because so much of what matters is visible if the limb is fully exposed. Clothing is cut away rather than pulled over the injury, the limb is compared with the other side, and the position in which it was found is written before anyone moves it. The wound is described in the words of what is seen, which are its length in centimeters, its edges, whether it is bleeding, whether it discharges, whether bone or tendon is visible in its depth, and whether foreign material such as grit, cloth, or plant matter lies within it. That description is a record of findings and not a diagnosis, and no name for the severity of the wound is invented by the person who describes it. Feeling is confined to the parts of the limb away from the wound, because pressure on the wound is painful and because a finger that enters the wound carries organisms into a space that sees no light and cannot be cleaned. The lay first aider reports only what can be seen from outside, and the examination of the wound itself belongs to the physician or to the orthopedic surgeon.

Three acts are forbidden in the field, and each one is forbidden for a reason that can be said plainly. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be pressing on a torn vessel and its removal can release bleeding that no one can then stop, so the object is left where it lies, the wound is covered around it, and the patient travels with it. Exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the act drives contamination deeper into the limb and turns a contaminated wound into a deep and contaminated one, so the bone end is covered instead. An open wound is never explored blindly with a finger or an instrument, because the exploring finger cannot see the vessels and nerves that lie in the depth of the wound and carries its own organisms in with it. Nothing is poured into the wound either, since the substances that clean a wound are used in an operating room under anesthesia and in a controlled setting, and a wound that has already been treated at home with a leaf, a powder, or an oil is reported as it is found. No attempt is made to close a wound in the field, because closing a wound over dead tissue and contamination traps the infection inside and produces a wound that will open again.

Bleeding is the first thing stabilized, because an open wound on a limb can bleed in a way that a closed one cannot, and because the patient who bleeds is the patient who dies first. The lay first aider presses firmly on the wound with the cleanest material at hand, keeps pressing, and does not lift the material to look underneath it, since looking interrupts the pressure that is doing the work. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician work with personal protective equipment, which protects the responder and the patient both, and they cover the wound with a sterile dressing while maintaining pressure. A dressing that becomes soaked is reinforced with another dressing placed on top rather than removed, and the amount of blood on the dressing is reported, because a dressing that has been lifted has told the receiving team nothing and has cost the patient blood. When pressure cannot control bleeding, a trained responder or paramedic may apply a manufactured tourniquet within the procedures the service authorizes, and the time of application is written down at once, because a tourniquet without a record is a hazard of its own. The technique of applying a tourniquet belongs to supervised training and to the local protocol, and this course does not teach it from a book.

The sterile covering is a simple act that is often done badly, and the reason it matters is that a covered wound is protected from further contamination and shows the receiving team how much it has bled. A sterile dressing from a sealed pack is the standard, and the responder opens it without touching the surface that will lie against the wound. When no sterile dressing is available, the cleanest material at hand is used, and the responder does not delay transport in a search for a better one, because minutes of bleeding and hours of contamination cost more than the difference between one clean covering and another. The dressing is placed over the wound and held there, and if an object is embedded in the wound the dressing is built around the object rather than pressed onto its tip. The covering does not replace the pressure and it does not replace the splint, because the aim is to protect the wound, to keep the bone ends from moving, and to reach a surgeon. The dressing stays in place until a clinician in an appropriate setting removes it, since each examination of the wound in the field raises the risk of contamination and requires the covering to be renewed.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is recorded in writing, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin beyond the wound, feels the pulses on both sides and compares them, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and tests sensation with a light touch on each side. The patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes, and any movement that was present a moment earlier and is now gone is treated as an emergency rather than as a curiosity. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to a vessel, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency, although a pulse may occasionally be absent for a time in a limb that is still viable. Numbness, tingling, weakness, a cold and pale limb, and pain out of proportion to the injury are recorded and reported rather than explained away, and a sign that is unreliable in one patient may be reliable in another, so the comparison with the other side is what carries the weight. The lay first aider observes warmth, color, and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse, or the clinician.

Immobilization follows the neurovascular examination and precedes any movement of the patient, and its purpose is to keep the bone ends from moving so that they cannot tear what is still intact. The limb is splinted in the position in which it was found, and a deformed limb is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear them, and because straightening can turn a closed injury into an open one. The splint includes the joint above and the joint below the fracture, since a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joints at either end, and it is padded where it presses on bone. It is secured firmly enough to hold the limb without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and it covers the wound without pressing on the dressing or on any object that has been left in place. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the nurse checks the skin, the dressing, and the circulation at intervals during the wait. The physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace, or a surgical fixation, and casting, traction, and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, never from a book.

Whatever is used as a splint, the limb is checked after it is in place rather than only before. A commercial splint, a padded board, a folded magazine, a sling, or the body of the patient can each serve, and an improvised device is checked more often because it shifts and because its padding is usually thinner. Cold is treated as a complication in its own right, so the patient is insulated from the ground, wet clothing is cut away, and the covering is applied over the splint rather than under it. The spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a patient with a suspected spinal injury is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. During the wait and during the journey, the same observations are repeated in the same order, which are color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement, and pain, together with the tightness of the splint and whether blood has struck through the dressing. Any change in those observations is spoken aloud to the team and written in the record, because a change that is not communicated is a change that does not exist for the person who takes over.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it never replaces the examination, the covering, or the splint. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly one that enters a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues including ligaments, cartilage, and muscle, and either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done. The decision to image and the interpretation of the image belong to a clinician trained to make them, while the lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging and the trained responder does not decide which study is needed. An image is a picture of one moment, so the limb is examined and the findings recorded again after the picture has been taken. In a patient who is bleeding, cold, or losing consciousness, imaging is deferred until the patient is stable enough to travel, because the picture can wait and the patient cannot.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment rather than by the injury. The complication this course fears most in a limb that has been splinted or cast is a rise in pressure inside a compartment, where muscle and nerve are enclosed by bone and fascia with very little room. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects it does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, pain that is worse when the fingers or the toes are stretched, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. Where the local protocol permits and someone authorized is present, a constricting bandage, splint, or cast is released, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently. A pulse that remains present does not exclude a compartment syndrome, and the responder who waits for the pulse to disappear has waited too long.

Antibiotics and protection against tetanus follow the local protocol, and this course gives no substance, no amount, and no schedule, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from a book. The decision belongs to the physician or to another prescriber authorized by the local protocol, and the finding that makes it urgent is an open wound contaminated by soil, manure, or standing water, a wound made by machinery, a wound neglected for hours or days, or a wound that lies over a joint. The time from the injury to the first appropriate treatment matters, and the receiving team will ask for it, so the time of the injury and the time of arrival are written down and handed over. The state of protection against tetanus is recorded as a fact, which means whether the patient has been immunized, when the last protection was given if the patient knows, and whether any record of it exists, and the clinician decides what is required. The nurse prepares the patient, carries out the orders that the local protocol and the prescriber authorize, and never decides the substance or the amount, while the responder in the field gives nothing by any route. Antibiotics given before the wound is cleaned and the dead tissue removed do not replace the operation, and nobody in the field should believe that they do.

What the operating room does is the definitive treatment that the field cannot provide, and the task of the responder is to deliver the patient to it without having made the injury worse. Cleaning the wound, removing dead and contaminated tissue, and washing the surfaces under anesthesia are surgical acts, and the number of operations needed cannot be known in advance because dead tissue declares itself over the following days. Stabilizing the bone may require a cast, a brace, a metal device, or an external frame, and the choice belongs to the orthopedic surgeon who can see the wound from the inside. Reducing a fracture means restoring the position of the bone ends, and traction means holding them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and both are used in the operating room or under close supervision with imaging at hand. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. In each of those situations an attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique, so if a movement meets resistance the attempt stops and the limb is supported where it lies.

Referral is a transfer of responsibility rather than a telephone call, and an open fracture is referred to a facility that has an operating room, imaging, and an intensive care unit. The receiving team needs the age of the patient, the time and mechanism of the injury, the environment in which it happened, the wound as it was first seen and how it has changed, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, what anyone has already done to the wound, the medicines that matter, and the state of protection against tetanus. The responder says plainly what was done and what was not done, because a transfer that hides a delay repeats that delay in a new place. The patient is kept warm and still during the journey, the wound stays covered, the limb stays splinted, and the splint is checked at intervals and the neurovascular status examined again if the condition changes. If the patient becomes unstable on the way, the nearest facility able to stabilize the patient takes priority over the facility able to repair the fracture, because life comes before limb. A patient who arrives late is not a patient for whom the urgency has passed, and the transfer is arranged with the same speed as though the injury had just happened.

Every act in the initial management of an open fracture has a provider level attached to it, and a chapter that leaves the level unsaid invites someone to act beyond that training. The lay first aider presses on bleeding that can be controlled, covers the wound with the cleanest material available, keeps the patient warm and still, and calls for help, and does nothing else. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician or paramedic expose the limb, cover the wound with a sterile dressing under personal protective equipment, maintain pressure, apply a manufactured tourniquet only where the service authorizes it and the training has been completed, splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and record the neurovascular status before and after each intervention. The nurse observes, records, reassesses, prepares the patient for transfer, and carries out the orders that the local protocol and the prescriber authorize, without deciding the substance or the amount of any medicine. The physician examines the wound, orders imaging, decides what analgesia and what protection against infection are needed, and refers the patient onward, while the orthopedic surgeon cleans the wound, removes dead tissue, stabilizes the bone, and closes the wound in the operating room where the true extent of the injury is finally seen. Where this chapter names a provider, it names the level at which the act is normally learned and certified, and the law of the country in which the reader works decides what may be done without supervision.

The record is part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and it is written while the patient is in front of the responder rather than reconstructed later. The time of the injury and the time of each intervention, the position in which the limb was found, the appearance of the wound as it was first seen, the neurovascular findings before and after every act, and any change in the condition of the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one. The record does not name a severity grade, because grading an open fracture is a judgment made by the surgeon who can see how much tissue has been destroyed and how heavy the contamination is. A wound that begins to smell, that discharges, or that bleeds more heavily is reported at once rather than noted for later. Where a number appears in this chapter it is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because times, distances, and thresholds differ between services, countries, and editions. Everything described here is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on one another, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision.

A few errors are so common and so damaging that they deserve to be named in the plainest words. Lifting a dressing to look underneath it interrupts the pressure that was controlling the bleeding, and it shows the receiving team a wound that has been disturbed twice. Straightening a deformed limb to make a splint fit can tear a vessel or a nerve that the injury had left intact, and it can convert a closed fracture into an open one. Pushing exposed bone back into a wound drives contamination inward, and removing an embedded object can release bleeding that cannot then be stopped. Closing a wound in the field traps dead tissue and organisms inside, and giving an antibiotic instead of arranging the operation treats the anxiety of the moment rather than the wound. Force is not a technique, so an attempt that meets resistance stops at once, and every intervention is followed by the same observations in the same order, because the treatment is the most likely cause of the next problem.

To summarize, the initial management of an open fracture is a short sequence of protective acts, and the sequence is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What to look for is a wound anywhere on an injured limb, bleeding that will not stop, bone or tendon in the depth of the wound, soil or plant material inside it, a wound near a joint, a limb that is deformed, and any loss of pulse, sensation, or movement. What to do is to make the scene safe, to work through the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, to cover the wound with a sterile dressing under personal protective equipment, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, to record the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, to splint the limb in the position found with the joint above and the joint below included, to keep the patient warm, and to arrange urgent transfer to a facility with an operating room, imaging, and an intensive care unit. What never to do is to straighten a deformed limb, to remove an embedded object, to push exposed bone back into a wound, to explore a wound blindly, to pour anything into a wound, to close a wound in the field, or to believe that an antibiotic replaces the operation. Antibiotics, analgesia, and protection against tetanus follow the local protocol and belong to the prescriber, and this course gives no substance, no amount, and no route. Reduction, traction, and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique of each belongs to supervised clinical training rather than to this book. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 49 — Principles of Dislocation Management

A dislocation is the injury in which the surfaces of a joint lose contact with each other, and it is best understood as an injury of the whole joint, because the capsule tears, at least one ligament tears, and the displaced bone end comes to rest where vessels and nerves are lying. The direction in which the bone end has moved decides which structures are at risk, and the state of the skin decides how urgent the injury has become. This chapter follows the order this course follows everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

A joint whose surfaces are only partly out of contact is described as subluxated, so the difference between a subluxation and a complete dislocation is one of degree rather than of kind. Many dislocated joints also tear the rim of the socket or pull a small piece of bone away with the capsule, which makes the injury a fracture and a dislocation at once, and that combination changes both the urgency and the plan. A joint can also slip back into place before anyone arrives, which is called a spontaneous reduction, so the examiner is left with a swollen, tender joint and no clear account of what happened. The absence of a visible deformity therefore proves very little, because the displaced bone end may already have returned to a position in which it still causes harm. A joint that has reduced by itself is examined, recorded, and referred in the same way as one that is still out of place.

Time matters in a dislocation for three separate reasons, and each of them runs on its own clock. The first is the blood supply of the bone end, because a bone that is levered out of its socket can stretch or tear the vessel that feeds it, and a bone end that loses its supply may die, which is called avascular necrosis. The second is the nerve and the vessel that travel against the bone, because they are compressed or torn by the displaced bone end and may recover once the pressure is relieved but not if the relief comes days later. The third is the cartilage, because joint surfaces that stay out of contact suffer changes that lead to pain and stiffness long after the injury has healed. Teaching often attaches a number of hours to the window before these risks rise, and any such figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services and editions.

Before anything is done about the joint, the patient is assessed, and the assessment begins with the scene and with the mechanism of injury. The question that comes first is whether the patient is stable enough to be examined at all, and the steps of that primary survey are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. A patient who has fallen from a height may have injuries to the head, the chest, the abdomen, or the spine that matter more than any joint, and the principle that decides the order of work is that life comes before limb. The lay first aider looks for danger, calls for help, and does not move the patient unless there is an immediate threat. The trained first responder, the emergency medical technician, and the paramedic carry out the survey within the procedures their service authorizes, and only when the patient is stable does attention turn to the injured joint.

The history of a dislocated joint is short but worth taking carefully, and several of its details change what happens next. The time of the injury matters, because the length of time a joint has been out of place bears on the urgency of reduction, and the mechanism matters, because a fall onto an outstretched hand produces a different pattern of injury from a direct blow. The number of previous dislocations matters, because a joint that has dislocated before comes out again more easily, and a joint that has already been operated on behaves differently again. The illnesses and medicines of the patient matter, because joint disease, a connective tissue condition, and medicines that thin the bone all change the picture.

Examining the joint itself means looking, feeling, and asking the patient to move, and it never means forcing the limb to prove a point. The examiner looks at the shape of the limb compared with the other side, at the skin, and at whether the patient is holding the limb in a guarded position. Feeling is done gently, over the joint and along the bone above and below it, because tenderness far from the joint suggests a second injury. Asking the patient to move is different from moving the patient, and a joint is never put through a range of motion by the examiner in the field, because the movement can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. Comparing the two sides is the single most useful habit, because the patient's own healthy limb is the best available reference. The lay first aider observes and reports, while the formal examination of the joint belongs to the trained responder and to the clinician.

Stabilization of a dislocated joint in the field is a small set of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found and is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with direct pressure, and an embedded object is never removed, because it may be plugging the hole in the vessel beneath it. An open wound is covered with a sterile dressing and is never explored blindly, and cold is treated as a complication of trauma, so the patient is insulated from the ground and the limb is kept warm while it waits. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands or with a pillow, while the trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes.

The neurovascular examination is the step this course will not allow anyone to skip, and in a dislocation it is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin beyond the injury, feels the pulse beyond the injury, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes that the injured joint controls. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and numbness, tingling, or the loss of a movement is recorded in the patient's own words as far as possible. The result is written before the support is applied and again after it is applied, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. An intact pulse does not exclude serious injury to a vessel or a compartment syndrome, so a pulse that is present is reassuring rather than conclusive. The lay first aider observes color, warmth, and the ability to move and to feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician.

The findings that suggest damage to a vessel are pallor, coolness, a pulse that is weaker than on the other side, and pain that is out of proportion to the injury. The findings that suggest damage to a nerve are numbness, tingling, weakness, and the loss of a movement that was present before. Which structures are at risk depends on the joint, because the nerve and the vessel lie against the bone in a different place at the shoulder than at the elbow, the hip, the knee, or the ankle. Knowing which one is most often injured at a particular joint tells the examiner what to test and what to watch, and that interpretation belongs to the clinician, while the responder records what is found and reports it without delay.

An associated fracture is looked for in every dislocation, and the search begins with the assumption that one is present rather than with the hope that one is not. The reason is simple physics, because the energy that dislocates a joint also acts on the rim of the socket and on the tendons that insert near it, so an avulsion of a small piece of bone is a common companion of a dislocation. A fracture may also be produced by the dislocation itself, as the displaced bone end strikes the edge of the socket on its way out, and the fracture may then be the reason the joint will not go back in. None of this can be told apart by looking and feeling alone, and a joint that seems to have simply come out of place may conceal a fragment lying between the surfaces. The responder therefore treats every dislocation as though a fracture were present, while the clinician confirms it with imaging.

When a dislocation and a fracture are present together, the injury is described as a fracture dislocation, and it is managed differently from a simple dislocation in almost every respect, because a fragment of bone may sit in the way of the returning bone end. An open dislocation, in which the joint has communicated with the outside, is contaminated even when the wound looks small and clean, because the skin carries organisms that reach the joint in the moment of the injury. The responder's part is to cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control the bleeding that can be controlled, examine and record the neurovascular status, immobilize the limb in the position found, keep the patient warm, and arrange urgent transfer. Blind exploration of the wound adds harm, exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, and definitive cleansing and closure belong to the operating room.

Analgesia has a place in the care of a dislocation, and that place is decided by a prescriber rather than by the responder or by the patient's family. Pain relief is not a comfort measure alone, because severe pain produces muscle spasm that holds the joint out of place, and because pain masks the very findings that the neurovascular examination depends on. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, escalating, or out of proportion to the injury, and such pain is treated as a sign of a developing problem. The lay first aider does not give any medicine, and the trained responder gives only what the local protocol authorizes that level of provider to give, while sedation and strong analgesia belong to a physician. No dose, no route, and no regimen is given in this course, because the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber.

Imaging is ordered when the answer it gives will change what is done, and its place in the sequence of a dislocation is dictated by that purpose. The first study is usually a plain radiograph, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below the injured one so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint, and it is often the study that reveals a fragment lying within the joint surfaces. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons, and muscle. Each of these studies is requested by a clinician trained to interpret it, while the lay first aider never orders and never interprets imaging.

Whether reduction is needed urgently is a clinical decision, and it is made on findings. The findings that place a dislocation in the urgent group are a limb with a failing pulse, a limb with a new and persistent nerve deficit, a joint whose displacement threatens the skin from within, an open dislocation, and a joint whose blood supply is known to be fragile. A hip dislocation and a knee dislocation are treated urgently in most services for this reason, and any figure quoted for how quickly such a joint must be reduced is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A dislocation that has been out of place for a long time, even without a failing pulse, is also treated with urgency, because the risk to the cartilage grows with every hour. The responder's task is not to make this decision but to recognize the findings that make it urgent and to move the patient toward the person who will make it.

Reduction is not attempted when the source lists a contraindication, and each contraindication carries its own reason. A suspected complex fracture dislocation is one, because a fragment may be caught between the surfaces and the attempt may drive it deeper or break more bone, and entrapped fracture fragments are another, for the same reason. Significant neurovascular compromise that needs a specialist is a third, because the specialist may need to repair a vessel, and a reduction performed on the way to the operating room may destroy the tissue that was to be repaired. An open injury is a fourth, because the wound must be managed in an operating room. An unclear diagnosis, inadequate training or equipment, and a previous failed attempt complete the list, and in every one of those situations the correct act is to stop rather than to try harder. Force is not a technique, and resistance during an attempt is a signal to stop and to escalate.

Reduction within the limits of scope of practice means that the person who reduces a joint is the person the local protocol and the law authorize to do it. Reduction is the act of restoring the joint surfaces to their normal relationship, and it is done to relieve the pressure on the vessels and on the nerves, to restore the blood supply to the bone end, to protect the cartilage, and to make the joint stable again. It is performed by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon, or by an emergency physician or an advanced practitioner whose service has granted that privilege, and it is not performed by the lay first aider, the trained first responder, or the emergency medical technician. The technique itself, with its holds, its direction of pull, and its timing, is learned under supervision on real patients and is not taught from a book in this course or in any other. A joint that cannot be reduced safely in one place is moved to another.

What can go wrong during a reduction is worth stating plainly, because a responder who understands the risks will not be tempted to improvise. The bone can break during the attempt, particularly when it is fragile or when a fragment is already present, and a closed injury can be converted into an open one. A nerve or a vessel that was stretched can be torn, the cartilage can be scuffed, and a fragment can be pushed into the joint. A reduction performed without adequate relaxation may fail and leave the joint worse than before, and repeated attempts are more dangerous than the first one. The reason this course describes the risks rather than the method is that the method belongs to supervised clinical training, and the risks are what a listener needs in order to recognize when to call for help instead of acting.

The setting in which a reduction is performed is part of the decision, not a detail that follows it. Adequate lighting, monitoring of the patient's breathing and circulation, suction, oxygen, and a plan for what will be done if the attempt fails are the ordinary requirements of a procedure that may suddenly become an emergency. Muscle relaxation is often what makes a reduction possible at all, and the medicines that produce it belong to a physician working under the local protocol. In some services a large joint is reduced in an operating room with an orthopedic surgeon present, and in others it is reduced in an emergency department by a physician with the equipment the protocol requires.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and in the management of a dislocation it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison rather than any single measurement that has value. The examiner checks the color, the warmth, the pulse, the sensation, the movement, and the pain, and checks the support or the splint for tightness. The findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation are pain that increases instead of settling, pain that is out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen. A pulse that disappears after a reduction is an emergency, and so is a limb that becomes pale and cool, because both suggest that the reduction has disturbed the circulation rather than restored it.

Compartment syndrome is the complication this course fears most after a dislocation, and the reason is that it can begin quietly and progress while everyone is reassured by a pulse. The pressure inside a closed space of the limb rises after the injury or after the reduction, and the flow through the smallest vessels fails even while a large pulse at the wrist or the ankle can still be felt. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and time is muscle, so a responder who suspects it does not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late. The constricting bandage, splint, or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol and by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is kept warm and referred urgently. The finding that most often gives the diagnosis away is pain when the muscles of the compartment are stretched, and that test is one a clinician performs.

Immobilization of a dislocated joint means preventing movement of the joint and of the bones above and below it, because a joint that is splinted alone can still be moved by the limb around it. The support is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position in which the joint was found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, and a folded magazine, a padded board, or the body of the patient can each serve the purpose. After a reduction the joint is often unstable in one direction, and the support is chosen to block that direction, which is a clinical judgment rather than a household one. A support that is too tight is as dangerous as no support at all, because it can produce the very compartment syndrome the immobilization was meant to prevent. The responder checks the fingers or the toes after the support is applied and records what was found.

The scope of practice for immobilization differs by provider level, and it is worth naming at each step. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands and with whatever padding is at hand, keeps the patient warm, and waits for help. The trained first responder, the emergency medical technician, and the paramedic apply splints and supports within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. The nurse prepares the materials, monitors the limb, and reports changes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace, a sling, or a surgical fixation. Casting is a technique learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and it is not taught from a book. The position in which a joint is held after a reduction, and the length of time it is held there, are clinical decisions as well, and every figure quoted for that time is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline.

Imaging again after a reduction is not optional, and the reason is that the clinical appearance of a reduced joint can be reassuring when the radiograph is not. The joint surfaces may be back in contact while a fragment lies between them, or the reduction may be incomplete in a way that is not visible from outside, or a fracture that was hidden before the reduction may now be obvious. The post-reduction study is taken in the same directions as the pre-reduction study so that the two can be compared, and it is interpreted by the clinician responsible for the care of the patient. The responder's part is to keep the limb supported and the patient still while the image is taken, and to report any change in the neurovascular findings. Reassessment continues after the imaging, because the sequence followed in this course is not a line that ends but a loop that returns to the patient.
