Referral is the final step of the sequence for most dislocations, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. The patients who are referred without delay include the one with an open dislocation, the one with a fracture dislocation, the one with a nerve or vessel deficit that has not recovered, the one whose joint will not stay reduced, and the one who arrives long after the injury. The receiving facility needs imaging, an operating room, and access to an intensive care unit, because a dislocation can become a vascular emergency within minutes of arrival. The receiving team is given the same story that the record tells, with the time of the injury, the position found, the findings before and after each intervention, and the treatment already given, because a referral that omits what was done invites the next team to repeat it. A dislocation of the spine is treated differently from a dislocation of a limb, since it is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear the spine has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe.

Children are a separate case, because the bone of a child is still growing, and the end of a long bone contains a growth region that can be injured without the bone breaking. The threshold for immobilization and for referral is lower in a child, and the threshold for reduction is higher, because a careless attempt can change the growth of the limb for years. An older adult presents a different difficulty, since a bone that has lost density can break with little force, and a joint that has been replaced with a prosthesis can dislocate in a way that belongs to the surgeon who knows the implant. A patient who has dislocated the same joint several times is describing a third kind of problem. The plan in all three of these groups is made by a clinician, while the responder protects the limb, keeps the patient warm, and moves the patient toward that person.

Several errors recur in this work, and each of them has a reason attached. The first is straightening a deformed limb in the field, which risks the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone, and the second is attempting a reduction more than once after a failed attempt, which adds damage with every repetition. The third is delaying referral in order to obtain an image that will not change the immediate plan, and the fourth is failing to record the neurovascular findings, which makes it impossible to know afterwards whether a deficit is new. The fifth is attributing a new numbness or a new weakness to the original injury without having looked for it before the intervention. The patient is told what to watch for, which includes increasing pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes pale or cool.

To summarize, a dislocation is an injury of the whole joint, so the capsule, the ligaments, and often a piece of bone are injured with it, and the displaced bone end rests where vessels and nerves are lying. The sequence is always the same, which is to assess the patient, to examine and record the neurovascular status before and after every intervention, to look for an associated fracture, to relieve pain within the limits of the prescriber and the protocol, to image when the answer will change what is done, to decide whether reduction is urgent, to reduce only within the scope of practice that authorizes it, to reassess, to immobilize, and to image again afterwards. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction, and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught between them, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the training or the equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed. Compartment syndrome is treated as an emergency, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, cold is treated as a complication, and the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 50 — Major Dislocations

A dislocated joint is an injury in which the surfaces that should glide over one another lose contact, and at the major joints it can cost a limb within hours. What it costs depends on where the bone end comes to rest, because that is where the vessels and the nerves are lying. This chapter asks of every major joint three questions, whether the injury threatens the limb, whether it threatens a nerve, and whether it can wait for definitive care. The order of work is the order this course follows everywhere, to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Three clocks start when a major joint leaves its socket, and each runs at its own speed. The first is the clock of the blood supply, because the bone end may have torn the vessel that feeds it, and a bone end that loses its supply can die, which is called avascular necrosis. The second is the clock of the nerve and the vessel that lie against the bone, because they may recover once the pressure is relieved but not if the relief comes days later. The third is the clock of the cartilage, because surfaces out of contact undergo changes that cause pain and stiffness long afterwards. Teaching attaches a number of hours to the first two clocks, and any such figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Ranking the joints by urgency rests on which structure is trapped rather than on how dramatic the deformity looks. The knee, the hip and the ankle threaten the whole limb within hours, because at each of them a major artery passes close to the bone. The shoulder, the elbow and the wrist threaten a nerve more often than the limb, because a nerve lies in a narrow passage that the displaced bone end can compress. The small joints of the fingers, the thumb and the patella usually wait, provided the skin is intact, the pulse is present and no fragment is caught between the surfaces. Waiting is a decision about the clock and never a permission to leave the patient unexamined.

Assessment comes first, and it begins with the scene and with the mechanism of injury. The mechanism matters, because a fall onto an outstretched hand, a blow to the knee and a collision against a dashboard each produce their own pattern of damage. The history adds the age of the patient, the time of the injury, any earlier dislocation of the same joint, and the illnesses that change the strength of bone. The primary survey follows, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because a patient with a dislocated hip may also have injuries to the head or the spine. Life comes before limb whenever two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands. The lay first aider looks for danger and sends for help, while the trained first responder and the emergency medical technician work within the procedures their service authorizes.

Stabilization of a dislocated joint in the field is a short list of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. A deformed limb is supported in the position found and is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what was intact. Pulling a limb straight can also convert a closed dislocation into an open one. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with direct pressure, and an open wound is covered with a sterile dressing and never explored blindly. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be plugging the hole in the vessel beneath it. Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated and the injured part is kept warm. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands or with a pillow, while the trained responder and the paramedic may splint within the equipment their service authorizes.

The neurovascular examination is the step this course will not allow anyone to skip, and at a dislocated joint it is done before any intervention and repeated after every one. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin beyond the injury, feels the pulse beyond the injury, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is compared between the two sides, and numbness, tingling or the loss of a movement is recorded in the words of the patient. The result is written before the support is applied and again afterwards, because a finding not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. The joint tells the examiner what to test, since the axillary nerve is at risk at the shoulder, the median nerve crosses the wrist, the sciatic nerve lies behind the hip, and the peroneal nerve is the one to watch at the knee.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured joint and of the bones above and below it, because a supported joint can still be moved by the limb around it. The support is padded where it presses on bone, applied over the position in which the joint was found, and secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation. A folded magazine, a padded board or the body of the patient can each serve, though an improvised device shifts and must be checked more often. A support that is too tight is more dangerous than none, because it can produce the very compartment syndrome that immobilization was meant to prevent. The lay first aider holds and pads, the nurse checks the fingers or the toes and reports any change, the paramedic applies splints within the equipment the service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required.

Imaging is ordered when the answer it gives will change what is done, and its place follows the examination rather than replacing it. The first study is usually a plain radiograph, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break and often reveals a fragment lying between the joint surfaces, while magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues. A joint that has been put back is imaged again afterwards, because the surfaces may be in contact while a fragment remains trapped. The study is requested and interpreted by a clinician trained to do it, and the lay first aider never orders and never interprets an image.

Reassessment is done after every intervention, and at a dislocated joint it catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison rather than any single measurement that carries the value. The examiner checks the color, the warmth, the pulse, the sensation, the movement and the pain, and checks the support for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that turns pale and cool are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. When compartment syndrome is suspected, the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is kept at the level of the heart rather than above it, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some joints cannot be managed where the patient lies. The patients moved without delay are the one with an open dislocation, the one with a fracture and a dislocation together, and the one whose pulse or nerve deficit has not recovered. The receiving facility needs imaging, an operating room and access to an intensive care unit, and the receiving team is given the story the record tells. Reduction, traction and casting, which restore the joint surfaces and hold them while the tissues heal, are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique is not taught from a book. A reduction is not attempted when the surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is trapped, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when training or equipment is lacking, or when an earlier attempt has failed. Force is not a technique, and resistance during an attempt is a signal to stop and to escalate.

The shoulder is the joint that dislocates most often, because its socket is shallow and it is held mainly by soft tissue rather than by bone. In most cases the bone end leaves toward the front, so the arm is held away from the body and the patient resists any attempt to bring it in. The nerve most often injured winds around the surgical neck of the bone, and the finding is numbness over the outer shoulder with weakness when the patient lifts the arm from the side. That nerve is recorded before anything is done and again after the joint has been put back, because a deficit that appears afterwards is an emergency. The shoulder may also tear the rim of the socket or dent the head of the bone, and none of that can be told apart by looking and feeling alone.

The age of the patient changes what a shoulder dislocation costs, and the change alters the threshold for referral. In a young patient the ligaments are strong and the force is violent, so the rim of the socket tears and the joint is likely to come out again, sometimes repeatedly. In an older patient the tissues are more brittle, so a dislocation that looks less violent may tear the tendons that raise the arm, injure the nerve far more often, and even tear the artery that supplies the arm. A shoulder that has dislocated before comes out again with less force each time, so that detail belongs in the history. The responder supports the arm in the position found, records the neurovascular findings and transfers the patient, and no attempt is made to put the shoulder back in the field, even when the deformity is familiar.

At the elbow the bone end usually leaves toward the back, and because the joint lies between the arm and the forearm it is surrounded by the nerves and the artery that cross its front. The median nerve is the one most often injured, and the ulnar and radial nerves are exposed as well, so the examination tests the ability to make a fist, to spread the fingers and to straighten the wrist. The artery that supplies the whole forearm passes in front of the joint, so a lost or weakened pulse at the wrist after an elbow dislocation is an emergency of the limb. The joint sits in a tight envelope of muscle and fascia, so swelling raises the pressure inside the forearm quickly, and the pressure can rise while a large pulse is still felt. The responder supports the limb in the position found, records the findings, keeps the patient warm and moves the patient to a clinician.

An elbow that has dislocated is treated with urgency in most services, because the artery lies in front of the joint and the compartment around it is closed. When the radial head and the small projection at the front of the ulna are also broken, the joint is unstable in every direction and needs an operating room rather than an emergency department. An open elbow injury is contaminated even when the wound is small, so the responder covers the wound, records the neurovascular state, immobilizes the limb and arranges urgent transfer. Blind exploration of such a wound adds harm, exposed bone is never pushed back into it, and definitive cleansing and closure belong to the operating room. Casting and the surgical repair of the ligaments are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and any figure for how long the joint is held still is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline.

The elbow of a young child is a separate problem, and one pattern of it is quiet. A small child lifted or pulled by the hand may hold the arm still at the side and refuse to use it, without swelling and without any injury to the skin, because the head of one of the forearm bones has slipped out from under the ring of ligament that holds it. That injury is a subluxation rather than a complete dislocation, it is common in the early years of life, and the child is otherwise well. The examination, the decision about imaging and the maneuver that restores the bone to its place all belong to a clinician, because a child's elbow can also hide a break at the growing end of the bone. The lay first aider supports the arm in the position found and takes the child for assessment, and no one pulls on the arm to test it.

Dislocations at the wrist and in the small bones of the hand are less dramatic and far easier to miss. The bone at the center of the wrist can slip out of its place and take its neighbors with it, a pattern called a perilunate dislocation, and the median nerve then loses its supply while the skin looks almost normal. The findings are numbness and tingling in the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger and half of the ring finger, with weakness when the patient brings the thumb away from the palm. The wrist itself can also be driven out of place, and that injury nearly always comes with a break of one of the bones around it, so an apparently simple dislocation is treated as a fracture until a clinician has shown otherwise. These injuries threaten the nerve and the function of the hand more than the limb, so the responder supports the wrist in the position found, records the findings and transfers the patient.

The joints of the fingers and the thumb dislocate far more often than any other joint, and most of them do so toward the back of the hand after the finger is bent backward. One pattern deserves particular caution, because the head of a bone of the hand has passed through the tough sheet of tissue on the palm and is caught there, and that joint cannot be brought back by pulling on the finger. A wound over a finger joint that was made by a tooth or by a fist is treated as a contaminated joint injury even when it looks trivial, and it needs an operating room rather than a dressing alone. These injuries rarely threaten the limb and rarely threaten a nerve, so most of them may wait a few hours for definitive care, but waiting never means leaving the hand unsupported or unreferred. The responder supports the finger in the position found, records the color, the warmth and the sensation, and passes the patient on to a clinician.

The hip is a deep ball and socket joint, and the bone end usually leaves it toward the back after a collision. Because the socket is deep, the bone end cannot leave without tearing the capsule and often without breaking the rim of the socket or the head of the bone itself. The patient typically lies with the injured leg shortened and turned inward, and any attempt to straighten it is painful and dangerous. The nerve at risk runs from the back of the pelvis down the whole leg, and the findings are weakness of the muscles that lift the foot with loss of sensation over the outer part of the foot. The blood supply of the head of the bone is also at stake, because the vessel that feeds it runs in the capsule the dislocation tears, and a head that loses its supply can collapse years later. The hip is therefore treated as an emergency, and any figure for how quickly it must be put back is an illustration to be confirmed against the local protocol.

A hip that is out of place is put back by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon, usually with medicine that relaxes the muscles and often in an operating room, and the responder never attempts it. Before and after that procedure the nerve is examined, the pulse in the foot is checked and an image is taken, because a second injury to the socket or the knee is common. In a child the same presentation may be a slip at the growing part of the thigh bone, and a slip treated as a sprain can lead to a lifetime of hip disease. An older adult whose hip has been replaced with a prosthesis presents a third difficulty, because that joint can come out of place easily and the decisions belong to the surgeon who knows the implant. In all of these groups the responder protects the limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm and still, and moves the patient without delay.

A dislocation of the knee is rare, and it is the most dangerous dislocation in the body, because the artery that supplies the whole leg passes behind the joint and is tethered above and below it. When the bone ends separate, that artery is stretched, torn or blocked, and the leg below the knee begins to lose its supply while the pulse may still seem reassuring. The nerve that runs around the head of the small bone below the knee is injured in a large share of these cases, and the finding is a foot that cannot be lifted with numbness on the outer side of the leg. A large fraction of knee dislocations go back into place by themselves, so the deformity is absent, yet the swelling is tense and the injury is still a vascular emergency. The responder supports the knee in the position found, records the pulse, the sensation and the movement of the foot, and transfers the patient to a facility with vascular surgery.

Because the limb itself is in question, the assessment of the vessels is repeated and recorded at short intervals while the patient waits. The clinician may measure the ratio of the pressure taken at the ankle to the pressure taken at the arm, but the meaning of the result belongs to the surgeon. A pulse that is present does not settle the question, because an artery can be injured while blood still flows through it and the flow can stop later as the vessel clots. The findings that make the situation urgent are a pulse that has become weaker, a limb that has turned pale and cool, increasing pain, and any new weakness or numbness, and any one of them is reported at once. In a constructed illustration, a patient who cannot lift the foot after such an injury is treated as a vascular emergency until a surgeon has said otherwise. The patient is moved to a facility that can repair a vessel, and the time allowed for that transfer is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The patella is the small bone that sits in front of the knee, and it usually leaves its groove toward the outer side of the leg when the knee is twisted with the leg straight. The joint fills with blood, the knee swells quickly and the patient holds it slightly bent, and the deformity is often obvious. It frequently slips back into its groove by itself, and when it does not, a clinician may restore it with a gentle act, and the responder does not attempt it. The injury is often accompanied by a small break at the inner edge of the patella, which can leave a loose body inside the joint, so an image is always taken. A patella that has come out of place is not usually a threat to the limb or to a nerve, so it may wait a few hours, but the knee around it is examined as carefully as the bone itself. The responder supports the knee in the position found, records the neurovascular findings, keeps the patient warm and passes the patient on.

The ankle is a joint in which the bone of the leg sits in a socket formed by the bones of the foot. A dislocation of the ankle almost always comes with a break of one or both of the leg bones, and the bone end can press the skin from within until the skin gives way, which turns a closed injury into an open one. The skin over the inner side of the ankle is thin and poorly supplied, so an injury that tents it is an emergency even before the skin breaks, and a clinician may need to restore the position of the bone. The bone at the center of the foot can also leave its place, and its blood supply is fragile, so that injury is treated with the same urgency. These injuries threaten the skin and the supply of the bone, and they are transferred urgently for imaging and definitive care. The responder supports the limb in the position found, covers any wound with a sterile dressing, records the findings and keeps the limb warm.

Pain is not only a symptom in this work, because severe pain produces muscle spasm that holds the joint out of place and masks the findings on which the neurovascular examination depends. Relief of pain therefore has a place, and the place is decided by a prescriber rather than by the responder or by the family of the patient. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, escalating or out of proportion to the injury, because that kind of pain is a sign of a developing problem. The lay first aider gives no medicine at all, the trained responder gives only what the local protocol authorizes, and strong analgesia and sedation belong to a physician. No dose, no route and no regimen is given anywhere in this course, because the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber. Splinting, position, reassurance, warmth and an explanation of what is happening are the comfort measures that stay within every scope of practice.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and at a dislocated joint they carry more weight than usual. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention and any change in the patient are written in a fixed order. Several errors recur in this work, and each has a reason attached. The first is straightening a deformed limb in the field, which risks the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone, and the second is attempting a reduction more than once after an attempt has failed. The third is delaying referral for an image that will not change the immediate plan, the fourth is failing to record the neurovascular findings, and the fifth is attributing a new numbness or weakness to the original injury.

To summarize, a dislocation of a major joint is an injury of the whole joint, and what it costs depends on which vessel, which nerve and which blood supply lie against the bone end that has moved. The sequence never changes, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine and record the neurovascular status before and after every intervention, to immobilize in the position found, to image when the answer will change what is done, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The knee, the hip and the ankle can cost the limb within hours, so they are moved without delay to a facility with an operating room, the shoulder, the elbow and the wrist threaten a nerve, so their nerve findings are examined with particular care, and the fingers, the thumb and the patella usually wait. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. A reduction is not attempted when the surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is trapped, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when training is lacking, and reduction, traction and casting are in every case learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. Compartment syndrome is treated as an emergency, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, cold is treated as a complication, and the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 51 — Principles of Reduction

Reduction is the act of restoring a displaced fracture or a dislocated joint to the position in which the surfaces meet again, and it is a principle rather than a procedure memorized from a page. The bone ends and the joint surfaces belong in a relationship that lets the limb work, and everything done before a reduction aims at reaching a place where a qualified clinician can restore that relationship safely. This chapter follows the order used in every part of this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The technique of reduction is not taught here and cannot be learned here, because it is acquired under supervision, on living patients, with a teacher who can correct a hand before it does harm. What a page can teach is the reasoning around the act, which is what a reduction is meant to achieve, what must be examined before and after it, and which situations forbid it altogether. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

A reduction is performed for reasons that have little to do with how the limb looks on an image. Restoring the alignment of a bone, or the contact between two joint surfaces, reduces the tension that a displaced fragment places on the soft tissues around it, and that tension is what threatens the skin, the vessels and the nerves. A joint that has been out of place for hours may recover its blood supply only when the surfaces are put back into contact, because the vessels feeding the head of the bone are stretched until the position is restored. An aligned fracture is also easier to immobilize, to image and to assess, and a limb left in extreme deformity may lose the skin over the bone and become an open injury. None of that authorizes anyone to attempt the movement without the training, the equipment and the authorization the act requires, and the purpose of the act is a limb that can heal rather than a limb that looks tidy.

Time is one of the tissues in this injury, and the window in which a reduction is easiest is the window in which the limb is least swollen. Swelling begins within minutes, continues for many hours, and stiffens the soft tissues that a clinician must move through in order to bring the bone ends together. A joint reduced early is usually easier to hold than the same joint reduced after the tissues have filled with blood and fluid, and a fracture reduced after a long delay may need an operation that would not have been necessary at the beginning. Teaching often names a number of hours as a threshold, and any such figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and editions differ and the state of the limb matters more than the clock. What a responder can rely on is the direction of the pressure, since earlier is generally easier and a long delay with a tight, swollen limb is a reason to involve a surgeon rather than to try harder. The exception is the patient too unstable to be examined or moved, because the limb can wait for minutes that the airway and the circulation cannot.

Reduction begins with anatomy rather than with force, and the anatomy that matters most is the relationship between the bone and the soft tissues against it. Nerves and vessels do not run through the middle of a limb, where a moving bone could not reach them, but along the surface of the bone, in the plane between the bone and the fascia. The bone is therefore the safest guide in health and the greatest danger in injury, because a displaced fragment has already traveled through the space where a vessel or a nerve was lying. The capsule of a joint and the ligaments that strengthen it also decide how a dislocation behaves, since a torn capsule may allow the bone end to pass into a position from which it cannot return by the same path. Knowing which structures lie at risk in a particular region is the first act of preparation, and it is why reduction is learned region by region under supervision rather than as one universal movement.

Assessment comes before any decision about reduction, and it begins with the scene, the mechanism of injury and the patient rather than with the limb. The primary survey follows the order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because a patient who cannot breathe will not benefit from a straightened arm, and life comes before limb whenever two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands. The history adds what the injury cannot say, which is the age of the patient, the time of the injury, the force involved, and the illnesses or medicines that weaken bone or make sedation unsafe. The limb is examined by looking at it, feeling it gently and asking the patient to move whatever can be moved, never by forcing a movement in order to see what happens. A limb examined once and then left alone until someone qualified arrives has been examined correctly, while a limb tested repeatedly by several pairs of hands is being injured further. The lay first aider observes and supports, the trained responder and the emergency medical technician record what they see and immobilize within the procedures their service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what the findings mean.

A displaced bone is rarely the only injury present, and the search for associated injuries is part of preparing for any reduction. The joint above and the joint below the fracture are examined and later imaged, because the energy that broke one bone often injured the next structure in its path. A fragment of bone may be pulled away by a tendon or a ligament, and a piece may come to lie inside a joint, where it blocks the surfaces from meeting and turns a straightforward reduction into an operation. The skin is inspected over the whole limb, because a small wound near a fracture changes the injury from closed to open and changes the urgency of everything that follows. A patient who has fallen from a height may have a fracture of the pelvis, the spine or the heel in addition to the limb that hurts most, and a patient struck by a vehicle may have injuries of the chest and the abdomen that matter more in the next hour. A dislocation may also be accompanied by a fracture of the same bone, which is one reason a reduction attempted without an image is a gamble rather than a treatment.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any attempt at reduction and repeated after it, and its result is written down before the next act begins. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and any numbness, tingling or loss of movement is recorded in the words the patient used, because a summary such as reduced sensation loses what those words carry. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to a vessel, since the flow through a limb can fail while a pulse at the wrist or the ankle remains, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency that changes every plan that follows. The record exists because a finding not written before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards, and because the clinician who reduces the injury must know what the limb could feel and do before the attempt. The lay first aider reports what the patient says about feeling and movement and touches nothing that hurts, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the clinician.

Analgesia and sedation are part of humane fracture care, and they are also the part of it most tightly bound to authorization, monitoring and law. The decision to give a medicine belongs to a prescriber, which in most services means a physician or a senior nurse acting under a written protocol, and the choice of substance, the amount and the way it is given belong to that protocol rather than to any page of this course. What a listener may take from this chapter is the reasoning around the decision, which is that an injury severe enough to need a reduction is severe enough to need relief, and that a calm patient is easier to examine, easier to position and safer to move. Sedation for a procedure requires the equipment and the trained staff to watch breathing, blood pressure and consciousness, which is why it is performed where those exist and not in the back of a moving vehicle. The trained responder and the paramedic give only the medicines their service authorizes, while the lay first aider offers comfort, covering, calm and a steady hand and gives nothing at all. Nothing in this course names a substance, an amount or a route, and no listener should be able to take a prescription from it.

Reduction is a planned act performed by a prepared team in a place that has what the act requires, and that setting is part of the principle rather than a detail of comfort. The team needs someone qualified to perform the movement, someone to support and steady the limb, monitoring of breathing and circulation where sedation is used, and a plan for what happens if the attempt fails. The environment needs light, space, warmth and enough quiet for the patient to be heard, because a frightened patient holds the muscles tight and a limb held tight is harder and more dangerous to move. Authorization decides who may do each part, so the nurse may prepare, monitor and document, the trained responder and the paramedic may support, splint and transport, and only the physician, the emergency physician or the orthopedic surgeon performs the reduction itself within the local protocol. Where no such clinician is available, the correct action is not improvisation but stabilization, documentation and the fastest safe transfer to a facility that has one.

There are situations in which the correct decision is to leave the deformity exactly as it was found, and a listener must recognize them before any movement of the limb is considered. The first is the suspected complex fracture with a dislocation, in which a fragment and a joint have both lost their normal relationship, because the path a reduction would take cannot be known without imaging and an operating room. The second is an entrapped fragment or a capsule caught in the gap, where soft tissue has closed around the bone and holds it, since pulling harder will not free it and will tear what is still intact. The third is a limb whose vessels or nerves are failing, because that situation calls for a specialist with instruments and a surgical theater rather than an attempt in a corridor. The fourth is an open injury, where the attempt may push contamination deeper and where the wound and its closure belong to a surgeon. The fifth is an unclear diagnosis or an image not yet obtained, the sixth is a responder without the training or the equipment the act requires, and the seventh is an earlier failed attempt, because repetition adds swelling and makes the next trial harder for everyone. In any of those situations the limb is supported in the position found, the neurovascular status is recorded, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently.

Stabilization is what happens while the decision about reduction is being made, and it is deliberately a small set of acts. A deformed limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because a movement that looks helpful can tear the vessel or the nerve that was still intact and can convert a closed fracture into an open one. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient still and warm, and waits for help. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint, a sling or a support their service authorizes, and a traction device is used only for the injuries and by the providers named in the local protocol, never as a general remedy for a painful leg. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with direct pressure over a dressing, an embedded object is left in place because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is covered rather than pushed back into the wound. Cold is treated as a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering.

Immobilization after a reduction protects what the reduction achieved, and its principle is that the joints above and below the injury must be held as well as the broken bone itself. A support that holds only the fracture leaves the bone free to move at either end, and that movement can displace the fragments all over again. Padding is placed where the device presses on a bony prominence, and the device is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. Casting is one form of immobilization, and it is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, because a cast applied too loosely fails and a cast applied too tightly damages the limb it was meant to protect. The physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides which form of immobilization is appropriate and for how long it is worn, while the trained responder and the paramedic apply the temporary devices their service authorizes. The patient is told what to watch for and when to return, and anyone who cannot be given that instruction reliably needs a place where they can be observed.

Imaging is the step that turns a clinical impression into a plan, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement lying in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly where a joint surface is involved or where fragments must be counted, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues such as ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. The image that matters most before a reduction is the one that shows where the fragments and the joint surfaces actually lie, because a decision taken without it is a decision taken blind. Whether a reduction is attempted before or after imaging depends on the urgency of the injury and on what the facility can provide, and that judgment belongs to the most senior clinician present acting within the local protocol. An image is a picture of one moment, so the limb is examined and reassessed after the picture has been taken, not instead of it.

A controlled reduction is one in which the clinician knows what the movement is meant to achieve before it begins, and that knowledge is the difference between a technique and a guess. In general terms, the movement follows the path that the bone or the joint took, in reverse, applied slowly and steadily rather than suddenly, with the limb supported so that the patient's own muscles are not left pulling against the hand. An assistant may provide countertraction at the trunk or at the proximal part of the limb so that the force is balanced rather than spent on sliding the whole patient across the stretcher. The clinician watches the limb and the patient rather than the clock, and recognizes the moment of reduction by the change in the contour of the limb and by the easing of the resistance under the hands. None of that description is a technique, and it is deliberately not one, because the angle, the handhold, the direction and the amount of force differ for every region and every patient. The technique belongs to supervised clinical training and to the local protocol, and a listener who has never performed a reduction under a teacher has not learned it from this paragraph.

Force is not a technique, and resistance is information rather than an obstacle to be overcome. When the limb will not move along the expected path, the usual causes are a fragment caught in the joint, a capsule or a tendon trapped in the gap, a fracture whose ends have interlocked, or a diagnosis that is wrong, and in each of those cases more force makes the injury worse. A clinician who meets resistance stops, reassesses the neurovascular status, looks at the image again, and either waits for better conditions or refers the patient onward. Repeated attempts deserve particular caution, because each one adds swelling, and swelling makes a joint harder to reduce and a compartment more likely to fail. A joint that reduces and then dislocates again is telling the listener that the injury is unstable and that holding it will need more than hands. Crepitus felt during an attempt is not a sign of success, and the absence of a satisfying click does not justify another pull.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and after a reduction it is the step that decides whether the patient improves or travels. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record made before the attempt, which means color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement, and the pain the patient reports. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the clinician and prompt escalation. A limb reduced into a splint or a cast is checked with particular care, because a device that is comfortable at first can become constricting as the limb swells. A finding that is worse after the intervention is a reason to undo the intervention or to escalate, never a reason to wait and see.

A compartment is a closed space bounded by bone and fascia, and it holds muscle, nerves and vessels with very little room to spare. When bleeding or swelling raises the pressure inside such a space, that pressure is transmitted to everything within it, and the first structures to suffer are usually the muscle and then the nerve. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for a measurement or for the diagnosis to be confirmed, and acts within the local protocol so that a constricting bandage, splint or cast is released by someone authorized to release it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, because raising it can lower the pressure that is still pushing blood through the smallest vessels, and the patient is kept warm and still. The patient is then referred urgently to a facility that can measure the pressure and, if it is needed, open the compartment in an operating room. The diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle, so the interval between suspicion and surgical care is the interval that decides what the limb can do afterwards.

The record and the handover carry more weight after a reduction than at any other point in the sequence, because the next clinician must be able to tell what the limb was like before the attempt and what changed after it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, the imaging obtained, and the patient's own description of pain and sensation are written or spoken in a fixed order. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so a patient with a possible spinal injury is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Some patients need a lower threshold for referral rather than a different sequence, because the bone of a child bends and its growing regions can be injured without an obvious break, so a child who will not use an arm after a fall deserves the same caution as a child with a visible deformity. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break a hip in a fall from standing height with surprisingly little pain, and the injury may be far less dramatic than its consequences. In those patients a sign that is usually reliable may be absent, and an examiner who trusts a single sign will miss the injury.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with a complex fracture and dislocation, an entrapped fragment, an open injury, a failing vessel or nerve, a fracture that enters a joint, or a fracture that crosses the growing part of a child's bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Definitive treatment may be a reduction held by a cast, a brace or an external support, or an operation in which a surgeon holds the fragments with metal devices, a procedure called open reduction and internal fixation. Every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught from a book, including in this course. Traction, which holds a limb in line with a gentle continuous pull, is likewise a supervised technique with its own indications and its own dangers, and it is not a field remedy to be improvised.

Consider a constructed illustration rather than a real patient, since no example in this course describes a real person or a real institution. A middle-aged person falls from a ladder and arrives with a deformed forearm, an intact pulse at the wrist and numbness along the thumb side of the hand, so the limb is supported in the position found, the findings are written down, and the image shows a fragment lying inside the joint. The correct decision in that illustration is not to attempt a reduction at the bedside, because the fragment blocks the surfaces and the numbness warns that a nerve is already involved, so the limb is immobilized as found and the patient is referred for an operation. A second illustration might show a similar deformity with no fragment in the joint, in a facility with imaging and a clinician trained in that region, where the reduction is performed under appropriate pain relief and the limb is reassessed immediately afterwards. The two situations look alike from across the room and are managed differently, and that difference is exactly why the decision belongs to a clinician who has the image and the examination in front of them.

A few limits are worth stating plainly before this chapter closes. This course describes principles and the order in which they are applied, and it deliberately does not describe the movements, the handholds or the forces that a reduction requires. Every number it names, whether it is an interval of hours, a distance or a threshold, is an illustration whose value differs between services, countries and editions and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. The rules that decide who may perform a reduction are not the same everywhere either, so a listener works within the authorization, the equipment and the law of the place where they practice. Where the local answer is unclear, the safest course is to stabilize, to record, to protect the limb and the patient from cold, and to hand the patient to someone who is qualified to decide.

To summarize, reduction is the restoration of the normal relationship between bone ends or joint surfaces, and it is a principle of care rather than a movement that a listener learns from a book. The sequence never changes, which is to assess the patient before the limb, to stabilize the limb in the position found, to record the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, to immobilize the joints above and below the injury, to image when the image will change what is done, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, naming who is authorized to perform each act. A reduction is never attempted when there is a suspected complex fracture with a dislocation, an entrapped fragment, a failing vessel or nerve, an open injury, an unclear diagnosis, a lack of training or equipment, or an earlier failed attempt. Force is not a technique, resistance means stop, and a limb that is worse after an intervention is a reason to escalate rather than to try again. Pain relief and sedation belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, the suspected compartment is acted on at once, the constricting device is released by someone authorized to release it, and the limb is kept at the level of the heart rather than above it, because time is muscle. This chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

# Chapter 52 — When Not to Attempt Reduction

Reduction is the act of restoring a dislocated joint or a displaced fracture to its proper position, and it is one of the few acts in musculoskeletal care that can heal and harm in the same movement. There are situations in which the correct decision is to leave the deformity alone, to support it as it was found, and to hand the patient to someone who has everything the attempt requires. This course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and reduction belongs at the end of it. A rule without a reason is forgotten and then broken, so every situation in this chapter is named with the reason it exists. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

A reduction forced through fragments that cannot be guided will drive those fragments through the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone. One attempted on an open injury pushes organisms from the skin into the deep tissues, and one tried again after an earlier failure strips the periosteum, grinds the articular cartilage and leaves the joint more firmly locked than it was before. Each of these harms comes from the treatment rather than from the fall, and each of them is the kind of complication this course is most afraid of. Force is not a technique, so a deformity left alone in the field is not a failure of care but a decision that protects the patient until the right hands and the right equipment are available.

The contraindications this chapter takes one by one are a suspected complex fracture-dislocation, entrapped fracture fragments, significant neurovascular compromise that needs a specialist, an open injury, an unclear diagnosis, inadequate training or equipment, and a previous failed attempt. They overlap, because a limb with an open wound and an absent pulse carries several of them at once. What they share is one consequence, which is that in each of them the attempt is more likely to add an injury than to remove one. The task of the responder is to recognize that one of these conditions is present, to say which one, and to act on the alternative pathway rather than on the reduction, while the judgment that a reduction is contraindicated remains a clinical decision. The lay first aider needs only the shape of the rule, which is that a deformed limb is left as it is found and help is called.

Assessment decides whether the contraindication exists at all, and it begins before the limb is touched. The responder establishes the mechanism and the time of the injury, whether the patient is awake and breathing normally, and whether there is more than one injury. The limb is examined by looking at it, by feeling it gently and by asking the patient what can be moved, never by forcing it through a range of motion. A deformed limb that is not moved can still be examined, by inspecting the skin for a wound, comparing the shape with the other side and writing down the position in which the limb lies. Where the patient cannot describe the injury because of a head injury, intoxication, shock or the pain of another wound, the history is incomplete and the diagnosis is uncertain, which is itself one of the contraindications. Life comes before limb, so the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, is completed first.

Stabilization is what happens while the assessment is completed and the patient waits, and it is a small set of acts performed with the hands and with whatever is at hand. The limb is supported as found, the patient is kept warm, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, and the patient is protected from further injury. The lay first aider does those things and nothing more, because they need no equipment and no authorization, while the trained first responder and the emergency medical technician work within the procedures their service authorizes, apply dressings, use personal protective equipment where it is available and move the patient no more than is necessary. Nothing in stabilization is a reduction, and no step of stabilization requires the deformity to be corrected.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is recorded, because a finding not written down before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the hand or the foot, feels for the pulse beyond the injury, and asks the patient to move the fingers and the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and the words the patient uses are recorded as closely as possible. Numbness, tingling, weakness and the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier suggest injury to a nerve, while pallor, coolness, a diminished pulse and pain out of proportion to the injury suggest injury to a vessel. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency. This examination is the most important reason not to attempt a reduction in the field, because a limb that has lost its nerve or its supply cannot afford what a forced maneuver costs.

The first contraindication is a suspected complex fracture-dislocation, which means a joint that has come out of place at the same time as the bone around it has broken into several pieces. The fracture may run into the joint surface, the rim of the joint may be broken off with the capsule still attached, or the shards may sit where no hand can feel them through the skin. In such an injury the fragments cannot be guided, and a pull that would put a simple dislocation back will instead drive a sharp fragment into the vessels behind the joint and the nerves around it. The reduction is performed by an orthopedic surgeon in an operating room, with imaging during the procedure and with the means to fix the bone once the joint is restored. The responder keeps the limb as found, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes and refers urgently, and the word suspected carries the rule, because the field diagnosis does not have to be certain.

The second contraindication is an entrapped fracture fragment, which means that something has been caught between the two surfaces of the joint and is holding them apart. The picture is a joint that looks as though it should go back into place and simply does not, and the examiner may feel a soft or a hard block that stops the movement before it is complete. Traction can tighten that trap rather than open it, because the interposed tissue is drawn more firmly across the joint as the surfaces are separated, and a sustained pull can strangulate the tissue that blocks the way. The longer the block is worked on, the more the tissue swells, and a joint that might have been closed with a small procedure becomes one that needs an open operation. The finding that a joint will not reduce is a report to be made rather than an obstacle to be overcome, so every level of responder stops, immobilizes in the position found and refers without delay.

The third contraindication is significant neurovascular compromise that needs a specialist, and it is the one in which the temptation to act is strongest and the harm from acting is greatest. The findings are an absent or barely palpable pulse beyond the injury, a hand or a foot that is pale or blue, skin cool to the touch, a limb that has become tense, pain out of proportion to the visible injury, and a numbness or a weakness that is progressing rather than fading. A brief tingling that settles when the limb is supported may be positional and is watched, but a deficit that is growing is a surgical emergency. A vessel may be torn, crushed, in spasm or compressed by a fragment, and the treatment is a vascular and orthopedic assessment with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, none of which a pull in the field can replace. The responder records what was found and when, keeps the limb as found, keeps the patient warm and refers as a priority, naming in the referral the level of care that is needed.

The fourth contraindication is an open injury, and the rule is broader than the wound suggests, because any wound in the same region as a broken bone makes that fracture an open fracture, however small the wound. The organisms that live on the skin enter the deep tissues in the moment of the injury, so those tissues are contaminated whether or not bone can be seen. A reduction on such a limb pushes that contamination deeper, tears the damaged soft tissue envelope and can enlarge the communication between the outside and the bone. Exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because it may be the one thing holding pressure on a torn vessel, and an embedded object is never removed for the same reason. A wound is never explored blindly, because a finger in a wound finds tissue it cannot identify and displaces what was tamponading the bleeding. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the limb as found, keeps the patient warm and refers urgently, because definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else.

The fifth contraindication is an unclear diagnosis, and it is the quietest of the seven because it is the state of the responder's own knowledge rather than a finding in the limb. The diagnosis is unclear when the mechanism does not fit the deformity, when the patient cannot give a history, when the limb cannot be examined because of pain or because the patient is not awake, or when the injury could be a fracture, a dislocation, an injury of the growth region of a child or a combination of them. A joint that is out of place is not the same injury as a broken bone, and either can produce the same outward shape, so an attempt made on a guess may complete a fracture that has not been recognized. In a child an injury near the end of a bone may involve the growing region, which can be damaged with no fracture visible at all and with consequences that last for years. Until the diagnosis is clear the limb is splinted as found and the patient is referred, because waiting costs hours while a wrong reduction costs a lifetime.

The sixth contraindication is inadequate training or equipment, and this one is about the person and the place rather than about the injury. Reduction is a procedure learned under supervision, practiced on models and in the operating room and performed according to local protocol, and it is not a technique that can be learned from a book or from a recording. The lay first aider supports the limb and calls for help, the trained first responder and the emergency medical technician immobilize and transport, the paramedic works within the procedures the service authorizes, the nurse and the physician act within their licenses and their protocols, and the orthopedic surgeon performs the reduction where imaging, anesthesia, assistance and an operating room are available. Equipment matters as much as training, because a reduction performed without monitoring, without a means to control pain, without imaging and without a plan for failure is an experiment on a patient. When in doubt, the answer is to keep the limb as found, to record, to immobilize, to keep the patient warm and to refer.

The seventh contraindication is a previous failed attempt, and it includes the attempt just made as well as any attempt made before the responder arrived. Every pass at a joint or a fracture costs tissue, because the periosteum is stripped from the bone, the articular cartilage is scuffed and ground, the capsule is stretched further, and bleeding and swelling increase inside a space that has no room for them. The tissues lose their elasticity as they are worked, so the second attempt meets more resistance than the first and needs more force, which is exactly the direction in which harm lies. A joint or a fracture that has been tried and has not moved has already answered the question, and the answer is that something about this injury is beyond what the field can do. Repeating the attempt also adds pain, and pain brings muscle spasm that makes the limb even harder to move. The rule is to stop, to immobilize, to document the attempt and who made it, and to refer, and that documentation is not an accusation but clinical information the receiving team needs.

Running through all seven situations is one instruction a responder can carry in the hands, which is to stop if there is resistance or a complication. Resistance may be felt as a hard block that does not give, as a limb that will not follow the direction in which it is guided, or as a muscle that grips and holds. The correct response is not a firmer pull but an immediate stop, a return of the limb to the position in which it was found, a fresh neurovascular examination and a report of what changed. Restraint after resistance is the whole of the technique this chapter teaches, and no target seen on an image justifies the loss of a nerve or a vessel.

One situation deserves to be described because it is often mistaken for an exception, and that is the limb that is obviously dislocated and has no pulse. A knee that has been dislocated may also have reduced itself before the responder arrived, so that it looks almost normal while the vessel behind the knee has been torn, and this is one of the few injuries in which a normal appearance is a warning rather than a reassurance. Some services authorize a gentle positioning of the limb under a specific protocol and by a named level of provider, and where that authorization exists it is followed exactly as written, with the neurovascular status recorded before and after. This course does not teach that maneuver and does not describe how it is performed, because it belongs to supervised clinical training in the service that authorizes it. Where the authorization does not exist the limb is splinted in the position found and the transfer is made as urgently as the service allows.

What, then, does a responder do when reduction is contraindicated? The answer is the rest of the sequence, performed in order and performed well. The limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found, with the joints above and the joints below included, and the splint is padded where it presses on bone. The neurovascular status is examined and written down before the splint is applied and again after it is in place, and any change is acted on. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with pressure and dressings, an embedded object is stabilized in place, and an open wound is covered rather than explored. The patient is kept warm, is given nothing by mouth without an instruction that belongs to the local protocol, and is moved no more than is necessary, and the receiving facility is told what is coming, what was found and what was done.

Pain is a finding and a harm in itself, and in this setting it must be addressed without any of the details belonging to this book. The decision to give a medicine, the choice of the substance, the amount, the way it reaches the patient and how often it is repeated belong to a prescriber working within the local protocol, and they are never taken from a recording. What the responder can do is recognize the findings that make the decision urgent, which are pain out of proportion to the injury, pain that increases instead of settling, a limb that becomes tense and swollen, and a patient who cannot be made comfortable. Those findings are reported at once, because a compartment under pressure produces pain of that kind rather than ordinary pain, and the treatment for it is not a stronger medicine but a surgical assessment. The lay first aider offers comfort, position, warmth and reassurance and gives no unauthorized substance, while the trained responder may assist with an ordered medicine within the scope and the protocol of the service.

Immobilization after a refusal to reduce is not a compromise and it is not a delay, because it is the act that protects the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone. A deformed limb is splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because the tissues a movement would tear are the same tissues the reduction was declined to protect. The splint holds the joints above and below the injury, is padded where it presses over a bony point, and is secured firmly enough to hold the limb without stopping the circulation. Improvised materials serve well, and a rolled magazine or a padded board can do the work, but an improvised device shifts, so it is checked more often than a manufactured one. A splint is not a place to correct angulation, and a splint tightened to straighten a limb has become a tourniquet. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, and casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision rather than from a book.

Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and a patient whose reduction has been declined often waits longer than one who has been treated. Wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, the patient is insulated from the ground, and the head and the limbs are covered, because heat is lost fastest where the surface is largest and the covering is thinnest. A cold limb is also harder to examine, since cool skin, a faint pulse and a sluggish return of color can all be produced by cold alone. Where a number such as a target temperature is named in the guidance of a service, it is an illustration confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A word belongs here about the spine, because a spine that has been injured is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no chapter in this course may describe a lone manual handling technique as safe. A dislocated vertebra, a fracture through the body of a vertebra or a fracture through the bony arch can each press on the spinal cord or on the nerves that leave it, and a movement made in the field can turn a patient who could walk into a patient who cannot. Reduction of an injury of the spine is performed in a hospital, with imaging, with monitoring and with the means to act if the neurological picture changes. The responder keeps the head and the body in line, uses the precautions and the equipment the local protocol requires, moves the patient only with a trained team, and keeps the patient warm and still until the transfer is made.

Imaging converts a suspicion into a diagnosis, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician, never by the responder. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly where the fracture runs into a joint surface, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. An image is a picture of one moment, so the patient is examined again after it has been taken, and a limb that deteriorates while waiting for a study is reported at once. Where reduction is contraindicated the image is still needed, because it tells the surgeon what the injury is and how it must be approached.

Reassessment follows every intervention and every wait, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement, and they are color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement, pain and the tension of the limb. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, a limb that becomes tense and swollen, numbness and tingling, weakness, pallor, coolness and a pulse that fades are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A compartment syndrome is suspected on those findings alone, and no pulse is required to be absent before the suspicion is raised, because the flow through the smallest vessels can fail while a large pulse is still felt. Where one is suspected, the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. A responder not authorized to release a splint asks someone who is, without waiting for a confirmation that would arrive too late.

Referral is the final step of the sequence, and when reduction is contraindicated it becomes the most important one. A patient with a suspected complex fracture-dislocation, an entrapped fragment, a failing pulse or a progressive nerve deficit, an open injury, an unclear diagnosis, an attempt that has already failed, or a limb the responder is not trained or equipped to touch is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, and where possible to one with the specialists that injury needs. The referral is a story told in a fixed order, which is the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, what was done and by whom, and what has changed since. The receiving team continues that story instead of starting a new one, and the difference is measured in minutes. The level of care is named in the referral, so that a patient who needs a vascular specialist is not received by a team expecting a simple splint.

A responder who writes down the neurovascular status before a splint, the position in which the limb was found, the attempt that was declined and the reason for the decision is protecting the patient from a later mistake and protecting the record from a gap. Everything in this chapter is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, and the recording of every finding is part of the clinical act rather than a formality. Where this chapter names a time, a distance or a threshold, it names an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries and editions. The course repeats its order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

To summarize, reduction can restore a joint or a fracture and can also destroy the tissues that surround it, so there are situations in which the only defensible act is to leave the deformity alone. Those situations are a suspected complex fracture-dislocation, an entrapped fragment, significant neurovascular compromise that needs a specialist, an open injury, an unclear diagnosis, inadequate training or equipment, and a previous failed attempt, and in each of them the attempt is more likely to add an injury than to remove one. What the responder does instead is to support and splint the limb in the position in which it was found, never to straighten a deformed limb in the field, never to remove an embedded object, never to push exposed bone back into a wound, and never to explore a wound blindly. The neurovascular status is examined and recorded before every intervention and repeated after every one, the patient is kept warm, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and a compartment syndrome is suspected clinically, released within the local protocol and referred urgently. Pain is treated within the scope and the protocol of the service and by a prescriber, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. Stop if there is resistance or a complication, refer the patient to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, and tell the receiving team the story in its fixed order.

# Chapter 53 — Immediate Complications

Some fractures kill within the first minutes, and the instrument is rarely the bone itself. The bone breaks, the vessels it has torn continue to bleed, the pressure inside an unyielding compartment continues to rise, and the rescue can add harm to harm when it is hurried or forceful. This chapter is about those first minutes and hours: hemorrhage that may be hidden, injury to the nerves and vessels that travel against the bone, a compartment syndrome already developing while the limb still has a pulse, and the damage the rescue itself can do. Every injury in this course is taught through one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows that order while naming who may perform each act. This is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The first thing to understand about bleeding from a broken bone is that the skin tells almost nothing. A closed fracture can empty blood into the thigh, the pelvis or the soft tissues around a bone until the circulating volume falls far enough to threaten life, and not one drop appears on the surface.
