A break of the thigh bone is taught as capable of releasing enough blood to cause shock, and that volume is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because estimates differ between services and editions. The chest, the abdomen and the pelvis can hide a loss just as large, since an injured rib, a lacerated organ or a fractured pelvis can bleed without any deformity of a limb. The pelvis is never rocked, sprung or squeezed to test whether it is unstable, because that maneuver can disturb a clot that was holding the bleeding in check, and where a pelvic binder is used it is placed by a trained responder or a paramedic under the local protocol. This is why the course repeats that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a heart and a brain cannot.

The body defends itself against blood loss for as long as it can, and that defense is what makes the first hour deceptive. A young patient with a strong heart and constricted vessels may keep a normal pulse and a clear mind while much of the circulating volume has already been lost, and then deteriorate very quickly when the compensation fails. The findings that give the loss away are a pulse that climbs, skin that becomes pale, cool and moist, a patient who grows anxious or drowsy, a thirst reported without being asked, and a delay in the return of color to a pressed nail. An older adult whose arteries are hardened, a patient who takes a medicine that prevents clotting, and a frightened child may show those findings late or in an unusual order, so a single normal measurement proves nothing. Bleeding after an injury is therefore treated as present until someone qualified has excluded it, and the examiner who waits for the classic picture has waited too long.

The acts that control bleeding are few, and every one of them belongs to a named level of practice. The lay first aider applies firm direct pressure with a clean dressing to a wound that is bleeding on the outside, and does not remove a dressing that has soaked through but adds another on top of it. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician work within the procedures their service authorizes, and they may use a pressure dressing or a tourniquet where the protocol provides for one and direct pressure has failed. A tourniquet is not a casual device, because a limb deprived of its blood supply is a limb at risk of being lost, so the time of application is written down and it is not loosened in the field by a responder acting alone. Bleeding that cannot be seen is treated by keeping the patient warm and still and by moving the patient quickly to a hospital, and no volume to be infused and no substance to be given is named here, because those decisions belong to the prescriber and to the surgeon.

Nerves and great vessels do not run through the middle of a limb, since they run along the bone, often pressed against its surface with only muscle and fascia between them and the outside world. That arrangement is efficient in health and treacherous in injury, because a displaced bone end travels exactly through the place where the vessel and the nerve were lying. The familiar illustrations are a break just above the elbow, which can injure the vessel that supplies the forearm, and a dislocation of the knee, which can injure the vessel behind the knee, and either can leave a limb without a blood supply while the bone injury looks unremarkable. A dislocation deserves suspicion, because a joint that has lost contact has already stretched or torn its capsule, its ligaments and whatever vessel or nerve crossed it. A bruised or torn nerve announces itself with numbness, tingling, weakness, or the loss of a movement the patient could perform a moment earlier, while an injured vessel announces itself with pallor, coolness, a diminished pulse, and pain out of proportion to the injury.

A pulse that can be felt beyond the fracture does not exclude serious damage to a vessel or to a compartment, and this is among the most dangerous misunderstandings in musculoskeletal trauma. The smallest vessels that feed muscle and nerve can fail while the large artery still carries a pulse to the wrist or the ankle, so a responder who feels a pulse and relaxes has learned only that one vessel is open. These findings are also less trustworthy in particular patients, including an older adult with hardened arteries, a limb already cooled by exposure, a patient who cannot report numbness, and a frightened child. The neurovascular examination is therefore performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and it is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The lay first aider reports only what needs no training, such as color, warmth and whether the fingers or the toes still move, while the formal examination of pulses, sensation and movement belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the physician.

Certain injuries carry a higher risk than others, and knowing which ones keeps the responder alert. A break of the upper arm can injure the nerve that winds around the bone and lifts the wrist, so the finding is a hand that drops when the patient tries to raise it. A break of the forearm can raise the pressure inside a compartment that is already tight, and a break of the shin can threaten the vessel behind the shin bone and the nerves that supply the foot. An open fracture adds contamination to the list, because the moment bone communicates with the outside, organisms from the skin reach deep tissue, and the size of the wound says nothing about the amount of contamination. In every one of these injuries the responder records the finding and refers the patient urgently, the interpretation belongs to the clinician, and the definitive repair belongs to the operating room.

The compartment syndrome is the complication this chapter most wants the listener to suspect early, and it is already developing in the first hours, often before the patient reaches a hospital. A compartment is a closed space bounded by bone and by the tough sheet of fascia, and it holds muscle, nerve and blood vessels with almost no room to spare. Bleeding from a fracture or swelling from a crush injury raises the pressure inside that space, and because fascia does not stretch quickly, the pressure keeps rising instead of dispersing. Muscle suffers first, then nerve, and flow through the smallest vessels fails long before the large pulse at the wrist or the ankle disappears, so a palpable pulse is worthless as reassurance. Pain out of proportion to the injury, pain that increases instead of settling, pain when the muscles of the compartment are gently stretched, a limb that feels tense and hard, and numbness where a nerve crosses the compartment are the findings that should stop the responder. The diagnosis is clinical, time is muscle, and a test that arrives late is no help at all.

A compartment syndrome is hardest to recognize in the patient who cannot complain. A child who is frightened, a patient who is unconscious after a head injury, a patient who has been given sedation, and a patient whose limb has been numbed for a procedure may all be developing one and report nothing. The examiner must then rely on the appearance and the feel of the limb and on the trend of the observations rather than on the patient's words, watching for a limb that becomes more swollen and tense, a hand or a foot that becomes cool and pale, and a pulse that weakens. Where a service measures the pressure inside a compartment with a device, that measurement supports a clinical judgment, and the threshold quoted for it differs between services and editions and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A single normal reading does not exclude the diagnosis, and a normal reading never outvotes a limb that is tense, swollen and painful.

Once a compartment syndrome is suspected, the acts that follow are few and each has an owner. An encircling bandage, splint, cast or dressing is released within the local protocol by someone authorized to do it, because the device applied to hold a limb still can be the very thing stopping the circulation. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, since raising it lowers the pressure that drives blood through already failing capillaries, and this is one of the few places where the instinct to raise an injured limb is plainly wrong. The patient is kept warm, because cold adds constriction and pain to a limb already short of blood, and the patient is transferred urgently to a facility where a surgeon can open the compartments, an operation called a fasciotomy that belongs to the operating room. Pain relief is often needed, and who may give it and in what form are set by the prescriber, the local protocol and the law, and none of those details belongs in this course.

The fourth subject of this chapter is the harm that comes with the help, and it is why every intervention is followed by a reassessment. A deformed limb that is straightened in the field can tear a vessel that was intact, release the pressure holding a torn vessel closed, and turn a closed fracture into an open one, so a deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never pulled straight. A splint applied too tightly, or a bandage tightened again as the limb swells, can create the very compartment syndrome the splint was meant to prevent. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be pressing on a torn vessel and the bone end may be the only thing closing the wound. A wound is never explored blindly, because fingers carry organisms into deep tissue and can displace a clot that was doing useful work, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room.

Other harms come from hurry rather than from force. A patient dragged or rolled by untrained hands may have a spinal injury converted into a spinal cord injury, so a spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no single manual handling technique is safe on its own. Traction applied by untrained hands, or a pull maintained while the patient is moved, can damage the soft tissues holding the fracture together, and traction is a clinical act learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. Moving a patient before the neurovascular status has been recorded destroys the only comparison that would later show whether the journey or the splint caused a new deficit, so the record comes before the movement. A long rescue in cold weather cools the patient, and a cold patient bleeds more readily, so covering is part of the rescue and not an afterthought.

One more harm in the first hours comes from good intentions rather than from force, and it is the injury that nobody looked for. A patient with an obvious deformity of one thigh may also have a broken wrist from the same fall, a dislocated shoulder, or a rib that has injured the lung, and the obvious injury draws every eye away from the rest. The examination that follows the primary survey therefore looks at the whole patient, and the joints above and below the injured part are examined before the splint is applied, because a splint crossing an unnoticed second fracture can displace it. The second injury is missed most easily in the patient who is unconscious, the patient in shock and the patient distracted by severe pain, and those are precisely the patients in whom it matters most. Recording which areas were examined, as well as what was found, shows the next clinician where the unknowns still lie.

The sequence this course follows begins with assessment, and in this chapter assessment has one purpose above all others, which is to find the patient who is bleeding or losing a limb before the limb is studied in detail. The scene is made safe first, because a responder who becomes a second patient helps nobody, and personal protective equipment is worn whenever blood or another body fluid may be present. The mechanism of injury, the time of the injury, the age of the patient, and the illnesses and medicines the patient takes are gathered next, because a patient whose blood does not clot normally is a different patient. The primary survey follows the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limb, and the limb is assessed by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing a movement. Life comes before limb at every step of that order, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot.

Looking at the limb means noting its position, its shape and its color and comparing it with the other side, which is the oldest and least expensive comparison available. Swelling, a wound, bleeding, deformity, bruising and the exact position of the limb on the stretcher are recorded as they are found, because the position found is the position that will be splinted. Feeling means touching gently along the bone for tenderness and for a step in the contour and feeling the skin for temperature and moisture, but it never means pressing hard on a suspected fracture or probing a wound. Asking the patient to move the fingers or the toes, and asking whether the limb feels numb or tingling, gives information that no device can supply, and the answer is written in the words of the patient. The lay first aider performs only the acts that need no training and no equipment, such as supporting the limb, covering a wound with a clean dressing and noticing that the patient can no longer move a hand.

Stabilization comes next, and here it means three things, which are to keep the patient warm, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, and to support the injured part in the position in which it was found. Supporting the limb is done with the hands of the first aider, with a pillow, with a rolled blanket or with whatever is at hand, and the aim is to remove the movement that hurts rather than to change the shape of the limb. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint or a commercial immobilizer within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and both levels protect the limb from further movement while the patient is transferred. Keeping the patient warm is part of stabilization rather than a comfort measure, because cold worsens bleeding, so the patient is separated from the ground and covering is added from the feet upward. Nothing in field stabilization includes straightening a limb, reducing a dislocation, removing an object, or pushing bone back into a wound.

The neurovascular examination is the step that must be performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and it is the step most often compressed into a single word in the record. Color is compared side to side, temperature is compared with the back of the examiner's hand, and the pulse beyond the injury is sought and its character described rather than simply noted as present. The nail bed is pressed briefly and the time taken for color to return is observed and written as a comparison rather than as an absolute number, because a threshold quoted in one service differs in another and must be confirmed against the local protocol. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and the patient is asked to move each finger and each toe, with the result recorded in the patient's own words. The finding before the splint and the finding after the splint are both entered with the time, because a deficit that was not documented before an intervention can neither be attributed afterwards nor defended.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and in the presence of a suspected vascular injury it also means resisting the temptation to correct anything. A splint is padded where it presses over a bony point, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, since a padded board, a folded magazine, a sling or the body of the patient can each serve, provided the device is checked often because an improvised one shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what immobilization will hold the bone for healing, which may be a cast, a brace or surgical fixation. Casting, reduction and traction are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them can be learned from a book, so what a book can explain is why they are done and what can go wrong.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joints above and below are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissue, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle, and neither is ordered merely because it is available. An image is a picture of one moment, and a patient who is bleeding into a thigh or losing the blood supply to a leg must not wait in a radiology department while the picture is taken, so imaging follows resuscitation and never precedes it. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, the trained responder does not decide which study is needed, and the choice belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and in a chapter about immediate complications it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison rather than any single measurement that carries the value. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, the splint is checked for tightness, and the patient is checked for the general signs of blood loss, which include a climbing pulse, skin that is becoming pale and cool, and a level of consciousness that is drifting. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain far worse than the injury appears to explain, numbness, tingling, weakness, a limb that becomes tense and hard, and a wound that begins to bleed through its dressing are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A patient who was comfortable ten minutes ago and is distressed now is telling the responder that something has changed, and the answer is to examine again and to call for help.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a damaged nerve or vessel, a dislocation, or a fracture that enters a joint is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The referral is made by the clinician responsible for the patient, while the lay first aider and the trained responder call for help early rather than deciding what treatment is needed. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, and all of those acts are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A reduction must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing, when the injury is open or the diagnosis is unclear, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

Across all of these complications the division of labor is the same, and it is worth stating plainly. The lay first aider recognizes danger, calls for help, supports the limb, covers a wound, keeps the patient warm and reports what can be seen, and nothing more is safe at that level. The trained first responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic work within the procedures and the equipment their service authorizes, which usually include splinting, wound coverage, control of external bleeding and the recording of the neurovascular examination. The nurse monitors, records, gives what has been prescribed and escalates a change to the physician without delay, while the physician assesses, orders imaging, decides about fluids and analgesia within the local protocol, and calls the orthopedic or vascular surgeon. The surgeon repairs the vessel and releases the compartment, and the operating room is the only place where those acts are done. The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality after it, so the time of the injury and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written down in a fixed order.

To summarize, the first minutes and hours after a fracture or a dislocation are decided less by the bone than by the bleeding, the nerves, the vessels and the pressure inside a closed compartment, and by whether the rescue adds harm to harm. Bleeding from a broken bone may be entirely hidden, so a closed fracture of the thigh or the pelvis can cause shock with no blood on the skin, and a pulse that remains present does not exclude damage to a vessel or a compartment syndrome. The course follows one order in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and it names the provider level for every act. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and an encircling bandage or splint is released only within the local protocol by someone authorized to do it. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, or when the vessels and the nerves are failing and need a specialist. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, the patient is reassessed after every intervention, and the surgeon is called early, because time is muscle and time is blood. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 54 — Early Complications

A fracture that is survived in the first hour can still be lost in the first days, and the complications that take it are quieter than the injury that caused it. The limb has been splinted, the bleeding has stopped, the radiograph has been taken and the patient is comfortable, and it is exactly then that the pressure inside a closed compartment keeps rising, that a wound begins to smell, that a lung which is not taking deep breaths begins to close, and that a clot forms in a leg which has not moved. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows that order while naming the provider level for every act. This is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The reason the first days are dangerous lies in two simple facts about the tissues around a broken bone. Swelling does not stop when the splint is applied, because bleeding and the leak of fluid from injured vessels continue for hours, so a limb can be far larger on the second day than it was in the first. Pain is the messenger that reports that increase, and the patient who says the pain is worse than it was, or worse than the injury appears to explain, is handing the examiner the most valuable finding in this chapter. A comfortable patient is not automatically a safe one, because a limb that has lost its blood supply may hurt less once the muscle inside it has died, and the same false comfort follows a strong painkiller given before anybody examined the limb. Life comes before limb when two correct actions compete, and in the first days the threat to the limb is the one that is missed most easily.

The compartment syndrome declares itself as a limb that is tense, swollen and painful out of all proportion to the injury, and the pain matters most because it arrives before function is lost. A compartment is a closed space bounded by bone and by the tough sheet of fascia, holding muscle, nerves and blood vessels with almost no room to spare. When bleeding or swelling raises the pressure inside that space, the smallest vessels fail first, so muscle starves and then nerve, and the large pulse at the wrist or the ankle can still be felt while both are dying. Pain when the muscles of the compartment are gently stretched, a limb that feels hard, numbness or tingling in the territory of the nerve that crosses it, and weakness in a movement the patient could perform earlier are the findings that declare it. Pallor, coolness and an absent pulse are late signs, and a responder who waits for them waits for a limb that can no longer be saved. The diagnosis is clinical and belongs to a clinician, and where a service measures the pressure inside a compartment, that reading supports the judgment rather than replacing it, and the threshold differs between services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Once a compartment syndrome is suspected, the acts that follow are few and each has an owner. The responder who applied an encircling bandage or splint does not tighten it, and a constricting bandage, splint, cast or dressing is released only by someone the local protocol authorizes to do so, because the device applied to protect the limb can be the very thing strangling it. The limb is not raised above the level of the heart, since lifting it lowers the pressure that drives blood through capillaries already failing, and here the instinct to elevate an injured limb is plainly wrong. The patient is kept warm, because cold adds constriction and pain to a limb short of blood, and the time of every observation and every intervention is written down. The nurse escalates a change at once rather than at the next round, while the physician makes the diagnosis and calls the surgeon, because the operation that opens the compartments, called a fasciotomy, belongs to the operating room and to nobody else.

When a compartment syndrome is missed, the damage is permanent and it is measured in what the patient can no longer do. Muscle deprived of blood for hours dies and is replaced by scar, and the resulting contracture pulls the fingers or the toes into a fixed position that no splint can correct, which is why this course repeats that time is muscle. Dead muscle releases pigment into the bloodstream, and a patient whose urine turns dark, like tea or cola, may be suffering the kidney injury that follows a large crush or a large area of dead tissue. That patient belongs in an intensive care unit, where the physician supports the circulation and the kidneys while the surgeon completes the removal of dead tissue. The lay first aider and the trained responder make none of those decisions, and their task is to notice the tense limb, the dark urine or the deteriorating patient and to say it aloud, early, to someone who can act.

Infection is the second complication that declares itself in the first days, and the open fracture is the injury that invites it. The skin carries organisms that reach the bone and the deep tissues in the moment of the injury, so a wound that looked clean at the roadside is contaminated, and the size of the wound says nothing about the amount of contamination. The signs that should raise alarm are pain that increases instead of settling, swelling, redness and warmth around the wound, discharge that may be thin or thick, a wound that begins to smell, and a patient who feels unwell, shivers, or has a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, a figure to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A wound that was dry and becomes wet is worth reporting even when the patient feels well. The lay first aider covers the wound with a clean or sterile dressing, the trained responder records the appearance and the neurovascular findings, and neither explores the wound blindly, removes a dressing that is stuck, or squeezes anything out of it, because blind exploration pushes organisms deeper and can displace a clot that was doing useful work.

A deep infection announces itself less clearly than a wound infection, because the wound may have healed before the pain begins. A patient whose pain increases days after an operation, whose wound leaks a little, or who feels generally unwell and cannot say why may be developing an infection in the bone or in the tissues around the metal placed to hold it, and that diagnosis belongs to the physician and the surgeon, who examine, image and take samples. Fever, a rapid pulse, rapid breathing and confusion in an injured patient point to infection that has spread through the body and constitute a medical emergency. A limb whose pain is severe, whose skin is changing color and whose tissues feel stiff or crackle under the fingers may be carrying an infection that requires the operating room within hours and admits no delay for pictures. The nurse sees the wound, the temperature and the behavior of the patient at every round, so a change reported then is worth more than one discovered the next day.

Antibiotics are selected and prescribed under the local protocol by those authorized to prescribe and to give them, and this course names no substance, no amount, no route and no frequency, so that no listener can carry a prescription away from these chapters. Protection against tetanus is likewise a decision for the treating clinician and for the local protocol, and the question belongs in the first conversation rather than in the memory of the patient. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. Definitive closure of a wound, the washing out of an infected joint and the removal of infected bone belong to the operating room, and a wound is never closed in the field by anyone at any level of practice.

The lung is the organ that suffers most from a patient who cannot move, and the first days after a fracture are when that suffering begins. A patient who lies still, especially one whose ribs hurt or who is afraid to take a deep breath, stops opening the small airways at the base of the lungs, and the secretions that collect there become a chest infection. A cough that brings up sputum, a fever, a rising breathing rate, breathlessness and a falling oxygen level measured on a finger probe are the findings, and they appear gradually rather than suddenly, which is why they are compared with the record rather than judged alone. A patient who becomes breathless and confused in the first day or two after a fracture of a long bone, and who develops a fine rash of tiny red spots across the chest, the neck and the armpits, may be suffering the fat embolism syndrome, which is a clinical suspicion rather than a diagnosis a responder can make. That suspicion is reported urgently to the physician and is managed in an intensive care unit.

Prevention of the chest complications of immobility is shared work, and most of it costs nothing. The nurse sits the patient up as soon as the injury and the protocol allow, encourages deep breaths and an effective cough, and uses whatever device the service provides to help the lungs open. The physical therapist teaches the patient how to clear secretions and how soon to move, within the limits set by the surgeon and by the local protocol, and the physician decides whether a chest infection is present and whether anything is to be prescribed. The lay first aider and the trained responder contribute by keeping the patient warm, supporting the injured part so that coughing hurts as little as possible, and reporting a cough, a fever or a change in breathing to the receiving team. Nothing in that list contains a drug or a dose, because any program of movement is set by the treating team for that particular patient.

Blood that does not move clots, and a patient immobilized by a fracture, a splint or pain is a patient whose leg veins are asking for a clot. A clot in the deep veins of the leg is called a deep vein thrombosis, and it may announce itself with a calf that is tender, swollen, warm and painful when the foot is bent. It may equally announce itself with nothing at all, and the classic sign of calf pain on bending the foot is taught as unreliable. The clot is dangerous not because it blocks the leg but because a piece of it can travel to the lungs, and that risk lasts through the first days and the first weeks of immobility. A patient who is dehydrated, older, or has had a clot before is at greater risk, and that assessment belongs to the physician.

A pulmonary embolism is a clot that has traveled to the lungs, and it can be the first sign that a clot existed anywhere. The patient becomes suddenly short of breath, may clutch the chest, may cough blood, may have a racing pulse and may faint or collapse. In the worst case the collapse is the first event, and the patient then needs CPR at once while emergency help is called, performed by anyone trained to perform it. A patient with a swollen and tender calf is not massaged, not walked about to test the leg and not treated as a curiosity, because handling a clot can help it travel, so the leg is left alone, the patient is kept still and the physician is called. The measures that reduce this risk are chosen by the treating team, and the physician decides what prevention is appropriate, whether mechanical or prescribed, under the local protocol.

A splint that is too tight or too long does its damage slowly and silently, and the first sign is usually the only chance there is to prevent a deep wound. The device presses hardest over the bony points, which include the ankle, the heel, the knee, the elbow and the back of the wrist, and the skin under a splint cannot be seen, so the report of burning pain under an edge carries more weight than any inspection. The first visible change is a red area that does not pale when it is pressed, and if the pressure continues the skin blisters, breaks and then dies, leaving a wound that takes weeks or months to heal and can become infected. Nerves suffer in the same way, and pressure from a splint or a sling can weaken the hand or produce a foot that drops when the patient tries to raise it. The nerve that lifts the foot passes around the head of the smaller bone of the lower leg, and the nerve at the inner side of the elbow is exposed in the same way.

Prevention of a splint injury is largely a matter of padding and of checking, and both have a named owner. A splint is padded over every bony point and along its edges, it is not applied over a wet, dirty or already reddened limb, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band. Whoever applied the device, whether a trained responder, a paramedic or a physician, remains responsible for checking its edges and for teaching the patient to report pain beneath it, while the nurse inspects the skin at every opportunity, especially at the heel and the ankle. Only someone the local protocol authorizes removes or replaces a cast, splits a cast to relieve pressure, or cuts a window in it, and the orthopedic practitioner decides what device the injury needs once the swelling has changed. A collar or a spinal board left in place too long produces the same skin injury, so the spine is treated as unstable only until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and the device is then removed by that person rather than by a responder acting alone.

A splint that is not checked can also lose the position of the bone, and the loss may stay invisible until somebody looks for it. The fracture is held not only by the device but by the swelling around it, so when the swelling subsides over the first days the device that was tight becomes loose and the bone ends can move again. A splint that does not include the joint above and the joint below leaves the fracture free to be moved by one of those joints, and a splint that does not control rotation allows the far end of the bone to turn while the patient shifts in bed. A patient transferred with a loose splint and no record of how the limb was positioned may arrive with a deformity nobody can explain. The check that prevents this is simple, and it consists of looking at the limb, comparing it with the other side and comparing it with what was written down.

The findings of a lost position are the return of a deformity that had settled, a new angulation or rotation, pain that increases where it had been easing, and a hand or foot the patient can no longer move as well as before. Those findings are reported at once to the clinician responsible, who decides whether a new radiograph is needed, taken in at least two directions so that a change in the third is not hidden. Restoring the position of the bone ends is called a reduction, and holding them with a gentle continuous pull is called traction, and both are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, with the sedation and the setting decided by the clinician who performs them. No responder attempts a reduction in the field to spare the patient a journey, because force applied to a broken bone can convert a closed injury into an open one and can tear a vessel that was intact, and force is not a technique. A reduction is also not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when an earlier attempt has failed.

Assessment in a chapter about the first days differs from assessment in the first hour, because the patient is already splinted, already imaged and often already comfortable. The history begins with the injury, its time and its mechanism, and then continues with everything done since, including every device applied, every transfer and every change reported by anyone who has touched the patient. The examination of the limb is repeated in the same order as before and compared with the earlier record rather than judged alone, because a limb that is tense today was described yesterday and a hand that is weaker today was tested yesterday. The general condition of the patient belongs to the same examination, and a rising pulse, a rising temperature, a falling oxygen level, a new cough, confusion or a calf that has become swollen all change what is done next. The interval at which these observations are repeated differs between services and injuries, and it must be confirmed against the local protocol rather than assumed.

Stabilization for a patient in the first days still means keeping the patient warm, controlling any bleeding that can be controlled and supporting the injured part, and it now includes protecting the patient from the complications that are already developing. Warmth matters for the same reason it mattered in the first hour, because a cold patient clots badly, feels pain more keenly and resists infection less well, so insulation is part of the treatment rather than a comfort measure. The splint is supported rather than adjusted by the responder, and any device that is cutting into the skin or constricting the limb is brought to the attention of someone authorized to modify it rather than loosened in a corridor. Whether the patient may eat or drink before a possible operation, and what relief of pain is appropriate, are decisions of the treating clinician and the local protocol, and the substance, the amount and the route belong to the prescriber. Any relief given before an examination is recorded, and the examination is performed anyway, because a patient who is comfortable can still be a patient whose limb is in danger.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and in the first days it is repeated again because the limb itself keeps changing. Color is compared side to side, temperature is felt with the back of the examiner's hand, the pulse beyond the injury is described rather than merely noted as present, and the nail bed is pressed briefly to watch the color return. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and the patient is asked to move each finger or each toe and to say whether the limb feels numb, tingling or weaker than it did. The findings are written with the time, because a deficit that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and in the first days the same rule applies to a deficit discovered after a transfer or after an operation. The lay first aider reports color, warmth and whether the fingers or the toes still move, while the trained responder, the nurse and the physician perform the formal examination and the clinician interprets it.

Immobilization in the first days is a matter of keeping the decision that was made and of noticing when it has stopped working. The device is checked for tightness, for edges that press, for padding that has slipped and for a fit that has changed as the swelling has fallen, and the check is repeated rather than performed once. A splint is never tightened by a responder to make it feel secure, and an improvised device is checked more often than a commercial one because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply and adjust splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization the injury needs, which may be a cast, a brace or surgical fixation. Casting, reduction and traction are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and nothing in this course teaches a listener to perform them, because a book cannot see the limb and cannot feel the resistance that means stop.

Imaging in the first days answers specific questions, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is used to check that the position of the fracture is being held and that the device has not allowed movement, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a change in the third direction is not hidden. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint and is used when the answer will change what is done, while magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissue, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. An image is a picture of one moment, and a patient who is developing a compartment syndrome must not wait in a radiology department while pictures are taken, because that diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, the trained responder does not choose the study, and the decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient.

Reassessment is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment, and in the first days it is performed after every intervention and at the intervals the local protocol sets. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the value lies in the comparison rather than in any single measurement. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain far worse than the injury appears to explain, numbness, tingling, weakness, a limb that becomes tense and hard, a wound that begins to discharge, a cough or a fever, a calf that swells and a patient who becomes confused are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A patient who was comfortable an hour ago and is distressed now is telling the team that something has changed, and the answer is to examine again, to check every device and to call for help rather than wait. The responder also says aloud what would make the situation unbearable, which here means a tense limb with rising pain, a wound that is spreading infection, a patient who cannot breathe, or a patient who collapses.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and most of the complications in this chapter are the reason a patient is referred rather than watched. A patient with a suspected compartment syndrome, a spreading infection, a clot in the leg or in the lung, a chest infection that is not settling, or a fracture whose position has been lost is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The referral is made by the clinician responsible for the patient, while the lay first aider and the trained responder call for help early rather than deciding what treatment is needed, and the nurse escalates a change at once. The surgeon opens a compartment, washes out an infection and removes dead tissue, and everything given to the patient is decided and provided under the local protocol by those authorized to prescribe and to give it. The record and the handover travel with the patient, so the time of the injury, the position of the limb and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written in a fixed order.

To summarize, the complications that decide the first days are quieter than the injury that caused them, and they are found by looking for them before the patient complains. Compartment syndrome declares itself with pain out of proportion to the injury, a tense and swollen limb and numbness or weakness, it is diagnosed by a clinician and treated by a surgeon in the operating room, a pulse that is still present proves nothing, and the limb is not raised above the level of the heart. Infection in an open fracture or around an implant shows itself as increasing pain, redness, warmth, discharge, smell and fever, and it is treated by the surgeon while every substance and every amount belongs to the prescriber and the local protocol. Immobility threatens the lungs with infection and the veins with clots that can travel to the lungs and kill, so the patient is sat up, encouraged to breathe and to cough, moved as soon as the treating team allows, and watched for breathlessness, chest pain or a swollen calf, and a patient who collapses needs CPR at once. A splint that is too tight, too long or no longer checked injures the skin over the bony points, presses on nerves and lets the bone lose the position it had, so it is padded and watched, and only someone the local protocol authorizes modifies it. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, a deformed limb is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, an open wound is never explored blindly, and the patient is reassessed after every intervention and referred early. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 55 — Late Complications

A fracture or a dislocation is often called healed long before the patient has recovered, and the weeks and months that follow are when the slow complications appear. The wound has closed, the splint has come off and everyone is relieved, and that is exactly when a bone that has stopped uniting, a bone that has united crooked, a joint that has stiffened, a bone that has lost its blood supply and a child's growth region that has been injured begin to decide the rest of that patient's life. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows it while naming the provider level for every act. These complications are missed because they arrive without an audience: in the first hour the injury is loud, while in the sixth week the patient is at home and the only witness is a limb slowly losing alignment or movement. The follow-up appointment exists for that reason and is part of the treatment rather than a courtesy at the end of it, so a responder supports it instead of replacing it. This is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Bone heals through a sequence worth describing in words, because the words explain why some fractures take so much longer than others. The first step is the bleeding between the broken ends, which forms a collection called a hematoma, and the next is the arrival of cells that build a soft bridge of cartilage and fibrous tissue across the gap. The third is the replacement of that bridge by woven bone, called callus, which appears on a radiograph as a cloud around the fracture, and the fourth is the slow remodeling that reshapes the rough bone into the column it was before. The blood supply is the most important factor at every stage, since no stage happens without vessels reaching the fracture, and the mechanical environment is the second, since a fracture that still moves is one whose bridge keeps breaking. As an illustration, most breaks in the shaft of a long bone have joined by 3 to 6 months, a span that differs between bones, ages and editions and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A fracture that heals slowly is not the same as a fracture that has failed to heal, and the distinction belongs to a clinician working with time and with imaging. What the patient reports is consistent: the fracture site still aches after a long day, it hurts when weight goes through the limb and it hurts when the limb is twisted in a way a united bone would not allow. What the examiner finds is tenderness that has never left the site of the break and sometimes a hinge of movement where there should be none. A responder does not test for movement at a fracture site by pulling on it, because that examination belongs to a clinician and the test itself can disturb a bridge that is trying to form. When the ends have still not joined by the time the clinician expects, the condition is called a nonunion, and the gap may stay open and filled with scar or the ends may grow rounded and sealed over. The causes are few: the blood supply to a fragment may have been destroyed at the moment of injury, an infection may be present in bone that looks healed from the outside, the ends may be held apart by muscle caught between them, and the fracture may have been left free to move. Illness, poor nutrition, smoking and medicines that suppress healing all work against the patient, and the diagnosis is made by the orthopedic surgeon with imaging rather than from the outside by a responder.

A bone that unites in the wrong position is described as malunited, and the position is judged against the normal anatomy of that bone and against the other side of the same patient. An arm or a leg that is visibly bent, a limb that has become shorter and a limb whose shape differs from the one opposite are all signs, and rotation is the one most often missed, because a bend is easy to see and a twist is not. A forearm that can no longer turn the palm upward, a wrist that sits at an angle so that grip feels weak, a foot that points inward or outward so the shoe wears unevenly, a finger that crosses its neighbor when the hand closes and an elbow that can no longer reach the mouth are the complaints that follow. Pain often joins them, because the joint above or below a malunited bone is loaded in a direction it was not built for.

Whether a malunion is accepted or corrected is a decision of the orthopedic surgeon, and it turns on how much the deformity costs the patient, how old the patient is, how much the joint has suffered and what an operation would risk. A small bend in a bone that does not cross a joint may cause no trouble at all, while the same bend in a forearm stops the hand from doing its work, so function matters more than the size of the bend. When a limb has shortened by 2 centimeters or more the patient may limp, and the effect of that difference on the joints above and below is assessed by the clinician, since such figures differ between patients and services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The lay first aider, the trained responder and the nurse do not straighten a healed limb, do not force a joint through a deformity and do not tell the patient that nothing can be done. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no part of that learning comes from a book.

Stiffness of a joint is the late complication patients notice most and resent longest, and it is the one most often accepted as inevitable when it is not. A joint held still loses the looseness of its capsule and ligaments, the cartilage that lines it is nourished by movement and suffers without it, and the muscles that cross it lose length and strength, so a joint immobilized for the safety of the bone pays a price that appears weeks later. The price is a range of movement that no longer reaches where it did, first in the direction the device restricted most and later in every direction. The patient reports difficulty with the small acts of daily life, and those acts are the true measures of a joint: combing the hair, reaching a back pocket, fastening a shoe, kneeling and rising from a low chair. The older patient and the patient whose limb stayed swollen for a long time lose movement fastest, and a joint guarded through fear loses it as surely as one that is splinted.

The management of a stiff joint begins with finding out whether the stiffness comes from the capsule, from scar tissue, from a block of bone, from a displaced fragment, from an infection or from pain, because each answer leads somewhere different. A joint that is simply tight after immobilization is treated with graded movement, with therapy and with patience, and that program is set by the physical therapist together with the surgeon for that particular patient, and a joint that is left in one position for weeks can stiffen into a fixed contracture that is far harder to undo than simple tightness. Where the joint does not respond, the orthopedic surgeon may consider an operation to release the tightened tissue or to remove a block, and that decision belongs to the surgeon and to the operating room. Nothing in this chapter teaches a technique for stretching, because a joint forced past its limit tears and bleeds, and blood inside a joint produces more scar and less movement than before. A responder never pulls a stiff joint straight and never tells a patient to push through the pain, and the nurse reports a joint that becomes hot and swollen after exercise rather than increasing the exercise.

The pain that persists deserves attention of its own, because pain brings the patient back and is the finding most often explained away. Pain is expected while a fracture heals and while a joint regains its movement, but the pain of a late complication has a different character. Pain that increases over weeks instead of easing, pain that wakes the patient at night, pain far worse than the injury appears to explain and pain in a limb that has changed color, temperature or sweating all point away from ordinary healing. One condition in which those changes come together is the complex regional pain syndrome, in which severe pain, altered skin color and temperature, altered sweating and extreme sensitivity to a light touch follow an injury that may have seemed minor. Its signs overlap with those of infection, of a blood clot and of a nerve injury, so the diagnosis is clinical and belongs to a clinician. Assessment begins with the account of the patient, who is asked where the pain is, when it began, what eases it, what worsens it, what it prevents and whether it disturbs sleep, and the answers are written down so that the next visit has something to compare. Relief of pain is part of good care and is also the step that can hide a complication, so any relief given is recorded, the examination is performed anyway, and the choice of substance, amount and route belongs to the prescriber and to the local protocol.

Some bones break in a way that destroys their blood supply, and the death of that bone is a late complication that unfolds over months. The head of the thigh bone, the small bone at the base of the thumb side of the wrist, the bone that forms the lower part of the ankle joint and the head of the upper arm bone are the sites where this is most feared, because each depends on a vessel that enters through a narrow place and can be torn by a fracture or a dislocation. The bone dies quietly, and for a long time the patient notices nothing, and then the dead segment loses its strength and collapses under the load of the joint. The findings are pain in the groin, in the wrist or in the ankle that worsens with use, stiffness of the joint and pain that continues long after the fracture should have settled. A radiograph may look almost normal at the beginning, and magnetic resonance imaging can show the change much earlier, which is one reason it is used when pain does not match the picture. A dislocation left unreduced, a bone already weakened by illness, a heavy use of alcohol and long treatment with medicines that thin the bone or suppress inflammation all make the death of bone more likely, and when the dead segment collapses the joint becomes arthritic, so the choice among the operations that may help belongs to the orthopedic surgeon.

A child's bone is not a small adult bone, and the late complications of injury in a child follow from that difference. Near each end of a growing bone lies a region called the growth plate, where cartilage is produced and then turned into bone, and it is that region which makes the bone longer rather than merely thicker. The plate is softer than the shaft and it sits close to the joint, so an injury that looks like a sprain may have crossed the plate, while an injury that breaks the shaft may spare the plate altogether. When the plate is injured, part of it may stop growing while the rest continues, and the result is a bone that grows crooked, or a limb that ends up shorter than the other, or a joint whose surfaces tilt as the child grows. Sometimes the injured plate grows faster for a time instead, so the injured limb becomes longer rather than shorter, which is the opposite of the expected direction and is no less of a disturbance. The damage depends on the pattern of the injury, on the age of the child and on how much growth remained, and those are estimates that differ between children and are confirmed by the specialist.

The difficult part of a growth disturbance is that nobody sees it at the moment it begins. A child whose limb length changes by a little each year may have no pain at all, and the family notices that one shoe is worn differently, that one sleeve is short or that the child limps when tired. A child who stops using an arm after a fall, who cries when the arm is handled or who refuses to bear weight deserves an examination and an image rather than reassurance, even when the skin is unmarked, because the growth plate is injured more often than it is seen. Follow-up after such an injury continues for as long as the bone grows, which means years rather than weeks, and the family has to be told why in words they can keep, or the appointments will be dropped exactly when they are doing their work. Comparison with the opposite limb, measured in the same way at each visit, is the simple observation the clinic repeats, and the interpretation belongs to the pediatric orthopedic surgeon. Nothing done at the roadside prevents a growth disturbance, and only the follow-up finds it in time, which is why the appointment belongs to the treatment rather than to the paperwork.

Assessment in the late phase is a comparison rather than a single examination, and the sequence is the same one this course follows everywhere. The history comes first and it begins with the injury, the time it happened, how it was treated and what has happened since, including every operation, every device and every missed appointment. The patient is then asked what the limb prevents and what it permits, because the function of the limb is the outcome that matters and it is heard rather than seen. The examination repeats the order used in the first hours and compares the two sides: the shape of the limb, its length, the alignment of its joints, the movement at each joint, the strength, the sensation and the pulses. The general condition of the patient belongs in the same examination, since a late infection, a clot or another illness can present at a follow-up visit as easily as at any other time. The record carried from the earlier visits is what turns today's finding into a change.

Stabilization in the late phase looks modest, because the emergencies of the first hours lie behind the patient, and it still has content. It means keeping the patient warm, protecting a limb that is painful or unstable from a load it cannot carry, supporting the limb in the position the treating team has chosen rather than in the position that feels easiest, and controlling any bleeding from a wound that has begun to discharge. A patient whose fracture is not united needs support for walking, and the device that provides it is chosen, fitted and adjusted by the clinician, the orthopedic practitioner or the physical therapist according to the local protocol, never improvised by a responder. A patient who arrives at a clinic with unrelenting pain is not stabilized by being sent home with reassurance, and a patient who is short of breath, confused or feverish after an injury is stabilized as any other seriously ill patient is, with attention to the airway, to the breathing and to the circulation. Life still comes before limb when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, and here the competition is usually between the general illness of the patient and the limb that brought them in. Any relief of pain and any medicine belong to the treating clinician and to the local protocol.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and in the late phase it is repeated because the limb itself has changed since the last visit. The patient is asked whether the limb feels normal, numb, tingling or weaker than it did, and the answer is recorded in the words of the patient wherever that is possible. Color and temperature are compared side to side, the pulses beyond the injury are felt and described rather than merely noted as present, and the movement of each finger or each toe is tested against the other side. Sensation is tested through the territory of the nerves that cross the injured region, because a nerve can be pressed months later by scar or by a bone that healed crooked and the loss can be partial and easy to miss. A pulse that is present does not exclude a problem, and a change in the neurovascular findings is an emergency until a clinician says otherwise. The lay first aider reports color, warmth and whether the fingers or the toes still move, while the trained responder, the nurse and the physician perform the formal examination.

Immobilization in the late phase is mostly a matter of continuing a plan and noticing when it no longer fits the limb. A cast or a brace that was correct in the first week may be wrong in the sixth, because the swelling has fallen and the limb has changed shape, and a device that has become loose lets the bone move while a device that has become tight presses on the skin. Whoever applied the device, whether a trained responder, a paramedic or a physician, checks the edges, the padding and the fit, and the nurse checks the skin wherever it can be seen, especially over the heel, the ankle, the elbow and the back of the wrist. Only someone the local protocol authorizes removes or replaces a cast, splits it to relieve pressure or alters a brace, and the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization the injury needs once the late phase has begun. Casting, reduction and traction are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and nothing in this course teaches a listener to perform them. A responder never tightens a device to make it feel secure and never scratches an itch beneath a cast with any object.

Imaging in the late phase answers questions the examination has already framed, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is the first study in most clinics, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a change in the third direction is not hidden, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second problem is not overlooked. Computed tomography shows the detail of a bone that has healed crooked or failed to unite, especially near a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues and for bone that may have lost its blood supply, since it can show that change before a radiograph does. An image taken today is compared with the images taken before, and that comparison is the reason the earlier pictures are kept and carried with the patient. Imaging is never ordered or interpreted by a lay first aider, and the trained responder does not choose the study, because the decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient. An image is a picture of one moment, and a patient whose pain has changed must still be examined.

Reassessment is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment, and in the late phase it catches the complication caused by time as well. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the value lies in the comparison rather than in any single measurement. The findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation are pain that increases instead of settling, pain that wakes the patient at night, a new deformity in a limb that had none, a joint that is becoming stiffer rather than looser, a wound that has begun to discharge, a limb that has become hot and swollen, a new numbness or weakness and a child who has stopped using the limb. A patient who says that something feels wrong, even when the examination is unremarkable, is reporting a change that deserves a second look rather than an explanation. A responder also says aloud what would make the situation unbearable, which here means a limb losing function week by week, a wound that is spreading, a patient who can no longer walk or a patient who is becoming unwell for a reason nobody has explained. The intervals at which these observations are repeated differ between services and injuries and are confirmed against the local protocol.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and the late complications are almost all reasons to refer rather than to watch at home. A suspected nonunion, a malunion that costs the patient function, a bone that may have lost its blood supply, a growth disturbance in a child, a joint that has become arthritic and a bone that may be infected each belong to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. The referral is made by the clinician responsible for the patient, while the lay first aider and the trained responder call for help early rather than deciding what treatment is needed. The orthopedic surgeon decides what the bone needs, which may be a different device, a graft of bone, an operation to correct a deformity, an operation to restore a blood supply or the replacement of a joint, and every one of those decisions belongs in that surgeon's hands and in the local protocol. The record and the handover travel with the patient, so the time of the injury, the treatment given, the position of the limb and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written in a fixed order. A patient with an injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so.

The follow-up appointment is part of the treatment because these complications cannot be prevented by anything done in the first hour and cannot be found by anyone who is not looking. A bone that is failing to unite does not announce itself with a fever, a joint that is stiffening does not hurt while it stiffens and the growth plate of a child does not complain. What finds them is a patient who returns, a clinician who compares today with last time and a record that carries the earlier findings forward. The system that makes that possible is made of ordinary things: a clear appointment, a written plan, a copy of the images, a telephone number to call when something changes and a patient who understands why any of it matters. Where the patient cannot return, the responder and the community health worker who see the limb between visits become the eyes of the team, and their report of a new deformity, a new pain or a new weakness is worth more than a perfect examination performed a year later.

To summarize, the complications of the late phase are quieter than the injury that caused them, and they are found by looking for them rather than by waiting to be told. The findings to watch for are pain that increases instead of settling, pain that wakes the patient at night, tenderness that never leaves the fracture site, movement where a healed bone should be solid, a limb that is bent, twisted or shorter than the other, a joint that is becoming stiffer rather than looser, a wound or a sinus that discharges, a new numbness or weakness, and a child who has stopped using a limb. A fracture that has not united, one that has united crooked, a bone that has lost its blood supply, a joint that has become arthritic and an injured growth plate are all conditions the clinician assesses with the history, the examination and the images, and none is diagnosed from the outside by a responder. The acts of the responder are to support the limb in the position found, to keep the patient warm, to protect the skin under any device, to record the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, to arrange the appointment and the transport and to report a change early rather than to explain it away. The acts that must never be performed are these: a deformed limb is never straightened in the field, a healed deformity is never forced or remanipulated, a stiff joint is never pulled straight, a cast is never tightened or split by anyone the local protocol does not authorize, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and no responder takes a prescription from this book. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear or when an earlier attempt has failed. Who to call is decided before the emergency rather than during it: the clinician responsible for the patient, the orthopedic surgeon, the emergency service and the facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit, and for a patient who collapses, the emergency number with CPR started at once. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 56 — Plain Radiography

The plain radiograph is the oldest and still the most widely used picture in the care of an injured limb, and it earns that place because it is quick, it is inexpensive, and it is available where nothing else is. It is also a shadow rather than a limb, and what a listener does with it depends on understanding what kind of shadow it is. A radiograph answers a question that someone has already asked about a patient, so it never replaces looking at the limb, feeling it, and asking the patient what happened. Every chapter of this course follows one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the picture comes after the hands for a reason. The reason is that a film can be repeated and a nerve cannot. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

To understand what a plain film can and cannot show, it helps to remember how the image is made. A beam of X-rays is passed through the part, and the tissues absorb different amounts of it, so the picture is a map of absorption rather than a portrait. Bone absorbs a great deal of the beam and appears white, air absorbs almost none and appears black, and muscle, fat and fluid lie between them in shades of gray. The beam crosses the whole thickness of the limb on its way to the detector, so every structure along that path is printed on top of the others and none can be separated afterwards, which is why a radiograph is a projection rather than a slice.

Assessment comes before the picture, and its purpose is to turn a general worry into a precise question. The mechanism of injury, the age of the patient, the point of greatest tenderness, the deformity, the swelling and the loss of function all point toward a particular bone and a particular place on it. A request that says only that the limb hurts asks the radiographer to search an entire region, and a search produces more exposures, more time and more radiation than a question does. The clinician who orders the study is the one responsible for the patient, which in most services means a physician, and in some services a nurse practitioner or a physician assistant working within an agreed protocol may order it. The lay first aider and the trained responder do not order imaging and do not decide which study is needed, and nothing here permits a listener to request a study that the local rules reserve to someone else.

Stabilization comes next, and it decides whether the patient goes to the imaging room at all. A patient whose airway, breathing or circulation is failing is treated where the team can act, and the film waits, because a picture of a limb is worth nothing to a patient who is bleeding somewhere else. When an image genuinely cannot wait, a portable machine may be brought to the bedside, and that decision belongs to the clinician leading the resuscitation together with the team that will perform the study. The responder keeps the limb supported in the position in which it was found, keeps the patient warm, and keeps the patient still while the exposure is made. Pain is not a detail that a patient must endure in order to obtain a better picture, and analgesia is decided by the prescriber, with the substance, the amount and the route belonging to that decision and to the local protocol. A patient with a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone handling technique is safe, so such a patient travels with a trained team and the precautions the local protocol requires.

The neurovascular examination is performed before the patient leaves for the imaging department and repeated when the patient returns, because the journey and the positioning can change what the nerves and vessels are doing. The examiner looks at the color and the warmth of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, tests sensation on both sides and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. The result is written in the record before the film and written again afterwards, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed to it later. The radiographer positions the limb for the exposure and must never be asked to straighten it or to pull it into line, and a limb that cannot be placed for a standard view is imaged as it lies. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious damage to the vessels, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency that no picture will explain.

Immobilization usually comes before the image, because a limb splinted in the position found is safer to move and easier to radiograph than one that is left free. A splint may obscure the fracture it is meant to protect and may hide the soft tissues the clinician needs to see, so the order bends when the clinical situation requires it, and the decision to image first belongs to the clinician. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required. Casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and neither is taught from a book in this course. A splint that is tight enough to stop the circulation is worse than no splint at all, which is one reason the film taken after a splint is applied is read for the position of the bone and for the fit of the splint.

What is asked for matters as much as how the picture is taken. The request names the region, the side, the clinical question and the reason the study is needed, and it names the projections the local protocol uses for that region. The side must be marked on the image itself, because a film shown against the wrong side of a patient is a hazard that has harmed people, and the marker is placed by the radiographer rather than added to the record later. Earlier films, where they exist, travel with the patient, because an old study may show the fracture that the new one is too early to reveal. The clinician writes the request, the radiographer chooses the technical factors and may add a view the protocol allows in order to answer the question, and the radiologist or another trained clinician interprets the result. The lay first aider does none of those things and is never asked to hold a film up to a window.

An injury has three dimensions and a radiograph has two, so a single exposure leaves one direction unexamined. The rule that follows is that a fracture is not excluded by one view, and the practical form of the rule is that every injured bone is examined in at least two projections taken at right angles to each other.
