The common pair is one view taken from front to back and one taken from the side, and in many regions a third view taken at an angle is added because it opens a joint surface that the first two overlap. Displacement of the broken ends can lie entirely within the plane of a single beam and leave no trace in the picture it produces, so a confident answer built on one image deserves distrust. The far end of a broken bone may also be rotated about its long axis, and rotation is the displacement a film shows least clearly, so the two limbs are compared and the patient is examined.

Two projections of the injured bone are still not the whole study, because the joints at either end must be included in the picture as well. A fall onto an outstretched hand can break the wrist and dislocate the elbow, and a blow to the knee can break the shin bone and injure the ankle, so the second injury is missed when the study stops at the ends of the shaft. A long bone is part of a chain, and a break anywhere in the chain changes the forces that reach every other link in it. The clinician who writes the request therefore names the joints above and below the suspected fracture, and the clinician who reviews the images checks that both of them are on the film. The forearm is a special case, because its two bones form a joint with one another along their whole length, so a break in one of them may be accompanied by a dislocation at either end. When any part of that chain is missing, the image is incomplete, and the answer is to obtain the view that was omitted rather than to assume that nothing is there.

A fracture announces itself on a plain film in a small number of ways, and a listener who knows them can follow a clinician's description. The most direct sign is a dark line across the pale bone, which is the gap between the broken ends, and it is often irregular, stepped or branched rather than a clean cut. A break may show instead as a kink or a step in the cortex, the dense white edge of the bone, with no obvious line within it, and an impacted fracture may look brighter rather than darker because the bone is compressed. A small piece pulled away where a tendon or a ligament attaches is called an avulsion, and a bone broken into more than two pieces is described as comminuted. The film also shows how the ends are sitting, since angulation appears as a bend in the line of the shaft, translation as an offset of the outlines, and shortening as a bone that looks shorter than its fellow on the other side. The soft tissues are part of the same picture, so swelling or a joint filled with blood adds to the story rather than decorating it.

A dislocation has its own appearance, and it is usually easier to see than a fracture because a joint that has lost its fit looks wrong even at a glance. The rounded head of one bone no longer sits within the hollow of the other, so the two outlines overlap instead of nesting, or a gap opens where the surfaces should touch. On the view taken from the side the far bone usually lies in front of or behind its socket rather than within it, and the smooth curves that run along the edge of the joint are broken rather than continuous. A joint that has dislocated has almost always torn its capsule and at least one ligament, and a fragment of bone may have come away with it, so the film is read for a chip as well as for the displacement. Reduction restores the position of the joint surfaces, and it is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol by a clinician qualified to do it, never from the pages of a book. A film taken after a reduction shows whether the surfaces are back in contact, and it never decides by itself whether the joint is stable enough to be left alone.

When a dislocation and a fracture occur together, the picture becomes harder to read, and the combination is one of the injuries in which a reduction attempted by the wrong person does the most harm. A fragment caught between the joint surfaces, a fracture of the socket, or a break of the bone that carries the joint can all be hidden by the displacement itself and appear only after something has been moved. That is one reason a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique. The part of the plain film here is to show the clinician what is present before anything is done, and the part of the responder is to support the limb in the position found.

Some fractures are invisible on the first film, and a listener who does not know this will send a patient away with a broken bone. The small bone at the base of the thumb side of the wrist is the classic example, because its fracture line may be too fine to see at first and the bone has a poor blood supply that punishes a delay. The neck of the thigh bone in an older adult can also break without a line that the first film reveals, and the patient may still be able to stand, which makes the picture even more misleading. A stress injury from repeated loading, common in runners, dancers and soldiers who march, often appears only as a faint thickening of the bone or not at all. The signs that point to a fracture the film does not show are indirect but real, and they include tenderness over one exact point, swelling of the soft tissue beside the bone, and fluid within a joint that has no other explanation. A tiny avulsion flake may be dismissed as an artifact, and the growth region of a child can conceal an injury that later disturbs the growth of the limb.

What is done when the film is normal and the patient is not is the test of whether the study is being used well. The patient is treated rather than the picture, so a limb that is painful, swollen and tender over one point is immobilized and protected even when the report says that no fracture is seen. The clinician may arrange a repeat film after an interval, and a commonly taught figure is 10 to 14 days, which is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because the interval differs between injuries and between services. A child with a tender elbow and a normal film receives the same caution, since a growth region can be injured without a visible break. In each of these situations the decision belongs to the clinician, and the part of the responder is to immobilize, to protect, and to make certain the patient will be seen again.

The soft tissues are not invisible on a plain film, and what they show can change what is done next. Swelling appears as a widening of the shadow around the bone, and a joint filled with blood appears as a bulge over the joint, which at the elbow may push the pad of fat that lies against the bone away from it and produce a dark crescent that warns of an injury within the joint. A foreign body may be visible if it is dense enough, such as metal or glass, while wood and many plastics often are not, so a normal film never excludes a retained object. An embedded object is never removed in the field and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. An open wound is never explored blindly; it is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the neurovascular status is recorded, the limb is immobilized, and the patient is referred urgently.

Reassessment follows every one of those steps, and it is the step this course is most afraid to see skipped. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. The examiner checks the color and the warmth of the skin, the pulse beyond the injury, sensation on both sides, the ability to move the fingers or the toes, and the level of pain, and then checks the splint for tightness. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A tense and painful limb may be developing a compartment syndrome, whose diagnosis is clinical and whose treatment is time critical, so the responder acts within the local protocol rather than waiting for an image or a laboratory result to confirm it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the constricting bandage or splint is released only by someone the protocol authorizes to release it, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently.

The radiograph is not free, and the cost it carries is invisible. The beam that makes the picture also deposits energy in the patient and in anyone who remains in the room, so the study is requested only when its answer will change what is done and never as a routine before a clinical decision. The clinician who orders the study is responsible for asking whether the patient may be pregnant, because the growing child is more sensitive to radiation than the adult, and local protocols differ in how that question is asked and what is done with the answer. The radiographer shields the patient and the team according to the local rules, wears personal protective equipment where those rules require it, and may ask everyone who is not needed to step behind the barrier. A patient is never left unsupported in order to keep a staff member out of the room, and nobody holds a fracture by hand during an exposure when a splint can hold it instead.

A film does not read itself, and the person who takes it is not always the person who interprets it. The radiographer is trained to produce a diagnostic image and to recognize when it is not good enough, and in some services the radiographer may comment on an obvious abnormality within a local protocol, but the formal reading belongs to a radiologist or to another clinician trained to interpret it. A responder who is not trained does not read the film aloud to the patient, does not name a diagnosis from it, and does not use it to decide that treatment is unnecessary. An obvious deformity with a limb that has no pulse is treated as an emergency whether or not a film has been taken, because the examination outranks the picture when the two disagree. A report that has not yet arrived never delays the care of a patient who needs it, and a normal report does not erase the findings that were recorded before the study was taken. When the report and the examination disagree, the patient is examined again and the clinician decides which to trust while the patient is kept safe.

The record of the study is part of the treatment, and it is written before the film is taken and after it is read. The request states the region, the side, the clinical question and the reason the study is needed, and the record states the findings that sent the patient there and the neurovascular status before and after the journey to the imaging room. A normal film of the spine does not clear it, because a spine is cleared only by someone qualified to clear it, using the examination and the rules of the local protocol rather than a picture alone. A normal film does not exclude a compartment syndrome, a ligament injury, a tendon injury or a stress injury that has not yet changed the bone, and it does not measure how much pain a patient has. The report may state that no fracture is seen, and that sentence describes the picture rather than the patient, so the examination and the reassessment continue after the film has been filed.

The images travel with the patient to the next facility, because a receiving team that cannot see the first study may repeat it or may miss what it showed. A handover that includes the pictures, the question they were meant to answer and the answers they gave lets the next team continue a story instead of starting a new one. Where the study can be done is also a question of resources, and the honest answer differs from one country to another, since a hospital may have a radiographer at all hours, a clinic may have one on certain days, and a remote station may have no machine at all. When imaging is delayed, the limb is immobilized and the patient is kept warm while the plan is made, because an unmanaged wait becomes a complication, and the decision to move a patient in order to obtain a study belongs to the clinician in charge of the case and to the local protocol.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the order, and the plain film usually decides nothing by itself while settling a great deal. A break that is displaced, a joint that has lost its fit, a fracture that reaches the joint surface, a bone broken into fragments, a fragment left within the joint and an injury in a growing child are all findings that send the patient onward to a facility with an orthopedic surgeon and an operating room. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals, and every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A surgeon may hold the fragments with metal devices, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, and the images taken during and after that operation belong to the surgeon's judgment. The responder rarely decides where the patient goes, but the quality of the record and the honesty of the handover travel with the patient into that decision.

Consider a constructed illustration, which describes no real patient and no real institution. A middle aged person falls onto an outstretched hand and arrives with a painful wrist, swelling on the thumb side and tenderness over one small bone, and the films are taken in the views the local protocol uses for that region and are reported as showing no fracture. The clinician knows that this bone is one of those whose first film is often silent, so the wrist is immobilized in the position found, the person is told not to use the hand, and a further appointment is made instead of a discharge home. Another constructed illustration concerns an older adult who cannot bear weight after a fall indoors, whose first film is read as showing nothing, and who is admitted for observation and repeat imaging rather than helped back onto the feet. In both illustrations the film was not wrong but incomplete, and the examination supplied what the picture could not. That is the habit this chapter asks for, which is to treat the patient and to use the film as one witness among several.

To summarize, the plain radiograph is a shadow of a living limb and not a substitute for examining it, and it is requested after assessment and after stabilization by the clinician responsible for the patient, never by the lay first aider or the trained responder. Every injured bone is examined in at least two projections taken at right angles, the joints above and below the suspected fracture are included in the study, and the side is marked on the image, because displacement can hide in the plane of a single beam and a second injury can be missed when the picture stops at the shaft. A fracture appears as a dark line, a step in the cortex, a denser impacted band, an avulsion fragment or a break into several pieces, and a dislocation appears as a joint that has lost its fit, with overlapping outlines and broken curves along the edge of the joint. Some fractures are invisible on the first film, especially in the small bone of the wrist, the neck of the thigh bone in an older adult and the growth regions of a child, so a painful limb with a normal report is immobilized, protected and seen again instead of discharged. The neurovascular status is recorded before the patient goes to the imaging room and after the return, and the reassessment is repeated after every splint, every reduction and every journey, because the complication this course fears most is the one caused by the treatment. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, a deformed limb is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly. The film does not clear a spine, does not exclude a compartment syndrome and does not replace the hands, and the patient is handed over with the images, the question they answered and the findings that came before them. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 57 — Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Ultrasound

The radiograph is the first picture taken of an injured limb, and for most fractures it is the only one that is ever needed, but there are questions it cannot answer. A break that reaches a joint surface may be far more complex than the plain film suggests, a ligament may be torn while the bone remains whole, and a fracture may be present and invisible for days after the injury. Three further examinations are available for those questions, and this chapter is about what each of them adds, what each of them costs the patient, and where each of them belongs in the order of care. That order does not change, and it is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. Imaging never leads that order, because a picture is taken of a patient who has first been examined, protected and recorded, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Every image begins as a question, and a study that was not ordered for a reason is a study that will not change anything. The clinician who orders it has already examined the patient, recorded the neurovascular findings and decided what the answer would do, whether that is to confirm a suspicion, to plan an operation or to exclude an injury that must not be missed. The lay first aider never orders imaging and never interprets it, the trained responder does not choose which study is needed, and the emergency medical technician or paramedic may only pass on the findings that the receiving clinician will use. Computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasound are each requested by a physician, and the choice among them belongs to that physician together with the radiologist who will report the study. When the answer cannot change what is done, the correct decision is often to take no picture at all, because every examination has a cost and some of those costs are borne by the patient alone.

The sequence that governs this course places imaging after immobilization, and the reason is not order for its own sake. A limb that is moved for a scan is a limb that may bleed again, and a fracture that is not yet supported can shift on the trolley, in the doorway and on the table of the scanner. The neurovascular status is therefore examined and written before the patient leaves the place where the injury was assessed, and it is examined again at the destination, because a finding that was not recorded before a journey cannot be attributed after it. Immobilization before imaging also protects the picture itself, since a limb that is held still produces an image that is easier to read and easier to interpret. Nobody in this sequence is permitted to straighten a deformed limb in order to obtain a better view, and the reason is that vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact.

Computed tomography takes many radiographs from many directions around the patient and uses a computer to reconstruct them as cross sections. It shows bone with a detail that a plain film cannot match, and it can display the same information in other planes or as a three dimensional shape that a surgeon can turn over in the mind. What it adds is geometry, which means the path of a fracture line, the number of fragments, the step where a broken edge meets a joint surface, and the small piece that has come to rest inside the joint or between the bone ends. It is information of that kind that decides whether an injury can be treated in a cast or needs an operation, and that decision belongs to the orthopedic surgeon who will perform it. Computed tomography is a hospital examination, performed in a department staffed by radiographers and reported by a radiologist, and it is not a tool that is carried to the roadside.

The fractures that most often need computed tomography are those near or inside a joint, where a step of a few millimeters can change the future of the limb. Examples used in teaching include breaks of the tibial plateau, the calcaneus, the acetabulum and the vertebrae, and these are illustrations of a principle rather than a list to be memorized, because the more a fracture involves a joint surface, the more the surgeon needs to see its geometry. A scan may also find a fragment that has rotated and now blocks the movement of a joint, and that is one of the situations in which reduction must not be attempted by an untrained hand. In the spine, computed tomography shows the bone of the vertebral body and the arch with great clarity, and it is combined with other studies when a neurological deficit is present, because the question then concerns the cord and the nerve roots as well as the bone. Clearing a spine is a decision made by a clinician qualified to clear it, and no image replaces that judgment.

Radiation is the cost that computed tomography imposes on the body, and it is a real cost rather than a theoretical one. A single scan of one region delivers a dose many times that of a single radiograph, and any figure quoted for that difference must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the values change with the machine, the technique and the edition of the reference. The tissues most sensitive to radiation are those that divide quickly, so a child, a young person and a pregnant patient deserve a deliberate conversation before any scan is ordered. A pregnant patient who has been injured presents a decision that no responder can make, and the clinician weighs the injury that must be diagnosed against the exposure that the study would cause, with the radiologist and, where it is possible and appropriate, with the patient herself. A clinician may decide that the answer is worth the dose and may be right, but that decision is made with the radiologist and recorded with the reason. Alternatives are always considered first, because a radiograph may answer the question, ultrasound may answer part of it, and magnetic resonance imaging uses no ionizing radiation at all.

Computed tomography is poor at showing the soft tissues that the examination is often most concerned about. A ligament, a tendon, a piece of cartilage and the marrow inside a bone are all seen far better by other means, so a normal scan does not exclude a torn ligament or a fracture that is only a crack in the spongy bone. Metal in the field, whether a surgical implant or a fragment from the injury itself, scatters the beam and produces streaks that can hide the very thing being looked for, and the radiologist must be told what is inside the patient. A splint, a brace or a binder that stays in place during the scan may also affect what can be seen, and it is left in place unless a clinician has decided otherwise, because the limb is still injured after the picture is taken. The report is read by the clinician who ordered it, and a printed result is never handed to a patient as an explanation.

Magnetic resonance imaging places the patient inside a strong magnetic field and uses radio waves to build a picture, so it uses no ionizing radiation and shows soft tissue in extraordinary detail. Ligaments, tendons, cartilage, muscle, the fluid within a joint, the marrow of bone and the spinal cord with its nerves are all within its range, and it is the study of choice when the question concerns a structure rather than a broken cortex. It shows a fracture that a radiograph has not yet revealed, because blood and swelling inside the marrow change the signal of the bone, and that change appears long before the fracture line itself becomes visible. For the same reason it often finds the injury in an older adult whose bone has lost density, whose fracture may be present with little pain and a radiograph that looks almost normal. It shows the growth region near the end of a child's bone, and it shows the spinal cord when a patient has weakness or numbness. It is ordered by a clinician, reported by a radiologist, and performed by radiographers trained for the magnet room.

The magnet is the part of magnetic resonance imaging that every responder must respect, and the reason is that the field is always on, even when the machine is not scanning and even when the room appears empty and quiet. Any ferromagnetic object that enters the room becomes a projectile, including an oxygen cylinder, a stretcher, a pair of scissors, a tool and a key, and the list is limited only by the imagination of the people who have been hurt by it. A patient with a pacemaker, a cochlear implant, certain surgical clips, an older heart valve, a metal fragment in the eye or an implanted pump may be harmed by the field, and the decisions about those devices belong to the radiologist and the physician responsible for the patient. The screening questionnaire is completed and verified before anyone crosses the line, and the staff who enter wear personal protective equipment and follow the rules of the facility. The radiographer has both the authority and the duty to stop anyone who has not been screened, and a monitor, a pump or a cylinder that travels with the patient must be approved for the magnet room, while equipment that is not approved stays outside. The patient must also be able to lie still through a long examination, and sedation for a patient who cannot cooperate is a decision for a physician working within local protocol.

The journey to the magnet room is itself an intervention and must be treated as one. A patient with an injured limb arrives in a splint or a binder that has been applied and checked, and the limb is examined before departure and again on arrival, with the color, the warmth, the pulses, the sensation and the movement all compared with the record. The magnet room cannot receive the monitor that was used in the resuscitation room, so the patient is observed by a person who stays within sight and by equipment that is safe for the field, and any change is reported at once. Warmth is maintained throughout the journey, because a patient who is cooled in a long corridor is a patient in whom shock and clotting worsen. A splint that has become tight on the way is loosened by someone authorized to do so, and a limb that becomes tense, swollen and painful out of proportion to the injury is a reason to stop and escalate rather than to continue.

Ultrasound uses sound waves that are too high for the ear to hear, sent from a probe held against the skin, and it builds a picture as the clinician watches. It uses no ionizing radiation, the machine is small enough to be wheeled to the bedside, and the examination can be repeated as often as the question changes, which makes it the one imaging method that can be brought to a patient who must not be moved. It is used by clinicians trained and credentialed in its use, by emergency physicians, by sonographers and, in some services, by trained prehospital teams working under a protocol that authorizes it. Its greatest strength is also its greatest weakness, because the picture is produced and interpreted by the person holding the probe, so the value of the study depends on the training of that person and on knowing what to look for. A study performed by someone who is not trained in it, and interpreted by someone who was not present, is a study that can mislead.

Ultrasound answers a small number of questions about an injured limb very well, and those questions are worth naming. It shows fluid inside a joint, which tells the examiner that something within the joint has bled, and it can show a joint that has filled after a dislocation or a fracture that enters the joint surface. It shows tendons and can demonstrate a gap or a retracted end after an injury, particularly where the tendon lies close to the skin, and it can find a foreign body such as a piece of glass or wood that a wound has hidden. It can follow the flow of blood in a vessel and can help to show whether an artery has been injured or compressed, although a normal flow signal does not exclude an injury to the wall of the vessel. It can also confirm that a joint has returned to its place after a reduction performed by a qualified clinician, which is useful when that confirmation must be obtained without moving the patient to another room.

Ultrasound also guides procedures that a trained clinician performs, and the guidance is a skill learned on patients under supervision rather than from a page. Aspiration of a tense joint, drainage of a collection, the placement of a needle or a catheter and the injection of a substance into a joint are each performed only by a clinician credentialed for that act and only within the local protocol, and the substance and the amount are never taught here. The probe gives the operator a view of the needle as it advances, which reduces the number of attempts and the harm that repeated attempts can cause, but it does not make the procedure safe by itself. The person who performs it is also responsible for the sterile field, for personal protective equipment, for confirming the identity of the patient and the side of the limb, and for recording what was done. A responder who is not credentialed for the procedure assists with the comfort of the patient and with holding the limb still, and does nothing more.

What ultrasound cannot be trusted for is as important as what it can do. Sound does not pass through bone, so the interior of a bone and the joint surface behind it are hidden, and a normal examination of a limb therefore never excludes a fracture. Deep structures are poorly seen in a large or swollen limb, and the probe cannot be pressed firmly against a wound, an open injury or a very tender area without adding pain and risk. A small crack in the cortex, a fracture that does not displace and an injury that lies behind another bone are all easy to miss, and the person who reports the study may be the person who most wants it to be normal. The finding that must never be reported as a clear limb is the limb that hurts, because pain after an injury is a finding in its own right and it outranks a picture that looks reassuring.

The choice among these examinations depends on the question, the patient and the place, and it is made in a conversation between the clinician and the radiologist. A patient with a suspected break of a long bone in a well equipped hospital is assessed, splinted, examined and sent for a radiograph, and computed tomography is added only if the geometry of the fracture will change the operation. A patient with a painful knee and a normal radiograph may need magnetic resonance imaging for a ligament, while a patient with a swollen joint that must be aspirated now may need ultrasound at the bedside. In a small facility with no scanner the question changes from which study to choose to whether the patient must travel, and that decision weighs the injury against the journey. Where two studies could answer the same question, the one that is faster and safer for this patient is chosen, and the reason is written down.

The cost of imaging to a patient begins with time, and time is not an abstraction in a person who is in pain, frightened and far from home. A scan may be available at once or may wait behind other patients, and the patient who is unstable or in severe pain is given priority while the patient with a stable injury waits. Waiting is a period of risk rather than an empty pause, because a splint can tighten, a limb can swell and a patient can become cold, so the responder uses that time to keep the patient warm, to keep the limb supported in the position found and to report every change to the clinician who can act on it. Transport is the second cost, and for many patients it is the largest, because a study that is not available where the injury was assessed means a journey by road or by air, an escort trained to watch the patient and a receiving facility that has been warned. The limb is splinted before the journey and checked during it, the neurovascular status is recorded before departure and after arrival, and the record travels with the patient so that the next team continues a story instead of starting a new one. There is a third cost, which is money, because a scan may be charged for, the days away from work may cost more than the scan, and a study that will not change the treatment takes from a household that has already been injured. Pain must be treated for the patient to wait and to travel at all, and the choice and the amount of any analgesic belong to the prescriber within local protocol, because this course names no dose, no route and no frequency.

Reassessment after imaging is the step that closes the loop, and it is performed with the same observations in the same order as before. The limb is examined for color, warmth, pulses, sensation, movement and pain, and each finding is compared with the record rather than remembered, because the comparison is what has value. The splint, the cast or the binder is checked for tightness after the patient has been moved, positioned on a table and moved again, since a device that fitted in the emergency department may not fit after swelling has increased. A patient who has been lying flat and still for a long examination may be cold, may be in more pain than before and may be frightened by what is happening, and each of those findings is acted on. The complication this course is most afraid of is the one caused by the treatment, and the reassessment is the only reliable way to catch it early.

A patient who becomes worse during or after a study is a patient who stops the process, because the study serves the patient rather than the other way around. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, a limb that becomes pale or cool and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. When a compartment syndrome is suspected, the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle, so the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of local protocol, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently. A pulse that remains present does not exclude that diagnosis, and waiting for a confirmation that will arrive too late is the mistake this course warns against. The responder records what was found, what was done and at what time, and passes that record to whoever takes over the care.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step, and imaging exists to inform it rather than to replace it. Some injuries are managed without an operation, in a cast, a brace, a splint or a boot, and that decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the follow-up, who also decides when the next radiograph will be taken. Other injuries need an operation, which may hold the fragments with metal devices placed inside the body, an operation called open reduction and internal fixation, or with a frame that holds them from outside, and the choice between those methods is made by the surgeon after examining the patient and the images together. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and this course describes what they are meant to achieve rather than how to do them. The part of the responder ends with the safe transfer of a patient who has been assessed, stabilized, examined, immobilized, imaged and reassessed, and with a record that makes the next decision easier.

Certain things must never be done, however strong the temptation and however good the intention behind them. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field or in the imaging department in order to obtain a better picture, and the reason is the risk to the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone. An embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room and to nobody else. A patient who is unstable, who is bleeding, who is not breathing or who is in cardiac arrest is not sent to a scanner alone, because imaging must never delay resuscitation. A reduction is never attempted by an untrained hand, and never when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear or when an earlier attempt has failed, because in each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot.

The spine deserves one further word in a chapter about imaging, because the studies described here are often the ones that decide whether it can be cleared. A patient with a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no image and no examination by an unqualified person changes that rule. The clinician who clears a spine is trained and authorized to do it, using the criteria of the local protocol, and until that moment the patient is moved by a trained team with the precautions the protocol requires. A normal scan in a patient who cannot be examined reliably does not by itself make movement safe, and a scan that is not available does not justify an exception. Where the patient has a neurological deficit the question about the spinal cord and the nerve roots is urgent, and the referral is made without waiting for a picture that can be obtained later.

Nothing described in this chapter is learned by listening to it, and that sentence is not a formality. The scope of practice that authorizes a procedure, the credential that proves a person has been trained for it and the protocol that governs it are defined by the service, the institution and the law of the country, and they differ from place to place. A responder who has been taught to hold a probe in one service is not thereby qualified to hold it in another, and the safe course for anyone who is unsure is to support the limb, keep the patient warm, record the findings and hand the decision to a person who is qualified to make it. Computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasound are each performed by trained professionals inside a department with rules, and each is interpreted in the light of an examination performed by a clinician.

To summarize, the radiograph remains the first and often the only picture taken of an injured limb, and the other three examinations are added when a specific question cannot be answered without them. Computed tomography shows the geometry of a complex fracture, magnetic resonance imaging shows the ligaments, the cartilage, the marrow and the spinal cord, and ultrasound shows fluid, tendons, foreign bodies and the flow of blood at the bedside, and each of them has limits the clinician must keep in mind. Every study is ordered by a physician, performed by trained professionals and reported by a radiologist, and the lay first aider never orders imaging and never interprets it. The order of care never changes, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the neurovascular findings are recorded before and after every intervention, including the journey to the scanner. A deformed limb is never straightened to improve a picture, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a patient who is unstable is not sent to a scanner alone, because resuscitation comes before imaging. The spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, cold is treated as a complication, and every number in this course is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 58 — Conservative Treatment

Most fractures in the world are treated without an operation, and so are many dislocations once they have been put back into place. Conservative treatment is not the treatment left over when nothing better is available, because a cast, a brace, a splint, a boot and, in some settings, traction are each a deliberate choice made by a clinician. That clinician has judged that the bone can be held well enough from the outside while it heals, and each device carries its own risks and its own way of failing. This chapter follows the order used throughout this course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The decision to treat an injury conservatively belongs to a clinician trained in fracture care, and it rests on a judgment about the injury and about the patient. That clinician asks whether the bone ends lie in a position the body can accept, whether the pattern of the break tends to stay where it is put, whether the joint surface is involved, and whether the nerves and vessels are intact. The clinician also asks whether the skin and the soft tissues can tolerate a device pressing on them for weeks. A second set of questions has nothing to do with the radiograph, and it asks whether this patient can return for follow-up, whether someone can bring them, and whether they can keep a device dry and in place. Where a service has no operating room and no orthopedic surgeon, conservative treatment may be the only treatment available, and then the urgent question is how the patient reaches a place where an operation exists. The lay first aider, the trained first responder and the paramedic do not make this decision, because it depends on images and on an examination that only a clinician performs.

Assessment begins before the limb is touched, and in conservative treatment the history carries as much weight as the examination. The responder notes the scene, the mechanism of injury, the time that has passed and the age of the patient. The primary survey follows, in the order remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, because life comes before limb. Certain details decide whether a bone will be easy to hold in a device, and among them are a medicine that thins the bone, a previous fracture in the same place, tobacco use and poorly controlled diabetes. The patient's circumstances belong in the same history, because a treatment that needs many visits cannot be given to a patient who has no way to make them. Exposure means uncovering the patient enough to see the whole limb, and it is followed at once by covering the patient again, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a matter of comfort.

The limb itself is examined by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing it. Both sides are uncovered and compared, because a limb that looks almost normal may still hold a fracture, and a fracture that has not moved is the very injury most often treated conservatively. The responder looks for swelling, for a wound, for a change in color and for skin that is stretched and shiny. Feeling is done gently and in a fixed order, moving from the joint above to the joint below. Pain far worse than the appearance of the limb suggests is itself a finding rather than a complaint, and a limb that cannot be moved may mean that a tendon is torn. Everything is recorded in the words that describe it, and the record is begun before the first device is applied, because a finding that was not written down cannot be settled afterwards.

Stabilization is a small set of acts performed in a deliberate order, and the most important of them is restraint. A deformed limb is supported and immobilized in the position in which it was found, and it is never straightened in the field. The reason is that the nerves and the vessels lie against the bone, and the pressure holding a torn vessel closed may be the only thing preventing further bleeding. Pulling a limb straight may also drive a sharp bone end through skin that was intact, which turns an injury that could have been treated in a cast into one that needs an operating room. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with a dressing, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an embedded object is never removed, because it may be plugging a torn vessel. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with a rolled blanket, keeps the patient warm and still, and calls for help. The trained first responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while an open wound is never explored blindly by anyone.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is written down. A finding that was not recorded before a device was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color of the hand or the foot and compares it with the other side, feels its temperature, and presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return. Sensation is tested on both sides in the same places, and the patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes and to say whether the movement feels normal and strong. In conservative treatment it has a second purpose, because a cast, a brace or a boot hides the skin beneath it, so it is the only way to know that the device is not pressing on a nerve or a vessel. It is repeated immediately after the device is applied, after any adjustment of a strap, a hinge or a weight, and at every follow-up visit. A pulse that can be felt does not exclude serious injury, while a pulse that cannot be felt, a hand or foot that is pale and cool, or a new numbness is an emergency that stops the process at once.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it. The devices that do this work form one family, and the splint is the device of the field and of the first hours. The cast is a rigid shell that encircles the limb, the brace is a removable support that often allows some movement, and the boot or the stiff-soled shoe holds the foot and the ankle while allowing protected weight bearing. All of them are padded where they press over a bone, all are applied over the position in which the limb was found, and all are secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The splint is also used in hospital while swelling is at its worst, because a limb that is still swelling inside a rigid cast will be squeezed by it. The trained first responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the choice among the devices belongs to the clinician who has examined the patient and seen the image. What every level must avoid is wrapping a device so tightly that it presses, because what was meant to protect then becomes the cause of the complication that follows.

The cast is a rigid shell, made of plaster or of a synthetic material, that is applied soft and molded around the limb and then hardens where it sits. Its purpose is to hold the bone ends in the position the clinician has accepted while the bone heals, and because it grips the limb it controls movement in every direction rather than in one. A cast is applied by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon, or by a trained technician working under a written protocol. The technique of applying it, molding it and judging its fit belongs to supervised clinical training rather than to a book, and a cast is never applied in the field. What can go wrong is worth saying plainly, because the device itself is silent, and a limb that swells inside a rigid shell is squeezed. The pressure can close the small vessels and press on a nerve, the material can heat as it sets and burn the skin, and skin beneath a cast can become infected without anyone seeing it. A stain, a bad smell or new pain is reported at once, nobody splits, cuts, tightens or removes a cast outside the local protocol, and nobody makes a cast comfortable by pushing padding under its edge.

The brace is the removable member of the family, and it trades a little security for the ability to see the skin and to move the joint. A brace may be a molded shell held by straps, a hinged frame that limits how far a knee or an elbow may bend, or a soft support used for a stable injury. It may be chosen for a fracture expected to stay in place, for an injury in which the ligaments rather than the bone carry the problem, or after an operation when the surgeon wants the joint to move within a defined range. Because it is removable, its value depends on the patient wearing it and on the straps and hinges being set as the clinician ordered. Straps that are too tight press on skin and on the nerves beneath them, straps that are too loose let the brace slide, and a brace worn over a swollen limb may be far tighter in the evening. The boot and the stiff-soled shoe let a patient walk while a bone in the foot or the ankle heals and are used for stable fractures and for stress injuries. A boot can be taken off, and a device that can be taken off will be taken off, so the fit is checked and the instruction about when to wear it is given. A brace or a boot is fitted by a clinician, a nurse or a physical therapist, and a patient who limps away with a boot but no instruction has been supplied rather than treated.

Traction is the oldest of these treatments and the one that must be handled most carefully, because it is still used in some settings when an operation is not available or not safe. Traction means a gentle and continuous pull along the long axis of the limb, held steady to overcome the pull of the muscles that have shortened it. Its purpose is to hold the bone ends in better alignment, to reduce movement at the fracture, to reduce bleeding and pain and to make the journey to hospital safer. It is never a way of setting a fracture or of putting a dislocated joint back into place, because a pull strong enough to force bone ends into position can tear vessels, nerves and skin. Skin traction transmits the pull through straps or a boot, while skeletal traction transmits it through a metal pin placed in the bone, and the second requires sterile technique and an anesthetic decision that belongs to the physician. Both forms are applied only by a clinician trained and authorized to apply them, according to a written protocol, and the placement of the pin and the adjustment of the weight belong to supervised practical training. Traction is not applied when there is a suspected pelvic fracture, when an open wound lies under the device, when a fragment is caught in the joint, or when the pulse is failing and the foot is numb. In each of those situations the limb is immobilized in the position found and the patient is referred, and a weight is never increased to overcome resistance, because force is not a technique.

Imaging is the step that tells the clinician what the hand cannot, and in conservative treatment it has two jobs. The first is the study that confirms the injury and shows its pattern, usually a radiograph taken in at least 2 directions with the joint above and the joint below included. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint, while magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. The second job is the follow-up study, taken after the device has been applied and then at intervals the clinician sets. The bone ends can move in the first weeks as the swelling goes down, and a device that fitted a swollen limb becomes loose on a thinner one. That loss of position is the commonest reason a conservative plan is abandoned, and it is often silent, since the limb is inside a device and the patient feels less pain rather than more. Every figure quoted for the interval between those studies is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services differ in how often they look. The lay first aider never orders or interprets an image, and only the clinician responsible for the care decides what the picture means and what is done next.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention and at every visit, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment rather than the one caused by the injury. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and it is the comparison that carries the information. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the device is checked for tightness, for slipping and for moisture. The skin is inspected at the edges of the device, under every strap and at the heel, where pressure is easiest to miss. The findings that stop the process are pain that increases instead of settling, numbness, tingling, weakness, a hand or foot that becomes pale or cool, and a limb that grows tense and swollen. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for confirmation, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle, and the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the local protocol by someone authorized to do it. The limb is kept at the level of the heart rather than raised above it, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently.

Weight bearing is the instruction that patients misunderstand most often, and the misunderstanding is not a failure of attention but a failure of our words. Not weight bearing means that none of the patient's weight goes through the injured limb at all, and the limb is held clear of the ground with crutches or a frame. Touch-down weight bearing means that the foot may rest on the floor only to help balance, with no more pressure than it takes to feel the ground beneath it. Partial weight bearing means that some share of the body's weight is allowed through the limb, and that share is defined by the clinician and often practiced on a scale in a training session. Weight bearing as tolerated means that the patient may put weight on the limb as comfort allows while the device is worn, and full weight bearing means that the limb may carry the whole body as it normally would. Each of those instructions belongs to the clinician who examined the patient and reviewed the images, and none of them is changed or guessed by the responder, the nurse, the physical therapist or the patient.

What goes wrong with those instructions is easy to predict and is worth saying in advance. A patient told to bear weight as tolerated hears that the leg is healed and begins to walk without the boot. A patient told to bear weight partially hears that the leg must be protected and stays in bed until the joint stiffens. Pain is a poor guide to how much weight is safe, because a device that holds a bone still also dulls the signal that would otherwise warn the patient. A patient whose sensation is impaired by diabetes or by a nerve injury may have no warning at all. Hopping on one leg is not a way of keeping weight off the injured side, because it is how patients fall, and a fall can undo a position that took weeks to hold. The instruction applies to every step, at home, in the bathroom and on the stairs, with the device on and fastened, and it applies until the clinician says otherwise rather than until the pain stops. When a patient reports that the limb feels better, the reply is not permission to do more but an explanation that a bone which has stopped hurting has not necessarily joined.

The way the instruction is given decides whether it is followed. The clinician authorizes the amount of weight, the device and the walking aid, while the nurse and the physical therapist teach the patient how to use them. The instruction is spoken and written in the same words, it is stated in terms the patient uses, and it names the activity rather than the abstract category. The patient is asked to say the instruction back in their own words and then to demonstrate it while someone watches, because a patient who can repeat the category may still be doing the opposite. The commonest way conservative treatment fails is not the device but the patient who does not come back, and the reason is usually distance, cost, lost wages or the care of children. At every later encounter the responder asks when the next appointment is and what the patient was told to do, and a missed appointment is treated as an urgent finding rather than an administrative one. A patient whose device has been ruined by water or who describes new numbness should be seen before the scheduled date, because those findings change what the next image will show.

A device that stays on the limb for weeks carries its own list of instructions, and the patient should hear all of them before leaving. The device is kept dry unless the clinician says that water is allowed, because wet padding holds moisture against the skin and a wet cast loses strength. Nothing is inserted into the device to scratch, no powder or cream is put beneath it unless it has been prescribed, and the edges are not cut or bent by anyone outside the treating team. A device that becomes loose, soft, cracked or foul smelling is a reason to seek care at once rather than at the next appointment. The patient is shown where to look and to feel for redness, blisters and pressure marks, and is told to use a mirror where the device hides the skin from view. Driving, work, sleep, keeping the device clean and managing dependents are part of the plan too, because a patient who is given a treatment that cannot be lived with will quietly abandon it.

Some patients need a different plan, because a device that cannot be checked safely is more dangerous than no device at all. A young child cannot describe numbness or tingling and grows out of a device within weeks, so the follow-up must be closer and the instruction belongs as much to the parent. An older adult may have thin skin that breaks down under a strap and a poor sense of balance that a rigid boot makes worse, so the walking aid and the home are assessed with the same care as the fracture. A patient whose sensation is impaired by diabetes, by a nerve injury or by a spinal cord injury may feel no warning at all and must be taught to inspect the skin at fixed times. A patient who is confused or intoxicated needs a plan that does not depend on cooperation, and the decision about what that plan should be belongs to the clinician. In every one of those situations the responder's part is to recognize the finding, to say it aloud in the handover and to bring the patient back rather than to adjust the device.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step, and for conservative treatment it means knowing when the plan must be changed. A fracture that has lost its position on the follow-up image, a fracture that shows no sign of joining, an infection beneath a device and a limb that is painful out of proportion are all reasons to involve the orthopedic surgeon. So are the injuries in which conservative treatment was never the first choice, which include an open fracture, a dislocation that has not been reduced and a fracture in a child that crosses the growth region. A patient who cannot return for follow-up or who has no one to help at home may need to be admitted rather than sent home, and that is a decision about safety rather than about bone. When the plan is changed, the patient is told that this is a change in the treatment and not a failure of the patient, because a person who feels blamed will not report the next problem. The orthopedic surgeon decides what form the definitive treatment takes, whether that is a longer period in a cast or an operation with plates, screws, nails or an external frame.

The levels of practice in this chapter are easy to keep in order, because every act described here has an owner. The lay first aider supports the limb in the position found, controls the bleeding that can be controlled with a dressing, keeps the patient warm and still, calls for help, and observes color, warmth, movement and feeling, but never straightens the limb and never applies anything rigid to it. The trained first responder performs the neurovascular examination and records it, applies splints within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes, and reports any change before arrival. The emergency medical technician and the paramedic work within a broader written protocol, may apply a traction device where the service trains and permits it, and may give a medicine for pain only as that protocol directs. The nurse examines and records, checks the skin under straps and cast edges, maintains the position the clinician has ordered, teaches the patient within the plan that has been set, and reports any change at once. The physician and the orthopedic surgeon examine the patient, order and interpret the images, decide whether treatment is conservative or operative, and set the amount of weight bearing. The physical therapist teaches the patient to walk with the aid and the device the clinician has chosen, and no dose, no route and no regimen appears in this chapter. The substance given for pain, for infection and for tetanus belongs to the prescriber and the local protocol, and the finding that makes any of those decisions urgent is reported rather than treated by a listener.

The record and the handover carry the plan as well as the injury. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the device that was applied and by whom, the weight bearing that was authorized, and the date of the next appointment are written or spoken in a fixed order. It is worth saying aloud that the limb was not straightened and that no object was removed, because the absence of an act is as important to record as its performance. A patient with a fracture of a long bone has often taken energy through the trunk or the spine, so the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, and where a number appears here it is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, a cast, a brace, a splint, a boot and traction are treatments in their own right, each chosen by a clinician who has examined the patient and reviewed the images, rather than the treatment that remains when an operation is unavailable. What to look for is a device that has become tight, loose, wet or cracked, a limb that is pale, cool, numb, weak or painful out of proportion to the injury, a stain or a smell from beneath a cast, and a patient who cannot return for follow-up. What to do is to follow the order this course uses in every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The neurovascular findings are recorded before and after every intervention, the patient is kept warm, and the instruction about weight bearing is said plainly, in the patient's own words, and checked. What never to do is to straighten a deformed limb in the field, to remove an embedded object, to push exposed bone back into a wound, to explore an open wound blindly, to apply a cast in the field, or to increase a weight to overcome resistance. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a responder who suspects a compartment syndrome releases the constricting device within the local protocol, keeps the limb at the level of the heart and refers urgently, because time is muscle. Who to call is decided by the service and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 59 — Surgical Treatment

An operation is one step in the same sequence this course follows everywhere, and it is neither the first step nor one that a responder performs. That sequence is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. Surgery belongs to the last of those steps, so everything done before it either prepared the patient for an operation or made one unnecessary. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

An operation on a fracture does three things, and any account of one can be judged by asking which of the three it addresses. The first is to put the broken ends into a position the body can heal and the limb can use, which is the act called reduction. The second is to hold that position without depending on a cast or on the stillness of the patient, which is done with a device fixed to the bone or passing through it. The third is to deal with everything else the injury damaged, which means the skin, the muscle, the vessels, the nerves and sometimes the surface of the joint itself.

The decision to operate belongs to the orthopedic surgeon and to the patient, and it is made after a conversation rather than from a picture alone. The surgeon brings the assessment of the bone, the state of the soft tissues and the resources of the facility, while the patient brings the life that has to continue afterward, including work, dependency and fear. A fracture that can be treated in more than one way is treated by explaining the choices, including what each choice asks of the patient and what each choice risks. A responder who tells a patient that an operation will certainly be needed has promised something that belongs to a surgeon's judgment and to a consent conversation.

Assessment comes before any decision about an operation, and it begins with the patient rather than with the radiograph. The mechanism of injury and the energy involved tell the clinician how much tissue the energy passed through, and a fall from a height or a collision at speed does far more than break the bone that finally stops it. The history includes illnesses and medicines that change how bone behaves and how it heals, and the general condition of the patient decides whether an operation is safe to offer at all. The primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, is completed before the limb becomes the priority. The limb itself is assessed by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, never by forcing it, and the findings are recorded in the words of the patient as far as possible.

Stabilization is what happens while the operation is still being decided, and in the field it is a small and disciplined set of acts. A deformed limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. The lay first aider supports the limb, keeps the patient warm and waits for help, while the trained first responder and the paramedic work within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by pressure, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and nothing done in the field should make the operation harder.

Cold is treated in this course as a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and it follows the injured patient into the operating room. A patient who has lain on a cold surface, whose clothing is wet, or whose limb has been uncovered for examination loses heat quickly, and that loss disturbs clotting, the heart and the response to blood loss. Covering the patient, insulating the limb, removing wet clothing and warming the environment are acts within the reach of the lay first aider and of every level above it. Warming belongs to whoever is present, provided the local protocol is followed, while the measurement and the correction of a low body temperature belong to the clinical team.

The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down. A finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterward, and that is the whole reason the record matters. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers and the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and numbness, tingling, weakness and the loss of a movement are recorded plainly. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency.

Immobilization prevents movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, and before an operation it serves two purposes at once. It protects the soft tissues from the sharp ends of the bone, and it holds the patient in a condition in which imaging, transfer and preparation for surgery can proceed. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician and the orthopedic surgeon decide what immobilization is required next. Casting, traction and surgical fixation are learned under supervision with real patients and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught in this course as a technique to be taken from a book.

Imaging confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician trained to do both. A radiograph is usually the first study, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in a third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below. Computed tomography shows the detail of a break that enters a joint or shatters a segment of bone, and it is often the study that decides which operation is possible. Magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues, and an image is a picture of one moment, so the patient is still examined and reassessed after it has been taken.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, because the comparison is what has value rather than any single measurement. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed, and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage, splint or cast to be released by someone authorized to do it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Referral or definitive treatment is the final step of the sequence, and it begins with the recognition that some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, or a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Transfer is arranged by the clinician responsible for the patient and carried out by a team trained and equipped for it, and it is not delayed for a study that will not change what is done. The receiving facility is told what was found, what was done, what has changed and what is suspected, in a fixed order, so that it continues a story instead of starting a new one.

A plate is a strip of metal that lies against the surface of the bone and is fixed to it with screws, and it can hold the broken ends in several different ways. It can press them together so that they unite directly, it can bridge a shattered segment and hold the length while the body fills the gap, and it can lock each screw into the plate so that the plate and the bone behave as one piece. The surgeon chooses among those behaviors according to the shape of the break and the quality of the bone, because a plate that presses works poorly in bone that has lost its density. Screws may also be used without a plate to hold a single fragment, and thin wires may be added where a small piece of bone must be kept in place. Placing any of these devices requires an open operation and a trained surgical team, and the technique is not something this course can teach.

A nail is a long rod passed into the hollow center of a long bone, so that it lies inside the bone rather than against it and holds the broken ends by running through both of them. A break in the shaft of the thigh bone, the shin bone or the arm bone is often treated this way, because a rod along the axis of the bone resists bending and carries load close to the line the bone itself would carry. The rod is introduced through a small opening at one end of the bone, guided into position with imaging used during the operation, and locked with screws across each end so that it can neither slide nor rotate. The operation is performed by an orthopedic surgeon in an operating room, and how much the canal is prepared beforehand belongs to the surgeon and to the current literature rather than to this course.

External fixation takes a different route, because the frame that holds the bone sits outside the limb and reaches it through the skin. Pins or wires pass through the soft tissues into the bone above and below the break, and they are joined by bars that the team can see and reach. Because the frame does not cross the zone of injury with a large implant, it is often chosen when the soft tissues are badly damaged, when the wound is contaminated, when the patient is too unstable for a long operation, or when the pelvis must be held together while bleeding is controlled. It may be the definitive treatment, and it may equally be a temporary measure that holds the limb until the soft tissues are ready for something else. The pins create a route from the outside world into the bone, so the pin sites are a place where infection begins, and a responder who sees spreading redness, increasing pain or discharge there reports it rather than touching the frame. The frame is applied, adjusted or padded only by the team qualified to do it, and it is never leaned on or used as a handle for the patient.

When the surface of the joint itself is destroyed, holding the bone is not enough, and the joint may be replaced. The worn or broken ends of the bones that form the joint are removed and replaced with an artificial joint, and the operation is called an arthroplasty when it redoes the whole joint and a hemiarthroplasty when it replaces only one side of it. This is a common operation in the older adult who has broken the hip, where the blood supply to the head of the thigh bone has been damaged and the bone will not unite, and it allows the patient to stand sooner than a healing fracture would. The choice among fixing the bone and replacing part or all of the joint depends on the age of the patient, the state of the bone, the ability of the patient to cooperate with protected movement and the wishes of the patient. It is decided by the orthopedic surgeon together with the patient or the family, and it is never a decision for a responder.

After the operation a responder may meet the limb again in a ward, in a vehicle or at home, and what is visible is the wound and the dressing rather than the device. A closed wound is usually held with stitches, staples or strips of tape, and it is covered with a dressing whose job is to keep it clean, to absorb what seeps and to let the team see whether bleeding continues. A drain may be left in place briefly to carry collected blood and fluid out of the wound, and it is removed by the team that placed it. A dressing that has become soaked is reinforced rather than taken down, because taking it down opens the wound to the environment and to hands that have no reason to be in it, and a change of dressing is done by a nurse or a physician following the local protocol. The lay first aider does not touch a surgical dressing at all, and the trained responder reports what is seen and leaves it covered. How much weight the patient may put on the operated limb is a decision the orthopedic surgeon makes and records, it is stated in words such as no weight, some weight or full weight, and a responder never decides that a limb looks strong enough to bear weight.

Infection is the complication that turns a good operation into a long illness, and it is watched for in every patient who has had one. The findings are a wound that becomes more painful rather than less, skin that is red and warm around it, swelling that increases, a fever, and a patient who feels unwell in a way that is hard to describe. In the first days after an operation those findings may be caused by something other than infection, and only the clinical team can tell the difference, so the responder reports rather than concludes. Whether an antibiotic is given, which one and by what route are decisions of the prescriber, and this course names no substance and no amount.
