A compartment syndrome can develop after an operation as well as before one, and the treatment that was meant to help is sometimes the cause. A cast, a tight bandage, a dressing that becomes soaked and then dries, or bleeding inside a closed space can each raise the pressure within a compartment, and the earliest and most reliable finding is pain that grows instead of settling. The limb may look normal from the outside, the pulse may still be felt, and the patient may still move the fingers or the toes, which is why an intact pulse is not a reassurance. Pain relief that numbs the limb can hide the pain that would otherwise give the warning, so the team watches the limb even when the patient is comfortable. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for confirmation, does not elevate the limb above the level of the heart, keeps the patient warm, and refers the patient urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Two further problems are common enough after an operation to be mentioned in any handover. A clot may form in the deep veins of the leg when a patient is still and has had a major injury, and the signs are a swollen, tender calf, while a clot that travels to the lungs causes sudden breathlessness and chest pain and is an emergency. Whether a medicine is given to reduce that risk, which medicine, in what amount and by which route are decisions of the prescriber working to the local protocol, and this course names none of them. Pain is treated for a reason as well, because a patient in severe pain cannot breathe deeply, move or sleep, but the choice of substance and the amount are again the prescriber's. The responder describes the pain in the words of the patient and reports it, and never takes a prescription from a book.

Repeating the neurovascular examination after an operation is as important as performing it before, and the record of the earlier examination is what gives the later one its meaning. A nerve may be injured by the original trauma or by the operation itself, and a weakness or numbness that was not present before is a finding to be reported at once rather than explained away. The responder records what the patient can feel and move, compares the two sides, and reports any change. Interpretation belongs to the clinical team, and the observation and the record belong to whoever is with the patient.

Rehabilitation begins earlier than most patients expect, and the reason is that a joint held still for a long time becomes stiff in a way that is hard to undo. Movement is often started while the bone is still healing, because the device holds the fracture and the movement keeps the muscle and the joint working. A typical interval for a long bone in the shaft of a limb to unite is given in teaching as 8 to 12 weeks, a figure offered here as an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs with the bone, the patient and the service. The physiotherapist teaches the exercises, the nurse supports them through the day, and the patient, whose understanding matters as much as the device, does the work. In the older adult the goal is to restore walking as early as it is safe, because a person who loses the ability to walk loses independence as well.

The reason the decision belongs to the surgeon and the patient together is that an operation trades one set of risks for another, and only the patient can weigh the trade. The surgeon explains the injury, the options, the likely result of each option, and the complications that are known as well as those that are rare, and the patient answers with the life he or she wants to return to. Consent is not a signature collected at the door of the operating room, and a patient who does not understand what is proposed cannot consent to it, which is why an interpreter, a family member or a simpler explanation may be needed. Where the patient cannot decide and no one is authorized to decide for that patient, the law and the local protocol govern what happens, and those differ between countries and between editions of the same guideline. A responder who is asked whether an operation is necessary answers with the name of the person who can say, and not with an opinion.

Some operations are not a choice but a rescue, and they follow a different logic from the planned ones. A patient who is bleeding into the pelvis or the abdomen, whose limb has lost its blood supply, whose wound is open and heavily contaminated, or who is deteriorating for reasons that are not yet clear may go to the operating room before there is time for every study. In that situation the operation may aim only to control bleeding, to clean a wound, to hold a bone temporarily and to keep the patient alive, with the definitive reconstruction planned for a later day. The decision is made by a surgical team with anesthesia and an intensive care unit behind it, and it is not a decision for a responder to make or to delay. The responder's part is to recognize how fast the patient is changing, to say so plainly, and to keep the patient warm while the transfer proceeds.

Two groups of patients need their own arithmetic, and the reason lies in the bone rather than in the operation. In a child, the growth region near the end of a bone can be injured without the bone breaking, and an operation that crosses it carelessly can slow or stop the growth of that limb, so these injuries belong to a surgeon used to treating children. In an older adult, the bone may have lost density, so a device that holds well in strong bone may cut through it, and the surgeon may prefer a joint replacement to a plate for that reason. Neither fact changes the sequence that begins with assessment, and both mean that a responder should lower the threshold for getting a senior opinion rather than settle for an explanation that the injury is minor.

Carrying the operation into the next phase of care is the work of the record and the handover, which are part of the treatment rather than a formality after it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, the operation performed, the device used and the wound care ordered are written or spoken in a fixed order. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so the patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. What the next team needs is not an opinion but an accurate story with the times attached, because a finding without a time cannot be interpreted. Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision.

Consider a constructed illustration, which is not a real patient and is offered only to show how the parts fit together. A man in middle age is struck by a car and breaks the shaft of his shin bone, and the skin over it is torn, so the fracture is open and the soft tissues are badly bruised. At the scene the trained responders control the bleeding, cover the wound, find the pulse and the sensation intact, splint the limb in the position found and keep him warm. In the hospital the wound is cleaned in an operating room, the bone is held temporarily with a frame outside the limb, and the wound is left covered while the tissues settle. Some days later the orthopedic surgeon replaces the frame with a rod inside the bone, and the wound is closed. Weeks afterward a responder meets him at home with a healed wound, a limb that is beginning to bear weight as the surgeon allowed, and exercises taught by a physiotherapist, and nothing in that illustration is a rule.

Certain acts lie outside the scope of everyone except the team that owns them, and the reason is that each of them can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot. A responder never straightens a deformed limb, never removes an embedded object, never pushes exposed bone back into a wound, never explores an open wound blindly, and never takes down a surgical dressing to look underneath it. No chapter of this course teaches a listener to reduce a fracture, to apply traction or to apply a cast, because those skills are learned under supervision with real patients and are performed according to local protocol. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. Force is not a technique, and resistance is a reason to stop.

To summarize, an operation is the last step of the sequence this course follows, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the decision to operate belongs to the orthopedic surgeon and to the patient together. The operations that hold a fracture use a plate and screws against the bone, a nail inside it, a frame outside it, or an artificial joint that replaces the surface the injury destroyed, and each of them is chosen for one patient and one fracture. The neurovascular status is recorded before any intervention and repeated after it, the limb is reassessed after every intervention, and a limb that becomes tense and painful out of proportion to the injury is treated as a compartment syndrome until someone qualified decides otherwise. A responder never straightens a deformed limb, never removes an embedded object, never pushes exposed bone back into a wound, never explores an open wound blindly, and never takes down a surgical dressing. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, no dose and no route appears in this course, the patient is kept warm, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and who to call is settled by the local protocol before the injury happens. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 60 — Rehabilitation

Rehabilitation is not the period that begins when the fracture has healed; it begins in the first hour after the injury and continues long after the last radiograph has been filed. It is the part of treatment that decides whether the limb works, and a limb that has united perfectly on an image but cannot reach the mouth, bear weight or hold a cup is a treatment that has failed the patient. Everything this course teaches leads to one question, which is whether the person can do again what they did before, and rehabilitation is the work that turns a healed bone into a working limb. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The same sequence that governs the acute injury governs the whole of recovery, and it is worth naming again because it does not stop when the splint is applied. Assess, stabilize, examine the neurovascular status, immobilize, image, reassess, and then refer or treat definitively. In rehabilitation the assessment is the progress the patient has made, the stabilization is the protection of what is healing, and the reassessment is the scheduled review that catches the complication before the patient loses function. The sequence is a habit of mind rather than a list to be recited, and it is repeated at every visit, in the clinic, at home and on the telephone.

Healing is the work of the body, and no exercise, machine or program makes bone unite faster than it will. What rehabilitation does is protect the conditions in which healing can happen and preserve everything around the injury that the healing process does not repair by itself. Muscle that has wasted, a joint that has stiffened and a nerve that has been compressed do not recover on their own simply because the fracture has joined. The outcome measure of this phase is therefore function, and the union of the fracture is only one of the conditions that make function possible.

The goals of rehabilitation are few and can be said plainly. The first is to keep moving every joint that the injury did not involve, because a joint that is not moved becomes stiff and the cartilage within it is nourished by movement. The next is to keep as much muscle as the injury and its treatment will allow, because muscle is lost far more quickly than it is regained. Then comes the control of swelling and the control of pain, since both of them, if they are allowed to persist, prevent the movement that the first two goals require. The last is the restoration of the patient's own independence, which is the goal the patient cares about most and the one that a measurement can easily miss.

Before any of this begins, the treating clinician decides what the injury will tolerate, and nothing in this chapter gives a listener permission to make that decision. A bone fixed with metal, a bone healing in a cast, a joint that has been put back into place and a ligament that has been repaired each allow a different amount and a different kind of movement, and the difference is not visible to the person holding the limb. The physical therapist designs and progresses the program, the nurse supports it at the bedside and in the clinic, and the patient performs it. Every one of them works inside the instruction of the treating physician or orthopedic surgeon and inside the local protocol.

The assessment at the start of rehabilitation is a full one, because a patient who has been immobilized for weeks is not the patient who was injured. The examiner asks what the patient can do now that they could not do a week ago, and what they could do a week ago that they cannot do now, because a loss of function is more informative than any single measurement. The limb is looked at, felt and moved, the joints above and below the injury are examined, and the strength of the muscles that cross them is tested against the other side. Nothing in this examination forces a joint or reproduces pain deliberately, because an examination that injures the tissue it is measuring has done harm rather than good.

The neurovascular examination recorded on the day of the injury is repeated at every stage of recovery, and its result is written down in the same form. The color and the temperature of the skin are observed, the pulse beyond the injury is felt, and sensation is tested and compared with the other side. The patient is asked to move the fingers or the toes, and any weakness is recorded in the words of the patient as far as possible. A finding that has changed since the previous visit matters more than one that has always been abnormal, which is why the earlier record is part of the examination. The lay first aider and the trained responder report what they observe, while the interpretation belongs to the clinician.

A new numbness, a new tingling, a new weakness, a limb that has become cool or pale, and pain that increases instead of settling are the findings that stop the program and send the patient back for urgent assessment. The complication this course fears most is the one caused by treatment, and in rehabilitation that usually means a cast, a splint, a bandage or a brace that has become too tight as the limb swelled. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for confirmation and does not elevate the limb above the level of the heart; the constricting device is released only by someone authorized to do it under the local protocol, and the patient is transferred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. This is why the neurovascular findings are recorded before a device is applied and again after it is applied or changed.

Swelling after an injury is expected, and it is also a mechanical problem that slows everything else. Fluid that collects in a limb makes the joints stiff, weakens the muscle that has to work against it, and presses on the small vessels and nerves at the edge of the healing tissue. Movement of the joints that were not injured pumps that fluid back toward the trunk, which is one reason early movement of the uninjured parts is worth the trouble it takes. Elevation of the limb above the level of the heart helps in most situations, with the important exception of a limb in which a compartment syndrome is suspected or not yet excluded. Compression, when it is applied by someone trained and authorized to apply it, works in the same direction, and a poorly applied bandage works in the opposite one.

Pain has to be respected, because pain that is not controlled prevents movement and sleep, and a patient who cannot sleep cannot heal well. The physical measures that reduce pain belong to the patient, the nurse, the physical therapist and the trained responder according to what their service authorizes: rest and protection of the injured part, a supported position, elevation when it is appropriate, and the careful application of cold within the limits the local protocol sets. The choice of a medicine, its amount and the way it is given belong to the prescriber, and this course deliberately gives no dose, no route and no regimen. Pain relief becomes urgent when the pain is out of proportion to the injury, increases instead of settling, is not relieved by the measures that usually work, or comes with a change in the neurovascular findings.

A constructed illustration may make the shape of this clearer. A patient with a fracture of the lower leg treated in a cast is taught to move the toes and the knee, to keep the leg supported, to keep the cast dry and to return if the pain increases or the toes change color. Suppose that some days later the toes become pale and the pain becomes worse rather than better; the illustration is meant to show that this finding is not the ordinary course of healing but an emergency, and that the response is urgent assessment rather than loosening the cast at home. An illustration is not a patient, and the details here are invented for teaching.

Early movement of the joints that were not injured is the single most valuable and most neglected part of recovery. A shoulder that is not moved while the forearm is in a cast becomes the joint that limits the arm long after the fracture has healed, and the same is true of a knee left still while the ankle is treated, or of a hip kept flexed in one position for weeks. The movements are chosen by the physical therapist and authorized by the treating clinician, they are performed gently and within the range that causes no more than mild discomfort, and they stop at any moment when the patient feels something give way or when the pain becomes sharp. The lay first aider and the trained responder can encourage and remind, but the prescription of movement belongs to the clinical team.

The order matters, and it can be described without teaching a technique. The first step is to keep the uninjured joints moving through their available range in a way the clinician has approved. The next is to teach the patient to tighten the muscles around the injured part without moving the joint, a contraction that is felt rather than seen, since this keeps muscle working while the bone is protected. Only then, and only when the treating clinician has confirmed that the bone or the repair will tolerate it, is movement of the injured joint itself begun, and even then under the supervision of a physical therapist rather than on the initiative of the patient, because force has no place in any of these steps and a movement that produces sharp pain or a sense of instability is stopped and reported.

Muscle is the tissue that punishes immobility most quickly, and the loss begins within days rather than weeks. Muscle that is not used loses its bulk and its strength, and in an older adult the loss is faster and the recovery slower, so a period of bed rest that would cost a young patient little can cost an older patient the ability to stand unaided. The program therefore keeps every usable muscle working, using contractions that do not move the joint while the fracture is unprotected, and later using movement against resistance once the clinician has authorized it. No weight is borne through an injured bone or an unhealed repair until the treating clinician allows it, because a limb loaded too early can lose the position that the treatment achieved. The physical therapist decides the exercise, the clinician decides when the limb may be loaded, and the patient decides how much effort to give.

The decision about bearing weight is a clinical one, and the words used for it are worth understanding even by those who will never make the decision. Some patients are told to keep the limb off the ground entirely, others that only the weight of the limb may be taken, others that part of the body weight may be taken with support, and others that full weight is allowed. Each of those instructions is specific to one injury, one operation and one stage of healing, and none of them can be transferred from one patient to another or from one week to the next. A patient who is unsure must ask rather than guess, and the nurse or the physical therapist who is unsure must ask the clinician rather than improvise.

Immobilization protects the healing tissue, and it also creates most of the problems that rehabilitation later has to solve. A cast or a brace holds the bone while it knits, and at the same time it holds the joints still, hides the skin, and takes away the sensation that would warn the patient of trouble. Where a limb is found deformed it is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found, and it is never straightened by anyone outside a supervised clinical setting, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone. Skin under a device can be rubbed sore, can become macerated by moisture, and can break down without the patient feeling it clearly, so the patient is asked at each visit about itching, burning, a damp feeling, a bad smell or a new pain over a bony point. Nothing is ever pushed under a cast, and the cast itself is never removed by the patient at home. Removing, trimming, splitting or replacing such a device is a clinical act performed by someone trained and authorized to do it, within the local protocol, because the position it holds may be lost as soon as it comes off.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention and at every stage, and in rehabilitation the interventions are spread over weeks rather than minutes. Each visit repeats the same observations in the same order and compares them with what was recorded before, because the comparison is what carries information. The patient is asked about pain, sleep, mood and what they can do for themselves, the limb is examined, the device is inspected, and the neurovascular status is recorded again. When a program is advanced, the patient is observed performing the new activity before being sent home with it, since an exercise understood in the clinic and done differently at home is worse than none. A change in the findings is the signal to stop the progression and to refer the patient back to the clinician responsible for the injury.

Imaging belongs to the clinician and continues to be used during recovery for reasons that are specific. A radiograph may be taken to see whether the bone is uniting, to check that the position has been kept, to look for a break in the metal that holds a repair, or to look again at an area where pain persists without explanation. Computed tomography shows the detail of a bone that is healing slowly or a joint that has become irregular, and magnetic resonance imaging is used when the question concerns the soft tissues, such as a ligament, a tendon, a cartilage surface or an infection deep to the skin. The physical therapist may report a finding and the nurse may ask for an opinion, but ordering and interpreting the image belong to the clinician trained to do both. It is worth saying plainly that a good image and a stiff limb are entirely compatible, which is why the program is guided by function and not by the picture alone.

The times and the thresholds that surround recovery are illustrations and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because they differ between services, between countries and between editions of the same advice. It is reasonable to describe the phases of healing in general terms, such as a period of protection while the tissue is fragile, a period in which controlled movement is introduced, a period of strengthening, and finally a return to the activities the patient wants. The length of each phase depends on the bone, the injury, the operation, the age and the health of the patient, and the presence of any complication, and no chapter can give a listener a number that will be right for the person in front of them. Where a clinician names a time, that time is a plan to be reviewed rather than a promise.

Referral during recovery is as important as referral in the first hour, and the findings that prompt it are not always dramatic. A fracture that is more painful after several weeks rather than less, a limb that will not take weight when the clinician expected it to, a joint that is losing movement instead of gaining it, a wound or a surgical site that becomes red, hot and swollen, a new deformity, and a numbness that does not resolve are findings that send the patient back to the clinician responsible for the injury. Infection, a bone that fails to unite, a repair that has loosened, a tendon that has pulled apart, and a nerve compressed by scar tissue all present in these quiet ways. The decision about what to do next belongs to that clinician and to the orthopedic surgeon, and the task of everyone else is to recognize the finding, record it and arrange the review without delay.

Some patients heal differently, and rehabilitation has to be written for the patient rather than for the injury. A child's bone remodels and a child's rehabilitation is often shorter and better tolerated, but an injury that crosses the growing part of the bone still needs scheduled follow-up until growth is finished, because a problem there can appear long after the child has stopped complaining. An older adult who has lost bone density, or who has lost muscle during even a short admission, needs a program that addresses strength, balance and the prevention of another fall, since the next fracture is often the one that takes independence away. A sign or a measurement that is reliable in a healthy adult may be absent or misleading in any of these patients, so the plan is adjusted and the review is earlier rather than later.

The conversation about how long recovery takes is part of the treatment, and it is the part most often avoided. A patient who is told that a bone takes about 6 weeks to knit, which is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and who then finds that the limb is still stiff and weak after several months, may conclude that something has gone wrong or that they were misled. The bone unites, then the muscle must be rebuilt, then the joint must regain its movement, and then the patient must regain confidence in the limb, and none of those steps is the same as being able to use the arm or the leg normally. Nerves recover slowly, often over months, and some never recover fully, which the patient deserves to hear early. The honest answer to the question of how long is a description of the phases, an explanation of what can slow them, and a promise of review rather than a date.

Adherence is where most programs quietly fail. The patient who does not do the exercises at home is rarely lazy; they may be in pain, afraid that movement will break the bone again, depressed, sleeping badly, or unable to reach the clinic because of distance, cost or work. A program that a patient cannot perform in their own home is not a program, so the physical therapist builds it around the space, the help and the time the patient actually has, and the nurse asks at every contact what is getting in the way. Returning to work, to driving, to caring for others and to the ordinary tasks of a household are goals that motivate more than any measurement, and they belong in the plan from the beginning.

The mood, the sleep and the confidence of the patient are not a separate subject from the limb, and a patient who is frightened of using an arm will not use it however strong it becomes. Pain that has lasted for weeks disturbs sleep, disturbed sleep lowers the tolerance for pain, and the two together make every exercise harder, which is a circle broken by treating the pain, protecting sleep and progressing slowly enough to succeed. Returning to a job may depend on an employer's willingness to accept modified duties, and returning to driving depends on the limb, the law and the local rules rather than on the opinion of the patient. The occupational therapist addresses the tasks of daily living and the return to work, the physical therapist addresses movement and strength, and the clinician addresses the injury, and none of them can replace the others.

Rehabilitation after a dislocation follows the same logic, with the difference that the joint itself has been injured and the tissues that hold it have torn. The joint is protected while those tissues heal, the muscles around it are kept working in the ways the clinician permits, and movement is restored in a controlled way, because a joint moved too far too early can come out again. The decision about how far and how fast belongs to the clinician and the physical therapist, and it is made for that joint and that patient. Anyone who has been taught to put a joint back into place from a book has been taught something dangerous, because reduction is a procedure learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

There are complications that belong specifically to this phase, and the program is designed to catch them. A joint that becomes painful, swollen, warm and stiff some weeks after an injury, with skin that changes color and sweats more than the other side, is a picture that the clinician must assess, because it may not be the ordinary stiffness of recovery. Prolonged immobility can also lead to a deep vein thrombosis in the leg, and a swollen, tender and painful calf in a patient who has been still for days needs urgent clinical assessment rather than massage. Pressure on a nerve can produce weakness and numbness that worsen while the patient is following the program correctly, and that too is a reason to stop and refer.

Throughout this phase the record and the handover carry the same weight as they did in the first hour. What the patient could do at the last visit, what the neurovascular examination showed, what the device looked like, what was changed and who authorized the change are written in a fixed order so that the next clinician continues a story instead of starting a new one. The patient is given the same information in words they can repeat, including what they may do, what they must not do, and which findings should bring them back before the next appointment. A patient recovering from an injury of the spine is still treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, no lone manual handling technique is safe, and the rehabilitation plan for such a patient is written with the team that manages the spine. Protection against cold remains part of care wherever a patient is exposed, waiting, or has a limb that is swollen and immobile, because cold slows healing and adds its own complications to an injury that already has enough.

Two things are deliberately absent from this chapter, and saying so is part of teaching safely. The first is the technique of reduction, of traction and of casting, all of which are learned under supervision, practiced on models and on patients under a teacher, and performed according to local protocol; a listener who learns the steps from a spoken description has learned nothing that is safe to do. The second is any medicine, its amount or the way it is given, because those belong to the prescriber and to the guideline. What a listener may take from this chapter is the shape of recovery, the findings that interrupt it, and the discipline of measuring function again at every visit, and every time it has named a time or a threshold it has named an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, rehabilitation begins on the day of the injury and is the part of treatment that decides whether the limb works, so function and not the image is the measure of success. The same sequence continues through recovery, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and the neurovascular findings are recorded before any intervention and repeated after it. Uninjured joints are kept moving, muscle is kept working, swelling and pain are controlled, and the program of the physical therapist is progressed only within the authorization of the treating clinician, because the amount and the kind of movement an injury will tolerate is a clinical decision. A cast or a brace is never removed by the patient, nothing is pushed under it, weight is not borne through an unhealed bone until the clinician allows it, and a limb is not elevated above the level of the heart when a compartment syndrome is suspected. Increasing pain, new numbness, new weakness, a cold or pale limb, a red and swollen surgical site, a swollen and tender calf and a joint that is losing movement are the findings that stop the program and bring the patient back for urgent assessment, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. The honest conversation about time is part of the treatment, because the bone unites long before the limb works, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 61 — Scenarios of the Road, the Home and the Workplace

Most of the fractures and dislocations that fill emergency departments begin in an ordinary place at an ordinary hour, on a road at dusk, on a staircase in a familiar house, or on the floor of a familiar workshop. The three settings are different, yet the injury is not, because bone fails at the same load wherever the energy arrives, and what changes is the scene, the hazards, the number of patients and the help available. This chapter walks through four constructed scenarios, which are illustrations rather than descriptions of real patients, and it speaks the reasoning at each step, because a rule without a reason is forgotten and then broken. Every scenario is followed through the same order that this course uses everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Safety comes before assessment and before everything else, because a responder who becomes a second patient has helped nobody. The lay first aider stops at the edge of the scene, looks for moving traffic, spilled fuel, broken glass, live electricity and unstable machinery, and calls for help before moving closer. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician wear the protective equipment their service provides and position a vehicle to shield the scene when the local protocol allows it. The mechanism of injury is read from the scene rather than guessed, from where the patient was found, what the patient struck and whether a belt or a helmet was worn, because energy tells the examiner where to look for the injury that is not yet visible. Nobody at any level straightens a deformed limb, removes an embedded object, or pushes exposed bone back into a wound, because each of those acts can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot.

The first scenario is a constructed illustration of a motorcyclist who has left his machine on a wet road and is lying on his side near the curb, still wearing his helmet. The lay first aider does not lift the head, does not roll the patient and does not remove the helmet, because the head and the neck are treated as injured until someone qualified to clear them has done so. The trained responder manages the airway with the maneuvers and the equipment the service authorizes, and if the airway cannot be kept open with the helmet in place, the decision to remove it belongs to that trained level and the local protocol, not to a bystander. Breathing and circulation are checked next, and catastrophic bleeding from a torn vessel is controlled at once by direct pressure, with a tourniquet used only by a responder trained and authorized to use one. The patient is kept warm from the first minute, because a person lying on wet asphalt loses heat quickly, and the neck is supported in the position found while help is organized. Only when the patient is stable enough does the assessment turn to the limbs.

The thigh is swollen, and the leg lies at an angle that the roadside rather than the patient's anatomy has decided, so the limb is assessed by looking and by gentle feeling and never by pulling it straight. The lay first aider supports the limb in the position found, with the hands, with a rolled blanket, or with whatever is at hand, because a movement that looks helpful can tear a vessel or a nerve that is still intact. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a splint within the procedures their service authorizes, and a splint holds the joint above and the joint below the fracture rather than the fracture alone. Traction splints are used for a break of the thigh bone in some services and not in others, so their use follows the local protocol instead of a rule from a book. Before any of this is done, the neurovascular status is examined and written down, and it is examined again afterwards, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. What is recorded is the color and the warmth of the foot, the pulse beyond the injury, the ability to move the toes, the sensation on the top of the foot and the sole, and the pain the patient reports.

A break of the thigh bone bleeds into the soft tissues around it, so a patient who is pale and restless and whose pulse is rising is treated as a patient who is losing blood even when the skin is unbroken. The trained responder and the paramedic monitor the breathing, the pulse and the level of consciousness within the procedures their service authorizes and prepare for urgent transfer, while the lay first aider keeps the patient still, warm and reassured. The physician in the receiving facility decides what imaging is required, and the usual first study is a radiograph taken in at least two directions, with the joint above and the joint below included so that a second injury is not hidden. Computed tomography is used when the shape of the break or an injury to the trunk needs more detail, and magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for the soft tissues, when the answer it gives will change what is done. Reassessment is performed after every intervention and repeats the same observations in the same order, because the comparison with the earlier record is what carries the information. Definitive treatment of that thigh bone, whether it is held with a rod, a plate or a frame, belongs to the orthopedic surgeon in an operating room, and reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol rather than from a book. A transport time or a pressure belongs to the local service, and any such figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs between countries and editions.

The second scenario is a constructed illustration of a pedestrian struck by a car while crossing a street, and her injuries follow the direction of the energy rather than the place where the bumper touched her. A pedestrian struck from one side often has an injury to that leg, an injury to the pelvis or the chest, and a head injury from the secondary impact with the road, so the examiner looks at the whole patient rather than at the obvious wound. The primary survey comes first, and its steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and each step is completed before the next begins, because a problem in the airway makes every later finding irrelevant. The lay first aider keeps the patient still, speaks to her to judge whether she is awake and answering sensibly, and covers her against the cold while someone calls for help. The trained responder examines the pelvis once and gently, because repeated springing of a broken pelvis can restart bleeding, and a pelvic binder is applied only where the local protocol authorizes a trained responder to apply one. An arm or a leg that is shortened and rotated may indicate a break in the thigh bone or the hip, and it is splinted as found, without any attempt to restore its length.

Blood lost into the pelvis or the abdomen can be considerable without a wound to be seen, so the findings that matter are those of the whole patient, which are a pulse that becomes faster and weaker, skin that becomes pale and cool, and a level of consciousness that drifts. The lay first aider reports those changes as they are observed instead of judging them, and the trained responder measures and records them within the procedures the service authorizes. A patient with a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so movement happens only with a trained team and the precautions the local protocol requires, and only when movement is necessary. The physician orders the imaging and interprets it, and the receiving team repeats the examination, because a patient who was talking a minute ago and is quiet now has given the most important finding of the assessment. The responder also passes on the mechanism, the position in which the patient was found and the time of the injury, because the next team should continue a story instead of starting a new one. Pain relief is decided by the prescriber and given according to the local protocol, and this course gives no substance, no amount and no route, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from a book.

The third scenario is a constructed illustration of an older woman who misses the last step of the staircase in her own house and is found by her daughter sitting on the floor and unable to stand. The home is the most common place for a fracture in an older adult, and the height of the fall is a poor guide to the severity of the injury, because bone that has lost density can break in a fall from standing. The lay first aider does not try to lift her into a chair, because a hip that has broken can be displaced further by that effort, and because the effort also places the helper's own back at risk. The trained responder assesses the scene, asks what happened and when, and completes the primary survey before turning to the limb, remembering that a patient who is confused after a fall may have struck her head. Pain in the groin, a leg that lies shortened and turned outward, and an inability to bear weight all suggest a break in the hip, but the sign may be absent or slight, and an older patient with a painful knee after a fall deserves the same caution as one with an obviously deformed hip. The wrist and the shoulder are examined as well, because a patient who puts out a hand to break a fall commonly injures both the hip and the wrist.

The examination of the injured limb begins with the neurovascular status, which is recorded before anything is applied and repeated after everything is applied, and that record is the reason the examiner can tell later whether a change was caused by the treatment. The limb is supported in the position found, with a pillow under the leg and a rolled blanket at either side, so that it is held without being straightened, and only a responder trained and authorized by the service applies a splint. The physician decides which radiograph is needed and whether an image of the chest or the pelvis is also required, because a fall in an older patient can injure more than the bone that hurts most. Reassessment follows each step, and the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation are pain that increases rather than settles, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for a diagnosis to arrive, and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting bandage or splint to be released by someone authorized to release it, while the limb is not elevated and the patient is referred urgently. The definitive treatment of a broken hip is an operation performed by an orthopedic surgeon, and the choice of operation and its timing belong to that surgeon and to the team that knows the patient's other illnesses. Casting, traction and reduction are described here so that a listener understands what is being done and why, but the techniques themselves are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

The fourth scenario is a constructed illustration of a worker whose hand has been caught between the rollers of a machine in a workshop, and the assessment begins with the machine rather than with the hand. The lay first aider does not touch the controls, because starting a machine that has stopped, or reversing one that has jammed, can pull the hand further in or release it suddenly, so the power is isolated by someone authorized to isolate it and the emergency services are called at once. Machinery that has trapped a person is a rescue problem before it is a medical one, and the responder's task is to keep the patient still, warm and talking while a trained team performs the extrication. The trained first responder and the paramedic assess the airway, the breathing and the circulation while the hand is still in the machine, and they control the bleeding that can be controlled without exploring the wound, because blind exploration of an open wound adds harm. Where the local protocol allows it and the responder has been trained, a tourniquet may be applied for bleeding that pressure cannot control, and the time it was applied is written down. An object embedded in the hand is left where it is, and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel.

If a part of the hand has been separated, it is wrapped in clean gauze that is only slightly dampened with a sterile salt solution, and the sealed bag that holds the gauze is cooled in a container of cold water and ice, so that the tissue is cooled but never frozen and never in direct contact with the ice. The lay first aider can do this, and can keep the patient warm and still, and the trained responder carries it out within the procedures the service authorizes. The decision about whether a separated part can be rejoined belongs to the hand surgeon, and no responder should promise that it can, because the outcome depends on the level of the injury, the crushing and the time that has passed. A duration or a temperature named in that teaching is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such figures differ between services and countries. Nothing is applied to the wound except a sterile dressing, no antiseptic, no ointment and no powder, because the receiving surgeon must see the tissue as the accident produced it. The patient is given nothing by mouth in anticipation of anesthesia, since that decision belongs to the treating team, and the patient is reassured while transport is arranged.

The hand repays a careful examination, because a finger that cannot be moved or a patch of skin that cannot feel tells the examiner where the damage lies before any image is taken. The trained responder tests sensation along both sides of each finger and asks the patient to bend and to straighten the fingers, and the result is written down before a splint is applied and checked again after it. Immobilization of the hand follows the position of function, which is the softly curved position the hand takes when it is at rest, and the splint is padded where it presses and secured firmly enough to hold without narrowing the circulation. The lay first aider supports the hand on a padded surface and does not attempt to shape it, and the trained responder applies the dressing and the splint that the equipment authorized by the service provides. The clinician orders the radiograph, and a hand that has been crushed may need more than one view. The reassessment after immobilization is not optional, because a crushed hand swells quickly, so the responder checks the color, the warmth, the pulse, the sensation, the movement and the pain, and loosens what the local protocol permits loosening.

Referral for this patient is to a facility with a hand surgeon, and it is arranged early, because the repair of a tendon, a nerve or a vessel, and any attempt to rejoin a separated part, are time dependent and cannot be performed in a clinic room. The definitive care of a crushed hand takes place in an operating room, where the surgeon explores the wound under anesthesia, removes what is dead, fixes what is broken and closes what can be closed, and closure is the surgeon's decision and never the responder's. The workplace itself becomes part of the medical history, because the machine, the guard that was missing and the task the worker was performing are recorded for the safety investigation that will follow. The lay first aider writes nothing about cause and nothing about blame, and simply reports what was seen, what was done, at what time and by whom. The record carries the time of the injury, the position in which the hand was found, and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention. That record travels with the patient, and the handover is spoken in the same order, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one.

Four settings, four mechanisms and one order, and that order is what a listener should be able to say aloud while working. The first step is assessment, which begins with the safety of the scene and continues through the mechanism of injury and the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE. The next step is stabilization, which means keeping the patient warm, controlling the bleeding that can be controlled, and supporting the injured part in the position in which it was found. The neurovascular examination follows and is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Immobilization then holds the joint above and the joint below the injury rather than the injury alone. Only then does imaging begin, and it is ordered and interpreted by a clinician, because a picture confirms what the examination has suggested and does not replace it. Reassessment comes after every intervention, and the last step is to refer the patient or to treat definitively, decided by the clinician who knows the injury, the patient and the resources of the facility. The order is not a ritual, because every step in it protects the next, and the step that protects the patient from the treatment is the reassessment.

The complication this course is most afraid of is the one caused by the treatment, and in each of these scenarios it has the same name. Compartment syndrome occurs when bleeding or swelling raises the pressure inside a closed space bounded by bone and fascia, and the muscle and the nerve inside that space suffer first while a pulse at the wrist or the ankle can still be felt, so an intact pulse does not exclude it. The findings that raise the suspicion are pain that increases rather than settles, pain out of proportion to the injury, a limb that is tense and swollen, numbness, tingling and weakness. The trained responder and the clinician do not wait for a measurement to confirm the diagnosis, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. Where the local protocol allows it, a constricting bandage, splint or cast is released by someone authorized to release it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently to a facility that can operate. A patient who improves after the bandage is loosened has given useful information, and a patient who does not has given an instruction to escalate at once. Anyone at any level who is unsure whether a limb is becoming tighter should ask early, because the answer to a question costs nothing and the answer to a missed compartment costs a limb.

Two of these scenarios carry an open wound, and that finding changes the management, because the deep tissues have met the outside world and are contaminated even when the wound looks clean. The part played by the responder is limited and precise: cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control the bleeding that can be controlled, record the neurovascular status, immobilize the limb in the position found, keep the patient warm, and arrange urgent transfer. The wound is not explored with a finger or an instrument, no antiseptic is poured into it, and exposed bone is never pushed back into it, because the surgeon needs to see the injury as the accident produced it. Antibiotics and protection against tetanus are decisions made by the prescriber according to the local protocol, and the responder's part is to report the time of the injury, the state of the wound and the environment in which it happened, since a wound from a farmyard and a wound from a clean kitchen floor do not carry the same risk. The question of how soon the wound must reach an operating room belongs to the surgical team, and any window of hours is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. What the responder must not do is to close the wound, to delay the transfer in order to clean it further, or to give the patient anything to eat or drink, and pain relief remains the prescriber's decision.

Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and every one of these four patients is at risk of it. The motorcyclist lies on wet asphalt, the pedestrian lies on a cold road, the older woman lies on a bare floor, and the worker stands in an unheated workshop, and each of them loses heat through wet clothing, exposed skin and a long wait. The lay first aider insulates the patient from the ground, replaces wet clothing with dry covering, and covers the head, and the trained responder does the same within the procedures the service authorizes. Transport is arranged by the service that owns the protocol, and the choice of the receiving facility and of the route belongs to those who know the local capacity and the condition of the patient. An injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has cleared it, and no single manual handling technique is safe on its own, so such a patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Anyone at any level who is uncertain about the spine says so at the handover, and the receiving team decides how the patient will be moved from that point onward.

Children, older adults and pregnant patients appear in these settings more often than any other group, and each of them changes the threshold for acting rather than the order of the steps. The bone of a child bends further before it breaks and has a growth region near each end that can be injured without the bone breaking, so a child who is unwilling to use an arm or a leg after a fall down the stairs deserves the same caution as a child with an obvious deformity. An older adult whose bone has lost density may break a hip or a wrist in a fall from standing height, and the fracture may be far less painful than its severity suggests, so the absence of severe pain is not a reason to wait. A pregnant patient who has fallen is assessed with the same sequence, and the decision about monitoring the pregnancy belongs to the obstetric team, while the responder's task is to keep the patient still and warm and to arrange transport without delay. In all three groups the sign that a book treats as reliable may be absent, so the responder lowers the threshold for immobilization and referral rather than trusting a single finding. The judgments about imaging, about pain relief and about definitive treatment in these patients belong to the clinicians who know them, and the responder's part is to recognize that the ordinary rule may not hold and to say so out loud.

To summarize, the road, the home and the workplace produce the same injuries by different routes, and the responder meets all of them with one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The motorcyclist is not moved and his helmet is not removed by a bystander, the pedestrian is examined as a whole patient because the energy leaves more than one injury, the older woman with a painful hip is not lifted into a chair, and the worker whose hand is in the machine is helped by people who isolate the power before they touch the hand. The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it and is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and the reassessment after every intervention is what catches the complication caused by the treatment. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, an open wound is never explored blindly, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, or when the vessels and the nerves are failing and need a specialist, and no substance, amount or route for pain relief appears anywhere in this course. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and the record travels with the patient to the handover. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 62 — Scenarios of the Fall, the Crush and the Sporting Injury

This chapter is built from four constructed illustrations, and none of them is the record of a real patient. A fall from a roof, a crush in an industrial accident, a twisted knee on a field and a dislocated shoulder in a match are situations a listener may meet. Each turns on a decision rather than a diagnosis, and the same decision made early or late produces two very different patients. Every chapter of this course follows one sequence, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. What follows is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The fall from a roof begins before anyone touches the patient, with the scene itself. The height of the fall and the surface that ended it tell the listener how much energy the body absorbed. A fall of 4 meters onto a hard surface is taught as high energy, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The lay first aider secures the scene and moves the patient only for an immediate hazard such as fire or traffic, while the trained responder works in personal protective equipment within the procedures the service authorizes.

The mechanism is followed by the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The principle that orders everything is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and no lone manual handling technique is safe. The lay first aider keeps the head still and waits, while the trained responder may apply a rigid collar within the procedures the service authorizes.

Only when the patient is stable does the assessment turn to the limb, which is assessed by looking, by feeling and by asking, never by forcing. The responder looks for a wound, a deformity and a change in color, and compares the limb with the other side. A thigh that is swollen, shortened and rotated outward is a fracture of the thigh bone until proved otherwise, and it may bleed enough to threaten the circulation. Feeling is done gently over the bones rather than over the wound, and asking the patient to move the fingers and toes is a request, not a command.

Stabilization in the field is a short list of acts whose most important member is restraint. A deformed limb is splinted in the position in which it was found and is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone. Pulling a limb straight can tear what remained intact, can convert a closed fracture into an open one, and can release the pressure holding a torn vessel closed. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm and waits. The trained responder may apply a splint and control the bleeding that can be controlled, within the procedures the service authorizes.

The neurovascular examination is never skipped and never assumed, and it is performed before the limb is splinted and again afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and warmth of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury and asks the patient to move the fingers and toes. Sensation is tested on both sides, and numbness or tingling is recorded in the words of the patient. The result is written before the splint and after it, because a finding not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. The lay first aider reports color, warmth and movement, while the formal examination and its interpretation belong to the clinician.

Immobilization prevents movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone splinted alone can still move at either end. A splint is padded where it presses on bone, applied over the position found, and secured firmly enough to hold without stopping the circulation. A device that pulls gently on a fractured thigh is used by trained responders, but its technique belongs to supervised training. The trained responder applies splints within the equipment the service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually first, taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissues. Either study is requested when the answer will change what is done, and that decision belongs to the clinician responsible for the patient. The lay first aider never orders or interprets imaging, the trained responder does not choose the study, and an image is a picture of one moment.

Reassessment is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The limb is checked for color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and the splint is checked for tightness. Pain that rises instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling and a limb that becomes tense and swollen stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for confirmation and acts within the local protocol, which may allow a constricting splint to be released by someone authorized to do it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the referral is urgent, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle.

Referral or definitive treatment is the last step of the sequence, and some injuries cannot be managed where the patient lies. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture entering a joint, or a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging and an operating room. The lay first aider calls for help and stays with the patient, and the decision about definitive treatment belongs to the physician. Definitive treatment includes reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which holds the position while the bone heals. Every one of those acts is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol.

The same fall, told too late, is a story about hands that were too helpful. A responder took the shortened, rotated thigh in both hands and pulled it straight because the leg looked wrong. The artery that had been compressed against the broken bone rather than torn began to bleed inside a thigh that swelled hard and fast, and the closed fracture had become an open one through the skin. The neurovascular examination had not been recorded before the pull, so the numbness that followed could not be attributed to the injury or to the hand. A compartment syndrome declared itself during the night, and by the time the operating room was ready the muscle had died.

The crush injury of an industrial accident is the scenario in which the environment itself is the first patient. A worker is pinned by a fallen load or a machine part, a limb is compressed, and the space is loud, dusty and unsafe. Power is isolated and locked out by the people authorized to do it, and no responder enters a space that has not been declared safe. The lay first aider stays outside, keeps the patient talking and sends for help, while the trained responder works in personal protective equipment. The release of a compressing object is a planned act involving the rescuers and a physician, and it is not the work of a single responder.

Crush injury and crush syndrome are not the same thing, and that difference is the reason the release is planned rather than improvised. Crush injury is the local damage that pressure does to muscle, nerve and skin at the point of compression. Crush syndrome is what happens to the whole patient when the damaged muscle is reperfused, because substances held inside the injured cells enter the circulation and can damage the heart and the kidneys. A patient pinned for hours may therefore look surprisingly well while still trapped and then deteriorate within minutes of release. The duration of compression and the bulk of muscle involved drive the plan, and any interval named in it is an illustration to be confirmed against the local protocol.

For the trapped patient the responder's work is monitoring, warmth and the honest passing of information. The patient is kept warm and insulated from the ground, the load and the machine, and bleeding that can be controlled is controlled without disturbing the compressing weight. The neurovascular status of the limb beyond the compression is recorded and repeated, and the findings are spoken to the physician directing the plan. Anything given to that patient is decided by a physician under the local protocol, and the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber. A lay first aider gives nothing unless a clinician has asked for it, and a trained responder gives nothing beyond what the service authorizes.

The same crush, told too late, begins with an unplanned release. A team lifted the load before the receiving hospital had been told that a patient with a crushed limb was coming. The pressure came off, the substances entered the blood, and within minutes the patient became pale, confused and then pulseless. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started by trained responders, and the hospital later found an injured heart and failing kidneys. The correct version of that story is telephone calls before lifting, a physician directing the preparation, warmth, continuous monitoring and transport to a facility with an intensive care unit.

A crush injury is also a wound, and the rules that govern any wound govern this one. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the neurovascular status is recorded, the limb is immobilized and the patient is referred urgently. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. Nobody explores such a wound with a gloved finger or an instrument in the field, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. Protection against infection and against tetanus is a decision for the physician and the local protocol.

The twisted knee of sport is the quietest of the four scenarios and the one most often got wrong. A player plants a foot, the knee buckles inward without contact, and the player goes down with a joint that swells within minutes and will not bear weight. Rapid swelling after a twisting injury usually means blood inside the joint, which is called a hemarthrosis, and it says that something within the joint has torn. The decision is that nobody tests the stability of this knee on the field, since pulling on a joint is a clinical skill learned under supervision and can convert a partial tear into a complete one.

Assessment of the swollen knee follows the same order as everywhere in this course, and it begins with the primary survey and the mechanism rather than with the joint. The responder looks at the position of the limb, the swelling, the wound and the color of the skin, feels the bones and the pulse beyond the injury, and asks about the pain rather than pushing on the joint. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are requested when the soft tissues need to be seen and the answer will change what is done. The lay first aider may support the limb and reassure, while the formal assessment belongs to the trained responder, the nurse or the physician.

Stabilization of the knee means holding it in the position found, keeping the patient warm and keeping weight off that limb until a clinician allows it. A trained responder may apply a splint within the equipment the service authorizes, padding the bony points and checking that the device does not stop the circulation. Cooling is used by many services for a swollen joint, and how it is applied, for how long and by whom is set by the local protocol rather than by this book. Nothing in this step straightens a joint, and nothing in it forces a locked knee to bend.

The neurovascular examination of the injured knee is written before the splint and after it, and it is brief enough to be done on a sideline. A knee that has gone out of place and slipped back by itself is more dangerous than one that stayed out, because the deformity has gone and with it the visible warning. Tingling, numbness, a cold foot, a weak pulse or pain far greater than the injury suggests are the findings that stop the responder and turn a sporting injury into an emergency. The lay first aider notices and reports these findings, and their interpretation belongs to a clinician.

The same twisted knee, told too late, is the story of a player who was sent back on. The knee had become much less painful after a few minutes, which was read as recovery but was the sign of a joint that had reduced itself. The player returned to the game, the knee was never examined neurovascularly and the pulse behind the knee was never recorded. By the evening the foot was pale and cold, and the artery damaged at the time of the injury had clotted, so the limb could not be saved. The right version of that story ends on the sideline with a splint, a warm patient, a written examination and a referral.

The dislocated shoulder of sport is the scenario in which the right decision is the hardest to watch. A player falls on an outstretched arm or is pulled by the arm, the shoulder becomes square instead of round, and the upper arm cannot be brought to the side. The instinct of everyone present is to pull the arm and put the joint back, and the decision that saves the limb is to refuse. The lay first aider supports the arm in the position found and sends for help, while the trained responder records the neurovascular status and applies a support. Reduction is performed by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon trained and authorized to do it, where imaging is available.

Reduction restores the position of the joint surfaces, and it is not a first aid maneuver, however simple the movement may look. It must not be attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment of bone is caught within the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed. Each situation carries its own reason, because a shattered surface cannot be held by pulling on it, a trapped fragment blocks the way back, and a failing vessel needs a vascular surgeon. In each case the attempt can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique.

The correct handling of a dislocated shoulder in the field is therefore almost entirely about what the responder does not do. The arm is supported in the position found, with a sling, a folded garment or the opposite hand of the patient, and the joints above and below are included in the support. The neurovascular examination is repeated after the support is applied and recorded again, with attention to sensation over the outer shoulder and the ability to lift the wrist, because the nerve closest to the joint is the one most often injured. Pain is reported honestly and treated by the physician under the local protocol, and the substance, the amount and the way it is given belong to the prescriber. 

The same shoulder, told too late, is the story of a well-meant pull on a touchline. A bystander took the wrist, braced a foot against the chest of the patient and pulled, and the joint did not return. The pull fractured the upper arm and stretched the nerve that supplies the muscles around the shoulder, and because no examination had been recorded before it, nobody could say whether the weakness came with the injury. In another version the shoulder was reduced successfully in a dressing room and the player was sent home without examination. Both versions share one root, because an act belonging to an authorized clinician was performed by someone untrained.

Across all four scenarios the same habits decide the outcome, and they are habits rather than talents. The first is that the neurovascular examination is done before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is written down. The next is that reassessment follows every intervention, including the application of a splint, the release of a bandage, the movement of a patient and the journey in the vehicle. The third is that the responder stops when there is resistance, because resistance means that the tissues are telling the hand something theory cannot. The last is that the record travels with the patient, since a finding spoken into a radio and never written is a finding lost.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality after it. The time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, and any change in the patient are written or spoken in a fixed order, so that the receiving team continues a story. The lay first aider reports what was seen and when, the trained responder and the paramedic report the observations of the service, and the nurse or the physician adds the findings and the decisions of clinical care. The last sentence of a handover should say what the responder is worried about, because that sentence is often the most useful one.

Cold runs through all four scenarios and is treated in this course as a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort. A patient lying on a roof in the rain, a worker pinned to a concrete floor and a player on a wet bench all lose heat, and a cold patient bleeds more easily. The ground is insulated, wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, and the patient is covered from the head down, with the injured limb included. The lay first aider can do all of this without equipment. A responder who keeps one hand on the patient is doing more than one who looks for something clever to do.

Pain is the finding that ties the four scenarios together, and it is managed by a physician rather than by a book. Pain that rises instead of settling, or that demands more attention than the injury appears to justify, is a finding to report urgently, because it may be the first sign of a compartment syndrome. The responder's part is to ask, to believe the answer, to record it in the words of the patient and to pass it on. Any substance used for pain, any amount of it and any way of giving it are decided by the prescriber under the local protocol, and this course deliberately names none of them.

Open injuries in these scenarios follow rules that do not change with the setting, and they are the rules most often broken by people who want to help. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with pressure around the wound, the neurovascular status is recorded, and the transfer is urgent. An embedded object is left where it lies, exposed bone is never pushed back, and the wound is never explored with a finger or an instrument, because all three acts can start bleeding that cannot be stopped outside an operating room.
