Cleaning, exploration and definitive closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. The lay first aider covers and supports, and the trained responder does the same within the procedures the service authorizes.

Injury of the spine appears in two of these scenarios and is treated in all of them as unstable until it has been cleared by someone qualified to clear it. The fall from a roof and the tackle that dislocated a shoulder can both involve the neck without any sign the responder can detect. No lone manual handling technique is safe, and a patient who must be moved is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. The lay first aider keeps the head still and waits, and the trained responder may apply a collar within the procedures the service authorizes. The decision to clear the spine belongs to a clinician with the imaging and the examination to support it, and it is never made in the field by elimination.

Every number in this chapter is an illustration rather than a rule. A height, a duration, an interval, a distance or a threshold is given only to make a mechanism understandable, and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is used. Where practice differs, the chapter says that it differs rather than choosing one version as universal. A duration that one service treats as urgent may be ordinary in another, so the local protocol is the only reliable source.

Everything described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no chapter of this course teaches a listener to perform them from a book, however clearly the words describe them. A listener who wants to perform them should seek the supervised training that leads to certification, and should treat this chapter as preparation for understanding what that training is for. These acts are judged by feel as much as by sight.

The four scenarios end with a decision about escalation, and that decision is always safer when it is made out loud. A patient who is deteriorating, a limb that is changing, a wound that is open, a joint out of place and a compression lasting hours are each reasons to call for a more capable provider. The lay first aider calls the emergency number and follows the instructions given, and the nurse or the physician calls the specialist service that will receive the patient. The call is not an admission of failure, and it is often the single most useful intervention available, because it turns a lonely scene into a prepared receiving team.

What separates the early version of each story from the late version is not courage and not equipment. It is a refusal to do the dramatic thing, an examination performed and written before any intervention, and a message sent ahead of the patient. The responder who supports a limb in the position found, who records what the hand and the foot can feel and do, and who telephones before acting will deliver the better patient. Every one of these scenarios is a constructed illustration and not the care of a real patient, and the protocol of the place where the listener works, together with the law of that country, decides what may be done there.

To summarize, the fall from a roof, the crush of an industrial accident, the twisted knee of sport and the dislocated shoulder all turn on one sequence, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and on the same restraint. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly, because definitive closure belongs to the operating room. The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one, and its result is written down. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, or when an earlier attempt has failed. A trapped patient is released once, deliberately, with a physician directing the plan and a receiving team ready. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, pain and any substance given for it belong to the prescriber and the local protocol. Stop when there is resistance, reassess after every intervention, and call for a more capable provider early, because the call is treatment. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 63 — Scenarios of the Child, the Older Adult and the Open Injury

Three patients in this course are frightening for the same reason, and none of them looks frightening at the door. The child whose elbow is swollen and who will not use the arm, the frailer older adult whose hip hurts although nobody saw a fall, and the patient whose open fracture looked like a scratch each carry an injury larger than the finding that announces it. What follows are constructed illustrations rather than real patients, and they are educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work. Every one of them is carried through the same order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and every act along the way is named with the level of provider who may perform it.

The bone of a child behaves differently from the bone of an adult, and that difference explains both why these injuries are missed and why they matter. The bone is more elastic, its outer sleeve is thicker and stronger, and near each end of a long bone there is a growth region where cartilage is turning into bone. Because that sleeve resists tearing, a child's bone may bend, buckle or break on one side only and then spring back toward its usual shape, so that a limb which appears almost straight still contains an injury. Because the growth region is softer than the shaft, force may damage it without cracking the hard bone at all, and an injury there can disturb the future length and shape of the limb. A child also loses heat quickly through a large surface and small reserves, so warmth matters from the first minute.

Consider a constructed illustration of a child of 7, who is carried into an urgent care room by a parent after falling from a low garden wall, and the parent says the child cried at once, held the arm against the body, has refused to use it since, and now has a swollen elbow. Assessment begins before the elbow is examined, because the scene is made safe, the mechanism and the time are established, and the child is taken through the primary survey whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure. The principle that decides the order when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands is that life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The history is taken from the carer as well as from the child, and it includes what the child was doing, whether the arm was pulled by the hand, whether the child has been unwell with a fever and how the child normally uses that arm, while the judgment about the severity of the injury belongs to the clinician.

The swollen elbow of a child has many possible explanations, and telling them apart is clinical work rather than a field skill. Among the possibilities are a pulled elbow, in which a ligament slips over the head of one of the forearm bones after a sharp pull on the hand, a break just above the elbow, a break of the upper end of one of the forearm bones, bleeding into the joint from a torn structure, and an infection of the joint or of the bone. That is why the responder protects the elbow, records what is seen and leaves the testing of movement, of stability and of tenderness to a clinician trained and equipped for it. Nobody in the field should pull on the hand of a child with a swollen elbow in the hope of making it better, because that movement may convert an injury that needed protection into one that needs a surgeon.

Stabilization of the child is a short list of acts, and the most important of them is restraint. The limb is supported in the position in which it was found with the hands, with a pillow or with a folded garment, and a deformed limb is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. A child loses heat quickly, so wet clothing is replaced with dry covering, the child is insulated from the ground and the head is covered, since cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. Any medicine is chosen and given by a prescriber working within the local protocol, with the substance and the amount belonging to that prescriber rather than to this course, while the lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment and the trained responder works within the procedures the service authorizes.

The neurovascular examination is performed before the limb is supported or splinted and repeated after every intervention, and its result is written down, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the hand and compares it with the other hand, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, feels the pulse at the wrist, and asks the child to move the fingers or watches whether the child grasps a toy. Sensation is tested lightly on both sides and compared, and in a child the answer may come as a word, as a grimace or as nothing at all, so the absence of a complaint is not evidence that sensation is intact. The vessels and the nerves at the elbow run directly against the bone, so a break just above the elbow can injure the vessel that supplies the forearm and the nerve that moves the thumb, and the pulse may remain palpable while that vessel is damaged, so the trained responder or the clinician repeats and records the examination after every intervention.

Immobilization means preventing movement of the injured part and of the joints above and below it, because a bone that is splinted alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. The splint is padded where it presses on bone, it is applied over the position found, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and it is checked at intervals because an improvised device shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, which may be a cast, a brace or an operation. Casting, reduction and traction are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the technique of each of them belongs to supervised clinical training and never to a book. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught inside the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed, and in each of those situations the attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot.

Imaging is the step that confirms what the examination has already suggested, and it is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it. A radiograph is usually the first study, and in a child the growth regions and the cartilage that has not yet turned to bone make the picture harder to read, so more than one view may be needed and a break that is invisible on the first film may show itself when the limb is imaged again a little later. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for soft tissue and for the growth region when the clinical question demands that detail, and the choice belongs to the clinician responsible for the child's care. A child with a swollen elbow, an obvious deformity or any change in the neurovascular status is referred urgently to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an orthopedic surgeon, and the timing of any operation differs between services and is confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Reassessment of the child is performed after every intervention, and it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with the record, and the comparison is what carries the value rather than any single measurement. The findings that stop a responder and prompt escalation are pain that increases instead of settling, a forearm that becomes tense and swollen, numbness or tingling in the fingers, weakness, pallor, coolness and a pulse that has changed or disappeared. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle, and the constricting bandage or splint is released by someone the local protocol authorizes to release it. The limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the child is kept warm, and the child is referred urgently with the times and the findings written into the handover.

The second patient is an older adult, and here the constructed illustration is a woman of 84 found sitting on the floor of her living room, complaining of pain in the groin and the front of the thigh, unable to stand, and with no fall remembered by her or by the carer who found her. The absence of a fall is the detail that misleads, because the bone may have given way first and the fall, if there was one, may have been the consequence rather than the cause. A break of the hip can also follow a twist in bed or a turning movement that nobody would call a fall, and it can happen in a patient whose bone has lost density over years without any symptom at all. The responder therefore treats the mechanism as a whole and refuses to be reassured by the story that there was no accident, while the clinician takes the fuller history, including the illnesses and the medicines that affect bone and bleeding, from the patient and the carer.

The examination of an older adult carries traps of its own. A limb that is shortened and turned outward is a well known sign of a broken hip, yet the bone ends may be impacted into one another so that the limb looks almost normal, the patient may be able to take a few steps with support, and the pain may be felt in the knee rather than in the hip. A sign that is treated as always present will be believed even when it is absent, so no single finding excludes the injury, and the threshold for referral is set by the mechanism, by the age of the patient and by the inability to bear weight rather than by the shape of the leg. The responder does not ask the patient to stand or to walk in order to settle the question, does not pull on the leg and does not turn the limb to see how far it moves, because each of those acts can displace an impacted break and add to the bleeding. Injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and some injuries of the pelvis and of the spine present with pain in the hip or the groin.

Stabilization of the older adult begins with leaving the patient where she was found and keeping her still, while the neck and the back are protected if the mechanism is unknown. No lone manual handling technique is safe, so moving the patient is the work of a trained team using the equipment and the precautions the local protocol requires, and the lay first aider waits with the patient and supports the limb as it lies. A leg that is turned outward is never straightened and never pulled, and the trained responder immobilizes the limb within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required. Warmth is a priority in this patient, because a thin older adult on a cold floor loses heat quickly, so the patient is insulated from the ground, wet clothing is replaced and the head and the feet are covered. Pressure injury can begin within a short time on a hard surface when the skin is thin and the patient cannot move.

The neurovascular examination of the older adult follows the same order and answers a different baseline question. The examiner looks at the color and the warmth of the foot, presses a toenail to watch the color return, feels the pulses at the ankle, tests sensation on the top of the foot and on the sole, and asks the patient to move the ankle and the toes, comparing the injured limb with the other one. Many older patients have narrowing of the vessels that has developed over years, so the pulse may be weak and the skin cool on both sides before any injury occurred, and what has value is the difference between the two limbs and the change from the record rather than an absolute standard of health. A break of the thigh bone can release enough blood to threaten the circulation, with a figure offered in teaching as an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services and editions. A rapid pulse, pale and cool skin and a falling level of consciousness are findings of shock, so this examination is performed by the trained responder or by the clinician and the findings are written before any intervention and repeated after each one.

Imaging and definitive treatment for the older adult are decided by clinicians, and the part played by the responder is to make those decisions possible quickly. The physician orders the radiographs, and a break of the hip may be invisible on the first film, in which case the clinician may request another view, a computed tomography scan or a magnetic resonance imaging scan, because the examination says the injury is there although the picture does not show it. Definitive treatment for most of these injuries is surgical and belongs to the orthopedic surgeon, who may hold the bone with metal devices or replace the worn joint, and the choice depends on the patient, on the pattern of the break and on what the local service can offer. Reduction, traction and casting are part of that work, they are learned under supervision, and they are performed according to local protocol rather than from anything a listener has heard or read. The transfer of an older adult with a suspected broken hip is urgent, and the record must say plainly that the patient cannot bear weight, when the pain began and what the neurovascular status was at each stage.

The third patient is the one whose open fracture looked like a scratch, and the constructed illustration is a man of middle age who came off a bicycle at low speed a short while ago. He is standing, he is speaking in full sentences, there is a small wound on the front of his shin with a spot of blood on the trouser leg, and he would like to go home. Everything about the scene suggests a trivial injury, and that is precisely why this patient is in the chapter, because an open fracture is defined by communication between the broken bone and the outside world and not by how large the opening is. The wound may be a puncture, a scratch or a small hole, and it may lie some distance from the broken bone because the skin slides over the bone when the limb moves, so a wound at the knee can belong to a break in the middle of the shin, and bone may not be visible at all. Bleeding may be slight or absent because the wound is small or because the broken end has moved back inside the limb, so the question that decides the management is not how the wound looks but whether anyone suspects that it reaches the bone, and that question is settled by a clinician and never by the size of a stain.

Recognition of the open injury therefore requires a deliberate search rather than an impression. The whole limb is inspected in good light, front and back, including the back of the thigh and the calf and the spaces between the fingers and the toes, and the patient is asked directly whether there was blood at the scene, on the clothing or in the shoe. Nothing is inserted into the wound to see how deep it goes, and no probe is passed along it, because that act carries contamination deeper and can start bleeding that was not there before. An open fracture is contaminated from the moment it happens, since the skin carries organisms that reach the broken bone during the injury itself, and it remains contaminated even when it looks clean.

Stabilization of the open injury is a short and disciplined set of acts, and it begins with the safety of the responder. Gloves and protection for the eyes, which are part of personal protective equipment, are put on before the wound is touched, because blood carries infection and a responder cannot help anyone after becoming a patient. The wound is covered with a sterile dressing, and bleeding that can be controlled is controlled by pressing on the tissue around the wound rather than on any exposed bone or protruding fragment. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the bone is contaminated and the limb will not tolerate the attempt. A wound is never explored blindly, and the part played by the responder is to cover the wound, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, to record the neurovascular status, to immobilize the limb in the position found, to keep the patient warm and to arrange urgent transfer, while definitive closure belongs to the operating room and to nobody else.

The neurovascular examination of an open injury is performed before the dressing is applied and repeated after every intervention. Color, warmth, the pulse beyond the injury, the return of color to a pressed nail, sensation on both sides and movement are all recorded in words, together with the pain and the time of the observation. A pulse that is present does not exclude damage to a vessel or the beginning of a compartment syndrome, and an open wound does not protect the limb from swelling inside the closed compartments that lie deeper. The dressing applied in the field is not lifted in order to look again at the wound, because looking adds contamination and bleeding and changes nothing, whereas a change in the neurovascular status or in the general condition of the patient changes everything. Pain that increases, a limb that becomes tense and swollen, numbness, tingling and weakness are the findings that stop the responder, and the response within the local protocol is to release a constricting bandage or splint, to keep the limb level rather than raised above the heart, to keep the patient warm and to refer urgently, while the lay first aider reports only what is seen and felt.

Two questions about medicine always arise with an open injury, and this course answers both by naming the decision maker rather than the medicine. The first is whether the protection of the patient against tetanus is up to date, and the responder asks when the last protection was given and passes the answer on, while the decision about what is given and how belongs to a prescriber working to the local protocol. The second is whether an antibiotic is needed, and here the finding that makes the decision urgent is the open fracture itself, together with a wound that has been in contact with soil, manure or standing water. No substance, no amount, no frequency and no route appears anywhere in this course, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from a book. The scope of practice forbids the responder to give any medicine outside a specific authorization, and those authorizations differ between services and between countries.

Imaging of the open injury is ordered by the clinician, and the radiographs are taken together with an assessment of the wound, so that the injury of the bone and the injury of the soft tissue are understood as one problem. In the operating room the surgeon removes the contaminated and the dead tissue, washes the wound out, stabilizes the bone and decides whether and when the skin can be closed, and every part of that work is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, with the timing differing between services and between countries. The duty of the responder is finished before that point, and it is to cover the wound, to control the bleeding that can be controlled, to record the neurovascular findings, to immobilize the limb in the position found, to keep the patient warm and to move the patient urgently to a facility with an operating room. An open fracture is an emergency even when the patient feels well and even when the wound has stopped bleeding, and the record must say that the wound was found, where it was, how it looked and what was done to it.

The three patients in this chapter share one property, and it is the property that makes them worth remembering. In each of them the injury is larger than the finding, which is a swollen elbow in a child whose bone bent instead of breaking cleanly, a hip that hurts in a patient who cannot recall falling, and a small wound over a bone that has communicated with the outside world. A listener who waits for the textbook picture waits past the moment when the outcome could still be changed, and the response is a lower threshold for immobilization and for referral rather than a different sequence. The sequence itself does not change, and it is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The record carries the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, the measures taken to keep the patient warm and any change in the condition of the patient, so that the receiving team continues a story instead of starting a new one.

None of this licenses a listener to act outside the law, the training or the equipment that applies where the listener works. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, a deformed limb is splinted in the position found and never straightened in the field, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, and an open wound is never explored blindly. The injury of a child, the injury of an older adult and the open injury are all referred to a facility with the people and the equipment to treat them, and the decisions about imaging, about medicine and about operation belong to those people and to no one else. Every time, volume, distance and threshold named in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, between countries and between editions.

To summarize, three patients in this course mislead by appearing less injured than they are, and they are the child with a swollen elbow who will not use the arm, the frailer older adult with pain in the hip and no remembered fall, and the patient whose open fracture looked like a scratch. In each of them the sequence is the same, and it is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the neurovascular findings recorded before every intervention and repeated after it. The bone of a child bends and buckles and can injure its growth region, so a quiet swelling and a refusal to use the limb are taken seriously, and nobody pulls on the hand of the child to put the elbow back. An older adult may break a hip without falling, may feel the pain in the knee and may still take a few steps, so the leg is not straightened, not pulled and not tested by walking, and the patient is kept flat, still and warm. An open fracture is contaminated however small the wound, so the wound is covered with a sterile dressing, bleeding is controlled around it, an embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back, the wound is never explored, and the patient is moved urgently toward an operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, no dose, no route and no regimen appears in this course, and the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so.

# Chapter 64 — The Practical Skills Laboratory

This course has taught the assessment and the management of fractures and dislocations in words, and words are enough for the reasoning, because a listener who understands why a deformed limb is splinted in the position found will not straighten it in the field. Words are not enough for the hands, because the pressure that holds a fractured forearm firmly without squeezing it, and the difference between a pulse that is faint and a pulse that has gone, are learned by doing the act on a model or on a colleague and by being corrected while doing it. The practical skills laboratory is the place where that correction happens, and it rehearses the same order that every chapter of this course follows, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Between knowing a step and performing it lies a distance that is wider than it looks from a page, because knowledge is tested in a quiet room and skill is tested in a noisy one. A responder who can recite the elements of the neurovascular examination may still hesitate when a limb is swelling under the hands, and a responder who has read about a log roll may still pull the shoulders while the pelvis stays behind. The laboratory narrows that distance by making the noise and the clock safe, so that an error costs a correction instead of a limb. Repetition does the rest, and a learner is allowed to fail in front of an instructor precisely so that the failure is not stored up for a patient. The laboratory is run by an instructor the training program authorizes, and what is taught there is defined by the curriculum of that program and by the body that certifies the learner.

A station begins with a briefing, which states what the skill is for, what the patient must gain from it, and what would make the attempt unsafe, so that the learner meets the failure before meeting a patient. The next step is a demonstration by the instructor, performed at the speed of a real patient rather than at the speed of a teaching video. Only then does the learner perform the skill, first on a manikin and then on an uninjured colleague who can say what the hands felt like. The station ends with a debrief in which the learner describes what went well and what went wrong before the instructor adds anything, because a learner who finds the error is more likely to keep the correction. Order matters in the practice room for the same reason it matters at the roadside, since each step protects the next one and a skill assembled out of order will be performed out of order.

One rule governs every station and is spoken before the learner touches anything, which is that no skill is practiced on a patient for the first time. The first attempt belongs to the manikin, to the padded model limb or to the uninjured colleague who has volunteered to take part, and the patient meets the skill only after the learner has performed it correctly under supervision. A learner in a recognized training program may then carry out the act on a patient within the authorization that the program and the local protocol give, with a supervisor present who is qualified to take over. A learner who is not in such a program never performs the act on a patient at all, however well the manikin went, and no learner is ever the most senior pair of hands on an unstable limb. The rule exists because a patient is not a rehearsal, and because the harm done by an untrained hand is done in the moment when help is furthest away.

Assessment of the injured limb is the first skill of the laboratory, and its purpose is to produce a description rather than a diagnosis. The learner looks at the limb as a whole and compares it with the other side, noting the position, the swelling, the color of the skin and any wound. The learner then feels with the flat of the hand and with the fingertips, beginning away from the most painful place, and notes the temperature and where the tenderness begins and ends. The patient is asked to move the limb gently, and the movement is never forced, because the examination is meant to gather information rather than to test the injury. The learner writes down what was seen and what the patient said, using the words the patient used, and leaves the interpretation to the clinician who will see the patient next.

The assessor follows the order rather than the answer, and looks for the comparison with the other side, for movement that was requested rather than imposed, and for a record that names findings instead of conclusions. An attempt ends immediately if the learner forces a joint, pulls a limb to see whether it moves, or hunts for the grinding felt when broken ends rub together, because each of those acts adds pain and can add damage. The attempt also ends if the learner continues while the patient reports pain that is rising, and stopping at the right moment counts as a pass rather than as a failure. In a constructed illustration that describes no real patient, a learner holds a simulated forearm, feels the swelling increase under the fingers, and says aloud that the examination stops there and that the limb will be splinted as it lies, which is exactly the answer the station is designed to hear.

Every station is also a station in dignity, warmth and hygiene, and these are judged as strictly as the technique. The learner wears personal protective equipment when the scenario calls for it, cleans the hands before and after contact, and asks the patient before exposing a limb. The part is uncovered only as far as the task requires, and it is covered again as soon as the hands have finished. A manikin cannot complain of cold, so the learner rehearses the covering as a deliberate act, since cold is a complication of trauma and a patient left uncovered while a splint is adjusted is being harmed by the treatment rather than by the injury. The assessor watches for the blanket and for the quiet words that tell the patient what is about to happen.

Restraint is the word the laboratory uses for the second skill, because stabilization in the field is a matter of holding still rather than of correcting. The learner supports the injured part in the position in which it was found, takes the weight with both hands, and holds the joints above and below the injury still. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, not even in a practice scenario, because the habit is built by the hands rather than by the intention, and because vessels and nerves lie against the bone where a helpful-looking movement can tear them. Holding is tiring, so the learners practice the exchange of a hold, in which the new pair of hands takes the load before the old pair releases it. The lay first aider performs this skill with the hands, a pillow or whatever is at hand, while formal splinting belongs to the trained responder and the paramedic.

The neurovascular examination is its own station and the one that is repeated most often, because it is performed before every intervention and again after it. The learner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and tests sensation on both sides so that the two can be compared. The patient is asked about numbness, tingling and weakness, and about any movement that was possible a moment ago and is not possible now. The learner practices saying the findings aloud in a fixed order and writing them at the bedside rather than from memory, because a finding that was not recorded before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. The lay first aider is taught the simpler version of this observation, which is color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder and to the clinician.

An important part of this station is the lesson that a pulse is a poor comfort, because a pulse can still be felt at the wrist or the ankle while the pressure inside a compartment is already strangling the muscle. A present pulse therefore never excludes a serious injury, and an absent pulse turns the moment into an emergency. The examiner should be the same person before and after an intervention wherever the service allows it, since two examiners may disagree about a faint pulse and neither of them will be wrong. Where a service requires the examination to be repeated at a fixed interval, that interval is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services differ in how often they require it and in who is authorized to perform it.

Applying a splint is the third skill, and it is taught as a way of preventing movement rather than as a way of correcting position. The learner pads the splint where it will press on bone, applies it over the limb as it lies, and includes the joint above and the joint below the injury, because a bone that is held alone can still be moved by the joint at either end. The straps are tightened until the limb is held and no further, and the material matters less than the principle, since a folded magazine, a padded board or a molded splint each serves the same purpose. The learner then checks the fingers or the toes for color, warmth, sensation and movement, and writes the finding beside the earlier one. Splinting in the field is the work of the trained responder and the paramedic within the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required.

A splint is a treatment that can injure, so the laboratory teaches its complications with the same care as its benefits. A strap that is too tight, a knot that presses on a nerve where the bone lies close to the skin, or a pad that has slipped while the patient was moved, each causes damage that appears after the splint and is blamed on the fracture. The learner is therefore taught to check the splint as part of the reassessment, to lift the edge and look at the skin, and to ask the patient about new numbness or new pain. If there is resistance, if the skin changes color, or if the pain rises rather than settles, the responder stops, does not force the device into a better position, and calls for a higher level of care. Force is not a technique in the practice room, and it is not a technique in the field.

The sling and the swathe are small skills that are easy to perform badly, and the laboratory treats them as seriously as the splint. A sling supports the forearm and takes the weight of the arm away from the shoulder girdle, and it is used for injuries of the shoulder, the clavicle, the upper arm and some injuries of the forearm and the hand. The learner is assessed on whether the fingertips stay visible so that the circulation can be watched, on whether the knot sits away from the back of the neck, and on whether the arm hangs in the position the injury tolerates rather than in a position the learner finds tidy. A swathe binds the arm to the chest to limit movement, and it is never drawn so tight that breathing becomes an effort. Binding the chest to splint fractured ribs is avoided in many services because it restricts breathing and increases the risk of a chest infection, and where practice differs the local protocol decides.

The log roll is the skill that most often reveals whether a team can work as one body. It is a way of turning a patient onto the side so that the back can be examined, a device can be placed beneath the body, or a blocked airway can be cleared, and what it must achieve is a turn in which the head, the shoulders, the pelvis and the legs move together. The team has one leader who gives the count and one person at the head who owns the alignment of the neck, and every other pair of hands owns a named part of the body. The patient is turned only as far as the task requires and is returned without delay, because the position is a means and not a destination. The log roll is not a technique for the lay first aider, and it belongs to the trained responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic, performed within the procedures their service authorizes.

The station is judged on the stop as much as on the turn, because the maneuver is abandoned whenever it becomes unsafe. If the patient fights the hands that hold the neck, if a limb cannot move with the body, if the alignment is lost, or if the team disagrees about the count, the leader stops the maneuver and the team returns the patient to the position found. No single responder performs a manual handling technique alone, and no chapter may describe a lone technique as safe, because an unstable spine moves as a unit only when the people around it move as a unit. The spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and clearing it is a judgment that combines the mechanism of injury, the examination and the imaging rather than a single test. The learner practices the words that ask for that clearance, because the request is a part of the skill and not a pause before it.

The stretcher and the devices that go with it are taught as answers to particular problems rather than as a list of equipment. The scoop stretcher separates into two halves that slide beneath the patient and lock together, so that a patient found on the ground can be raised with as little movement of the trunk as possible. The long board is rigid and flat, and its greatest value lies in freeing a patient from a confined space, while a hard surface that does not give transmits every bump of the road to the skin of the back, the heels and the head. The padded stretcher and the vacuum mattress spread the weight of the body, and the choice among these devices belongs to whoever is leading the move, within the equipment the service carries and the protocol it follows. Practice differs between services about how long a patient may be carried on a hard board, and any figure for that belongs to the current guideline rather than to this course.

The transfer drill is practiced until the plan comes before the hands, which means that the move is spoken aloud before it begins. Every responder knows which part of the body they own, where the patient is going, and who is watching the injured part, and the fractured bone is never used as a handle, because the bone is a lever and the soft tissues attached to it take the strain. Where the patient can be slid along a surface rather than lifted above it, the slide is preferred, since it needs fewer hands and moves the spine less. The straps and the locks are checked before the lift, the skin is inspected where a device meets the body, and the leader watches the patient rather than the equipment. The number of responders a move requires depends on the size of the patient, the device and the protocol, so any figure offered for it is an illustration to be confirmed against the guideline in force and the procedure of the service.

Imaging is the step that the laboratory can teach only from the outside, because interpretation is a clinical skill that belongs to the radiographer who takes the study and to the clinician who reads it. What the learner can practice is everything around the study, which is the safe transfer of the patient to the imaging table, the immobilization that travels with the patient, the warmth that is maintained in a cold room, and the neurovascular examination that is recorded before and after the journey. A radiograph is usually the first study and is taken in at least two directions, while computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues. The learner is assessed on knowing that a study is ordered by a clinician and that a lay first aider never orders or interprets one. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined after it has been taken.

Reassessment is drilled as a skill in its own right, because it is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment. The same observations are repeated in the same order after every intervention, and the record of the earlier examination is read before the new one is written. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. A constricting bandage, splint or cast is released only by someone the local protocol authorizes to release it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently.

The laboratory teaches the definitive treatments by name and by purpose, and leaves the technique where it belongs. Reduction restores the position of the bone ends, traction holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and a cast or a surgical fixation holds the position while the bone heals, and none of those acts may be learned from a book. The learner may watch a demonstration, may handle the devices, and may be told what each one is meant to achieve, but the technique itself is acquired in supervised clinical training and is performed according to local protocol by a physician or an orthopedic surgeon. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when the responder lacks the training and the equipment. In each of those situations an attempt can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and the learner is assessed on recognizing those situations rather than on attempting the act.

The open fracture has its own station, because it is the injury in which the wrong reflex causes the most harm. The learner covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm, and prepares an urgent referral. An embedded object is never removed and exposed bone is never pushed back into a wound, because the object may be holding pressure on a torn vessel and the bone may be the only thing closing the wound. An open wound is never explored blindly, since exploration adds contamination and pain, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. The learner is assessed on what is not done as much as on what is done, which is the mark of a skill that has been understood rather than memorized.

Pain, tetanus protection and antibiotics appear in the practice scenarios, and they are handled there with deliberate vagueness. The scenario states who decides, which finding makes the decision urgent, and what the scope of practice of the responder forbids, and it says plainly that the substance, the amount and the way it is given belong to the prescriber and to the protocol in force. A learner must not be able to take a prescription from this course, and the laboratory is no different, so the station is assessed on the recognition of severe pain, on the request for help, and on the accurate reporting of what the patient said and what has changed. The nurse and the physician act within the authority the law and the employer give them, and the learner observes that boundary rather than rehearsing an act that is not theirs.

Some patients change the practice without changing the sequence, and the laboratory keeps manikins of different sizes for exactly that reason. The child is not a small adult, because the head is large in proportion to the body and a device sized for an adult will not hold a small body in line, so the learner practices on a child-sized model and practices the words used to explain the examination to a frightened parent. The older adult brings thin skin that tears under a grip, bone that breaks under a hand laid on a rib cage, and a fracture that may hurt far less than its severity suggests. A pregnant patient is two patients for the purpose of assessment and one patient for the purpose of handling, so the position in which she is carried is decided by a clinician or by the protocol of the service. In each of these patients the learner rehearses a lower threshold for immobilization and for referral rather than a different order of steps.

The skills of talking are assessed beside the skills of the hands, because a frightened patient who is not told what is about to happen will tense against the very hands that are trying to help. The learner says what will be done, asks permission before exposure, warns the patient before a movement, and takes the answer seriously even when the answer is a request to stop. The debrief of a station is blame-free, since a learner who is humiliated does not report the near miss, and a near miss reported in the practice room is an injury prevented at the roadside. Every station ends with a written record of the practice, signed by the supervisor who watched it, and the certifying body that recognizes the training defines what the learner may do afterward and what still requires supervision.

The intervals for refreshing a skill differ between services, countries and certifying bodies, so any schedule named in a course or a policy is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the rule of the authority that certifies the responder. Simulation also has honest limits, because a manikin does not bleed, does not feel pain and does not deteriorate, so the feel of a limb that has become tight, or of a pulse that has become hard to find, is learned on real patients under supervision. What the laboratory can give is the order of the actions, the habit of the neurovascular record, and the reflex to stop and to call for help, and those three are worth the hours. The lay first aider learns a smaller set of acts, which are to call for help, to keep the patient still and warm, to cover a wound, and to support a limb as it lies.

To summarize, the practical skills laboratory is where the reasoning of this course becomes the work of the hands, and it follows the same order as every chapter, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The skills practiced there are the examination of the injured limb, the support of that limb in the position found, the neurovascular record written before and after every intervention, the splint, the sling and the swathe, the log roll, the transfer onto a stretcher, and the reassessment that catches the complication caused by the treatment. No skill is practiced on a patient for the first time, because the first attempt belongs to a manikin or to an uninjured colleague, and a learner acts on a patient only within the authorization of a training program and the local protocol. Never straighten a deformed limb in the field, never remove an embedded object, never push exposed bone back into a wound, never explore an open wound blindly, and never perform a manual handling technique alone. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when vessels or nerves are failing, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when the training and the equipment are lacking. Any interval, temperature or number of responders named in a policy is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, the patient is kept warm, the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and the responder stops and escalates when there is resistance or a complication. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 65 — The Clinical Decision-Making Framework

Every injury in this course is met with the same questions in the same order, and this chapter gathers those questions into one framework that a responder can run in the head at the roadside, in a corridor, or at the foot of a bed. The framework does not replace the sequence that every chapter of this course follows, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively; it is that sequence spoken as questions a person can remember when nothing can be looked up. The first few questions are usually answered in seconds, while the rest may take minutes, and several of them are answered again after every act of care. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The reason the questions are fixed rather than left to the moment is that a frightened memory does not sort priorities by itself. Under pressure the eye goes to the obvious deformity, to the blood on the jacket and to the limb that is bent the wrong way, while the quiet problem that will kill first may be a chest that does not move or a pulse that is fading. If the order is fixed, the responder does not have to decide what to think about first, and the decision that matters most, which is that life comes before limb, is made before the patient is even reached. A fixed shape also makes the assessment repeatable, so that the second person to arrive continues the same examination instead of beginning a different one.

The framework asks thirteen questions, and it asks them in a fixed order: what happened, what is injured, whether the patient is stable, whether there is a life-threatening problem, whether there is a limb-threatening problem, whether there is a neurological injury, whether the fracture is open, whether the injury is unstable, whether it requires reduction, how it should be immobilized, what imaging is required, where the patient should go, and what needs to be reassessed. The first two belong to assessment, the next two decide how quickly everything else must happen, and the questions that follow move through the examination of the limb, its immobilization, its imaging and its destination. In practice the framework is not walked from the first question to the thirteenth and then put away, because an unstable patient sends the responder back to the beginning, and an intervention sends the responder forward only as far as the next reassessment. A useful way to hold it is as a loop with a gate, where the gate is the stability of the patient and everything about the limb waits behind it.

Question one is what happened, and it is answered from the scene before it is answered from the patient. The responder notes the position of the patient, the height of a fall, the nature of a collision, the object that struck or the surface that was struck, the time of the injury, and whether the patient has been moved since. The mechanism of injury is the best early guide to which tissues took the energy, and it predicts which injuries may be present even when the patient cannot tell the story. The environment belongs to this question as well, because traffic, machinery, fire, water, electricity and the risk of a further collapse decide whether anyone may approach at all. The lay first aider stays out of an unsafe scene and calls for help, while the trained responder enters only with the authorization of the service, and personal protective equipment is put on before contact whenever blood or other body fluids may be present.

The mechanism also tells the responder how much energy was involved, and energy is the part of the injury that the skin conceals. A fall from a low height and a fall from a roof can produce the same swollen ankle and a very different set of hidden injuries, so the height, the landing surface and the part of the body that landed first are all recorded. As a constructed illustration, a patient who strikes a knee against a dashboard may have a break of the thigh bone and a dislocation of the hip on the same side, and the hip may be noticed only when the whole body is examined. Any threshold for a dangerous height or a dangerous speed is also an illustration, and the current guideline and the local protocol define the figure your service uses, because services and countries set them differently. The age of the patient and the illnesses and medicines that have weakened the bone belong here too, since a fall that leaves one person unhurt can break the hip of another.

Question two is what is injured, and it is answered by the whole-body examination that follows the primary survey rather than by the part the patient complains about. The head, the neck, the chest, the abdomen, the back, the pelvis and each limb are examined in turn, and each limb is compared with its fellow on the other side. The limb is examined where it lies, by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it if the patient is able, and never by forcing a movement the patient cannot make. Swelling, deformity, bruising, an open wound and tenderness over a bone point toward a fracture, while a joint that is empty, locked or sitting in the wrong direction points toward a dislocation.

No single finding proves that a bone is broken and no single finding excludes it, because a fracture may be present in a limb that looks straight, that moves without grating and that is not badly swollen, particularly in a child and in an older adult whose bone has lost density. Grating, which is the sensation when two broken ends move against each other, is reliable when it is present and dangerous to seek, because the movement that produces it can injure the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone. A patient who is distracted by a more painful injury, intoxicated, confused or unable to speak may not report a second injury at all, so the examination is completed whatever the patient says. The responder records what was seen and felt instead of what it is called, because a description can be judged later and a diagnosis made in the field cannot.

Question three is whether the patient is stable, and it is the gate through which every other question must pass. Stability is judged by the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and it is judged again whenever the patient changes. An airway that is not open, a breathing that is not adequate and a circulation that is failing are treated before the limb is examined, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The trained responder and the paramedic perform the primary survey and the interventions their service authorizes for it, while the nurse repeats the observations that show whether the patient is holding and the physician directs the resuscitation. When two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, the principle that decides between them is that life comes before limb. A falling level of consciousness, a changed pattern of breathing, a weak and rapid pulse and skin that has become cold and pale send the responder back to the beginning without apology.

Question four is whether there is a life-threatening problem, and at the roadside it is most often bleeding, both the bleeding that can be seen and the bleeding that cannot. Blood pouring from a wound is controlled by direct pressure, and the trained responder may use a tourniquet or another device that the local protocol authorizes, applied by someone trained and certified to apply it, while the lay first aider presses on the wound and calls for help. Blood collecting inside the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis or the thigh cannot be seen, and it is suspected from the mechanism, from a rising pulse and from skin that is cold and clammy. A pelvic binder is applied by a trained responder or a clinician within the local protocol when the mechanism and the examination suggest an unstable pelvis, and it is part of stabilization rather than of diagnosis. An operating room and a blood bank, and not the roadside, are what finally treat these problems, so the task of the responder is to recognize them and to shorten the time until the patient reaches them. No drug, no dose and no route is given from this book, because prescribing belongs to a prescriber who works within the local protocol.

Stabilization is the second step of the course sequence, and in the field it is a small set of acts performed in the right order. The patient is kept warm, wet clothing is replaced with covering, the body is insulated from the ground and the head is covered, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled, the injured limb is supported in the position in which it was found, and nothing is straightened. A patient with a suspected injury of the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear it has done so, and the patient is moved only by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires, because no single manual handling technique is safe on its own. The lay first aider supports, warms and waits, the trained responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic act within their equipment and their procedures, and the nurse and the physician continue the same work with the resources of the facility. Stabilization is never allowed to delay the transport of a patient who cannot be made stable where the patient lies.

Question five is whether there is a limb-threatening problem, and it is answered by the neurovascular examination together with the look of the limb. A limb whose pulse has weakened or disappeared, that is pale and cool beyond the injury, that is painful out of proportion to what is seen, or that has lost sensation or movement is a limb at risk, and each of those findings is recorded before anything is done and repeated afterward. A compartment that is tense, swollen and painful when it is stretched is an emergency even when a pulse is still present, because an intact pulse does not exclude a compartment syndrome and the diagnosis is clinical. An open fracture, a limb that has been crushed or partly amputated, and a joint that remains dislocated are the other limb-threatening problems a responder must recognize. A limb-threatening finding means urgent transfer to a facility with an operating room and a surgeon, and it means that nothing is done on the way that could add to the injury. Diagnosis and treatment belong to the clinician and to the orthopedic surgeon, while recognition, recording, immobilization and movement belong to the responder.

Question six is whether there is a neurological injury, and it is asked about the limb and about the spine at the same time. In the limb, the question is whether the patient can feel a light touch and can move the part that the nerve beyond the injury supplies, and the answer is compared with the other side and written down. In the spine, the question is whether there is weakness, numbness or a loss of bladder or bowel control, because those findings change the urgency of the transfer. A patient who is unconscious, confused, intoxicated or sedated cannot give a reliable answer, and the absence of a complaint is not the absence of an injury. A neurological finding that appears or worsens after a splint, a move or a journey is reported at once, because it may mean that the treatment caused it.

The neurovascular examination is the step this course turns on, and it is performed before any intervention and repeated after every one. The examiner looks at the color and the temperature of the skin, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. Sensation is tested on both sides and compared, and the words the patient uses are recorded as far as possible rather than translated into a term the patient did not say. The result is written before the splint is applied and after it is applied, and it is written where the next person will find it, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterward. The lay first aider observes color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, the trained responder and the paramedic perform the formal examination, and the nurse and the physician repeat it and interpret it.

Question seven is whether the fracture is open, and the answer changes the destination, the urgency and the precautions of the whole plan. A fracture is open when the bone or the deep tissues have communicated with the outside, whether the wound is large or a puncture the size of a fingertip, and an open fracture is contaminated even when it looks clean. The responder covers the wound with a sterile dressing, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, records the neurovascular status, immobilizes the limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm, and arranges urgent transfer. An embedded object is never removed, because it may be holding pressure on a torn vessel, and exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, because the movement can carry contamination inward and tear what remains intact. The wound is never explored blindly with a finger or with an instrument, and definitive cleaning and closure belong to the operating room and to nobody else. Antibiotics, tetanus protection and pain relief are decided by a prescriber according to the local protocol, and this book gives no substance, no amount and no route, because those belong to the prescriber and to the guideline current where you work.

Question eight is whether the injury is unstable, and the word unstable describes behavior rather than appearance. A fracture is unstable when the broken ends will not hold their position without support, as they often will not when the bone is broken into several pieces. A joint is unstable when its surfaces no longer stay in contact, which is what a dislocation is, and the same joint may remain unstable after it has been put back if a ligament or the rim of the joint has been torn. Instability matters to the responder because an unstable injury can move during handling, during a transfer and during a journey over a bad road, and each movement can injure a vessel or a nerve that lies against the bone. The response of the responder is not to test the instability but to immobilize the limb in the position found, to handle the patient gently, and to say in the handover what was seen. Judging how unstable an injury is and what will hold it belongs to the clinician and to the orthopedic surgeon.

Question nine is whether the injury requires reduction, and this is the question in which the framework most needs its discipline. A reduction is the act of restoring broken ends or dislocated surfaces to their proper position, and it is done to relieve pressure on vessels and nerves, to restore the length and the alignment of the limb, and to make the injury holdable while it heals. Whether it is needed, when it is done, who does it and where it is done are decisions for a clinician, most often an orthopedic surgeon in a facility with imaging and an operating room. A deformed limb is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone, and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact or turn a closed fracture into an open one. The technique of reduction is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and it is not taught from a book, because the hands that perform it must have felt resistance and known when to stop. Traction, which holds broken ends in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting, which holds the position while the bone heals, are learned in the same way and belong to the same supervised training.

A reduction is not attempted when the source lists a reason to leave the injury alone, and those reasons are worth naming because a rule is followed only when the reason behind it is understood. The attempt is not made when the injury is a suspected complex fracture and dislocation, when a fragment of bone is caught within the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has already failed. In each of those situations the attempt can convert an injury that might have healed into one that cannot, and force is not a technique. Resistance met during any maneuver is a signal to stop, to support the limb where it now lies, to record what has changed and to escalate. For the lay first aider, the trained responder and the paramedic, the answer to this question in the field is almost always the same, which is to immobilize the limb as found and to leave reduction to the people and the place equipped for it.

Question ten is how the injury should be immobilized, and the principle is that movement is prevented at the fracture and at the joints above and below it. The limb is splinted in the position in which it was found, the splint is padded where it presses over bone, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation. The material matters less than the principle, because a folded magazine, a padded board, a pillow and the body of the patient can each serve, and an improvised device is checked more often because it shifts. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints and the authorized traction devices within the equipment and the procedures their service permits, and they recheck the neurovascular status after the splint is on. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands or with whatever is at hand and applies nothing that presses on the injury, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is needed, which may be a cast, a brace or a surgical fixation. A splint is a treatment that can cause its own complication, which is why the limb is examined again after it is applied and why a tight splint is a reason to stop and escalate.

Question eleven is what imaging is required, and the word required carries the weight of that question. A radiograph is usually the first study, and it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, while the joint above and the joint below the fracture are included so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography, which is often called CT, shows the detail of a complex break, particularly where it enters a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging, which is often called MRI, is used mainly for soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. Imaging is ordered by a clinician trained to interpret it, never by the lay first aider, while the trained responder and the paramedic report the findings and the mechanism that may make a study necessary. Either study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done, and it is performed after the limb has been immobilized so that the journey to the imaging room does not move the injury. An image is a picture of one moment, so the patient is examined and reassessed after the picture is taken, and the image never replaces the hands.

Question twelve is where the patient should go, and the answer follows from the answers to the questions before it. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, an injured vessel or nerve, a dislocation, a fracture that enters a joint, or a fracture in a child that crosses the growing part of the bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. A patient with a suspected injury of the spine is taken to a facility able to assess and to stabilize the spine, and the transfer is made with the precautions the local protocol requires. The choice also depends on distance, weather, the resources of the nearest hospital and the hour of the day, and those belong to the dispatcher, the receiving clinician and the local protocol rather than to the preference of the responder. The trained responder and the paramedic communicate the mechanism, the findings, the interventions already made and the neurovascular status before and after each one, because the receiving team continues a story rather than starting a new one. The lay first aider keeps the patient warm and still and keeps the time of the injury, because those three things change what the hospital can do.

Question thirteen is what needs to be reassessed, and the honest answer is almost everything, in the same order, after every intervention and at every change in the patient. The observations that matter are the same ones throughout, which are the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the level of consciousness, the color and the temperature of the limb, the pulse beyond the injury, the sensation, the movement and the pain. They are compared with the record rather than judged alone, because the meaning lies in the change and not in any single measurement. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness and a limb that becomes tense and swollen are the findings that make the responder stop, and they are also the findings that make the responder escalate. A responder who suspects a compartment syndrome does not wait for the diagnosis to be confirmed, and within the local protocol the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released by someone authorized to release it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. The framework loops back at this point rather than ending, since every intervention changes the answers to the questions that came before it.

The complication this framework most fears is the one caused by the treatment, which is why reassessment is a question in its own right and not a habit left to goodwill. A splint applied too tightly, a bandage that has become a band, a patient left too long in one position and a patient who has become cold while waiting are complications that follow care rather than injury. Each of them is found by looking at the patient again with the same questions in mind, and each is corrected within the limits of the local protocol by a person authorized to correct it. Some patients need the questions asked with a lower threshold for action, although the framework itself does not change: a child's bone bends before it breaks, an older adult's bone may break in a fall from standing height with little pain, and a patient who is intoxicated, confused or distracted may report nothing at all. The record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality after it, so the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention are written or spoken in a fixed order.

To summarize, the framework is thirteen questions asked in a fixed order, and it follows the sequence this course uses everywhere, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. Look for the mechanism and the energy behind it, for the injuries the patient does not mention, for bleeding that cannot be seen, for a limb that has lost its pulse, its color, its warmth, its feeling or its movement, for a wound over a fracture, and for a nerve or a vessel that has changed. Stabilize by warming the patient, controlling the bleeding that can be controlled, supporting the limb in the position found and treating the spine as unstable until someone qualified clears it, and record the neurovascular status before every intervention and after every one. Never straighten a deformed limb in the field, never remove an embedded object, never push exposed bone back into a wound, never explore an open wound blindly, and never attempt reduction, traction or casting unless you are trained, authorized and supervised to do it. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and a reduction is not attempted when the joint is shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, or when an earlier attempt has failed. Reassess after every intervention, hand the patient over with the same story in the same order, and call the receiving facility and the specialist that the local protocol names. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 66 — Documentation, Communication and Assessment

This final chapter is about the two things that decide whether everything you have heard in this course ever reaches a patient: the story that carries the findings from the roadside to the operating room, and the way your competence in all of it is judged. A fracture can be assessed perfectly and still be treated badly, because the team that received the patient never learned what the first responder saw, and a course can teach a sequence flawlessly and still fail if the listener is never asked to perform it.
