Every chapter of this course has followed one order, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and this chapter follows that order once more, though it follows it through the record rather than through the limb. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The record exists because memory is the least reliable instrument in trauma care, and the more urgent the situation the less it can be trusted. Adrenaline narrows attention to the task in front of the hands, so a responder who has just splinted a leg may genuinely believe that the foot was warm and the toes moved, when what was actually noted was the absence of an obvious problem. The neurovascular examination is performed before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding that was not written before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards, and no one can tell later whether a nerve was injured by the bone or by the bandage. A written or spoken note therefore protects the patient, who receives care based on facts rather than on a reconstruction, and it protects the responder, who is not asked to defend a memory against a bad outcome. The lay first aider, who carries no chart and no pen, still contributes to the record by reporting aloud, in the same fixed order, what was seen and what was done. The trained first responder, the emergency medical technician and the paramedic write within the forms and the procedures their service authorizes, and the nurse and the physician write in the clinical record.

A handover is not a fresh beginning, and the patient is not a new patient to each team that touches the stretcher. The receiving team is handed a story already in progress, and the value of the handover lies in the fact that the story continues in the order in which the events happened. When that order is kept, the receiving clinician can see the trajectory, so a pulse that was present at the roadside and absent on arrival means something very different from a pulse that was never recorded at all. The same sequence that governs treatment governs the telling of it, which is why the assessment findings come first, then what was done to stabilize, then the neurovascular status before and after each act, then the immobilization, then the images, then the reassessment, and last what is being asked of the receiving facility. A handover that begins with a conclusion and works backwards leaves the listener unable to judge how much of it to trust. The record travels with the patient, and the patient is never separated from the account of what has already been done.

Assessment begins with the scene and with the mechanism, and both belong in the record because the mechanism predicts the tissues that were loaded. The time of the injury is the first thing anyone will ask for, and it is written as a clock time rather than as a duration, because the window for certain treatments is measured from the moment of the injury; the exact figure that defines that window is confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since it differs between services and editions. The primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, is recorded in the order it was performed, with the level of consciousness and any change in it written in the same place every time. The limb assessment is then written as findings rather than as a diagnosis, which means what the examiner saw, what the examiner felt, what the patient said about the pain, and which movements the patient could and could not perform. Describing findings rather than naming a diagnosis is not a matter of modesty, because a label written early travels far and is believed long after the finding that produced it has changed. The lay first aider reports the mechanism and the time as well as the appearance of the limb, while the primary survey and the examination of the limb belong to the trained responder, to the nurse or to the physician according to local protocol.

What was done to stabilize belongs in the record in the plainest words available, because the next team has to know not only that the limb was supported but how. The position in which the limb was found is written down before anything is applied, since a deformed limb is splinted in the position found and never straightened in the field, and the reason is the risk to the vessels and the nerves that lie against the bone. The record notes that bleeding was controlled by direct pressure where it could be controlled, that an embedded object was left in place and stabilized, that exposed bone was not pushed back into a wound, and that an open wound was covered with a sterile dressing and not explored. Warmth belongs in the same paragraph as the splint, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, so the patient was insulated from the ground and wet clothing was replaced with covering. The lay first aider performs the acts that need no equipment, while the trained responder and the paramedic act within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes.

The neurovascular examination is written in the words of the examination itself, and it is written twice. Color, warmth, the pulse felt beyond the injury, the color of a pressed nail as it refills, sensation compared on both sides, and the movements the patient can perform are recorded before the limb is immobilized and again after it, because the comparison between the two notes is the only thing that can later separate an injury of the nerve from an injury of the treatment. The strength of a pulse is described rather than graded, so that the next examiner reads that it was present and equal to the other side rather than a mark whose meaning was never defined. Sensation is recorded where the patient can point to it, and the patient's own words for numbness or tingling are written down where possible, because a paraphrase loses the difference between a limb that feels asleep and a limb that feels nothing at all. The result is entered even when it is normal, and a normal entry is not a formality, because the normal record of a finding before an intervention is what allows the same finding to be trusted after it. The lay first aider observes and reports what can be observed without equipment, which is color, warmth and the ability to move and to feel, and the formal examination belongs to the trained responder, to the nurse or to the physician within the limits of their practice. A pulse that is present excludes nothing, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency that ends the examination and begins the referral.

Some findings are recorded precisely because they are unreliable, and the record must say what was found rather than what was concluded from it. An intact pulse at the wrist is compatible with a compartment syndrome that was already established when it was felt, because the pressure that closes the smallest vessels may not be enough to silence a large artery, so a note that reads that the circulation was intact conceals the observation that mattered. A patient whose limb is swollen and tense and whose pain is out of proportion to the injury has a finding and not yet a diagnosis, and the note should carry that finding forward without attaching a name to it that the next clinician may accept too quickly. The same discipline applies to the older adult whose fracture hurts less than its appearance suggests, and to the child who will not use a limb after an injury that looked minor, because in both the expected sign is missing and the record of its absence is what will change the next decision. Where a number is written, whether a temperature, a pulse rate or a distance, it is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than a threshold that this course has established.

Immobilization is recorded as an act with an author, so the note names what was applied, to which joints it extended, and who applied it. A splint holds the injured part and the joints above and below it, it is padded where it presses on bone, and it is secured firmly enough to hold without becoming a band that stops the circulation, and the record should say which of those was checked and when. An improvised device, such as a folded magazine, a padded board or a sling, is recorded as improvised, because a device of that kind shifts and must be checked more often than a manufactured one, and the check belongs in the record as well. The trained responder and the paramedic apply splints within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, while the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required. Casting belongs to that definitive stage, it is learned under supervision, and it is performed according to local protocol, and no chapter of this course teaches the technique of applying one.

Imaging is recorded as a question and an answer, because a study is requested when the answer it gives will change what is done. The record names who requested the study, what question it was meant to answer, and who interpreted it, since interpreting an image is the work of a clinician trained to do it and is never the work of the responder who carried the patient. A radiograph is usually the first study, it is taken in at least two directions so that a displacement in the third direction is not hidden, and it includes the joint above and the joint below so that a second injury is not missed. Computed tomography shows the detail of a complex break, particularly around a joint, and magnetic resonance imaging is used mainly for the soft tissues, including ligaments, cartilage, tendons and muscle. An image is a picture of one moment, and the patient must still be examined and reassessed after the picture has been taken, which is why the note of the reassessment follows the note of the study and never replaces it.

The reassessment is written immediately after every intervention, and it repeats the same observations in the same order so that the comparison can be made by whoever reads the note next. Pain that increases instead of settling, pain out of proportion to the injury, numbness, tingling, weakness, a limb that becomes tense and swollen, and a pulse that changes are the findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation. When a compartment syndrome is suspected, the constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of local protocol by someone authorized to do it, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently, because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. The record then states what was found after the release, what changed, and whom the finding was reported to by name or by role, so that the next team does not have to reconstruct whether anyone acted. Reassessment is the step that catches the complication caused by the treatment, and a course that feared only the injury itself would have no reason to insist on it.

Referral is where the record changes hands, and the questions asked at the receiving end are always the same. They are what the injury is, when it happened, what has been done, what the neurovascular status is now and what it was before, whether the patient is warm and stable, and what the referring clinician believes is needed. Reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting or surgical fixation, which hold the position while the bone heals, are all described rather than taught, because the technique of each is learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed, and the note should state which of those applies rather than only that no attempt was made. A patient with an open fracture, a suspected compartment syndrome, a dislocation, a damaged nerve or vessel, a fracture that enters a joint, or an injury that crosses the growing part of a child's bone is referred to a facility with imaging, an operating room and an intensive care unit. Force is not a technique, and a responder who meets resistance stops, splints what is there, and escalates. What is written at that moment is what the surgeon reads first.

The spoken handover is a performance with a structure, and the structure is worth practicing aloud until it becomes automatic. The first step is to identify yourself and the patient and to say where the patient is going, the next is to describe what happened and when, only then to give the relevant background of illness and treatment, then to report the findings of your examination in the order this course has used, and finally to state clearly what you are asking for. The receiving clinician is told the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention in the same breath as the interventions themselves, because a handover that lists what was done without the state of the limb around each act gives the listener actions with no results. A closed loop is used for anything that must be acted upon, which means that the instruction is repeated back by the person who will carry it out. The lay first aider gives a short spoken report in the same order and hands over the patient rather than the story. Where the patient is transferred from one service to another, the same order is used again, in speech and in writing, so that nothing depends on which form the receiving service happens to prefer.

Communication is not only professional, and the way the findings are told to the patient and to the family belongs to the same discipline as the record. The patient is told what has been found, what is being done, what will happen next and when, in the ordinary words of the language the patient speaks, and an interpreter is used rather than a passing bystander when that language is not shared. The patient's own account of the pain and of the mechanism is valuable evidence and is recorded as the patient tells it, since a description that comes from the person experiencing it is often sharper than anything the examiner can see. Consent for an examination or for an intervention is obtained by whoever is authorized to obtain it, it is explained in terms of what will be done and what the alternative is, and the fact that it was obtained is written down. Relatives are told what can be said within the limits of confidentiality and by the person designated to speak with them, because a course of treatment announced to a family by three different people in three different versions is a harm of its own.

A handover fails for ordinary human reasons far more often than for want of knowledge, and naming those reasons is part of preparing for them. Noise is the first, because a handover shouted across a moving vehicle competes with an engine and a siren, so the receiver must be close enough to hear and unhurried enough to ask. Hierarchy is the second, because a junior responder may not correct a senior clinician who has misstated a finding, and a service that treats the record as the authority rather than the rank removes that problem. The third is the shift change, where a patient arrives at the moment when attention is divided, and the answer is to write before speaking rather than after. Fatigue and the end of a long shift change how much is remembered rather than how much is known, so the note is written while the details are fresh and is never reconstructed from memory hours later. Where a note is corrected, the correction is made openly and visibly, so that the record shows what was thought at the time and what is known now.

The record has a legal and an ethical life of its own, and the rules that govern it are local, so they must be learned where you work rather than assumed from a course. What is written is written to be read by those who need it for the care of the patient and by no one else, so confidentiality is a duty and not a courtesy. An entry is made at the time or as close to the time as the situation allows, it is dated and signed by its author, and it states what was observed rather than what was inferred. Notes are never altered long afterwards to improve the story, and a later correction is added as a separate entry that says what changed and why, because a record that has been rewritten is worth less than a record that was imperfect and honest. The record may be requested by a court, by an insurer, by a regulator or by the patient, and in each case what stands is what was written at the bedside. No real patient, no identifiable case and no institutional detail belongs in any teaching example, which is why the examples used in this course are constructed illustrations and are described as such.

There are places where the record has no printed form, no computer and sometimes no electricity, and the duty to document does not disappear with the stationery. The minimum set of facts is always the same, and it is the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, what was done and by whom, the neurovascular status before and after each act, the images taken and what they showed, the findings on reassessment, and what is being asked of the receiving facility. Those facts can be written on a card, on a dressing wrapper, in a notebook or on a part of the patient that will not be washed before arrival, and the note travels with the patient rather than in a pocket. Where nothing can be written, the handover is spoken at the receiving door in the fixed order and repeated back, and the receiving clinician is asked to write it down while the account is fresh. The patient's own identification and the name of the person who made the note are the two details most often lost, and they are the two that make everything else traceable.

The written assessment of this course is meant to be used as a rehearsal of the sequence rather than as a test of memory, and it will ask you what you would look for, what you would do, in what order, and who may do it. It will not ask you for a dose, because no dose has been given anywhere in these chapters, and it will not ask you to describe the technique of a reduction, because a technique learned from a page and never practiced under supervision is a technique that has not been learned. Questions about an intervention are answered by naming the step of the sequence it belongs to, the finding that indicates it, the provider level that is authorized to perform it, and the reassessment that must follow it. A question about an open fracture is answered with covering, bleeding control, the neurovascular record, immobilization in the position found, warmth, and urgent referral, and a question about a suspected compartment syndrome is answered with escalation and with release of the constricting device within local protocol by someone authorized to do it. The reason the assessment is written this way is that a listener who has internalized the sequence can apply it to an injury the course never described, while a listener who memorized a list of answers cannot.

The practical assessment is where the course is finally used, and it is conducted on models, on simulators and on willing colleagues under the supervision of an instructor who is qualified to certify competence. The candidate is observed performing the sequence whole, which means assessing, stabilizing, examining the neurovascular status, immobilizing, obtaining and discussing imaging, reassessing, and then stating the referral or the definitive plan, while naming the provider level for each act as though the act were real. A candidate who skips the neurovascular examination before applying a splint fails that station regardless of how neat the splint is, and a candidate who straightens a deformed limb in order to make it easier to splint fails the whole scenario, because the examination exists to protect the patient from exactly that instinct. Feedback is given against the sequence rather than against the candidate, so that the same order can be used at the next station and in the next hospital. Certification is issued by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision, and that definition differs between countries, between services and between professions, so it is checked rather than assumed. Skills decay quietly, so drills, briefings and debriefings are scheduled rather than hoped for, and none of them substitutes for the authorization that the local authority requires. Nothing performed in the practical assessment of this course is a license to perform it on a patient.

Documentation and communication come last in this course because they carry everything that came before, and they carry one idea above all, which is that the patient is the whole person who was healthy the day before and the fracture is only the part of the injury that can be seen. Life comes before limb, because a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot, and the complication this course fears most is the one caused by the treatment. The neurovascular examination before and after every intervention is written down so that the course of the injury can be told apart from the course of the care, and the reassessment exists so that the first sign of harm caused by a splint, a bandage or a cast is caught while it can still be reversed. Immobilization in the position found, an embedded object left alone, exposed bone left where it lies, an open wound covered and not explored, and a deformed limb never straightened in the field are rules that survive only when the reason travels with them, which is why every chapter of this course has attached a reason. The spine is treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it. Reduction, traction and casting remain acts of supervised clinical training performed according to local protocol, and this course has described them without ever teaching them.

To summarize, the record and the handover are part of the treatment rather than a formality that follows it, and a finding that was not written before an intervention cannot be attributed after it. Write and speak in the order the course has used, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, and say who among the lay first aider, the trained responder, the paramedic, the nurse, the physician and the orthopedic surgeon may perform each act. Describe findings rather than diagnoses, name the provider level for every intervention, keep the patient warm, treat the spine as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and stop and escalate at the first sign of resistance or of a complication. Never straighten a deformed limb in the field, never remove an embedded object, never push exposed bone back into a wound, never explore an open wound blindly, and never take a dose, a route or a regimen from anything you have heard in this course, because the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and the prescriber. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and no chapter of this course has taught them. The sequence is not a ritual to be recited but a habit of mind that protects the patient at every step from the scene of the injury to the operating room, and if you keep it, you will have taken from these chapters the one thing they were written to give. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Appendix A — Practical Emergency Algorithms

These pathways are the emergency routes of the course, set out as ordered prose so that they can be followed by ear when the hands are busy. Each one begins with the finding that starts it, then gives the steps in the order in which they are performed, then marks the point at which the responder stops and calls for a higher level of care, and then names the scope of practice of each act. The same shape runs through all of them, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. The pathways are the unstable patient, the threatened limb, the suspected compartment syndrome, the open fracture, the suspected spinal injury and the dislocated joint. Nothing here replaces training, certification, supervision, local protocol or the law of the country in which you work.

Every pathway opens with the same two acts, and neither of them touches the injured part. The first is to make the scene safe enough to work in, which means traffic, fire, electricity, glass and the personal protective equipment that keeps blood off the skin of the rescuer, and a responder who cannot make the scene safe calls for help and waits, because a second casualty helps nobody. The second is to judge whether the patient is stable, since a patient who cannot breathe will not be helped by a perfect splint. The course therefore puts the primary survey before the limb and names its steps in the order in which they are spoken, which are airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, remembered as ABCDE, with the lay first aider doing the acts that need no equipment and everyone else working inside the equipment, the authorization and the local protocol that apply to their own level of practice.

The first pathway is for the patient who is unstable, and the finding that starts it is a patient who does not respond, who is not breathing normally, whose pulse is weak and rapid, whose skin is cold and damp, or who is losing blood faster than it can be replaced. The bleeding that kills first is usually outside the body and within reach, so the trained responder looks for a spurting wound, a dressing soaked through, a swelling that grows while the patient grows quieter, or a limb enlarging under its splint. The lay first aider who finds a patient unresponsive and not breathing normally calls for help at once and begins compression and rescue breathing if trained to do so, because CPR is a skill learned on a manikin with a teacher and refreshed in practice. A tourniquet, where it is used at all, is applied by a trained responder or a paramedic under the procedures of the service, and only for life-threatening bleeding from a limb that direct pressure has failed to control.

Once the catastrophic bleeding has been addressed, the order continues with the airway, which the trained responder opens with a simple position of the head or a device the service authorizes, while an advanced airway belongs to the paramedic or to the clinician trained to place it. Breathing comes next, and oxygen and assisted ventilation are given only by those whose authorization and equipment permit it. Circulation is supported by laying the patient flat, by keeping the patient warm, and by treating the injured limb as a source of concealed bleeding that is splinted rather than straightened, because moving the broken ends disturbs the clot and enlarges the loss. Disability is judged by the level of consciousness and by the pupils. Exposure means undressing the patient enough to find every injury and then covering the patient again at once, because cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort.

Throughout this pathway the injured limb waits, because life comes before limb in the order of the hands and not only in the order of the words. A deformed thigh or a dislocated ankle is supported as it was found, splinted by the trained responder within the equipment the service provides, and left alone until the patient is stable enough for the limb to be examined. The responder stops and escalates to the highest level available when the airway is lost, when breathing becomes inadequate, when the pulse disappears, when consciousness falls further, or when bleeding cannot be controlled by the means at hand. Reassessment follows each intervention and is compared with what was written before, and the receiving team is told before arrival what was found, what was done and what has changed, so that it continues a story instead of starting one.

The second pathway is for the threatened limb, and it begins with a finding rather than with a diagnosis. The finding is a limb that has turned pale or dusky, that is cool to the touch, that is painful out of proportion to the injury, that is numb or tingling, that is weak, or that has no pulse beyond the fracture, and any one of those signs starts the pathway. A pulse that is still present does not exclude serious injury, because the flow through the smallest vessels can fail while the large artery still carries a beat to the examining fingers. The injury that most often produces this picture is a fracture that has displaced, a break near a joint, a joint that has dislocated, or a fragment lying against a vessel. The lay first aider notices color, warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, keeps the limb supported as found, keeps the patient warm, and sends for help without delay.

The steps follow the order of the course, and the first of them is the neurovascular examination performed before anything else is done. The trained responder or the clinician looks at color and temperature, feels the pulse beyond the injury, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, tests sensation on both sides, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes, recording every finding as far as possible. The limb is then supported and splinted in the position in which it was found, and it is never straightened in the field, because vessels and nerves lie against the bone and a movement that looks helpful can tear what remained intact. A wound, if there is one, is covered with a sterile dressing, and the bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with pressure applied around the wound rather than into it. The patient is kept warm and the limb is not raised above the level of the heart, because raising it can reduce the flow the limb still has.

The responder stops and escalates at the moment the limb becomes pulseless, or at the moment its color, warmth, sensation or movement is worse than it was before the splint was applied, and any constricting material is then released by whoever the local protocol authorizes to release it. Nobody in the field reduces a fracture or a dislocation in order to restore a pulse, because force applied to an injured joint can turn an injury that would have healed into one that cannot, and because a reduction performed without imaging and without supervised training may trap the very vessel it was meant to free. The warning to the receiving team is spoken before the patient arrives rather than left as a note for later. Where a period of time is named in this pathway, it is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such periods differ between services, countries and editions.

The third pathway is for the suspected compartment syndrome, and it starts with pain rather than with a pulse. The finding is a limb that is tense and swollen, painful out of proportion to the injury, worse when the muscles inside are stretched, and accompanied by numbness, tingling or weakness that grows instead of settling. A compartment is a closed space bounded by bone and fascia, and bleeding or swelling inside it raises the pressure until the flow through the smallest vessels fails, even while a large pulse at the wrist or the ankle can still be felt. For that reason an intact pulse never excludes the diagnosis, and a limb that is painful beyond its appearance is treated as an emergency. The diagnosis is clinical and is made by a clinician, and the responder who suspects it does not wait for confirmation, because time is muscle.

The responder compares the injured limb with the other side, records what is found and the time, and reports it at once to the clinician responsible for the patient. The constricting bandage, splint or cast is released within the limits of the local protocol by someone authorized to release it, and if that person is not on scene the patient is moved toward whoever is. The limb is not raised above the level of the heart, the patient is kept warm and still, and any measure for pain is the decision of the prescriber, because the substance, the amount and the way it is given belong to the local protocol rather than to this course. A clinician may measure the pressure within the compartment in millimeters of mercury and compare it with the pressure at which the heart relaxes, and any threshold quoted for that comparison is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. The operation that opens the compartment, called a fasciotomy, belongs to the surgeon in an operating room and nowhere else, so escalation begins as soon as the diagnosis is suspected rather than after it is proved.

The fourth pathway is for the open fracture, and the finding that starts it is a wound anywhere near a broken bone, a wound that bleeds steadily, bone visible within the wound, or an object embedded in the limb. An open fracture is contaminated even when the wound looks clean, because the skin carries organisms that reach the bone and the deep tissues at the moment of the injury, so the injury is treated as a contaminated emergency from the first second. The responder puts on personal protective equipment before touching the wound, and where that equipment is not available the responder protects the hands with whatever the service provides and avoids contact with blood. Bleeding that can be controlled is controlled with pressure applied around the wound rather than into it, and the wound is then covered with a sterile dressing. The limb is supported and splinted in the position in which it was found, and the patient is kept warm while transfer is arranged.

Three acts are forbidden in this pathway, and the reason for each is the same, which is that the object or the bone may be holding pressure on a torn vessel. An embedded object is never removed, exposed bone is never pushed back into the wound, and the wound is never explored blindly with a finger or an instrument. The neurovascular status is recorded before the dressing is applied and again afterwards, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards. Antibiotic treatment and protection against tetanus are decisions of a prescriber working to the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route and the timing belong to that protocol rather than to this course. Definitive cleaning of the wound, removal of dead tissue and closure belong to the operating room and to the surgeon, and any interval quoted for the arrival of the patient there is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The responder stops and escalates when the bleeding cannot be controlled with pressure, when the part of the limb beyond the wound is pale, cold or pulseless, or when the patient becomes unstable for any reason.

The fifth pathway is for the suspected spinal injury, and it begins with the mechanism as much as with the patient. The finding that starts it may be a fall from a height, a dive into shallow water, a collision at speed, a blow to the head or the face, a heavy object falling on the back, or any injury in which the patient was found unconscious. Pain or tenderness in the neck or the back, numbness, tingling, weakness, or a change in the control of the bladder or the bowel raises the suspicion further. A patient whose attention is held by another painful injury may not mention the neck at all, which is why a distracting injury is a reason for caution rather than for reassurance. Until someone qualified to clear the spine has cleared it, the spine is treated as unstable, and that rule holds even when the patient feels well and asks to sit up.

The steps begin with the head, which the trained responder holds steady where it was found, without traction and without pulling, while the rest of the assessment continues around it. The patient is moved only by a team using the equipment and the number of trained people that the local protocol requires, because no lone manual handling technique is safe and one pair of hands cannot prevent movement of an unstable spine. The lay first aider keeps the patient still, warm and talking, and moves the patient only when the scene itself has become dangerous. Clearing the spine is a clinical decision based on the examination, on the way the injury happened and on imaging, and the studies used are computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, ordered by a clinician trained to interpret them. A responder who is unsure whether the spine has been cleared treats it as not cleared, and the patient is carried with the precautions the protocol demands until someone qualified says otherwise. The point of escalation is a patient who vomits, who becomes unresponsive, who cannot breathe, or who must be moved for safety, and in each of those cases the trained team moves the patient rather than the bystander.

The sixth pathway is for the dislocated joint, and the finding that starts it is a joint that no longer matches its partner on the other side. The limb is held in one position, the usual bony landmark is missing or has moved, the joint is swollen and painful, and the patient resists any attempt to move it. Numbness, tingling, weakness or a pulse difficult to find beyond the joint make the injury urgent rather than merely painful, and they are recorded before anything is done. A joint that has dislocated has almost always torn its capsule and at least one ligament, and it may have injured the cartilage or the bone at the edge of the joint. The one act that must never be performed in the field is the attempt to put the joint back, because a dislocation may be accompanied by a fracture that nobody has seen and because the attempt may compress the vessels on which the head of the bone depends.

The steps are to leave the joint alone, to support it as it was found with a sling, a pillow or the hands, which the lay first aider can do, to record the neurovascular status before and after that support, and to keep the patient warm. Any measure for pain is the decision of the prescriber, and the amount and the way it is given are not taught here. The trained responder may apply a sling or a splint within the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides how and when the joint is put back, with imaging available and with the means to manage whatever is found. Reduction is learned under supervision and performed according to the local protocol, and it is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open, when the diagnosis is unclear, when the training or the equipment is inadequate, or when an earlier attempt has failed. If an attempt has already begun and meets resistance, or if the pain, the sensation or the pulse changes while it is under way, it stops at once, and the responder escalates to the surgeon rather than persisting, because force is not a technique.

All six pathways end in the same discipline, which is reassessment after every intervention and a record the next person can read. The same observations are repeated in the same order and compared with what was written before, and the record names the time of the injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found, what was released or applied, and the neurovascular findings before and after every step. Cold is treated as a complication in every pathway, so the patient is insulated from the ground and wet clothing is replaced with covering. None of these pathways is a license to act beyond training, and every act in them is performed within the authorization of the service, the supervision of the clinician responsible and the law of the country in which the responder works.

To summarize, six emergency pathways run through this course and each begins with a finding rather than a diagnosis, which are the unstable patient, the threatened limb, the suspected compartment syndrome, the open fracture, the suspected spinal injury and the dislocated joint. In all of them the first acts are the same, which are to make the scene safe, to protect the hands, to follow the order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and to keep the patient warm, because life comes before limb. The steps that follow are to examine and record the neurovascular status before and after every intervention, to immobilize the limb as it was found, to image when a clinician orders it, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively, with the provider level named for each act. What must never be done is also the same in all six, which is never to straighten a deformed limb in the field, never to remove an embedded object, never to push exposed bone back into a wound, never to explore an open wound blindly, never to raise a limb that may be compartmented, never to move a patient with a suspected spinal injury by a lone untrained technique, and never to attempt a reduction that the source forbids. When the responder stops and escalates, the call is to the emergency service, to the trauma team, to the surgeon or to the intensive care unit, and it is made early rather than late. Everything in this appendix is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol or the law of the country in which you work.

# Appendix B — Practical Skills Laboratory Checklist

The practical skills laboratory is the place where this course stops describing and begins to check, and this appendix is the checklist a learner and an assessor work through together. Every item is spoken as a sentence or a run of sentences rather than as a mark on a form, and the whole of it is meant to be used with a teacher present. The skills below cannot be learned from a book, from a recording or from this course, because a hand learns a position by being corrected and not by being told. The learner practices on a manikin first and on a healthy colleague afterwards, with consent, and never on an injured patient until a qualified supervisor has signed the skill off and the service has authorized it. The assessor is a course instructor, a clinical educator, or a qualified practitioner designated by the service, and that assessor's judgment about safety overrides every other item on the list. This appendix, like the rest of the course, is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The general standard by which every skill is judged is the same, and it is worth stating before the individual items. The learner must name the step being performed, must perform it within the scope of practice of the level being trained, and must say what would make the step stop. A skill is demonstrated when it is performed in the right order, slowly enough to be watched, on the right patient, with the reason attached to it, and when the learner can describe what would count as harm. It is unsafe when the learner forces a limb, works outside the level they are authorized for, works alone where the protocol requires a team, or cannot say what they would do if the patient became worse. The sequence every skill in this appendix belongs to is the sequence of the whole course, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. An assessor who sees a step skipped marks the skill as not yet achieved, however neat the finished work looks.

The examination of an injured limb begins before the limb is touched, and the learner must demonstrate that order. The first part is the scene and the mechanism of injury, because the energy that broke a bone also passed through everything in its path. The second part is the primary survey, whose steps are remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and the learner states aloud that life comes before limb. Then the limb is exposed enough to be seen, with the patient covered everywhere else and kept warm, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. It is unsafe to walk to the injured limb first, to move the patient before the airway and the breathing have been assessed, or to remove clothing in a way that twists a limb. The lay first aider may check the airway and the breathing and summon help, while the trained responder and the clinician carry the survey further.

The limb itself is examined by looking, by feeling and by asking the patient to move it, and never by forcing it. Looking means the whole limb and both sides of the body for comparison, because a limb compared with its partner is read far better than one seen alone. Feeling means the temperature of the skin, the tenderness over a bone, the swelling, and the places where the skin has broken, and it is done gently enough that the patient does not pull away in pain. Asking means inviting the patient to move the fingers or the toes and to report what they feel, and the words of the patient are worth more than the interpretation of the examiner. What the learner then produces is a description rather than a diagnosis, naming the findings with the shared anatomical words and recording the position in which the limb was found. A sign that is reliable in one patient may be absent in another, so the learner says which findings are strong and which are weak in the patient in front of them. It is unsafe to test the stability of a joint by pulling on it, to push the ends of a suspected fracture against one another, to probe a wound with a finger or an instrument, and to try to straighten a limb that is deformed. Each of those acts belongs to a clinician trained to perform it, and each of them can convert an injury that would have healed into one that cannot.

Application of a splint is assessed as a way of protecting the limb and not as a way of making it look straight. The learner must demonstrate that the limb is held in the position in which it was found, that the splint is padded where it presses against a bone or a joint, and that it holds the joint above the injury and the joint below it, because a bone splinted alone can still be moved by the joints at either end. The splint is secured firmly enough to prevent movement and loosely enough that the circulation is not compromised, and the fingers or the toes are left visible so that they can be checked afterwards. The material matters less than the principle, and an improvised device is checked more often because it shifts. The trained first responder, the paramedic and the nurse apply splints within the procedures their service authorizes, while the lay first aider supports the limb with the hands and waits for help. The physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides what definitive immobilization is required, and casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol rather than from any page of this course. It is unsafe to straighten a deformed limb in order to fit a splint to it, to apply a splint so tightly that firmness is mistaken for safety, and to apply a splint over an open wound that has not first been covered.

Every splint is checked after it is applied, and that check is part of the skill being assessed rather than a separate item. The learner examines the color and the temperature of the skin beyond the splint, feels for a pulse that was felt before, presses briefly on a nail to watch the color return, tests sensation on both sides, and asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes. The findings are compared with those recorded before the splint was applied, and any new numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor, coolness or pain out of proportion to the injury is reported at once. Adjusting or releasing a splint is done within the local protocol by a responder authorized to do it, and the learner must say plainly what would make them stop and escalate rather than continue to adjust. The same rule governs the constricting bandage or splint released when a compartment syndrome is suspected, the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and the patient is referred urgently because the diagnosis is clinical and time is muscle. It is unsafe to apply a splint and never look at the limb again, to attribute new pain to the injury alone, and to hide uncertainty from the receiving team.

The sling and the swathe are assessed as one skill, because together they rest the upper limb and stop it from swinging. The learner must show that the hand is left visible below the sling so that its color and warmth can be watched, that the part of the sling crossing the neck is padded so that it does not cut into the skin or the vessels, and that the swathe crosses the chest without restricting the chest wall. The sling is set so that the elbow is supported and the hand rests higher than the elbow, because a hand that hangs down becomes swollen and painful. Any responder trained to apply a sling may do so, and the physician or the orthopedic surgeon decides how long the limb is rested and what definitive treatment follows. It is unsafe to secure a sling so tightly that the fingers change color or the patient cannot breathe comfortably, to cover the hand so that it cannot be seen, and to use a sling as a substitute for the examination that should have come before it.

The log roll is the skill with the highest penalty for failure, and it is assessed with the seriousness it deserves. The learner must demonstrate the team, the leader who gives the count, the hands placed where the protocol requires them, the head and the trunk moved together as one unit, and the airway watched by a member of the team whose only task is that. The learner must state aloud that an injury of the spine is treated as unstable until it has been cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and that no lone manual handling technique is safe. The roll is used to examine the back, to place a board beneath the patient, or to move a patient when the protocol requires it, and never simply because it is a skill that has been learned. The number of rescuers a roll requires is settled by the local protocol and by the size of the patient, and any number offered in teaching is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol of your service. It is unsafe to roll a patient alone, to roll without a count, to let one member pull on an injured arm, and to take hold of the head in order to steer it. A failed roll is a failure of the team, and the learner must say when the roll should not be attempted at all.

Transfer from the ground to the stretcher is assessed as its own skill, because a limb that survived the injury and the splint can still be lost during the lift. The learner must demonstrate the briefing before the lift, the position of each member of the team, the leader who gives the word, the hands that support the injured limb, the straps that hold the patient to the carrying device, and the check of those straps before the patient is raised. The patient is covered and insulated from the ground and from the wind during the transfer, and the receiving surface is padded where the injured part will rest. The paramedic and the nurse usually lead the transfer within the procedures their service authorizes, while the lay first aider keeps the head steady and the patient warm and does not lift alone. It is unsafe to lift a patient by the clothing, to let a limb hang unsupported, to leave a strap over the injured part, and to finish the transfer without repeating the neurovascular examination afterwards.

The reassessment after the transfer repeats the same observations in the same order, and the comparison with the earlier record is what has value rather than any single measurement. The learner must demonstrate the examination of color, warmth, pulse, sensation, movement and pain, and must say what has changed since the roadside, while the trained responder and the clinician decide what that change means. Where a pelvic injury is suspected, the learner states that the pelvis is stabilized with the device the local protocol provides, that the patient is not rolled onto the injured side for convenience, and that the receiving team is told the pelvis has not been cleared. Where a spinal injury is suspected, the learner states that the patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the protocol requires, and that the spine is not declared clear by anyone not qualified to clear it. It is unsafe to move a patient with a suspected pelvic or spinal injury on the strength of a single examination, and unsafe to treat a normal pulse as proof that nothing is wrong.

The neurovascular examination is assessed twice for every intervention, once before it and once after it, and the learner who performs it only afterwards has not achieved the skill. The learner must demonstrate the color and the temperature of the skin, the pulse felt beyond the injury and compared with the other limb, the color of a nail as it refills after brief pressure, the sensation tested on both sides, the movement of the fingers or the toes, and the pain the patient reports. The findings are spoken in a fixed order, written down before the intervention and written again after it so that the two records can be compared, and the words of the patient are recorded as far as possible rather than translated. A pulse that is present does not exclude serious injury to the vessels or to a compartment, and a pulse that is absent is an emergency, and the learner must be able to say both of those sentences. The lay first aider observes the color, the warmth and the ability of the patient to move and to feel, while the formal examination belongs to the trained responder or to the clinician. It is unsafe to skip the examination because the limb looks well, to assume findings from an earlier patient, to record a normal finding that was never tested, and to write the record after the splint rather than before it, because a finding that was not recorded before an intervention cannot be attributed afterwards.

What the learner must also demonstrate is the meaning of those findings and the action they demand. Numbness, tingling, weakness, pallor, coolness and pain that grows rather than settles are stated aloud as findings that stop the responder and prompt escalation, and the learner names the person who must be told and the urgency with which the patient must move. The learner must describe what a compartment syndrome looks like at the bedside, that it is diagnosed clinically, that the limb is not elevated above the level of the heart, and that a constricting bandage or splint is released within the local protocol by a responder authorized to do it. That item is assessed in words and through a constructed scenario, because a manikin cannot reproduce the pain of a compartment that is filling, and the scenario is an illustration rather than a patient. It is unsafe to wait for a confirmation that will arrive after the muscle has died, to elevate the limb in the belief that swelling will settle, and to apply something cold in a way that hides the skin from the examiner.

The record and the handover are assessed as clinical skills in their own right, because a finding that is not passed on has not been made. The record is completed by the responder who made the observation, and the handover is given to the receiving clinician or nurse. The learner must demonstrate a handover in a fixed order, naming the time and the mechanism of the injury, the position in which the limb was found, the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, the treatment given, and what has changed since the last assessment. The record must be legible to someone who was not present, must distinguish what was observed from what was concluded, and must carry the time at which each observation was made. It is unsafe to hand over a patient without the neurovascular findings, to describe a splint as applied without saying when it was checked, and to leave a change in the condition of the patient out of the story because it seemed unimportant.

Practicing the skills of this appendix has limits that the learner must be able to state, and the assessor marks those limits as part of the skill. Reduction, which restores the position of the bone ends, traction, which holds them in line with a gentle continuous pull, and casting, which holds the position while the bone heals, are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and none of them is taught as a technique by this course. A reduction is not attempted when the joint surfaces are shattered, when a fragment is caught in the joint, when the vessels or the nerves are failing and need a specialist, when the injury is open or the diagnosis unclear, when the responder lacks the training or the equipment, or when an earlier attempt has failed, and the learner must give the reason rather than only the rule. The learner must also state that no dose, no route and no regimen is given anywhere in this course, that the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber, and that the decision to give any medicine is made by someone authorized to make it. Practice on each other requires consent, personal protective equipment appropriate to the task, and a supervisor present, and a learner who cannot state the scope of practice for a step has not yet earned the step.

To summarize, this appendix is a checklist for supervised practice and not a substitute for it, and every item in it names the provider level that may perform the step. The examination of an injured limb is assessed as looking, feeling and asking the patient to move, always comparing both sides, never forcing a joint, never probing a wound and never straightening a deformed limb, which is splinted in the position found. The application of a splint is assessed as padding the bony points, holding the joints above and below, leaving the fingers or the toes visible and checking the limb afterwards, and the sling and the swathe are assessed as supporting the arm without hiding the hand or restricting the chest. The log roll and the transfer are assessed as team skills with a leader and a count, with the spine treated as unstable until it is cleared by someone qualified to clear it, and with no lone manual handling technique ever taught as safe. The neurovascular examination is assessed before every intervention and again after it, its findings are recorded in a fixed order, and a present pulse is never taken as proof that the limb is safe. Reduction, traction and casting belong to supervised clinical training and to local protocol, no dose and no route appears anywhere in this course, and any figure named here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol of your service. This appendix is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Appendix C — Quick-Reference Fracture Card

This appendix is a card to be listened to before or after an encounter rather than during one, because a responder recalling a region and a referral threshold at once gives neither enough attention. It holds the shape of each regional injury: the findings that identify it, the immediate management any responder may begin, the nerves and vessels at risk, and the urgency of referral. It names the level at which each act belongs, for the lay first aider, the trained first responder, the emergency medical technician, the paramedic, the nurse and the physician. Nothing here is a technique to be learned from a book, and nothing here replaces training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work. Practice differs between countries and between editions of the same guideline, so the protocol of your own service governs what you do. Where a figure is named, it is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Every region is read through the same sequence, which is to assess, to stabilize, to examine the neurovascular status, to immobilize, to image, to reassess, and then to refer or to treat definitively. Assessment begins with the scene and the mechanism of injury, moves to the primary survey remembered as ABCDE, meaning airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, and turns to the limb only when the patient is stable. The neurovascular examination is done before any intervention and repeated after it, and its result is recorded, because a finding not written down before a splint was applied cannot be attributed afterwards. Two prohibitions hold everywhere: a deformed limb is splinted in the position found and never straightened in the field, and a wound is never explored blindly, never emptied of an embedded object and never closed outside an operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and they are never taught from this book. The lay first aider supports the limb, controls the bleeding that can be controlled, keeps the patient warm and calls for help, while the trained responder and the paramedic work within the equipment and procedures their service authorizes. Anyone who meets resistance, or who finds the limb more painful, tenser or less sensate after an intervention, stops and escalates, because force is not a technique.

A break of the collarbone shows as pain and swelling over the bone, tenderness at the site and an arm held still against the body. It is usually closed and is managed by supporting the arm in a sling that the trained responder or the clinician applies within local protocol, with the neurovascular status recorded before and after. The nerves and vessels of the arm pass close beneath the bone, so numbness, tingling or a weak hand changes the urgency, and a blow that breaks the shoulder blade has often injured the ribs, the lung or the head as well. A dislocated shoulder shows a squared outline, a hollow where the rounded head of the bone should sit and a patient who holds the arm away and refuses to move it. The nerve wrapping around the surgical neck and supplying the outer shoulder is the one most often injured, so numbness there or weakness in lifting the arm is recorded. A weak pulse or a pale cool hand makes the injury an emergency, and the limb is supported in the position found and transferred urgently to a facility with imaging. Restoration of the joint is not attempted from this book, nor when the diagnosis is unclear, a fragment lies in the joint, the vessels or nerves are failing, or training and equipment are lacking.

A break near the elbow is more dangerous than its size suggests, because the vessel that supplies the forearm crosses the joint in front and the nerves that move the hand lie against the bone. A dislocated elbow shows the bone prominent behind the joint, a fixed position of the arm and swelling that follows quickly. A pulse that vanishes, a hand that is pale or cool or a hand that cannot move makes it an emergency, and the lay first aider does not pull the joint, test its movement or try to straighten the arm. Both bones of the forearm show as pain, swelling, a possible deformity and a refusal to turn the palm. The forearm is a closed space bounded by bone and fascia, so bleeding inside it can cause a compartment syndrome, and a tense, swollen and disproportionately painful forearm is an emergency from the first contact. An inability to make a circle with the thumb and the index finger is a nerve finding to record and report, because the nerves of the forearm supply the muscles that bend the fingers and the thumb. A break of the upper arm bone shows as pain, swelling and a limb the patient supports with the other hand, and the nerve spiraling around it is at risk, showing as a wrist that will not lift and numbness on the back of the hand.

Injuries at the wrist show as pain, swelling, tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb and a hand the patient will not use. A break of the far end of the forearm bone is the commonest and may leave the wrist bent backward, shortened or displaced sideways, a finding described for the record and never corrected in the field. The nerve passing through the wrist to the hand is at risk, so numbness in the palm, the thumb or the fingers is recorded before splinting and again after. Support on a padded splint that holds the wrist as it was found, protection of the joints above and below, warmth and referral are the acts of the responder, because the final position belongs to the clinician. A small wrist bone may hurt only when the hollow at the base of the thumb is pressed, so a wrist that stays painful after a fall deserves imaging. A dislocation of those small bones is suspected when the wrist is markedly swollen, the fingers cannot be felt properly or the hand is pale, and a numb, white or cool finger is an emergency for the hand. The hand itself shows as swelling, a finger rotated or shortened and a reluctance to make a fist, and a dislocated finger is never pulled back into place from a book, nor when the skin is broken, a fragment lies in the joint or the diagnosis is unclear.

The pelvis shows as pain in the groin, the hip or the lower back after a high-energy injury, tenderness over the pelvic bones and an inability to bear weight. Bleeding into the pelvis can be massive and hidden, so a pale, cool and anxious patient with a rising pulse is treated as a patient in shock. The pelvis is not sprung apart or pressed repeatedly to test it, and a break of the socket of the hip joint or of the bone running from hip to knee shows as pain, a shortened and outwardly rotated limb and an inability to lift the leg. Support the limb as found, keep the patient flat and warm, control the bleeding that can be controlled and arrange urgent transfer with the pelvic binder or splint that local protocol authorizes. A dislocated hip shows a limb fixed in an abnormal position, severe pain and an immovable joint, and the nerve running behind the hip is at risk, so sensation and movement at the foot and ankle are recorded. Restoring a hip to its socket is done by a clinician with sedation or anesthesia in a facility with imaging, and it is urgent because the blood supply of the head of the bone is at stake. None of these injuries is manipulated, straightened or moved without immobilization, and the part of the responder is support, warmth, the neurovascular record and rapid transfer.

A break of the thigh bone shows as severe pain, swelling, a guarded deformity and a limb that is shortened and rotated, and the hidden bleeding can threaten the circulation, so a pale, restless patient with a rapid pulse is treated as a patient in shock. Immobilize the limb as found with the joints above and below controlled, using the splints or traction device the trained responder's service authorizes, and never straighten the limb to make the splint fit. The vessel running from groin to knee and the nerve supplying the front of the thigh are at risk, so the foot pulse, the color and warmth of the skin and the movement and sensation of the foot are recorded before and after immobilization. Pain out of proportion, a tense thigh, numbness and weakness raise the suspicion of a compartment syndrome there, which is uncommon but severe, and the responder acts within local protocol instead of waiting for confirmation. A break just above the knee shows as swelling, joint pain and a knee that will not straighten, and it threatens the vessels behind the knee. Traction, casting and surgical fixation are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and the responder keeps the patient warm, records what is found and transfers without delay.

The kneecap shows as swelling of the joint, a gap or a tender fragment and pain when the knee is straightened, and the skin over it is inspected because the bone lies directly beneath. A dislocated knee is a rare injury of great violence, showing an obvious deformity, an immovable joint and a knee already very swollen, and the vessel behind the knee and the nerve crossing the outer side are both at risk, so a pulse that is present does not exclude damage to the vessel. Support as found, immobilize within the equipment and procedures the service authorizes, keep the patient warm, record the neurovascular status before and after, and arrange the most urgent transfer the service can provide. A break of the upper end of the shin bone shows as swelling, pain on the inner or outer side of the knee and an inability to bear weight, and its seriousness is rarely visible from outside. A break of the shin bone in its shaft is the broken bone most likely to be open because it lies just under the skin, and it shows as pain, swelling, a visible deformity and an inability to bear weight. The compartments of the lower leg are tight, so a break there is a classic cause of an acute compartment syndrome, recognized by pain that grows instead of settling, pain when the muscles are stretched, a tense swollen limb and numbness or weakness in the foot. A pulse that can still be felt does not exclude it, so immobilize the joints above and below, keep the limb at the level of the heart and never above it, and release a constricting bandage, splint or cast only if the local protocol authorizes you to do so, because time is muscle.

The ankle shows as swelling, bruising, tenderness over one or both bony prominences and pain on weight bearing. A break of the inner or outer prominence is the common form, and the joint may be visibly displaced, which is described for the record and never corrected in the field. Support the ankle as found on a padded splint that holds the foot as it was found, include the joints above and below, protect the limb from cold and refer for imaging. The nerve behind the inner prominence and the artery beside it are at risk, and the tendon crossing the front of the ankle can be injured by the same force, so sensation over the sole, the pulse behind the inner prominence and the ability to pull the foot up are recorded before and after every intervention. A tear of the ligament binding the two bones of the lower leg together shows as tenderness above the ankle and pain when the foot is turned outward, and it is easily missed. Restoring a displaced ankle belongs to the clinician, is often urgent because the skin over the bone can fail, and the responder never tests the joint by forcing it.

The heel bone shows as swelling of the heel, bruising of the sole, pain that prevents weight bearing and a history of a fall from a height, and the injury is often worse than the swelling suggests. Support the foot as found, immobilize the ankle and the foot together within the procedures the service authorizes, keep the patient warm and refer urgently for imaging. A break of the small bone below the ankle joint that carries the weight of the body shows as pain and swelling around the ankle and tenderness deep to the bony prominences, and it is serious because the blood supply of that bone is fragile. The middle of the foot shows as swelling, bruising across the sole and pain when it is squeezed, and a dislocation there can be subtle while the injury is severe. The nerves of the foot are at risk, so numbness, a loss of light touch and a foot that is pale or cool are recorded and reported at once. Breaks of the long bones of the foot and of the toes show as swelling, tenderness and pain on weight bearing, and their urgency is set by the skin and the circulation, while dislocations of the foot are never restored by the responder and definitive care belongs to the clinician.

A suspected spinal injury shows as pain in the neck or back after a fall, a collision or a blow, tenderness over the bones and any numbness, tingling or weakness in the limbs, and the absence of pain does not exclude a serious injury. Such a patient is treated as unstable until someone qualified to clear the spine has done so, and no lone manual handling technique is safe, so the patient is moved by a trained team using the precautions the local protocol requires. Keep the head and trunk as found, maintain the airway and the breathing while protecting the neck, keep the patient warm and transfer to a facility able to assess the spine. An injury of the spinal cord is suggested by weakness or paralysis, loss of sensation, loss of bladder control and a changed pattern of breathing, and the level of the injury decides what the patient has lost. Some patients break bones more easily and heal them less predictably, so the card is used with a lower threshold in each of them. The bone of a child bends before it breaks, and a growth region near the end of a bone can be injured without a break, while an older adult whose bone has lost density may break a hip or a wrist in a fall from standing height with far less pain than the injury deserves. Pain relief, antibiotics and tetanus protection belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, and the substance, the amount and the way it is given are never taken from this course.

An open fracture shows a wound near the bone, blood on the skin or bone that is visible, and it is contaminated even when it looks clean, which makes it an emergency at every level. Cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control the bleeding that can be controlled, immobilize the limb as found, record the neurovascular status before and after, protect against hypothermia and transfer to a facility with an operating room. The person who cleans, explores or closes such a wound outside an operating room is doing harm, and no listener to this card should be that person. Urgency can be read from a few findings rather than from a diagnosis: an absent or diminished pulse, a pale or cool limb, a part that is numb or weak, a wound over the bone, a deformity that threatens the skin, a suspected compartment syndrome, a suspected spinal injury or an unstable patient means emergency transfer with the receiving team warned in advance. A closed injury that is neurovascularly intact and comfortable in its splint is transferred promptly but without the same alarm, and every figure in this card is an illustration, because a teaching value for the time within which an open injury should reach surgery differs between services and countries. Gloves, eye protection and a barrier for the face are worn for every contact with blood or body fluid, and the record and the handover carry the time of injury, the mechanism, the position in which the limb was found and the neurovascular findings before and after every intervention, so that the receiving team continues a story rather than starting a new one.

To summarize, this card is a memory aid for the road and the bedside rather than a manual of procedures, and it is listened to before or after an encounter and never in place of the protocol of the service. In every region the order is the same: assess, stabilize, examine the neurovascular status, immobilize, image, reassess, and then refer or treat definitively, with the neurovascular findings recorded before every intervention and repeated after it. The findings that make an injury an emergency are a pulse that is absent or weak, a limb that is pale, cool, numb or weak, a wound over or near the bone, a deformity that threatens the skin, pain that grows instead of settling, a limb that is tense and swollen, and a patient who is unstable. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and never straightened in the field, a wound is never explored blindly, exposed bone is never pushed back, an embedded object is never removed, and definitive closure belongs to the operating room. Reduction, traction and casting are learned under supervision and performed according to local protocol, and they are not attempted when the diagnosis is unclear, when a fragment lies in the joint, when the vessels or nerves are failing or when training and equipment are lacking. Cold is treated as a complication, the spine is treated as unstable until someone qualified clears it, and the patient is kept warm, comforted and watched until the handover. The lay first aider supports, warms and calls for help, the trained responder works within what the service authorizes, and the physician or the surgeon decides what definitive treatment is required. Where this card names a time, a distance or a threshold, the figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is used.

# Appendix D — The Core Principle and Scope of Practice

Every injury in this course has been taught through one sequence, and this appendix names the principle that holds the sequence together. The aim of the responder is not to make the injury look normal, and it is not to produce a limb that appears straight and tidy on the outside. The aim is to protect the patient from further harm, to recognize what threatens life and what threatens limb, and to move the patient toward the care that can finish the job. A fracture that looks better after the responder has handled it may be a limb that has just lost its last intact vessel, and a joint that has been forced back into place may now be a wound that the skin can no longer hide. This appendix is placed last on purpose, because the judgment that decides whether to act matters more than any technique, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The first duty is restraint, and restraint is a skill and not the absence of action. A limb that is deformed is supported and immobilized in the position in which it was found, and it is never straightened in the field, because the vessels and the nerves lie against the bone and the movement that looks tidier may tear what was still carrying blood and feeling to the hand or the foot. Pulling a limb straight may also turn a closed fracture into an open one and release the pressure that was holding a torn vessel closed. The lay first aider supports the limb with the hands, with a pillow or with whatever is at hand, keeps the patient warm, and waits for help. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician or paramedic may apply a splint within the equipment and the procedures their service authorizes, and each of those levels works inside a scope that has been defined for it.
